exp.11:5:
This verse invites the people of Jerusalem to shout for joy and sing. The reason is that God, whom it calls "the Holy One of Israel," is present among them and is great. "Inhabitant of Zion" means the people who live in Jerusalem, seen as a single woman.

The prophet Isaiah closes with this song a section about the promise of rescue for God's people. After speaking of judgment, he announces that on that day, a future time of restoration, the people will praise God for his salvation. Interpreters apply it to the return from exile, and many Christians also see it fulfilled in Christ. The speaker is the prophet, calling the people to sing.

Today you can rejoice because God is not far away. Before asking him for anything, take a few minutes to sing to him or thank him aloud for what he has already done in your life.
exp.37:16:
Here the verse says that Hezekiah suffered great anguish just when he expected peace. But God, in love, rescued him from death. "Pit of corruption" is the grave or the place of the dead, and "cast all my sins behind your back" means that God forgave them and no longer holds them in view. The word "pleased" means "was pleased" or "willed."

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks in a song after recovering from a deadly illness. Isaiah had told him he would die, but he prayed and God granted him more years of life. Some understand "in peace" as a time of calm that became bitter because of the sickness; the text does not give more detail. Here he gives thanks for having been rescued.

For today: when you remember a failure or a painful season, do not stay bound by guilt. If you ask God for forgiveness, he has already cast your sins behind his back. Answer him with gratitude and tell others what he has done for you.
exp.9:5:
God says he will send Assyria against a nation that is "hypocritical," that is, false, one that does not keep its word, and he calls it "the people of my wrath." Assyria will take the spoil, seize the prey, and trample that people "like the mire of the streets," that is, with no respect at all.

God speaks through Isaiah. He addresses Judah and Israel, who had fallen into injustice and idolatry (see the beginning of the chapter). God uses Assyria as the instrument of his discipline. But the verses that follow show that Assyria acted out of pride, not obedience, and for that reason it too would be judged.

For today: God governs history and corrects his own people with justice. If he calls our attention, let us not harden our hearts; let us return to him in humility. And let us not forget that no human power escapes his judgment.
exp.52:5:
It says that all of us have gone astray, like sheep that wander off without direction, each one going its own way. But God laid on his Servant the guilt of all of us. "Going astray" means turning away from the right path. "Laid on" means he placed the weight of our sin upon him.

Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking, and the "we" is a people who recognize their own error. Before, they thought the Servant was suffering because of his own fault, but now they understand that he was suffering for them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament applies it to him (1 Peter 2:24-25). Other Jewish readings see the people of Israel.

Today we can honestly admit that we sometimes go our own way. And instead of hiding it, we can return to God with confidence, because he himself took responsibility for our guilt.
exp.2:6:
He says that, when the crisis comes, the person whom they want to make a ruler will refuse. "Shall he swear" means he will say it firmly. "I will not be an healer" means: I will not take on that responsibility. He says that in his house there is neither bread nor clothing, and so he does not want to be made a ruler, that is, a leader or governor of the people.

Isaiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem, announcing God's judgment for their sin. Before this he says that God would take away their leaders and their provision. The land is left so weak and disordered that people look for a head among anyone who has even a cloak. But even that man does not want to take on the ruin of others.

For today: leading is not only holding a position, but bearing responsibility. A people who turn away from God lose good guides. Pray for those who govern and, if God calls you to serve, do it with humility and honesty.
exp.55:1:
He says that the person who puts into practice what God has just asked is happy and blessed: keeping justice and doing what is right. "Blessed" here means happy. "Hold on to it" means clinging to something with devotion. "Polluting it" means treating it as something ordinary. "Keeping his hand from doing any evil" means not using his hands to do wrong.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His salvation is near, and so he calls his people to live righteously. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant with God. In the verses that follow, God opens his arms to foreigners and eunuchs, who felt excluded, and promises them a place in his house.

For today: set aside time to rest and to remember that God is your provision. Ask him to care for your hands as well, so that you treat others with justice and kindness in your work and in your home.
exp.44:18:
God says that he has never spoken in secret or from some dark corner. Nor did he tell the people of Jacob, that is, Israel, to seek him in vain. "I speak righteousness" and "I declare things that are right" mean that what God says is true and upright.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, and also the nations, at a time when many worshiped idols of wood that could neither speak nor save. God presents himself as the Creator who has made himself known clearly, unlike false gods and their hidden mysteries.

For today: you can seek God with confidence, because he wants to be found. Read his Word and pray sincerely, knowing that you are not searching blindly or in vain.
exp.6:20:
It says that in that day a man will keep only one young cow and two sheep. That is very little livestock. The word "nourish" means that he will feed and care for them. The verse does not say this is a great blessing, but something small and simple.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, when the kingdom was threatened by enemies and Ahaz did not trust God. Isaiah announces that judgment will come through Assyria. The land will be nearly empty, and the people will live on the bare minimum. The verses that follow show that there will be milk and honey, but in a desolate land. Some understand this as survival, and others as a sign that God sustains a remnant.

Even when we lose much, God can sustain us with what we need. We can learn to be thankful for little and to trust in Him, without seeking security in human powers.
exp.41:17:
This verse is a direct call. God tells the deaf to listen and the blind to look closely so that they may truly see. The reader's verse says "Hear, ye deaf," and "look, ye blind, that ye may see." It does not speak of a physical disability but of a spiritual condition.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will lead the blind and will not forsake them, and has warned that those who trust in idols will be put to shame. Now he addresses his own people, Israel, who had seen and heard much of God but did not take him seriously. The verses that follow show this: the servant sees many things but does not observe them. Scholars discuss how this servant relates to the earlier passages about the servant of the LORD.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are truly attentive to God or only accustomed to what we already know. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible in silence and ask God to open your eyes and your ears.
exp.9:22:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, will carry out a total and determined destruction in the midst of the whole land. A "consumption" is something brought all the way to its end, and a "consumption" in the sense of an ending or completion means the finish of what was decreed. It is not a half-measure punishment but a complete sentence.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, while Assyria was threatening the region. The prophet explains that the judgment would be severe, but just. Even so, only a remnant of the people would return to God. Right after this comes comfort: God asks His people not to fear Assyria, because the punishment would have a limit.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but He also cares for those who turn back to Him. If today you feel under pressure or correction, do not flee from God; return to Him with humility and trust that His justice is always joined with His mercy.
exp.53:4:
This verse says that God himself is like a husband to his people. "Maker" means the one who created you; "Redeemer" is the one who rescues you and gives you back your freedom; "Holy One of Israel" speaks of a God who is pure and set apart. Although he has a powerful name, "LORD of hosts," he also draws near with tenderness. And he will be known as the God of the whole earth.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from God to Jerusalem, which feels like an abandoned woman without children. Before this verse, God promises growth and that there will be no more shame. Afterward, he explains that he left her for "a little moment" and that he will gather her back with great mercy. It is a poetic picture of God's love.

For today: if you feel lonely or ashamed of your past, bring that pain to God in prayer. He not only made you, he also redeems you and cares for you.
exp.15:12:
This verse says that what Isaiah has just announced about Moab was not something new. God had already spoken it long before, from that time, that is, from some time ago. The word "spoke" means that God declared it openly.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, conveying the message of the Lord. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, proud and trusting in their gods of the high places. Earlier, the prophet showed grief over their fall. Then, in the following verse, God sets a near deadline: three years. Scholars debate which exact historical events this fulfillment refers to.

For today: God does not speak at random or change his mind without reason. His warnings are an opportunity to turn back to him in time, instead of trusting in our own strength or in things that cannot save us.
exp.5:4:
Isaiah says that he feels lost and destroyed. "I am undone" means that he believes he is condemned, and "a man of unclean lips" means that his way of speaking is not pure. Moreover, he lives among a people who speak the same way. And yet his eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord of the armies of heaven.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He has just seen a vision of the temple, with seraphim proclaiming the holiness of God. Faced with such purity, Isaiah sees his own sin. He does not defend it or hide it; he acknowledges it. Then, in the next verse, God cleanses him with a coal from the altar.

For today: when we draw near to God, we do not need to pretend that we are perfect. We can sincerely acknowledge our sins, including those of our words, and trust that God forgives and cleanses those who humble themselves before Him.
exp.27:23:
He says that a farmer does not spend the whole day plowing and breaking up the clods without ever sowing. Plowing is only the preparation; the time comes to set down the plow and scatter the seed. "Nigella" is a plant with aromatic seeds, and "cumin" is a spice.

Isaiah speaks to scornful leaders of Jerusalem, whom he warns of a judgment coming from God. He uses the picture of the field to show that God does not punish without end or without purpose. Like a wise farmer, he has a plan and a time for each task. Verse 26 says that his God teaches him. Some understand that the judgment aims to correct and bring to fruit; the text suggests this, though it does not fully explain it.

For today: if you are going through a hard season, trust that God does not prolong it without purpose. And examine whether you yourself keep "plowing" in worries or blame, without taking the step of sowing.
exp.62:12:
He says God led his people through the deep waters of the Red Sea with as much sureness as a horse walking across open, level ground without stumbling. The wilderness here is understood as open country or grassland, not as difficult sand. The picture is one of firm, calm steps with no stumbling.

The speaker is the prophet, speaking on behalf of the people, in a prayer of lament. He recalls the exodus with Moses in order to appeal to God: if God cared for them so well before, where is that same help now? The people feel far from God and ask that he show his compassion again.

For today: when you go through a situation that feels like a deep abyss, remember how God has helped you before. That memory can sustain your prayer and your trust, even when today you do not see the way clearly.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the land of Judah is in ruins. Its cities have been burned, and foreigners eat the produce of its fields while the people watch, unable to stop it. The word for "desolate" in the verse above is the one used here: it means laid waste or stripped bare. The phrase for "burned with fire" means set on fire.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, sent by God to Judah. The verses before this one describe the people as a body wounded from head to foot because of their rebellion. Many think this refers to an enemy invasion, perhaps that of Assyria, though scholars do not fully agree on the exact time. What matters is that God shows the consequences of sin and calls the people to return to Him.

For today: do not ignore the signs that something is wrong in your life. Wounds that are not treated get worse. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge what is harming you, and let Him heal and restore what has been broken.
exp.43:21:
God says that He has already blotted out the rebellions and sins of His people, the way the sun makes a cloud or a mist disappear. Then He invites them to return to Him, and the reason is that He has already redeemed them, that is, bought them back and set them free.

The Lord speaks to Israel, also called Jacob. Shortly before, He mocked idolatry, which is like feeding on ashes and trusting in a lie. Now He reminds His people that He formed them and that they are His servant. First God acts by forgiving and redeeming, and then He invites them to return. That is why a song of praise follows.

If you feel trapped by your failures, do not wait until you have fixed yourself before drawing near to God. He invites you to return because He already offers forgiveness. Confess today what weighs on you and rest in His mercy.
exp.16:4:
It says that what is coming upon Israel will be like a harvest: the reaper gathers the stalks of wheat, takes them in one hand, and with his arm cuts off the heads of grain. It is also compared to someone who gathers loose heads of grain in the valley of Rephaim. The mature crop is the grain standing in the field, and the heads are the tips of the stalk where the kernels are. The image speaks of almost everything being taken away, with very little left behind.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces judgment on Damascus and on Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, which had allied itself with Syria. It is thought that the valley of Rephaim lies near Jerusalem and was known for its harvests, though its exact location is debated.

For today: do not place your security in alliances, money, or power, because all of these can vanish. Trust in God, who even in judgment leaves a remnant and invites us to turn our eyes back to Him.
exp.9:8:
The king of Assyria proudly asks whether some cities did not suffer the same fate. Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, and Damascus are cities he had already conquered. He means that none of them could resist him, and that Jerusalem will not be able to resist him either.

The Assyrian king speaks here, boasting of his victories. He does not know that God is using him to correct His people. Even so, his heart is arrogant and he wants to destroy without limit. Later, God will hold him accountable for that pride. Scholars debate the exact location of Calno.

For today: when we have success or power, let us remember that everything is under the hand of God. Boasting about our achievements draws us away from Him. With humility, let us give Him thanks and use what we have to serve.
exp.27:6:
They also stagger from wine and reel from strong drink: the priest and the prophet reel from strong drink, they are swallowed up by wine, they stagger because of strong drink. They go astray in vision, they stumble when they judge.

This verse says that the spiritual leaders of Judah, the priest and the prophet, drank so much wine and cider (a fermented drink, usually made from apples or other fruit) that they were unsteady on their feet and confused. Their confusion is described as losing sound judgment. That is why they failed in their vision, that is, in receiving and passing on the word of God, and why they stumbled in judgment, that is, when deciding just cases.

Speaking on God's behalf, Isaiah had announced that God would be a crown for the faithful. Now, in a sharp contrast, he denounces the leaders of Jerusalem, who were meant to guide the people with clarity. Their disorderly way of life left them unable to teach or to judge. The verses that follow show how repugnant their condition was.

For today: be careful about what clouds your mind, because whoever guides, advises, or decides for others needs to be sober and attentive to God.
exp.4:0:
He says the prophet is going to sing a song for his beloved, and that the song is about his beloved's vineyard. This vineyard was on a fruitful hill, that is, a slope on a mountain, a place of good, productive soil.

The one speaking is Isaiah, who begins as if he were a singer dedicating a love song. The verses that follow show that it is a parable: the vineyard represents God's people, Israel and Judah, and the beloved is God himself. The prophet uses a song so that the people will listen and then realize that the judgment applies to them.

For today: God has given us care and good opportunities. Ask yourself honestly what fruit of love, justice, and faithfulness your life is bearing in response.
exp.25:3:
Trust in the Lord always, without growing weary, because he is firm and does not change. The phrase "for ever" in the verse conveys the idea of lasting through all times. The expression "everlasting strength" can be understood as an eternal rock: a secure refuge that endures through every age.

It is part of a song that the prophet Isaiah announces for the people of Judah, directed toward a future time of restoration. The song contrasts the righteous who trust in God with the proud city that he humbles, as the following verses say. Scholars debate which city is meant; the text does not name it clearly here.

Today, when everything seems unstable, you can choose to trust God one day at a time. Speak to him honestly about your worries, and remember that he remains firm even when your circumstances change.
exp.43:2:
God promises to give water to dry ground, and with that image he announces that he will pour out his Spirit and his blessing on the children and descendants of his people. A dry, parched land is what the picture describes, and the shoots that spring up are the children and grandchildren. The word "generation" here refers to the descendants.

The Lord speaks to Israel, called by the names Jacob and Jeshurun (an affectionate name meaning something like "the upright one"). The people were discouraged, and God comforts them with the words "Do not fear." The verses that follow show the result: the descendants will grow like willows beside the water and will gladly say that they belong to God.

For today: if you worry about your children or about loved ones who seem spiritually dry, pray with hope. God is the one who gives life, and you can entrust them to him while you live out your faith and set a good example.
exp.33:7:
This verse says that God has an appointed time to act with justice. "Vengeance" here is not human resentment; God is setting right what is wrong. "Recompences" means paying back what is due, and "the controversy of Zion" is the cause of his people, who were mistreated.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the nations, and especially on Edom, Israel's neighbor, which often treated Israel with hostility. The images of sword, blood and sacrifice are very strong poetic language meant to show how serious this judgment is. Some believe it refers to a historical event, and others believe it also announces a final judgment.

For today: do not take justice into your own hands. If someone has harmed you, hand your pain over to God and trust that he sees everything and judges with justice. That helps you let go of bitterness and act with mercy.
exp.16:11:
It says a "Woe!" or lament is coming upon many peoples who make a great noise, like the roaring of the sea or the thunder of many waters. It is an image of armies and nations stirred up with force and seeming impossible to stop.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The chapter concerns Damascus and Ephraim (the northern Israel), who joined forces against Judah and forgot God. Afterward the Assyrian invasion would follow. The verses that come next show that, although the noise is enormous, God rebukes it and everything vanishes like chaff before the wind. Many understand the warning to be both for the enemies of God and a comfort for His people. Scholars debate exactly which peoples are meant.

Today: when the noise of the world frightens you, remember that God remains above all things. Pray and trust in Him.
exp.25:18:
He says that God will give life again to those who died in him. The promise "your dead shall live" is a promise of resurrection. Those who lie in the dust are the buried, and they are commanded to wake up and sing for joy. The "dew of herbs" is an image of the life God brings forth, like the dew that wakes up the plants. The phrase "the earth shall cast out the dead" means that the earth will give them back. The words "together with my dead body" are hard to translate, and other versions read them differently.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a song of God's people. Before this, the people confess that their efforts were like labor pains that brought no fruit: they could not save anything by themselves. Here God answers with hope: He himself will bring life. Many see in this one of the first clear hopes of resurrection in the Old Testament, although it is debated how Israel understood it at that time.

When your own efforts seem empty, remember that God has the last word. You can face grief and weariness with a real hope, and begin to sing with gratitude today.
exp.25:4:
He brings down those who dwell on high, with their pride and their sense of security. The "lofty city" is a city that thought itself great and untouchable, but God humbled it until it lay on the ground, "even to the dust." The word "dwell" means to live, and "lofty" means high. "Humbled" and "brought low" are the same action: God laid the city low.

Isaiah speaks within a song of trust that the people of Judah will sing in the future. He contrasts God, who gives peace to those who trust in Him, with the proud powerful ones who fall. Scholars do not agree on which city is meant: it may have been Moab, Babylon, or another, or it may be a symbol of all arrogant power.

Today: do not put your security in success, money, or reputation, since these can fall. Trust in God, and let Him teach you to live with humility and peace.
exp.64:2:
This verse speaks of a people who offend God openly, "to my face," and who keep doing it without stopping. Their sin was false worship: they offered sacrifices in gardens, that is, in orchards used for pagan worship, and they burned incense on altars made of brick, probably altars they had built for themselves. Some scholars think it refers to idolatrous rituals, although the exact detail is understood in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he stretched out his hands all day to a rebellious people who sought him little, and now he shows the pain and seriousness of that rebellion. God was patient, but they kept following their own path.

For today: examine whether your way of worshiping God is sincere and according to his Word, or whether you are following your own ideas. Come to him with humility and obedience, not out of habit or appearance.
exp.62:5:
It says that God, in anger, trampled the peoples like someone crushing grapes, made them stagger like drunkards with his fury, and brought their power down to the ground.

The word "trample" here means to step on something and crush it.

The Lord speaks in a vision in Isaiah about God as a warrior who comes to judge the enemy nations and to rescue his people. The verses before speak of "the day of vengeance" and "the year of my redeemed": judgment for some, deliverance for others. Some see here an image of Edom; others, a broader picture of the final judgment. Christian interpreters often also connect it with the work of Christ.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not leave it without a response. This allows us to leave vengeance in his hands, trust that he will do justice and, in the meantime, live with humility and mercy toward others.
exp.2:8:
Their faces give them away: their guilt and their brazenness show. Like the people of Sodom, they speak openly of their sin and do not hide it. To hide something means to conceal it or pretend it is not there. Their own harm was gathered upon themselves, so the prophet cries out: "Woe unto them!"

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem, who were in crisis. The verses before this one describe a fallen leadership, and the people no longer wanted to take responsibility. The prophet says their words and their deeds were against the Lord. Sodom appears as an example of shameless sin. But right away Isaiah affirms that it will go well for the righteous.

Today this invites us to be honest with God and not to grow used to sin. If something in our life no longer makes us ashamed, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer and seek his forgiveness and his help to change.
exp.16:6:
This verse says that after a time of judgment and loss, the people will once again look to God. The word "Maker" means Creator, the One who made us. "The Holy One of Israel" is a title for God that stresses that He is pure and set apart from everything else. "Look" here means to fix one's attention and trust on Him.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks on God's behalf. He announces judgment on Damascus and on the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim) for their idolatry and their alliances. Very little will remain, like a few olives left on the branch after the harvest. But in the midst of that loss, some will leave their altars and idols and turn back to God.

For today: sometimes God allows us to lose things we were trusting in, so that we lift our eyes toward Him. Today you might ask yourself: where am I placing my security? Give it to God in prayer, and look to Him again.
exp.10:12:
In the time of God's restoration, the rivalry between the two great families of the people will come to an end: Ephraim (the northern kingdom) and Judah (the southern kingdom). "Envy" here means jealousy and resentment. "Cut off" means cut down or removed. "Vex" means to trouble or harm. The enemies of Judah will disappear, and the brothers will no longer fight among themselves.

Isaiah is the one writing, speaking on behalf of the LORD. After announcing the righteous king who would come from the root of Jesse (the father of David), the prophet describes how God will gather his people scattered among many nations. Israel had been divided into two kingdoms, and between them there was tension and war. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others see it already beginning in Christ.

For today: if God promises to heal divisions between brothers, we can move toward that now. Think of someone with whom you have jealousy or resentment, and take a step toward peace: a phone call, an apology, or a sincere prayer for that person.
exp.40:5:
This verse says that the people of the nations helped one another. Each one supported his neighbor and said to his companion: "Be strong," that is, "take courage, be of good courage."

Here God speaks through Isaiah. He presents himself as the Lord of history, who calls the generations from the beginning. The nations see his work and become afraid. Then they encourage one another to make idols, as the following verses show. Contrast this with Israel, whom God calls his chosen servant. Many understand that this mutual encouragement is in vain, because it rests on idols made by hand.

Encouraging others is a good thing, but it depends on where we place our trust. Today we can comfort someone who is weak, but we can also point him to the living God, who does not move or fall like an idol. Look for someone discouraged this week, offer him concrete help, and remind him that God sustains him.
exp.9:13:
Here the king of Assyria boasts of his conquests. He says he took the riches of the nations as easily as someone gathers eggs from an abandoned nest. No one defended themselves: no one moved a wing, or opened their mouth to cry out, that is, to raise the alarm or protest. The conquered nations are what the verse calls "the people," and "found" means to come upon and take.

The one speaking is the king of Assyria, quoted by Isaiah. God had used Assyria to correct his people, but the king became full of pride and claimed all the credit for himself. For this reason God announces that he will judge him, and then compares the king to an axe that thinks itself greater than the one who wields it.

For today: what we achieve comes from God, who gives us strength and opportunities. Let us give thanks to him, and use our successes with humility and service, without boasting.
exp.13:26:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, has already decided what he is going to do, and no one can cancel it. His hand is stretched out in action, and no one can make him withdraw it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God said about Assyria, a powerful empire that oppressed many peoples. God promises to break the Assyrian in his land and remove his yoke, that is, his heavy domination. The verse closes that promise by affirming that God's plan cannot be stopped. Scholars debate exactly how everything was fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that no human power, however great it may seem, is stronger than God's purposes. When you face something that overwhelms you, pray and trust that he continues to govern.
exp.36:13:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah received a letter from the messengers sent by Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He read it, went up to the temple of the Lord, and spread it out before the Lord, that is, he opened it and laid it in front of God, as if showing it to Him.

The writer describes a moment of crisis. Assyria had conquered many cities and now threatened Jerusalem. The letter mocked God and said that He could not deliver His people, just as the gods of other nations had not saved theirs. Hezekiah did not respond with fear or with a hasty alliance, but by bringing the problem before God.

For today: when news comes that troubles you, a message, a diagnosis, or a debt, before reacting, bring it to God with sincerity. You can lay it out before Him in prayer, tell Him what you feel, and entrust the outcome to Him.
exp.0:5:
It says the people are wounded from the sole of the foot to the head, with no healthy part left. They have open wounds, swollen bruises, and infected sores. Nobody has cleaned them, bound them up, or eased them with oil. The words "no soundness" mean there is no part without harm; "putrifying sores" are sores that have become infected; "neither mollified with ointment" means they have not been soothed or relieved.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. He describes Judah as a body mistreated because of its rebellion and its abandonment of God. Many understand this as an image of their spiritual ruin and of the consequences they were already suffering, such as the devastation of the land described next. Scholars debate which exact moment in history it refers to.

For today: let us not hide our spiritual wounds or assume they will heal on their own. Let us acknowledge our sin honestly, return to God, and let Him heal what we cannot heal ourselves.
exp.41:13:
God says that for a long time he has held his peace and stayed quiet, not acting. Now he will not keep silent any longer: he will cry out like a woman in labor, with force and all at once. The phrase "for a long time" simply means that he has been still for a long while. "Destroy" means to lay waste completely, and "devour" means to finish off everything, here whatever stands against his work.

The Lord himself speaks, in the prophecy about the Servant and the deliverance of his people. His silence may have looked like indifference, but it was patience. Now he announces that he will act against evil and idolatry. The verses that follow show that his action also brings hope: he will guide the blind and will not forsake them.

For today: when God seems silent in the face of injustice or your pain, do not conclude that he is absent. Keep trusting that his patience has a purpose, and that the time to act will come. In the meantime, let him guide you.
exp.50:13:
The prisoner is said to be in a hurry to be set free, so that he will not die in the dungeon, which is a dark, underground prison, nor be left without food. Other translations read the Hebrew differently: the bowed-down captive will soon be set free, will not die in the pit, and will not lack his bread. It is a somewhat difficult text.

God speaks here, presenting himself as the comforter of his people. Many understand that he is addressing Israel in captivity, or on the verge of it, in Babylon. He reminds them that the oppressor is mortal and that the Creator, who gave freedom to his people before, can give it again.

Today, if something or someone has you bound by fear, debt, or anguish, remember that God sees your need. Speak to him honestly and trust that he cares for you, even in the everyday things, like bread.
exp.31:0:
This verse announces that a time is coming when a king will reign in righteousness, and his officials will also rule with justice and fairness. "Princes shall rule in judgment" means that they will lead and decide matters with equity.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had suffered under unjust rulers and under the threat of Assyria. After harsh warnings, the prophet offers hope. Many Christians see here an anticipation of Jesus, the righteous King, though some think the first meaning points to King Hezekiah. Both readings have been held, and they need not be set entirely against each other.

For today: trust that God has not forgotten justice. While that King reigns in full, seek to be, in your home, work, or church, someone who protects, listens, and acts uprightly, without taking advantage of any authority you hold.
exp.38:1:
Hezekiah was pleased with the envoys from Babylon and showed them everything he had: the house of his treasures, the silver and the gold, the spices and the precious ointment, and the house of his armour. Nothing was held back.

The text presents this as a fact. Babylon had sent letters and gifts when they learned that Hezekiah had recovered from his illness. Soon after, Isaiah will confront him. Interpreters do not fully agree: some see pride, others a lack of political wisdom or trust placed in resources rather than in God. Later, it would be Babylon that carried those treasures away.

For today: when God blesses us or heals us, it is easy to boast about what we have. It is wise to give glory to God and to be careful about whom we show everything to, and why.
exp.59:3:
It says that Zion, or Jerusalem, should lift up her eyes and look around her. A crowd has gathered and is coming toward her. Her sons return from far away, and her daughters are carried in the arms. The phrase about being carried at the side is an old expression: it means they are carried carefully on the hip or at the side, like small children. The word for "round about" simply means all around.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a promise of God to his people. After a time of sorrow and scattering, God promises restoration. His light and glory will shine over Jerusalem, and even the nations will draw near. Scholars connect this with the return from exile, and many Christians also see a broader fulfillment in Christ and his Church.

For today: when you find yourself in darkness or alone, lift up your eyes. God can restore what seems lost, so pray with hope for those who are far from him or from your family.
exp.29:6:
The help of Egypt will be of no use; it is worthless and empty. For this reason God cried out about it, that is, He warned that their strength would be to "stay still": not to rush after Egypt, but to remain calm and trust in Him. The Hebrew text of this last phrase is difficult, and some translations express it differently.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah faced a military threat, and its leaders were sending riches on donkeys and camels to Egypt to seek protection. God tells them that this alliance will bring them shame, because they did not trust in Him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, before rushing to find human solutions, stop for a moment to pray and ask God for direction. Being calm before Him is not passivity, but trust.
exp.64:14:
It says that the rebels will leave their name as a curse for God's chosen people. That is, when someone wants to curse, they will say, "May it happen to you as it did to them." God will judge them, but He will call His servants by another name.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He contrasts two groups: the faithful servants, who receive blessing, and those who abandoned Him and followed other practices, who suffer the consequences. It does not say with certainty what the new name is, but it points to a renewed identity. The passage moves toward the promise of new heavens and a new earth.

For today: God sees the difference between living for Him and living far from Him. If you are faithful to Him, your identity rests on what He says about you, not on your failures. Ask Him today to remind you who you are in Him.
exp.9:19:
It says that in the coming time, the few who survive from Israel will no longer lean on the one who struck them down. To lean on something means to rely on it or trust in it, like a person leaning on a walking stick. Instead, they will rely on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth, meaning with sincerity and faithfulness.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the kingdom of Judah, which was surrounded by threats. The one who struck them down is usually understood to be Assyria, though Judah also looked for security in alliances with other nations. God announces judgment, but he also promises a remnant: a small group who return to him after suffering.

For today: think about what holds you up when everything around you is shaking, such as money, other people, or your own strength. Even if these fail you or hurt you, you can return to God sincerely and rest your life on him.
exp.50:4:
God says that his righteousness is near and that his salvation has already gone out, meaning it is already on its way. With his arm, which represents his power, he will judge the peoples. The distant lands, which in the Bible often point to faraway regions, will wait on him and place their hope in his power.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to a weary and discouraged people. He has just promised comfort for Zion and that his law and his judgment will be a light to the nations. Then he asks them to look at the heavens and the earth, which will pass away, and to trust in his salvation, which lasts forever. Scholars debate exactly which moment he has in mind, but the message of hope is clear.

For today: when you feel tired or without a way out, remember that your hope rests not on passing things but on the faithful power of God. Today, bring to him in prayer whatever you cannot resolve.
exp.62:10:
The verse says that, after God had become an enemy to his people because of their rebellion, someone remembers the days of old, when Moses led Israel. It asks: where is the God who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of his flock, and who put his Holy Spirit within them?

This passage is a lament prayer. Some interpreters think the people themselves are speaking, and others think God is speaking as he remembers; the Hebrew text allows both readings. What is clear is that the people, in the middle of the punishment, look back and remember how God rescued them at the Red Sea.

When you feel God is far away, do what Israel did: remember how he has helped you before. That memory can sustain your faith and lead you to cry out with hope.
exp.9:20:
It says that a small group of the people of Israel, those who survive, will return to God. "Remnant" means those who are left over, the survivors. "Shall return" means they will turn back and come home. "The mighty God" is a title of the Lord that highlights his power.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the kingdom of Judah, at a time when the Assyrian empire threatened to destroy nations. God warns that judgment will come because of the people's injustice, but he promises that he will not wipe them out completely. A remnant will stop trusting in the power that had wounded them, which was Assyria, and will lean on God. The name of Isaiah's son, Shear-jashub, means "a remnant shall return" (Isaiah 7:3), although some connect it to this passage in different ways.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, God can still raise up a new life from what little remains. Return to him and lean on him, not on what has hurt you.
exp.9:14:
It would be absurd for an axe to think itself more important than the person who uses it to cut, or for a saw to show off in front of the one who moves it. It is as if a staff could lift up the person who holds it, or as if a rod could claim to be in charge. In the end, they are all just wooden tools.

God speaks through Isaiah. Assyria, the empire God used to discipline Israel, boasted that it had achieved everything by its own strength and wisdom. God reminds it that it was only an instrument in his hands. That is why judgment comes upon its pride.

For today: everything we do well, our talents, achievements, and opportunities, comes from God. We can work with effort and joy, but without thinking we own the success. If we remember that we are instruments, we live with humility and gratitude.
exp.52:11:
This verse says that God will reward his Servant with a portion among the great and the strong, like a victor who divides what he has won. The reason is that he poured out his life even to death, was treated as a wrongdoer, bore the sin of many, and interceded for those who did him wrong. "Transgressors" are those who disobey God's law. "Was numbered" means that he was treated as one of them.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the fourth Servant Song. Christians see this passage fulfilled in Jesus, and the New Testament quotes it in this way (Luke 22:37). Jewish interpreters have understood it in other ways, for example as referring to Israel.

For today: if Christ prayed for those who mistreated him, we can ask him for help to pray for someone who offends us, and trust that God sees and rewards what is done in love.
exp.35:17:
It says not to let yourselves be deceived by Hezekiah when he assures you that the Lord will deliver you. "Beware" means "be careful" or "take notice." "Let not Hezekiah persuade you" is "do not let them deceive you." The speaker asks whether the gods of the other nations managed to save their lands from the king of Assyria. The idea is that, if they could not, the Lord will not be able to either.

Rabshakeh, an officer of King Sennacherib of Assyria, speaks before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to stir up fear and distrust among the people so that they will surrender without a fight. He places the Lord on the same level as the gods of the conquered nations, and so his argument is a mockery against God.

Today, many voices tell us that trusting God is naive when everything seems lost. We can remember that God is not like the idols people invent. When doubt comes, it is good to pray and rest in his faithfulness, as Hezekiah did.
exp.27:8:
Says: "Whom do they think they are teaching? To whom are they explaining their message? To infants just weaned, just taken from their mother's breast?" Here "knowledge" means understanding, "doctrine" is a message or teaching, and "weaned from the milk" refers to children who have already stopped nursing.

Isaiah speaks to the priests and prophets of Judah, who were drunk and confused. Many understand these words as mockery of them: they felt insulted because Isaiah was correcting them as if they were children. Others think it is the prophet's own irony. The text does not make this entirely clear. In any case, it revealed a proud heart that did not want to listen to God.

Today: when the Word of God corrects us, let us not become defensive. Let us learn with humility, like someone who always has something more to learn.
exp.40:6:
They say the craftsmen encourage one another to make an idol. The carpenter encourages the goldsmith, and the one who smooths the metal with a hammer encourages the one who strikes on the anvil. Someone checks the soldering and says, "It is ready." Then they fasten the figure with nails so that it will not wobble or fall.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just called the nations to judgment, and they, frightened, respond by making gods and encouraging one another. God lets the absurdity show: an idol needs nails to hold it up. Right away He contrasts this with Israel, His chosen servant, whom He Himself upholds.

For today: when you feel afraid, do not look for security in things you hold up with your own hands. Rest in God, who holds you up.
exp.35:0:
This verse tells us that in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah's reign, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. The word "took" is an older way of saying "captured." The "fortified cities" were the ones that had walls and defenses.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, introducing a new section of Isaiah (chapters 36 to 39). It shows the crisis Judah faced before the powerful Assyrian empire. Hezekiah was known as a king who sought to honor God, and yet he faced this threat. Scholars debate how exactly to fit the date together with other chronologies of the period, so it is best to take it with caution.

Even faithful people can go through great trials. When everything that seemed secure falls apart, it is time to turn to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and not to trust only in our own defenses.
exp.53:12:
This verse promises that the children of Jerusalem will be taught directly by God. As a result, they will have abundant peace. The phrase "shall be taught of the Lord" means that God himself will guide them and give them understanding. The phrase "great shall be the peace" means that peace will grow and fill their lives.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, pictured as a grieving woman, battered by the storm and without comfort. After the suffering and exile, God promises her restoration, beauty, righteousness, and security. Jesus quoted the first part of this verse in John 6:45, and many Christians see it as a reference to those who are drawn to God and learn from him.

For today: it is not enough to give our children good habits; let us pray that God will teach their hearts. And let us also seek his daily guidance in the Bible, trusting that his teaching brings peace.
exp.31:9:
It says that women who live at ease and feel secure about themselves will be troubled for a long time, "many days and years." The reason is that there will be no grapes for the vintage (the grape harvest) or any other fruit to gather. "Careless" here means carefree, feeling safe without good reason.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. Earlier he announced a righteous king (ch. 32:1), and now he warns the comfortable women who do not take the warning seriously. Many understand it to refer to a judgment that would come upon the land; scholars do not agree on the exact date.

For today: do not confuse comfort with security. Check whether your peace rests on your possessions or on God, and heed his voice before the crisis arrives.
exp.37:3:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Isaiah. The word "came" is the old form of the word that the verse uses, so the sentence can be read as plain speech about a message arriving. The phrase "the word of the Lord" means that God himself gave him a message. It is a short phrase, but it marks an important moment: God answers.

Here the narrator speaks, telling what happened. King Hezekiah was seriously ill and had received the news that he would die. He turned his face to the wall, prayed, and wept. God did not delay in answering. Right away he sent Isaiah with a reply: God had heard his prayer and seen his tears.

For today: when you pray sincerely, even weeping and without many words, remember that God hears you. He does not always answer in the same way, but he is always attentive to you and to your need.
exp.28:3:
This verse describes Jerusalem brought low, fallen so far that her voice seems to come up from the ground. A "familiar spirit" was a spirit of divination, and people believed that mediums or spiritists spoke in a faint, muffled whisper, as if from beyond the grave. The city will sound weak, like a voice murmuring out of the dust.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The name for Jerusalem used here is one that some take to mean "lion of God" or "altar of God"; there is no single certain interpretation. God warns that he will allow a siege against a city that is proud and religious only in appearance. But the message continues: in the end, God himself will intervene against the enemies.

For today: when pride or false security fill us, God may humble us in order to correct us. If you feel brought down to the dust today, cry out to him with humility; he lifts up those who sincerely draw near.
exp.21:0:
This verse opens a message of judgment, or "burden," which means a heavy warning from God. It is addressed to the "valley of vision," and then asks what is wrong with the people, that they have all gone up to the housetops, that is, to the flat roofs of the houses.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Almost everyone understands that the "valley of vision" is Jerusalem, although the text does not name it here. The verses that follow show a city in uproar and celebration, while its leaders flee. Some think of an invasion; the exact details are debated.

For today: when a crisis comes, let us not settle for noise, celebration, or distractions. Let us stop and ask what God is trying to tell us, and return to trusting Him with humility.
exp.12:10:
God says he will "visit" the evil of the world, that is, call it to account and punish it. His judgment reaches the wicked because of their wrongdoing. He will bring an end to the arrogance of the proud and bring down the pride of the powerful. To "lay low" means to humble or bring down. "Haughtiness" is the pride of someone who thinks they are better than others.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This passage is part of a message against Babylon, which begins in chapter 13. The "day of the LORD" is described with images of darkness in the sky. Some see it fulfilled in the historical fall of Babylon, and others also see a look toward the final judgment. It can be understood in both ways.

For today: God opposes pride and the injustice of the powerful. Today we can examine our hearts, lay aside arrogance, and live with humility, trusting that God will do justice.
exp.47:9:
God tells Israel that he has tested and cleansed them, but "not as silver is refined," that is, not in the way silver is refined, or not to the level of complete purification, and this phrase is understood in several ways. The verse's "I have chosen you" is the same as saying "I have chosen you." The "furnace of affliction" is the suffering God used to test his people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a stubborn and rebellious people. Soon they will live in exile in Babylon. God makes clear that he does not leave them for their own merits, but for love of his own name. Even the punishment seeks to cleanse them and not to destroy them.

For today: when you go through a hard time, do not assume right away that God has abandoned you. He may use the trial to remove pride and strengthen your trust in him. Ask him to teach you what he wants to form in you, and keep walking in faith.
exp.13:10:
It says that the pride of the king of Babylon and the music of his feasts went down to the grave with him. The "grave" is the place of the dead, and the "viols" are stringed instruments, like harps or ancient guitars. Instead of a luxurious bed, he will have worms beneath him and over him.

Isaiah delivers this poetic mockery against the king of Babylon, who oppressed the nations. The dead, once powerful kings, receive him in astonishment: he is now no more than one of them. Some see in the passage that follows a reference to Satan, but others understand it only as the human king. Christians have interpreted this in different ways.

For today: power, money, and prestige do not accompany us to the grave. It is worth asking God for a humble heart and using what we have to serve, not to dominate others.
exp.9:11:
It says that God will first finish what He intends to do with Jerusalem and Mount Zion, that is, His correction of His people. Then He will "visit," that is, call to account and punish, the king of Assyria for the fruit of his pride, for his arrogance and the haughtiness of his looks.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria was the empire God used as a rod to discipline His people, but the king believed he was the master of his own power and boasted of his conquests, as seen in the verses that follow. God shows that He does not overlook that pride.

For today: everything we achieve comes from God's hand. It is worth examining whether we are boasting of our successes, and asking Him for a humble and grateful heart.
exp.26:4:
God asks whether anyone will dare to take advantage of his strength, that is, of his protection. And immediately he invites: let that person make peace with him, yes, let them truly make peace.

Here "take hold" means to seize by force, and "strength" can be understood as refuge or shelter. Some see this as an invitation to take refuge in God.

The Lord speaks, and in this passage he cares for his people, whom he calls his vineyard. He says he has no anger toward her and that he will destroy the enemies, compared to thorns and briers. Even so, he leaves the door open: whoever opposes him may be reconciled and find peace. Scholars interpret this phrase in various ways.

For today: if there is something in your life that keeps you from God, do not put it off. Come to him with sincerity, for he offers peace and care to those who come to his refuge.
exp.13:28:
God tells Philistia not to celebrate too soon. The rod that struck them has broken, but from that same family of enemies something worse will come. The serpent is a snake, the viper is a poisonous snake, and the flying fiery serpent is a burning snake that strikes quickly.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, in the year King Ahaz died. It is not known for certain which rod was broken: some think of the death of King Ahaz, others of the death of an Assyrian king. What is clear is that a greater judgment would come, and no one could stop what God had decided.

For today: do not trust that a problem is over just because a visible threat has fallen. Before you celebrate, ask God whether there is something more in your life that needs correcting, and entrust your future to Him, not to circumstances.
exp.6:15:
This verse says that, before that child is old enough to tell good from evil, the land of the two kings that Ahaz fears will be abandoned. The word "abhorrest" means that it caused him fear and rejection. The idea behind the verse is "to reject," meaning to refuse.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who was frightened by the threat from the kings of Syria and Israel. God offers him a sign so that he will trust in Him and not in human alliances. Christians see in the child Emmanuel a final fulfillment in Jesus, as Matthew 1 says. Some scholars think there was also a nearer fulfillment in the time of Ahaz. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

When fear presses on you, remember that God keeps His promises in His own time. Before looking for hasty solutions, ask Him to increase your trust in Him.
exp.59:20:
It says that God's people will be completely righteous, that is, they will be in a right relationship with Him and will live uprightly. They will inherit the land forever. They are called "branch of my planting": shoots of a plant that God Himself has sown. They are also "the work of my hands," and all of this is "that I may be glorified," that is, to show who God is.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who had suffered greatly. He promises them a future in which He Himself will be their light and their mourning will end. Interpreters differ on how this is fulfilled: some see restoration after the exile, others see something final and future, and others see both.

For today: if God is shaping you, you are not an abandoned project. Trust that He finishes what He begins, and let your life, with its processes, honor Him.
exp.42:26:
It says that Israel's sin goes back a long way. "Your first father" could refer to Adam, Abraham or Jacob, or to the nation's first leaders; scholars understand it in several ways. "Teachers" were God's spokesmen or interpreters, such as priests and prophets. "Transgressed" means they betrayed or failed their duty, rebelling against God.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just offered free forgiveness: "I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake." Then he invites the people to present their defense, and he answers that they have no argument: the sin goes back through generations, and even their guides failed. The next verse shows the consequences of judgment.

For today: do not defend yourself or make excuses based on your past, your family or your leaders. Acknowledge your wrong sincerely and receive the forgiveness that God gives by his grace.
exp.21:21:
It says God will give Eliakim the key of David's house, as a sign of full authority. The key laid on the shoulder represents the right to govern the palace and decide who enters and who does not. What he opens, no one will shut; what he shuts, no one will open. The belt or strap of office is a sign of his role.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked Shebna, the proud steward of the king, and announces that he will replace him with Eliakim, whom God calls "my servant." Eliakim would be like a father to Jerusalem and Judah. Later, the New Testament takes up this image in Revelation 3:7 to speak of Christ; Christians often see it that way, although Isaiah speaks first of Eliakim.

For today: true authority comes from God and is exercised through service. If you have any responsibility, use it with humility, caring for others, and trust that God opens and shuts the doors in your life.
exp.41:5:
God speaks to his Servant and tells him that he has called him in righteousness, that is, with a right and faithful purpose. He promises to take him by the hand, to care for him and to protect him. He appoints him as a covenant for the people, meaning as someone through whom God joins himself to his people, and as a light for the nations, who are the non-Jewish peoples.

The Lord speaks, the Creator who gives life and breath to all. This passage is one of the Servant songs in Isaiah. Some see it as referring to Israel, and Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus, whom the New Testament calls a light to the nations. God assures him of his support in opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners.

For today: if God calls you to serve, he also promises to sustain you. Walk with confidence, not in your own strength, and let your life bring his light to others.
exp.50:8:
Here the people ask God to act. "Arm of the Lord" is a way of speaking about his power. They tell him to awake, to clothe himself with strength, and to act as he did in the past. "Rahab" and "the dragon" are figures of chaotic and hostile powers; many think they allude to Egypt and its defeat in the Exodus. And the verbs "cut" and "wounded" mean that God won.

The one speaking seems to be the people of Israel, or the prophet speaking on their behalf, crying out in the midst of exile. Earlier, God had told them not to fear human beings, because his righteousness endures. Then the memory of the Red Sea becomes hope: the redeemed will return to Zion singing.

Today, when you feel weak or afraid, you can pray with sincerity and remember what God has already done for his people and for you. His faithful past feeds your hope.
exp.4:7:
It says that God laments and condemns those who keep buying house after house and field after field, until they have taken up all the space. "Gather in" means to pile up and accumulate; "inheritance" refers to the family land; "leave no room" means leaving nothing for anyone else. The closing question sounds like a rebuke: will you be the only ones living on the earth?

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. It comes from the song of the vineyard, where Israel is the vineyard that was meant to produce justice and produced injustice. This is the first "woe" against specific sins. In Israel the land was divided among the families as an inheritance, so hoarding property left others without a livelihood. What follows announces empty houses and poor harvests.

For today: check whether your desire to gain more is leading you to forget your neighbor. Strive to be just and generous, and share what God has given you.
exp.15:10:
This verse says that the grief over Moab goes very deep. The words that describe the inner self, the seat of the emotions, point to the heart and the core of the person, and the phrase about sounding like a harp speaks of a trembling or vibration, like strings that sound with sorrow. The name of the place mentioned at the end was an important city of Moab.

Isaiah prophesies God's judgment on Moab, a proud people who would be destroyed and would lose their vineyards and their joy. The one speaking expresses sorrow over that ruin. Some think it is the prophet, others that it reflects the feeling of God. The text does not make this fully clear, and both ideas can stand side by side.

For today: even when someone faces the consequences of their pride or their mistakes, we should not rejoice in their fall. We can ask for justice and also feel compassion, praying for that person.
exp.35:16:
He says that the king of Assyria promises the people of Jerusalem that, after a while, he will take them to another land like their own, fertile and full of harvests. "Corn" is wheat or barley, "wine" is the juice of the grape, and "vineyards" are the fields where grapes grow.

The one speaking is Rabshakeh, a spokesman for King Sennacherib, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants the people to surrender and stop trusting in Hezekiah and in God. It sounds kind, but it is an offer of exile: he asks them to leave their land in exchange for peace and comfort.

For today: sometimes temptations come with pretty, attractive promises. Before accepting an offer that pulls us away from trust in God, it is wise to ask where it really leads and what it asks us to leave behind in exchange.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that when God rises to judge the earth, people will flee to hide in the cracks of rocks and in caves. The word "clefts" refers to cracks or openings, and the verse speaks of a terror and awe so great that people will run to hide. The "glory of his majesty" is the bright, radiant greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. He denounces the pride and idolatry of the people, who trusted in wealth and idols. He announces the day of judgment, when everything man exalts will be brought low and only God will be great. The verses that follow call people not to trust in human beings, who are as fragile as a breath.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or people. All of that can fall. Trust in God, who alone is firm, and live with reverence toward Him.
exp.28:16:
What it says: Isaiah asks whether it is not yet a very little while before Lebanon, a place of thick forests, is turned into a fertile field (Carmel), and before Carmel, already fertile, is regarded as a forest. Being turned means being changed, and being regarded means being considered. It is a picture of great change: what once looked one way will be seen another way.

Context: The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Earlier he rebuked those who pretended to obey God and made their plans in secret, as if God did not see them. Afterward he promises that the deaf will hear and the humble will rejoice. Interpreters differ: some see here a future restoration, others a reversal of values, where the proud fall and the humble are lifted up.

For today: God can transform situations that seem unchangeable. We can stop hiding things from Him, trust Him with humility, and wait for His work, even when today we see little change.
exp.17:6:
It says that when the time set by God comes, a people will be brought as an offering to the Lord of hosts, to Mount Zion. They are described as "scattered and peeled" (tall and smooth-skinned, or perhaps mistreated and stripped), feared from their beginning until now, worn out from waiting, trodden under foot, and with a land ruined by rivers. "Present" means gift or offering.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, in a message against Cush (the region south of Egypt), whose messengers were going about seeking alliances. God says that He will act in His own time, like someone who prunes before the harvest. Scholars disagree about who this people is: some think of Cush, others of Israel.

For today: God does not hurry or forget, even when we feel weary of waiting. Instead of looking for human ways out, we can trust that He knows when to act, and bring Him our waiting and our wounds with patience.
exp.27:5:
This verse continues the promise from the verse before: God himself will be a crown for his faithful people, and he will also give a spirit of judgment to the one who sits in judgment, that is, wisdom and justice. He will also give strength to those who turn the battle to the gate, meaning those who push back the enemy and hold it at the entrance of the city.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. He has just announced punishment for proud Samaria, compared to a flower that withers. Then he shows that God will care for those who remain faithful to him. Right after, he criticizes the leaders of Judah, priests and prophets, who were drunk and judged badly. That is why the contrast is so strong.

For today: if you have responsibility over others, in the home, the church, or the workplace, ask God for wisdom and firmness, and take care of your own clarity of mind and character.
exp.57:8:
It says that when the people live with justice, God will answer their prayer right away. The words "call" and "cry" mean asking God for help. "Here I am" means "I am here." But it sets a condition: to take away from among you the yoke (the oppression of others), the pointing of the finger (accusing and despising others) and the speaking of vanity (saying words that are evil, false, or harmful).

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and seemed religious, yet oppressed their workers and were harsh toward the needy. God tells them that their faith is not genuine if it is not shown in justice and compassion. The verses before this one speak of sharing bread and clothing the naked.

For today: before asking something of God, examine how you treat others. Stop criticizing and accusing, and help someone who is in need.
exp.32:20:
In Zion, the Lord himself will be our strength and our protection, as if the city were surrounded by wide rivers and streams. But those rivers cannot be crossed by a rowed vessel, nor by a great ship. That is to say, the enemies will not be able to come near.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of foreign threat. Jerusalem had no great river to protect it, so the image is symbolic: God is a better defense than any wall or river. The verses that follow confirm this: the Lord is judge, lawgiver, and King, and he will save.

For today: when you feel fear or lack resources, remember that your security does not depend on your own defenses, but on God. Pray, trust in him, and walk with peace.
exp.52:10:
He says that the Servant of the LORD, after suffering greatly, will see the fruit of his pain and be content. Through his knowledge, he, being righteous, will make many righteous, because he will carry their guilt. "Iniquities" are sins and wrongdoings; to "justify" means to declare righteous or free from blame; to be "satisfied" means to be content.

It is part of the fourth Servant song in Isaiah. God speaks and announces that the suffering of this Servant has a purpose and ends in victory. Jews have interpreted it in various ways, for example as referring to Israel; Christians, from the New Testament onward, see it fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:24).

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through your own effort. You can rest in what Christ has done for you and respond with gratitude, forgiving others as God forgave you.
exp.37:20:
Here the text says that Isaiah had already given an instruction to heal King Hezekiah. They were to prepare a lump of figs, that is, figs pressed until they formed a paste, and place it on the boil, which is a sore or inflammation. The promise is that in this way he would recover.

The book presents Hezekiah as very sick, and God adds years to his life after his prayer. This verse seems like a separate detail, placed almost at the end, that explains how the illness was treated. The text does not say exactly what the boil was, so it cannot be specified. Some see here a common remedy of the time used under the word of the prophet.

For today: God can heal, and He can also use simple means, such as medicine or the care of others. Praying and receiving practical help are not opposed; we can trust God and thank Him for both.
exp.23:11:
This verse says the city was left empty and silent. "Desolation" here means abandonment, and "ruin" means ruin or destruction. The gate, which used to be a place of trade and gathering, was left "struck down," that is, beaten and shattered.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the earth for its rebellion (Isaiah 24:5-6). The "city of emptiness" is a city that lives without God; interpreters debate whether it refers to a specific city or serves as a symbol of all human pride. After the judgment, the passage ends with hope: a group will sing about the greatness of the LORD.

For today: whatever we build without God, whether money, fame, or security, can crumble. Today you can ask yourself what you are trusting in and place your life in the hands of God, who endures.
exp.12:6:
This verse says that, when the day of the Lord comes, all hands will grow weak and every person's heart will melt with fear. "Shall be faint" means they will be left without strength, limp and drained. "Melt" means to dissolve or lose all firmness, like something that loses its solidity.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces judgment against Babylon and, in a broader sense, against the pride of the nations. The verses before this one describe God gathering an army to act. That is why verse 7 shows the human reaction: neither strength nor courage helps when divine judgment arrives. Some see this as already fulfilled in history, and others also read it as a warning of the final judgment.

For today: do not trust in your own strength or your own security. Live with humility and draw near to God now, for He offers forgiveness and rest to whoever turns to Him.
exp.32:17:
It says that when deliverance comes, the faithful person will look back in wonder at the time of terror. They will ask where the enemy's officials are: the one who recorded and wrote things down, the one who weighed the tribute or the plunder, and the one who counted the towers or important houses in order to plunder them. "Distinguished" means notable or important.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, threatened by the Assyrian invasion. Earlier he announces that the one who lives in righteousness will be protected, and will see the King. Many understand that this verse looks back at a fear already past; the officials who caused it are no longer there. Some interpret it differently, but the overall sense is one of relief.

For today: when fear makes you feel that your problems are enormous, remember that God can make you one day look at them as things of the past. Trust in Him and keep doing what is right.
exp.43:19:
It says that whoever worships an idol feeds on ashes, that is, on something that gives neither life nor nourishment. A deceived heart turns him from the path, and so he cannot deliver himself. Nor does he stop to ask himself: "Is there not a lie in my right hand?" The right hand speaks of what a person takes hold of and what he trusts in.

God speaks through Isaiah. He mocks idolatry with sorrow: the man uses part of a tree to cook with, and with the rest he makes a god. This prepares the call that follows, where God tells Israel to remember Him and return, because He has redeemed them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we hold on to as if they could save us: money, success, approval. Let us ask God to show us honestly what we trust in, and let us return to Him, who truly forgives and sustains.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that Israel, the northern kingdom, did not turn back to God even though He was disciplining them. "The one who struck them" is the Lord, who allowed the suffering to wake them up. "Turned" means to turn around, to repent. "Sought the Lord" means to come to Him sincerely. They felt the blow, but they did not seek God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here in the name of God. He explains why the punishments keep coming: attacks by the Syrians and Philistines, and a judgment that continues. The leaders and the false prophets had led the people astray, and no one was changing course. Some understand these blows as God's discipline, not as simple bad luck.

When difficulties come, it is not enough to complain or to look only for relief. Let us ask ourselves with humility: "Lord, what do you want to teach me?" And let us return to Him in prayer and obedience.
exp.46:6:
Here Babylon boasted: "I shall be a lady for ever." The word for "latter end" refers to the final outcome, what comes afterward, the consequences. She believed her power would never end, and she did not think about how her actions would turn out.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon, called the daughter of the Chaldeans, was used to discipline Israel, but she treated the elderly with cruelty and showed no mercy. God judges her for her pride and her false sense of security.

For today: do not trust that what you have, your success or your strength, will last forever. Think about the end of your decisions, treat others with mercy, and live with humility before God.
exp.25:17:
This verse says that the people suffered like a woman in labor pains, but in the end nothing was born. The verse says "we have as it were brought forth wind." The word that is translated as "deliverance" here means salvation or liberation. Nothing they did was able to rescue the earth. The last phrase can be understood in two ways: that no new inhabitants were born, or that the oppressors were not brought down.

The people of God in Judah speak here, in the midst of trouble and discipline. They honestly acknowledge that their own efforts failed to free them. That confession prepares the hope of the next verse: God himself will give life to the dead.

For today: when your efforts leave you with empty hands, do not give up or pretend otherwise. Bring your weariness to God honestly. He is the one who gives true salvation, and he can give life where we see only emptiness.
exp.21:19:
God says that when that day comes, he will call Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, whom he calls "my servant." That is, he will choose him for an important task. Here, "call" means to choose and place someone in an office.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just announced that he will remove Shebna, a high official of the king's palace, from his position because of his pride (Isaiah 22:15-19). Eliakim will take his place. God shows that he decides who serves and who falls. The verses that follow describe the authority he will be given as administrator of the kingdom of Judah.

For today: positions and influence are a responsibility to serve, not an occasion to boast. If God gives you a task, carry it out with humility and care for others, because he is the one who entrusted it to you.
exp.21:17:
He will surely violently turn and toss you like a ball into a large country: there you shall die, and there the chariots of your glory shall be the shame of your lord's house. Explanation: It says God will throw this man with force, the way one throws a ball, into a wide and distant land. There he will die, and there his chariots, which symbolized his prestige, will remain. The phrase about the ball means he will be tossed and sent away; the word "ball" refers to a round object thrown through the air, and "large country" refers to a land with very wide borders. His pride turns into shame for the house of his lord.

God speaks through Isaiah. He addresses Sebna, a high official of the king (v. 15), who had carved himself a luxurious tomb as though he would stay forever. His ambition and pride offended God, and for that reason he will be removed from his post. The text does not say which land he will go to; it only announces exile and death far from home.

For today: take care that your service does not become a pursuit of fame. Every position or achievement is a temporary assignment from God, and true security lies in living with humility before Him.
exp.23:1:
What it says: The verse lists pairs of people: the people and the priest, the servant and the master, the one who buys and the one who sells, the one who lends and the one who borrows. It says that judgment will come to all alike.

Context: Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. In chapters 24 to 27 he announces a judgment on the whole earth because of human wickedness. Here it is shown that no one is left out: not those who hold authority, not those who have money, and not those who serve.
