Some understand this passage as judgment on Judah and the nations of his time, and others also see it as an announcement of the final judgment.

For today: God shows no favoritism. Our position, money, or prestige does not protect us from having to give an account to him. Today we can examine our hearts with humility and live honestly, whatever our place in society.
exp.1:0:
This verse works like a kind of title. It says that what follows is something Isaiah "saw," that is, a message God showed him. Isaiah was the son of Amoz, and his message is about Judah and Jerusalem. The spelling "Jerusalem" in the verse is an older form of the name.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, introducing the prophet. Isaiah prophesied in Judah, the southern kingdom, and the book itself mentions several kings of his time. What follows in the chapter is a vision of hope: one day the nations will seek God in Jerusalem. Some understand this as something still in the future, and others see a partial fulfillment in history.

For today: before hearing a message from God, it is good to remember that it comes from Him, not from human ideas. Read the Bible with attention and humility, ready to receive what God reveals.
exp.25:13:
It says that Israel's former oppressors are dead and will not live again. "Deceased" means that they died. "You visited them" means that God intervened to judge them. "You made their memory perish" means that their power and their name were wiped out.

The people of God speak in a song of confidence. Earlier they say that other lords dominated them, but now only the name of the Lord is remembered. The "dead" are those masters, probably powers that oppressed Israel. Some scholars see specific kings here, and others see a general image. Afterward, the text speaks of God making his people grow.

Today we can remember that no unjust power is eternal. If something oppresses you, such as fear, an injustice, or a difficult situation, hand it over to God and trust that he has the last word. In the meantime, try to remember his name and seek him in prayer.
exp.2:22:
This verse continues a list of ornaments and fine clothing worn by the women of Jerusalem. The mirrors were made of polished metal. The fine linen garments were pieces of fine cloth or fine fabric. The gauzy garments were dresses of very thin, see-through cloth. The hoods were ornaments or head coverings worn on the head.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah and Jerusalem. He warns of a judgment coming because of their pride and their injustice. The list of luxuries shows a vanity that led them to forget the poor. The verses that follow announce that all that splendor will be replaced by loss and sorrow.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we care for more than people. Examine whether your security rests in your appearance or in what you own, and ask God for a humble and generous heart.
exp.42:15:
Here God presents himself with a very well-known image: he is the one who makes a way through the sea and a path through the mighty waters. The word "mighty" here means strong and turbulent, with great force.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who would be taken captive to Babylon. He reminds them that he is their Redeemer, their Holy One, and their King. This image is often connected with the crossing of the Red Sea, and the following verse speaks of how God defeated the Egyptian army. In this way he gives them hope that he will again rescue them.

For today: if you face a situation that seems closed off, remember that God has already opened impossible ways before. Trust him and take the next step in faith, even though you cannot yet see the whole route.
exp.44:13:
This verse says that God promises that the wealth of Egypt, the trade of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans, a people of great stature, will come to belong to his people. The word "labour" here means what is produced by effort, that is, riches. Those nations will come after Israel, in chains, will bow down, and will acknowledge: "Surely God is in thee; and there is none else."

The Lord speaks, and addresses Israel through Isaiah, while the people live in captivity or are about to live in it. Shortly before, God announces Cyrus, who would free the captives. Interpreters debate whether the chains speak of submission or of a willing acknowledgment. In any case, the central point is that the nations will see that only the Lord is God.

Today, when you feel small or without resources, remember that your worth does not depend on what you have, but on the fact that God is with you. Trust that He can show his power through your life.
exp.41:16:
This verse says that those who trust in idols will be put to shame and forced to turn back. Their "graven images" are carved figures, and "molten images" are figures of melted and shaped metal. Those who say to them "You are our gods" will be completely confounded, that is, humiliated when they see that their idols cannot help them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will lead the blind, turn darkness into light, and not forsake his people. By contrast, the verse shows the fate of those who place their hope in things made by human hands. God is faithful; idols are not.

For today: an idol is not always a statue. It can be money, success, or the approval of others, anything we look to for security in place of God. Today, ask yourself what you trust most and surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that a throne will be established on the basis of mercy, that is, on love and compassion. There a king will sit firmly, in the house or "tabernacle" of David (his royal line), one who will judge with uprightness, seek what is just, and not delay in doing justice. "Hasting" means that he acts promptly.

Isaiah announces this to Judah concerning Moab, a neighboring people who have been destroyed and have desperate refugees. The Moabites are told to seek refuge in Judah. Many understand that this throne of David points to the ideal king, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. Others see it first as a hope for the Davidic dynasty in the time of Isaiah.

Today we can ask God for a heart that joins justice with mercy. If you have authority, even in your home or workplace, treat the weak with compassion and do not put off doing what is right.
exp.0:26:
Zion, that is, Jerusalem, will be saved and restored through judgment, meaning through God's just action. Its ones who turn back to God, those who repent, are the people who will be rescued by righteousness, because God acts with uprightness. The idea of those who turn back can also be understood as those who return.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. They had become corrupt, with unjust judges and an empty religion. God promises to cleanse them the way metal is refined, removing the dross. The text then warns that the rebels who abandon God will be destroyed.

For today: God corrects because He wants to restore, not merely to punish. If He shows you something you need to change, do not harden your heart; return to Him with humility and trust that His correction seeks to heal you.
exp.28:14:
This verse says that God laments the situation of those who want to hide themselves from Him. "Seek deep to hide their counsel" means trying to conceal their plans, and "their works are in the dark" refers to actions done in secret because they know they are wrong. They think, "Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?", as if God did not notice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in Judah. Shortly before, He accuses the people of honoring Him only with words, while their hearts are far away. Many understand that here He is referring to leaders who made political plans in secret, seeking alliances without consulting God. Then He reminds them that the clay cannot say the potter has no understanding.

For today: do not live a faith that is only outward appearance. When you are tempted to hide something, remember that God already sees it and loves you. It is better to bring it to Him in prayer, confess it, and seek someone you trust who can help you walk in the light.
exp.13:14:
It says that the one who dreamed of rising up to heaven ends up "brought down," that is, thrown down, into the grave. The word translated "to the sides of the pit" in this verse refers to the deepest and most hidden part of the pit. Some other versions read "to the bottom of the abyss."

Isaiah directs this mocking song against the king of Babylon, a proud and cruel ruler who oppressed many nations. His ambitious words, "I will be like the Most High," stand in sharp contrast with his end. Some Christians see here also an echo of Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of the human king; there are different interpretations.

For today: pride promises to rise, but it ends in falling. Let us ask God for a humble heart, for He Himself "gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6).
exp.21:6:
It says that the most beautiful valleys of Jerusalem, which had once been quiet and fertile, were filled with war chariots. The horsemen took up positions in front of the city gate, ready to attack. The horsemen are not named in the verse above, so I should not refer to them that way. Instead, the verse describes them simply as the horsemen who took their stand at the gate.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Jerusalem, which is called the valley of vision. The city faced an invasion, and its people trusted in their weapons and walls, but they did not seek God. Scholars debate which exact attack is described: it may be the Assyrian threat or a later event. The text does not make this fully clear.

For today: it is not enough to prepare defenses and plans if we forget God. Before crises arrive, we can draw near to Him and entrust our security to Him.
exp.40:7:
God speaks to his people and says: "You are my servant." Israel and Jacob are names of the same people. God chose them, and he calls them the descendants of Abraham, whom he calls "my friend."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the neighboring nations would encourage one another to make idols, out of fear and with a great deal of human effort. Here God contrasts that with how he treats Israel: they do not need idols fastened with nails, because God himself chose them and sustains them. The verses that follow say: "Fear not, for I am with you."

Today we can remember that our security does not depend on what we build or on our own strength, but on the fact that God calls us and walks with us. When you feel afraid, rest in his faithfulness and speak to him as you would to a friend.
exp.60:3:
This verse says that God's people will rebuild what lay in ruins. "Old wastes" and "desolations" refer to places destroyed and left abandoned for a long time. Cities laid waste for generations will be raised up again.

The context is a prophecy of comfort. The one speaking is a servant anointed by the Spirit of the Lord, and Christians see in him Jesus, who read part of this passage in Luke 4. It speaks to a battered and grieving people, most likely thinking of Israel after the exile. God promises to exchange their ashes for glory and their sorrow for joy, and that they themselves will take part in the restoration.

For today: God can restore what has seemed lost for a long time, such as families, relationships, or communities. We can trust that he invites us to work with him, step by step, in that rebuilding.
exp.0:1:
God calls the heavens and the earth to listen, as if they were witnesses at a trial. Then he says that he raised his children and made them grow, that is, he cared for them and helped them flourish, but they rebelled against him. The words "hear" and "listen" are the same idea here, to pay attention and take in what is said.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, who received this vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of several kings. God brings a complaint like that of a wounded father. What follows shows that his people do not even recognize him, while an ox knows its owner.

For today: let us remember how much we have received from God and not take it for granted. One practical way is to thank him each day for something specific, and to ask him to help us obey him with a grateful heart.
exp.21:11:
He says that the Lord God of hosts called the people on that day to weep, to lament, to tear out their hair, and to put on sackcloth, which was a rough cloth worn as a sign of grief and repentance.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was under threat, and its people trusted only in walls, torn-down houses, and stores of water, but they did not look to God, who had made all of it. God asked for humility, but they answered with feasting and with the attitude of "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

For today: when a crisis comes, make your plans wisely, but do not leave God out of them. Stop, pray, and humbly acknowledge your faults, instead of distracting yourself so you do not have to think about what matters.
exp.37:15:
It says that true life depends on the "mercies" of God, that is, on his compassion and goodness. Hezekiah affirms that in them lies the life of his spirit, and that he will tell this to everyone. "Consist" here means "rests on." It ends with confidence: God will restore him and make him live. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and that is why the translations vary a little.

King Hezekiah of Judah is the one speaking. He had fallen gravely ill and received word that he would die. He prayed with tears, and God granted him more years of life. He wrote this song after he recovered, looking back with pain and now with gratitude, as the following verses show, where he speaks of the forgiveness of his sins.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not keep silent about what God has done for you. Write down how he sustained you and tell someone. In this way your gratitude can encourage others to trust in his mercy.
exp.18:22:
It says that a time will come when there will be an open road between Egypt and Assyria, two nations that were once rivals. People will go back and forth from one country to the other without fear. And together, Egyptians and Assyrians will worship the LORD.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking, on God's behalf, within a message about Egypt. First he announces judgment, but he ends with hope: God wounds in order to heal. Assyria was a feared power. Interpreters differ on when this is fulfilled: some see a partial historical fulfillment, others see it in Christ or in the future.

For today: God can bring together those who seem to be enemies. Ask Him to help you let go of a grudge and take a step toward reconciliation with someone.
exp.18:12:
The leaders of Egypt, those of Zoan and those of Memphis (Noph), are described here as having lost their way. They thought they were wise, but they were mistaken and led the whole country down the wrong path. The "stay of the tribes" refers to the chiefs or pillars of the tribes and clans, the ones who held the nation up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from the LORD against Egypt. The Egyptians boasted of their wisdom and their royal lineage, and Judah sometimes sought their help. God shows that their counselors cannot understand or stop what He has determined.

For today: let us not place our final trust in leaders, titles, or the opinion of people who call themselves "experts." Let us seek God's wisdom first in His Word and in prayer, and weigh every piece of advice in its light.
exp.21:13:
God told the prophet Isaiah directly, and the message was very serious: the people's sin would not be forgiven while they were still alive. The verse says it was revealed in his ears, meaning Isaiah heard it from God. The title "Lord of hosts" speaks of God's power over all things. The words "till ye die" show that the consequences would last until the end of their lives.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Jerusalem when the city was under threat. God called them to weep and to repent, but they held a feast, saying, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Their sin was ignoring God and failing to trust in Him. Some understand this as a punishment that would no longer be lifted; others see it as a hardening of the heart.

Today it invites us not to take lightly God's call to repentance. When He speaks to us, it is wise to answer Him with humility and not with indifference.
exp.28:17:
He says that a time will come when God will change the condition of his people: the deaf will be able to hear what the book says, and the blind will be able to see even in the middle of the darkness. "Darkness" means a deep dark. It is a picture of people who did not understand and who now do.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. Before, the people had a faith of lip service only and did not understand God's ways, and for that reason they are compared to clay that does not recognize the potter. "The book" may refer to the words of the prophecy or to Scripture; some see here an announcement of times of restoration and others a promise that points to the Messiah. Interpreters understand it in several ways.

For today: ask God to open your ears and your eyes when you read the Bible. Read it with humility, hoping that He will give you light and understanding.
exp.20:15:
God tells Isaiah that within a year, counted precisely, the way a hired worker counts his years of service, all the glory of Kedar will come to nothing. A hired worker is one who receives a fixed wage for a set period of time, so the term will not be extended by even one day.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert, known for its archers and its wealth. The passage announces that war will strike them, while the people of Tema are to help the fugitives with water and bread. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical event the passage refers to.

For today: human strength and reputation are passing, but God governs history. Trust in Him more than in your achievements, and when you see someone fleeing or exhausted, offer them concrete help, such as water and bread.
exp.48:18:
God tells Zion (Jerusalem) that the ruined, destroyed and empty places of her land will now be too small for her, because many people will come to live there. The destruction of those places will be complete, and the land that was made narrow will have no room left to hold the crowd. Moreover, those who destroyed her will be sent far away.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people who felt abandoned and exiled. Zion is pictured as a woman alone and without children. God promises that her children will return in great numbers, so many that she herself will be amazed. Many see this as a promise of return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment.

For today: even if your life seems to be in ruins, God can restore it beyond what you imagine. Keep waiting on Him and pray with confidence, without counting out what He is able to raise up.
exp.61:3:
God tells Jerusalem that she will no longer be called "Forsaken," nor her land "Desolate," which means ruin or destruction. Her new name will be Hephzibah, meaning "my delight is in her," and her land will be Beulah, meaning "married." The reason is that the LORD's love will be upon her.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were suffering the consequences of exile and of a city in ruins. God promises restoration and a new name, one that expresses a relationship of closeness, like that of a marriage. Christian interpreters also see here a promise of God's love for his people in general.

For today: if you feel abandoned, or believe your past defines you, remember that God can give you a new identity. When you doubt it, repeat what He says about you, not what others have said.
exp.28:9:
Here Isaiah says that God himself brought down upon the people a "spirit of deep sleep," like a very heavy sleep. He closed their eyes, that is, he took away their ability to understand. The prophets and the "seers" (those who received visions from God) were left as if a veil lay over them, unable to see clearly.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Jerusalem, also called Zion. The people practiced a religion of lips, but their hearts were far from God. For that reason they did not understand his message. Some scholars see here a judgment from God; others see it as the result of the people's hardness.

For today: if we hear the Word of God but do not want to obey it, it can become difficult for us to understand. Let us ask God for a humble and willing heart, and let us read the Bible with prayer.
exp.27:26:
Says that not all seeds are beaten the same way. The fitches (a small plant with delicate seeds) and the cummin (another aromatic seed) are not threshed with the heavy threshing instrument nor with the cart wheel. The fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod, that is, a gentler blow.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had become hardened and mocked God's correction. He uses the example of the farmer, who knows what to do at each sowing and harvest, because God teaches him. In the same way, God also knows how to treat his people with wisdom. Scholars understand that he is speaking of divine discipline, measured and purposeful.

For today: when God corrects you or you go through trials, trust that it is not harshness without meaning. He knows your strength and treats you with wisdom. And with others, correct with measure and not with more severity than necessary.
exp.58:8:
The people thought God would give them justice and a good way forward, but justice moved far away and did not reach them. They hoped for light and found darkness. Here "judgment" means justice or what is right, and "brightness" refers to moments of clarity and hope, which the verse above expresses with the word "light."

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel and includes himself with the word "we." Before this verse, he describes the violence, the injustice, and the crooked paths of the people. His message is that sin and wickedness raise a barrier between the people and the blessing of God. The verses that follow show his confession and his despair.

For today: if we feel that we walk in darkness, it is good to examine ourselves humbly and see whether there is something we should correct. We can confess it to God and seek again the paths of justice and peace, trusting that he is merciful.
exp.21:16:
It says that God himself will take Shebna out of his land and carry him away into a harsh captivity. "Carry away" means to take far away, and "cover the face" probably speaks of shame or a complete fall, though some understand it as an image of humiliation or death.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Shebna was a high official of the king, in charge of the treasury and the palace. He had made an elegant tomb, as if his place were permanent and his fame secure. God confronts him for his pride and for seeking his own glory. The Bible does not detail all of his sin, so it is best not to invent more.

For today: position, success, and prestige are not our security. We receive everything we have from God, so it is good to serve with humility and not to exalt ourselves.
exp.53:5:
God says that he calls his people like a woman who has been abandoned, with a wounded heart, or like a young wife whom her husband has rejected. "Forsaken" means abandoned, "wife of youth" means a wife from her youth, and "refused" means rejected and sent away. But the verse speaks of a calling: God is seeking her.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Jerusalem, or Israel, which has lived through punishment and exile and felt abandoned. God uses the image of marriage to say that he has not forgotten her. The verses that follow explain that the abandonment was brief, and that he returns to her with everlasting mercy. Some see here also a promise for the Church, but the text speaks first to Israel.

If you feel rejected or have a broken heart, God does not leave you in that place. He calls you by your name. Speak honestly with him about your pain, and trust that his compassion is greater than your wound.
exp.26:8:
This verse says that God will purge the wickedness of the people of Israel (Jacob). The intended result is that sin is taken away, and it is seen when the altars of the idols are broken down until they are like chalkstones that are beaten to pieces. The groves and images are not to stand up again.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, passing on what God said. It comes after speaking of the measured punishment God gave his people. His purpose was not only to punish but to cleanse Israel of idolatry. Some scholars see this fulfilled after the exile, and others think it will also be fulfilled later on.

For today: God corrects in order to heal. Ask him to show you which "altars" have taken his place in your heart, and let them fall with confidence.
exp.6:1:
A report reached the royal palace of Judah: Syria had made an alliance with Ephraim, that is, with the northern kingdom of Israel. When they heard it, the king and all the people were filled with fear. Here "shaken" means trembling, and the image is that of the trees of the forest swaying in the wind.

Here the narrator of the book of Isaiah is speaking. "The house of David" refers to King Ahaz and his court. Syria and Israel meant to attack Jerusalem, and Ahaz felt he had no defense. That is why, in what follows, God sends Isaiah with a message: do not be afraid, because those enemies were only smoldering stumps of firebrands, that is, logs nearly burned out.

For today: when bad news makes you tremble, do not rely only on what you can see. Stop, pray, and remember that God is greater than whatever threatens you.
exp.12:11:
It says God will make people scarce, as rare and precious as the finest gold. "Ophir" was a region famous for its gold; no one knows for certain where it was. "Man" and "a man" in the verse are two ways of saying the same thing: human beings.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a message of judgment against Babylon. Before and after, the passage describes the day of the LORD: darkness in the sky, the end of pride, and the trembling of the earth. Many understand that very few people will be left because the judgment will be severe, and so each life that remains will be worth more than gold.

For today: if God considers each person so precious, let us treat others with respect and care, and not with pride or contempt. Our worth comes from God, not from what we have.
exp.41:4:
This verse presents God in all his power. He is the Creator who made the heavens and stretched them out like a cloth, and who also spread out the earth along with what comes out of it (the plants and vegetation that grow from the ground). Furthermore, he is the one who gives breath and life to all the people who live on the earth. "Creator" means the same as Maker, and "spirit" here refers to the breath of life.

God speaks here about his Servant, who was described in the verses before: someone gentle, who does not break a bruised reed. Before saying what he will do with him, God reminds us who he himself is. Many Christians see in this Servant Jesus, and the New Testament applies this passage to him (Matthew 12:18-21). Others also emphasize its meaning for Israel.

For today: the God who sustains your breath can also sustain you when you are weak. Trust in him, even if you feel like a bruised reed.
exp.0:9:
Here God calls the rulers and the people of Jerusalem "rulers of Sodom" and "people of Gomorrah." "Hear" means listen, and "law" here means God's teaching or instruction. He asks them to pay serious attention to what he is about to say.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the previous verse it was said that, without God's mercy, Judah would have ended like Sodom. Now God uses those names as a strong rebuke: they were behaving like those cities. What follows shows that they had a religion of rituals and sacrifices, but without a sincere heart or justice.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious practices if we do not truly listen to God. Before we pray, sing, or serve, we can ask ourselves humbly, "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" And then we can obey in concrete ways, such as treating others with justice and kindness.
exp.4:13:
It says that the grave, like an enormous mouth, opens without limit to swallow the proud people of Jerusalem and Judah. There their honored people will go down, along with their crowds, their luxury and the noise of their festivities, and everyone who took pleasure in it. The place of the dead is what the Hebrew word Sheol refers to, and it is the place of the dead. Those who took pleasure in it were enjoying themselves.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he denounces a people who held banquets with music and wine but ignored what God was doing. For this reason he announces judgment, which would mean captivity, hunger and death. Scholars debate whether all of this refers to a single invasion or to several stages of judgment. What is clear is the message: God will be recognized as holy and just.

For today: examine whether your pleasures and your comfort make you forget God. Enjoying what is good is not a sin, but it is wise to set aside time each day to pray, read the Bible and give thanks to him.
exp.43:11:
He describes a smith who takes his tools, works the metal in the coals, shapes it with hammer blows, and forms it with the strength of his arm. But he grows tired: he becomes hungry, loses his strength, and if he does not drink water, he faints. The tongs are what the smith uses to hold the hot metal, and the coals are the glowing embers.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He mocks idolatry with irony. He shows that the one who makes an idol is a limited human being, who wears himself out and needs to eat and drink. How could such a weak being create something that could be a god?

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by our own hands, such as work, money, or success, we are treating as if they could save us. Only God, who never grows weary, deserves our complete trust.
exp.42:16:
It says that God is the one who brings out a powerful army, with chariots, horses and soldiers. But that same army falls down together and does not rise again. It is put out like a wick, the thread of a candle or lamp, and goes out completely.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah to his people Israel. He reminds them how he made a way through the sea, most likely alluding to the exodus from Egypt, when Pharaoh's army was defeated. He encourages them in the midst of their distress, because he is still their King and Savior, and right after this he promises to do a new thing.

For today: no human power is so great that it can stop God. If you face a problem today that seems impossible, trust that God has rescued before and can open a new way. Rest in him and not only in your own strength.
exp.59:6:
It says that the peoples of the desert will bring their best animals to Jerusalem. Kedar and Nebaioth were nomadic tribes, descendants of Ishmael, rich in flocks. "All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together" means they will be gathered and brought. "With acceptance" means God will receive them gladly. "The house of my glory" is the temple, which God promises to glorify.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem. The chapter announces that, after times of sorrow, God's light will shine upon her and the nations will come to worship. Scholars understand it in several ways: as hope for the return from exile, or as a announcement of a greater future time. Many Christians see here an image of people from all nations coming to God.

For today: God gladly receives what is offered from the heart. Put your time or your talents at God's service today, with joy and without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.9:15:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, will send weakness on Assyria's "fat ones," that is, its strong soldiers and its proud leaders. Weakness means a weakness or wasting sickness that consumes. And under its glory, that is its fame and its power, God will kindle a fire that will burn like a flame.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria had conquered peoples, and God used it to discipline Israel and Judah. But the Assyrian king became full of pride, like an axe that boasts against the one who wields it. That is why God announces that he will judge that arrogance. Some understand the fire as a plague or a military disaster; the text gives no further details.

For today: everything we have comes from God, so there is no reason to boast. Ask him to give you a humble and thankful heart.
exp.47:21:
It says that those who live in wickedness do not have true peace. "Wicked" refers to the ungodly, that is, to those who turn away from God and live against His will. "Peace" is more than calm: it is complete well-being and tranquility of the soul.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. God has just invited His people to leave Babylon, where they were held captive, and He reminds them how He cared for them in the desert. This sentence closes that section as a warning: deliverance is for those who trust in Him. Those who reject Him will remain without inner rest. Some scholars see here a call not to stay bound to Babylon.

Today we can examine what takes away our peace. If there is something we know does not please God, we can confess it and turn back to Him sincerely. His forgiveness and His guidance restore a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.5:6:
In this verse, the seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with the burning coal from the altar. Then he declares to him that his iniquity has been taken away and his sin purged. "Iniquity" is the guilt that weighs on a person, and "purged" here means cleansed or forgiven.

Isaiah has seen God in his glory in the temple and feels lost, because he recognizes that his lips and those of his people are unclean. The seraph, a heavenly being, speaks on behalf of God. The forgiveness comes by divine initiative, from the altar, and not through any effort of Isaiah's own. After this, Isaiah hears God's call and responds. Scholars interpret the symbolism of the coal in various ways, but all agree that it shows the purification that God gives.

Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, acknowledging our faults without hiding them. He forgives and cleanses, and from that forgiveness he invites us to serve him with gratitude.
exp.36:34:
It says that God himself will defend Jerusalem and deliver it. The word translated "defend" means to protect, shelter, and care for. God gives two reasons: he does it for his own sake, that is, for his name and his faithfulness, and for the sake of his servant David, because of the promise he made to that king.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. King Hezekiah was terrified because the Assyrian army, led by Sennacherib, surrounded Judah and mocked his God. Hezekiah prayed, and God answered with this promise. Afterward, an angel struck down the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, pray as Hezekiah did and rest in the fact that God is faithful to his promises. Your security does not depend on your own strength but on the character of God.
exp.25:20:
God says he comes out of his place, that is, out of the heavens where he reigns, to call to account the wickedness that the inhabitants of the earth have done. The phrase about coming to judge the wickedness is rendered here in plain terms: he comes to judge it. The earth will reveal the blood of those who were murdered, and it will no longer hide those unjust deaths.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. This passage belongs to the section often called the "Little Apocalypse of Isaiah" (chapters 24 to 27), which speaks of God's judgment on the world and of hope for his people. Just before it, God invites his people to hide for a moment while his anger passes. Scholars interpret these images in different ways, but all see here the promise of justice.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that God sees every injustice, even the one no one else knows about. Hand over your pain, leave vengeance in his hands, and keep practicing justice and mercy.
exp.0:4:
What it says: God asks why he should keep striking his people if they will not change, since they keep rebelling. Here "stricken" means struck or corrected. Then he describes the nation as a sick body: the head, which thinks and directs, is unwell, and the heart, the center of life and desire, is hurting and without strength.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the beginning of his book. He has just said that even an ox knows its owner, yet Israel does not recognize God. The punishments that had already come, such as the land laid waste, did not lead them back to him. Many understand that the image of the wounded body shows that sin had already damaged the whole people.

For today: If we repeat the same mistakes and only feel the pain, we do not heal. This week, ask God to show you something you keep repeating, and take one concrete step of repentance, turning back to him with sincerity.
exp.29:29:
He says God will make everyone hear his powerful voice and see the strength of his arm when he acts. His anger appears as a consuming fire, and also as a storm: a flood, scattering, and hail. "Furious anger" describes very strong wrath. A "flood" is a rush of water. "Scattering" is a storm that sweeps everything away.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who were afraid of the Assyrian empire. God promises that Assyria, which had struck down many nations, will be broken by his voice. For those who trust in him, that judgment brings relief and song, as at a festival.

Today we can remember that no human power is final. When you feel fear before something that seems bigger than you, pray and entrust that situation to God, trusting that he does justice in his own time.
exp.0:21:
It says that what was once valuable in Jerusalem has been ruined. "Dross" refers to the worthless residue left behind when a metal is refined. Wine mixed with water becomes watered down, of lower quality and deceptive.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just lamented that the faithful city, Jerusalem, has become like a prostitute, unfaithful to God. The silver and the wine are images of her moral corruption: justice and loyalty have been degraded. The verses that follow make this concrete: the leaders accept bribes and neglect the orphan and the widow.

For today: examine which part of your faith has been diluted, like wine with water. Ask God to purify you, and look for one concrete act of justice or compassion toward someone who is vulnerable.
exp.27:12:
It says that the word of God, for this people, becomes teaching that is repeated: precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little. But they, instead of learning, stumble, fall backward, are broken and snared and taken.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Judah who mocked his message. God had offered them rest, but they would not listen. They trusted in covenants with death and in lies. Many think the repetitive tone imitates how they mocked the teachings, as if they were for children. Some also see it as a judgment: if they do not listen, that word will make them stumble.

For today: do not despise the simple or repeated teaching of the Bible. Listen to it with humility every day, because God often shapes us little by little.
exp.5:8:
God tells Isaiah to go and speak to the people. The words "Hear indeed" and "see indeed" are commands to listen and look carefully, yet the result will be that they do not understand or perceive. It is a harsh, almost ironic statement: they will hear and see, but without grasping its meaning.

The Lord speaks right after Isaiah was cleansed and said, "Here I am, send me." Isaiah is sent to a people who have hardened themselves against God. His message will be faithful, but many will not respond. Some understand this as God's judgment on a people who had already rejected his voice; the text does not explain every detail.

For today: obeying God does not depend on the results we see. We can speak faithfully, pray for those who do not listen, and ask God for a humble heart, one that hears and understands his Word.
exp.1:10:
It says that human pride, that look of superiority with which someone thinks of himself as better than others, will be brought down. "Lofty looks" and "haughtiness" are pride and arrogance. The lofty looks of man will be humbled, and the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day, the day when He acts in judgment.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks to the people who trusted in their wealth, their power and their idols. The verses nearby describe people hiding themselves before the majesty of the Lord. Then the day of the Lord is mentioned, along with tall trees like the cedars, images of everything people consider great. Some see here a historical judgment, and others also see the end of time.

Today we can examine what we take pride in: success, money or knowledge. It is better to recognize with humility that everything comes from God and to live grateful, without looking down on anyone.
exp.9:32:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, will lop the bough with terror, that is, break the branches of a tree with force. The high ones of stature will be cut down, and the haughty will be humbled.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The Assyrian army advances toward Jerusalem, and the text describes it as a great forest. When it seems that nothing will stop it, God himself intervenes and brings it down. Many understand the high ones as the proud leaders of Assyria, though others also see a general warning against all pride.

For today: when powerful people or great problems make you feel small, remember that God rules over all. Trust him, and examine your heart so that you may live with humility.
exp.16:2:
It says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel) will lose its protection, and that Damascus, the capital of Syria, will cease to be a kingdom. The word "fortress" means a place of protection or defense. What little remains of Syria will be like the "glory" of Israel, that is, it will share the same fate: a glory that fades away. "The Lord of hosts" is the Lord, the owner of all power.

Isaiah announces this message against Damascus. Israel and Syria had formed an alliance, perhaps seeking security against Assyria. God warns that this alliance would not save them. Many understand that the judgment came because they trusted in human alliances rather than in God, although the historical details are explained in several ways.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, connections, or plans. All of these can fail, but God remains faithful. Trust in Him first and seek His guidance.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that a day of great confusion had come, of people trampled down and of anguish, and that all of it comes from the Lord, the LORD of hosts. It happens in the valley of vision, which is Jerusalem. The word "treading down" means trampling or crushing. The phrase "crying to the mountains" can be understood as cries of panic or a shout that echoes across the mountains. Breaking down the walls speaks of the city being left defenseless.

Isaiah speaks in chapter 22 about Jerusalem, and it is not known for certain which siege he has in mind; many think of the Assyrian threat or the later fall of the city. The leaders fled, the people were in ruin, and the prophet wept for them. The text affirms that God allowed that judgment.

For today: do not place your security only in your "walls," such as your money, your job, or your own strength. Trust God first, and when you see ruin, weep and pray instead of ignoring it.
exp.29:9:
This verse describes a people who did not want to hear the truth. They said to the seers (those who received visions from God), "See not," and to the prophets, "Prophesy not unto us right things," that is, what is correct. They asked for "smooth things," which are pleasant and flattering words, even if they are "deceits," or false.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah, at a time when the people sought security in political alliances, especially with Egypt, instead of trusting the Lord. God calls them rebellious because they rejected his law. For this reason he commands that the message be recorded in writing, so that it may serve as a witness. The people preferred not to be confronted, and God warns that rejecting his word brings consequences.

For today: examine whether you seek out voices that only confirm what you want to hear. Ask God for humility to receive his Word, even when it corrects you, and surround yourself with people who tell you the truth with love.
exp.53:8:
God compares his promise to Israel with the one he made after the flood. Just as he swore he would never again flood the earth, he now swears that he will no longer be angry with his people or rebuke them with punishment. Here, "to be angry with" means to reprove or punish harshly.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem, seen as an abandoned and suffering woman. The people had gone through judgment and exile, and they felt forsaken. God assures them that that season of discipline was brief, and that now comes a restoration based on his mercy and his covenant of peace.

For today: when you feel guilt or fear that God has let you go, remember that his compassion is firmer than your failures. Rest in his word and return to him with confidence, without fear of rejection.
exp.37:21:
It says that King Hezekiah had asked what sign he would have that he would go up again to the temple. "Go up to the house of the Lord" means going to worship God in the temple in Jerusalem, which stood on a hill. A "sign" is a visible proof or confirmation. It is a question asking for assurance.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and God promised to heal him and add fifteen years to his life. After his song of thanksgiving, this verse adds a detail: Isaiah had ordered a poultice of figs placed on the sore, and Hezekiah asked for a sign. In 2 Kings 20 it is told that God gave him as a sign that the shadow would go back. Some think the verse is out of its proper place, but that does not change its message.

Asking God for assurance is not always a lack of faith. If you have doubts, bring them to him honestly, and remember that healing and giving thanks lead you into the community of worship.
exp.35:20:
This verse says that the officials of Jerusalem stayed silent in the face of the mockery of the Assyrian messenger. They did not answer him a single word, because King Hezekiah had commanded them: "Answer him not."

Rabshakeh, spokesman of the king of Assyria, had just spoken with arrogance. He said that no god had delivered other cities, so the God of Israel would not deliver Jerusalem either. It was an attempt to frighten the people and make them doubt. Hezekiah, knowing that arguing would be useless, asked for silence. Afterward, his officials brought him the message with their clothes torn, a sign of grief.

There are moments when it is not necessary to answer every insult or provocation. Sometimes silence is wisdom, and it is better to bring one's worry to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did afterward.
exp.49:3:
This verse says that God gave the Servant a "tongue of the learned," meaning a tongue that has been taught, so that he would know how to speak a word in due time, that is, at the right moment, to encourage the weary. Every morning God awakens his ear to listen the way disciples listen, with attention and a readiness to learn.

The Servant of the Lord speaks in the third of Isaiah's "Servant songs." Before this, God reproached Israel because no one answered his call. Now the Servant does answer and listen. Many Christians see Jesus here, who suffered without rebelling, as the following verses show. Others first emphasize the meaning for the prophet or for Israel.

For today: before speaking with someone who is exhausted, begin by listening to God yourself, in the morning, in prayer and in his Word. In this way your words will be timely and will bring encouragement, not just opinions.
exp.34:1:
It will blossom abundantly and be filled with joy and singing. It will receive the glory of Lebanon, known for its cedars, and the splendor of Carmel and Sharon, green and fertile lands. The people will see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who have endured judgment and fear. He announces a promise of restoration: the dry land becomes life, and this shows that God himself is coming to save. The verses that follow call for encouraging the weak. Many understand this as hope for the return from exile; others also see it pointing to the work of Christ.

For today: if you feel dry or weary inside, God can make bloom what seems dead. Trust his promise, and encourage someone today who is discouraged.
exp.53:11:
God promises his people a beautiful and secure city. Its windows will be made of precious stones, its gates of a gem called "carbuncle" (a bright stone, probably red, though it is not known for certain which stone this was), and all its border or boundary wall of pleasant stones, that is, carefully chosen and beautiful stones.

The LORD speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as a poor, weary, and comfortless woman. He first assures her that his mercy and his covenant of peace will not change, even though the mountains may be moved. The image of jewels expresses restoration, care, and worth, more than a literal description.

For today: if you feel tired or discouraged, remember that God not only comforts you, but also rebuilds with care what is broken. You can hand over a difficult situation to him today and trust that his faithfulness does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.51:7:
This verse says that the watchmen, that is, the lookouts who guard the city from the walls, lift up their voices and sing together for joy. They see clearly, face to face and up close, that the Lord is bringing back Zion, that is, Jerusalem, his city.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who were living in exile or in the aftermath of it. The watchmen were waiting for news of liberation, and the messenger had already announced that your God reigns. Many understand this as referring to the return from Babylon, and others also see a broader fulfillment in God's work in Christ. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: God does not leave his people forgotten. Even in difficult times, we can live alert and full of hope, and praise him together, remembering that he is faithful to restore.
exp.61:4:
The verse uses the image of a wedding. Just as a young man marries his bride, so your sons will be joined to you, Jerusalem. And as the bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God will rejoice over you. The word "young man" in the verse means a young man, and "virgin" here refers to a bride who has never been married. There are different readings of "your sons": some understand it as the inhabitants who will live in the city again, and others see an image of the land wedded to its people.

Isaiah speaks to a people who lived through exile and a city in ruins. God promises to restore them: they will no longer be called "Forsaken" but will be called by a new name that means "my delight is in her." The prophet wants to comfort and give hope with the most tender image of human love.

For today: even when you feel abandoned or without worth, God does not approach you with anger but with joy. Pray today by receiving that love, instead of trying to earn it.
exp.12:1:
It says to raise a banner on a bare hilltop, a signal that everyone can see. A loud call is made and a hand is waved to gather an army. "Lift ye up the voice unto them" means shouting to the soldiers. That army is to go in through "the gates of the nobles," that is, through the entrances of the lords and rulers of Babylon.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, and God himself gives the command. He wants to show that he directs the nations and that Babylon's power is not final. Interpreters explain in different ways which historical events the passage refers to, but the central message is that God judges the pride of empires.

For today: trust that God governs history, even when the powers of the world seem untouchable. This invites us to live with humility and not to place our security in money, politics, or prestige.
exp.58:11:
It says the people have sinned enormously against God. "Rebellions" refers to deliberate acts of disobedience. "Testify against us" means the sins are like witnesses who accuse us. "Our iniquities are with us" means the guilt goes with them everywhere, so they can no longer deny it: "we know our sins."

Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel and includes himself with the word "we." It is a corporate confession. Earlier, the prophet explained that their sins had separated them from God (v. 2). That is why they live as if in darkness, waiting for justice and salvation that do not arrive. After this verse, they name their sins: lying, slander, and injustice.

For today: honest confession is the first step back to God. Instead of making excuses or blaming others, we can tell him sincerely what we have done, trusting that he forgives those who come near with humility.
exp.20:1:
Isaiah says he received a very harsh vision. A treacherous one keeps betraying, and a destroyer keeps destroying. Then Persia and Media are called to go up and lay siege, that is, to surround a city in order to attack it. The word "treacherous" here means acting with deceit and betrayal. At the end, God says that he has made all the sighing cease, that is, the suffering caused by that oppression.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and in the last sentence it seems that God is speaking. The message is a heavy burden, a weighty warning, concerning the wilderness of the sea, a phrase that many connect with Babylon. The text does not name it here, so there are different opinions. Many understand that the sighing that ceases is that of the peoples oppressed by Babylon. Isaiah trembles at what is coming.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it forever. If you find yourself suffering or witnessing abuse, you can pray and trust that He governs history, while you choose to act with truth and justice.
exp.29:5:
It says that Judah sends a caravan loaded with riches toward Egypt, the south. To get there, it crosses a dangerous desert full of lions, vipers, and swift poisonous snakes. They carry the treasure on donkeys and camels, but the people they are taking it to will be of no use to them.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The leaders of Judah, threatened by Assyria, were seeking a secret alliance with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities. God warns them that they will pay a high price for help that will do them no good.

For today: when we are afraid, let us not spend the best of ourselves on solutions that promise much but cannot sustain us. First let us turn to God in prayer, and then use wisely the means He gives us.
exp.31:15:
It says that when God renews all things, judgment (uprightness, acting with fairness) and righteousness will live in every place: both in the wilderness, a dry and abandoned land, and in the fruitful field, land that is cultivated and fertile. In other words, nothing will be left outside its reach.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Before this, he announces ruin: empty palaces and cities laid waste because of their sin. But he adds a hope: "until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high." Many Christians see here a promise of God's Spirit; others connect it with the future restoration of the people. Then the text says that righteousness will bring peace and security.

For today: even where you see areas of dryness in your life, family, or work, ask God's Spirit to renew them, and practice righteousness with honesty in small things.
exp.13:0:
This verse says that God will have compassion on Jacob, that is, on the people of Israel, and that He will choose them again. He will give them rest in their own land. Moreover, people from other nations will join them and be added to the family of Jacob. To join with them means to come near and become united.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. This message comes just before a song against the king of Babylon. It announces that Israel, who would suffer exile and oppression, would be restored. The verses that follow speak of a change of fortune among the nations. Some interpret this as referring to the return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment in the future.

For today: even if we have passed through hard times or have failed, God is faithful and compassionate. We can trust that He restores and gives rest, and welcome with open arms those who come near to Him.
exp.21:5:
Elam and Kir are said to be preparing an army to attack Jerusalem. Elam carried the quiver, the case for arrows, and came with chariots of men and horsemen. Kir uncovered the shield, that is, he took off its cover to make it ready for battle. It is a picture of an armed and determined army.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, and he is deeply sad over the suffering of his people. The valley of vision is usually understood to refer to Jerusalem. God allows this attack, and the text shows that the city trusted more in its weapons than in Him. Scholars are not completely sure which specific enemy is described, or when it happened.

For today: let us not rely only on our defenses, plans, or resources. Preparing ourselves is good, but God should be our first security. When difficulty comes, let us return to Him with humility.
exp.55:7:
The Lord God, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says he will not stop there. He promises to bring in others to join those he has already gathered. The word "outcasts" means people who have been driven out or scattered.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he promises that foreigners who love him and serve him will be welcomed into his house of prayer, which will be for all peoples. For this reason, the verse shows that God's people will grow larger. The verses that follow change in tone and criticize the leaders who do not care for the people. Some understand this as a reference to the future inclusion of the nations.

God opens his arms to those who feel distant or left outside. We can imitate him by warmly welcoming the new or overlooked person in our church, and not treating the group as closed.
exp.4:12:
It says that God's people would go into exile because they had no knowledge: they did not know or consider God and his ways. For that reason their honourable men would die of hunger, and the multitude would be dried up with thirst. The verb is in the past tense, as something so certain that it is already a fact.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah. It comes after a "woe" against those who lived among feasts and wine, without looking at what God was doing. Many understand that it announces the captivity that would come later, though some see it as a general warning of judgment.

For today: do not let noise, entertainment, or routine dull your attention to God. Set aside time each day to read his Word and reflect on it.
exp.64:1:
God says that he spread out his hands all day long, meaning that again and again he reached out with open arms to a stubborn people. That people does not walk in the good way; they follow their own thoughts, that is, their own ideas.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The verses before this one show that he let himself be found even by those who were not looking for him. Then he describes Israel, who offended him with idolatrous practices. Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10:20-21 and applies it both to the Gentiles and to Israel.

For today: if God still holds out his arms, do not wait until everything is settled in your life. Ask yourself in what area you are following only your own ideas, and return to him with humility and simplicity.
exp.5:2:
Here the seraphim, beings who stand around the throne of God, call out to one another and proclaim that God is holy three times. "Lord of hosts" means the Lord of the heavenly armies, the one who commands all power. They say that the whole earth is full of his glory, that is, of his greatness and his presence.

Isaiah describes a vision he had in the year King Uzziah died. The seraphim speak in praise, and their voice shakes the temple. Repeating "holy" three times is a way of giving the strongest possible emphasis, though some also see a hint of the Trinity; this is interpreted in several ways. Before this holiness, Isaiah feels unworthy and confesses his sin.

Today we can begin our prayer with awe, not only with requests. Before speaking of what we need, let us take a moment to acknowledge who God is. And as we look at creation, let us remember that it speaks of his glory.
exp.24:11:
It says that God will bring down the fortresses of Moab. The word "bring down" means to level something, to knock it flat. "High walls" are the walls that gave security. "Bring low" means lowering it, and "bring to the ground, even to the dust" describes a total fall, ending up on the ground.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a song of praise (chapters 24 to 27), where he celebrates that God will reign and save his people on this mountain. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears as an example of human pride. Many understand that it represents everyone who trusts in their own power. Some think that "your" refers to Moab, although the shift of person in the text is explained in several ways.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, fame, or your own strength. The walls we build out of pride fall, but whoever trusts in God rests safe.
exp.12:0:
This verse is the heading of a prophetic message. "Burden" does not refer to a physical weight, but to a serious message of judgment, a sentence that God places upon a nation. "Did see" is the old form of "saw." It is a message against Babylon that Isaiah received from God, in a vision.

Here God does not speak directly; the one who introduces the book is Isaiah, the son of Amoz, a prophet in Judah. The following verses do show God summoning armies to carry out his judgment. Babylon was then a power that would later be an enemy of Judah. Scholars debate exactly when this message was fulfilled, but the text presents it as the word of God.

For today: God sees and governs over all nations, even the most powerful. You can trust that injustice will not have the last word, and that God cares for his people.
exp.57:3:
God says that his people fast, but meanwhile they quarrel, argue, and strike out wickedly. "Strife and debate" are fights and arguments; "smite with the fist of wickedness" is to strike unjustly. He warns them that fasting in this way will not make their prayer reach "on high," that is, up to God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people complain that they fast and God does not answer. But on those days of fasting they were seeking their own advantage and treating their workers badly. God shows them that their fasting was only outward religion, without justice or compassion.

For today: before you pray or fast, examine how you treat others. If you have an unresolved dispute or have been harsh with someone, seek peace and do what is right. In this way your devotion will be sincere.
exp.52:0:
The prophet here asks two questions that express wonder and sorrow: who has believed the message we heard? And to whom has the power of God been shown? The "report" is what was heard or proclaimed, and the "arm of the Lord" is an image of his strength to save. The suggested answer is that very few have believed it.

This question opens the song of the suffering Servant, which begins in Isaiah 52:13. It seems to be spoken by a group ("our report"), which then confesses that it despised the Servant. Jews and Christians have interpreted it in different ways, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus (John 12:38).

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly believe what God says, even when his work does not seem great or impressive. Sometimes his power comes in a humble form, and we need faith to recognize it.
exp.56:1:
This verse says that the righteous person enters into peace. When they die, they rest in their beds, a poetic way of speaking about the rest of death. Walking uprightly means living with sincerity, aware that God sees us. Beds are places of rest.

God speaks through Isaiah. Many righteous people died and no one noticed or asked why. The previous verse says the righteous are taken away before calamity, and many understand this as God's protection from the evil that was coming. Afterward, God addresses with harshness those who mocked and lived in rebellion.

For today: if you live faithfully before God and feel that no one values it, remember that He does see it. Your faithfulness is not lost, and your final rest is in His hands.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that those who rebel against God and keep on sinning will be destroyed together. The verse of the old phrase is no longer needed for the English reader, since the verse itself says "together" and "consumed" directly. The words "broken in pieces" and "completely finished" are likewise shown by the verse's own wording, so they are not explained here. Those who "forsake the Lord" are those who turn away from God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Earlier, He promises to cleanse the city, restore righteous judges, and redeem Zion with justice. But here He makes clear that not everyone will be restored: those who refuse to return to Him will face the consequences. The verses that follow speak of the shame of having trusted in places of worship dedicated to idols.

For today: God offers forgiveness and a fresh start, but it must be accepted. Today you can ask yourself whether there is anything in which you have drifted away from God and, with humility, return to Him in prayer, before pride hardens your heart.
exp.44:19:
God invites the people of the nations who have managed to survive to gather together and draw near. The word translated "draw near" here carries the sense of coming close. Those who "escaped" are the ones who saved their lives, perhaps from wars or disasters. God points out that those who carry an idol made of wood and pray to it for help have no understanding: that god cannot save.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he is the Creator, that he speaks plainly, and that he deceives no one. Now he calls the nations to compare. Right after, he challenges them to see who announced these things long ago. Many interpret this as referring to the return of the people from exile, but the text leaves it open.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. An idol can be money, fame, or control. If it cannot save us, let us return simply to God, who does listen.
exp.63:8:
This verse says the people ask God not to be angry too much or forever. The phrase "be not wroth very sore" is the wording of the verse itself, and it means "do not be angry beyond measure." They ask that he not remember their sin forever, and that he look upon them, because they are his people.

The passage is a prayer spoken by the prophet Isaiah on behalf of the nation. He confesses that the people turned away from God and are suffering the consequences. The verses that follow describe deserted cities and the temple burned, which many understand as the destruction of Jerusalem. Scholars disagree about the exact moment in which the prayer is set.

We can come before God with sincerity, acknowledging our failings without making excuses. Even so, we rely on his relationship with us, not on our own merits. God is a Father who listens to anyone who returns to him with humility.
exp.18:1:
Here God says that he will set the Egyptians against one another. There will be fighting between relatives, neighbors, cities, and even kingdoms. "Stir up" means to provoke conflict and disorder. "Neighbour" is the person who lives nearby or is close to us.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, in what is called a "burden," that is, a message of judgment against Egypt. This country trusted in its idols, its fortune-tellers, and its own wisdom. God shows that none of these will protect it. It is not known with certainty which specific historical event is meant; scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: when a society, a family, or a church is divided and filled with conflict, it is good to ask ourselves whether we have placed our trust in passing things instead of in God. Let us seek peace and humility before him.
exp.15:2:
It says that Moab, a people in trouble, must make a wise and just decision. Take counsel and act justly means to deliberate and then act with justice. Make your shadow in the midst of the noonday as the night is an image: give the pursued a shade so deep that they can hide even in broad daylight. The ones who were driven from their land are those who were expelled from their home, and the wanderers are the fugitives. They should not be handed over to their pursuers.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, and the Moabites ask help from Judah, which stands on Mount Zion. Moab flees before a destroyer, probably an invasion, though the text does not give the name with certainty. The suggested answer is that Judah should protect the refugees. Then a just and merciful kingdom is promised in the line of David.

For today: when someone flees violence or injustice, God calls us to be a refuge, not to hand them over. We can help with lodging, practical aid, or by defending the one who suffers.
exp.37:0:
Hezekiah the king became seriously ill, very nearly at the point of death. The prophet Isaiah went to see him with a message from God: "Set your house in order," meaning put your affairs in order and leave instructions, because you will die and not recover.

Here Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, carries God's word to the king of Judah. This happens at a time of threats, when Assyria was pressing on the kingdom. The verses that follow show that Hezekiah prayed weeping, and the story continues with God's response. For that reason, the statement is not to be understood as final, but as the beginning of a dialogue with God.

For today: do not wait until you are sick or in crisis to put your life in order. Speak with God honestly, take care of important unfinished matters, and look after your family. And if hard news arrives, you can bring it to God in prayer.
exp.0:25:
God promises that he will set good judges and counselors back in Jerusalem, like those who served in the best days of his people. When this happens, the city will be known as the city of righteousness and the faithful city.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he had told them that the city was corrupted, and that he would cleanse it the way metal is purified, removing the impurities. This restoration comes after a judgment that purifies. Some understand that it was partly fulfilled after the exile, and others also see a future fulfillment in Christ; interpreters explain it in several ways.

God does not settle for punishing; he wants to heal and restore. If today we see injustice or a lack of integrity, we can pray for our leaders and begin by being faithful and just in our home, our work, and our church.
exp.3:4:
God says that he himself will cover and protect all of Zion, both the houses where his people live and the places where they gather to worship him. "Will create" here means "will make." By day there will be a cloud, and by night a glow like a flaming fire. A "covering" is like a roof or canopy: over all the glory there will be protection.

Isaiah is speaking to Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier he spoke of judgment and cleansing for sin; now he promises that those who remain, called holy, will have God's protecting presence. The cloud and the fire recall how God guided Israel in the wilderness, though the text does not say this directly. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others apply it to the church.

After being cleansed, God does not leave us alone. If today you feel exposed or afraid, remember that his presence covers you. Ask him to cleanse you, and rest in his care.
exp.48:8:
God says that the Servant will be used to tell the prisoners, "Go forth," and to those who live in darkness, "Show yourselves; come out into the light." And like a shepherd, God will feed them along the ways, and even on the highest hills there will be pasture for them.

Here the LORD speaks to the Servant, who was seen as despised and worthless. God promises that He will be faithful to him and that He will use him to set others free. Some understand the Servant to be Israel; many Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus. Both readings have been held.

Today, if you feel trapped by guilt, fear, or sadness, God invites you to come out into His light. And if you know someone like this, you can encourage them, with love, to trust in the Shepherd who cares for and provides for them.
exp.13:20:
This verse says that the children of the wicked king will be handed over to death, like animals led to the slaughter, because of the sins of their fathers. The sentence about "prepare" is to be rewritten for the verse's word "Prepare": the word "Prepare" in the verse means to get something ready. "Face of the world" is the surface of the earth. The purpose is that these children will not rise up to rule or fill the world with cities.

Isaiah announces a mocking song against the king of Babylon, a cruel ruler who destroyed peoples. God speaks through the prophet, and the verses that follow confirm this. God promises to bring an end to the name and descendants of that dynasty. Some believe the passage also echoes the general pride of power; scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered. We can leave vengeance in his hands, trust his justice, and take care that our decisions bring blessing, not harm, to those who come after us.
exp.12:4:
It says that God himself comes from a faraway country, from the end of heaven, meaning from the most distant horizon. He comes with the weapons of his indignation, that is, armies he uses to carry out his judgment. "To destroy the whole land" may refer to the whole territory of the empire being judged, although the language also anticipates a wider judgment.

Isaiah speaks against Babylon. God gathers nations and troops to judge its pride and its violence. Those who are set apart are the ones God has dedicated to that task. Many understand this to refer to the Medes, although the text also points to the final day of the Lord.

For today: God rules over the nations and does not overlook injustice. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in human power, and to seek his mercy now, while there is still time.
exp.36:36:
This verse says that King Sennacherib of Assyria, after losing his army, left Judah, returned to his country, and stayed to live in Nineveh, his capital. "Departed, and went and returned" means that he withdrew at once. "Dwelt" means that he settled there.

The one telling the story is the prophet Isaiah, who recounts what happened when Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem in the days of King Hezekiah. God had promised to defend the city, and that night his angel struck the Assyrian camp. This verse shows the result: the proud king who defied God went back humbled and without his army.

God keeps his promises, even when the danger seems greater than we are. When you face a problem that is bigger than you, pray as Hezekiah did and trust that God is faithful. He knows how and when to act.
exp.7:7:
It says that the army of Assyria, like a river that has burst its banks, will enter Judah, rise up to the neck (almost covering the people, like water that reaches the throat), and spread across the whole land, like a bird that spreads its wings. The word "overflow" means that it will pass over, flooding past its limits. The land is called Immanuel ("God with us").

God speaks through Isaiah, around 730 BC. The people rejected the gentle waters of Shiloah, which many understand as a sign of trusting God, and placed their hope in human alliances. God says that Assyria will come as judgment. Even so, the name Immanuel shows that God does not abandon his people.

For today: when difficulties seem to flood over you, do not look for security only in human resources. Trust in God, who remains with you even in the middle of the trial.
exp.48:7:
God tells his Servant that he has heard him in an acceptable time, that is, in a time of favor and goodwill. The phrase "in a day of salvation" means in the day of salvation, and there God helped him. He promises to keep him and make him a covenant for the people, that is, the means by which God renews his agreement. He also sends him to raise up the land and to divide the ruined inheritances again, which are the lands laid waste.

The LORD speaks to the Servant, whom people despise. The context shows that his mission reaches Israel and also the nations. Many Christians see Jesus here, and Paul quotes the first part in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Others think first of Israel as the servant. Both readings recognize that God restores.

For today: even when you feel despised or in ruins, God hears you and sustains you. Today is a time to draw near to him with confidence.
exp.56:7:
It says that the people set their symbols of idolatry hidden behind the door and the doorpost of their house. The word "remembrance" here may refer to pagan signs or emblems; some scholars understand it this way, while others dispute it. Then, using the image of a bed, it describes Israel as an unfaithful wife: she uncovered herself before others, enlarged her bed, and made a covenant with them. "Thou hast discovered thyself" suggests stripping oneself bare.

God speaks through Isaiah. He accuses Judah of abandoning him to follow idols and alliances with other nations. He presents their sin as spiritual adultery, because God had made with them a covenant of faithfulness.

For today: examine what things you hide and love more than God, even if it is in secret. God does not ask for a faith of appearance, but for a faithful heart. If you have given your loyalty to other things, return to Him with sincerity; He continues to invite repentance.
exp.6:21:
It says that when that time comes, whoever raises one cow and two sheep will have so much milk that they will eat curds, a kind of thick cream or soft cheese rather than butter as we know it, along with honey. The same food will be eaten by those who are left in the land, that is, the survivors who remain in the country.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz of Judah, who feared his enemies and sought help from Assyria. Assyria would be like a razor that God uses to bring judgment. The land would be left empty and poor, and the few who remain would live on simple things. Some understand that food as a sign of scarcity; others see it as a sign of provision for the survivors.

For today: trust that God cares for you even when everything is reduced to little. Instead of seeking security in human powers, rest in Him.
exp.9:31:
