This verse says that the enemy army, advancing toward Jerusalem, will stop at Nob, a town very close to the city. From there it will raise its hand, a gesture of threat, toward the mount of Zion, also called "the hill of Jerusalem." The word "remain" means that it stops for a moment.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. He describes the march of Assyria, naming towns along the road, as if the danger were drawing closer step by step. Many understand this as a prophetic picture rather than an exact itinerary. Right after, God shows that He Himself will bring down the pride of the invader, like someone cutting down a forest.

For today: when the problem seems to be at the gates, remember that God still rules over it. Bring your fear before God in prayer and trust that no power, however great it may seem, has the final word.
exp.10:6:
It says that animals that are normally enemies or dangerous will live in peace. The cow and the bear will eat together, their young will lie down side by side, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. The word "feed" in the verse means they will graze on grass. In other words, even violent nature will be transformed.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who lived among injustice and threats. He first announces a righteous king, a descendant of Jesse, the father of David. Many Christians see in him Jesus. Some understand these images literally, and others as a picture of peace among the nations. The Bible allows room for both ideas.

For today: if God promises such peace, we can practice it now. Seek to be reconciled with someone with whom you have tension, and treat with gentleness those who think differently.
exp.10:14:
God promises to dry up the arm of the Egyptian sea and strike the river into seven streams, meaning seven small channels. In this way people will be able to cross it with their shoes on, that is, with sandals and without getting wet. The sentence about the word for "will strike it" is removed, since that wording does not appear in the verse you are reading. Many understand "the river" to be the Euphrates, but this is not certain.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. He announces that God will gather the survivors of his people, scattered among the nations. He recalls the crossing of the Red Sea: what God did before, he will do again. Some see in this also a sign of the kingdom of the Messiah.

For today: if before you there is an obstacle that seems impossible, remember that God has opened paths before. Trust in him, take the next step, and let him take care of the rest.
exp.65:21:
He says that God is making new heavens and a new earth, and that this new creation will last forever before him. In the same way, he promises that the descendants of his people and their name, or their identity, will also endure. "Descendants" here means offspring. "Endure" means to stand firm and not disappear.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. After speaking of judgment, he announces hope: people from all the nations will be brought to worship him in Jerusalem, and some will even become priests. Interpreters debate whether this refers to Israel, to the church, or to both, and whether it is fulfilled in the present time or in the future.

For today: if your life feels fragile or uncertain, remember that God upholds what he promises. You can entrust your future and that of your family to the one who will make a creation that never ends.
exp.31:18:
This verse says that when the hail comes, it will fall on the forest, and the city will be completely destroyed or brought low.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. Earlier, he promises a just kingdom, with peace and security for his people. This verse is difficult: some think it announces judgment on the proud (the forest and the city as symbols of power), while others believe it contrasts the judgment outside with the peace of God's people. There is no single certain interpretation. Then the text speaks of blessing for those who sow beside the waters.

For today: do not place your security in what seems strong, such as money or reputation. All of that can fall. Trust in God, whose justice gives a peace that truly lasts.
exp.37:17:
This verse says that the dead cannot praise God the way the living do. The word "grave" is the tomb, or the place of the dead (in Hebrew, Sheol). "Pit" is the burial pit, the tomb. "Hope for thy truth" means trusting in your faithfulness. The text expresses that, from the tomb, one can no longer proclaim God's faithfulness.

The speaker is King Hezekiah, who was gravely ill, and God granted him more years of life. This is his song of gratitude. His words reflect a limited view of what lies beyond death; the Bible reveals more about that in other passages.

Today, every day of life is an opportunity to give thanks to God and to tell others, especially our children, what He has done for us. Do not leave it for later: praise Him today.
exp.40:2:
He pursued his enemies and moved forward without any stumble, secure and unharmed. He was walking along a new road, where his feet had never trodden before. The phrase "pursued them" means he went after them, and "passed safely" means he got through without being hurt.

God speaks, calling the nations to judgment as if in a courtroom. He asks who raised up that righteous man from the east. Many understand this as Cyrus, king of Persia, though others see it differently, even as Abraham. The point is that the LORD directs history, and so the nations should not trust in their idols.

For today: when you face an unfamiliar path, such as a change of job, city, or season of life, remember that God already knows that ground. Ask him for direction, take the next step with humility, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.23:12:
It says that when God judges the earth, very few people will be left among the nations. It is like when the olive tree is shaken to bring down the olives, or like when someone looks for the grapes that were left behind after the grape harvest. The verse calls these few forgotten grapes "gleanings," and the grape harvest is the "vintage." Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking. Chapters 24 to 27 describe a judgment on the whole earth for its sin, and joy disappears. But this verse looks ahead to a small remnant that survives. According to the context that follows, that remnant lifts up its voice and praises the LORD. Some scholars see here a historical judgment, and others see an announcement of the end of time; the text allows both readings.

For today: even in dark times, God cares for those who are faithful to him. You can choose to praise him today, even when everything around you seems lost.
exp.1:14:
It says that the day of the LORD will also come against every high tower and every fortified wall. The towers and walls were defenses and symbols of human security. "Fortified" here means strongly built, hard to bring down.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He announces a day of the LORD in which God will bring down everything that people raise up in pride: mountains, cedars, towers, ships, and riches. The list in the nearby verses ends by saying that human haughtiness will be humbled and that only the LORD will be exalted. Interpreters debate when and how this is fulfilled: some see historical judgments, others also a final day.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, reputation, work, or your own strength. Having things is not sin, but trusting them more than God is. Today you can hand over to God your "walls" and rest in Him.
exp.44:12:
He says that God himself "stirred up" a man to carry out a just purpose. This man will rebuild God's city, Jerusalem, and will set free God's captives, that is, his people who were carried away into exile. The phrase "I will make straight his ways" means that God will clear the road before him. And he will do this "not for price nor reward": without taking payment or a bribe.

The Lord speaks, the Creator of all things. From the context, the verse before it and the name of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, many understand this to refer to the Persian king Cyrus, who allowed the Jews to return from exile in Babylon. Some also see in this a shadow of the deliverance that Christ brings, though that is an interpretation. God wants to show that he directs history.

For today: if God could use a pagan king to carry out his plan, he can also work in your difficult circumstances. Trust that he is still guiding, even when you cannot see how.
exp.25:10:
The verse says that, although God's hand is raised to act, the wicked do not see it. They are blind to what He is doing. But in the end they will see, and those who envied God's people will be put to shame. And the fire, that is, divine judgment, will consume His enemies.

Isaiah speaks in a song of confidence that the people of Judah will sing. Shortly before, the prophet says that the wicked receive kindness and still do not learn righteousness. That is why the verse acknowledges that some do not understand even when God acts. Then the song affirms that God will give peace to His own.

Today, if you see that those who mock God seem to get their way, do not become bitter or envy them. God sees everything and works in His own time. In the meantime, seek God steadily, as the passage says, and trust that He puts everything in its place.
exp.56:16:
He says that God was angry with his people because of their greed, that is, their desire to gain more and more by unjust means. For this reason he punished them and turned his face away from them, meaning he withdrew his nearness and his favor. The phrase about being angry with force means that he was angered intensely. Even so, the people remained rebellious, walking wherever their heart wanted to go.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Isaiah. Shortly before, he is presented as the High and Exalted One, but also as one who dwells near the humble and the broken. Here he reminds them that his anger was a just correction, not an eternal rejection. In the next verse he announces that, although he saw their wicked ways, he will still heal them and comfort them.

For today: when you feel that God is correcting you, do not take it as abandonment. Examine honestly whether there is some craving or desire that is pulling you away from him, and return to him with humility. His discipline seeks to heal you, not to destroy you.
exp.42:14:
It says that the Lord presents himself with three titles: he is the "Holy One" of his people, the "Creator" of Israel, and their "King." "Holy One" means unique, set apart, perfect. "Creator" is an older way of saying "Creator" (the word "creator" as it appears in the verse). It is God affirming who he is and what place he holds with his people.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were about to be taken to Babylon, and God promises to act on their behalf and defeat their enemies. Before and after this verse he reminds them that no one can stop his hand, and that he has already made paths through the sea, as in the Exodus. With these titles he strengthens Israel's confidence.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember who your God is. Before asking him for something, take a moment to declare who he is: holy, Creator, and King. That affirms your trust.
exp.5:3:
This verse describes what happened when the seraphim proclaimed the holiness of God. The posts of the door, the frames on which the doors turn, shook at the force of that voice. The phrase about the house being filled with smoke means that the temple was filled with smoke.

Isaiah recounts a vision he had in the temple, when he saw the Lord seated on his throne. The seraphim, who are heavenly beings, sang that God is holy. Smoke often calls to mind the presence of God, although the passage does not explain this in detail. This scene leads Isaiah to feel himself a sinner and to be purified, and then to be sent out.

When one takes the holiness of God seriously, prayer stops being routine. Today we can draw near with reverence and humility, acknowledging our faults, and trust that God forgives and equips us to serve him.
exp.44:8:
It says that woe is coming to the one who argues with God, his Maker. A "potsherd" is a broken piece of a clay vessel. In this way, the person is like one broken piece of clay among many others on the earth. The clay has no right to ask the potter, "What are you making?" Nor can the vessel say, "He has no hands," meaning that the potter does not know what he is doing.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is announcing that he will use Cyrus, a foreign king, to free his people from exile. Some Israelites doubted or complained that God would act in this way. God reminds them that he is sovereign and that his plans have a purpose.

Today we can trust God even when we do not understand what he allows. We can bring our questions to him honestly, as the psalms do, but without accusing him of not knowing what he is doing. His hand is wise and loving.
exp.33:16:
God himself divided the land among the birds and wild animals, like one who casts lots and measures out ground with a measuring line. That land will belong to them forever, and they will live there from generation to generation.

Isaiah speaks of God's judgment against Edom, which had been left desolate. Where people once lived, desert creatures would now dwell. The prophet invites readers to examine the book of the LORD to confirm that everything happens just as God said. Some interpreters see in Edom a symbol of all the nations that oppose God.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. We can trust that everything he says comes to pass, and for that reason it is worthwhile to read his Word with seriousness and faith.
exp.27:21:
Now therefore, do not keep mocking, or your chains will grow tighter. He says that they should stop mocking God and his warning, so that their bonds will not be made stronger. The bonds are the chains of punishment that were already threatening them. Complete and determined destruction is what the phrase about consummation and end means. The prophet states that he heard this directly from the Lord, the LORD of hosts, that is, the God of the armies of heaven.

Isaiah speaks to the rulers of Jerusalem, who were mocking his warnings and trusting in political alliances to protect themselves. The preceding text recalls God's past victories at Perazim and Gibeon, but now his strange work would be to act against his own people. Scholars debate historical details, but the message is clear: mockery would not save them.

For today: when the Bible or our conscience corrects us, let us not take it as a joke. Let us listen with humility and change in time, because God corrects in order to rescue.
exp.16:10:
He says that someone plants with great care and sees that their plants grow quickly, even sprouting in the morning. But when the day of the harvest comes, everything is lost. Instead of joy, there remains a sorrow with no remedy, a grief that cannot be healed. The seed is what is planted, and gathering in the crop is the harvest.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom, Israel, together with its ally Damascus. He rebukes them for having forgotten God, their salvation and their rock. They looked for security in alliances and in strange and beautiful plants, and this probably refers to practices or supports foreign to God. Some interpreters see idolatry in this; others see political strategies.

We can work hard and see quick results, but if we leave God out, nothing endures. Today you might ask yourself: on what do I base my security? Before making plans, pray and place your projects in his hands.
exp.7:14:
It says that many among the people will stumble, fall, and be broken. They will also be snared, like an animal in a trap, and be taken captive.

Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God showed him. Judah and Israel were threatened by foreign powers and looked for safety in human alliances instead of in God. The verse before says that God would be a sanctuary for those who trust in him, but a stone of stumbling for those who ignore him. Scholars agree that this is a warning of judgment; the exact historical details are explained in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust most when we are afraid: in money, in people, or in God? Take a moment to bring your worry to God and to give him first place in your heart.
exp.36:15:
Here King Hezekiah begins his prayer by calling God "Lord of hosts," that is, the Lord who commands all the powers of heaven and earth. "Thou that dwellest between the cherubims" refers to God's presence above the ark of the covenant, where there were figures of cherubim (angelic beings). Hezekiah declares that the Lord alone is God over all the kingdoms and that He made the heavens and the earth.

Hezekiah speaks in the temple, after receiving a threatening letter from Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who mocked God and wanted Jerusalem to surrender. The king does not respond with fear or with pride, but spreads the letter out before God and prays.

When you face a threat or a piece of news that troubles you, before doing anything else, bring it to God. Remind Him, and remind yourself, who He is: the Creator, greater than any problem.
exp.64:19:
In the renewed Jerusalem, it says, there will no longer be babies who die after only a few days, nor old people who die without having lived a full life. Dying at a hundred years old will be seen as dying young. And the sinner who reaches a hundred years will suffer the curse, that is, the consequences of his sin.

God speaks through Isaiah. He promises his people new heavens and a new earth, where weeping and crying will come to an end. Christians understand this in different ways: some see it as a picture of eternity, and others as a stage before it. All agree that God will restore life and justice.

For today: when death or pain weighs on you, trust that God promises to restore everything. In the meantime, care for the lives of others and live with integrity.
exp.11:3:
This verse calls for praising God out loud. The commands to sing and to shout for joy are calls to celebrate with gladness. To make his deeds known among the peoples means to make known among the nations what God has done. His name is exalted means that his name is lifted up, or made very high. The word for salvation in the previous verse means deliverance.

Isaiah 12 is a short song of thanksgiving. It announces what God's people will say in that day, that is, when God restores them after his judgment and comfort, as Isaiah describes in chapter 11. Scholars connect it with the restoration of Israel and, for many Christians, also with the work of Christ. Here the people, now saved, encourage others to praise.

For today: when God helps you with something, do not keep it to yourself. Tell a friend or family member, or share it in your church, so that others also come to know his goodness.
exp.12:3:
It says that a great noise is heard in the mountains, like that of a huge crowd. It is the sound of kingdoms and nations coming together. Here "noise" means a loud roar, not a quiet whisper. "The Lord of hosts" is the Lord in command of all the forces, and it is he who organizes and prepares the armies for battle.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon. God himself speaks in the verses nearby and calls his "consecrated ones," that is, those he has set apart for this task. Scholars understand this to refer to armies that God would use to judge Babylon's pride and violence. Some also see here an image of the final judgment of the whole earth.

For today: even when the world seems like a chaos of nations and conflicts, God remains sovereign. You can rest in the fact that he governs history and is just, and live with humility and confidence.
exp.41:24:
He says that God poured out on Israel the heat of his anger and the violence of war. It was like a fire that surrounded them on every side, yet the people did not understand what was happening. It burned them, and still they did not take it to heart.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of the defeat and exile that Israel would suffer for having turned away from God. In the verses before, it is acknowledged that it was the Lord who allowed the plundering, because the people refused to walk in his ways or obey his law. Many understand this to refer to foreign invasions, such as that of Babylon, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when difficulties come, it is not enough simply to endure them; it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God what he wants to teach us. He corrects in order to restore, not to destroy.
exp.41:2:
It says that God's chosen servant will treat the weak with gentleness. A "bruised reed" is a reed already broken or split, and the "smoking flax" is a lamp wick that barely gives off smoke, with almost no flame. He does not crush the fragile person or snuff out the one who is about to give up. The phrase about bringing forth judgment in truth means he will carry out justice faithfully and surely.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He presents his chosen servant, upon whom he places his Spirit. Christians see Jesus here, and Matthew 12:18-21 quotes this passage in that sense. God shows that his justice comes with patience and kindness, not with shouting or violence.

For today: if you feel tired, wounded, or low in faith, God does not discard you. And when dealing with weak people, imitate him: correct with firmness when needed, but care for them without crushing them.
exp.40:24:
He says that God has stirred up a man from the north, and that he is coming. From where the sun rises, that is, from the east, this man will call on God's name. He will trample rulers as if they were mud, just as the potter treads the clay to shape it. "Trample" is the meaning of the word here.

God speaks, challenging the idols of the nations to declare the future, and they cannot. God shows that he alone directs history. Many understand this man to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who conquered Babylon and allowed the Jews to return. Others also see a broader announcement of God's plan. The text does not give the name here.

For today: God governs history, even when the powerful seem to have no limits. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your life and the world are not adrift. Trust him with your worries.
exp.56:14:
This verse says that God is great, eternal, and holy, and yet he lives near those who are crushed and humble. "High and lofty" speaks of his greatness. The phrase about inhabiting eternity means that he is not limited by time. Someone who is crushed is a person whose heart is wounded or brokenhearted. To revive means to give life and courage again.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he had condemned idolatry and trust in human helpers that the wind would carry away. Now he promises that whoever waits on him will receive the inheritance. Then he explains that he will not be angry forever, because the human being would faint before his discipline.

For today: if you feel tired, guilty, or hurt, do not think that God is far away. Come before him with humility and sincerity, and trust that he can give you new strength and hope.
exp.8:13:
He says that God will cut off from Israel, in one day, everyone: from the most important to the least important. The phrase for "head and tail" refers to those above and those below. The "branch and rush" are similar images: the high branch of the palm tree and the low reed of the marsh. That is, no one will be left outside the judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had already suffered attacks from enemies such as Syria and the Philistines, but they did not return to God or seek him. The following verse explains the image: the head is the elders, and the tail is the prophets who teach falsehood. Interpreters agree that it speaks of a broad and sudden judgment.

For today: when difficulties come, let us not ignore them or blame others. Let us ask ourselves humbly whether God is calling us to return to him, and let us respond by seeking him wholeheartedly and sincerely.
exp.23:5:
It says the earth suffers a curse that devours it, and that its inhabitants pay the consequences. "Desolate" means laid waste or left in ruins. "Burned" means consumed or reduced to very little. In the end, few people are left.

Isaiah speaks as a prophet of God in a passage that many call the apocalypse of Isaiah (chapters 24 to 27). It describes a judgment that reaches the whole earth. The previous verse gives the reason: the people broke the laws and the everlasting covenant, that is, God's eternal covenant. Scholars debate which covenant is meant: it could be Noah's, Moses', or the moral law in general.

For today: our decisions have consequences that go beyond ourselves. Today you can choose to be honest and just in small things, trusting that God cares for the earth and for those who obey him.
exp.47:13:
Gather together, all of you, and listen. God invites everyone to come together and hear. He asks, with a certain challenge: who among the idols or the nations was able to announce these things in advance? Then he declares that "the Lord loves him," someone whom he has chosen, and that this chosen one will carry out God's purpose against Babylon and the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). "His arm" means his power in action.

God himself is speaking, addressing Israel, which lived surrounded by idols and doubts. Many understand "the beloved" to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who would later defeat Babylon and set the people free. Some scholars debate the exact identity, but the central meaning is clear: only God knows and directs the future.

For today: when the future fills you with fear, remember that the God who announced everything in advance still governs history. Trust in him and rest.
exp.15:0:
It says that a lamb, that is, a tribute or gift, should be sent to the ruler of the land. "Ruler" is the word in the verse that translates the old term meaning one who governs or holds authority. The sending goes from Sela, "the rock of the wilderness," to Jerusalem, "the mount of the daughter of Zion." Some believe the ruler is the king of Judah; others hold that it refers to the Messiah who is to come.

Isaiah prophesies against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. Moab lies in ruin, and its women flee like frightened birds. Moab is advised to seek refuge and help in Judah, sending the tribute it once gave. Scholars debate the exact historical details.

For today: when everything falls apart, let us not rely only on our own strength or our pride. Humbly seeking the help of God and of his people is wisdom. Asking for help in time is not weakness; it is a step toward hope.
exp.39:8:
This verse calls a bearer of good news to go up onto a high mountain and cry out without fear. Her message is for Zion, Jerusalem, and all the cities of Judah: "Behold your God!" The word "bringest" in the verse means the one who brings and proclaims the news. "Lift it up" refers to the voice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who are weary and discouraged, probably in or near the time of exile. Earlier he said that all human things are fragile like grass, but that the word of God endures. Now that God comes with power, and also as a tender shepherd who carries his lambs. Some scholars see Jerusalem herself as the messenger; others see a group of messengers.

For today: do not keep quiet the hope you have received. With humility and without fear, encourage someone who is tired, reminding them that God is strong and also cares with tenderness.
exp.50:1:
God tells his people to look back, to Abraham and to Sarah, from whom all of them descend. The old form of "a" is sometimes spelled differently in older texts, but that is not something your reader will see in this verse. Where the verse says "parió," it means that Sarah was the one who gave birth to them as a nation: she bore them. God reminds them that Abraham was alone when he called him, and yet he blessed him and gave him many descendants.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israelites who are discouraged, probably in times of exile or great weakness. They are few and feel forsaken. God reminds them that their beginning was humble: one man alone and a woman without children. If God could do that then, he can fulfill the promises of comfort that still follow.

For today: when you feel small or alone, remember that God often begins with little. Trust that he can make grow what seems weak, and take the next step of obedience.
exp.45:5:
Some people, the verse says, take gold out of their bag or purse and weigh silver on scales. With that money they pay a goldsmith, a craftsman who works metals, to make them a god. Then they bow down before what they had made themselves and worship it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he presents himself as the God who made, carries, and sustains his people into old age. He then compares that faithfulness with the idols of Babylon, which have to be carried on people's shoulders, do not move, and do not answer. God wants his people to come to their senses.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we are putting in God's place, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Everything we make ourselves and then expect to save us falls short. Today we can once again trust the God who sustains us.
exp.65:17:
God says that he knows very well what people do and what they think in their hearts. For this reason he announces that the time will come to gather all nations and tongues. They will come and see his glory, that is, his presence and his shining power. "I know" here means that God knows thoroughly.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah, at the close of the book. He has just said that he will judge those who practice a false and mixed religion, even though they appear to be holy. Then he shows that his plan goes beyond Israel: he will send survivors to distant peoples who never heard of him, to proclaim his glory. Interpreters disagree on the details of how this is fulfilled.

Today we can remember that God looks at the heart, not only at appearances. And we can share with love what we know of him, because he desires that all peoples come to know him.
exp.65:1:
God says that He Himself made everything that exists, the heavens and the earth, and that nothing is lacking to Him. Therefore, the one He looks upon with favor is the person who is poor and humble in spirit, who trembles at His word. Trembling here does not speak of a fear that runs away, but of a deep reverence that takes seriously what God says. Looking here means paying careful attention with kindness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were very interested in the temple and the sacrifices, but their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow show that their offerings, without obedience, were offensive to Him. God does not seek buildings to dwell in, but hearts willing to listen to Him.

For today: before fulfilling religious duties, open the Bible with humility and ask yourself, "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Then obey what you understand.
exp.6:13:
It says that God himself will give a sign: a virgin will conceive, have a son, and name him Immanuel, which means "God with us." The verb "will bear" means "will give birth." The Hebrew word for "virgin" can also be translated "young woman," and that is why there are different views about its original meaning.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz, of the house of David. Judah was threatened by two enemy kings, and Ahaz, instead of trusting God, refused to ask for a sign, pretending to be humble. Then God gives one anyway. The child would be a sign that those two kings would soon fall. Christians also see in this passage a greater fulfillment in Jesus, as Matthew 1:22-23 says.

When you are afraid, remember that God is with you. Trust his promise instead of looking for ways out on your own.
exp.35:18:
Here the spokesman of the king of Assyria mocks and asks where the gods of Hamath, Arphad and Sepharvaim are, and whether the gods of Samaria were able to save it.

Speaking is Rabshakeh, envoy of King Sennacherib, before the walls of Jerusalem, in the days of King Hezekiah. He wants the people to lose hope and surrender. He places the LORD on the same list as the idols of other nations, as if He were no different. The Assyrians had indeed conquered those cities, but Rabshakeh overlooks that idols are human handiwork, while the LORD is the living God.

For today: when voices of fear or mockery compare God to anything else, do not become anxious or argue endlessly. Keep silent as the people did, and seek God in prayer, trusting that He is different and faithful.
exp.23:6:
It says that the new wine has spoiled, that the vine has dried up, and that those who once lived with joy now grieve. Where the wording reads as it does here, the verse itself speaks of the wine mourning and the vine languishing, and the sense is the same: a plant that weakens and no longer bears fruit. The wine and the vine were common symbols of joy and celebration.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the earth. In the verses before, he explains the cause: the people broke the laws, twisted justice, and broke the everlasting covenant. Some understand this covenant as the one made with Noah, others as the law given to Israel. Scholars interpret it in different ways. Here the sorrow is the result of sin.

For today: let us not look for joy only in things that can come to an end, such as festivities, money, or success. Living justly and faithfully before God gives a joy that is more firm.
exp.32:2:
It says that when God acts with power, there is a great noise or uproar, and the peoples flee in fear. "Lifting up of thyself" means that God rises up to act, and then the nations are scattered.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. He has just pronounced a "woe" against a cruel and treacherous plunderer, and then he prays to God asking for help. Many think it refers to Assyria, but the text does not name it here, and some see it as a broader message. What is clear is that God does not leave violence and treachery unanswered.

For today: when you feel that evil or injustice seems stronger, pray as Isaiah did: "be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee." Trust that God will rise up in his time, and in the meantime, do not repay evil with evil.
exp.13:30:
God tells Philistia to cry out in grief. "Howl" means to cry out with weeping, and "gate" is the entrance of the city, where decisions were made. "Dissolved" means melted away by fear. "From the north" refers to the direction of the north, and from there comes "a smoke," probably an invading army. Scholars do not fully agree on this. No one will be left behind: all will be overtaken.

Isaiah delivers this message on behalf of God. The Philistines were celebrating the fall of a king who had struck them, but God warns them that something worse is coming. The following verse shows that, while they fall, God protects the afflicted of his people in Zion.

Today: do not place your security in a problem or an enemy disappearing, because another may come. Trust in God, who sustains the humble and offers firm refuge.
exp.6:18:
They say the enemy armies, compared to flies and bees, will come in force and occupy the whole land: even the empty valleys, the holes in the rocks, the thornbushes and the shrubs. No corner will be left free of them.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and did not trust God. He looked for help to Assyria. The prophet warns him that this same empire, which he wanted to use as a protector, would bring very hard days upon Judah. Egypt also appears in the picture, and many scholars see there the clash of great powers in the region.

For today: when you are afraid, do not place your security in human solutions that seem easy but leave God out. Before deciding, pray and seek his guidance. Trusting in him is safer than leaning on what may later turn against you.
exp.57:0:
God tells the prophet to speak loudly and without fear. The phrase "Cry aloud" means to shout with all your strength. "Spare not" means not to hold back or pull away. The voice should sound like a trumpet, which wakes people up and warns them of danger. The message is clear: to show the people their rebellion and their sin.

Here God speaks to the prophet Isaiah. The people seemed very religious: they sought God every day and fasted. But, according to the verses that follow, their lives did not match their practice. God confronts them because their religion was only on the outside. Scholars debate the exact date, but the message is directed to Israel.

Today, it is worth asking ourselves honestly whether our faith shows in our daily life. And if we speak to others about their mistakes, let us do it with truth and with love, seeking that they return to God.
exp.48:13:
Here the text says that Zion, that is, the people of God in Jerusalem, complains and thinks that God has abandoned her. The phrase "hath forsaken me" means "has forsaken me," and "my Lord hath forgotten me" expresses the pain of feeling forgotten. It is not a fact, but what she feels.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of exile, when Israel was suffering far from its land. Just before, God promises comfort and the return of people from far away. But Zion says that God has forgotten her. Immediately God answers with the image of a mother who does not forget her nursing child, and says that even if she could, He will not forget His people.

For today: when you feel forgotten by God, do not keep that pain silent. Bring it to Him honestly, as Zion did, and rest on what He has promised, not only on what you feel.
exp.39:27:
Doesn't this verse ask whether we have not known or heard that the Lord is the everlasting God? He is the one who created the ends of the earth. He never grows tired or weary, and no one can fully grasp his wisdom.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, also called Jacob, who felt forgotten and thought God did not see their suffering. So the prophet reminds them who God is: the Creator who calls the stars by name. Then he promises that he gives strength to the weary.

For today: when you feel exhausted or believe God does not see your situation, remember that he does not grow tired or forget you. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that his wisdom is greater than what you are able to understand.
exp.24:5:
God, the Lord of hosts, will prepare on his mountain a great feast for all peoples. The old wording describes the finest food: the "fattened" things are choice meats, the "rich marrow" is the most nourishing and substantial food, and the "refined wines" are aged wine, well strained and clear. It is a picture of abundance and joy.

Isaiah speaks in a song of praise to God, who protected the poor and humbled the proud. After that judgment, God invites all nations, not only Israel. Many understand "this mountain" as Zion, Jerusalem. The passage that follows speaks of God taking away death and tears.

For today: when you feel weary or in need, remember that God is preparing for you a future of abundance and comfort. In the meantime, share your table with someone who needs it.
exp.22:6:
Isaiah asks Tyre: "Is this the city that once rejoiced, so ancient?" Now its own feet will carry it far away, like someone exiled or made a refugee. "Wandering afar" here means going through foreign lands, not a religious pilgrimage. The phrase about ancient days speaks of a city with a long history.

Isaiah prophesies in God's name against Tyre, a great trading city on the Phoenician coast. Its fall is announced with astonishment: even Egypt will grieve at the news. The following verses say that God decreed this to humble the pride of those who thought themselves glorious. Scholars debate exactly how and when it was fulfilled.

For today: wealth, reputation, or years of success are not a secure foundation. We can thank God for what He gives us, but without placing our trust in it. Let us put our security in Him, who endures when everything else changes.
exp.59:17:
It says that in the land of Israel there will no longer be violence, ruin, or destruction within its borders. The source's explanation of a word for serious damage and the word for territory's limits must be rewritten: "Ruin" in the verse's sense means serious harm, and "borders" are the limits of the land. The walls will be called Salvation (safety, protection) and the gates Praise. That is, security will come from God, and the people will respond with gratitude.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who had suffered wars and exile. He promises them restoration: peace instead of oppression, and Himself as light and Savior. Some understand this as the restoration after the exile; others see it as a hope looking toward God's final kingdom.

For today: when you live with fear or wounds, remember that true security comes from God. You can "name" your walls: instead of repeating your fears, give thanks today for a concrete protection you have received.
exp.32:8:
The earth mourns and grows weak. Lebanon, famous for its cedars, is put to shame and cut down. Sharon, a fertile plain, looks like a wilderness. Bashan and Carmel, known for their pastures and trees, are shaken, that is, left without leaves.

Isaiah speaks in a time of threat from Assyria. The treaties were broken, the roads stood empty, and even the messengers of peace were weeping. Many understand that the land reflects the consequences of violence and of trusting in human alliances. Interpreters explain it in several ways, but the picture is clear: without God, everything withers.

For today: when everything around you seems to be drying up, do not place your security in human promises. Bring your anxiety to God, who remains the Lord, and listen to his voice.
exp.39:13:
No one gave God counsel or taught him how to decide well. The questions are rhetorical: the answer is "no one." To "be advised" means to be instructed or to become wise. "Judgment" is the right way of deciding, "knowledge" is understanding, and "prudence" is wisdom for acting well.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, who were living, or were about to live, in exile and felt that God did not see their situation. After announcing comfort, the prophet shows the greatness of God: he measured the waters and weighed the mountains. If God is so wise and powerful, his people can trust him, even when they do not understand everything.

Today, when something does not make sense, avoid judging God by your limited sight. Bring your anguish to him honestly and rest in the knowledge that his wisdom is perfect, even though you cannot yet see the way ahead.
exp.48:2:
He says that God speaks to his servant and calls him "Israel." He assures him that God will be honored through him. The verse as it reads in your Bible says, "Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified," so the phrase "in whom I will be glorified" means that God will show his glory, or be glorified, in this person.

The one speaking is the servant, who tells how God called him from before he was born. Here there is a detail that is interpreted in several ways: some see in this servant the people of Israel; others, a faithful figure within Israel; and many Christians see Jesus, who fulfills what Israel did not accomplish. The next verse shows weariness, but also trust in God.

For today: even if you feel tired or think your effort is not worth it, your worth does not depend on results. God has called you, knows you, and can be glorified in your life. Rest in Him.
exp.47:15:
He says, "Come near to me and listen. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time it happened, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and also his Spirit." The phrase "come near" is the same as "come ye near unto me," and "listen" is the same as "hear ye this."

The context is that God calls Israel, who is in exile and tempted to trust in idols, to remember that he announced ahead of time what he would do, even against Babylon. Who speaks at the end of the verse is a matter of debate: some see the prophet Isaiah, others the Servant of the Lord, and many Christians see here a shadow of the Messiah. The mention of the Lord God and his Spirit alongside the one who is sent is remarkable, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God does not act in secret or leave us in the dark. Come near to him, read his Word, and trust that his promises will be fulfilled in his time.
exp.51:10:
This verse is an urgent call to leave a place and separate oneself from what is unclean. "Depart" means to go away. "Unclean" means impure or contaminated. Those who carry "the vessels of the Lord" are the ones who bear the sacred objects of the temple, and they are asked to make themselves clean.

God speaks through Isaiah to his people, who are in exile in Babylon. He has just announced comfort and redemption for Jerusalem. Now he invites them to return home. He promises that they will not leave in a hurry, because he will go before them. Many see here a reference to the temple objects that were to be returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:7-11).

For today: if God has redeemed us, he also calls us to live differently. Think of a habit or environment that pulls you away from him, and take one concrete step to leave it, trusting that he goes ahead of you.
exp.48:23:
This verse asks two questions that seem to have an obvious answer: can the plunder be taken from a strong man? Can a prisoner escape who was taken lawfully? The word "prey" refers to what a warrior has captured. "Lawful captivity" sounds like those taken in a righteous war. Some older translations read "the captive of the righteous," and scholars explain that difference in the texts.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, who in exile felt abandoned and without a way out. The question expresses the people's doubt: it seemed impossible that Babylon would let its captives go. The following verses give the answer: God himself will deliver them.

For today: when a situation seems impossible to change, do not measure the problem by its strength, but measure God by his power. Bring him your doubt honestly, and trust that he is able to set you free.
exp.0:24:
God says that he will turn his hand against Jerusalem to purify it, as one does with metal. The impurities left behind when silver is melted down are the dross, and tin is a less valuable metal mixed in with it. "Purely purge away" is understood to mean "take away all thy tin," that is, with great thoroughness, depending on the translation used. God promises to remove what contaminates.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he denounced the leaders of Judah for accepting bribes and not defending the fatherless or the widow. His hand here is correction, not only punishment, since the following verse promises to restore righteous judges and a faithful city.

For today: God corrects because he wants to heal, not to destroy. We can ask him to show us what dross is in our hearts, such as selfishness or injustice, and accept his correction with trust, seeking to help those who most need it.
exp.44:23:
This verse says that the day will come when people will recognize that true righteousness and strength are found only in the Lord. The phrase "shall one say" in the King James wording means that people will say it about him. Those who are angry at God, who rebel against him, will end up ashamed, and those who come to him will find refuge.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel and all the nations. He has just invited all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved, and has sworn that every knee will bow before him. The verses that follow say that Israel will be justified in the Lord and will glory in him.

For today: instead of relying on your own strength or your own righteousness, come to God with humility. Tell him sincerely that in him are your strength and your hope.
exp.29:24:
It says that upon the lofty mountains and the high hills there will be rivers and streams of water. This will happen in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. A raised hill is a high ridge, and the towers may stand for strongholds or for human pride.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting God. He announces that God will judge the proud, but also that He will restore His people with abundant blessing. Scholars disagree about whether the day of the great slaughter refers to the fall of Assyria, to a future judgment, or to both. The text joins judgment and blessing in one moment.

For today: God can bring life where we least expect it, even in hard times. Trust in Him and not in your own towers, such as money, status, or human plans. He knows how to care for His people.
exp.6:3:
God tells Isaiah to say to King Ahaz that he should calm down and not be afraid. Be calm and keep still, and do not lose heart. The "smoking stumps of firebrands" are pieces of wood that are nearly burned out and no longer have fire. Rezin is the king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel, is the one who is pictured here. His anger looks terrible, but God sees it as weak smoke.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Judah was threatened because Syria and Israel (Ephraim) had joined forces against King Ahaz. He and his people were trembling like trees in the wind. God wants to reassure them and to have them trust in Him.

For today: When a problem seems enormous, remember that God is greater. Pray, breathe deeply, and trust in Him before acting out of fear.
exp.15:11:
It says that Moab will exhaust himself greatly at his high places, where he worshiped his gods, until he is worn out. Then he will go to his sanctuary to pray, but it will do him no good. The word "shall come to pass" means "will happen," and "when it is seen" means "when it is noticed," and "the high places" were places of worship on the hills.

Isaiah announces a judgment on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. The verses before this one show the ruin of its vineyards and the end of its joy. God himself says he feels grief for Moab, and the prophet compares this to a harp that sounds sad. Even so, Moab trusted in its gods, and that trust was empty. Afterward it is announced that the judgment would come within three years.

For today: intense religiousness does not replace a real relationship with God. Praying only when everything is falling apart, and without trusting the living God, does little good. Let us seek him now, with humility and sincerity.
exp.18:5:
This verse says that the rivers of Egypt will be turned far away, meaning their flow will drop until they are dry. The canals or channels that carried water will be emptied, and the plants along the banks, such as the reeds and flags (a plant similar to the rush), will be cut down or will wither.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God, the Lord of hosts, against Egypt. In that country everything depended on the Nile: food, work and trade. When the river dried up, God's judgment would strike the foundation of its security. Scholars debate exactly which historical events it refers to, and some also see a broader meaning.

For today: ask yourself what things you place your security in, such as money, employment or health. All of these can fail, but God remains. Trust Him first.
exp.22:13:
It says that the great ships of Tarshish must howl, that is, cry out loud in grief, because their strength has been destroyed. "Tarshish" was a distant place across the sea, and its ships were trading vessels. "Strength" here may refer to the harbor or safe refuge of Tyre, where they came.

It is part of Isaiah's prophecy against Tyre, a city rich from maritime trade. God speaks through the prophet and announces that this power will fall. The sailors of Tarshish mourn because they lose their great trading partner. Scholars debate where Tarshish was located, and some think of Spain, but this is not certain.

For today: our security should not rest on money, success, or business, for all of that can fall suddenly. Today you can hand your plans over to God and trust Him more than your resources.
exp.5:9:
He says God tells Isaiah to make the heart of this people fat, to make their ears heavy, and to shut their eyes, so that they do not see, do not hear, do not understand, do not turn back to God, and are not healed.

Isaiah has just seen God in the temple and offers himself as a messenger. God warns him that the people will not listen. Many understand that the passage describes how the people had already hardened themselves, and that God confirms that direction as judgment. Others stress that the language expresses the result of the mission. The text does not fully settle the question. Jesus quoted this passage when speaking of those who rejected his message.

For today: let us not assume that hearing the Word is enough. Let us ask God for a soft heart, and let us respond quickly when he speaks, before habit makes us indifferent.
exp.15:3:
It says that the outcasts of Israel (or of Judah) can take refuge in Moab, and that Moab should protect them from the spoiler. A hiding place is a place to hide; the one who tramples and oppresses is the oppressor; and the word for ending means that it will come to an end. The promise is that oppression will not last forever.

Isaiah announces judgment on Moab, and here he gives it a piece of advice: that it help the fugitives. Scholars disagree about who the spoiler is and who the outcasts are; they could be Jews fleeing an invader, or Moabites themselves. What can be seen is that it is followed by a promise of a throne of mercy in the house of David, and Moab's pride remains as an obstacle.

For today: God calls us to be a shelter for the one who flees or suffers. We can open the door, our time, or our help to someone vulnerable, trusting that God puts an end to all oppression.
exp.23:4:
The earth was defiled because of the people who live on it. Its being defiled means that it was made dirty and corrupted. The inhabitants disobeyed God's laws, twisted justice, and broke the everlasting covenant.

Isaiah the prophet announces what the LORD says will come upon the whole earth. This judgment is not a whim: it comes as a consequence of sin and injustice. Some think the everlasting covenant refers to the covenant with Noah; others, to God's law in general. It is not certain which it is.

Today we can take seriously that what we do has consequences. Let us ask God for help to be honest and just in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in our dealings with others.
exp.63:4:
He meets those who gladly do what is right, that is, those who remember you and walk in your ways. Then the people admit that God was angry because they had sinned. The phrase "in those is continuance, and we shall be saved" is hard to understand. It could mean that there is ongoing life and hope of salvation in God's ways, or it could mean that their sin lasted a long time and they still hope to be saved.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of repentance. They remember God's mighty works in the past and ask him to act again. They acknowledge that their spiritual condition is bad, as the following verses show.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God. Admit your sin honestly, remember how faithful he has been to you, and return to his ways, trusting that he gladly receives anyone who seeks him.
exp.39:6:
This verse compares people to the grass of the field. The grass dries up and the flower falls because the breath of the Lord blows on it. In other words, human life is fragile and fleeting, and God is in control. The words "surely the people is grass" confirm this: we are weak and temporary.

A voice asks the prophet to proclaim a message, and he asks what he should say. The answer is this: every human being is like grass, but the word of God endures forever. Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, and this contrast gives them comfort: what is human passes away, but God does what he says. Some scholars see the "wind" as a dry desert wind; others see it as the breath of God himself.

Today we can stop placing our security in success, fame, or our own strength, and rely on the Word of God, which does not fail and never ends.
exp.13:22:
It says God will turn Babylon into an abandoned place: a territory of hedgehogs (some translations say "birds of prey" or "porcupines") and of marshes or pools of water. It also says he will "sweep it with the broom of destruction," that is, he will clean it out completely, like someone taking the trash out of a house.

God himself speaks, "the Lord of hosts," within a prophecy of Isaiah against Babylon, the great power that oppressed other peoples. That judgment answers its pride and violence. The nearby passages also speak of the fall of Assyria, which shows that God governs over all empires.

For today: no human power is eternal, and God has the last word over injustice. If you suffer from abuse or feel small before the powerful, you can trust that God is just and keeps what he says. It is also a call to personal humility.
exp.28:18:
God says that, when he acts, humble and needy people will be filled with a joy that keeps growing. The phrase about joy increasing means their gladness will become greater and greater. The most needy among people are the ones meant here, and the Holy One of Israel is a title for God, the only one who is perfect and set apart from evil.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people with proud leaders and a religion that is only on the lips. First, the prophet announces a surprising change: the deaf will hear and the blind will see. Then he promises that the violent and the mockers will fall. Scholars debate whether all of this was fulfilled in Isaiah's own time, in Christ, or also in the future.

For today: if you feel small or lacking, you do not have to wait until everything is settled before you can rejoice. Today you can draw near to God with simplicity and look to Him for your joy.
exp.2:10:
It says that the one who lives in wickedness will have a bad end, because he will receive the payment for what he did. The word "wicked" refers to the person who lives without reverence for God. "Woe" is an expression of grief and warning. "For the reward of his hands" means according to his own deeds.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah and Jerusalem. The people had unjust leaders, and many sinned openly, without shame, as in Sodom. The verses around it contrast the wicked with the righteous, who will eat the fruit of their deeds. God appears as a judge who defends his people and calls to account those who deceive them.

Today it reminds us that our decisions have consequences. Before acting, ask yourself: "What am I sowing with this?" Ask God for help to sow honesty, justice and kindness, trusting that he sees everything.
exp.26:9:
It says that a city which seemed very strong will be destroyed and abandoned. Where there were once people, there will be a desolate place. The animals will graze there and feed on the branches that grow up.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Israel. The verses before this one speak of purging Jacob of idolatry. Commentators do not agree on which city is meant: it may be Jerusalem, Samaria, or an enemy city. What is clear is that judgment comes because of the people's lack of understanding and faith.

For today: there is no lasting security in what we build without God, whether money, reputation, or power. We can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and return to God with humility. He corrects, but He also desires to restore.
exp.27:24:
He says that the farmer, once he has leveled the ground, plants each seed with care. The fitches are a plant with aromatic seeds, similar to cumin. Each crop goes in its place: the wheat in rows, the barley in its marked spot, and the rye (or spelt, it is not known for certain) at its edge.

Isaiah speaks to the proud leaders of Israel and Judah who did not want to hear his warning. He uses the example of the field to show that the farmer does not act without order or without limit. The verses that follow say that God taught him. Thus, God also works with wisdom and measure when he corrects his people.

For today: trust that God knows what he is doing with you. If you go through a difficult time, it is not by chance or without limit. Ask him for wisdom and obey him with patience.
exp.35:8:
This verse says that the Assyrian commander mocks Judah. He asks how they could expect to defeat even one officer from the weakest group of the servants of the king of Assyria, since they are relying on Egypt for chariots and horsemen. "Captain" here refers to a governor or military leader. The phrase "turn away the face" means to drive back or to defeat. "Horsemen" are those who ride on horses.

Rabshakeh, a high spokesman for King Sennacherib of Assyria, speaks before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and Hezekiah, and so he tells them that Egypt will not save them. His words are war propaganda; he mixes truths, taunts, and half-truths, even when he speaks about God.

For today: when someone tells you that your situation has no way out, do not measure everything only by visible strength. Evaluate honestly, but place your trust in God, not in human resources or in voices that try to frighten you.
exp.9:29:
The verse is a cry of alarm. The people of that town, called here "daughter of Gallim," are told to raise their voices to give warning. The warning must be heard as far as Laish, and the prophet expresses pity for poor Anathoth, a village that lies on the enemy's path. The word "poor" here expresses pity.

Isaiah describes, in poetic tone, the march of the Assyrian army toward Jerusalem. He names northern villages one after another, which grow frightened as they see it advancing. These places were near Jerusalem, and the prophet thus announces the danger that was drawing close. Scholars are not sure whether it is a real march or a vision of the prophet, and the exact location of Gallim and Laish is debated.

When a threat arrives, one should not stay silent or pretend that everything is fine. Warning in time, praying, and asking others for help is an act of love and wisdom, and God cares for those who cry out to Him.
exp.49:4:
It says that God "opened his ear" to his servant, that is, gave him the ability to truly listen and obey. In response, the servant was not "rebellious" (he did not oppose God) and did not "turn away back" (he did not draw back or withdraw).

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, in the third Servant Song in Isaiah. Each morning he receives God's teaching so that he can sustain the weary. What follows shows that obeying cost him suffering: blows, mockery, and spitting. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus; others first connect it to the prophet or to Israel, and it can be read on more than one level.

For today: begin the day by listening to God before the rush of your schedule. Read a passage, be quiet, and ask him for a heart willing to obey, even when it costs you.
exp.39:11:
This verse asks questions to show the greatness of God. It asks who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, who set the heavens in order with the span of a hand, who gathered the dust of the earth in a measure, and who weighed the mountains in scales. The hills are the hills. The answer is: only God.

The prophet Isaiah comforts the people of Israel, who were discouraged and felt that God had forgotten them. Just before this, God appears as a tender shepherd who carries the lambs. Here the same God is presented as the enormous and powerful Creator, so that they may trust in Him.

For today: when your problems seem enormous, remember that the God who holds up the universe also cares for you with tenderness. Give that worry to Him today in prayer.
exp.58:10:
This verse says that the people groan in deep distress, like bears that roar and doves that mourn. They were hoping that God would set things right, but it did not come. "Judgment" here means justice, and "salvation" means deliverance or rescue. The word "far off" refers to something that stayed at a distance.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, joining himself to them with the word "we." He acknowledges that the injustice and darkness they live in come from their own sins, as the following verses say: lies, rebellion, and turning away from God. God had not lost his power; sin had created a barrier.

For today: when you feel that justice or help is slow in coming, examine your heart honestly. Confess what God shows you, and return to Him with confidence, for He receives whoever draws near with humility.
exp.30:7:
It says that Assyria, the great enemy power, will fall by a sword that is not wielded by a human warrior. The words for "knife" and "sword" in the verse mean the same thing. The word that means "will destroy her" is the verb used for what will happen to Assyria. The young men are the ones who will end up as tribute-payers, that is, forced to pay and to serve.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking military help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. He asks them to return to God and to set aside their idols. The text does not say precisely how Assyria will fall; many connect it with the defeat of Sennacherib at Jerusalem (Isaiah 37:36), although this is an interpretation.

For today: when a problem feels too big, do not place your security only in human resources or in things that take the place of God. Return to him sincerely, because he can act in ways we do not expect.
exp.4:25:
It says that God will raise up a signal, like a banner (a standard), to call nations who live very far away. He will also call them with a whistle, as one summons someone from the farthest corner of the earth. And those nations will come quickly, without delay.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, whom he earlier called his vineyard. The people rejected the Lord's law, and so God announces judgment. The verses that follow describe a strong and tireless army. From the context, many understand this to refer to Assyria, though some also see a broader warning. God is shown directing even the nations.

For today: let us not take God's word lightly. His correction seeks to wake us up, so when He speaks to us through His Word, let us respond promptly with humility and return to Him.
exp.59:11:
This verse says that any people or kingdom that refuses to serve Zion, that is, Jerusalem and God's restored people, will be destroyed. "Will perish" means it will come to an end, and "utterly wasted" means laid waste, left in ruins.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who had suffered punishment and exile. God promises to restore Jerusalem, and that nations will come to it. Many understand that serving Zion means recognizing God's work among his people. Some see this fulfilled in the return of Israel, and others in Christ and his kingdom. Not everyone interprets it the same way.

For today: no human power can stand firm by opposing God. We can rest in the knowledge that his justice and his mercy will prevail, and also live with humility, seeking to be on the side of his work rather than against it.
exp.35:2:
This verse says that three officials of King Hezekiah went out to meet the messenger from Assyria. Eliakim was the steward, that is, the one in charge of the palace. Shebna was the scribe, the secretary who kept the records. Joah was the recorder, an older term for the one who kept the annals or archives of the kingdom. The phrase "Came forth unto him" means that they went out to speak with Rabshakeh.

The account is told by the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had conquered many cities of Judah and now threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah sent these three men as his spokesmen, and immediately Rabshakeh uses them to intimidate the people and undermine their trust in God.

For today: when pressures come and voices try to discourage us, there is no need to respond with fear or to argue endlessly. We can act with calm and bring the situation to God, as Hezekiah later did.
exp.47:7:
God tells his people that these new things he had never heard of or understood before. Their ears were not open, meaning they had no readiness to listen. God already knew they would be disloyal, that is, unfaithful, and that they would disobey him. That is why he called them "rebels from the womb," a way of saying that this tendency went back to the very beginning of their history.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel. He announces new things so that they cannot say, "We already knew it," nor credit them to their idols. Even so, the next verse shows that God, for the sake of his name, holds back his anger and does not destroy them.

For today: humbly recognize that at times your heart resists God, and yet he does not reject you. Ask him for open ears to listen to him and obey him, trusting in his patience and his mercy.
exp.9:18:
It says that, after God's judgment, the trees left in Assyria's forest will be so few that even a child will be able to count them. Here "forest" is an image of a great army and a proud nation, not of real trees.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria had been used to discipline Judah, but it became arrogant. For this reason God announces that He will bring it down. Many understand that the forest refers to Assyria, although some also see a broader application. What follows shows the contrast: a small remnant of Israel will stop trusting the one who struck them and will trust in God.

For today: do not place your security in what seems large and strong, but in God. What impresses today can disappear soon; the Lord remains faithful to those who turn to Him.
exp.45:8:
Isaiah 46:9 tells the people to remember what God did long ago. The reason is clear: God alone is God, and no one is like him. The word "of old" here means ancient times, or from long ago. The phrase "none like me" means no one is similar to him or equal to him.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he mocks idols: they are objects that must be carried on people's shoulders, that do not move and do not answer. God calls the rebellious to think it over and return to him. Then he shows that he does announce the future and fulfills what he says.

For today: when you feel fear or doubt, call to mind the times God helped you, or your family. Write them down and thank him. Remembering his faithfulness helps you trust in him and not in things that promise security but cannot answer.
exp.7:18:
This verse warns that when someone tells you to seek answers from spirits or fortune-tellers, we should remember that God's people ought to seek their God. The "spirit-mediums" are people who claim to contact the dead, and their "mysterious whispering" describes the murmuring voices they use. The closing question means: does it make sense to seek the dead to guide the living?

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Judah lived in fear because of threats from other kingdoms, and many people sought answers through the occult. Isaiah had decided to wait on the LORD, even though God seemed silent. Then he directs the people to "the law and to the testimony," that is, to what God had already said.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, do not run after horoscopes, mediums, or mysterious voices. Pray, open the Bible, and wait on God, even when the answer takes a long time.
exp.5:0:
Isaiah tells us that, in the year King Uzziah died, he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, very high and exalted. Grand and exalted is what the word "high and lifted up" means. The lower edges of his robe are what the verse refers to when it speaks of his train, and the phrase about them filling the temple means that they covered the whole temple.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, remembering the moment when God called him. Uzziah had reigned for many years in Judah, and his death may have brought uncertainty. It is not known for certain whether the vision took place in the temple in Jerusalem or in a heavenly scene; it is interpreted both ways. What is clear is that, although a human king had died, the true King still sits on his throne.

When everything changes or someone you trusted is no longer there, remember that God still reigns. Ask him to give you peace and confidence, and praise him for who he is.
exp.37:14:
He says that Hezekiah cannot find words to describe what he is going through. He acknowledges that God himself was the one who spoke and the one who acted. Then he resolves to go softly, moving slowly and thinking with seriousness, remembering the bitterness of his soul all the years of his life. Some understand that he says this with humility, and others with a sense of solemn reverence.

The speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, after a serious illness. Isaiah had announced that he would die, but he prayed and God added years to his life. This song is his response of gratitude. His suffering has passed, but he does not want to forget what he learned.

For today: when God brings you out of a difficult trial, do not let it lie buried. Write down what you felt and what God did for you. Review that memory from time to time, so that your gratitude and your humility stay alive.
exp.58:3:
This verse says that among the people no one stands up to call for justice or to judge with honesty. They put their trust in empty things ("vanity" means something without worth or truth) and speak lies. "They conceive mischief, and bring forth iniquity" is an image of pregnancy: they plan evil and end up producing wickedness. The word "mischief" here means harm or trouble.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He explains that their sin, and not some supposed weakness of God, separates them from Him. He describes a corrupt society, with violence, lies and injustice in the courts. Then he compares their works to spider webs: they seem to be something, but they neither serve nor protect.

For today: before speaking or deciding, ask yourself whether what you say is true and whether it is just. Be encouraged to defend honestly the one who is treated unjustly, even when no one else does.
exp.43:4:
This verse describes several people who, one after another, identify themselves with God. One says plainly, "I am the Lord's." Another takes the name Jacob. Another writes "To the Lord" on his hand and takes the name Israel. "Take the name" means that he adopts that name as his own, and writing on the hand seems to be a way of marking oneself as belonging to the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will pour out his Spirit on the descendants of Israel, like water on dry ground. This comes at a time of discouragement for the people. As a result, many will openly declare themselves his.

For today: when God renews the heart, faith becomes something a person confesses without shame. We can ask him to fill us with his Spirit and dare to say, simply, at home and at work, "I am the Lord's."
exp.34:4:
This verse promises that God will heal. The blind will see and the deaf will hear. The word "Then" points to a future time, when God will act to save his people.

Isaiah speaks to a people who are tired and afraid. He asks them to strengthen those who are weak and to tell them not to fear, because God is coming to save them. The chapter uses images of a desert that blooms and of people being healed to describe that restoration. Christians see a partial fulfillment in the miracles of Jesus (Matthew 11:5), though many understand that the complete promise still awaits its fullness.

For today: if you are tired or afraid, remember that God does not forget you. Encourage someone who is weak with a word of hope or with concrete help, and trust that God is still at work and that one day he will restore everything.
exp.32:11:
This verse says that the enemy peoples of God will be utterly destroyed. The "burnings of lime" are limestone which, when burned, turns into white, brittle dust. The "thorns cut up" are dry branches thrown into the fire, which burn quickly. Both images speak of a total and swift end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah lived threatened by Assyria, and God promises to act against those who oppress and betray. The verses before it say that their plans are like straw: they produce nothing, and their own fire consumes them. The verses that follow call everyone, far and near, to acknowledge the power of God, and they also make the hypocrites in Zion tremble.

For today: do not trust in violence or in plans made without God, because they do not last. Ask Him to examine your heart, and live with sincerity before Him.
exp.31:5:
This verse says that the vile person, that is, the one who acts with wickedness and selfishness, speaks and thinks according to what is in his heart. He plans evil, lives without respect for God, and speaks with mockery against the Lord. Furthermore, he leaves the hungry person empty and denies water to the thirsty.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He announces a time when justice will reign, and so people will no longer be confused: the selfish person will not be called generous. This verse shows what the heart of the vile person is really like, and the next one contrasts it with the generous person.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our words and actions reflect a generous heart. One practical way is to help someone with a concrete need this week, such as food or companionship, without expecting anything in return.
exp.44:24:
This verse says that all the people of Israel, that is, their descendants, will be declared righteous and will have reason to rejoice and take pride, but not because of their own merits, but because of what God does. To be declared righteous means to be accepted as right before God. To rejoice and boast in him means to find joy and confident praise in him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just sworn that every knee will bow before him and that those who oppose him will be put to shame. This verse is the other side of that: those who turn to him receive righteousness and joy. Some see here a future fulfillment for Israel; others also see a promise open to all the nations, since the context invites "all the ends of the earth."

For today: do not look for your worth in what you achieve or in comparing yourself with others. Rest in the fact that God is the one who declares you righteous when you trust in him, and let that give you a quiet and humble joy.
exp.53:14:
If someone joins together in secret to harm God's people, the verse says, that evil does not come from God and does not have his approval. The verse's wording about this kind of joining together means plotting something harmful with others. Its other phrase, "not by me," means God is not behind such a plan. The text adds that whoever attacks this people will fall, that is, they will fail.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, pictured as a woman who was once barren and is now restored. After the exile, God promises her protection, peace, and justice.
