Some interpreters read this as a promise to Israel, and others also apply it to the church. But it does not promise that attacks will never come. It promises that they will not have the final word.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly criticized, do not respond with revenge. Pray, do what is right, and trust that God cares for you and is just.
exp.24:4:
He says that God subdues the pride of the powerful who oppose him, just as strong heat dries out parched ground. But then he compares it to heat softened by a cloud: in the same way, God makes the arrogance of the violent fade away. "Strangers" here means people who are foreign and hostile; "a shoot" is the bud or new growth; "the terrible ones" are the strong and the tyrants. Their strength withers like a plant.

Isaiah speaks in a song of praise to God. He celebrates that the Lord protects the poor and the needy, and that he restrains the oppressors. Scholars do not agree on which city or power the text refers to; it may be a specific enemy or a symbol of human pride in general. Then comes the promise of a feast for all peoples.

For today: there is no need to fear those who abuse their power. We can trust that God cares for the weak, and ask him to free us from our own pride too.
exp.1:8:
It says that the lowly man and the great man have bowed down and humbled themselves, but before idols. The phrase "have bowed" is the same as the word "bowed" in the verse. The final clause, "therefore forgive them not," is understood in several ways: as a statement that judgment will come, or as a question or plea from the prophet. The text is not entirely clear.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. The land was full of wealth, horses and idols, and they trusted in these more than in God. The verses that follow announce that God will bring low all pride and that he alone will be exalted.

Today we all bow down before something. Ask yourself honestly: what holds first place in my heart, money, success, or the opinion of others? Give that place to God, who alone is worthy of it.
exp.12:7:
This verse describes the fear of the people when the day of judgment comes. They will be filled with terror, and pain will seize them like a woman about to give birth. They will be stunned, speechless with amazement, looking at one another. Their faces will be flushed and burning with distress.

Isaiah prophesies about God's judgment against Babylon (Isaiah 13:1). He speaks on God's behalf and warns that the day of the Lord is drawing near. Some scholars also see in these words an announcement of the final judgment of the whole earth, because the language is very broad. Both readings are possible.

For today: let us not live as if God did not see injustice and pride. Today we can come to Him in humility, ask for forgiveness, and trust in Christ, so that we can await His justice with peace and not with dread.
exp.19:2:
Here God explains the meaning of something strange that Isaiah had been doing. For three years, the prophet went about stripped and barefoot, and this was a sign and warning, that is, a visible announcement of what would come upon Egypt and Ethiopia. The word for "stripped" probably means without the outer cloak, wearing only his inner garment, though this is not certain.

The Lord speaks, and his servant Isaiah obeys. Assyria had just conquered Ashdod, and some nations were thinking of seeking protection in Egypt and Ethiopia. God uses this act to warn that such hope would fail: Assyria would lead them away captive, in shame.

For today: trusting in what seems strong, such as money, power, or influence, can leave us disappointed. Ask yourself where you have placed your security, and give it over to God, who never fails.
exp.7:8:
The passage says that the enemy peoples may join together, arm themselves, and prepare for war, yet they will still be broken. The word repeated three times emphasizes that the outcome is certain.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of threat from Assyria against Judah. Shortly before, he had announced that Assyria would come like a flooding river, but now he turns his attention to the hostile nations. The name Immanuel means "God with us," and the following verse declares it: the plans against God's people will not succeed. Scholars debate exactly which peoples are meant, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel that troubles are gathering against you, remember that God is with you. Pray, trust, and take the next step without fear, knowing that his presence is greater than any threat.
exp.57:5:
God asks what kind of fasting truly pleases him. It is not only giving up food, but setting others free: loosening unjust chains, easing heavy burdens, giving freedom to the mistreated, and breaking every yoke. The "crushed" are the oppressed, and the "bundles of oppression" are burdens tied together with injustice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted with great devotion, yet still fought and mistreated others. He tells them their fasting had no value if their daily lives were unjust. He then adds that sharing bread and clothing the naked is also part of that fast.

Today, when we pray or fast, let us also ask ourselves whom we can help. We can pay a fair wage, forgive a debt, stand up for someone, or share food with those who need it.
exp.53:9:
God says that even the firmest things in nature, such as the mountains and the hills, could move or shake, but his mercy (his compassionate love) will not depart from his people. His "covenant of peace," that is, his promise of well-being and reconciliation, will not waver either. The Lord says this, the one who has mercy.

God, called the Redeemer, speaks to Jerusalem, described as an abandoned and beaten woman. She had gone through judgment and exile, and God acknowledges that he hid his face "for a moment." Now he comforts her and compares his promise to the one he made after Noah's flood: just as he swore not to destroy the earth with water again, he swears not to be angry with her like that again.

For today: when you feel that everything is being shaken, in your family, your health, or your work, remember that God's love does not depend on your circumstances. Rest in his promise and pray with confidence.
exp.18:4:
It says the water of the sea will fail, and the river will be drained and left dry. In this verse, "the sea" probably refers to the Nile River, which the Bible sometimes calls by that name because of its great size. It is an image of complete drought.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, in a message of judgment against Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile for its harvests, its food, and its economy. It also trusted in its idols, magicians, and fortune-tellers. God shows that none of these could save it. Scholars debate which exact historical event is meant, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work, or plans. All of these can dry up like a river. God, however, remains faithful, and we can trust in Him first.
exp.50:3:
God calls on his people to pay attention and listen to him. He tells them that the law will come forth from him, that is, his teaching and his guidance. He also says he will make known his judgment, that is, his righteousness, and that it will be a light for the peoples, a light for all the nations. The word "hearken" in the verse means to listen closely, and "make known" in the verse means to reveal or announce.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, a discouraged people in difficulties. He has just reminded them of Abraham, whom he called alone and then multiplied, and he promises them comfort for Zion. God assures them that his teaching and his righteousness will not remain only in Israel, but will reach other peoples. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, the light of the world.

When our spirits sink, let us turn again to listen carefully to God. His word not only comforts us; it also guides us and makes us a light for others.
exp.36:3:
This verse is part of the message that King Hezekiah sends to the prophet Isaiah. It says that perhaps the Lord your God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, the spokesman sent by the king of Assyria to mock the living God. The "remnant" is the part of the people who are still left alive, and to "reprove" here means to insult or defy. Hezekiah asks Isaiah to pray for them.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks through his servants. Jerusalem is threatened by the Assyrian army, and Rabshakeh has scorned the people's trust in God. Hezekiah, distressed and dressed in mourning, does not rely on his own strength but seeks the prophet's prayer. God answers with the words, "Fear not."

For today: when you feel powerless before a problem, do not face it alone. Pray to God sincerely and also ask for the prayers of people of faith. He hears those who trust in Him.
exp.65:23:
It says that the redeemed will go out and see the dead bodies of those who rebelled against God. Their worm will not die and their fire will not be put out, meaning their ruin does not come to an end. Words such as "abhorring" mean something that causes horror or disgust, and "all flesh" refers to all of humanity.

The words are spoken by the LORD through the prophet Isaiah, as the book closes. Before this, he promises new heavens, a new earth, and worship from all the nations. This ending contrasts the faithful with the rebels. Interpreters disagree: some see it as a picture of the final judgment, others as a symbolic scene. Jesus used similar words in Mark 9:48 to warn about judgment.

For today: let us take God's warning seriously, but also his invitation. If there is rebellion in your heart, come to him in humility and trust in his forgiveness, while there is still time.
exp.10:15:
This verse promises that there will be a clear road for the rest of God's people who were left in Assyria, that is, those who survived and were scattered there. The word "remnant" refers to those who survived and remained. Their return will be compared to the departure of Israel from Egypt, when God brought them out of slavery.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking. In this chapter he announces the reign of the Messiah, a time of justice and peace. Then he says that God will gather his scattered people a second time. The dried-up rivers and seas recall the Red Sea. Some see here the return from exile, and others also see it fulfilled in future times; there are several interpretations.

For today: if you feel far away, exhausted, or without a way out, remember that God knows how to open paths where you cannot see them. Trust that he can guide you back and give you hope, even when your situation seems impossible.
exp.21:12:
This verse describes a feast. Instead of weeping and repenting, the people slaughter cattle and sheep, eat meat, drink wine, and say, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die." Slaying here means killing the animal by cutting its throat.

The Lord had called Jerusalem to weep and to dress in mourning, because the city was under threat. But the people chose to ignore the danger and did not turn their eyes to God, who governs all things. That is why God later says this sin would not be forgiven until they died. It is a very serious judgment, and scholars understand it as a hardness of heart without repentance.

For today: when a difficulty comes, let us not cover it with entertainment or distractions. Better to stop, pray, and return to God with humility, for He does listen to us and restore us.
exp.18:13:
It says God allowed the leaders of Egypt to become confused. "A spirit of dizziness" means a spirit of reeling, disorientation, or twisting. So their counselors made the whole country stagger in everything it undertook, like a drunken man who staggers and befouls himself in his own vomit.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf within a prophecy against Egypt. Pharaoh's counselors, like the princes of Zoan and Noph, prided themselves on their wisdom, but they could not understand what God had determined. Some believe this is a judgment on their pride; the text does not give an exact date.

Today we can remember that human wisdom, without God, can easily be lost. Before deciding something important, it is wise to pray, ask for humility, and seek sound counsel in God's Word.
exp.40:21:
Here God challenges the idols and those who worship them. He tells them to bring forward their evidence: to announce what is going to happen and to explain what took place from the beginning.

The Lord, the King of Jacob, speaks as in a courtroom. The nations and their gods of wood or metal are called to defend their case. The challenge is that a true god must know and direct history. Later, God himself will show that he does announce what is coming, and the idols fall silent.

For today: our trust can be placed in many things that promise security, such as money, success, or fashionable opinions. Ask yourself which of them can truly guide you through what is uncertain. Rest in the God who knows the beginning and the end.
exp.44:16:
Israel receives salvation from the Lord, and that salvation lasts forever. Here "salvation" does not mean being healthy, but being saved and rescued. The promise is that God's people will not live in shame for all time.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and the context sets this against those who make idols, who will indeed be confused and put to shame. Idols cannot save, but the God of Israel, though at times he may seem hidden, does save. Scholars differ on how this promise applies to Israel today; some see it fulfilled in Christ and his people, while others also see a future fulfillment for the nation.

For today: if you trust in God and not in what you build yourself, you can rest. He does not fail, and whoever takes refuge in him will not be ashamed.
exp.46:10:
It says that a disaster will come upon Babylon, and she will not know where it comes from. "Ruin" is a hard blow or collapse. "Remedy" is to fix or prevent. "Destruction" will come "suddenly," without warning. She will be unable to stop it or understand what is happening to her.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Babylon, pictured here as a proud woman who trusted in her wisdom, her diviners, and her astrology, and who said, "I am, and there is none else beside me." God announces that these things will not save her. Scholars often see here a judgment on Babylon for her arrogance and cruelty.

For today: do not place your security in your own intelligence, your plans, or your superstitions. Live with humility, trusting in God, who sees everything and sustains what we cannot control.
exp.63:6:
This verse says that almost no one truly seeks God with eagerness. The phrase about waking up to hold on to him means that no one makes an effort to take hold of him. That is why God "hid his face," that is, he seemed distant, and the people were "consumed," like a dry plant, under the weight of their own wrongdoing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people, in a prayer of repentance. Many understand that he looks toward the time of exile or later, when Israel felt God's distance. He confesses sin honestly, and then, in verse 8, he holds on to God as Father and potter.

For today: if you feel spiritual coldness, do not stay in complaint. Wake up, pray sincerely, and confess whatever is pulling you away. God is still a Father, and he receives those who return to him.
exp.2:18:
It says that the Lord will take away from the women of Jerusalem their adornments: the necklaces, the pendant earrings (hanging jewels), and the bracelets (wristbands). It is part of a long list of jewelry and accessories that the prophet mentions. Some of the Hebrew terms in this list are difficult, and the translations vary a little.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem, the daughters of Zion. The problem was not the jewelry itself, but the people's pride, luxury, and injustice (see Isaiah 3:16 and 3:14-15, where the poor are oppressed). God warns them that what they took pride in would disappear.

For today: ask yourself where you are placing your worth, in what you have or in God. And check whether your comfort goes hand in hand with indifference toward those in need.
exp.60:5:
This verse says that God's people will be recognized as priests of the Lord and servants of our God. "Servants" means those who serve; "you will eat the riches of the nations" means they will enjoy the goods of the nations; and "glory" here speaks of honor or splendor.

The one speaking is the anointed servant of the Lord (Isaiah 61:1), who brings good news to the afflicted. God promises to restore Israel after ruin and shame. Some see this as a promise for Israel; the New Testament also calls the Church a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). How the riches of the nations come about is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if God has called you to serve him, your daily life is a sacred service. Pray for others, serve with humility, and trust that God restores what seemed lost.
exp.57:6:
This verse says that the fasting which pleases God is shown in acts of kindness: sharing your food with someone who is hungry, welcoming into your home the poor who have no place to live, clothing the one who has no clothes, and not turning your back on your own flesh, that is, your relatives or anyone in need, who is of your very same human nature. Those who are wandering without direction or shelter are the ones described here.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people fasted with great outward religiosity, yet they continued to oppress others. God makes clear to them that he does not want only external rituals, but justice and compassion. Afterward he promises light, healing, and his closeness to those who live this way.

Today we can ask ourselves: who near me needs concrete help? It may be sharing a meal, giving away clothing in good condition, or supporting a family member. Praying and fasting are good, but God also calls us to love through deeds.
exp.42:1:
He says that God promises to accompany his people in the midst of trials. The waters, the rivers, and the fire represent dangers and difficult moments. The promise does not say that there will be no trials, but that God will be present and you will not be destroyed. The verse says the waters will not overflow you, meaning they will not cover you and drown you.

The LORD speaks to Israel, the people he created and redeemed. Before this, the people had suffered because of their disobedience, and for that reason he sent them into exile. God reminds them that they belong to him, that he called them by name and loves them. For this reason he says to them: "Do not be afraid." His companionship is based on that covenant relationship.

For today: when you face an illness, a loss, or a crisis, remember that you are not alone. Pray and rest in the presence of God, even if you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.23:9:
It says that the city is broken and destroyed. It is called "the city of confusion," that is, an empty city with no firm foundation, and it is also called "the city of chaos," as other versions translate it. The houses are shut up, with no one left to come in: there are no more visitors, no feasts, no life in the streets. It is a picture of fear and loneliness.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's judgment on the earth (chapters 24 to 27). Joy disappears because humanity broke its covenant with God (v. 5). It is not stated with certainty which city is meant; some think of a specific city, and others of a symbol of all human pride without God.

For today: what we build without God, whether success, pleasure or security, can end up empty. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your trust, and hand it over to God in prayer.
exp.33:2:
They say that the bodies of the dead will be thrown out, unburied, and that the stench of the corpses will rise up. The text also says that the mountains will be melted, that is, they will dissolve and their soil will be washed away, because of so much blood spilled.

The one speaking is God through the prophet Isaiah. He calls all the nations to listen, because God is angry with them and hands them over to judgment. It is poetic and very intense language. At the end of the chapter the judgment focuses on Edom, though some scholars see here also an image of the final judgment. Interpreters debate how much of this is historical and how much is symbolic.

For today: this text reminds us that God takes injustice seriously and that no one escapes giving an account to him. That should move us to live with humility, to seek his forgiveness, and to trust that he will do justice in the end.
exp.43:20:
God tells his people to remember what they have just heard: that he formed them and that they are his servant. "Jacob" and "Israel" are names for the same people. The phrase about not forgetting him is an invitation not to turn away from God. The old word meaning "and" and the phrase meaning "since" would be rendered today with the ordinary words "and" and "since."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he mocks the person who uses half of a log to warm himself and cook food, and with the other half makes an idol to worship. That deception leaves the person without understanding. In contrast, God reminds Israel who its Creator is. Next he promises to forgive its sins and redeem it.

For today: when something takes the place of God, such as money, success, or the opinion of others, stop and remember that he made you and does not forget you. Return to him with confidence, because he already offers forgiveness.
exp.0:7:
It says that Jerusalem, called "the daughter of Zion", was left very alone and fragile. It is like a hut that a watchman builds in a vineyard, or a shelter in a field of cucumbers: poor, temporary shelters that are abandoned after the harvest.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. He has just described the people as a body wounded from head to foot, and the land as devastated by invaders. Scholars debate which invasion is meant, but the point is clear: the people's rebellion brought painful consequences. Even so, the next verse speaks of a small remnant that God preserved.

For today: when you feel your life lies in ruins because of your own choices, do not hide the wound. Bring it honestly before God, because he preserves a remnant and can heal and restore.
exp.17:5:
It says that the bodies of those who were cut down will be left lying on the mountains, and the birds of prey and the wild animals will feed on them all year round. The words "summer upon them" and "winter upon them" mean that the birds and beasts will be there through the summer and the winter, that is, the whole time.

God speaks through Isaiah about a powerful nation beyond the rivers of Ethiopia (Cush). It is not known for certain which nation this was. God watches calmly, and just when everything seems to be ripening, he steps in and cuts off the branches. Judgment comes at the least expected moment. Afterward, a people will come to bring an offering to God in Zion.

For today: do not despair when the powerful seem to have no restraint. God watches calmly, has his own timing, and governs history. Trust in him and live righteously.
exp.30:2:
This verse says that the Egyptians are simply human beings, not God, and that their horses are flesh, not spirit. That is, they are strong in appearance, but limited. When the Lord stretches out his hand, both the one who helps (Egypt) and the one who is helped (Judah) will fall together. "They shall all fail together" means that they will all fail at the same time.

Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C., when Judah, threatened by Assyria, was seeking a military alliance with Egypt. The prophet warns them that trusting in chariots and horses, and not in the Holy One of Israel, is a mistake. The verses that follow show that God will indeed protect Jerusalem.

For today: it is good to use resources, plans, and human help, but let us not place our ultimate security in them. Before rushing to look for solutions, we can stop to pray and ask God to guide us.
exp.65:18:
God promises to set a sign among his people and to send some of those who survive to distant nations: Tarshish, Pul, Lud (known for their archers), Tubal, Javan, and the far-off coastlands. Those peoples had never heard of God or seen his glory. They will make his glory known among the nations. The word "Gentiles" in the verse simply means the nations.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah near the close of the book. First he warns those who practice a false and hidden religion, and then he announces that he will gather all the nations to see his glory. It is not known for certain what the "sign" was or who the survivors are; there are several interpretations. The exact locations of all these places are also uncertain.

God wants his glory to reach all peoples, even the most distant. We can take part by praying for missionaries, supporting them, and speaking of God with those around us, with humility and joy.
exp.36:20:
This verse says that Isaiah, the son of Amoz, sent a message to King Hezekiah. The prophet tells him that the Lord, the God of Israel, answers his prayer about Sennacherib, king of Assyria. The phrase "sent unto" means he sent word through messengers. "Hast prayed" means you asked or pleaded.

Hezekiah was in great distress. Assyria had conquered many cities and threatened Jerusalem. Sennacherib mocked God. Hezekiah brought his problem to the Lord in prayer, and now God responds through the prophet Isaiah. The one speaking in the message is God himself, and Isaiah only passes it on.

For today: God hears the sincere prayers of those who trust him. When you face a situation that is beyond you, bring it to God honestly and wait for his answer, even if it does not come in the way you had imagined.
exp.18:23:
It says that in a future time, Israel will join with Egypt and Assyria as a "third," that is, it will form with them a trio of nations living in peace. And Israel will be "a blessing in the midst of the land," meaning a source of blessing for the whole world. The word "third" does not speak of a place of rank, but of a union among equals.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks in a message about Egypt. First he announces judgment, but then he promises healing and conversion. Egypt and Assyria were powerful enemies of Israel, and yet God calls them "my people" and "the work of my hands." Scholars disagree about whether the fulfillment is still future, spiritual, or both.

For today: God loves peoples who seem like enemies to us and wants to reconcile them. Ask him to help you be someone who builds bridges and blesses those who think or live differently from you.
exp.7:0:
God told Isaiah to take a large tablet or scroll and write on it in ordinary script, "in the common way of a man's hand," that is, in plain writing that anyone could read. What he was to write was a name that is usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the prey."

The Lord spoke to his prophet in a time of threat to Judah, when neighboring kingdoms were pressing King Ahaz. According to the verses that follow, Isaiah calls witnesses, and then his son is born with that name. It was a public sign: the power that now frightens Judah would soon be taken away. Scholars debate some details, such as exactly who "the prophetess" is, but it is commonly understood to be Isaiah's wife.

For today: God keeps what he says, and so we can trust his word even when fear seems stronger. Write down God's promises and remember them when distress comes.
exp.56:6:
He says that the people set their bed on a high and lofty mountain, and that there they also went up to offer sacrifices. The bed is an image of the place where they gave themselves to other gods. "Lofty" means very steep and high.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Israel of being unfaithful, like a wife who leaves her husband. High mountains were places where idolatry was practiced. Many understand the bed as a symbol of spiritual adultery, not only of a literal act. Some details of the passage are debated, but the central message of unfaithfulness is clear.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we give the time, effort and heart that belong to God. God does not want divided loyalty. We can return to Him sincerely, knowing that He receives us with mercy.
exp.18:3:
He says that God himself will hand Egypt over into the power of a cruel master, and that a violent king will rule over them. "Cruel master" means a harsh ruler, without compassion. The phrase that describes this ruler's control means that he will govern them with force. All of this is affirmed by the Lord of hosts, that is, the God who has power over everything.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a message against Egypt. Before this, he announces divisions and confusion among the Egyptians, and that they will look for answers in idols and in fortune-tellers. It is not known with certainty which king he means; scholars have understood it in various ways, since the prophecy does not give a name.

For today: trusting in what is passing, such as power, money, or the occult, leaves us empty. Let us seek the guidance of God, who governs over all nations and is just.
exp.33:13:
It says the place will be left desolate and filled with wild animals. The "wild beasts of the desert" are animals of the desert, and the "wild cats" are untamed felines. The "satyr" is probably a male goat or a goat-like creature, and some understand it as a spirit of the desert. The "night creature" is a difficult word: some think of a nocturnal animal, others of a creature from legend, and the Hebrew Bible uses "Lilith." All of them find rest there.

The prophet Isaiah announces God's judgment against the nations, represented here by Edom. Its palaces, once full of power, will be abandoned. The message is that no human kingdom can defy God and remain standing.

For today: do not place your security in what the world calls great, such as money, power, or prestige. All of that can disappear. Trust in God, whose word endures, and seek first what lasts forever.
exp.1:1:
It says that in a future time ("the last days"), the mountain where God's temple stands will be firmly established and recognized as the most important, above all other mountains and hills. People from all the nations will come flowing toward it.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks to a people living under threats and spiritual failures. Before the warnings of judgment, God shows them a hope: one day Jerusalem will be a center of peace and teaching for everyone. Some understand this as the kingdom of Christ and the church; others as something future and literal. Christians have read it in both ways.

For today: when the world seems confused or violent, remember that God has a plan of peace. Draw near to Him with a desire to learn His ways and to live in them.
exp.3:2:
It says that, after God's judgment, the few who remain in Jerusalem will be called "holy." The phrase "written among the living" refers to people recorded in a register of the living, that is, those whom God kept alive. "Holy" means set apart for God.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces this after describing a harsh judgment on Jerusalem, with war and great loss of life (chapter 3). Then he promises a future of restoration. The "branch of the LORD" has been understood in several ways: as God's blessing on the land, or as a sign pointing to the Messiah. Interpreters do not fully agree. What is clear is that God purifies and leaves a faithful remnant.

For today: God does not stop at punishment, but cleanses his people so that they may live close to him. If you are going through correction today, trust that his aim is to restore you. Ask him to cleanse you and set you apart for himself.
exp.20:16:
It says that of the brave archers of Kedar only a few will be left, very few. The verse's "remnant" in the sense of what is left over. Some explanation about old wording: the word "diminished" in the verse means made smaller, reduced. And it is the Lord, the God of Israel, who declares it, so this is no mere guess.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, repeating what the Lord told him. Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert, known for its archers and descended from Ishmael. This message closes a prophecy about Arabia: people fleeing from war. God announces that within a year their glory will come to an end. The Bible does not detail here which army defeats them; some think of Assyrian invasions, but this is not certain.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, is final. If you today trust in your strength, your money or your reputation, remember that God has the last word. Rest better in Him.
exp.56:9:
They wore themselves out going down many wrong roads, yet they never admitted that all of it was useless. Saying "there is no hope" would have meant recognizing the hopelessness of those roads. Instead, they found strength in their own hand, meaning they found the strength to keep searching on their own, and for that reason they did not repent or return to God.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, whom he describes as an unfaithful wife who seeks alliances and idols. Scholars debate whether this refers mainly to idolatry, to political alliances with other nations, or to both. God shows them that their stubbornness kept them from seeing their error.

For today: sometimes we grow weary seeking security in work, money, or people, and we tell ourselves, "one more effort." Today you can stop, admit that this does not save you, and return to God with humility.
exp.59:21:
This verse says that the smallest and weakest will grow to be enormous: the little one will become a thousand, and the least, a strong nation. God promises that he will do it "in his time," that is, at the moment he has chosen. The phrase "in his time" is the verse's own wording, so it stays as it is in the reader's version; no separate word needs explaining.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem and its people. Earlier he spoke to them of mourning and ruin, and now he promises light, justice, and restoration. Interpreters read it in different ways: some apply it to Israel's return from exile, others to the Church, and others to a future fulfillment. In every case, the center is God's faithfulness.

For today: if you feel small or have little, do not despise your beginning. Remain faithful, and trust that God works on his own schedule, which is not always ours, and that he keeps what he promises.
exp.60:4:
It says that people from other nations, called "foreigners" and "strangers" here, will do the field work for Israel. They will tend the sheep and work the land and the vineyards. To "feed" the flocks means to lead the livestock out to graze on pasture, and the "plowmen" and "vinedressers" are those who cultivate the ground and the grapes.

The one speaking is the prophet, announcing God's message to a people who suffered destruction and exile. God promises comfort, restoration, and honor. The verses around it speak of ruined places being rebuilt and of a people called "priests of the LORD." Some see here the return of Israel; others see a wider promise that Christ fulfills (Luke 4:18-21 quotes the beginning of this chapter).

For today: when you feel ruined or without strength, remember that God knows how to restore what was lost and raise up those who have fallen. Trust in Him, and let His grace return hope to you.
exp.39:25:
Isaiah 40:26 tells us to lift up our eyes to the heavens and consider who created the stars. God brings out their whole host and calls each one by name; not one is missing.

The verse's wording for the star-host refers to the stars as a whole, and the phrase about God's great might and strength is rendered as "by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power."

Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who are discouraged and feel that God has forgotten their situation. Earlier in the chapter, the text showed that powerful rulers wither like plants before God. Then the people complain that their way is hidden from the Lord. This verse answers them: the God who knows every star also knows his people.

For today: when you feel forgotten or small, go outside at night, look at the sky, and remember that God sustains everything with care. If not one star is lost, neither is your life lost to him. Bring your worry to him today with confidence.
exp.9:23:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, speaks to his people who live in Zion, that is, Jerusalem. He asks them not to be afraid of Assyria. Although Assyria will strike them with a rod and lift up its staff against them, as the Egyptians did in the past, God does not want them to live paralyzed by fear. "Staff" and "rod" are instruments of punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah had lived in disobedience, and God allowed Assyria, a feared power, to be a rod of correction. But the following verse says that his anger will soon pass, and that God himself will judge Assyria. Thus, the punishment has a limit, and God still calls them "my people."

For today: when you face a trial or correction, do not see it as abandonment. God remains your Father and has control. Come to him with humility and trust, without letting fear dominate you.
exp.12:20:
This verse describes Babylon as an abandoned place, where no people live anymore but only wild animals. "Wild beasts of the desert" are animals of the wilderness; "doleful creatures" are probably animals that howl or cry out (the Hebrew term is uncertain); "owls" may be owls or ostriches; and "satyrs" refers to creatures that leap or dance, sometimes understood as desert spirits or simply wild goats.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, announcing judgment against Babylon, the proud power of its time. It is a warning that no empire, however great it may seem, stands above God. Interpreters debate when and how this was fulfilled: some see it in the city's gradual fall, others in a fulfillment that is still broader.

For today: do not place your security in what seems great and strong, such as money, power or prestige. Trust in God, who always endures.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that the strong man will be as fragile as tow, the flax or hemp fibers that burn very quickly. What that man made, his work, will be like a spark. Both will catch fire together, and no one will be able to put out the fire.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Judah. They practiced idolatry, worshiping under trees and in sacred gardens, and they lived with injustice. Many understand "the strong" as the leader or the rich man who trusted in his power; others see it as the people themselves or their idols. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not put your trust in your strength, your achievements, or anything made by human hands. All of that can burn up quickly. Seek God with humility and place your security in Him, for He alone endures.
exp.4:22:
It says that God laments those who accept money to declare the guilty person innocent, and to take away the rights of the honest person. "Bribes" are payoffs. To "justify" the wicked means to acquit them, and to "take away the righteousness" of the innocent is to deny them fair treatment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. In this chapter, after the song of the vineyard, he pronounces six woes against injustices. Here he points to corrupt judges who, along with the proud and the drunkards, no longer respect the Lord's law. For that reason he announces judgment.

For today: God cares about justice in small things and in great ones. We can refuse to give or take bribes, even when they are common "favors," and honestly defend someone who is treated unfairly at work, at school, or in the community.
exp.13:15:
They that see you will look closely at you and consider you with wonder, and they will ask: "Is this the man who made the earth tremble and shook kingdoms?" The phrase about bowing down means they will stare at him up close. The word about shaking means he stirred up and destroyed the order of the nations.

Isaiah announces a prophetic mockery against the king of Babylon (v. 4). His pride went so far as to say he would be like the Most High, but he ends up in the grave. Some see in these verses also a wider look at pride and its fall; others limit them to the historical king. The texts do not fully settle this.

For today: power and fame do not last, and God opposes the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and use whatever influence we have to serve and care for others, not to dominate them.
exp.34:0:
It says that the desert, the dry land and the empty place will be filled with joy. The "wilderness" is abandoned ground where nothing grows. It will bloom "like the rose"; some translators think the Hebrew word may refer to a different flower, perhaps the saffron or crocus, and this is not known with complete certainty.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah, after announcements of judgment in the earlier chapters. It is a promise of restoration: God will bring renewal, and his glory will be seen. The verses that follow encourage the weary and fearful to take heart, because God is coming to save.

For today: if you are going through a dry or exhausting season, do not think that God has forgotten you. You can wait on him with hope, and encourage someone who is tired with a kind word or a simple act of help.
exp.34:9:
This verse says that the ransomed of the Lord will return and enter Zion singing with happiness. A joy that never ends will crown them like a garland, and sorrow and mourning will run far away. The "ransomed" are those whom God has bought back or redeemed. The "sighing" is the weeping or complaint of pain; and the phrase "they shall obtain" means they will keep or reach that joy.

Isaiah, a prophet of the eighth century B.C., speaks to the people of Judah, who faced threats and later exile. This chapter describes the restoration in poetic images: the desert blossoms and God comes to save. Scholars understand this as a promise of return from captivity and also as an announcement of a still greater, final hope.

Today, when you are tired or sad, remember that God promises you an ending of joy, not of weeping. Walk with that hope, give thanks for what He has already given you, and help others trust that He will bring them home.
exp.50:6:
God calls the attention of those who "know righteousness," that is, those who know what is right and have his law written on their heart. He asks them not to be afraid of the reproach (the insult or humiliation) that comes from men, nor to lose heart because of their revilings, which are the insults and mockery.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a believing people who feel weak and surrounded by people who mock them. Before and after this, God reminds them that the world is passing, like clothing eaten by moths, but that his righteousness and his salvation last forever. For this reason they should not fear what is temporary.

If you are criticized or mocked for living your faith with honesty, remember that those words pass away, but what God says remains. Keep his Word in your heart and let it weigh more than the opinion of others.
exp.36:30:
This verse says that the people of Judah who survive will once again take root downward and bear fruit upward. It is an image of a plant: first it becomes firm beneath the soil, and afterward the fruit can be seen. The word "remnant" means those who are left, and "shall again" means will return.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. The army of Assyria, under King Sennacherib, had invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem. God promises to stop the invader and gives a sign: two years of eating what grows on its own, and in the third year, sowing and reaping as usual. It is a promise of restoration.

For today: when we go through a crisis, let us not expect quick results. God often heals what is hidden first, such as faith, prayer, and character, and in his time visible fruit comes. Let us cultivate those roots today.
exp.7:16:
Isaiah says that he will wait for the Lord and trust in him, even though God has hidden his face from the house of Jacob. The phrase "hide his face" means that God has withdrawn his favor and his visible help. To "wait" means to hope with patience and confidence.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. The people of Judah lived under the threat of enemies and, instead of trusting in God, many sought security in human alliances and in fortune-tellers. God had announced judgment, and Isaiah decides to remain faithful, keeping God's word with his disciples while others stumbled.

There are moments when we feel God is silent or distant. This verse invites us not to run after easy solutions or doubtful voices, but to keep trusting, praying, and obeying his Word while we wait. Faith does not always see, but it keeps waiting.
exp.16:1:
It says the cities of Aroer will be abandoned and will become grazing land for flocks. The sheep will lie down there, and no one will frighten them.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in an oracle, a message of judgment, against Damascus, the capital of Syria. Damascus had allied itself with Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel) against Judah. Aroer was probably in territory east of the Jordan, though it is not certain which Aroer is meant. The message announces that this alliance will collapse and that places once inhabited will be left empty.

Today we can remember that no human power or political alliance is safe forever. Trusting in God, and not in what appears strong, gives a peace that does not fall apart.
exp.21:23:
He says that all the weight of honor of his father's house will be hung on this man, as objects are hung on a firm nail in the wall. The "vessels" were household utensils: from the cups used for drinking up to the instruments used for music. That is, from him will depend everything from the most important relatives down to the smallest things.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He will replace Shebna, a proud administrator of the palace, with Eliakim, to whom He will give authority and the key of the house of David. The following verse makes clear that this "nail" will also fall: no man is an eternal support.

For today: if many depend on you, carry that responsibility with humility and do not think yourself indispensable. Only Christ, whom the New Testament connects with "the key of David" (Revelation 3:7), is a support that never fails.
exp.17:3:
This verse says that the Lord spoke to the prophet and told him that he would remain still, as if at rest, watching everything from his dwelling, that is, from his place in heaven. This calm is compared to clear sunshine after rain and to a cloud of dew in the heat of the day. "I will take my rest" means "I will stay calm and still."

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, who tells what God said to him. The chapter mentions a distant nation, which many believe is Cush (Ethiopia), though this is not certain. God does not act in a hurry; he observes calmly and waits for the right moment, which the following verses compare to pruning before the harvest.

For today: when it seems that God is slow or silent, this does not mean he is absent. He sees everything and works in the perfect time. You can rest and wait patiently, trusting that He is in control.
exp.59:13:
This verse says that the descendants of those who oppressed Jerusalem will come to her in humility. Those who once mocked her will bow down before her. The mockery is scornful ridicule, and the bowing means they will lower themselves in a sign of respect. Then they will call her "the city of the Lord" and "the Zion of the Holy One of Israel."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who had endured exile and contempt. He promises to restore Zion and to show that she belongs to him. Many believers see here a hope for Israel, and others also see an image of the Church. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

For today: if you have been hurt or looked down upon, do not carry the burden of revenge. Trust that God defends his own and knows how to restore your dignity in his time.
exp.6:23:
It says that people will have to enter that land armed with arrows and a bow, because the whole field will be covered with thorns and thistles. There will no longer be crops, only weeds, and the land will be dangerous or used for hunting.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid of his enemies, Syria and Israel. God promises that this threat will pass, but He also warns of judgment: the land will be left abandoned and uncultivated. Interpreters often see here the invasion of Assyria, although the details are explained in several ways.

For today: when we trust in our own securities instead of in God, what seemed fruitful can become weeds. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our trust, and return to God with humility, knowing that He cares for those who seek Him.
exp.61:10:
God has made an announcement that reaches to the farthest corners of the world. The message is for the daughter of Zion, that is, the people of Jerusalem: their Savior is coming. The reward and the work are understood as what God brings with him: the prize, the restoration, and the fruit of his labor on behalf of his people. Here, hearing means making known.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to a people who are returning from exile or waiting to be restored. The verses before this one call for preparing the way and raising a signal for the nations. What follows promises that they will be called a holy people and the redeemed of the Lord. Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, the Savior.

Today we can live with active hope: God is coming to rescue and to restore. Prepare your heart by removing a specific stone, such as a grudge or an excuse, and share a word of encouragement with someone.
exp.20:3:
Here the prophet says that his heart was troubled and that terror left him without strength. The "night of my pleasure" is a night he had looked forward to with gladness, perhaps for rest or celebration, but it was turned into dread for him.

Isaiah speaks here, having just seen a difficult vision about the fall of Babylon to the Persians and Medes. He does not celebrate the fall; he feels it in his body, with pain and anguish. The text refers to a night that was meant to be peaceful, and scholars connect it with the feast and the sudden fall of the city, though not all agree on the details. Soon after, God tells him to set a watchman.

For today: when God shows you a painful reality, do not harden yourself or ignore it. Feel its weight, and then remain alert and attentive to his voice.
exp.60:6:
This verse promises a complete reversal. Where there was shame and dishonor, there will be praise. The word "portion" in the verse refers to the share of land that falls to each person. The idea of "double" means twice as much. So God says the people will receive twice what they lost, and they will have joy that does not end.

The message comes from the prophet Isaiah, speaking on God's behalf to a humbled people, probably returning from exile. God promises to restore them and to make them his priests before the nations. Christians see here an announcement of the work of Jesus, who quoted the beginning of this chapter in Luke 4.

For today: if you carry shame over past mistakes or losses, do not stay there. Bring them to God in prayer and trust that he restores. His joy can replace what hurt you.
exp.35:4:
Rabshakeh, the messenger of the king of Assyria, tells Judah that talk of having a plan and strength for war is only "vain words," that is, empty talk with no real value. Then he asks: "on whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me?" He wants Judah to realize that they have no one to lean on.

The king's messenger is speaking before the walls of Jerusalem. Hezekiah's officials have come out to listen to him. His aim is to frighten the people and break their confidence so that they will surrender without a fight. He mixes half-truths with mockery, and he has not yet mentioned God, though he soon will.

For today: when the voices of fear question whom you trust, do not rely only on your own strength or on human plans. Examine honestly where your trust lies, and place it in God, who is faithful.
exp.40:4:
It says that the islands, that is, the distant peoples by the sea, saw what God was doing and were filled with fear. Even the most remote corners of the earth were frightened. Then they gathered together and drew near. The words "ends of the earth" mean the far edges or limits of the world.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that he raises up a conqueror, and many believe this is Cyrus, although the text does not give the name here. God affirms that he directs history. The nations react with fear, and what follows shows that they organize themselves and encourage one another to make idols, instead of seeking the living God.

Today, when the world is stirred up and people look for security in what they make or in mutual support, we can remember that God still governs. Instead of relying only on what is human, we can pray and trust him.
exp.29:4:
It says that the leaders of Judah will be ashamed for having trusted in a people who will not be able to help them. To be of use means to serve a purpose, and to be a shame means to bring disgrace or mockery. Egypt will give them no help or benefit, but just the opposite: humiliation.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was under the threat of Assyria, and its leaders sent envoys with gifts to Egypt, seeking a military alliance, without consulting the Lord. Isaiah warns them that this alliance will be useless. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities where the messengers arrived (the exact location of Hanes is debated).

For today: when you face a big problem, before rushing to your "resources from Egypt," whether money, connections, or plans, pray and seek God's direction. Human help can be useful, but it must not take the place of trust in Him.
exp.52:2:
He is said to be the Servant of the Lord, rejected and brought low by the people. He is a man of sorrows, one who came to know suffering up close. Grief here means deep pain. The phrase "we hid as it were our faces from him" means the people turned their eyes away, like someone avoiding a person who makes them uncomfortable. "Despised" means treated as having little worth.

Here a group speaks in the first person plural, "we," probably the people admitting their mistake. They recognize that they did not value the Servant, and in the verses that follow they understand that he was carrying their sins. Christians see in this a prophecy about Jesus; others have also read it as referring to Israel.

Today, do not turn your eyes away from the one who suffers, and do not judge by appearances. Jesus knows your pain and drew near to those who were hurting; seek to draw near to the wounded as well.
exp.13:9:
The verse says that the dead, that is, the ancient kings who are already in the grave, will all speak together to the king who arrives. They will ask him in astonishment whether he too has become weak and without strength, just as they are. "Art thou also become weak" here means that he has lost his power. "Hell" in the text is Sheol, the place of the dead.

Isaiah presents a mockery against the king of Babylon, famous for his pride and violence. The prophet imagines his arrival in the world of the dead, where the kings he once ruled rise to receive him. It is poetic and figurative language. Some see here only the Babylonian king; others also see a broader reference to pride and its fall.

For today: power, money and fame do not make us different in the face of death. Live with humility, use what you have to serve others, and remember that your worth comes from God, not from your position.
exp.30:3:
Isaiah says that the Lord spoke to him in an image: a lion roaring over its prey, which is not frightened even when a group of shepherds comes shouting against it. A group of men is the company of shepherds, and the uproar of many voices is the noise they make. In the same way, God will come down to fight for Mount Zion, which is Jerusalem, and for its hill, that is, the height on which the city stands.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. They were looking for help in Egypt, with its horses and chariots, instead of trusting in God. The prophet reminds them that the Egyptians are only men. There are different views on whether the lion here shows God protecting Jerusalem or also his firmness toward it; the context that follows favors the idea of protection.

For today: when you feel pressure and want to lean only on human resources, remember that God is not intimidated. Do what you can with wisdom, but place your trust in Him.
exp.25:8:
Here the prophet says that he desires God with his whole being. At night he longs for him with his soul, and while he has life and breath ("spirit") he will rise early to seek him. He also says that when God's judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn what is right.

Isaiah speaks in a song of trust on behalf of the people of Judah. They wait on God, who is upright, while they see evil all around them. The verses that follow show that not everyone learns: the wicked, even when shown kindness, keeps doing evil. For this reason some understand "judgments" as God's corrections, and others as his acts of justice.

For today: set aside a moment at the beginning or end of the day to seek God sincerely. Before the news or your phone, speak to him, listen to his Word, and ask him to teach you to live righteously.
exp.7:21:
He says that when these people look toward the earth, they will see only suffering, darkness and anguish, and they will be plunged into gloom. "Trouble" means great affliction or serious problems. "Plunged" means sunk down, completely immersed in something.

Isaiah speaks in a time of crisis for Judah, threatened by neighboring kingdoms. Many, instead of trusting God, sought answers from mediums and spiritists (verse 19). The prophet calls them to return to "the law and to the testimony," that is, to God's Word. Whoever rejects that light ends up angry, hungry and without direction. The text is followed by a promise of light (Isaiah 9:1-2), which the New Testament connects with Jesus.

For today: when distress comes, do not look for answers in just any voice. Open the Bible, pray, and let God's light guide you, even when the path seems dark.
exp.36:9:
Here the king of Assyria sends a message to Hezekiah, king of Judah. He tells him not to let his God deceive him, since that God promised that Jerusalem would not fall into the hands of Assyria. To be deceived means to be made to believe something false, and to be given into the hand of the enemy means that the city would be surrendered to them.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, speaks through messengers. He was at war and had learned that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, was coming to attack him. He wanted to frighten Hezekiah so that he would surrender. With his words he treats God as if he were just one more of the gods of the defeated nations. Later, God would show that this idea was a mistake.

Today there are also voices that tell us that trusting in God is an illusion, especially when problems seem enormous. Like Hezekiah, we can bring those threats to God in prayer and not decide by fear alone.
exp.50:12:
God asks his people whether they have forgotten him, their Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth. They have lived all day in fear of the oppressor, who seemed ready to destroy them. Then God asks, "Where is the fury of the oppressor?" To "oppress" means to crush or make suffer. The word "hast" means "have."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were in trouble, probably under the rule of foreign powers, and they were afraid. God has just told them that he is their comforter and that a mortal human does not deserve so much dread. He reminds them who he is in order to restore their confidence.

For today: when fear of a person or a situation takes hold of you, remember that the God who created all things still cares for you. Pray and tell him what you fear, and go over his promises. The problems are real, but his power is greater and the threat does not have the last word.
exp.49:10:
They say there are people who light their own way with their own fire, that is, with their own plans and resources, and not with the light of God. They are surrounded by sparks. God tells them to keep walking by that light if they want, but the result will come from his hand: they will end up in sorrow.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and at the end God himself speaks. The verse before shows two groups: the one who walks in darkness but trusts in the Lord, and the one who prefers his own light. Many understand the servant to be the Messiah, though it has also been interpreted in other ways. The passage invites trust in God and warns against self-sufficiency.

For today: when you are in the dark, do not invent your own way out. Pray, trust in God, and lean on his Word, even when you cannot yet see the path.
exp.36:14:
This verse says that King Hezekiah, after receiving a threatening letter, began to pray to God. Hezekiah is the name used here, and God is the one he calls on. It is a simple sentence that introduces the prayer that follows.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who is talking about Hezekiah, king of Judah. The Assyrian king Sennacherib had sent messengers with letters that mocked God and demanded surrender. Hezekiah took the letters to the temple, spread them out before the Lord, and prayed. He did not look first for a human solution but for the presence of God.

When you receive news that frightens or overwhelms you, do what Hezekiah did: bring it to God as it really is, with honesty. Before rushing to find solutions or giving in to fear, take a moment to lay everything before Him in prayer.
exp.44:1:
God tells Cyrus that he will go before him, preparing the way. "I will make the crooked places straight" means that he will level what is twisted or difficult. The gates of brass and the bars of iron represent obstacles that seemed impossible to pass, and God promises to break them down.

The LORD speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he calls "his anointed," meaning someone chosen for a task. God would use him to defeat nations, among them Babylon, whose cities had great gates. The purpose is to help Israel, his people, and to make known that the LORD alone is God. Many see here a reference to the fall of Babylon, although the historical details are explained in several ways.

When you face closed doors or crooked roads, remember that God governs history and can go before you. Trust, pray, and take the next step with humility, knowing that He fulfills His purposes.
exp.22:17:
It says that the profits Tyre makes from its trade will be set apart for God. They will not be stored away in warehouses or piled up. They will serve to support those who live before the Lord, so that they eat until they are full and are clothed with dignity. "Trade" is the word for merchandise, and "set apart" means dedicated to God. "Full" describes being satisfied.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces judgment on Tyre, a city rich from its commerce. Earlier he says it will be forgotten for seventy years and then return to its trade, described with the image of a harlot. This verse shows a final turn: its wealth will end up serving God and his people. Interpreters debate when and how this was fulfilled.

For today: money is not meant to be hoarded but to bless others. Today you can decide to set aside part of what you earn to help someone in need or to support the work of God.
exp.60:1:
It says that God's servant comes to announce a year of the Lord's good pleasure, that is, a time of favor and grace. It also speaks of a day of vengeance, which points to God's justice against evil. And his mission is to comfort all who mourn, that is, those who weep and suffer.

The one speaking is a servant anointed by the Spirit, and the passage goes on to speak of good news for the brokenhearted. It was probably addressed to a battered people living among ruins. Jesus read this text in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18-19), but he stopped before the day of vengeance, and that suggests this aspect is reserved for his return. Some interpret it this way; others see it differently.

For today: if you are grieving or weary, God sees you and wants to comfort you. Tell him your pain in prayer, and also look for someone you can comfort this week.
exp.64:8:
God promises that he will raise up descendants from among the people of Jacob and Judah who will receive his mountains as their inheritance. Those he has chosen, meaning those he selected, will possess the land, and his servants, those who serve him, will live there. The word "seed" in the verse means offspring, and "inheritance" means something received as a possession.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people had fallen into idolatry, burning incense on the hills and turning away from God. For this they deserved judgment. But God compares his people to a cluster of grapes with good juice: he will not destroy everything, because there is still blessing in them. So he preserves a faithful remnant. Scholars understand this promise in several ways: as the return from exile, as something still future, or as fulfilled in Christ.

For today: God is just, but he also cares for those who seek him. If you feel small or weak in faith, trust that he knows how to keep what belongs to him.
exp.1:17:
He says that God will completely remove the idols, that is, the images and the things to which people give the place that belongs to Him alone. "Utterly abolish" means that none will be left. The word "idols" here refers to figures made by human hands and worshiped as gods.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He describes a time when God will judge human pride. Earlier he mentions ships, riches, and valuable things in which people trusted. The message is that everything man exalts will fall, and only God will remain exalted. Scholars understand this "day" in different ways: as historical judgments, as the end of time, or as both.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, success, reputation, or comfort. We can give that place to God and trust in Him, before those things fail us.
exp.20:13:
This verse is a call to help: the inhabitants of Tema are asked to go out to meet the one who is thirsty and bring him water. They are also to give bread to the one who flees. The phrase "go out to meet" is what the verse rendered as "salgan a encontrar," and to help means to assist.

Isaiah announces a burden, that is, a message of judgment, concerning Arabia. The travelers of Dedan, people of the caravans, hide at night in the forest. They flee from war, as the following verses explain. Tema was an oasis, and that is why it is asked to show hospitality. Scholars do not agree on who the invader is, but the text announces that the glory of Kedar will fall within a year.

Even in times of crisis, God calls us to be generous. Today we can help with something concrete, such as food or companionship, for someone who flees from violence or need.
exp.7:13:
He says that God himself will be a refuge, a holy place, for those who trust in him. But for those who reject him, he will be like a stone in the road that makes people fall, and like a trap or a net. A stumbling block is an obstacle; a snare is a trap; an inhabitant is a dweller. The two houses of Israel refers to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

Isaiah speaks in a time of political threat, when Judah feared the neighboring kingdoms and sought alliances out of fear. God asks his people not to fear what others fear, but to honor him as holy. Whoever does not do this stumbles over him.

Today we can ask ourselves what we fear most. When we give God first place in our hearts, he becomes our refuge and our peace, even in times of uncertainty.
exp.29:3:
This verse describes the leaders of Judah and their messengers, who have already arrived in Egypt. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities, and there the princes (leaders) and ambassadors (envoys) were seeking an alliance with Pharaoh. Some scholars doubt exactly where Hanes was located, but all agree that it was a place in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was threatened by Assyria, and instead of seeking God, its leaders looked for military protection in Egypt. God warns them that this help will bring them shame and will not do them any good.

Today, when we are afraid, it is easy to rush first to our own solutions. Before deciding, let us ask God for direction in prayer and seek his Word. We may use the resources we have, but without placing our final trust in them.
exp.48:6:
God, who is the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, speaks to someone who is despised and rejected by the nations and who serves under harsh rulers. He promises that kings and princes will see him, will rise to their feet as a sign of respect, and will bow down in worship. The reason is that God is faithful, and it was he who chose him.

This is the second Song of the Servant. The one speaking is God, and he addresses the Servant, whom he sends to restore Israel and to be a light to the nations. Christians often see Jesus here, who was rejected and then exalted. Others also see a reference to Israel as a people. Both readings are possible.

For today: if you feel despised or ignored, remember that your worth does not depend on what people think of you, but on the faithfulness of God. Trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.64:18:
It says that God himself will rejoice over Jerusalem and be glad with his people. The old wording in the source uses forms of "rejoice" and "be glad" for this, and I will leave that as the sense of the verse. It also promises that the sound of weeping will no longer be heard in the city, nor the sound of crying out in pain.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a people who had suffered greatly. He promises a new heaven and a new earth, where past pain will no longer weigh on them. The verses that follow describe long life and houses and vineyards enjoyed. Some believers see here a restoration of Israel, others the final fulfillment in eternity, and others both.

For today: when pain wears you down, remember that God is not indifferent; he delights in his people and promises final comfort. That hope can give you strength to keep going and to comfort others.
exp.40:13:
God tells his people: "Fear not." He calls them "thou worm Jacob," an image of weakness, and "ye men of Israel," meaning a small group. Then he promises: "I will help thee." He presents himself as "thy redeemer," the one who rescues and frees, and as "the Holy One of Israel."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a frightened people, surrounded by powerful nations. He reminds them that he holds them by the hand and that their enemies will be reduced to nothing. He does not praise their strength; he shows them that their security lies in the one who rescues them. Then he promises that they will be like a new threshing sledge, a tool from the field, and that they will end up rejoicing in God.

When you feel small or without strength, do not trust in what you have. Remember who holds you up. Pray today like this: "Lord, you are my help; take my hand."
exp.37:19:
It says that the Lord was ready to save the one who speaks. Therefore, he and his people promise to sing his songs, that is, songs of praise, in the temple, "the house of the Lord," all the days of their life. The first sentence is brief; it can be understood as "The Lord saved me" or "The Lord is ready to save me."

The speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, after being very sick and close to death. In the verses before, he says that the dead can no longer praise God, but the living can. This song gives thanks for his healing. Then the text tells of the remedy with figs and the sign Hezekiah asked for.

For today: when God helps you in a crisis, do not let it be forgotten. Write down what he did for you, give him thanks out loud, and look for a community where you can praise him faithfully, not only in emergencies.
exp.52:6:
It says that the Servant of the Lord suffered greatly, yet he did not defend himself or protest. He is compared to a lamb led to be slaughtered and to a sheep that stays silent while it is being sheared. The shearers are those who cut the wool. The word for the place where animals are killed is slaughter, the place where they are put to death.

This is the fourth song of the Servant in Isaiah. The prophet speaks of this Servant's suffering on behalf of others, who had gone astray like sheep. Jews have read this in different ways (as Israel, or as a righteous man), but Christians see Jesus here, as Acts 8:32-35 does.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, you do not always have to respond with anger or revenge. Jesus shows you another way: to trust God, even in pain. And remember that this silence was for love of you.
exp.64:13:
It says there will be two very different outcomes. God's servants will sing for joy, with hearts full of gladness. Those who rebelled will cry out in pain, with wounded hearts, and they will howl, that is, lament with loud groaning, because their spirit will be broken.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people where many, although God called them again and again, did not respond and chose what is wrong. God contrasts those who are faithful to him with those who reject him. The verses that follow promise that the past troubles will be forgotten for the faithful.

Today we can examine whether we are responding when God speaks to us. Listening to his voice and obeying it today leads us to a deep joy, while ignoring it brings an emptiness that later hurts.
exp.51:13:
Many were astonished at him: his appearance was so marred, beyond that of any man, and his form beyond that of the sons of men. The verse of the verse is as follows. "Astonished" here means they were appalled. "Appearance" refers to how he looked. The second part of the verse is hard, and other translations say that his form was ruined more than that of any person.

Here God speaks and presents his servant, who first suffers and afterward is exalted. Christians see Jesus in this passage, since the New Testament applies it to him. Some Jewish interpreters understand it as a reference to Israel. The text prepares the way for chapter 53.

For today: do not measure the worth of people, or the working of God, only by what is seen. God can bring salvation through pain and humility. Trust him when the path seems hard.
exp.12:18:
This verse says that Babylon, the most admired city of its time, the pride and ornament of the Chaldeans, will end up destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah, cities that God overthrew because of their wickedness. The verse's wording "overthrew" means that they were completely wiped out.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces this message on God's behalf against Babylon. God says he will raise up the Medes to bring it down. Babylon was then a power that dominated other peoples, and the prophet shows that no empire stands above God. Scholars often connect this with the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians, although some also see a broader meaning, as a symbol of human pride.

Today we can remember that fame, success, and wealth do not protect us if we live with arrogance. It is wise to trust God and to live with humility.
exp.61:5:
God says he has set "watchmen" (guards, sentinels) on the walls of Jerusalem. They will not keep silent, either by day or by night. Then he speaks to "those who make mention of the Lord," that is, those who remind him of his promises, and asks them not to stop doing so.

Here God speaks through Isaiah, or the prophet himself speaks, to a people who felt abandoned. God has just promised that Jerusalem will no longer be forsaken, but loved, like a bride. These watchmen keep up prayer and waiting until the promise is fulfilled. Some think they are prophets; others, that they are those who pray. The text does not fully clarify this.

Today we can pray steadily for what God has already promised, even when it takes a long time. Choose a promise from the Bible and bring it before God each day, with confidence and without growing weary.
exp.3:0:
It says that, in a future time, seven women will take hold of one man. They offer to support themselves, with their own bread and their own clothing, if only they may be called by his name and so take away their reproach, that is, their shame.

Isaiah speaks of the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem, described at the end of chapter 3. Many men would fall in war, and so many women would be left alone that social shame would be great. Some think the number seven is a way of saying "many." The following verse announces hope: God would cleanse and restore his people.

For today: when shame or loss comes, let us not seek just anything that gives us identity or acceptance. God offers us his name and his restoration, and that is what truly sustains us.
exp.32:3:
It says that the plunder the enemy left behind will be gathered up, like when caterpillars strip a field. The people will rush over it, back and forth, like locusts. The words about the spoil and what was taken are explained by the verse itself: the spoil is what is taken in war, and the gathering is simply the collecting or seizing of it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of threat, probably when Assyria was pressing against Judah. First he prays to God asking for help, and then he announces that the nations flee before Him. Here he describes how God's people will gather, with great speed and abundance, what the enemy abandoned. Some think the picture is of looting; others, that it describes how the people strip the defeated enemy. The text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel that a problem is bigger than you, go to God with confidence, as Isaiah did. He can turn around what seemed like a total loss, and your part is to wait on Him and give thanks.
exp.8:15:
It says that the leaders of the people were leading them down the wrong path, and that the people, by following them, had gone astray. The words that describe the leaders as those who guide or direct, and the phrase saying that they made the people wander by means of falsehood, belong to the same idea of misleading. Those who let themselves be guided are the ones who were led, and the people who were lost were left confused and without direction.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the northern kingdom, Israel, in the eighth century B.C. God had already disciplined them, but they still did not turn back to Him. The previous verse accuses elders and prophets who taught lies. Here the verse of the result is given: false leaders and a people who followed them.

For today: do not follow anyone blindly. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray asking for wisdom, and if you are a leader, guide with truth and humility.
exp.39:4:
