It says that God will reveal his glory, that is, his power, his goodness and his presence, in such a clear way that all flesh, that is, all people, will see it together. The word "revealed" means that it will be shown plainly. What it states is certain, because the very mouth of God has spoken it.

Isaiah announces comfort to the people of Israel, who are discouraged and in exile. A voice commands that the way of the Lord be prepared, as when a road is leveled for a king. Christians see in this an announcement of John the Baptist and of the coming of Jesus, as the Gospels do. Afterward the text contrasts human frailty with the firmness of God.

For today: when you feel small or doubt God's promises, remember that his word does not fail. Prepare the way for him with humility, letting him straighten what is crooked in your heart.
exp.47:19:
This verse says that God's people must leave Babylon and move away from the Chaldeans. They must announce this with joy and shouts of gladness, to the farthest corner of the earth. The message is: "The Lord hath redeemed his servant Jacob." "Redeemed" means that God rescued and freed him. "To the end of the earth" means the most distant places.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces in advance that Israel would be freed from exile in Babylon. Earlier, God laments that his people did not obey, for they would have had peace that way. Even so, he promises to rescue them. Some also see here an image of leaving sin, although the text speaks first of a real liberation.

For today: if God has rescued you, do not stay silent or tied to what was enslaving you. Take a concrete step to leave it behind, and share with joy with someone what God has done for you.
exp.34:6:
This verse says that the dry ground, scorched by the sun, will become a pool, and the thirsty land will become springs of water. "Parched ground" is very dry earth, and "springs" are the places where water rises up. Even the place where the jackals used to lie down, wild animals of the desert, will be filled with grass, reeds, and rushes, plants that grow where there is water.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of God, who lived among threats and discouragement. This chapter is a promise of restoration: God will bring healing, joy, and a safe road for the redeemed. Many believe it speaks of the return from exile and also of a greater hope, still in the future. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: if there is an area of your life that feels dry, do not lose hope. God knows how to bring life where it seemed impossible. Pray with confidence and take one small step of faith today.
exp.27:1:
This verse says that God has at his disposal someone strong and mighty, who comes like a hailstorm, like a whirlwind that destroys everything, or like a flood of violent waters. "Downpour" refers to a sudden, heavy rain. The description of someone who turns everything upside down is that this person leaves everything in ruins. The idea of throwing down to the ground means casting something hard to the earth.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C. against Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel. Its capital, Samaria, stood on a fertile hill, and its leaders lived proud and drunk. Isaiah announces judgment. Many understand that the "strong and mighty one" is the army of Assyria, used by God, although the text does not name it here.

Today it reminds us that pride and careless living do not hold up when God acts. Today we can ask ourselves in what things we trust more than in Him, and turn back to God with humility before the storm arrives.
exp.22:12:
Look at the land of the Chaldeans, that is, Babylon. That people had no importance before. Assyria founded it or strengthened it for people who lived in the wilderness. They raised up towers and palaces, but in the end that land was left in ruins. The text is difficult, and it is not known for certain who "he" was that brought it to ruin: it may be Assyria, or God working through it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message against Tyre, the great trading city. He uses the example of Babylon to show that even what seems firm can fall. Tyre should not have trusted in its wealth or its reputation.

Today, let us not place our security in money, success or power, because all of that can change. Let us trust in God, who remains forever.
exp.37:8:
This verse is a short introduction. It says that what follows is a writing by King Hezekiah of Judah, made after he had been sick and was recovered. The word "writing" here means a written text, something like a poem or a written prayer.

The context is that Hezekiah was very ill, and God promised him more years of life. As a sign, he made the shadow on the dial of Ahaz go back. The speaker in the verse is the narrator of the book, and then Hezekiah himself speaks. His writing recalls his distress before possible death and his gratitude for having been healed.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not let it pass by. Write down what you lived through, your fears and your gratitude. Writing it will help you remember God's faithfulness and encourage others.
exp.54:10:
This verse says that God's word is like a mission with a sure destination. When God speaks, that word does not come back empty, that is, without result. It accomplishes what God desires and achieves the purpose for which he sent it. It also says that the phrase "the Reina-Valera" is no longer needed... [omitted; see note below]

Correction: here is the full translation.

This verse says that God's word is like a mission with a sure destination. When God speaks, that word does not come back without result. It accomplishes what God desires and achieves the purpose for which he sent it. In this verse, the idea of "not returning" means it will not come back without having done its work.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were living in exile or coming out of it (scholars debate the exact date). God compares his word to the rain and the snow, which come down from heaven and make the earth produce. In the same way, his promise of forgiveness and restoration will be fulfilled, even though his ways may seem hard to understand.

For today: read the Bible with confidence, knowing that God works in you through his word, even when you do not see the fruit right away.
exp.55:11:
Here the wicked leaders of Israel invite one another to a party. They say they will bring wine and get drunk on strong drink, which in this version is a potent beverage, not the apple juice of today. They expect tomorrow to be just like today, or even better.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just described the watchmen and shepherds of the people as blind, silent, and selfish. Instead of caring for and warning the people, they only seek their own pleasure. This verse shows their attitude: pleasure today and great confidence that tomorrow will stay the same.

For today: let us not live with the idea that there will always be time later. Whoever leads others, in the church or in the family, must care with responsibility and not merely seek their own comfort. Let us ask God to keep us alert.
exp.62:16:
Here the people ask God why he let them wander from his ways and why their hearts became hard so that they stopped fearing him. "To wander" means to turn aside, and "inheritance" is the people God chose as his own. They ask God to return to them, for the sake of his servants.

The people of Israel are speaking, probably in a time of ruin and exile. They acknowledge that God is their Father and Redeemer, even though their ancestors can no longer help them. It is a painful and bold prayer. Some understand that God allowed their hardness as a consequence of their rebellion; others see a language of sincere complaint, not an accusation against God.

For today: when you feel far from God, do not hide. Bring him your confusion honestly, acknowledge your part, and ask him to draw you near again. He remains a Father.
exp.27:10:
He says God will speak to his people with voices that sound like babbling, in a foreign tongue they do not understand. The word "stammering" refers to people who speak in broken phrases, with sounds that are hard to make out. The phrase "to this people" refers to Judah.

Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Jerusalem who were mocking his messages and treating them as if they were meant for children. God answers that, since they will not listen to his clear word, he will speak to them through foreign invaders, the Assyrians, whose language they will not understand. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 14:21 when speaking about tongues. It is a judgment for having rejected the rest that God was offering them.

When God speaks to us clearly and we ignore him, he may later speak to us through difficult circumstances. Let us listen to his Word today with humility, before correction becomes harder.
exp.33:14:
It says that in the ruined land there will be wild animals that make their home there. The phrase about gathering them under her wings means that she will gather them and care for them. The vultures are scavenging birds, and "each one with her mate" shows that they gather in pairs.

Isaiah announces God's judgment against Edom and the nations that opposed his people. The city will be left desolate, and only wild life will inhabit it. This is presented as the fulfillment of the word of the LORD, written in his book.

For today: God is just and his word is fulfilled. When we see injustice, we can trust that he will not overlook it. That invites us not to take revenge, to live with humility, and to place our hope in his just judgment.
exp.43:10:
It says that all who join themselves to idols will be put to shame. The makers of those gods are only human beings. Even if they gather together, present themselves side by side, and try to defend their idols, they will be struck with terror and, all together, they will be put to shame.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people Israel. Shortly before this, he told them that only he is the true God. Now he mocks idolatry with seriousness: an object made by human hands cannot see, understand, or save. The verses that follow show the blacksmith and the carpenter growing tired as they make their "god."

For today: examine what things you treat as your own source of security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If you build it and hold it up, it cannot hold you up. Trust today in the God who created you.
exp.43:5:
God introduces himself with three titles: King of Israel, Redeemer, and the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord of all powers. To say "the first and the last" means that he was before everything and will continue after everything. "Beside me there is no God" means that there is no other true God.

The same God speaks to Israel, his people, who lived surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this, he promises to pour out his Spirit and bless the children of the people. Here he reminds them who he is so that they will not be afraid. Later he calls them his witnesses.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember that God was already there at the beginning and will be there at the end of your story. Bring to him in prayer today whatever worries you most, and trust that he remains the Lord.
exp.29:20:
God says he will guide his people with a clear voice. That voice will be heard "behind thee," like a teacher who walks behind you and tells you which way to go. The message is: "This is the way, walk ye in it." Turning "to the right hand" or "to the left" means not straying off to either side.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, a people who sought help in Egypt instead of trusting God. Before this promise, he announces that God will be merciful and will answer their cry. Even though there will be days of "bread of affliction," that is, of suffering, God's teachers will not disappear. Then the people will give up their idols.

For today: when you have to make a decision, do not rush or rely only on your own opinion. Read the Bible, pray, and listen to the advice of wise people. God usually guides step by step, and his direction never contradicts his Word.
exp.64:12:
God says he will make a clear difference between two groups. Those who serve him will have food, drink, and joy. Those who reject him will have hunger, thirst, and shame. The word "ye" is an older way of saying "you." "Ashamed" means they will be disappointed and humiliated when they see that their hopes have failed.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses those who had abandoned him and who set out tables of offerings to Luck and Fate, which were false gods of fortune. God had spoken to them, and they refused to listen. That is why he announces this contrast between the faithful and those who turned away.

For today: do not place your trust in luck, money, or anything else that promises security. Respond when God speaks to you, and seek in him your provision and your joy.
exp.60:8:
This verse says that the descendants of God's people will be known among the nations. "Seed" means descendants, and "offspring" are the young shoots, like new branches on a tree. Everyone who sees them will recognize that the Lord has blessed them.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's promise to a people who were humbled and wounded. God tells them that he will turn their shame into honor and make an everlasting covenant with them. Many believe this refers to a restored Israel; Christians also see in the passage Christ (Isaiah 61:1-3 is quoted by Jesus in Luke 4) and those who belong to him.

Today we can live in such a way that others notice God's goodness in us: with honesty, kindness, and hope, trusting that he restores what seemed lost.
exp.13:7:
It says that even the trees rejoiced when this tyrant fell. The "fir trees" are what this version called the cypresses or junipers (scholars are not sure of the exact plant). The phrase "rejoice" simply means that they were glad. The cedars of Lebanon, famous for their wood, speak as if they were saying: since he has fallen, no woodcutter comes up against us anymore.

Isaiah announces a mocking song against the king of Babylon (v. 4). He was a cruel ruler who oppressed peoples and laid waste to nature for his building projects and wars. The trees appear in poetic language, as if all creation were breathing a sigh of relief. Afterward, the world of the dead also receives him with astonishment.

For today: oppressive power does not last forever, and God sees the harm done to people and to creation. We can use whatever authority we have, at home, at work, or in our community, to care for and not to destroy.
exp.60:0:
This verse says that the Spirit of God is upon the one who speaks, because God anointed him, that is, set him apart and equipped him for a mission. He was sent to bring good news to the afflicted (those who are humbled and discouraged), to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and to open the prison to those who are bound. The word "sent" in this verse is the one that "he hath sent me" expresses.

The one speaking is not named here. Many believe he is the prophet Isaiah, and others see the Servant of God who would bring comfort to a people in distress. Jesus read this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in Him (Luke 4:16-21). For that reason Christians see it fulfilled in Christ.

For today: God draws near to those who suffer. We can accompany someone who is hurt through a visit, a prayer, or a word of encouragement, trusting that God also heals our own heart.
exp.45:7:
God asks his people to remember what they have just seen: the absurdity of worshiping idols. "Show yourselves men" means recognizing with humility that you were wrong. "Bring it again to mind" means coming back to your senses and reflecting. "Transgressors" are those who rebel and betray their commitment to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just described how someone pays a silversmith to make a god that must be carried, that does not move and does not answer. Then God reminds them that he is the one who announced the future and carries out his plan. This contrasts the living God with powerless idols.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in the place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If they cannot answer us or save us, it is time to come to our senses and return to God with sincerity.
exp.18:24:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, will bless Egypt, Assyria and Israel. He gives each of them a affectionate title: Egypt is "my people," Assyria is "the work of my hands," and Israel is "my inheritance," that is, his treasured possession.

Isaiah speaks to Judah at a time when neighboring powers threatened it. Egypt and Assyria were longtime enemies of Israel and of other peoples. Here God speaks of a future time, when these nations will worship him together. Interpreters differ on when and how this is fulfilled: some see a partial historical fulfillment, others see it in Christ and the church, and others see it in a time still to come.

For today: God loves and seeks people whom we see as enemies. We can pray for someone with whom we are in conflict and ask God to help us treat them with respect and a desire for peace.
exp.48:9:
They shall not hunger or thirst, and neither the heat nor the sun will harm them. God, who has compassion on them, will lead them like a shepherd to places where fresh water flows.

The Lord speaks in the second song of the Servant. He addresses his Servant, whom many Christians see fulfilled in Jesus, and also the people returning from captivity. God promises to free the prisoners and bring them back along safe paths. Some scholars see this as a promise for Israel of that time, while others add a broader spiritual fulfillment.

For today: when you feel weary or in need, remember that God cares for you like a shepherd. Trust his guidance, ask him for direction each day, and rest in his compassion.
exp.9:10:
What it says: Here the king of Assyria speaks with pride. He says that just as he destroyed Samaria and its idols, he will do the same to Jerusalem and its own. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and the idols are false gods made by human hands.

Context: God had used Assyria as a rod to correct his unfaithful people. But the Assyrian king believed himself master of everything and boasted of his victories, without acknowledging God. He also placed Jerusalem on the same level as the idolatrous nations. That is why, in the verses that follow, God promises to call him to account for his arrogance, after finishing his work on Zion.

For today: Everything we accomplish, whether work, studies or success, is a gift that God allows. When we believe we are the authors of everything, pride blinds us. Today, before celebrating an achievement, give thanks to God for it.
exp.10:4:
It says that justice will be like the belt that fits around this king's waist, and faithfulness like the sash that holds his lower body in place. The words "loins" and "kidneys" both refer to the area of the waist. In that time, tightening the belt was a way of getting ready to work or serve. The idea is that justice and faithfulness are an inseparable part of his character and his work.

It is the prophet Isaiah who speaks. He describes a future king from the line of David, the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa. 11:1). Christians recognize him in Jesus, the Messiah. This king judges with uprightness, protects the poor, and brings a peace that changes even nature, as the image of the wolf and the lamb shows.

For today: ask God to make righteousness and faithfulness your belt. Keep your word and deal fairly with the weak, without letting yourself be swayed by appearances.
exp.48:0:
It says that someone speaks to the islands and to distant peoples, that is, to nations all over the world, and asks them to listen. It affirms that God called him before he was born and that, from his mother's womb, God already had his name in mind. "God kept my name in mind" means that God remembered him and chose him for a purpose.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, and his message reaches all the nations. In the verse that follows he is called "Israel," so many understand him to be the people of Israel. Others, based on what follows in the chapter, see in him the Messiah, and Christians apply it to Jesus. Some see both: a mission that Israel received and that Christ fulfills completely.

God knows and calls each person with purpose. Your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that God knows you and has had you in mind from the beginning. Today you can rest in that and serve with confidence.
exp.21:3:
Here the prophet says he wants to be alone to weep bitterly. He asks that people not strive to comfort him, because the grief over the ruin of "the daughter of my people" (a poetic way of speaking of Jerusalem and its people) is too great. The word "labour" in the verse means to work hard at something, and "look away from me" means leave me alone.

The speaker is Isaiah. The chapter is headed by a reference to Jerusalem, called "the valley of vision." It describes a city that thought itself safe and lived in festivity, but whose leaders fled and were captured. Isaiah does not rejoice in the judgment; he suffers for his people. Scholars debate which exact historical moment the passage refers to.

For today: sometimes pain needs time, not just quick words. We can accompany others with presence and silence, without rushing them. And when something hurts us, it is right to weep honestly before God.
exp.51:0:
Says that Jerusalem, also called Zion, must awake and put on her finest clothes, like someone getting ready for a festival. Strength speaks of power, and glorious garments of splendid clothing. She is promised that the uncircumcised (someone who did not belong to the covenant people) and the unclean (someone who was ceremonially impure) will no longer enter her.

The prophet Isaiah passes on God's word to the people of Judah, who lived in humiliation and captivity. God encourages them to rise, because their deliverance is coming. The verses that follow speak of shaking off the dust and loosing the chains. Interpreters debate whether "no more" refers only to the return from exile or also to a future, spiritual restoration.

For today: if you feel fallen or discouraged, God calls you to rise up, trusting in his rescue. Today you can pray, remember his promises, and take one concrete step of faith.
exp.38:2:
Isaiah the prophet comes to King Hezekiah and asks him two questions: what those men said, and where they came from. Hezekiah answers that they came from a far country, from Babylon. Notice that he answers only the second question; he does not say what they had told him or what he showed them.

The messengers of the king of Babylon had come to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery. He was glad and showed them all his treasures and weapons. Isaiah asks as a messenger of God, since he is about to announce a judgment. Some think Hezekiah became proud or sought human support; the text does not explain all his motives.

Today, God invites us to be sincere and to guard our hearts when we receive praise or success. Everything we have is a gift from God; let us give the glory to Him.
exp.35:10:
Here the three officials of King Hezekiah ask Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, to speak in Syriac (Aramaic), a language they understood, and not in Hebrew. They did not want the people listening from the wall to understand what was being said. The request is that he speak to them in the language they understood and not in the language of the people, in hearing of those on the wall.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Assyrian army. Rabshakeh was trying to spread fear and break the people's trust in God and in Hezekiah. The officials wanted to negotiate in private, but Rabshakeh refused and shouted in Hebrew so that everyone could hear him. His plan was to sow panic.

For today: when words arrive that only aim to frighten and discourage you, do not let yourself be carried away by them. You can ask for wisdom to respond with calm, to guard what you listen to, and to remember that your trust is in God, not in the noise of those who threaten you.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that on that day the people will flee in fear, like a startled and hunted deer, or like sheep without a shepherd. Each one will turn toward his own people and escape to his own land.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in his message against Babylon. He announces the day of the LORD, a time of judgment on that empire's pride and violence. The foreigners who lived there, without protection or leader, would try to return to their own countries.

For today: human powers may seem firm, but they are not our security. Trust in God, and in Christ, the Good Shepherd, who cares for his sheep and does not leave them lost.
exp.39:23:
This verse describes powerful rulers as plants that hardly had time to put down roots. As soon as they begin to grow, God blows on them and they wither. Then the whirlwind, or strong wind, carries them away like chaff, that is, like dry leaves and light straw.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who live under the shadow of very strong empires. He wants to remind them that God is far greater than any king or nation. That is why, in what follows, God asks: "To whom then will you liken me?" No one is his equal.

For today: when you feel afraid before people or situations that seem enormous and unstoppable, remember that none of them is greater than God. You can bring your worry to him in prayer and trust that he still governs.
exp.12:16:
It says that God himself will stir up or rouse the Medes against Babylon. They are described as a people who have no interest in silver or gold, meaning they cannot be bought or stopped with bribes. The phrase "they will not care for silver" means that it will mean nothing to them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God against Babylon, which was a proud and violent empire. The harsh scenes of war show judgment on a nation that oppressed others. Historically, the Medes were part of the coalition that later defeated Babylon. Some understand the passage as fulfilled in that event, and others also see a broader picture of God's judgment.

God rules over the nations and does not overlook injustice. Today we can trust that no human power lasts forever, and we can live with humility, seeking justice rather than pride or wealth.
exp.23:18:
This verse says that the earth will be completely broken, shattered, and shaken with great force. These are three phrases that repeat the same idea for emphasis: the judgment will be total. The word "utterly broken down" means the earth will be fully broken, and "clean dissolved" means it will be reduced to pieces, like something ground to dust.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in chapters 24 to 27, sometimes called "the apocalypse of Isaiah." Before this verse, the prophet describes judgment on the earth because its inhabitants broke God's laws and his covenant (v. 5). Some believe he is speaking of a final judgment; others also see it as a warning to the nations of that time. Both readings have been held.

For today: do not place your security in what can be shaken. Today you can entrust your life to God, who remains steadfast, and live with humility and obedience.
exp.24:1:
It says that God turned a city into a heap of rubble. That strong city, with its walls, was left in ruins. The word "turned" in this verse means "made" or "brought," and the phrase "a palace of strangers" refers to a walled fortress or palace. "Strangers" are people who are outsiders, enemies of God's people. And the idea of the fortress being rebuilt means that this fortress will never be raised up again.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, praising God for His just and faithful works. It is not stated clearly which city is meant; some think of a real city, such as Babylon, and others of a symbol of human pride and power that opposes God. What matters is that God brings down the proud and protects the poor, as the following verses say.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever, but God is faithful. When you see injustice or powerful people who seem untouchable, do not lose hope: trust in God and praise Him, because He cares for the weak.
exp.41:1:
This verse says that God's servant will not cry out, nor raise his voice, nor make himself heard with commotion in the squares, which were the public places where people gathered. "Cry out" here means to shout loudly; "make his voice heard" refers to making noise to attract attention.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He presents his chosen servant, whom he upholds and fills with his Spirit, to bring justice to the nations. Many Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the Gospel of Matthew (12:18-21) quotes it this way. The point is that his manner of acting will be humble and gentle, not noisy or proud.

For today: we can serve and bear witness with gentleness, without fighting or seeking applause. Truth does not need shouting; it needs love, patience, and steadfastness.
exp.27:13:
God calls the leaders of Jerusalem "scornful men," that is, men who mock the divine warning. They "rule" (hold authority over) the people. God asks them to hear his word, even though until now they have refused to listen.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. The rulers of Judah mocked the prophet's message and trusted in political alliances, which the following verse calls a "covenant with death" and a refuge in lies. Some scholars think this refers to pacts with foreign powers, but the text does not say so with complete clarity. God responds by announcing a firm stone in Zion, where trust can truly be placed.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, let us not mock it or seek false refuges. Let us stop to listen to it with humility and trust in the foundation that God offers.
exp.29:22:
It says that when the people turn back to God, he will send rain on the land that has been sown. There will be bread from the produce of the earth, and it will be rich and full of substance. The animals will graze in peace in wide pastures, that is, broad meadows. The sown land is the field that has been planted.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, the prophet announces that God will guide them with his voice and that they will abandon their idols of silver and gold. The promise is one of forgiveness and restoration after repentance. Scholars understand these blessings as a picture of real provision, and some also see a broader future hope.

For today: when you have gone astray, returning to God is not a loss but a receiving of care. Place today in his hands a worry about money or provision, and leave behind any false security that steals your peace.
exp.43:13:
This verse describes a man who gets wood to make an idol. He cuts cedars, chooses oak and cork oak (hard woods), and works hard among the trees of the forest. He also plants an ash tree, which grows because of the rain. The phrase "he heweth him down" means that he cuts the cedars down, and "which he strengtheneth for himself" means that he chooses and tends them with great care.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, who lived surrounded by nations with idols. With a touch of irony, he points out the absurdity of idolatry: the man uses the wood to warm himself, to cook, and also to make a god. Moreover, the ash tree grows because of the rain that God sends, not because of the man.

For today: check which things, jobs or achievements have taken God's place. Everything we have comes from Him. Let us give Him first place and thank Him for what He gives us.
exp.28:15:
This verse says that the people have turned things upside down, and this is rendered by the word "turning" in the verse. Thinking that the clay is wiser than the potter is absurd. A work cannot say of the one who made it, "He made me not," nor a vessel say, "He has no understanding."

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Jerusalem. Its leaders were making plans in secret, without consulting God, and they thought no one was watching. They pretended to be cleverer than He was. So God shows them how ridiculous that attitude is. Then He promises that the deaf will hear and the blind will see.

For today: before deciding something important, lay your plans before God with humility. He knows you and formed you, so trust that His wisdom surpasses yours, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.65:13:
It says that God's people will see their promises fulfilled and their hearts will fill with joy. "Your bones will flourish like an herb" is an image of renewed strength and life, like grass that springs back to life after the rain. "The hand of the Lord will be known" means that God's care for his servants will be noticed. "His indignation" means that he will show his anger against those who oppose him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. Earlier he has promised to comfort Jerusalem as a mother comforts her child. Then he announces judgment by fire. Thus the comfort for the faithful and the justice against the rebels go together.

For today: if you are tired or discouraged, rest in the knowledge that God cares for you as a mother cares for her child. Keep serving him with confidence, because he renews strength and will do justice in his time.
exp.47:0:
God calls the people's attention: "Hear ye this, O house of Jacob." They bear the name of Israel and have come forth from the waters of Judah, a phrase that speaks of their origin, like a spring. They swear by the name of the Lord and mention him, but not in truth or in righteousness, that is, without sincerity or an upright life.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who took pride in their religious identity but lived with a divided heart. His rebuke seeks to awaken them, not to destroy them. The verses that follow show that they relied on their holy city and on their name.

For today: it is not enough to say that we believe in God or to use Christian words. Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is sincere and whether it shows in how we treat others and in how we live each day.
exp.62:17:
This verse says that God's people, called "the people of your holiness" (that is, the people set apart for God), held the land or the sanctuary for only a short time. Now their enemies have "trodden down" the sanctuary, an old-fashioned way of saying they walked all over it and treated it with contempt. The sanctuary, the holy place of worship, has been defiled.

The one speaking is the prophet, praying on behalf of the people. It is a prayer full of grief, probably offered after the destruction of the temple and the exile, although scholars debate the exact date. The people acknowledge God as Father and Redeemer, and ask him to return to them with mercy.

For today: when you feel that you have lost something sacred, or that everything is falling apart, do as this people did. Come to God honestly, without hiding your pain, and call him "Father" again. He listens to his children.
exp.42:6:
He says God calls all who bear his name "my sons and daughters," that is, those who belong to him. He created them, formed them, and made them for his glory, meaning to display who he is. The word "created" here stands in for the verse's wording, and "formed" and "made" stress that God shaped them with care, like a potter.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, which was scattered and going through trials. He promises them, "Do not fear, I am with you," and that he will gather his children from the east, the west, the north, and the south. Then he presents them as witnesses that he alone is God.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements, because God made you with purpose. Today you can live without fear and do something simple, such as your work, the way you treat others, or your prayer, to honor him.
exp.47:1:
This verse says that the people identify themselves with Jerusalem, the holy city, and say they trust in the God of Israel. That God has a solemn name: the Lord of hosts, meaning the Lord who rules over all the powers of heaven and earth. "They call themselves" means they describe themselves as belonging to the holy city and claim to belong to it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Judah, which uses the name of Israel and swears by the Lord, but not in truth or in righteousness. God reminds them that their words and their religious identity do not match their lives. Next he will tell them that he knows them as a stubborn people.

For today: it is not enough to say "I am a Christian" or to belong to a church. Ask God that your trust in him be sincere and that it shows in the way you live, speak, and treat others.
exp.62:2:
He says God trod the winepress alone, the place where grapes were pressed to get the wine. No one was with him. He trod the peoples in his anger and crushed them in his fury, and their blood stained his garments. It is a strong image: the red juice of the grapes is compared with judgment on the nations.

The Lord speaks, arriving from Edom and Bozrah, a land hostile to Israel. He answers the question of why his clothing is red. It is poetic language that shows God as a warrior who executes justice and rescues his people. Some see here a foretelling of the final judgment; others, a specific historical judgment.

For today: we do not have to carry revenge or all the injustice of the world. We can trust that God sees evil and will act with justice, and so let go of resentment and seek peace.
exp.23:0:
This verse says that God himself is about to leave the earth empty and stripped bare. "Stripped bare" means that it is left without its riches and its beauty. The phrase about turning it upside down means that he changes the appearance of the earth, disfiguring it. And the phrase about scattering its inhabitants means that the people who live there will be dispersed, sent far away.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God. This chapter opens a section where the judgment reaches the whole earth, not just one nation. The verses that follow explain that no one escapes, neither priest nor servant, neither rich nor poor. Scholars debate whether it refers to a near historical event, to the final judgment, or to both.

For today: let us not place our security in things that can be lost, such as money, status, or plans. Let us place our trust in God, who remains when everything else is shaken.
exp.57:1:
It says that the people seek God every day and seem eager to know his ways. They act like a nation that practices justice and has not abandoned the law of their God. They ask him for fair decisions and appear to want to draw near to him. The phrase "rights of justice" refers to upright judgments; "practiced" means carried out or done.

God speaks here, commanding the prophet Isaiah to denounce the sin of his people. The verse describes their religious appearance, but the following context shows that it was superficial. They fasted, yet they kept seeking their own benefit, oppressed others, and lived in quarreling and violence. Many interpreters understand that God does not deny that they sought him, but that their religion was not accompanied by a just life.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our prayer, our attendance at church, or our fasting is reflected in how we treat family, coworkers, and those in need. Let us seek God with sincerity and obedience.
exp.44:7:
It says that God invites the heavens to "drop down" or pour out righteousness like rain, and invites the earth to open like a furrow so that salvation together with righteousness may sprout. Both grow together, like a seed that germinates. At the end, God declares: "I the Lord have created it," meaning that He is the one who makes this happen.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel and the Persian king Cyrus, whom He would use to free His people from exile. God insists that there is no other God and that He governs everything, the light and the darkness. Many understand "evil" as calamity or judgment, not moral wickedness. Some see here also a promise of the Messiah.

For today: when the world seems dark, trust that God is still at work and causing salvation to spring up. Pray in waiting, without trying to control everything.
exp.41:19:
This verse describes someone who sees many things but does not really take notice of them, and who has open ears but does not listen. Where the verse says "Advierte," it means noticing or paying attention. It is like seeing and hearing without understanding or obeying.

God speaks through Isaiah to his people Israel, whom he calls his servant. He had given them his law and his works, but they did not respond. The text that follows speaks of their ruin as a consequence. Some understand that the one described is Israel in its calling, while others connect it with the ideal Servant. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

We can hear sermons and read the Bible, and yet change nothing. Today, before reading or listening to the Word, ask God for an attentive heart, and choose one specific thing you will obey this week.
exp.62:18:
This verse says the people feel as though God had never been their Lord and had never called them his own. The reader's verse says "thou never barest rule over them," so I'll rewrite the comment about that word: "Ruling over them" means governing them or having authority over them. "Thy name was called upon them" means they belong to God. "We are become" is "we have become."

Here the prophet speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of lament. Enemies have trampled the sanctuary, and the people feel that God is far away. Some scholars think it refers to the time of the exile or to the period after Jerusalem fell, but there is not full agreement. Their complaint is that they seem just like the nations that do not know God.

For today: when you feel far from God or abandoned, do not hide that pain. Bring it to him honestly, as the prophet did, and rely on what God has promised concerning you, not only on what you feel.
exp.18:6:
It says that the green plants growing along the Nile, on its banks, and all the crops that depend on its water, will dry up. They will be carried off by the wind, will spoil, and will cease to exist. The "green plants" are the leafy growth, and the "sown land" is the ground where seed has been planted. The phrase "will be no more" means they will vanish completely.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile for its livelihood: food, fishing, flax, and trade. Here God shows that He has power over the very things that people trusted. Many think this refers to a drought or to a judgment on the land, although scholars do not agree on the exact time.

We can ask ourselves where we place our security: in work, money, or health. All of these can fail, but God remains. Today you can thank Him for what you have and trust Him first.
exp.50:7:
This verse says that God's enemies and the enemies of his people will disappear like a garment that the moth and the worm gradually eat until it is gone. What God does, on the other hand, endures forever. "Righteousness" here includes his faithfulness and his action to rescue, and "salvation" means deliverance or rescue. "Forever" means without end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who are weary and exposed to mockery and pressure. He tells them not to fear the contempt of men, because their power is passing. Then the people respond by calling on God to awaken his arm, as in the past.

Today we can remember that the criticisms, threats, and fears of this world wear away with time. When someone despises you for following God, rest in the knowledge that his salvation does not come to an end. Place your trust in what lasts.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that God has a solemn message, a "burden," against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. In a single night its main cities, Ar-moab and Kir-moab, fell, and they were brought to silence, that is, ruined and without life. The word "burden" means a heavy prophecy of judgment.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces this message on behalf of God. Moab was a nearby people with a complicated history with Israel. Scholars do not agree on when or how exactly this fall happened; the text does not make it clear. What is clear is that God speaks as Lord of all nations, not only of Israel.

For today: let us not trust in what seems firm, such as money, power, or prestige. Everything can change in a night. Let us place our security in God, who endures and is just.
exp.26:1:
He says that, when that promised day comes, God's people will sing with joy about a vineyard of red wine. "Sing ye" is an invitation to celebrate. The vineyard represents Israel, and the red wine speaks of a vineyard that yields good fruit. Some older translations read "a pleasant vineyard," since the Hebrew text has that variant.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Earlier, God promises to judge Leviathan, a symbol of the powers of evil. Then He Himself says that He tends His vineyard, waters it, and does not leave it alone. This contrasts with Isaiah 5, where the vineyard produced bad grapes and was judged. Here there is restoration.

For today: if God cares for His own with such careful attention, you can rest in His protection. Before you worry, give thanks to Him and sing a song of praise for His daily care.
exp.31:17:
This verse promises that God's people will live in a peaceful place, with safe homes and places of rest. A peaceable habitation is a home without fear. Sure dwellings and quiet resting places mean places of calm rest, free from hurry and threat.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name. Just before this, he describes a time when a just king will reign and the Spirit will be poured out from on high (v. 15). There, justice produces peace. Some believe the promise points to the reign of Hezekiah, others to the Messiah and the future. Then comes a warning of judgment against the proud city.

For today: true peace grows where people live with justice and trust in God. Today you can care for honesty at home and at work, and rest by handing your worries over to God.
exp.65:19:
It says that people from all the nations will bring your "brothers" back, that is, the scattered people of God, to Jerusalem. They will bring them as an offering to the Lord, on horses, in chariots, in litters (stretchers or seats carried by people or animals), on mules, and on camels. It compares this to the Israelites who brought their offering in clean vessels to the temple.

God himself speaks at the end of the book of Isaiah. He announces that he will gather all the nations so that they see his glory. He will send messengers to distant lands that have never heard of him. Scholars understand who these "brothers" are in different ways: scattered Jews, or believers from all peoples. The text that follows speaks of priests taken from among them, which is a very open idea.

For today: God wants his glory to reach all peoples, and every person brought to him to be a clean offering. We can pray for someone far from God and help draw them near with love and patience.
exp.40:20:
Here God invites the idols and those who worship them to present their defense. "Produce your cause" is like saying: "Present your case, as in a trial." "Bring forth your strong reasons" means: "Show your proofs and solid arguments." God calls himself "the King of Jacob," that is, the King of Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is a courtroom scene before the nations and their false gods. The verses that follow ask the idols to declare the past and the future. God has just shown his power by transforming the desert, and now he challenges the idols to demonstrate something similar. They cannot.

For today: God does not fear questions or tests. We can examine where we have placed our trust, whether in money, success, or people, and return to trust in the God who does what he says.
exp.5:1:
These verses describe beings called seraphim, who stood above the throne of God. Each one had six wings: with two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. The word "seraphim" probably means "burning ones," and they appear only here in the Bible.

Isaiah tells what he saw in a vision, in the year King Uzziah died. The seraphim do not speak yet; in the next verse they proclaim the holiness of God. Many understand that covering the face and the feet shows reverence and humility before God. The feet may be a gentle way of referring to the body, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if even the seraphim cover themselves before God, we too can approach Him with respect and gratitude. Before you pray, pause and remember who God is.
exp.52:7:
He was arrested and condemned without justice, and his life was taken away. "Cut off from the land of the living" means that he died. No one thought about his descendants, or about his future. The phrase "who shall declare his generation?" can be understood in several ways. What is clear is that he suffered for the people's rebellion.

In this passage, the prophet speaks of the Suffering Servant. Some believe the speakers are the people and the nations, admitting their guilt. Jews have understood it in different ways. Christians see Jesus here, as Philip did in Acts 8.

Today, this verse invites us not to see Christ's suffering as something distant. He bore what we deserved. We can respond to him with gratitude, confessing our wrongs and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.47:18:
It says that if Israel had obeyed, their children would have been countless, like the sand of the sea. "Seed" refers to their descendants, and the children born from them are their offspring; "pebbles" are small stones. "Cut off" means erased. God says that his name would never have been removed from his presence.

The Lord, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, speaks to a people who did not listen to him. With sorrow, he shows them what they would have received: peace like a river and a large family. Even so, he immediately invites them to leave Babylon, because he still redeems them.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but the path to a life of peace. Before deciding something, ask yourself what God says, and trust that his correction seeks your good. If you have drifted away, he still calls you to return.
exp.58:1:
It says that sin raises a wall between people and God. The "iniquities" are the wrongdoings and crooked deeds. "Hid his face" means that God does not look on them with favor or answer. "That he will not hear" explains the result: their prayers are not heard.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel. They thought God was far away or weak, but the verse before says that his hand has not been shortened nor his ear made dull. The problem was not God but the sin of the people: violence, lies, and injustice, as the following text describes.

For today: if you feel distant from God, do not first blame Him. Examine your life with honesty, acknowledge your sin, and return to Him. The Bible teaches that God forgives those who repent (1 John 1:9).
exp.61:9:
God commands that the way be prepared. "Go through the gates" means to leave the city. "Clear the road" means to make it open. "Level the highway" means to smooth out the main road. "Remove the stones" means to take away whatever is in the way. A "standard" is a banner raised high so that everyone can see it and draw near.

God speaks to Jerusalem after promising her that she will no longer be plundered. The verses that follow announce that her Savior is coming. Many understand that the return of the exiles is being prepared. Christians also see in this an image of the coming of Christ. Both readings have been held for a long time.

For today: ask God which "stones" are standing in the way in your life or in your church, such as resentment, laziness, or pride. Remove one this week. In this way you help others draw near to Jesus more easily.
exp.36:29:
God gives Judah a sign: this year and the next they will eat what grows on its own, what springs up without being sown. In the third year they will be able to sow, reap the harvest, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Hezekiah. The army of Assyria, under King Sennacherib, threatened Jerusalem and had ruined the fields. God promises to deliver his people and give them back a normal life. Scholars debate the details of those years, but the message is clear: restoration will come.

For today: when you go through a time of scarcity or little progress, trust that God can sustain you step by step. He cares for you today and prepares better times.
exp.36:24:
Here the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, boasts about what he has achieved. He says that he dug wells in foreign lands and drank their waters, and that with the sole of his feet he dried up the rivers of Egypt. The phrase "fortified places" refers to places that are strongly walled or defended. He feels unstoppable.

God speaks through Isaiah, and God himself quotes the proud words of the king. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel, and King Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. God answers by saying that this king has really only been an instrument in his hands, and that his arrogance is an offense against the Holy One of Israel.

For today: when you accomplish something, do not take all the glory for yourself. What you have and what you are able to do comes from God, so use your strength with humility and gratitude, and remember that whoever boasts of his power falls, but God upholds the one who trusts in him.
exp.59:9:
It says that people from other nations will help rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and that their kings will serve her. God explains the reason: he once punished her in anger, but now, out of his good will, he shows her mercy. The word "smote" means "struck" or "punished." The word "build up" means "rebuild."

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem, his people. The chapter announces a glorious restoration after the punishment. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as the return from exile and the rebuilding; others see it as a promise fulfilled in Christ or at the end of time.

For today: God disciplines, but his discipline is not his final word. If you are going through a correction or a failure, do not shut yourself in guilt. Return to God with humility, trusting that his mercy can rebuild what has fallen, and that he often uses unexpected people to help you.
exp.33:10:
He says that the land of Edom will be left abandoned, and only desert birds will live there, such as the pelican, the owl, the screech owl, and the raven. Some of these birds are hard to identify with certainty, and translations vary. The "measuring line" and the "plumb line" were tools for measuring: God measures the land, but not to build it, only to destroy it. "Desolation" means total ruin.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces God's judgment on the nations, and here Edom is especially mentioned (v. 5). The chapter shows that God is just and that violence and pride do not go unanswered. Many see in the language a poetic and exaggerated picture of judgment, not only a literal description.

For today: do not trust in your strength, your success, or your pride; only what God builds endures. Ask him today to give you humility and to teach you to build your life on his truth.
exp.63:0:
Here the prophet cries out to God with great urgency: "Oh that you would tear open the heavens and come down!" He asks that God intervene in a powerful and visible way. "The mountains would quake" means that the mountains would melt or slide down as if they were liquid before his presence.

The one speaking is the prophet, on behalf of the people of Israel. It comes from a prayer that remembers God's past deeds and feels that now he seems far away. Many understand that the people live in a time of ruin or exile, though scholars debate the exact moment. The people acknowledge their sin and plead for help.

Today we can pray sincerely when we feel God is far away. There is no need to pretend: we can ask him to act, confess our faults, and remember how he has helped us before.
exp.9:16:
God, whom Isaiah calls the light of Israel and the one who is holy to his people, will be like a fire and a flame. That fire will burn up in one day the thorns and briers, which are images of undergrowth: the people and the power that do harm. Burning means that it sets on fire, and destroying completely means that it wipes out everything.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria was like an axe or a rod that God used to discipline his people. But Assyria became filled with pride, as if the power were its own. God answers that he rules and that he will judge that arrogance. Scholars understand the undergrowth and the forest as the Assyrian army.

For today: do not boast of your achievements or your strength, because everything you have comes from God. And if you feel small before powerful people, remember that God is still just and has the final word.
exp.35:9:
Rabshakeh asks: "Am I now come up without the Lord against this land to destroy it?" In other words, he claims that the very God of Judah sent him to attack Jerusalem. The words "without the Lord" in the verse above mean the same as "without his permission or approval."

Rabshakeh speaks as the spokesman of the king of Assyria, before the envoys of King Hezekiah. He wants Jerusalem to surrender without a fight, and so he weakens their trust in God. There is no evidence that he actually received such an order from the Lord; it seems to be war propaganda. Isaiah 10 shows that God can use a nation, but it also judges that nation's pride.

For today: do not accept every voice that claims to speak in God's name. Compare what you hear with Scripture, especially when it tries to frighten you or pulls you away from trust in Him.
exp.52:9:
It says that, although the Servant of the Lord was innocent, God allowed him to suffer and to be crushed. "Crushing him" means beating him down, and "subjecting him to suffering" means placing him under affliction. "An offering for sin" is a sacrifice that covers guilt. After that sacrifice, the Servant will see descendants, will live many days, and the purpose of God will prosper in his hand.

Isaiah 53 is the fourth Servant Song. Here the prophet speaks, and in other passages it seems God is speaking. The verses before it show a righteous man who dies because of the people's rebellion. Christians see in this Jesus, as the New Testament does. Some Jews interpret it differently, for example, as referring to Israel.

For today: when pain seems meaningless, remember that God can bring life and good out of what looks like loss. Look to Christ with gratitude and trust.
exp.28:10:
It says that, for the people, the whole vision of God had become like a letter closed with a seal. If it is handed to someone who knows how to read, they answer: "I cannot, because it is sealed." The word "vision" refers to the message God gave through the prophets. "Sealed" means closed, impossible to open.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD to Jerusalem. God says that he sent them a "spirit of deep sleep": his people were spiritually dull and did not understand. The problem was not that the message was missing, but that their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow explain this: they honored him with their lips, but their hearts were far away, and their religion had become merely human custom.

For today: it is not enough to own a Bible or to talk about God. Before reading it, ask God for a humble heart willing to obey. In this way his Word stops being a closed book and becomes a light for your life.
exp.29:0:
He says God grieves over the situation of his rebellious children. "Woe" is an expression of sorrow and warning. They turn away from God to ask advice from others, and not from him. "Covering with a covering" means seeking protection and shelter, but not in the Spirit of God. In this way they keep adding sin to sin, that is, one wrong after another.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. At that time they were threatened by neighboring powers, and instead of trusting in God, they made plans to ally themselves with Egypt. The verses that follow make this clear: they went down to Egypt without consulting God. He warns them that this help would leave them ashamed.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we turn first when we are afraid or facing difficult decisions. Praying and seeking God's guidance in his Word before we act protects us from trusting only in human resources.
exp.7:17:
Isaiah says that he and the children God gave him are "signs and wonders" in Israel. "Signs" are things that point to a greater truth, and "wonders" are events that draw attention. All of this comes from the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of fear and political pressure in Judah. Many people were looking for help from mediums and spirits. Isaiah's children had names that carried a message (Isaiah 7:3; 8:3), and their lives reminded the people of what God was saying. In this way, his family was a living message for the people.

For today: our lives also speak. Let your way of living and of trusting God, even in difficult times, be a clear witness to those around you, one that rests on his Word.
exp.13:4:
It says that God broke the power of the wicked. The "staff" and the "scepter" are symbols of authority: the staff can also be a rod for striking, and the scepter is the sign of a ruler. The "wicked" are those who live without respect for God, and the "rulers" are those who dominate others.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. He announces that, when God frees his people from harsh servitude, they will be able to sing a mocking song against the king of Babylon. He refers to an oppressor who treated the peoples cruelly. Scholars debate whether he speaks of one particular king or of Babylon's arrogance in general.

For today: no unjust power lasts forever. If you suffer abuse or pressure, trust that God sees and knows how to bring oppression to an end. In the meantime, be someone who uses their authority to serve and care, not to hurt.
exp.47:14:
He says that God himself has spoken, has called a certain person, and has brought him, and for that reason that person's way will go well. The word "prosperous" means that things will go well for him in his task. The repetition "I, even I" stresses that everything depends on God and not on human strength.

The Lord speaks to Israel, who was about to live in exile in Babylon. He reminds them that he is the Creator and that he announced things before they happened. The "he" is not named here, but many understand it to be Cyrus, king of Persia, whom Isaiah mentioned earlier (44:28; 45:1). Others see it in a broader way, as God's plan to deliver his people.

For today: when God calls you to something, trust that he also sustains the path. Obey step by step, without relying only on your own strength.
exp.36:32:
God promises that the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, will not enter Jerusalem. He will not shoot even one arrow there, he will not approach with shields, and he will not build a siege ramp against the walls.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. Assyria had invaded Judah and threatened to take Jerusalem. Hezekiah had prayed with humility, and God answered with this promise. The verses that follow say that God would defend the city for his own sake and for the sake of David, to whom he had made promises. The text then tells how the Assyrian army withdrew.

For today: when a threat seems bigger than you are, bring the problem to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. He is faithful to his promises, and we can rest in his care, even when we do not always know how or when he will act.
exp.1:9:
It says that people should get into the rocks and hide in the dust to flee from the Lord. The "dreadful presence" is his presence that causes fear, and the "brightness of his majesty" is the shining glory of his greatness. It is a command given with both irony and seriousness: before God, no one can stand proud.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah. The people were full of idols and worshiped what their own hands had made. For this reason he announces "the day of the Lord," a time when God would judge human pride. Scholars debate whether it refers to a judgment near in history, to a final one, or to both.

For today: do not place your trust in things made by human hands, such as money, success, or your own strength. Instead, humble yourself before God today with sincerity, so that you will not have to hide from him later.
exp.5:12:
It says that although God's judgment will be very harsh and almost everything will be destroyed, a tenth of the people will remain. Even that remnant will pass through the fire again. But just as a cut elm or oak leaves a stump that is still alive, a stump will remain: the holy seed, that is, a remnant set apart for God, from which the people can grow again.

Isaiah recounts his calling as a prophet. God tells him that the hardened people will suffer judgment and exile. Isaiah asks how long this will last, and God answers that it will continue until the land is left desolate. Even so, this last verse adds hope. Some scholars disagree about how parts of the sentence should be translated, but the central idea of the faithful remnant is clear.

For today: when everything seems lost, remember that God still cares for what belongs to him. Trust that he can bring forth new life where you see only a cut stump.
exp.18:11:
God asks Egypt where its wise men and counselors are, the ones who prided themselves on their discernment. He challenges them to tell the king what the Lord of hosts has decided concerning their country. If they were truly wise, they would know God's plan.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message against Egypt. Pharaoh's counselors, in Zoan and Noph (Memphis), took pride in their wisdom and their lineage. But their advice failed, and the text says that God himself confused them, showing that no human wisdom stands above him.

For today: It is good to seek advice and to keep learning, but we should not trust our own intelligence or that of others as if it were the final word. Before deciding something important, seek God's direction in prayer and in his Word.
exp.39:20:
God asks four questions in a row to wake up his people. He reminds them that they already know the truth about him: they have been taught it from the very beginning, and creation itself shows it. The phrase "since the earth was founded" simply means since the world was created.

The prophet's message brings comfort to a tired and discouraged people. Earlier he speaks of idols that a craftsman shapes with wood and metal, and that must be fastened in place so they do not fall. Then he shows God ruling over the whole earth. The questions are meant to help the people remember who their God is.

For today: when you feel small or worried, take time to recall what you already know about God. Remember what you have heard about him and what you have seen of him in your life, and trust him again.
exp.51:12:
It says that God's servant will succeed and will be lifted up to a very high place. The words "magnified, exalted and raised up" repeat the same idea: great honor and exaltation. "Prospered" here means that he will act with wisdom and accomplish his purpose.

God is speaking, presenting his servant. Earlier, he called his people to leave Babylon with confidence, knowing that he would go before them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes it about him. Other Jewish readers have understood the servant to be Israel. What follows shows that before being exalted he will go through great suffering.

For today: when the path of obedience costs you or seems to bear no fruit, trust that God knows how to finish what he begins. Keep doing good with patience, without rushing or looking for shortcuts.
exp.6:10:
God tells King Ahaz to ask for a sign, that is, a proof that would confirm his promise. It can be as great as the deepest part of the earth or the highest part of the heavens. The word translated as "ask" here means asking for it. God gives him complete freedom to ask.

The LORD speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to the king of Judah. Ahaz was afraid because Syria and Ephraim (Israel) had joined forces against him. God promises him that this threat will not succeed, but Ahaz does not trust. Then he answers with a false humility: "I will not ask." In reality, it seems he was already looking for another way out, and the Bible shows him to be distrustful.

God invites trust, not living in fear. When you doubt, you can speak to him honestly and ask him for strength to believe. But avoid hiding your distrust behind phrases that sound pious.
exp.9:25:
He says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, will punish Assyria with a scourge. It will be like when he defeated Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will also lift up his rod over the sea, as he did on the way out of Egypt. A scourge is a whip used for punishment, and a rod is a staff of authority. The sea is the sea.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had been used to discipline Judah, but it became proud and cruel. God comforts his people by reminding them of two past deliverances: the one over Midian, in the days of Gideon, and the one at the sea during the exodus. It is not known with certainty which sea is meant here, but the comparison points to the exodus.

For today: when you feel that evil oppresses you and seems to have no end, remember how God has delivered before. Trust that he has the final word and that he does not forget his own.
exp.28:4:
It says that the great crowd of Jerusalem's enemies, called "strangers" and "terrible ones," will become like fine dust and like chaff, the light straw that the wind carries away. And this will happen suddenly, in an instant.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Ariel is a name for Jerusalem. First he announces that the city would be humbled and besieged, and then he promises that the armies that attack it will disappear, like a dream. Scholars debate which historical event is in view, perhaps the siege of Sennacherib, though there is no full agreement.

For today: when a problem looks huge and threatening, remember that God can change the situation in a moment. Hand your fear over to Him in prayer and keep trusting in Him.
exp.23:15:
From the farthest parts of the earth we hear songs of praise: "Glory to the righteous." But the prophet, instead of joining in with joy, laments. "Leanness" here is understood as wasting away or ruin; some translations say "I am wasted away." Then he repeats that the treacherous dealers keep betraying; "to deal treacherously" means acting with deceit and disloyalty.

Isaiah speaks within a long announcement of God's judgment on the earth (chapters 24 to 27). Before this, voices of praise are heard from a faithful remnant, but the prophet looks at the wickedness and the judgment that is coming, as the following verses show with their terror, pit, and snare. Scholars debate exactly who "the righteous" refers to.

For today: we can praise God and, at the same time, take seriously the sin and pain of the world. Pray with sincerity, without pretending, and ask for faithfulness for yourself.
exp.60:10:
It says that just as the earth brings forth its bud, and as the garden makes the things sown in it spring up, God will make righteousness and praise spring forth before all the nations. A new shoot is a bud, and the seed is what is sown. The nations are the peoples of the earth.

The one speaking seems to be God's anointed messenger, who comes announcing good news to the afflicted (Isaiah 61:1-3). Christians often see Jesus here, who read this passage in Nazareth (Luke 4). God will restore his people, clothe them with salvation and righteousness, and the nations will see that God has blessed them.

For today: you cannot force a seed to grow, but you can plant it and trust. Plant patiently works of kindness, truth, and prayer, and let God bring forth the fruit in his time.
exp.46:9:
Babylon felt secure in her wickedness. She thought, "None sees me," as if she could do whatever she wanted without consequences. Her wisdom and her knowledge led her astray, and in the end she came to see herself as the center of everything: "I am, and none else beside me," that is, "I, and no one else like me."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah against Babylon, a proud nation that had treated its people harshly. She trusted in her diviners and omens (signs they interpreted to predict the future). God announces that her fall will come suddenly, and that these practices will not save her.

For today: let us be careful not to think that no one sees us. God sees the heart. It is wise to be humble, to recognize that our knowledge is limited, and to ask God to guide us, rather than trusting only in ourselves.
exp.7:19:
To the law and to the testimony: the verse says we should return to God's law and his testimony, that is, to what he has said in his Word. If someone speaks and does not agree with that, the verse says there is no light in them, that they are like someone still walking in the darkness of night. The "pythones," the spirits or mediums who claimed to speak with the dead, are also mentioned here.

Isaiah speaks in a time of fear, when Judah was threatened by enemy kings. Some were suggesting that the people seek answers from mediums and fortune-tellers. The prophet replies that the people should consult their God, not the dead. The verses that follow show the distress of those who reject that guidance.

For today: when you hear opinions, advice, or teaching, compare them with the Bible. Before you decide out of fear or confusion, read Scripture and pray; there you will find firm light to walk by.
exp.9:27:
He comes to Aiath, he passes through Migron; at Michmash he leaves his baggage. This verse says that an enemy army advances step by step toward Jerusalem. First it arrives at Aiath (also called Ai), then it passes through Migron, and at Michmash it leaves its baggage and counts its troops. The phrase about counting the army means that it reviews and organizes them. These are names of towns north of Jerusalem.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He describes the arrival of the Assyrian army, which draws near quickly. Scholars debate whether this is a real military march or a poetic picture of what could happen. What is clear is the message: the threat seems enormous, but God still governs and promises to bring an end to the power that oppresses.

For today: when a problem seems to advance without a brake, do not look at it alone. Remember that God sees every step and has the final word. Pray with confidence and take the next step in faith.
exp.58:0:
It says that God is indeed able to save and indeed able to hear. "The hand is not shortened" means that his power has not grown weak. "His ear is heavy" means "his ear has become dull," like someone who can no longer hear well. Isaiah affirms that this is not the case.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who felt that God was far away and did not answer. The verses that follow explain that the problem was not God, but the sin of the people: violence, lying, and wickedness were separating Israel from their Lord.

For today: when you feel that God is not listening to you, do not begin by doubting his power. Examine your heart honestly, confess whatever needs to be confessed, and return to him, for he remains ready to forgive and to save.
exp.29:21:
It says that when God restores them, the people will treat their idols with complete contempt. "Defile" here means to declare impure something that was once revered. The silver images were overlaid with silver, and the "molten image" was a figure of cast metal, overlaid with gold. They will cast them away like a filthy cloth, a rag that was considered unclean under the law, and say to them: "Get thee hence!"

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking help in Egypt and in idols instead of trusting the Lord. Although suffering would come, Isaiah says God promises to guide them with his voice and lead them to repentance. Then comes the blessing of rain and abundant harvests.

For today: ask yourself what thing has taken God's place in your heart. When you recognize it, do not adorn or justify it: surrender it to God and cast it out with determination.
exp.30:1:
He also is wise, and not only the counselors of Judah or the Egyptians. If He decides to bring judgment, He will do it, and He will not take back what He has said. "Evil" here means calamity or judgment, not wrongdoing on God's part. The "evildoers" and "workers of iniquity" are those who do wrong, and the "help" is the aid they offer. The word "arise" here means that God will rise up.

Isaiah speaks to Judah in a time of military threat. The people sought an alliance with Egypt, trusting in its horses and chariots instead of trusting in God. The prophet warns them that this human help will not save them, and that God would act against those who leaned on it.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, connections, plans. Planning is not wrong, but above all we must seek God, ask Him for direction, and trust Him more than any human resource.
exp.44:20:
God invites everyone to present their best arguments. "Tell ye" and "bring them near" mean to declare and to bring forward evidence; "take counsel together" means to gather and deliberate. Then he asks who declared these things long ago, and answers: he himself, the Lord. He declares that there is no other God, that he is just, and that he saves.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah, addressing the nations and those who worship idols of wood, which cannot save. God shows them that he spoke clearly, not in secret, and that his promises come true. That is why he can invite them to look to him and be saved.

For today: when you feel confused or tempted to trust in things that cannot rescue you, such as money, success, or the opinions of others, remember that only God is faithful and saves. Pray sincerely today and entrust your need to him.
exp.58:9:
This verse describes a people who have lost their way, like a blind person feeling along the wall to find the path. Groping along is the picture: moving forward without seeing, feeling the way step by step. Even in broad daylight they stumble as if it were night. And the verse speaks of living in desolate places, a life without light or hope, almost like that of the dead.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God's people and includes himself in the confession with "we." Earlier in the chapter he says that injustice and crooked paths have drawn them away from God. Then he acknowledges that their sins are the cause of this darkness. It is not that God is unable to help; the problem is the sin that separates them.
