For today: when you feel confusion or stumbling, ask yourself humbly whether there is something you need to acknowledge before God. Confessing and returning to Him is the first step toward the light.
exp.10:0:
It says that from what seemed like a cut-down tree, the trunk of Jesse (the father of King David), a new shoot would come forth. The words for the young shoots that spring up from the roots are not used here; the verse itself speaks of a rod and a Branch growing from the roots. The idea of a branch that grows again after the tree has been cut is what this picture conveys.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Before this, chapter 10 announces that God would bring down the pride of Assyria, the way a forest is cut down. Now he offers hope: the family of David would look finished, but God would raise up a righteous king, filled with the Spirit. Christians see Jesus here, as the New Testament does; the original passage was addressed to Judah in a time of crisis.

For today: when something in your life seems cut off or without a future, remember that God can bring new life to grow where you no longer expect it. Trust him and keep taking small steps of faith.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that the watchman, the sentinel, answers someone who asks him about the night. He replies that the morning is coming, but that afterward the night returns. Then he invites them: the phrase "if ye will enquire, enquire ye" means that if you wish to ask, then ask, and "return, come" is an invitation to turn back and draw near again.

Someone from Seir, a region of Edom, asks the watchman how long the night will last, that is, the time of distress. Isaiah presents the watchman as a spokesman for God. His answer is not entirely clear, and scholars interpret it in several ways: it may speak of a brief relief followed by more trials. What is certain is that the invitation to return remains open.

For today: when you go through dark moments, do not settle for quick answers. Keep asking God, return to Him again and again, and trust that He always receives you.
exp.51:6:
This verse speaks of a messenger who comes running over the mountains with good news. His feet are beautiful because they bring joy: peace, good, and salvation. "Salvation" here means deliverance or rescue. The central message is: "Your God reigns!" "Zion" is Jerusalem, the people of God.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who are oppressed and exiled, whose name was mocked. God promises that He will make Himself present. The watchmen of the city see the messenger coming and sing for joy, because God will comfort and redeem Jerusalem. The New Testament quotes this text in Romans 10:15 to speak of those who proclaim the gospel.

Today we can bring words of hope to someone who suffers. You do not need to be an expert: it is enough to tell them, with love, that God has not abandoned them and that He reigns.
exp.32:23:
It says that in the city of God no one will complain of being sick, and that the people there will have their guilt for sin taken away. "Inhabitant" means someone who lives in a place, and "shall be forgiven" means they will be pardoned, declared free of guilt. "Her" refers to Zion, the city of God.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and distress. The chapter shows God as judge, lawgiver, and King who saves. The verses before this compare the enemy to a poorly rigged ship that cannot hold together. This verse promises a future of restoration. Some see it fulfilled in part in the deliverance of Jerusalem, and others see it pointing to the fullness of God's kingdom. Both readings are possible.

For today: God's forgiveness is the greatest healing we need. Today you can bring him your guilt with confidence, knowing that he offers a future of fullness.
exp.48:17:
God tells Zion, who feels abandoned, to lift up her eyes and see her children coming back. They are like a garment of honor and like the adornment of a bride. "I live" is an oath from God, and the word for "bind" means to be adorned or tied on, as with a belt. "To you" is simply "to you."

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to the people of Jerusalem, who were living in exile or in ruins. She had said that God had forgotten her (v. 14), and he answers that he has her engraved on the palms of his hands. This promise refers to the restoration of the people. Some also see a broader fulfillment in God's people of all times.

For today: when you feel alone or abandoned, remember that God does not forget you. Lift up your eyes, trust in his faithfulness, and wait for him to restore what seems lost.
exp.48:12:
This verse says that the whole universe should sing for joy: the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. The reason is that God has comforted his people and has compassion on the afflicted. The word "break forth" means to burst out with force in praise. "Afflicted" here refers to the humble and those who suffer.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Israel, who lived in exile, far from their land. God promises to bring them back from distant places. This song announces that hope. But in the following verse Zion feels forgotten, and God answers that he will never forget her, as a mother does not forget the baby at her breast. So the praise rests on God's promise, even though the people did not yet feel it.

Today, when you feel lonely or abandoned, you can praise God for what he has said about his faithfulness, even though you do not yet see the change. His comfort is real, and it can grow in you as you praise him.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that human pride has an expiration date. "Mankind" and "the mighty" refer to ordinary people and important people alike: everyone will be brought low. "Brought down" means knocked down or lowered. "The lofty" are the proud, the ones who look down on others, and their eyes will be humbled, meaning they will have to lower their gaze.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. He has just described injustice, luxury, and indifference toward God in the nation, and he announces that punishment is coming, including exile. The verse that follows shows the outcome of all this: God will be recognized as just and holy.

For today: ask God to show you the areas where you feel superior or self-sufficient. It is better to humble yourself willingly, asking forgiveness and serving others, than to wait for life to humble you by force.
exp.5:11:
It says the judgment will last until God has carried the people far away (the exile), and that the land will be left almost empty. The phrase about the abandoned land means the land left desolate, without inhabitants. Here "many" means that the places left empty will be numerous.

Isaiah has just received his call in the temple. God assigns him to speak to a people who will not listen. Isaiah asks, "How long, Lord?", and God answers with this announcement of destruction. Many connect it with the Babylonian invasion and the exile, though some also see a broader scope. But the next verse leaves a hope: a stump remains, a holy seed.

For today: when you see that your efforts to speak of God bear no fruit, remain faithful. God disciplines, but never stops preserving a remnant and preparing a new beginning.
exp.21:24:
God announces that the nail, fastened in a place that seemed secure, will be pulled out. It will break and fall, and everything hanging from it will be destroyed. "Fastened" means driven in firmly, and "will be ruined" means it will be spoiled and fall apart.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah, in a message about the officials of the palace of Judah. The nail represents a trusted man, on whom his family hung all their honor. Scholars disagree about who he is: some think it is Eliakim, others see a reference to Shebna. What is clear is that no human support lasts forever, and that what was said will come to pass, "for the Lord has spoken."

For today: value the strong people who hold you up, but do not hang all your security on them. Place your ultimate trust in God, who never fails and never breaks.
exp.37:12:
He says the man spent the night counting the hours, waiting for morning to come. He feels that his pain is like the attack of a lion that broke all his bones. He believes God is bringing him to an end, from morning until evening.

The words "quebró" and "trituró" mean broke or crushed, and "terminarás conmigo" means you will finish with me.

Here the speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, after he recovered from a serious illness. Earlier, the prophet Isaiah had told him that he would die (Isaiah 38:1). Here he recalls his anguish, when he believed his life was ending before its time. His language is poetic and very honest.

For today: there is no need to hide pain and fear from God. Hezekiah put them into words and brought them to God, and the text then shows that God responded. When you go through a difficult night, speak to him with sincerity.
exp.0:19:
It says that God sets two paths before his people. If they refuse to obey and persist in rebelling, they will be "devoured by the sword", that is, destroyed by war, by their enemies. The phrase "if you refuse" in the verse means "if they refuse". And it ends with a statement of authority: "for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it", that is, God himself declared it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he offers them complete forgiveness: their sins, red as crimson, would become white as snow. He asks them to decide. Then the text describes a city that was once faithful and is now full of injustice and violence.

For today: God's forgiveness is real and generous, but it also invites us to respond. Today you can identify one area where you have hardened your heart, speak with God about it honestly, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.4:19:
It says that God laments and warns with a "Woe" to those who reverse the values: they call evil good and good evil. The quoted word "Woe" in the source appears in your verse as "Woe unto them," so it stays as is. The verse's note on the old form of a word does not carry over, since that word does not appear in your verse. Light and darkness, and bitter and sweet, are images of what is right and wrong, of what heals and what harms.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks in God's name within the song of the vineyard (chapter 5). He denounces a people who mock God's judgment, pride themselves on their wisdom, and live in excess and injustice. The problem is not only doing wrong, but justifying it and changing its name.

Today we can honestly ask ourselves: am I excusing something the Bible calls sin, or criticizing something that is good? Measuring everything by God's Word, and not by fashion or by my own desires, protects my conscience.
exp.4:3:
God asks what more could have been done for his vineyard. He had done everything that was needed: he tended it, protected it, and planted it well. Even so, he expected good grapes and received wild grapes, that is, sour fruit with no worth.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf, with a song or parable addressed to the people of Jerusalem and Judah. He asks them to be the judges of the case. Later, the prophet explains that the vineyard represents God's people, who, despite so much care, answered with injustice and wickedness instead of justice and righteousness.

For today: God has given us much, such as his Word, his care, and his grace. We can ask ourselves humbly what fruit of love, justice, and faithfulness we are bearing, and ask him to help us change wherever it is needed.
exp.47:10:
He says that God will act for his own sake, so that his name will not be dishonored. "Polluted" is an old word that means stained or slandered. "Glory" here refers to his honor. God states that he will not share that glory with anyone else.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who had been rebellious and stubborn. Even so, God restrains his anger and does not destroy them completely. He has tested them in the furnace of affliction, that is, in suffering. Some understand this to refer to the exile in Babylon, though the text does not say so in those words. What matters is that God shows his faithfulness, not the merits of his people.

For today: when you fail or go through trials, remember that your hope rests on the faithful character of God, not on your perfection. Trust in him and live in a way that honors his name.
exp.21:10:
This verse says that the people of Jerusalem built a channel between the two walls, using the water of an old pool (the word translated here as "pool" refers to a pool or reservoir of water). They did all this to defend themselves, but they did not take God into account, the one who had made and shaped everything long ago.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy, and the people rushed to strengthen walls, houses and their water supply. They were preparing well, but they did not even think of seeking God. Afterward, instead of repenting, some of them said, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Scholars debate exactly which pool is meant.

For today: It is good to plan and prepare, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before facing a problem, let us bring it to prayer and ask God for direction.
exp.12:12:
God says that he will shake the heavens, and the earth will be moved out of its place. This will happen when his indignation is shown, that is, his righteous anger. "The Lord of hosts" is a title that shows his power over all things. "The day of his fierce anger" speaks of a moment of judgment.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The chapter announces judgment against Babylon, and the verses before it speak of punishing wickedness and humbling the proud. Many believe that the images of shaken heavens and earth are poetic language for a very great judgment. Some also see an announcement of the final judgment; interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God does not ignore injustice or pride. We can live with humility, trust that he is a just judge, and seek his mercy today.
exp.36:6:
God tells King Hezekiah, through Isaiah, that He will put a spirit in the king of Assyria. This means that God will influence his mind or his decisions. That king will hear a rumor, that is, a piece of news, and return to his own land. There he will fall by the sword, that is, by the sword.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by Assyria, and its messengers had mocked God. Hezekiah was distressed, and God calmed him. Afterward, the Assyrian king hears that Tirhakah of Ethiopia is coming to fight against him, as the following account shows.

For today: when you feel fear over a threat that seems bigger than you, hand it over to God in prayer. He can act in ways we do not expect, and He still rules over every situation.
exp.14:3:
It says that Moab's crying will be so loud that it will be heard from one town to another. Heshbon and Elealeh were Moabite towns to the north, and Jahaz was farther away, though its exact location is not certain. The armed soldiers are the warriors, who are normally brave, but now they howl, that is, they cry out in pain. Their life will be grievous to them means that each person will suffer deeply inside.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. He describes the fall of its cities with images of mourning: shaven heads, sackcloth, and streets full of weeping. Scholars debate when this happened, but the text shows that God rules over all nations.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, money, or security, because everything can fall. Let us place our trust in God and show compassion to those who suffer, as the prophet does in the following verse.
exp.13:27:
This verse only marks the moment when Isaiah received a message. The king of Judah named Ahaz is the one who died, and the word translated "burden" means a solemn word from God, almost always an announcement of judgment. It says this happened in the year that King Ahaz died.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and behind him God himself. The message is directed to Philistia, a region neighboring Judah. Many think the year was around 715 B.C., although the exact dates are debated among scholars. The Philistines were rejoicing because a power that had struck them had weakened, but God warns them that their relief will not last.

For today: let us not celebrate too soon when a problem seems to be ending. God governs history, so let us trust him and not changing circumstances.
exp.40:9:
God tells his people not to be afraid or give up, because he is with them. He says he is "your God who strengthens you," meaning the one who gives you strength. "I will hold you up" means he will support you, and "the right hand of my righteousness" is his right hand, a symbol of his power, which acts with justice and faithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, whom he calls his servant, chosen and descended from Abraham, "my friend." The people were surrounded by hostile nations and felt weak. God reminds them that he chose them and did not abandon them. Then he promises that their enemies will be put to shame and left powerless.

Today, when you feel fear or weariness, do not lean only on your own strength. Pray and repeat this promise, remembering that God is with you and sustains you. Then take the next step with confidence, even if you do not yet see the solution.
exp.36:18:
This verse says that the kings of Assyria threw the gods of the nations they conquered into the fire. Hezekiah explains that those gods were not real gods, but things made by human hands, out of wood and stone. That is why they could be destroyed.

The one speaking is King Hezekiah, in prayer, in the temple. Assyria was threatening Jerusalem, and Sennacherib mocked the God of Israel as if he were just one more of the idols of the nations. Hezekiah acknowledges what the Assyrians did, but he marks the difference: the LORD is the living God, not a human work. That is why he asks him to hear and to act.

For today: when something big threatens you, do not just stare at the size of the problem. Pray as Hezekiah did, remembering who God is. And check where you have placed your trust, because what we build or make with our own hands cannot save us.
exp.64:11:
God says he will hand over to judgment those who rejected him. The verse's wording points to a sword and a slaughter. Being put to the sword and bowing down to the slaughter show that they will not be able to escape. The reason: God called them and they did not answer, he spoke and they did not listen, and they chose what was evil in his sight and what he did not delight in.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a group of the people who had left him and worshiped false gods of luck and fate. Scholars debate the exact details of who they were, but the point is clear. God contrasts this group with his faithful servants, who will be blessed.

For today: God still calls. Today we can put our trust in luck, money, or success instead of him. Let us listen to his voice soon and answer with humility, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.26:10:
The branches of a tree dry up and snap off, and women gather them to make a fire. In the same way, this people will be judged: because they had no understanding, meaning they did not want to know or obey God, their Maker will show them no pity. The one who will show no pity refers to the people, and the phrase "will have mercy" means he will not feel compassion for them.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier, the text speaks of cleansing the sin of Jacob by removing the altars and the false idols, and of a strong city left deserted. Scholars debate which city is meant. Even so, the verse shows judgment on spiritual foolishness, and then God promises to gather those who have been scattered.

For today: let us not harden our hearts. Let us seek to understand God through his Word and prayer, obey him while there is still time, and trust in his mercy.
exp.48:5:
He says that God speaks to his servant and tells him that merely restoring the tribes of Israel is a "light thing." His mission will be greater: to be a light to the Gentiles, that is, to the nations outside Israel. The word "salvation" in the verse is the Hebrew-to-English rendering of a term meaning deliverance, and here it means salvation. The phrase "the end of the earth" means the most distant places in the world.

The one speaking is the servant of the LORD, who felt tired and without fruit. God responds by expanding his calling. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes this text with reference to him (Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47). Others also understand it as a reference to Israel as a people. The passage allows both readings.

For today: when you feel that your effort was in vain, remember that God sees further than you do. Remain faithful and share his light with those near you, trusting that he can do far more with your life.
exp.55:10:
They say the people's leaders are like greedy dogs whose appetite is never satisfied. They are also shepherds who do not understand what they are doing. Each one goes off on his own path, looking out for his personal gain, every one for his own side, without caring about the others.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that foreigners and outcasts would be welcomed into his house. Then he accuses the watchmen, or lookouts, of Israel of being blind and asleep, failing to warn of danger. That is why the people are left exposed, like sheep before wild beasts. The next verse shows that they think only of feasting and drink.

Today the message invites us to examine our hearts if we lead others, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace. Ask yourself: do I care for people, or do I seek my own comfort? Ask God for a shepherd's heart that watches and serves.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that the people should cry out and weep loudly, because the day of the Lord is about to arrive. That day comes as a total destruction, and it brings the power of the Almighty. "Howl" means a loud crying out, of pain and terror.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter begins with a message against Babylon. The verses before describe a huge army gathered for battle, and God uses these nations as instruments of his judgment. The verses that follow show the fear of the people: weak hands and melted hearts. Some see here a historical judgment on Babylon, and others also see a picture of the final judgment.

Today we can take God seriously and not live distracted. Instead of fearing without hope, we can examine our hearts, ask for forgiveness, and live with humility, trusting in the mercy that God offers in Christ.
exp.13:11:
It says that someone very powerful and proud fell from a great height. "Lucifer, son of the morning" is a brilliant title, like the star that appears at dawn. The phrase "cut down to the ground" means struck down and thrown to the earth. The words about weakening the nations mean that he ruled over and oppressed the peoples.

Isaiah directs this prophetic taunt against the king of Babylon (see Isaiah 14:4). The dead receive him in the grave and are astonished that he too is mortal. Some Christians, since ancient times, see here also a reference to Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of a human king. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: pride promises to rise, but it ends in a fall. Ask God for a humble heart, and do not seek your worth in power or success, but in serving Him and others.
exp.36:5:
Isaiah answers the messengers of King Hezekiah with a word from God: do not be afraid. The mockery they heard from the servants of the king of Assyria is blasphemy, that is, insults against God.

The phrase "to your master" refers to Hezekiah, and "said to them" in the verse is simply a way of saying that Isaiah spoke to the messengers.

Hezekiah was in a desperate situation, since the Assyrian army threatened Jerusalem. Rabshakeh, a senior Assyrian spokesman, mocked the people's trust in God. Hezekiah asked the prophet for prayer, and God answered him through him. What follows in the text shows that God took the matter into his own hands.

For today: when the words of others frighten us or mock our faith, we can bring the matter to God in prayer. He listens, and we need not defend ourselves in fear, because our confidence rests in his care.
exp.60:7:
God says that he loves justice, that is, what is right, and that he hates robbery mixed in with offerings, as if an offering could cover over what was stolen. For this reason he promises to support the work of his people with truth and to make with them an everlasting covenant, a bond that never ends.

Here God himself speaks, in a message of comfort for a humbled people. Before this, he promises to change their shame into honor and their sorrow into joy. Many understand that his justice is the basis of that restoration. Christians also see in this passage, which Jesus read in Luke 4, a promise that points to Christ, although there is discussion about how all of it is fulfilled.

For today: God does not want offerings or service while we practice injustice. Review your work, your dealings, and your money, and seek to be honest and fair. In this way your worship will be sincere, and you can trust that God keeps his promises.
exp.42:17:
God tells his people not to stay looking back. "Remember" and "consider" here mean clinging to what has already passed, turning it over and over. "The former things" are events from the past, such as the exodus from Egypt, which the earlier verses recall with the sea and the army that fell.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, who was in exile in Babylon. He reminds them of what he did at the Red Sea, but tells them not to live only on the memory of it, because he is going to do something new: open a way in the wilderness and give water to his people. Some understand that he is not asking them to forget, but not to limit God to what they have already seen.

For today: do not let old failures, pains, or even past successes keep you from trusting that God can do something new in your life. Give him today what has already passed, and take the next step with hope.
exp.31:10:
It says that the women who are calm and confident should tremble and be troubled. The word for "calm" refers to women who live without worry. Stripping off clothes and making themselves bare means taking off their fine clothing. Girding the loins with sackcloth means putting on rough clothing of mourning, a sign of sorrow and repentance.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to well-off women of Judah. They lived secure while the people were turning away from God. The prophet announces that the harvest will fail and the land will be overrun with thorns. Many believe this refers to a near crisis, such as an invasion or famine, but the text gives no exact date.

Today, comfort can dull the heart. Ask yourself: what am I trusting in, my possessions or God? Set aside a few minutes this week to pray with humility, give thanks for what you have, and ask God to awaken you wherever you have become indifferent.
exp.42:18:
God says he is doing something new, and that it will soon sprout up, like a plant coming out of the ground. He asks whether the people will not notice it. He promises to open a way where there is only desert and to make rivers run in the wilderness.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israel, who was in exile or was about to be. Earlier, he reminded them how he defeated the Egyptian army at the sea. Now he asks them not to stay bound to those memories, because he is going to act again to rescue his people, who were created to praise him.

For today: if you feel that your life is a desert, do not conclude that God has finished working. Remember with gratitude what he has done, but keep your eyes alert and your heart open to see the new thing he is beginning.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that the women of Jerusalem will lose their luxury and their beauty. Instead of fine perfume there will be a bad smell; instead of an elegant belt or sash, a broken rope or cord; instead of carefully arranged hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, rough sackcloth worn in mourning; and instead of beauty, marks of burning, perhaps from slavery or captivity.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. He warns that their pride, their luxury, and their injustice will bring judgment. The verses that follow show that war, death, and desolation will come, and the city will be left like a woman sitting on the ground, weeping.

For today: taking care of our appearance is not wrong, but let us not place our security or our worth in it. Let us ask God for a humble, generous, and just heart, one that values more what lasts forever.
exp.16:7:
It says that, in that day, the people will stop putting their trust in the altars, idols and images they made with their own hands. The verse of "groves" here refers to the Asherahs, sacred poles or trees used in pagan worship. "Images of the sun" were symbols or pillars dedicated to the sun.

God speaks through Isaiah. The message is about judgment on Damascus and the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), which had turned away from Him. After the punishment, only a small remnant will be left, like a few olives left on the tree. That remnant will again look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel.

For today: ask yourself what things you have made with your hands, such as your work, your money or your image, that have taken the place of God. Honestly, look again to Him, who is your true security.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that the palaces of Babylon will be left empty and in ruins, and that only wild animals will live there. The "wild beasts" and "dragons" of the verse are the creatures meant by that picture. The phrase about her time coming near means that her end is very close, and the phrase about her days not being prolonged means that it will not be delayed.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Babylon, a proud and violent power. God promises to judge her arrogance and her injustice. Scholars debate how and when each detail was fulfilled, since Babylon fell into the hands of other empires and declined gradually.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever. If you feel admiration or fear before powerful people, place your trust in God, who is just, and live with humility.
exp.39:17:
To whom then will ye liken God? Or what likeness will ye compare unto him? The question is rhetorical. It means "with whom will you equal him?" To "make a graven image" means to fabricate or put together a figure. The expected answer is: with nothing and with no one.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, probably because of the exile in Babylon, where idols were everywhere. Earlier he had said that the nations are like nothing before God. Then he mocks the idols with irony: a craftsman makes them, a goldsmith covers them with gold, and they must be fastened so they will not move. In this way he contrasts the Creator with objects made by human hands.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God: money, success, or the opinion of others. None of them can sustain us. Trust God as he is, not as you imagine him.
exp.34:8:
It says that on the Highway of Holiness there will be no lions or fierce animals to threaten those who travel it. "Fierce beast" refers to a wild and dangerous animal. "Redeemed" are those whom God has rescued. The way will be safe for them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who lived in fear and under threat. Before this, he announces that the desert will bloom. Here he promises a safe return to Zion, with joy. Many see it as a promise for the exiles of Israel, and Christians also read it as a greater hope of final restoration.

For today: if God has rescued you, you can walk with confidence even when the path seems dangerous. Bring your fears to Him in prayer and take the next step of obedience, remembering that He cares for His own.
exp.4:29:
He says that, on the day of judgment, the invading people will roar against Israel with a noise like the sea stirred up by a storm. If someone looks toward the land, they will see only darkness and distress. Even the light in the sky will be darkened.

"Roar" means to make a loud, deep, rumbling noise.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. He has just described the song of the vineyard, which represents Israel, and the injustices of the people. Then he announces that God will bring a distant nation as an instrument of discipline. The verses before this one paint their army as swift and frightening. Exactly who that army is, the text does not say here; many think of Assyria, but others see it in a broader way.

For today: God takes justice and faithfulness seriously. Instead of ignoring the warnings, we can ask him to show us where we need to change, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.40:22:
God challenges the idols and those who worship them. "Tell us what is to come hereafter" means: let them announce what will happen in the future. If they can do this, we will know that they are gods. "Or do good, or do evil" is a simpler challenge: do something, anything, that can be seen. "That we may be dismayed" means that we would be amazed.

The LORD speaks, "the King of Jacob," in a kind of public trial against the false gods of the nations. Israel lived surrounded by peoples who trusted in idols. God shows that only He knows the future and announces it before it happens. The verses that follow say the idols are "nothing," and announce someone whom God will raise up. Many think this refers to Cyrus, although the text here does not name him.

Today, in what do you place your trust: money, fame, your own plans? None of these can guarantee tomorrow for you. Rest in the God who truly holds your future.
exp.31:11:
This verse describes a time of mourning. The people will beat their chests, showing grief, over the fields that once brought them joy and over the vine that bore good fruit. The phrase about the pleasant fields refers to fields that were lovely and agreeable.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the comfortable and self-assured women of Jerusalem. They were living at ease, without thinking about the consequences of their spiritual neglect. The prophet announces that the harvest will fail and a great loss is coming. Some understand the beating of the chest as a gesture of mourning; others render the phrase differently, but the general sense is the same: deep sorrow.

For today: comfort can give us a false sense of security. It is wise to examine whether we trust in what we have more than in God, and to return to him with humility before loss forces us to do so.
exp.33:8:
It says that the land of Edom, the enemy of God, will be turned into a landscape of judgment. Its streams will become like "pez," that is, pitch or tar; its dust will be sulfur, and the whole territory will be like burning pitch, a fire that never stops burning.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing the judgment of the LORD upon the nations, represented in this case by Edom. The passage says it is "a year of recompenses for the controversy of Zion": God defends his people and corrects injustice. Many understand the images as poetic and symbolic language for total destruction.

For today: God takes evil and injustice seriously, and he does not leave them without an answer. We can trust that he will do justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. In the meantime, let us live with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.45:6:
Here the passage speaks of people who make an idol. They lift it onto their shoulders, carry it, and set it in its place. There it stays, unmoving. If someone cries out to it, it does not answer, and it cannot save anyone from their distress.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he asked to whom they could compare him. Then he describes how people pay a goldsmith to make a god of gold and silver, and then they worship it. God contrasts that motionless image with himself, who does act and does save. After this, he calls his people to remember and return to him.

For today: ask yourself what you are holding onto to feel secure, such as money, status, or success. If it depends on you to keep it up, it cannot keep you up. Bring your distress to God today, for he does hear.
exp.4:18:
Here Isaiah quotes the mocking words of people who challenge God. They say: "Let him hurry, let him get on with his work so that we may see it with our own eyes." They call God "the Holy One of Israel" almost sarcastically, as if his warnings were nothing but a tale. The plan or purpose of God is what is meant here.

The prophet speaks to the people of Judah, who lived in sin and felt secure. In the "woe" just before this, Isaiah describes them dragging their wickedness along like animals tied to a heavy cart. They mocked the judgment announced against them because God had not yet acted. Another "woe" follows, directed against those who confuse good with evil.

For today: do not mistake God's patience for indifference. If He delays in acting, it is to give us time to return to Him. Use that time with humility, instead of mocking or hardening your heart.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that all the people of the northern kingdom, called Ephraim, and the inhabitants of Samaria, its capital, will come to know or feel the judgment of God. The word "shall know" refers to the word that God sent. They speak with pride, which is arrogance, and with a stubborn heart, that is, with a heart that thinks itself superior.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he announced hope through the eternal kingdom of David. Now he warns Israel, the northern kingdom, which had suffered blows and damage. Instead of turning back to God, they responded with confidence in themselves, as the following words show: they would rebuild better, with cut stone and cedars.

Today, when losses or failures come, we can react with pride and say, "I will rise up on my own." It is better to stop, listen to God, and humbly ask him for direction before rebuilding.
exp.29:23:
The oxen and the young donkeys that work the ground will eat fodder of very good quality. It is clean grain, winnowed with the shovel and the fan, that is, separated from the chaff with tools that clean it. It is choice food, not leftovers.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who had sought help in Egypt and in idols instead of trusting in Him. This passage describes what will come if they turn back to God: they will abandon their idols, and there will be rain, abundance, and healing. Scholars read it as a promise of near restoration and also as a foreshadowing of future blessings.

For today: God cares even for the small details of our lives. If we set aside what has taken His place and trust in Him, we can wait in peace for Him to provide.
exp.62:4:
I looked around, and there was no one to help; I was amazed that no one took his side. So I acted myself: "my own arm brought salvation" means that his own power won the victory, and "my fury upheld me" means that his righteous anger kept him steady.

The Lord speaks, pictured as a warrior who treads the winepress, that is, the place where grapes are trodden. That image of judgment against the nations contrasts with the year of his redeemed. Then the prophet recalls God's mercies toward Israel. Some Christians see here a shadow of Christ, but the text speaks directly of the Lord and his people.

For today: God does not depend on our strength to save. He rests in his work and responds with gratitude, remembering his mercies.
exp.43:25:
This verse says that God makes true what his prophets announce. The phrase about his servant's word means that he confirms it and fulfills it. His messengers are the prophets who spoke on his behalf. God promises that Jerusalem will again have inhabitants and that the cities of Judah will be rebuilt. The idea of raising up the decayed places means that he himself will restore what has been destroyed.

The Lord speaks, presented as Redeemer and Creator. Isaiah writes to a people who would be taken into exile, or who were already living it, depending on how one understands the book. God shows himself superior to diviners and to the wise men of the world. In the following verse he names Cyrus, who would have a role in the rebuilding.

For today: when you feel that something in your life has been left in ruins, remember that God keeps what he promises. Trust his word and wait for his work, while faithfully doing what is yours to do.
exp.9:17:
It says that God's judgment will completely destroy the greatness of Assyria, pictured as a forest and a fruitful field. The phrase "soul and body" means, in plain terms, the whole person, every part of them, entirely. The image of a standardbearer who falls and collapses is one way to read the last comparison; others understand it as a sick person who wastes away. Both images speak of an end with no remedy.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks at a time when Assyria was a powerful empire. God used it to discipline his people, but Assyria filled itself with pride. Therefore the Lord announces that he will bring it down, and that a small remnant of Israel will once again trust in him.

For today: no power, success, or wealth lasts if it makes us forget God. Examine what you rest your security on, and rest in the Lord, who remains faithful.
exp.29:27:
This verse describes God's judgment with powerful images. His breath is like an overflowing river that rises up to the neck. Sifting with a sieve means shaking and separating, the way grain is sifted. The bridle in the jaws is like the one put on a horse to lead it where it does not want to go; here it causes the peoples to turn aside.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Assyria was the threat. The text promises that God will heal his people and judge the nations that oppress them. Scholars debate how this is fulfilled in detail, but the central message is clear: God rules over all peoples.

Today we can rest in the fact that God is just and in control. When we feel fear or injustice, instead of depending only on human resources, we can pray and trust in Him.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that God, who created and formed his people, speaks to them with tenderness. "Creator" and "Former" mean that God made them and shaped them. To "redeem" is to rescue by paying a price. The phrase "I have called you by name" shows that God knows them personally, and "you are mine" expresses that they belong to him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel (Jacob), a people suffering the consequences of their disobedience and facing exile. The opening word "But now" marks a turn: after judgment comes comfort. The verses that follow promise that God will be with them in the waters and in the fire.

For today: when fear reaches you, remember that you are not a stranger to God. Christians see in Christ the fullest redemption. Pray, "Lord, I am yours," and take the next step with confidence.
exp.23:19:
It says that the whole earth will stagger like a drunkard who cannot keep his feet, and will sway like a flimsy hut or shelter that the wind shakes. The guilt of its sins will weigh so heavily that the earth will fall and not rise again.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God over the whole earth. These chapters (24 to 27) are often called the "apocalypse of Isaiah." Some see them as a final judgment, others as poetic language that also speaks of judgments within history. The text says that human sin is the cause, and that afterward God will act against the powerful.

For today: do not place your security in things that shake, such as money, power, or success. Trust in God, who does not move, and return to Him with humility every day.
exp.3:1:
It says that, after judgment, God will do something beautiful for his people. "The branch of the Lord" is a new shoot, and "the fruit of the earth" is the harvest of the land. Both will be a source of beauty and glory, of excellence and honor, for those who survived, that is, the ones who remained of Israel.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. The previous chapter announces a harsh judgment on Jerusalem, so severe that seven women would seek a single man to take away their shame. This verse changes the tone and promises hope. Many understand "the branch" as an image of the Messiah, that is, Jesus; others see it as the restoration of the land, and some see both.

For today: even when we go through loss or painful consequences, God can make something new grow. Trust that his final word is restoration, not ruin.
exp.1:11:
It says there will be a "day of the Lord," a time when God will act with power against everyone who is proud, haughty, or thinks himself superior. "Exalted" means lifted up or placed very high; "brought low" means cast down and humbled. No one who makes himself great will remain standing.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks to a people who trusted in their wealth, their armies, and their idols (vv. 6-8). The cedars, the mountains, and the hills in the verses that follow represent everything that seems great and secure. Many understand this day as a specific judgment of God in history and also as a sign of the final judgment; there are different interpretations.

Today we can examine where we place our trust, in our success, our money, or our image. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on Him and treats others with respect.
exp.37:18:
It says that only the living can truly give thanks to God. "Confess" here means to praise or openly acknowledge what God has done. "Made known" means to be well known, to be made known. Parents, then, will teach their children that God is faithful and does what he promises.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks in a song after being very ill, almost at the point of death. God healed him and forgave his sins. For him, death no longer offers the opportunity to praise God in this life. So, grateful, he promises to sing and testify of his deliverance.

For today: if God has helped you through a difficulty, tell it out loud. Share with your children, nephews, nieces, or young friends how you have seen his faithfulness. Your testimony can strengthen their faith.
exp.42:22:
God tells Israel that they did not bring him the sheep and goats for their burnt offerings, and did not honor him with their sacrifices. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar. A grain or food offering was given to God, and incense was the sweet smoke that rose from the altar. God makes it clear that he did not burden them with those offerings or wear them out by demanding incense.

God speaks through Isaiah and addresses Jacob and Israel. He reminds them that he made them to praise him, but they did not seek him. It is understood that their offerings were empty or did not come from a grateful heart, though scholars debate the details. What is striking comes next: God forgives by his own grace, not because of their merits.

For today: do not use your religious activities to try to satisfy God. Seek him with a sincere heart, and remember that your forgiveness rests on his love, not on your efforts.
exp.45:2:
God calls his people: "Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel." He reminds them that he has carried and sustained them since before they were born, from the womb of their mother. The word "womb" here refers to the place where a baby is formed, and the idea of being carried means being held up and supported.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, Babylon had gods such as Bel and Nebo, idols that had to be carried on animals when defeat came. In contrast, the Lord is not carried by his people; he is the one who carries his people. He speaks to those who remained of Israel, probably in times of crisis and captivity.

For today: when you feel tired or insecure, remember that God is not one more burden. He has sustained you your whole life. Rest in his care and speak to him with confidence today.
exp.36:25:
Doesn't God ask the king of Assyria whether he has not heard that God planned all of this long ago. What is happening now, that is, fortified cities falling into heaps of ruins, is something God himself prepared and now brought about. The phrase "long ago" in the verse above means "a long time ago."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Sennacherib of Assyria, who had mocked God and boasted of his conquests. God reminds him that his victories were not his own achievement: God allowed them within his plan. In this way the king is shown that he is not the master of history.

For today: when the powerful or circumstances seem to control everything, remember that God still governs history. You can rest in him and live with humility, without boasting of your achievements, because everything good comes from his hand.
exp.63:5:
This verse says that all of us are like something unclean. Even our best works, the "justicias," are compared to a filthy rag, that is, a stained and impure cloth. It also says that we wither like a dry leaf, and that our wickedness (our sins) carries us away like the wind.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God's people. It is a prayer of confession. The people acknowledge their sin and their need for God. Afterward, the text asks that God, as Father and potter, not abandon them, because they are the work of his hands.

For today: do not rely on your own merits to be accepted by God. Humbly acknowledge your failings and come to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy and not in your own goodness.
exp.39:9:
This verse announces that God himself is coming. The phrase "will come with strong hand" means that he arrives with power. The words "his arm shall rule for him" mean that his arm governs and has dominion. His reward is what he brings, and his work is the fruit of what he does; both come with him, "before him."

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who faced punishment and discouragement. The message of comfort begins in this chapter. Messengers are told to cry out with courage: "Behold your God!" Interpreters debate whether the "reward" refers to the recompense for his people or to judgment, and perhaps it includes both. Right after this, the text shows this powerful God as a tender shepherd.

For today: when you feel weak or weary, remember that God is not distant. He is strong and he is near. Give him one specific worry today and trust that he cares for you.
exp.28:0:
This verse says that a painful warning is coming to Ariel, a name given to Jerusalem, the city where King David lived. "Woe" expresses grief and a warning of judgment. "Add year to year" means they kept on with their cycle of festivals year after year. "Let them kill sacrifices" refers to the religious offerings they continued to make.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. The exact meaning of "Ariel" is debated: it may point to the "lion of God" or to the altar where the sacrifices were burned. The people kept their rituals, but their hearts were far from God, and for that reason an enemy siege would come.

For today: keeping a religious routine is not enough if the heart is not with God. Today you can ask yourself whether your prayer, your church, and your customs come from a sincere love for Him, and ask Him to renew your heart.
exp.44:2:
God promises Cyrus, king of Persia, "treasures of darkness" and "hidden riches of secret places," that is, riches stored away in hidden places. The purpose is that Cyrus will know that the Lord is the God of Israel, the one who calls him by his name. Calling him by name means that God knows him and gives him a place and a task.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Cyrus is called "anointed," that is, set apart for a task, even though he did not know God. The verses that follow explain that all of this is "for the sake of my servant Jacob," the people of Israel, who were in exile. Many understand this to refer to the riches of Babylon, but the text gives no further detail.

For today: God governs history and can use anyone to carry out his plans. When everything seems closed off or out of control, we can trust that he is still at work and still caring for his people.
exp.9:26:
He says that a day will come when God will take away the burden and the yoke that Assyria had placed on the people, just as a weight is lifted from the shoulder or the neck of an animal. The word for "come to pass" means "happen," and "neck" is the part of the body the yoke rests on. "Destroyed" means to rot or be broken down completely. The word "anointing" is understood in different ways: some see it as the power of God, others as the anointed king who would come.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing the word of God to Judah, which was threatened by Assyria. God allowed that oppression to correct his people, but he promises that the oppressor will come to an end, as in the victory over Midian and the deliverance from Egypt.

For today: if you carry a weight that seems endless, remember that God can break any yoke in his time. In the meantime, trust in him, pray, and keep doing what is right, knowing that he has not forgotten you.
exp.36:23:
This verse says that the king of Assyria mocked the Lord through his messengers. He boasted that with his many chariots he would climb the highest mountains, up to Lebanon, and cut down its tallest cedars and its finest trees. The word "reproached" in the verse means insulted. The "choice fir trees" refer to the best trees (other versions say cypresses). "Carmel" here means a fertile forest.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Sennacherib, who had threatened Jerusalem and sent messengers to insult the Lord. God shows him that, although he feels invincible, he has actually offended the Holy One of Israel and does not have as much power as he believes.

For today: it is easy to trust in our achievements, resources, or strength and forget that we depend on God. Today we can stop, thank Him for what we have, and hand over our plans with humility, remembering that He is the one who sustains everything.
exp.23:21:
This verse says that the powerful will be gathered together like prisoners and shut up in a dark jail. The word "pit" in the verse names an underground cell, a dungeon where prisoners are kept out of sight. "Shall be visited" means that God will call them to account, that is, he will judge them, and this will happen "after many days," that is, after a long time.

Isaiah speaks in God's name within a prophecy about judgment on the whole earth. The "host on high" is understood in several ways: some see rebellious spiritual powers, others see proud rulers. Then comes the promise that the LORD will reign in Zion with glory.

For today: no human power escapes God, and his justice arrives in its time. If something troubles you because of injustice, trust that God sees it. Better still, live today with humility, without relying on your own strength.
exp.22:8:
He says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, decided what would happen to Tyre. His purpose was to bring low, to humble and strip of worth, the pride that rests on human glory. He also meant to pull down, to cast to the ground, the honourable people of the earth, those famous and respected figures.

Isaiah speaks in a prophecy against Tyre, a Phoenician city very rich from sea trade. Its merchants were treated like princes. The prophet answers the question "who decided this?": it was not chance or only the politics of empires, but God. Scholars debate which exact historical moment is meant, and that remains open.

For today: money, prestige, or achievements can give us a false sense of security. Today we can examine what we boast in and place our trust in God, who gives everything we have and sustains what truly lasts.
exp.48:22:
He says that God promises to restore Zion, his people. Kings will be their protectors who care for and raise children, and queens will be wet nurses. Bowing with the face to the ground and licking the dust are Eastern images of great honor and submission. The result is that Zion will know that God is the Lord, and that those who wait for him will not be put to shame.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israel, which felt abandoned, alone, and exiled in captivity. God answers that he himself will lift up his hand and bring his children back. Interpreters debate whether the language of kings bowing down is literal or a picture of the honor God would give his people. Many Christians also see here a look toward the Messiah.

For today: when you feel forgotten or are waiting for an answer, remember that God does not forget his own. Keep trusting him with patience, because his faithfulness does not leave those who wait for him ashamed.
exp.21:20:
It says that God will clothe Eliakim with another man's robe of authority, strengthen him with his belt (a sash is a wide band worn around the waist) and give him the power that man once had. Eliakim will be like a caring father to the people of Jerusalem and to the people of Judah.

God is speaking through the prophet Isaiah. The verses before this are addressed to Shebna, a high official of the palace, whom God removes from his position, apparently because of his pride. In his place, God calls Eliakim, whom he calls "my servant." The text does not detail everything Shebna did, so it is best not to assume more than it says.

For today: authority is an assignment from God, not a prize to show off. If you have responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, exercise it with humility and care, like a father who protects and serves.
exp.9:21:
It says that even if the people of Israel became as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant would return to God. The word for what is left over, the remnant, is the part that remains. The idea of turning back means they will come back. A decreed destruction is a punishment decided by God, and the judgment will be completely just.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who trusted in alliances with foreign powers, while Assyria was threatening them. The prophet announces that judgment will come, but also that a faithful remnant will stop leaning on the one who struck them and will trust in the Holy One of Israel. Some see here also a promise that Paul quotes in Romans 9:27.

For today: when the consequences of drifting away from God arrive, let us not trust in our own strength or in human support. Let us return to Him sincerely, because God is just and always leaves the door open for a return.
exp.2:4:
It says that when a society falls apart, people mistreat one another. Each one oppresses his neighbor. The young man shows no respect for the elder, and the common man, that is, the person of low standing, rises up against the person of rank and honor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the kingdom of Judah. He announces that he will take away its capable leaders, such as judges, counselors and skilled craftsmen, because of the people's injustice. In their place will come immature rulers, and the disorder will be so great that no one will want to lead.

For today: when respect and justice are missing, everything begins to crumble. We can start at home, treating elders and younger ones with honor, and praying for our leaders.
exp.43:23:
God presents himself with three titles: the Lord, your Redeemer, and the one who formed his people from the womb. That is, he knows them and cares for them from their very beginning. Then he says that he makes all things, and that he alone stretched out the heavens and the earth. In today's language, stretching out the heavens is like unfolding them, and "by myself" means that no one helped him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people who would be taken into exile. He has just told them that he blotted out their sins and redeemed them. Now he affirms his power as Creator, so that they will trust in him and not in diviners or human wise men, as the following verses show.

For today: the God who created everything and knows you before you were born can also forgive you and sustain you. When you feel fear or uncertainty, pray and rest in his care, instead of seeking security in other sources.
exp.62:11:
This verse recalls how God led Israel through Moses. With the phrases "the right hand of Moses" and "his glorious arm," the text speaks of God's power working through his servant. The phrase "dividing the water before them" refers to the Red Sea, which opened so the people could pass through. In this way God made himself an everlasting name, that is, a name that is not forgotten.

The speaker is the prophet, in a prayer of remembrance. The people are in difficulty and look back to the past. They remember that Israel was rebellious and that God had nevertheless rescued them. The questions in the passage express longing and ask that God act again as he did before.

For today: when you feel lost or weak, remember the times God has sustained you. That memory can become a prayer and renew your confidence that he remains faithful.
exp.42:5:
God says he will tell the north to give up its captives, and the south not to hold them back. In this way he will bring back his sons and daughters, even if they are in the farthest parts of the earth.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people scattered and discouraged. Earlier he had told them that he loved them and that they should not fear, because he was with them. This promise to gather them from every direction points first of all to the return from exile. Some also see it fulfilled in a broader way in the gathering of people from all nations into God's people.

If you feel far away, forgotten, or lost today, remember that God knows where you are and has not let you go. Pray with confidence, leave your fear in his hands, and return to him, because his love is seeking you and calling you by name.
exp.8:3:
He says that God broke the burden that weighed down his people. The "yoke" is the wooden piece placed across the necks of working animals. The "rod" and the "staff" are the oppressor's sticks, and the one who collects taxes by force is the tax collector. All of that was broken. The day of Midian recalls the victory God gave Gideon with very few men (Judges 7).

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, addressing God. Judah lived under the threat of the Assyrian invasion, and the people were in anguish. Isaiah announces that God will bring freedom, and right away he connects it to the child who is promised, the Prince of Peace. Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: if you carry something that crushes you, such as fear, guilt, or pressure, remember that God knows how to break yokes. Bring that burden to him in prayer and trust that he acts, even when you feel weak.
exp.63:10:
It says that the temple in Jerusalem, the holy place where our ancestors worshiped God and which was the pride of the people, was burned. All the valuable things were also lost. "Was burned up" means "was destroyed," and "were destroyed" is the same idea.

The speaker is the prophet, praying on behalf of the whole people. These words seem to come from a time after the temple was destroyed, probably by the Babylonians in 586 BC, although some scholars believe the prophet sees it in advance. The people confess their sin, ask for mercy, and remind God that they are his.

For today: when you lose something very dear, do not keep silent or shut yourself away. Speak with God honestly, acknowledge your failures if there are any, and remind him that you belong to him. He listens to honest pain.
exp.41:9:
This verse calls everyone to sing a new song to God and to praise him from the farthest places on earth. It asks those who travel the sea, everything that is in it, and also the islands with their people, to sing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he alone is the Lord, that he will not share his glory with idols, and that he announces new things before they happen. That is why the song is "new": it responds to the new thing God is about to do. Many understand it to refer to the Servant of the Lord in the previous passage, although how that is fulfilled is debated.

For today: when God shows you his faithfulness, do not keep your thanks silent. Write or choose a new song, and sing it today, at home or with others, to give him thanks.
exp.46:8:
This verse says that two calamities will come together and suddenly, in a single day: losing children and losing a husband. The word "orphanhood" here refers to losing one's children, and "widowhood" means losing one's husband. They will come in full, in spite of the "enchantments" and the "sorceries," which were practices of magic and of reading signs to foretell the future.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is addressing Babylon, pictured as a proud woman who thought she would be a lady forever. She trusted in her power and her magic, and she did not expect to be held accountable. God announces to her that her fall will be sudden and that her resources will not save her.

For today: do not place your security in your success, your intelligence, or any practice meant to control the future. Trust God with humility, because He is the one who sustains our lives.
exp.12:19:
It says Babylon will be so desolate that no one will live there for generations. Not even the Arab nomad will pitch his tent there, nor will shepherds bring their flocks to rest in a fold. It will be an abandoned place, like a warning.

Isaiah announces this message on behalf of God against Babylon, the proud great power that oppressed the nations. God compares it with Sodom and Gomorrah, cities that were judged. Some believe the prophecy was fulfilled gradually, through the slow decline of the city after the Persian conquest. Others see poetic and symbolic language pointing to the end of all human pride. It is interpreted in several ways.

Today it reminds us that no human power, success, or fame lasts forever. Let us ask God for humility and place our trust in what is eternal, not in what we boast of.
exp.27:17:
This verse says that the agreement the leaders of Jerusalem believed they had with death and the grave will be annulled. They thought they were safe, but that will not be so. "Covenant" and "agreement" both mean pact. A "scourge" is a punishment that comes like an overflowing flood.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to rulers who mocked his warnings. In verse 15 they said they had made a pact with death and were taking refuge in a lie. Many think this refers to political alliances, perhaps with Egypt, but the text does not say so precisely. God offers them, as the alternative, the firm stone that He places in Zion.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, in influence, or in excuses. Every false refuge collapses. Trusting in God is the only foundation that does not move.
exp.62:7:
He says that when God chose Israel, he declared: "Surely they are my people," that is, "truly they are my people." He calls them "children that will not lie," meaning children who would not be false to him or betray him. And he concludes: "so he was their Saviour."

The writer is the prophet Isaiah, who gratefully recalls God's mercies toward Israel. He describes what God hoped for from his people when he rescued them. The following verses show the painful contrast: even so, they rebelled. Some see here God's hope, and others see an expression of his confidence in choosing them. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God saved us, hoping for a sincere relationship with us. Today we can answer him with honesty, without pretending, and trust that his mercy lifts us up when we fail.
exp.29:7:
God tells the prophet Isaiah to write his message on a tablet and also in a book, in front of the people. The word "vision" refers to the message God gave him. "Latter day" means the final day or the future time. God wants this message to be kept in writing forever.

God speaks to Isaiah. Judah was looking for help from Egypt against its enemies, instead of trusting in the LORD. God warns that Egypt will be of no use to them. Because the people were rebellious and did not want to hear the truth, God orders the message to be left in writing, so that later it can be seen that he had spoken clearly.

Today we can learn not to run away from God's words when they make us uncomfortable. If you are about to make an important decision, ask yourself whether you are looking for a flattering answer or for the truth. Read the Bible with humility, and trust that God guides you better than any human support.
exp.31:16:
It says that righteousness produces good fruit. "The effect" is the result, and "the work" is the labor or fruit of righteousness. That fruit is peace, quietness (a calm, restful state) and assurance (trust without fear), and it will last forever.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived with injustice, fear and threats from other nations. Earlier he announces a righteous king (32:1) and a time when God will pour out his Spirit from on high. Then the dry land would bear fruit, and justice would dwell in it. Christians often see here an announcement of Christ's reign, though it also speaks of a restoration for Israel.

Today, do not seek peace only by avoiding problems. Strive to live uprightly: be honest, treat others well and trust God. True calm is born from living in what is right with the help of his Spirit.
exp.39:14:
It says that, compared with God, all the nations weigh very little. They are like a drop that falls from a bucket, or like the fine dust that clings to the scale of a balance and that no one takes into account. The islands, distant and great as they seem, are to Him like light dust.

In this chapter, the prophet Isaiah brings comfort to God's people. The verses before ask who could ever have advised or taught the Lord, and the answer is that no one could. God depends on no one. This encourages a people who felt small in the face of powerful empires.

Today, when governments, the news, or the pressure of the world make you feel afraid, remember that God is still greater than all of that. Rest in Him and pray with confidence, without ceasing to act responsibly.
exp.59:5:
It says that Jerusalem will be visited so heavily that multitudes of camels will cover it, like a great caravan. They come from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba, regions to the south and east of Israel known for trade. They bring gold and incense, valuable gifts, and they proclaim the praises of the Lord. "Proclaim" means they will announce them and make them known. "Dromedaries" are one-humped camels.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, who had passed through judgment and discouragement. He promises restoration: their light will come, and the nations will come. Interpreters differ about the fulfillment: some see the return from exile, others the Church, others a future time. Many Christians also connect this with the wise men who bring gold and incense to Jesus (Matthew 2), although the text does not say so directly.

For today: when you feel small or without hope, remember that God can change your situation. And the best we can offer him is our life and our praise.
exp.43:8:
This verse says that those who make idols of wood or metal live in vanity, that is, in something empty. Even what they value most in those figures is of no use. The idols themselves bear witness against their makers, because they neither see nor understand, and so they expose how absurd it is to worship them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he alone is God, that he announced what would happen, and that his people are witnesses to it. Now he contrasts the living God, who speaks and guides, with idols made by human hands, which can do nothing.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval. If they depend on us and cannot sustain us, it is worth returning to trust in God.
exp.18:18:
It says that a day will come when Egypt, an old enemy of Israel, will have an altar dedicated to the Lord in the middle of its land. The word "pillar" here means a column or monument set up as a sign, and "border" means the edge of the country. In other words, there will be a visible reminder of God right at the country's boundary.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, announces what God will do. Before this, he speaks of judgment on Egypt, but now he shows hope: Egypt will come to know the Lord. Scholars disagree about when this will be fulfilled. Some think of Jews and believers in Egypt centuries later, others of the time of the Messiah, and others of a time still in the future.

God does not give up on anyone, not even on peoples who seem most distant. Today we can pray for people or nations we see as enemies, trusting that God can transform them.
exp.18:10:
They say that the leaders of Egypt, those of the city of Zoan, are fools. The counselors who thought themselves very wise no longer know what to do; their counsel has vanished, meaning it has disappeared and is of no use. God asks with irony how they dare tell Pharaoh that they are descendants of the wise and of ancient kings. Zoan was an important city in Egypt.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message of judgment against Egypt. Earlier, the crisis in its economy is described: linen, nets, and fish. Now its leaders are pointed out, people who boasted of inherited wisdom but cannot understand what God is doing.

For today: human wisdom, prestige, or experience is not enough without God. Before trusting in our own plans, it is good to ask him for direction with humility and to listen to his Word.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that some people will be frightened and put to shame, because they had placed their hope in Ethiopia and took pride in Egypt. They will be filled with fear and confusion. Here, the things they boasted in or leaned on with pride were their own sources of security.

God speaks through Isaiah. Isaiah walked without his outer clothing and barefoot as a sign for the people. The inhabitants of the region, probably Judah, were seeking alliances with Egypt and Ethiopia to defend themselves against Assyria. God warns that Assyria would defeat them, and that confidence would end in shame.

Today we can ask ourselves what we rely on for our security: money, influence, a job, or powerful people. All of these can fail. It is good to use the resources we have, but our deepest trust should rest in God, who does not fail.
exp.10:5:
It says that animals that are normally enemies or prey will live in peace: the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the young goat, the calf with the lion. And a little child will lead them.

The phrase "fatling" in the verse refers to an animal fattened and raised in the pen.

Isaiah speaks of a future king, whom Christians understand to be Jesus, of the line of David. His justice is described first: he defends the poor and the meek. This peace is the result of his just reign. Some read the images literally, others as a symbol of peace between peoples, and others combine both ideas.

For today: if God promises such deep peace, we can practice it now. Seek to be reconciled with someone with whom you have had conflict, and treat them with justice and gentleness.
exp.31:13:
It says that the palaces will be left empty and the busy city will fall silent. The towers and fortresses will become abandoned caves, where wild donkeys will roam and flocks will graze and rest. And this will last "forever," that is, for a long time, until something changes.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah. Just before this verse, he rebukes the women and the well-off people who lived calmly and confidently in their comfort. He warns that their prosperity will be lost through God's judgment. But the next verse brings hope: "until" God pours out his Spirit and everything is restored with justice.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, because all of that can disappear. Let us trust in God and ask him for his Spirit, who truly renews life.
exp.56:10:
God asks his people: "Of whom were you so afraid that you were unfaithful to me and did not even remember me?" To "break faith" means to be disloyal or to betray trust. Here "kept quiet" means that God was silent and patient, without punishing right away. And for that reason, says God, the people stopped showing him respect.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Israel of seeking help in alliances with kings and nations, and also in idolatrous practices, instead of trusting in him. Some understand the "king" as a foreign ruler or as a false god; the text does not fully clarify this. Even so, God ends by promising good to whoever waits on him.

For today: when you feel fear, do not rush first to your own solutions. Before you act, speak with God and remember that his patience is an invitation to return to him.
exp.42:19:
It says that even the wild animals of the field, such as the jackals and the young of the ostrich, will give honor to God. The reason is that He will make water spring up in dry and empty places. The word "solitude" here means uninhabited, arid land. That water is for His people, whom He calls "my chosen."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a discouraged people who were living, or would live, in exile. He asks them not to remain tied to the past, because He is doing something new. This promise of rivers in the desert is understood as an image of rescue and return, and many believers also see it as a sign of the renewal that God gives.

For today: if you are going through a dry season, do not conclude that God has forgotten you. Bring that area of your life to Him in prayer and wait with confidence, because He knows how to open a path where we see only desert.
exp.27:11:
It says that God offered his people a path of rest and relief: that they should care for the weary and give him rest. That was the true peace God gave them. But they would not listen. The word "refreshing" means relief or comfort for someone who is worn out.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in Jerusalem to leaders and people who mocked his message. They treated him as if he were speaking only in endless repetition, "line upon line," as if to children. God says that if they will not hear his clear voice, he will speak to them through foreigners, and that will be judgment. There are different ways to understand who the "weary" is, but the general sense is clear.

Today, we can seek rest in God and also be rest for others. This week, help someone who is exhausted with a visit, a meal, or a kind word, and listen humbly to what God is saying to you.
exp.15:7:
This verse says that the fields of Heshbon have withered, and also the vines of Sibmah. Some "lords of the nations," that is, rulers of other peoples, trampled its finest branches. "Branches" are the shoots of the vine. Those vineyards once reached as far as Jazer, spread out into the wilderness, and even crossed over the sea.

Isaiah announces a judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The prophet speaks on God's behalf and points to Moab's pride as the cause of its fall. The vineyards were its pride and its wealth. Scholars do not agree on who the invader was exactly, so it is better not to state it. Even so, the prophet shows sorrow for Moab, not satisfaction.
