For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or achievements. All of that can be lost. Trust in God, who gives what truly endures, and ask for humility so that you do not live in pride.
exp.36:22:
God asks Sennacherib, king of Assyria, pointed questions: whom have you mocked and spoken against, and against whom did you raise your voice with such pride? The words that were used for insulting and speaking with contempt, and the phrase describing a haughty attitude, all point to arrogance. The answer is clear: he did it against the Holy One of Israel, that is, against God himself.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Hezekiah, who had prayed asking for help. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel, believing his army was unbeatable. God answers that these mockeries will not go unnoticed.

For today: when you feel small before a threat or a taunt, pray as Hezekiah did and trust that God sees everything. And remember that human pride, however powerful it may seem, is not above God.
exp.38:7:
Hezekiah answers Isaiah that the word of God is "good," meaning he accepts it as just. He then adds that there will be peace and truth in his days. Here "truth" can be understood as stability and security.

Isaiah had just announced that Babylon would carry off the treasures of the palace and some of the king's descendants. Hezekiah had shown his riches to the Babylonian envoys. Scholars debate his attitude: some see humility and submission; others see a somewhat selfish relief because the punishment would not fall on him. The text does not make this clear.

We can learn to accept God's correction without arguing against it. But it is also wise to think beyond our own comfort: our decisions today affect those who come after us. Let us ask God to give us wisdom to care for the next generation.
exp.36:28:
God tells the king of Assyria that his pride and his rage against Him have risen up to heaven. Therefore He promises to put a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth, the way one controls an animal, and to make him return by the same road he came.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for God here. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah and mocked the God of Israel while threatening Jerusalem. God answers King Hezekiah, who had prayed in distress, and assures him that the invader will not have the final word.

For today: when someone powerful seems to be in control of everything, remember that God is still greater. You can bring your fear to Him in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and trust that He governs even what you cannot control.
exp.33:15:
Isaiah invites readers to search the book of the Lord and confirm that nothing of what has been announced is missing. The wording "search" appears in the verse as "seek ye out," and the phrase about the animals gathering in pairs fits the verse's wording that none shall want her mate. The birds and animals of the desert come in pairs, because God commanded it and his Spirit gathered them together.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The whole chapter announces judgment on the nations, and Edom is named in a special way. The land will be left desolate and inhabited by wild animals. Scholars debate whether "the book" is Isaiah's own written scroll or a broader divine record. In either case, the message is that the word of God is fulfilled.

For today: you can trust that what God says is firm. Read the Bible carefully, compare passages, and rest in the fact that He keeps what He promises, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.36:19:
Here King Hezekiah asks God to rescue him from the power of the king of Assyria. He is asking to be saved from the king's power. He makes this request so that all the nations will know that the Lord, Jehovah, is the only true God.

Hezekiah prays in the temple. Assyria had conquered many countries and burned their idols, and now it threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah recognizes that those gods were only wood and stone, but that Jehovah is different. His request seeks the glory of God, not only his own safety. God answers quickly through the prophet Isaiah.

When you face a big problem, you can pray sincerely and ask God for help. And you can add a deeper desire: that, whatever the outcome, your life will show who God is and honor him.
exp.54:7:
It says that God thinks and acts in a way that is different from ours. The word "your" in the verse means "of you," and "saith the Lord" indicates that it is God Himself who is speaking. This does not mean that God is beyond understanding, but that His plans are greater than ours.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were living in exile and felt far from Him. Just before this, He invites them to seek Him, to leave the wicked way, and to return, because He pardons generously. This verse explains why they can trust Him: His forgiveness is greater than they imagine.

For today: when it is hard for you to forgive yourself or to believe that God welcomes you, remember that His mercy does not work the way ours does. Return to Him with confidence, even if you do not understand everything.
exp.6:5:
Here the plan of Judah's enemies is told. Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) say: "Let us go up against Judah, and vex it," that is, we will frighten it or conquer it. Then they would divide it among themselves and set up as king the son of Tabeal. We do not know for certain who this man was; he was probably not of David's line.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz, who was afraid. Kings Rezin and Pekah were threatening him, and God calls them "two tails of smoking firebrands," almost burned-out sticks. With this, God asks Ahaz for calm and trust, because the enemy's plan would not come to pass.

Today, many threats seem enormous and make us fear. Before acting in panic, we can pray and remember that God still governs. The plans that frighten us do not have the last word.
exp.2:19:
This verse continues a list of adornments worn by the women of Jerusalem. The bonnets were embroidered caps or head coverings. The ornaments of the legs were small chains or decorations for the ankles. The headbands probably were ribbons or jewels for the hairstyle, though translators do not fully agree. The tablets were small flasks of perfume, and the earrings were earrings or charms.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. He announces judgment on Jerusalem, whose women, proud and luxurious, stood for a society that had forgotten justice and trusted in its wealth. The Lord says he will remove all that splendor.

For today: examine what your security rests on. What can be lost, such as money or appearance, should never be your foundation. Trust God first.
exp.30:4:
This verse compares God's care to that of birds flying over their nest. It says that the Lord of hosts will defend Jerusalem, that is, protect it and cover it. Then it uses four verbs: defend, deliver, pass over, and preserve. "Passing over" seems to recall Passover, when God passed over the houses of Israel in Egypt, although some understand it simply as passing over the city to protect it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Judah was tempted to seek help from Egypt, with its horses and chariots, in the face of the threat from Assyria. Isaiah reminds them that Egypt is only human, but God is the one who truly defends his people. Then he calls them to turn back to him.

For today: when you are afraid or in need, do not place your trust first in human resources. Use your wisdom, but turn to God in prayer and rest in the knowledge that he cares for you with tenderness and power.
exp.9:12:
Here the king of Assyria speaks with pride. He says he accomplished everything by his own strength and wisdom. He boasts of having removed the bounds of the nations, of having robbed their treasures, and of having put down their inhabitants like a mighty man.

The bounds are the borders or limits between the nations. The phrase about those who sat on their thrones probably refers to kings or rulers seated on their thrones.

God had used Assyria to discipline his people, who had filled themselves with idolatry. But the Assyrian king did not acknowledge God; he credited himself with all the glory. That is why, in the previous verse, God says he will punish him for his arrogance. Here the king speaks, but the prophet Isaiah shows that God sees his heart.

For today: when something goes well for us, let us give thanks to God instead of boasting. Everything we have, strength, talent, and opportunities, is a gift from him.
exp.36:33:
God says that the king of Assyria will go back by the same road he came, and that he will not manage to enter Jerusalem. The verse's wording, "by the way that he came, by the same shall he return," expresses this clearly, so no further explanation of a word is needed. The phrase "saith the Lord" stresses that this promise comes directly from God.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to King Hezekiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah and was threatening Jerusalem with his powerful army. The people were afraid, but Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. God responds by assuring that he will protect the city for the sake of his own name and because of the promise made to David.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, do as Hezekiah did and bring it to God in prayer. He does not always act as we expect, but he is faithful to his promises and can change the course of what seems impossible.
exp.49:2:
God says that he clothes the skies in darkness, that is, he covers them with gloom, as if he were putting them in mourning. And that their covering, or their cloak, he makes like sackcloth, a rough, dark cloth that was used for grief and sorrow. It is an image of God's power over all creation.

The LORD speaks to the people of Israel, who felt abandoned, like a wife who had been sent away. God answers that the people were punished for their own sins, and that his hand has not grown too short: he is still able to save. If he can dry up the sea and darken the heavens, he can also deliver his own people. Some think the darkness recalls the judgment on Egypt, although the text does not say so.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, do not doubt his power. Acknowledge your mistakes, return to him, and trust that he can help you.
exp.64:5:
It says that God keeps a record of what this people has done, and that he will not stay silent. The phrase about his coming to act means that he will come to take action. The phrase about repaying into their bosom means that he will give them back what they deserve, so that they receive it in full. The bosom is the chest or lap, where what was given was received.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He addresses a rebellious people who practiced idolatrous customs, such as eating what was forbidden and considering themselves holier than others. Their religion was false and proud. Even so, the passage goes on to show that God preserves his faithful servants, for he will not destroy them all.

For today: God sees everything, including what we do in secret and the pride with which we look down on others. Instead of boasting of being holy, we can humbly ask him to cleanse us and teach us to treat others with mercy.
exp.59:0:
It says that God calls his people to arise and shine. The phrase translated here as "light" means light, and the word about the light having come refers to God's light rising like the sun at dawn. The glory of the Lord, that is, his presence and his beautiful character, is revealed upon them. They do not shine by themselves; the light comes from God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, which is discouraged and in darkness after hard times. Many believe he is addressing a people who are returning from exile or who are waiting for it. God promises to restore them and says that other nations will see that light and draw near. Some Christians also see here an announcement of Christ and his church, although this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if you are tired or discouraged, do not wait to feel strong before getting up. Fix your gaze on God, receive his light, and let it show in your kind treatment, your honesty, and your hope toward those around you.
exp.4:17:
It says that it will be terrible for those who drag their wickedness along as if they were pulling an animal with ropes. "Vanity" here means something empty or deceptive. "Yokes" are the straps by which oxen were fastened to a cart. The image is of people who carry their sin with effort, pulling it along and making it heavier each time.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God, within a song about the vineyard of Israel and a series of "woes." God accuses the people of injustice. In the verses that follow, it is seen that they mock God's judgment, as if it were a threat of no importance. Some understand that the ropes show how sin binds them more and more tightly.

For today: do not let yourself be deceived into thinking that a small sin does not weigh anything. If something is tying you down, bring it to God sincerely today, and ask a trusted person to help you loosen it.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that God will allow a great flood of strong and numerous rivers to fall upon the people. That flood represents the king of Assyria with all his powerful army. It will advance over all the channels of the river and overflow all its banks.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a time of military threat. The people had rejected the quiet waters of Siloam, which many understand as a symbol of God's gentle and dependable protection, and preferred to lean on alliances with human kings such as Rezin and the son of Remaliah. For this reason God warns that a much greater force would come.

Today, when we trust in our own securities more than in God, we may end up facing bigger problems. Let us take a moment today to place in God's hands the things we rely on most.
exp.29:2:
This verse says that the protection Judah was looking for in Pharaoh would not help them. On the contrary, what they saw as a secure strength would end up bringing them shame. The word "refuge" here means protection or shelter, and the shame of being let down is what the passage is describing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The leaders of Judah, threatened by a neighboring power, sent envoys to Egypt to ask for military help, without consulting God. Many understand that the threat came from Assyria. God rebukes them because they chose to trust in a human power and not in Him.

It is easy to look first for a human solution and leave God for last. Using the resources we have is not wrong, but it is wrong to place in them the trust that belongs only to God. Before deciding something important, pray, seek His guidance in the Bible, and ask for wise counsel.
exp.41:10:
It says that even the driest and most remote places should raise their voices in praise. The "wilderness and its cities" are the villages that live in dry lands. "Kedar" was a nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert, a descendant of Ishmael. "The rock" probably refers to Sela, a rocky city, though some believe it is a region or a high place.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. After announcing that he will bring new things, he invites everyone, even distant peoples, to sing a new song. God shows that his salvation is not only for Israel but for all nations. Then comes the image of God as a warrior who acts on behalf of his people.

For today: don't wait for your life to be perfect before praising God. Even in your "wilderness," in times of dryness or loneliness, you can choose to sing to him and thank him for his works.
exp.17:1:
It speaks of a nation south of Egypt, beyond the rivers of Cush, that sends messengers in boats made of reeds, or papyrus, along the river and the sea. God calls them "swift messengers" and sends them to a people that is "scattered and peeled," that is, tall and smooth-skinned according to some, or stretched out and polished. They are "terrible," feared from their beginning until now, "trodden down" or trampled, and their land has been spoiled by the rivers.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of Assyrian threat. Cush was probably seeking allies, and Judah could be tempted to trust in them. Isaiah announces that God watches calmly and will act in his own time. The details about the people are interpreted in several ways.

For today: before rushing after alliances or human solutions, pause and trust that God sees everything and works in his own time.
exp.0:2:
It says that even the simplest animals, like the ox and the donkey, recognize who takes care of them and where they are fed. In contrast, Israel, God's people, does not recognize the one who has cared for them. The word "crib" is the trough where the animal eats, and "doth not consider" means that they do not reflect or pay attention.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he raised and exalted his children, but they rebelled. With this comparison, God expresses pain and reproach: his people forgot where all good things came from.

For today: let us not take daily blessings for granted. Today you can stop and thank God for something specific, such as food, health, or family, recognizing him as the one who cares for you, instead of living distracted.
exp.9:1:
He says that some rulers made unjust laws so that the poor would be left without protection in the courts. They took the rights of the afflicted among God's people, preyed on widows, and robbed the fatherless. The phrase "to turn aside the needy from judgment" means denying them fair treatment; to take away what they had is to rob them of what was theirs.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the people of Judah, especially to their leaders. He warns them with "Woe!" because they were abusing their power. The verses that follow announce that God will call them to account, and neither their wealth nor their position will save them.

For today: God cares for the weakest and expects the same from us. We can ask ourselves whom we might defend or help, and treat everyone with justice and honesty, above all those who have no one to speak for them.
exp.58:16:
He puts on a suit of armor, like a soldier about to go into battle. The breastplate is the piece of armor that protects the chest, and here it stands for righteousness. The helmet is the head covering, and it stands for salvation or deliverance. The "vengeance" is like the clothing that covers him: it refers to God doing justice and correcting evil. The "zeal" is his intense and steadfast love for his people and for what is right.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of a people full of injustice, lies, and violence. No one was defending what was right, and God was astonished that no one stepped in. So He himself acts. This passage presents God as a warrior who rescues and judges. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of the work of Christ, although Isaiah says it in the context of Israel.

Today we can trust that God is not indifferent to injustice. While He is at work, let us ask Him for the courage to defend the truth and help those who suffer, without taking personal revenge.
exp.33:3:
It says that everything in the heavens that seems firm and everlasting is going to come undone. "The host of heaven" is usually understood to mean the stars, and some think it may also point to spiritual powers. The idea of things being "dissolved" means they will be worn away or broken up. The heavens being rolled together like a scroll means they will be folded up like an ancient parchment. The stars will fall like dry leaves from the vine and the fig tree.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing the judgment of the LORD on all the nations that oppose Him. Then the passage focuses on Edom, a people neighboring Israel. It is poetic and very intense language; not everyone agrees on whether it describes only a historical judgment, the end of the world, or both.

For today: do not place your security in anything passing, not even in what seems immense. Trust in God, who endures, and live today with humility and hope in Him.
exp.25:1:
It says that someone commands the gates of the city to be opened so that a righteous people may enter, a people who keeps the truth. "Keeper of truths" means a faithful people, one that guards and practices what God has said. "Salvation" in the preceding verse means deliverance.

Isaiah announces a song that Judah will sing "on that day," that is, at a future time of victory. The city is strong because God himself is its wall. Interpreters see it as Jerusalem or as an image of God's restored people. What matters is that the one who enters is the faithful person, not the one who merely boasts of belonging.

For today: it is not enough to say that we trust God; he invites us to live with integrity. Today, choose one truth from his Word and practice it in a concrete decision, even when it costs you. After that comes the peace that verse 3 promises.
exp.18:14:
It says that Egypt will get no benefit from anything its people do, whether they are the most important or the most humble. The phrase translated here as "head or tail" refers to those at the top and those at the bottom, and the phrase rendered "branch or rush" refers to the top of the palm tree and the reed of the marsh, another way of saying the same thing. The verb "may do" means that the work will serve a purpose or produce a result.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God and directs a prophecy against Egypt. The counselors of Zoan and of Noph (Memphis) had led the nation down a wrong path, and the text says that the LORD allowed that confusion, like a drunkard who staggers. Scholars debate exactly which historical moment the passage refers to.

For today: human wisdom, without God, can become confused. Before deciding, whether at home, at work, or in church, ask God for direction and listen to humble counsel.
exp.33:12:
It says that the palaces and fortresses of this place will be left abandoned. Where the powerful once lived, thorns, nettles and brambles will grow. In their place will live wild animals: jackals (dog-like creatures of the wild) and ostriches. The word for "palaces" in the source here refers to fortified palaces, which the verse above calls palaces and fortresses.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God on the nations, and in this passage in particular on Edom, mentioned in verse 5. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and appears in the Bible as an opponent of God's people. The picture of total ruin shows that no human power can withstand God. Some scholars also see in it a general picture of the final judgment.

Everything people build with pride is temporary. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security: in our riches and achievements, or in God, who endures forever.
exp.6:11:
Here King Ahaz answers that he will not ask God for any sign. He says he does not want to "test" the Lord, that is, to put him to the proof. It sounds very respectful, but God himself had offered him the sign.

Judah was threatened by two enemy kings, and Ahaz was already looking for support from Assyria instead of trusting God. So his answer seems like piety, but it was really an excuse for not obeying. Isaiah rebukes him, and God gives the sign of Immanuel anyway, "God with us".

Today we too can pretend to be humble in order to avoid trusting God or doing what he asks. When God invites us to believe him, true faith responds with sincere obedience, not with excuses that merely sound religious.
exp.54:11:
It says that God's people will go out with joy and be led back in peace. The joy is so great that creation itself joins the celebration: the mountains and the hills will break forth into singing, and the trees of the field will clap their hands, that is, they will applaud. The hills are low rises or small mountains. The people will be brought back again, that is, they will be led home.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were, or would be, in exile, far from their land, and God promises them deliverance. The verses before this one say that his word, like the rain, accomplishes its purpose. Many understand this going out as a reference to the return from Babylon, although some also see a broader promise of salvation.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, trust that God keeps what he promises. Write down one of his promises and repeat it in prayer, waiting with peace and gratitude.
exp.41:7:
He declares that God presents himself with his proper name: Jehovah, the God of the covenant, who is always faithful. He affirms that he will not share his glory, that is, the honor that belongs to him alone, with anyone else. Nor will he give his praise to carved images, that is, idols made by human hands.

God himself is speaking, addressing Israel, which lived surrounded by idolatrous nations. Just before this, he presents his Servant, who would be a light to the nations and would free the prisoners and those who live in darkness. Many Christians see Jesus in that Servant. God makes clear that only he can accomplish this and that no idol will do it.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts: money, success, or the opinion of others. Let us give God the gratitude and the first place that belong to him.
exp.0:28:
It says the people will be ashamed of the trees and groves where they used to worship. The word the text uses for the trees is one that some render as "oaks" or "great trees"; the word for the groves refers to sacred gardens or orchards. To "confound" means to leave someone in shame.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the people of Judah. They practiced idol worship under leafy trees, a common practice in Canaanite religion. God announces that he will judge the rebels, but that he will redeem Zion with justice. What today seems a source of security will later bring shame.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust, such as money, prestige, or success. If they are not God, sooner or later they will leave you disappointed. Return to the Lord, who is faithful and does not put to shame those who wait for him.
exp.21:2:
It says that the city's leaders, its "rulers," fled from the bow, that is, from the enemy archers. But it did them no good: they were caught and bound all together. Even those who had got far away were overtaken. The word "fled" here means running away, and "bound" means captured, taken prisoner.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from God about "the valley of vision," which almost everyone understands to be Jerusalem. The city was festive and confident, but it did not see the danger. Scholars disagree about which historical moment is meant: some think of the invasion of Sennacherib, others of the fall before Babylon. The text does not make this clear. Isaiah weeps for his people.

For today: let us not place our security in leaders, money, or our own plans, because they can fail. Let us seek God first, listen to his warning in time, and live with humility, not with false calm.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that God, who saved Abraham, makes a promise to the family of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel: they will no longer suffer shame, nor will their faces turn pale with fear. The word "redeemed" means that God rescued them and set them apart for himself.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he announces the end of the violent, the mockers, and those who twisted justice at the city gates, where judgment was made. Then he promises that the children of Israel will recognize God as holy, and that those who have gone astray will learn. It is a promise of restoration. Scholars debate exactly when it is fulfilled: whether in the return from exile, in future times, or in both.

For today: if you place your trust in God, who has been faithful generation after generation, you can face your fears with hope. Ask him today to give you calm and to help you live with honesty.
exp.41:20:
It says that God was pleased, because He is just and faithful to Himself, to make His law great and worthy of honor. "Was pleased" means that He did it with delight. "Magnify" and "make it honorable" mean to exalt it, to give it value and honor.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Israel, the servant who was meant to be a light, but who did not see or hear what God was showing him. Before and after the verse, the text describes a people who are blind and deaf, and also plundered and punished. God does not change His law because of the people's disobedience; His justice remains firm. Some understand that the verse also points to the perfect Servant, Christ, although this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: value God's Word as He values it. Read it with attention and ask Him for open ears to obey it, not only to know it.
exp.47:4:
God says that long ago he told his people what was going to happen, before it took place.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a stubborn people, whom he describes as having a neck of iron and a forehead of bronze. Many understand this to refer to the years of exile in Babylon, when people were tempted to credit their fate to idols. God shows that he alone knows the future and directs history.

For today: when something good comes into your life, do not credit it to luck, money, or your own effort. Stop and give thanks to God, who cares for you and works even before you notice.
exp.41:6:
This verse says that God's servant has the mission of opening the eyes of the blind and bringing prisoners out of prison. It also speaks of those who "sit in darkness," that is, those who live sitting in the dark, with no way out.

God himself, the LORD, the Creator of all things, speaks. He addresses his servant, whom he called, holds by the hand, and sets as a light to the nations. Christians see Jesus here; others also understand it as a reference to Israel. The blindness and the prison may be literal or spiritual.

For today: if God has given us light, we can be instruments of that light. This week, approach someone who feels trapped or hopeless with patience and kindness, listen to them, and pray for them.
exp.32:16:
This verse promises that those who have remained faithful will see the King in all his beauty, and they will also look out over a wide and distant land. "Beauty" speaks of his glory and splendor. The phrase about a distant land can be understood as an expansive territory free from threats, or as a faraway place that has been promised. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah at a time of threat from Assyria. Before this, he describes the righteous person who will live securely. Afterward, the people will remember with relief the fear they once knew, when foreign invaders were besieging them. Many see God or a just king in view here, and Christians also see Christ.

Today, when fear or injustice weighs heavily on us, we can live with integrity and keep our eyes fixed on God, trusting that He has the final word.
exp.7:10:
It says that God spoke to Isaiah with a strong hand, meaning with a powerful and clear pressure upon him. He taught him not to follow the way of most of the people. The phrase "with a strong hand" is rendered here by the verse's own wording, and the sense of being firmly instructed is what the verse conveys.

Isaiah speaks in the first person. Judah was threatened by enemy kings, and many people looked for security in alliances and schemes of conspiracy. God warns the prophet not to be swept along by that shared fear. The verses that follow call for trust in the Lord and reverence for him, not for human threats.

For today: when everyone around you is moving out of fear, rumor, or pressure, stop and pray before you decide. Ask yourself whether you are following the crowd or the voice of God in his Word.
exp.31:14:
It says that the desolation will last until God pours out his Spirit from on high. "Spirit from on high" is the Spirit who comes from God. Then the dry and empty land, the wilderness, will become a fruitful field, or fertile ground. And that fertile ground will be so abundant that it will be counted as a forest, that is, a land full of life.

Isaiah speaks to Judah. He announces that, because of their pride and their spiritual neglect, the city will lie in ruins, with thorns and empty palaces. But the desolation does not have the last word: this verse marks the turning point, and the verses that follow say that justice, peace, and security will come. Some see it partly fulfilled in the restoration of the people, and others also at Pentecost or in the future; Christians have understood it in several ways.

For today: if there are dry areas in your life, do not rely only on your own effort. Ask God to fill you with his Spirit, and wait patiently for his renewing work.
exp.14:6:
Here the text says that the Moabites flee with everything they managed to gain and keep. They carry their goods to the brook of the willows, a stream that many believe lay on the border of Moab. Some think it may be the Zered brook, but this is not known for certain. The words that are older forms, "carry away" and "have laid up," are rendered in modern English as "shall they carry away" and "have laid up."

God speaks through Isaiah in a prophecy against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. He announces a destruction that sends the people fleeing, weeping. The prophet himself grieves for them (v. 5), which shows that God does not take pleasure in human suffering.

Today we can remember that possessions cannot save us in times of crisis. It is wise to trust God more than what we have piled up, and to have compassion for those who suffer.
exp.46:12:
This verse mocks Babylon's trust in its advisers. It says she has grown weary of so many counsels, and it challenges them: let the ones who watch the sky, the ones who study the stars to predict the future, and those who announce the months now stand up and save you from what is coming.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Babylon, pictured as a proud queen. She trusted in astrology and enchantments, but God announces a sudden judgment that no divination will be able to stop. The verses that follow show that these advisers will not be able to save even themselves.

For today: when we are afraid of the future, let us not place our security in horoscopes, superstitions, or people who promise to control what is to come. We can bring our worries to God in prayer and trust Him, who truly holds our days.
exp.29:17:
He says that God does not hurry to punish, but waits for the right moment to show mercy to his people. The word "But" introduces this contrast, and "will be exalted" means that his goodness will be recognized and honored. "A God of judgment" is understood as a just God, who acts with righteousness. "Blessed" means happy or fortunate. Those who wait for him are those who trust in him.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. They rejected God's help and sought to save themselves with horses and military alliances, probably with Egypt. Isaiah warns them that they would flee in defeat. Even so, this verse shows that God does not abandon them: he is willing to forgive them and restore them.

When you feel anxious, do not rush to hasty solutions that leave God out. Pray, ask him for direction, and wait with confidence. His timing may seem slow, but his mercy is certain.
exp.40:10:
It says that those who become angry and fight against God's people will end up humbled and powerless. "Become angry" means they are full of rage; "fight" means they quarrel or contend with hostility. "Confounded" here refers to being defeated and left bewildered. To be "as nothing" is to lose all strength and importance.

God, through the prophet Isaiah, speaks to Israel, whom he calls "my servant." The people were surrounded by powerful nations and felt afraid. God reminds them that he chose them and did not abandon them, and for that reason he promises to be with them and to uphold them.

For today: when you feel attacked or afraid, do not respond with resentment. Pray, trust that God sustains you, and leave justice in his hands while you keep doing good.
exp.49:5:
Here the servant says that he gave his body to those who struck him. He offered his cheeks to those who pulled out his beard (the phrase is rendered here as tearing out the hair, meaning pulling hard on the hair or the beard). He did not hide his face from insults or from spit. The ones who strike are the smiters.

This is the third Servant Song in Isaiah. It speaks of a servant of the Lord who listens to God every morning, obeys, and does not turn back. Christians read it as a foreshadowing of Jesus, since the Gospels recount that he was struck and spat upon. Others also understand it as the experience of the prophet or of the faithful people. His confidence rests in God helping him and vindicating him.

For today: if you suffer for doing what is right, you do not have to repay evil with evil. Listen to God each day, and rest in the knowledge that He sustains you and knows your cause.
exp.63:2:
This verse recalls a moment when God came down and acted with power. The phrase about the mountains means that the mountains melted or trembled before his presence, as if they were nothing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, praying on behalf of the people of Israel. He seems to ask God to intervene once more, as he did before, probably recalling the exodus from Egypt and Sinai, although some see it as a more general reference. The people feel far from God and need his help.

For today: when you feel tired or without hope, remember what God has already done in your life and in his history with his people. Pray with confidence, asking him to act, and wait on him with humility.
exp.52:8:
The passage says that the Servant of the Lord was placed with the wicked in his burial, yet in his death he was with a rich man. The reason is that he never committed violence and never spoke deceit. The word "made" in the verse is rendered as "was appointed" or "was determined" in other versions, and "wicked" refers to those who live without reverence for God.

The passage is part of the fourth song of the Servant in Isaiah. The prophet speaks, and in other verses God also speaks, about a righteous servant who suffers because of the rebellion of the people. Christians see Jesus here, who was crucified with criminals and buried in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man (Matthew 27:57-60). Some Jews have understood it in another way, for example, as Israel.

For today: Jesus suffered while innocent, for us. When you feel unjustly judged, trust in him and seek to respond with truth and gentleness.
exp.29:10:
Here the people of Judah tell the prophets to get out of their way. The phrases "get you out of the way" and "turn aside out of the path" are ways of asking them to leave them alone. "Cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us" means that they no longer want to hear about God or his commands.

Isaiah denounces a rebellious people who preferred pleasant words to the truth. Judah sought political help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. That is why God, through Isaiah, warns them that this sin will be like a crooked wall that suddenly collapses.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only want to hear what comforts us. A good practice is to read the Bible letting it correct us, and to listen with humility to someone who tells us the truth with love.
exp.39:30:
This verse says that those who wait on the Lord will receive new strength. Their life is compared to eagles that rise high, and to someone who runs or walks without growing exhausted. The word "wait" here means trusting and expecting with faith, and the verse's words "they shall renew their strength" and "faint" show that people lose their strength when they grow weary.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a tired and discouraged people of Israel, who felt that God had forgotten them. Earlier in the passage, the text shows that even the strongest young people grow exhausted, but God never grows weary and sustains the one who is weak. Many scholars connect this to the time of the exile in Babylon, though the exact period is debated.

When you feel you have no strength left, do not rely only on your own energy. Take a moment each day to pray, read the Bible, and hand your burdens over to God. He renews you step by step.
exp.40:25:
God asks the idols and those who follow them: who announced these things from the beginning, so that we might know, and who said them long ago, so that we could say, "He is right"? And he answers: no one. None announced, none taught, none heard the words of the idols. Here "right" means that something is true or correct.

The Lord speaks in something like a courtroom case against the false gods of the nations. He challenges them to prove that they are gods by showing that they can announce the future. Shortly before, he mentions one who will rise up "from the north," which many connect with Cyrus, king of Persia, though the text here does not name him. Only the God of Israel declares what is coming and fulfills it.

Today too there are voices that promise security and answers, but they cannot sustain what they say. Before you place your trust in something, ask yourself whether it has proven itself worthy of that trust. Rest in the God who has spoken and has kept his word.
exp.21:9:
This verse says that the people of Jerusalem counted the houses of the city and tore down some of them to get stones and space, in order to strengthen the wall. The word "Jerusalem" refers to Jerusalem itself, and to fortify means to make something stronger so that it can be defended.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy army. The people made practical plans: they inspected the defenses, gathered water, and repaired the wall. The problem, according to the following text, is that they did not look to God, who had made and directed the city. They did what was human, but they ignored what was spiritual.

For today: it is good to plan and work hard in the face of difficulties, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before we set our plans in motion, we can pray and seek God's guidance, and then work wisely, trusting in Him.
exp.53:1:
It says that God tells Jerusalem, compared to a woman, to make the place of her tent bigger. She must stretch out the curtains, not hold back, lengthen the cords, and drive the stakes in firmly. The words "tent" and "curtains" refer to field tents. "Spare not" means do not hold back or be stingy with the space. The "stakes" are the pegs that hold the tent up.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, seen as a barren and abandoned woman, probably during a time of exile or great desolation. God promises her a large family, and so she must prepare for a growth she does not yet see.

For today: if God has given you a promise or a calling, prepare with faith before you see the results. You can pray, organize your time, learn, or make room in your life and in your church, trusting that God keeps what he says.
exp.42:10:
It says that the Lord is the only true God and the only one who can save. The phrase "I, even I, am the Lord" repeats the pronoun for emphasis: there is no doubt about who is speaking. "Beside me" means "apart from me," and "saviour" means one who rescues or delivers from danger and evil.

God himself speaks here, addressing Israel, his chosen people. It is like an imaginary trial: God invites the nations to bring forward their gods as witnesses, to see whether any of them announced what was going to happen. None can. Israel, however, has seen God announce and fulfill, and for that reason Israel is his witness.

For today: when you feel trapped by fears, guilt, or problems you cannot solve, do not look for your security in things or people who cannot fully save you. Go to God with confidence, and tell others how he has helped you.
exp.13:8:
It says that the place of the dead trembled at the arrival of this fallen king. Down there the spirits of the departed were stirred, and the ancient kings and rulers rose from their thrones to receive him.

The word translated here as the place of the dead is the Hebrew Sheol, which means the dwelling place of the dead, not necessarily the place of final punishment.

It is part of a poetic mockery that Isaiah directs against the king of Babylon, an oppressive nation. He imagines the scene of his arrival in the world of the dead. Many see in the passage a reference to a historical king; others also see a broader background about pride and the fall of Satan. Scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: power and fame do not save us from death or from the judgment of God. It is better to live with humility, using what we have to serve and not to dominate.
exp.41:23:
This verse says that Israel was handed over to thieves and plunderers, and that God himself was the one who allowed it. To "give for plunder" means to hand something over so that others can take everything. "Plunderers" are those who steal by force. The people acknowledge that they sinned against the Lord, since they would not walk in his ways or obey his law.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who are suffering invasion and ruin, as described in the verses before. He asks a question and answers it: the punishment was not an accident, nor only the work of strong nations. Many understand that he is announcing the exile in Babylon, although the text does not give all the details. Then it says that, even in the fire of the trial, the people did not understand or take it to heart.

For today: when difficulties come, instead of blaming only others, let us ask God to show us whether there is something we need to correct. His discipline aims to bring us back to him, and he always welcomes the one who repents.
exp.53:7:
This verse says that God turned away from his people only for a moment and with a small anger, but now he embraces them with a love that never ends. "I hid my face" means that he withdrew his favor and his closeness. The one who rescues and pays the price to set someone free is the one who redeems them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, which had suffered the punishment of exile because of its unfaithfulness. The people felt like an abandoned wife. God promises restoration and compares his faithfulness with the promise he made after Noah's flood: his mercy will not move, even if the mountains move.

For today: if you feel that God is far away because of your mistakes, remember that his correction is brief, but his mercy is eternal. Return to him with confidence.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that in God's holy mountain there will no longer be violence or destruction. The reason is that the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as completely as the sea is covered with water. "They shall not hurt" means to do harm or to destroy. "Holy mountain" refers to the place where God reigns.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf and describes the king who would come from the family of Jesse, the father of David. Just before this, the prophet speaks of fierce animals living in peace with the weakest ones. Many understand this as a picture of God's kingdom; others also see it as a literal picture of the renewed creation. Christians often see it fulfilled in Christ, but with a fullness that is still to come.

For today: if true peace is born from knowing God, we can seek him every day in his Word and in prayer, and let that knowledge soften the way we treat others.
exp.35:14:
Here Rabshakeh, a spokesman for the king of Assyria, tells the people of Jerusalem not to let Hezekiah persuade them to trust in the Lord. The phrase "make you trust" is rewritten here as "persuade you to trust." The message is: "Don't think that God is going to save you, because this city will indeed be handed over to the king of Assyria."

Jerusalem was under siege by the Assyrian army. Rabshakeh shouted in Hebrew so that the people on the walls would understand him and be filled with fear. He wanted to take away their confidence in God and in their king so that they would surrender without fighting.

Today too there are voices that present faith as an illusion when trials arrive. When someone tells you that trusting in God does no good, remember that He is faithful. Speak to Him in prayer and seek His word before giving in to fear.
exp.46:7:
God speaks to Babylon, personified as a luxurious and self-assured woman. The word "given to pleasures" means someone accustomed to luxury and comfort. She feels so secure that she says, "I am, and none else beside me," as if no one were greater than she is. She believes she will never lose her husband or her children, that is, that she will never suffer ruin or loss.

God himself is the one speaking, through Isaiah. He used Babylon to discipline his people, but she was cruel and believed herself eternal. For this reason God announces that her fall will come suddenly.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, success, or our own intelligence. All of these can fail. Let us live with humility, remembering that we depend on God and that our firmest confidence rests in him.
exp.24:8:
This verse describes a shout of joy from the people on the day when God acts. They will say, "This is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us." They repeat that they waited for the Lord, and now they rejoice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and the verse is the people's response to what God promised before: to remove the veil covering the nations, to destroy death, and to wipe away every tear. After that, the text speaks of judgment on Moab, a symbol of pride against God. Interpreters debate whether this is fulfilled at a moment in history, at the end of time, or in both.

For today: waiting on God is not wasted time. While you wait for an answer, remember what He has promised, pray with patience, and keep alive the hope that His salvation will come.
exp.36:31:
It says that from Jerusalem a group of survivors will come out, and that deliverance will come from Mount Zion. "Remnant" means those who are left, a part that is saved. "Deliverance" is rescue or salvation. And "zeal" here is God's burning commitment to his people and to his word: he himself will bring it about.

It is part of God's answer to King Hezekiah through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Assyria, and the people were afraid. God gives a sign: although now it is not possible to sow normally, the land will again bear fruit. Then he promises that the Assyrian king will not enter the city.

For today: when you feel surrounded by a great problem, remember that your hope does not depend on your own strength, but on God's faithful commitment. Rest in him and keep taking simple steps of obedience.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. It says that what Isaiah is going to relate is a "vision," that is, a message God showed him, and that it concerns Judah and Jerusalem. Isaiah was the son of Amoz. It names four kings of Judah: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

Here Isaiah himself speaks as the author, though the message comes from God. The kings mentioned reigned for many years, so his ministry covered a long and difficult time for the people. The following verses show that God rebukes his people for rebelling, and at the same time calls them to return to him.

For today: God speaks in real situations and at specific times. You can read the Bible knowing that its message is not a distant idea, but a word addressed to real people, and to you as well.
exp.37:11:
He says his life is leaving him like a shepherd's tent that is taken down and carried away to another place. He also compares it to cloth that a weaver cuts from the loom: his life seems to be cut off before it is finished. The phrase "is removed from me" means that his home, that is, his life, is being taken from him. He feels that God is ending him between day and night, very quickly.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks here, when he was seriously ill. This song expresses his anguish at the thought that he would die young, in the middle of his days. After praying, God granted him more years of life (Isaiah 38:1-5).

For today: when you feel fragile or see that life is passing quickly, do not hide your pain. Speak with God honestly, as Hezekiah did, and place your days and your future in his hands.
exp.13:16:
This verse continues the question asked by those who look at the fallen king: "Is this the man who..." It says that he turned the world into a wilderness, laid its cities in ruins, and never let his prisoners go home. "Laid waste" means he tore down and left in ruins. "Grave" is the tomb. "Prisoners" are the captives.

Isaiah presents a mocking song against the king of Babylon (v. 4). Those who see him dead are amazed that someone so feared now lies weak. Many believe he speaks of a historical king, and some also see a symbol of pride and evil in general. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: power used to oppress comes to an end, and God holds people accountable. We can use our influence, small or great, to help, to free, and to lift others up, not to dominate or harm them.
exp.25:0:
This verse announces a song that will be sung in Judah when God restores his people. It says they have a strong city, but their security does not come from stones; it comes from God himself. In this context, "salvation" means rescue or deliverance. The walls and bulwarks are the protection that God himself provides in full.

It is the prophet Isaiah who speaks, describing a future song of praise. It comes after the judgments against the nations (chapters 13 to 25). "In that day" refers to a time of future deliverance. Some see it fulfilled in part after the return from exile, and others see it also pointing to the final restoration. The verses that follow speak of the righteous entering and of peace.

For today: when you feel fear or insecurity, do not first look for refuge in your own resources. Remember in prayer how God has saved and cared for you, and sing to him, even if only quietly, with gratitude.
exp.6:14:
The verse says that the child promised, Immanuel, will eat "butter and honey." Butter here is curds or cottage cheese, a simple food. This diet continues while the child grows until he knows how to "refuse the evil, and choose the good," that is, until he reaches discernment.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz and the house of David. Ahaz was afraid of two enemy kings and did not want to trust God. Then God gives him a sign: a child will be born, and before he grows up, those two kings will be removed. The simple food suggests hard times, since the land would be poor. Scholars debate whether the sign was first fulfilled in the time of Ahaz and then in Christ, as Matthew understands it.

For today: even in times of scarcity, God is with us. Ask him for wisdom to choose the good, and trust him when you are afraid.
exp.35:1:
This verse says that the king of Assyria sent his spokesman, named Rabshakeh, with a great army from the city of Lachish to Jerusalem, where Hezekiah was king. Rabshakeh is not a personal name but probably the title of a high official. He camped beside the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field, that is, where clothes were washed and worked.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sennacherib had already conquered many fortified cities of Judah and was now pressing Jerusalem to surrender. The place mentioned also appears in Isaiah 7:3, when Ahaz received another message from God there. That can remind us that God had already spoken in that place.

For today: when problems seem like giants and surround your life, do not just stand there staring at the threat. Put your trust in God, who remains faithful.
exp.41:15:
This verse says that God will lead the blind by a way they did not know and by paths that are new to them. The "darkness" will become light, and the "crooked places" (twisted and difficult roads) will become level ground. In the end, God promises: "I will not forsake them," that is, he will not abandon them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he announces that he will act with power after a long time of silence. Then he speaks against those who trust in idols. Many understand the "blind" to be his people, who could not see their situation or God's way clearly. Others also see it as a promise for everyone who is lost.

For today: when you do not know which way to take, hand your confusion over to God and take the step you can already see. He promises to go with you and not leave you alone.
exp.36:7:
This verse tells how Rabshakeh, the officer sent by the king of Assyria, returned from Jerusalem and found his king fighting against the city of Libnah. The king had already left Lachish, another city he had been attacking.

It is part of the account of King Hezekiah and the threat from Assyria. Rabshakeh had insulted God in front of Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah had already said that God would act and that the Assyrian king would hear a report and return to his own land. Here events begin to move, but the outcome is not yet in view. The Assyrians are still sending threats.

For today: when God promises to help you, you will not always see the result right away. Between the promise and its fulfillment there may be new pressures. Trust what God has said and keep praying, as Hezekiah did.
exp.59:8:
This verse says that the isles, that is, distant lands along the sea, will place their hope in God. The ships of Tarshish, large trading vessels, will bring back the sons of Zion from far away, together with their silver and their gold. All of this will be to honor the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and the Holy One of Israel, who glorified his people. To "wait" here means to trust and to look forward in expectation.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, which had gone through judgment and punishment. Here he promises restoration: the scattered will return and other nations will join in worship. It is not known with certainty where Tarshish was; some think it lay in the western Mediterranean.

Today we can remember that everything we have, our work, resources, and talents, can be offered to God with gratitude. He also restores those who return to him.
exp.36:2:
Hezekiah sends word to Isaiah that this day is a day of distress, of punishment, and of mockery against God. He compares their situation to a woman at the point of giving birth: the children are ready to be born, but there is no strength to finish the delivery. The word "rebuke" here means humiliation or disgrace. "Blasphemy" means speaking with contempt about God.

The messengers of King Hezekiah speak, dressed in mourning clothes. Rabshakeh, spokesman for the king of Assyria, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. The king, with no human way out, seeks God in the temple and asks Isaiah to pray for the people who remained.

For today: when you feel weak and without a way out, do not hide it. Bring your distress before God honestly, and ask someone of faith to pray with you. He listens to those who trust in Him.
exp.27:28:
This verse says that the farmer's wisdom is not his own but comes from God. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" is a title for God that stresses his power and authority. "Counsel" means plan or way of acting, and "wonderful" means admirable. The small-seeded plant and the heavy threshing tool are farming items used to separate the grain.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who felt secure and did not want to hear God's warning. Earlier, the prophet describes how a farmer treats each seed according to its need: with gentleness or with more force. In this way he teaches that God also works with wisdom, and that his correction has a purpose and a limit.

For today: when you go through a trial, remember that God does not act at random. Trust that his dealings with you are wise, and ask him to teach you what he wants to form in you.
exp.13:6:
It says that after the oppressor fell, the whole earth was calm and at peace, and the people broke out in joyful song. The idea of "rest" and "quiet" here speaks of a deep relief after much suffering. The "song" in this verse is a shout of celebration.

Isaiah speaks in a prophecy against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4). It is a mocking song about his fall. That king had oppressed many nations with cruelty, and God broke his power. Some think it refers to one particular king; others also see a broader message about pride and tyranny. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God sees injustice and does not let oppressors rule forever. If you are suffering abuse or the abuse of power today, trust that God is just. And if you have authority, use it with humility and with care for others.
exp.40:1:
This verse asks a question: who raised up someone from the east, one who is "righteous," called him to follow him, and put nations and kings in his path? It says that God gave them "as the dust" before his sword, and "as driven stubble," that is, chaff that the wind carries away. "Rule over" means to dominate.

God himself is speaking, and in verse 4 he identifies himself as the LORD. He calls the nations to a trial, as in a courtroom, to show that he directs history. Many believe the "righteous one" is Cyrus, king of Persia, although some connect him with Abraham. It is a debate among interpreters. God reminds his people that they should not fear empires.

For today: when the news or powerful people frighten you, remember that God still governs. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.57:9:
It says that if we truly give of ourselves to the hungry, and help the suffering until they are fully satisfied, God will make our light shine even in dark times. "Pouring out the soul" means giving yourself wholeheartedly, not just handing over what you have left over. To "satisfy" someone is to leave them well fed and content. "Noonday" is the hour of brightest light in the day.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and carried out religious practices, yet still treated others unjustly. He explains that the fasting that pleases him is joined to compassion and justice. The promises of light, guidance, and restoration come after that change.

Today you can help someone concretely: share food, accompany a person who is suffering, or give them real time. Do it with kindness, without seeking applause. God cares for those who give themselves in this way.
exp.10:10:
He says that God, in a future time, will once again stretch out his hand to rescue the remnant of his people who have been scattered. The word "remnant" means the survivors, those who were left behind. The phrase "a second time" is often connected with the return from exile, although some see it fulfilled in Christ or still to come in the future. Christians interpret it in different ways.

The places named (Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the islands of the sea) show that they were spread across the whole known world at that time.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat of powerful empires. After describing the righteous king who would come from the root of Jesse, the father of David, he announces that God will gather his people together.

For today: God does not lose sight of those who are far away or scattered. If you feel distant from Him, trust that He knows how to bring you back.
exp.38:0:
It says that Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to King Hezekiah of Judah. He did this because he had heard that Hezekiah had been very sick and had recovered. "Recovered" means that he got better from his illness. The "gifts" were presents.

Here the narrator of the book of Isaiah is speaking. This comes after God healed Hezekiah (chapter 38). Scholars think Babylon was also looking for allies against Assyria, although the text does not say so clearly. What follows shows that Hezekiah showed all his treasures to the visitors, and God corrected him through Isaiah.

For today: after receiving a blessing from God, we may be tempted to boast or to trust in people. Let us ask for wisdom to give the glory to God and to guard our hearts well in the face of flattery.
exp.24:0:
Isaiah says that the Lord is his God, and that he will exalt him and praise his name. The reason is that God has done wonderful things. "Exalt" means to lift up very high. The "counsels of old" are plans that God made long ago, and "firm truth" means faithfulness that never fails.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, after the judgments announced in the earlier chapters. From the verses that follow, the fallen city is a symbol of a proud power that God brought down. It is not known with certainty which city is meant; scholars interpret it in several ways. Isaiah responds with a song of thanksgiving, because what God planned has been fulfilled.

For today: when you look back, make a list of the times God was faithful to you. Give him thanks for them in prayer. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens your trust when the future looks uncertain.
exp.53:3:
God tells a woman not to be afraid or to feel humiliated, because she will not be put to shame. He promises that she will forget the shame of her youth and will no longer remember the disgrace of her widowhood.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for God. The woman represents Jerusalem, or the people of Israel, who felt abandoned after the exile. Earlier, God asks her to enlarge her tent, because a great growth is coming. Then God presents himself as her husband and redeemer, that is, the one who rescues her and cares for her.

If you carry a shame from the past or a feeling of abandonment, you can hand it over to God. He does not define you by your failures or your losses. Trust that he can give you a new future, and prepare your heart to receive it.
exp.15:6:
This verse says that all the people of Moab will weep and cry out in pain. Where the source explained one word as giving strong cries of anguish, that idea is carried by "howl" in the verse above. The "foundations of Kir-hareseth" refer to what supported that fortified city of Moab, probably its raisin cakes or its firm base (scholars interpret this in different ways). Being "stricken" speaks of a very hard blow.

Isaiah, speaking on behalf of God, announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The cause is their pride and their lies, mentioned just before. But the passage also shows hope: it speaks of a just throne in the tent of David, and even the prophet laments over Moab.

For today: pride may seem strong, but it does not hold up. We can examine what we place our security in, and ask God for a humble heart that also grieves for those who suffer.
exp.65:3:
God says that He too will choose the punishment that fits them: He will bring upon them the very thing they feared. The reason is that He called them and no one answered; He spoke and they would not listen. They did evil in His sight and chose what does not please Him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people practiced a religion that was only for show: they offered sacrifices, but with their hearts far from God, and for this reason He compares those offerings to detestable things. God contrasts this group with those who are humble and tremble at His word, that is, who take it seriously with reverence.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly answer when God speaks to us through His Word. Before carrying out religious acts, it is good to listen with humility and obey. God looks for an attentive heart, not just ceremonies.
exp.65:14:
It says that God will come with fire, and that his chariots will be swift and powerful like a whirlwind. The word "render" means to give back or repay: his anger will fall with its full force. "Rebuke" is his correction or judgment, which here is compared to flames.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. Shortly before, he promises comfort to his faithful servants, as a mother comforts her child. Then he announces judgment against his enemies and against those who practice a false religion, mixed with customs that God calls an abomination. Thus the same God who comforts also does justice.

For today: do not take God lightly or use religion as a facade. Live with sincerity, trust that he will do justice, and rest in his comfort.
exp.64:22:
God promises that his people will no longer live with efforts that come to nothing. What they work for, they will enjoy. Nor will they have children for sorrow or disaster, since the phrase about bearing children for a curse speaks of raising children who suffer calamity. They and their descendants will be blessed by the Lord.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises new heavens and a new earth to a people who had suffered losses, injustice and exile. Before, others ate what they had planted; now God gives them back peace, security and joy. Some see here a complete future fulfillment, others also see a foretaste in the restoration of Israel.

For today: when work or family wear you down or worry you, entrust them to God in prayer. He promises a future where nothing is lost. In the meantime, work with faith, knowing that God sees and cares for your effort.
exp.58:14:
Here the verse says that truth was lost in society: it was no longer allowed to act. Whoever turned away from evil was left as prey, that is, they were attacked or stripped of what they had. God saw this, and it grieved him that there was no justice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and describes their sin: lies, slander, and corruption in the public square, where justice was supposed to be done. This explains why God seems far away. The verses that follow show that God does not simply watch: he himself acts to save and to correct.

Today, if you are called to be honest and that costs you, do not be discouraged. God sees when truth is trampled and is not indifferent. Even so, keep speaking the truth with respect, and seek to be just in your work, your family, and your community.
exp.20:12:
Here God announces a "burden", that is, a message of judgment, concerning Arabia. He says that the travelling companies of Dedanim, who were merchants with caravans, will have to spend the night hidden in the thickets or among the bushes, far from the known roads, because they are fleeing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The verses that follow show that these travelers are escaping from war: swords, bows, and battle. The people of Tema are asked to bring them water and bread. Scholars do not know with certainty which invasion is in view; it is often linked to some military advance of the period, but this is debated.

For today: when someone arrives weary and fleeing from a difficulty, God calls us to offer concrete help, such as a plate of food or a cup of water. Small acts of kindness reflect his care for those who suffer.
exp.29:13:
It says God will break this sin and those who lean on it, the way a clay pot is broken: without pity, and into pieces so small that none of them is any use. Small fragments are tiny bits of broken pottery. A shard is a piece of baked clay. Not even one fragment is good for carrying coals from the fire or for drawing water from a well.

The Holy One of Israel speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah had rejected his word and trusted in violence, injustice and political alliances, probably seeking help from Egypt, as the chapter suggests. God warns that this false security will suddenly collapse. He then reminds them that their strength lay in quietness and in trusting Him, but they refused.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are resting our security on: money, influence or our own plans. In humility, let us ask God to teach us to rest in Him and to obey His word before what we hold on to breaks.
exp.18:0:
This verse says that God speaks of a judgment against Egypt. The word "burden" means a heavy message, a serious warning. The Lord appears riding on a swift cloud, that is, he arrives quickly and no one can stop him. The Egyptian idols shall be moved, that is, they tremble before him. The phrase about the heart melting means that the courage of the Egyptians melts away like wax.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, announcing what Jehovah will do. Egypt was a power with many gods and great confidence in its strength. Some in Judah looked to Egypt for protection against other empires. Scholars disagree about the exact historical moment this prophecy refers to.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, power or security, begins to totter when he acts. We can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and return to resting in him.
exp.60:9:
It says that the one speaking will be filled with a deep joy in God. The reason is that God himself has clothed him with "garments of salvation," that is, of salvation, and has covered him with a "mantle of righteousness." He compares him to a bridegroom who dresses up for his wedding and to a bride adorned with her jewels, or in other words, decked out with her jewels. Adorned means dressed and decorated.

In this passage the one speaking is the prophet, or the anointed servant of Isaiah 61:1-3, and it can also be understood as the voice of the restored people. Some see here a reference to Jesus; others, to Israel. The context speaks of God's eternal covenant and of his people being recognized as blessed. That is why this song is a response of gratitude.

For today: salvation and righteousness are not earned, they are received as a gift. When you feel unworthy, remember that God clothes you. Give thanks to him today with a song, a prayer, or a testimony.
exp.20:10:
Here is what the verse says about Isaiah 21:11. It tells us that God gives Isaiah a heavy message, an "oracle", concerning Dumah. Someone calls out to the prophet from Seir, a region of Edom: "Watchman, what of the night?" That is, "Watchman, how much longer until this darkness ends?" The question is repeated because of the distress behind it.

The prophet stands like a watchman, waiting for the word of God. Dumah may refer to Edom or to a place in Arabia; it is not known for certain. The one asking lives in a time of oppression and wants to know whether relief will come. The watchman's answer is ambiguous: morning is coming, but so is the night. Many read it as an invitation to keep seeking God.

For today: when you go through a difficult night, do not keep the question locked inside. Bring it to God, stay attentive to his word, and return to him with patience, even when the answer is not immediate or complete.
exp.47:11:
God asks his people to listen to him. He reminds them that they belong to him, because he called them. When he says "I am the first, I also am the last," he declares that he has always existed and will always exist. Nobody was before him, and nobody will come after him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people live through trials, and God says he chose them in the furnace of affliction. The verses that follow show his power as Creator and announce that he will act against Babylon. God wants Israel to trust in him and not in idols or human powers.

For today: when you go through a trial, remember that God did not begin with you and will not leave you unfinished. He is the first and the last, and your story is in his hands. Take a few minutes today to listen to him in prayer and in his Word, and rest in his care.
exp.50:11:
It is God himself who comforts his people. "I, even I" repeats the phrase to give force and assurance. Then he asks, almost tenderly: who are you to be afraid of a mere human being? The verse speaks of a man who will die, and of a son of man who will fade like grass, which soon withers and disappears.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were under pressure and fear before powerful oppressors. God reminds them how he opened the sea to rescue his own, and he promises that the redeemed will return to Zion with singing. His purpose is that they look to their Maker and not to their enemies.

When fear of people overwhelms you, remember who holds you up. Pray honestly, and place your fear before the power and faithfulness of God, which is greater.
exp.43:17:
They do not know nor understand those who make and worship idols. The verse of the word meaning covered over, like a crust that covers the eyes, is left out here. Because of this, they cannot see the truth, and their hearts cannot grasp it. It is a spiritual blindness that they themselves do not notice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel. He mocks idolatry with sadness: a man uses half of a log to warm himself and cook, and with the rest he makes a god and asks it for help. The verse explains why he does something so absurd: his heart is closed and deceived.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we put in place of God: money, success, approval. Ask God to open your eyes, and look honestly at whether you trust in something that cannot save you.
exp.34:7:
It says that God will open a special road, a raised and well-marked highway, called "The Way of Holiness." "Unclean" refers to someone who is not clean before God. "Err" means to go astray or lose one's way. So the passage promises that those who walk there will be accompanied, and that even the simple-minded will not get lost.

Isaiah speaks to a people facing threats and exile. In this chapter, the prophet announces restoration in poetic form: the desert blooms, the weak are healed, and the redeemed return to Zion with joy. Many see it as a hope for the return of Israel, and Christians also read it as pointing to the work of Christ. There are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: you do not have to find the way alone. If you feel lost or weak, ask God to guide you, and walk alongside other believers who can accompany you.
exp.50:18:
This verse speaks to Jerusalem and reminds her of her suffering. "Happen" means to take place, and "ruin" is complete destruction. "Being broken" is being shattered both inside and out. Two double disasters came upon her: ruin and breaking, famine and the sword. The question "who will grieve for you?" shows that no one seemed to pity or comfort her.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here in God's name. The city had suffered God's judgment for its sin, and its children lay fallen and without guidance. The text probably looks to the fall of Jerusalem, though not every detail can be pinned down. But the passage does not end in punishment: what follows (v. 22) is that God himself will take up her cause and remove the cup of his wrath.

For today: when you feel alone in your pain, do not stay silent. God sees your affliction and can comfort you in ways no one else can. Bring your brokenness to him in prayer.
exp.24:6:
It says that God will remove the veil that covers all nations. The "mask of the covering" and the "spread-out cover" are images of something that blocks sight, like a cloak that keeps one from seeing clearly. "This mountain" refers to Zion, the mountain of Jerusalem. Many understand this veil to be spiritual blindness and the shadow of death; the next verse speaks of destroying death.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces a promise for the future. Earlier he described a feast that the Lord will prepare for all peoples.
