Now he says that not only Israel, but all nations, will be invited to know him. Then comes the promise that God will wipe away every tear and save his people.

For today: if there are areas where you do not understand or where you feel pain, ask God to open your eyes. He promises light and hope, and you can trust that he will finish what he has begun.
exp.61:8:
They who have gathered in the harvest and picked the grapes will be the ones who enjoy the fruit of their labor. "Gathered" means brought together or collected; "picked" here means harvested the grapes. They will eat and drink, praising the Lord, and they will do this in the courts of the temple, that is, in the courtyards of his sanctuary.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who had suffered invasions, when enemies carried off their crops. God swears that this will not happen again. The promise announces restoration for Jerusalem. Interpreters see it fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and also pointing to a greater restoration, announced in the following verse with the coming of the Savior.

For today: God watches over the fruit of our efforts. When you enjoy what you have earned through your work, give thanks and praise him, recognizing that everything comes from his hand.
exp.59:2:
This verse says that peoples from other nations will walk guided by the light that shines over Jerusalem, and that even kings will come drawn by its brightness. The word "Gentiles" means nations or peoples who are not Jewish. "Rising" here is understood as the dawn, the rising of the light, as when the sun comes up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, a people who had come through punishment and discouragement. God promises restoration. The light is not their own merit: it is the glory of the LORD rising over her. Many Christians see here an announcement of Christ, the light of the world, though others read it mainly as a promise for a restored Israel.

For today: if God has brought light into your life, do not hide it or boast about it. Live with honesty and kindness, and let his glory be seen in you. Many people in the middle of their darkness will draw near, not because of you, but because of the light that shines on you.
exp.58:20:
God promises a covenant: his Spirit and his words will remain in the mouth of his people, and also in the mouths of their children and grandchildren, forever. The word "seed" that appears in the source means offspring, and the phrase "shall not depart" means that they will not be lost or taken away.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Earlier, the people had been accused of sin, but God promises that the Redeemer will come to Zion for those who turn from their wickedness. This verse is part of that promise of restoration. Some understand "thee" to refer to the Redeemer, others to the faithful people or to Isaiah as a representative; the text does not fully clarify this here. Many Christians see a fulfillment in Christ and in the Spirit given to his people.

For today: if you want your faith to reach your children, do it through example and through words. Read the Bible at home and speak about God naturally, trusting that he sustains his work.
exp.41:8:
God says that the things he announced earlier have already happened. "The former things" are what he had said and then fulfilled. Now he announces "new things," and he makes them known before they come to pass, that is, before they happen.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just introduced his Servant, who will open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of darkness. God declares that he will not give his glory to idols. His ability to announce the future sets him apart from them. Then comes a call to sing him a new song. Many believers see here a look toward Christ, although the text also speaks of what God would do in his own time.

For today: if God fulfilled what he promised before, you can trust that he will fulfill what you do not yet see. Today, bring your uncertainty to him in prayer and wait with patience.
exp.44:10:
Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who also formed them, that he invites them to ask him about what is to come. The one who "forms" is the one who shapes, like a potter. The phrase "command ye me" sounds bold; many understand it as an invitation to bring him their requests and concerns about his people, not as a command that God must obey.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were complaining about how he was acting. He was about to use Cyrus, a foreign king, to free the captives, and this seemed strange to some of them. God reminds them that he is the Creator and that his plan makes sense, even when they do not understand it.

For today: instead of arguing with God or doubting him when something does not make sense, bring him your questions and concerns in prayer. You can trust that the One who made you cares for you and for those you love.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues a list of leaders that God will remove from Jerusalem and Judah. It names the captain of fifty (the leader of a small group of soldiers), the honourable man (someone respected and in authority), the counsellor, the cunning artificer (a highly skilled craftsman), and the eloquent orator (someone who knows how to speak with wisdom and persuasion).

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the Lord will do because of the people's sin. Taking away these leaders and supports was a judgment: without wise and capable people, disorder would come, and the people would be left in the hands of immature rulers, as the verses that follow say.

For today: value and pray for those who guide you, whether in the church, the family, or the workplace. And remember that a society is not sustained by talent alone, but by humility before God. Ask Him for wisdom to serve where He has placed you.
exp.43:22:
This verse calls all of creation to celebrate. The heavens, the lower parts of the earth, the mountains, the forest and every tree in it are told to sing and shout for joy. The reason is that the Lord has done it: He has rescued His people. To redeem means to pay the price to set someone free. To break forth means to burst out into singing. To be glorified means that God will show His greatness in Israel.

The prophet Isaiah passes on what God says to a people who have failed and feel forgotten. Just before, God reminds them that He has wiped away their sins like a cloud that fades away, and He invites them to return to Him. Then He presents Himself as Redeemer and Creator of all things.

For today: when you doubt that God will forgive you, remember that He has already wiped away your sins. Respond with gratitude: take a moment today to thank Him out loud for His forgiveness.
exp.50:9:
This verse is a question that reminds us of what God has already done. The dried-up sea and the depths made into a way point to the people's crossing of the Red Sea during the Exodus. The "ransomed" are those who were rescued, and the word translated here means those who were brought back or made to return.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and asks God to act again as he did in the past. Israel was discouraged, probably because of the exile in Babylon. Remembering the Exodus gave them hope that God would bring them back to Zion, as the next verse says. The sea monsters and the dragon are poetic images of chaos and hostile power; some relate them to Egypt, and scholars do not explain them in just one way.

For today: when you face a "sea" that seems to block your path, remember what God has done before for his people and for you. Pray with confidence, knowing that he can open a way where no one else sees one.
exp.50:16:
It says that Jerusalem must wake up and stand up. She has taken from the hand of God a cup full of his anger, and she has drunk it all, to the very bottom. The sediment that remains at the bottom is the leftover dregs. Being stunned is being dizzy and unable to react. To have drunk it all means she left not a single drop.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The people had suffered severely because of their disobedience, and they were left like someone drunk with sorrow, without strength and without anyone to guide them. But God has just reminded them that he is their God and that he called them "my people." The call to wake up is the beginning of a promise of comfort.

For today: if you are exhausted by the consequences of past mistakes or pain, do not stay on the ground. God calls you to rise, not to condemn you, but to restore you. Today you can return to him with sincerity.
exp.35:11:
Here Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, answers the officials of Judah harshly. He says that his master did not send him only to the leaders, but also to the people who sit upon the wall. The crude words in this verse are about what those people will be reduced to: he warns that if the city stays under siege, they will face such hunger and thirst that they will suffer terrible things. The words "sent me" are the same as "hath he sent me" in the verse above.

Rabshakeh speaks during the siege of Jerusalem, in the time of King Hezekiah. The officials asked him to speak in Aramaic so that the people would not understand. He refuses and wants everyone to hear, in order to spread fear and push them toward surrender. It is psychological pressure.

For today: when someone tries to frighten you with threats or exaggerations, do not let fear carry you away. Stop, pray, and seek the truth in God. He sustains those who trust in Him, even when the voices around them shout loudly.
exp.64:10:
God speaks to those who abandon him and forget his holy mountain, that is, Jerusalem and its temple, the place of his worship. Instead of seeking him, they set a table with food for the god of fortune and pour out drink as an offering to the god of destiny. These names (in Hebrew, Gad and Meni) seem to be gods of luck, although scholars are not completely certain about them. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and "drink offerings" are drinks offered in worship.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he promises to save a faithful remnant who will inherit the land. Here he marks the contrast with those among the same people who rejected his call and gave themselves over to idolatry. Then he announces the consequences of that choice.

Today we too can put our trust in luck, money, or success instead of God. Ask yourself: where do I place my confidence when I am afraid of the future? Return to God with simple prayer and trust in his care.
exp.62:8:
God did not stay far away when his people suffered: he felt their pain along with them. "The angel of his presence" is a messenger or God's own presence, and it is understood in several ways. He saved them, and he redeemed them (rescued them) out of love and compassion, and he lifted them up and carried them "all the days of old," that is, from long ago.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and gratefully recalls what God did in the past, such as the exodus from Egypt. He does this because Israel is in a difficult moment. The verses that follow admit that the people rebelled, yet he still remembers God's faithfulness.

Today, when you go through distress, remember how God has cared for you before. Write it down and give thanks; that strengthens trust.
exp.45:1:
It says that the idols of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, fell down humbled and brought low together. They could not free from the burden those who carried them, and they themselves ended up going into captivity. The idols are the images or statues of the gods, and the phrase meaning "at the same time" describes how they fell together.

God speaks through Isaiah. Bel and Nebo were important gods of Babylon. Here they are described as statues loaded onto animals, that is, as a weight, while the enemy advances. Then God contrasts that picture with his own: he does not need to be carried, but carries his people from birth to old age.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up weighing us down and cannot sustain us. Today you can hand God a specific burden and rest in the knowledge that he carries you.
exp.45:12:
God promises that his righteousness will draw near and will not stay far away. He also says that his salvation will not be delayed. He will place salvation in Zion, which is Jerusalem, his people, and he will show his glory in Israel.

God himself is speaking through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he will call a man from far away to carry out his plan; many understand this to refer to Cyrus, king of Persia, although the text does not give the name here. God speaks to those who are stubborn of heart, people who doubted his help and lived far from what is right. In contrast with the idols of Babylon, which must be carried, God himself carries and rescues his people.

For today: when you feel that God's help is taking too long, remember that he does what he says. Trust his timing, and instead of hardening your heart, come to him with humility and wait for his salvation.
exp.27:18:
It says that when God's punishment begins to pass through, it will not be a matter of a single moment: it will come again and again, every morning, by day and by night, and it will carry off those who trusted in themselves. The word for "carry off" means to take away by force. The word for terror is fear; and the last sentence can be understood this way: only when the fear arrives will people understand the message they heard earlier and despised.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The leaders of Judah mocked his warnings and believed they were safe because of their political alliances, which the text describes as a covenant with death. God warns them that this false security will not withstand judgment.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to arrive before we take God's voice seriously. If He speaks to us today through His Word, let us respond with humility and trust in Him, not in false refuges.
exp.50:20:
He says that God calls Jerusalem "miserable," that is, afflicted and struck down, and "drunk, but not with wine." This drunkenness does not come from liquor, but from having drunk the cup of God's punishment, which left her dazed, staggering, and without strength.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The people suffered invasion, hunger, and the loss of their children because of their disobedience. No one seemed able to comfort them. But this call to listen prepares a good word: in the verses that follow, God, who defends his people, says that he takes away that cup and that they will no longer drink it.

For today: if you are stunned by pain, or by the consequences of your mistakes, do not stay alone in your sadness. Listen to the voice of God, who not only names your wound, but also promises comfort and restoration.
exp.51:8:
This verse calls the desolate places of Jerusalem, meaning the ruins and abandoned areas of the city, to break into singing and joy. The word "together" in the verse means all of them joining in as one. The reason for such joy is that the Lord has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem, that is, rescued and freed it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who had lived through exile and the destruction of their city. Just before this, watchmen announce that God is returning to Zion and reigning. What follows shows that God acts before all the nations. The message speaks as if the deliverance were already a certain fact. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of salvation in Christ.

For today: if there are areas of your life that you feel are in ruins, you can begin to praise God before you see everything restored. He is faithful to comfort and rescue.
exp.25:15:
When the people went through distress, they turned to God. "Distress" means suffering or a tight spot. "They poured out a prayer" means they prayed with an open heart, letting out everything they felt. "Thy chastening" refers to God's correction of them.

The people of Judah speak in a song of trust within Isaiah 24 to 27. They acknowledge that God had allowed the judgment, and that in that pain they sought him. The verses that follow compare their suffering to the pains of childbirth: they felt they could accomplish nothing. Some understand the chastening as divine discipline for their sins; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you are going through a difficult moment, do not hold back your prayer. Speak to God honestly, even with few words or with tears. Difficulty can draw you closer to Him rather than push you away.
exp.7:9:
It says that the plans of God's enemies will fail. "Take counsel together" means making plans or meeting to decide a strategy; "speak the word" means giving orders or declaring what they intend to do. But none of it will stand, "for God is with us," which in Hebrew is "Emmanuel."

The prophet Isaiah speaks at a time of great threat to Judah from the powerful army of Assyria. The people were afraid and looked for human alliances and conspiracies. Isaiah reminds them that God is with his people, and that no enemy power has the final word. The following verse asks them not to fear what others fear.

For today: when problems seem bigger than you, do not let yourself be carried away by the panic of the crowd. Do your part with wisdom, but rest in the fact that God is with you and still governs.
exp.54:8:
It says that the heavens are much higher than the earth, and that in the same way God's ways and thoughts are above ours. "Ways" refers to the way he acts, and "thoughts" refers to his plans and the way he sees things.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who are generally understood to have been in exile or close to it, and he invites them to return to him. Just before this, the wicked person is called to leave his evil way, because God is abundant in pardoning. This verse explains why he can forgive so much: his heart and his plans are not like those of humans.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, or find it hard to believe that he truly forgives, trust that his wisdom and mercy are greater than your view. Come to him with humility.
exp.13:13:
This verse shows what this figure was saying in his heart: "I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High." The word "ascend" expresses the wish to rise to the heights and to take the place of God.

Isaiah gives this message as a mockery against the king of Babylon, who thought himself very great and was brought down (Isaiah 14:4). Many Christians have long read this passage as also referring to Satan, but others believe it speaks only of the human king. For that reason it is wise to be careful: the text clearly points to pride that ends in a fall.

For today: examine your desires with sincerity. When success or recognition tempts you to believe you are sufficient without God, pray and choose humility, for He lifts up the humble in His time.
exp.64:24:
This verse describes a time of complete peace. The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, meaning animals that were once enemies or predators will live side by side without violence. The word for "feed together" in the verse's source means to graze and eat. The serpent will be given dust to eat, a sign that evil is brought low. In God's holy mountain, no one will hurt or destroy.

Here God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises his people "new heavens and a new earth" (v. 17). Many see this as a hope for Israel and also as a foretelling of God's final kingdom; Christians read it in the light of Christ. Scholars debate whether the language is literal or symbolic.

For today: God promises a future without violence, and that invites us to be peacemakers now. Today you can choose to respond with gentleness at home, at work, or in church, trusting that God will complete the work of peace.
exp.47:17:
God says with sorrow: "Oh, that you had paid attention to my commandments!" If you had done so, your peace would have been like a river, flowing steadily, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, arriving one after another without end. Here "hearken" means to obey.

The LORD, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, speaks to his people who were in exile or about to leave Babylon. He reminds them that he taught and guided them, but they did not listen. It is a lament from God, not only a rebuke: it shows what he longed to give them. Then he invites them to leave Babylon and to rejoice in their redemption.

For today: true peace grows when we listen to God and follow him. Today, before deciding something, take a moment to ask him what his Word says about it.
exp.43:3:
It says that the descendants of Israel will grow with strength and life, like green grass and like willows that grow beside the bank of a river. "They shall spring up" means they will come up and grow. The "banks" are the edges of the water. The willow is a tree that grows quickly where water is plentiful.

God himself speaks, the Creator of Israel. His people were downcast, and He tells them: "Do not be afraid." He promises to pour out his Spirit and his blessing on their children, like water on dry ground. The growth the verse describes is the result of that water, that is, of God's work and not of human effort.

For today: if you feel dry or tired, seek God in prayer and in his Word. Just as the willow depends on water, our life grows when we remain close to Him, who gives his Spirit to those who trust in Him.
exp.23:20:
It says that when the day of God's judgment comes, he will "visit," that is, call to account and punish, both the powers on high (the "exalted host") and the rulers of the earth. Here "visit" is not a friendly visit but an intervention by God to judge.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in chapters 24 to 27, which describe a judgment over the whole earth because of its sin. Scholars understand "the host on high" in several ways: as rebellious spiritual forces, as the heavenly bodies that were worshiped, or as exalted human powers. The text does not fully make this clear. The conclusion is clear: God will reign.

For today: do not place your ultimate trust in any human power, because only God reigns forever. Live with humility and hope.
exp.39:10:
He will care for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. The word translated "feed" means that he will give them food and lead them. He will take the small lambs in his arm and carry them close to his chest. The ewes that have just given birth are the ones he will guide with tenderness, without rushing them.

Isaiah announces comfort to Judah, a people beaten down and discouraged. The messenger is to shout without fear: "Here is your God!" The verse before this one shows God arriving with power and strength. This verse shows the other side: that same strong arm, which rules, also carries the weak with gentleness. The text then goes on to speak of God's incomparable greatness.

For today: if you feel tired or fragile, you do not have to pretend to be strong. God knows your limit and cares for you with patience. And if you have strength, you can treat those who are weaker with the same gentleness.
exp.11:2:
God's people will draw water with joy from the springs of salvation. "Salvation" here means rescue and deliverance. The springs are the sources from which fresh water flows. The picture is of people who are thirsty and find plenty of water, without having to search for it in anguish.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had suffered God's anger because of their sin. This chapter is a song for the day when God will restore and comfort them. The verses before it say that God is their salvation, strength, and song. Some see here also a promise of the Messiah; interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: do not live your faith as a dry burden. Each day, come near to God in prayer and in his Word as one who goes to a spring, trusting that he gives you what you need, and let that provision fill you with gratitude and joy.
exp.32:19:
Isaiah tells the people to look upon Zion, the city where the feasts of the LORD were celebrated. There they will see Jerusalem as a place of rest and peace, compared to a sturdy tent: its tent pegs will never be pulled up, and its cords will never be broken.

Isaiah speaks to Judah at a time when Assyria was threatening and fear was great. Before this, the people remember with dread the foreign officials who counted and collected tribute. Afterward, the prophet explains the reason for this security: the LORD is judge, lawgiver, King, and Savior. The promise rests on God, not on the walls.

For today: when you lack stability, do not place your peace in things that can be broken, such as work, money, or plans. Take a moment today to pray and remember that God is your King and your firm refuge.
exp.46:11:
It says that Babylon should keep relying on her enchantments (spells) and her omens (signs supposedly announcing the future), in which she has grown weary since youth. The verse's "Stand now" means "stay" or "keep at it." The words about possibly improving are ironic: God mocks her, because these practices will do her no good.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon believed herself secure, wise, and invincible. God judges her for her pride and for trusting in magic and astrology. The following verses show that her counselors will not be able to save her: they will fall like straw into the fire.

For today: examine where you place your security. It may be horoscopes, money, your own intelligence, or your pride. None of that will sustain you in a crisis. Trust instead in God, who truly knows the future and cares for those who seek him with humility.
exp.40:16:
This verse says that there are people who are afflicted and poor who desperately seek water and do not find it; their tongues are dry from thirst. The word for "poor and needy" refers to those in need, and "forsake" means to abandon. Facing that distress, God promises to hear them and not leave them alone.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, a small and weak people surrounded by powerful nations. Shortly before, he had called them not to fear and promised them strength to overcome their enemies. Then he announces that he will turn the desert into rivers, springs and trees. The thirst can be understood as a real need and also as an image of their difficult situation.

For today: when you feel dry, tired or without a way out, bring your need to God with sincerity. He hears and promises not to abandon you, even though his answer does not always come as or when we expect it.
exp.27:19:
It says the bed is too short for a person to stretch out on, and the blanket is too narrow to wrap oneself in. The word for "covering" in the original refers to the blanket or bedspread, and "wrap" here means to wrap or cover oneself with it. It is a saying about a discomfort with no remedy.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the leaders of Jerusalem. They trusted in political alliances, and perhaps in agreements with foreign powers, to save themselves from judgment, and they called these a covenant with death. Many understand the bed and the blanket as an image of that false security: it looks like a shelter, but it is not enough to protect them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we seek rest apart from God: money, influence, our own plans. If that "bed" leaves us short, it is better to trust the Lord again, who alone gives true rest.
exp.22:15:
Isaiah 23:16 tells Tyre, compared to a forgotten prostitute, to take up a harp and walk through the city. She is to play a good tune and repeat her song again and again, so that people will remember her once more. "Harlot" here is an image for a city that lives by trade and looks for customers. The phrase "so that she may be remembered" means to be remembered again.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah within his message about Tyre, the great trading city. After seventy years of being forgotten, Tyre would return to its business. Scholars debate how exactly to understand those seventy years. The tone is mocking: Tyre tries to attract customers once more. Even so, the text that follows says that her profits would end up serving God and his people.

For today: let us take care that our success is not based only on earning and being remembered. Let us put what we have at the service of God and of others.
exp.28:13:
God says that he will once again astonish his people with a great and amazing work. The result is that the wisdom of the wise men will perish and the understanding of the prudent men will vanish, that is, it will disappear or become worthless.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah, in Jerusalem. They practiced a religion of the lips, with fine words but with their hearts far away, following human rules. In addition, they trusted in their own plans and tried to hide them from God. For this reason he shows them that human intelligence cannot hide anything from him or take his place. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 1:19.

Today, examine whether your faith is only a habit or whether it comes from the heart. Before making a decision, pray and ask for God's guidance, instead of relying only on your own judgment.
exp.45:11:
God calls the attention of people who are "stouthearted," that is, stubborn, unwilling to listen or to change. He says they are "far from righteousness": they live apart from what is right and from what God approves. "Hearken unto me" is a serious invitation to pay attention.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to the people of Israel. He has just shown that his plans are fulfilled and that the idols of Babylon cannot save anyone. Even so, the people were doubting. That is why God confronts them, but right away he promises to bring his righteousness and his salvation near to Zion.

For today: if you notice that your heart becomes stubborn in the face of God's correction, stop and listen. Read his Word with humility and ask him for a heart willing to respond. He does not call you in order to condemn you, but to bring you near to his salvation.
exp.22:4:
When the news of Tyre's fall reaches Egypt, the Egyptians will be filled with anguish. "Report" here means news or rumor, and the word translated "report" means news. Some translators understand that Egypt will suffer because of what happened to Tyre; others understand that it will be distressed as it was when it heard the news of another disaster. The Hebrew text allows several readings.

Isaiah announces God's judgment on Tyre, the great trading city of the sea. Egypt was one of its partners, since it supplied Tyre with grain from the Nile. If Tyre fell, Egypt would lose a good customer and would see that not even the most secure powers hold firm. God is the one who speaks through the prophet.

For today: let us not place our security only in money, work, or business. All of that can change suddenly. Let us first trust in God, who endures.
exp.4:8:
Here Isaiah says that God himself made something known to him: many houses will be destroyed and left empty. The word translated as "desolate" means laid waste, reduced to ruins. The phrase "without inhabitant" means that no one will live in them, not even the great and fair houses. The phrase "In mine ears" indicates that Isaiah received this message directly from God.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he compares Israel to a vineyard that God tended, but which produced bad fruit: injustice instead of justice. He condemns those who were accumulating houses and lands, taking space away from others. For this reason he announces that such wealth will not last.

For today: the ambition to have more and more can make us forget about others. Today you might ask yourself whether you use what you have with generosity and justice, or only to secure more and more for yourself.
exp.42:13:
God presents himself as the Redeemer of his people and the Holy One of Israel. He says that, for their sake, he acted against Babylon: he brought all of them down like fugitives, and the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) cried out in anguish in their ships. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translators understand it differently.

God speaks to Israel, who would be carried off captive to Babylon. He promises them that this mighty empire will not have the last word. He announces its fall to set his people free, and he does this so that they will recognize that he alone is God.

Today: when you feel that something greater than you has you trapped, remember that God is your Redeemer and that no power stands above him. Trust in his care and pray with hope.
exp.38:6:
God announces through Isaiah that some of King Hezekiah's descendants will be taken away to Babylon. The word "eunuchs" probably refers to servants of the royal court, though some understand that it could also mean they would be made eunuchs.

Isaiah speaks to King Hezekiah after he proudly showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon. The prophet warns him that this nation, which now seems friendly, will one day carry off the riches and also part of his family. Later, the Bible shows that Babylon conquered Judah.

For today: what we boast about or hold onto with pride is not secure forever. It is wise to live with humility, to be thankful for what God gives, and to also think about the good of those who will come after us.
exp.65:10:
It says that those who love Jerusalem will be like a nursing baby who feeds and is satisfied at its mother's breast. That breast gives comfort, that is, consolation. The idea of drawing out milk with delight refers to the abundance of the restored city, and its glory and beauty are the fullness of the restored city. It is an image of nourishment, rest, and complete joy.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah at the end of the book. After the exile, the people were grieving and the city lay in ruins. God promises to restore Jerusalem like a mother who nurtures her children, and the verses that follow confirm this: he himself will comfort them as a mother does. Many also see here a broader hope for the future.

For today: when you are tired or sad, do not look for comfort only in distractions. Turn to God in prayer and to the community of believers, where he often gives nourishment and rest to the soul.
exp.31:8:
It says that God, through the prophet, calls to certain women who live at ease and without worries. He asks them to rise up, to listen to him, and to pay attention to his words. The verse's "at ease" means they are rested and comfortable. "Careless" means they feel secure and have no concern. "Speech" here refers to what is said, the message.

The one speaking is Isaiah, who passes on the message of God. Earlier he spoke about people who took advantage of the poor and others who acted with generosity. Afterward he warns that the comfort of these women will end, because years of scarcity are coming. Some think he means the women of Jerusalem in particular; others think he means the whole people, and the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not confuse comfort with security. Take a moment this week to listen to God and ask him whether there is something in your life you have stopped attending to because you feel settled.
exp.56:11:
God says he will reveal the "righteousness" of his people and their works, that is, everything they believe makes them good. But he says it with irony: those works will do them no good at all.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. He is addressing a people who had turned away from him, looking for support in idols and human alliances. They were worn out from all their effort, yet they did not want to return to God. The text then shows that those supports will be carried off by the wind, while whoever trusts in God will inherit the land.

For today: we can ask ourselves what we are trusting in to feel secure or accepted. Our works, though good, do not save us. We can rest in God and come to him with humility.
exp.42:23:
God says that Israel did not buy him sweet cane, the fragrant oil or fine incense used in worship, nor did they please him with the fat, the best part of the sacrifices. Instead, they made him serve under their sins; that is, they burdened him with their wickedness and wearied him with their faults.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who offered little from the heart and lived in rebellion. He does not say that sacrifices were wrong in themselves, but that there was no sincere love behind them. Right after, in verse 25, he promises to forgive for the sake of his own name.

For today: performing rituals or religious gestures is not enough if the heart remains far from God. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge your failures, and trust in his forgiveness, which is not earned with gifts but comes from his grace.
exp.35:12:
Rabshakeh stands up and shouts loudly in Hebrew, the language of Judah, so that everyone can hear him. He calls on them to listen to the words of the great king, the king of Assyria.

Rabshakeh was a senior officer of King Sennacherib, who had Jerusalem under siege. The officials of Hezekiah had asked him to speak in Aramaic so that the people would not understand. He did the opposite: he spoke in Hebrew to frighten the ordinary people on the wall and to take away their trust in their king and in God.

Today too there are loud voices that try to sow fear and doubt about God. Before you let yourself be carried along by them, stop, pray, and remember what God has promised. His voice is more trustworthy than the voice of fear.
exp.0:11:
God asks with sorrow: "Who asked this of you?" He is speaking about the people who came to the temple to present themselves before him. The word "require" means asked for or demanded. "Tread" means to trample underfoot. "Courts" are the courtyards of the temple. God says they only trample his courtyards, and their visit has no worth to him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah, whom he calls "Sodom and Gomorrah" in order to rebuke them harshly. They kept on with sacrifices and feasts, but their lives were unjust, as becomes clear later in the chapter. God does not reject worship itself, which he himself had commanded, but empty religion, without obedience or justice.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our life in church, prayer, and giving is joined to an obedient heart. Before we sing or give, it is good to examine how we treat others and correct what is wrong.
exp.56:12:
It says that when the people cry out for help, the idols and alliances they trusted will not be able to save them. Their "companies" are the groups gathered around them, that is, what was put together for protection. "But" is the word that turns the verse toward its contrast. The wind and the breath show that all of that is fragile. By contrast, whoever trusts in God will receive the land and will live on his holy mountain.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He rebukes a people who had forgotten Him, sought other gods, and feared people more than Him. Many understand that the land and the holy mountain speak of Jerusalem and the restoration; others also see a broader spiritual promise. Then God promises nearness to the humble.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, success. Those things help, but they do not sustain the soul. Today, hand over to God one specific worry and trust Him with it.
exp.45:3:
He says that God himself will care for his people all their lives, even into old age and gray hairs. The word "carry" here means to bear up and hold, not merely to put up with something. God repeats "I" several times: he made them, he will carry them, he will uphold them and keep them safe.

The passage speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It compares the idols of Babylon, which had to be carried on animals when they fell, with the God of Israel, who has carried his people since before they were born. The idols are a burden; the Lord is the one who carries the burden. He addresses a people who were facing captivity.

When you feel tired, old, or without strength, remember that God does not ask you to hold yourself up alone. You can give him your burdens in prayer, trusting that he walks with you through every stage of your life.
exp.7:3:
God says that, before the child is old enough to say "my father" and "my mother," the power of Damascus and the riches taken from Samaria will be carried away by the king of Assyria. "Shall be taken away" means they will lose their power. "The spoil" is the plunder taken in war.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. King Ahaz of Judah was afraid of Syria (Damascus) and of Israel (Samaria), who were threatening him. God gives him a sign through the son of the prophet, named Maher-shalal-hash-baz, a name usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the prey." The witnesses recorded the prophecy before it was fulfilled.

For today: when enemies or problems seem enormous, remember that God governs history. Trust in Him instead of seeking security in human alliances or in your own cleverness.
exp.30:0:
God laments the attitude of those who go down to Egypt seeking help. They place their trust in horses, chariots, and horsemen, because there are many of them and they are strong. But they did not look to the Holy One of Israel, nor did they seek the Lord. The word for horsemen here means riders, soldiers on horseback.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks in a time of threat from Assyria. Judah's leaders were seeking a military alliance with Egypt instead of trusting in God. Historians agree that it was a time of great political pressure. Isaiah reminds them that Egypt is only human, not God, and that God is wise and keeps his word.

Today we can trust more in our resources, contacts, or plans than in God. Planning is not wrong, but the question is: to whom do I turn first? Before seeking human solutions, let us pause to pray and seek God sincerely.
exp.35:5:
It says Egypt is like a walking staff made of a fragile reed. A "staff" is a stick a person leans on when walking. If someone leans on it, the reed breaks, goes into the hand, and wounds it. The phrase "it will go into his hand" means it will enter the hand, and "pierce it" means the wound will be deep. That is how Pharaoh is to all who trust in him.

Rabshakeh, an officer of the king of Assyria, speaks in front of the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and Hezekiah so that they will surrender. He mocks their alliance with Egypt and presents it as an empty hope. At this point, his criticism of Egyptian help was realistic, since Egypt was not a firm support. But Rabshakeh is an enemy and seeks to intimidate, so his words mix truth and pressure.

We may lean on things that seem strong, such as money, connections, or plans, and that fail us just when we need them most. It is wise to use them with discernment, but to place our final trust in God, who does not break.
exp.40:14:
God tells his people that he will make them into a new threshing sledge, a heavy tool with sharp edges or teeth that was used to separate the grain from the straw. With it they will crush mountains and hills until they are reduced to chaff, the fine straw that the wind carries away. These are figurative images, not literal ones.

God himself speaks to Israel and calls them a worm because of their weakness and smallness. He tells them not to be afraid because he is their Redeemer. The mountains represent the enemies and obstacles that seem enormous. The strength will not come from Israel, but from God, who holds them by the hand.

For today: when a problem looks like a mountain to you, do not trust your own strength. Bring it to God, who takes you by the hand, and move forward in faith, knowing that he gives you what you need for each step.
exp.21:14:
God tells the prophet Isaiah to go and see Shebna, a high official of the palace. The words "treasurer" and "steward" indicate that he managed the king's property. "Go, get thee unto this treasurer" means "go, present yourself before this official." What follows is a message from God to him.

Thus speaks the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord of all power. Before this, the people had lived in feasting and carelessness, without repenting. Now God confronts one particular leader. The following verses show that Shebna was carving himself a luxurious tomb, a sign of pride. Information about his life outside this passage is scarce.

For today: God sees those who have power and calls them to account. Examine whether you use your work, money, or influence to serve others or to exalt yourself. Ask Him for humility.
exp.10:9:
It says that, when the time of the kingdom God promises arrives, the descendant of Jesse (the father of King David) will be like a banner raised for all the peoples. A banner is a flag or standard that gathers people together. The nations will seek it. Rest is a place of quiet and ease, and the verse promises that this rest will be glorious.

Isaiah, a prophet of God, speaks to a people who lived in fear of the neighboring empires. Before this verse he describes a righteous king who would come from David's family and bring peace even to all creation. Christians see in that king Jesus; Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:12. Afterward, God promises to gather the scattered of Israel.

For today: if Jesus is the banner that gathers all the peoples, let us seek rest in him and welcome people from every background.
exp.35:13:
Here Rabshakeh, a spokesman for the king of Assyria, speaks. He says the king orders them not to let Hezekiah mislead them, because Hezekiah will not be able to deliver the people. The word "deliver" means to rescue or save from danger. The phrase "let not...deceive you" means not to let them be fooled by false hopes.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Assyrian army, a few years before 700 B.C. Rabshakeh shouted in Hebrew, the language of Judah, so that the people on the wall would understand him and lose their confidence. His aim was to separate the people from their king and from their faith in God. He presents as deception the very thing Judah was meant to trust in.

When loud voices tell us there is no way out, it is worth remembering that they do not always speak the truth. Before surrendering to fear, we can pray and seek God's voice in his Word, trusting that he can act even when everything seems lost.
exp.36:37:
Here "it came to pass" means "it happened," and "smote him with the sword" means that they killed him with the sword. While Sennacherib was worshipping in the temple of his god, two of his sons murdered him and fled to the region of Ararat. Another son, Esarhaddon, became king. It is not known with certainty who Nisroch was.

The writer of the book of Isaiah tells how the Assyrian king who had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel came to his end. This ending fulfills what God had announced earlier: that Sennacherib would fall by the sword in his own land (Isaiah 37:7). It happened years after his withdrawal.

Today we can trust that God keeps his word, even when it takes time. Human powers may seem enormous, but they pass away. A false god could not protect even his own worshipper, so let us place our trust in the living God.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that God's plan against Assyria is not something isolated. It is a "purpose," that is, a firm decision of God, and it reaches the whole earth. The "hand that is stretched out" is an image of his power in action, acting upon all the nations.

Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, who swore that he would break the Assyrian, the empire that oppressed Judah. It was a message of comfort for a threatened people. It is then added that no one can overturn what God determines. Many understand that the judgment on Assyria is an example of how God governs all the nations.

For today: when the world seems dominated by unjust powers or by chaos, you can rest in the knowledge that God still governs. Bring your fears to him in prayer and trust that his purposes will be fulfilled, even though you cannot see how.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that Syria, together with Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and the king of Israel, the son of Remaliah, made a bad plan against Ahaz, king of Judah. The name Syria here refers to the king of Syria, and an evil plan is a wicked scheme. The sentence ends with a colon because what they said continues in verse 6.

God speaks through Isaiah. Ahaz was terrified because two allied kings were coming to attack Jerusalem. God sends Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub (a name that means "a remnant will return") to tell the king not to be afraid. Here God reminds Ahaz what his enemies are planning, but he also shows him that their plan will not succeed.

For today: when someone plans something harmful against us, or when fear seems enormous, we can remember that God knows every plan and still governs. Let us speak to Him with confidence before we act out of panic.
exp.13:24:
He says that God himself will destroy the Assyrian army when it is inside the land of Israel, on the mountains of Judah. "Break" means to crush or shatter, and "trample" means to tread underfoot, as one tramples something that cannot resist. The "yoke" and the "burden" are images of the domination and weight that Assyria placed on the peoples. God promises to remove them.

The words are spoken by the LORD of hosts, through Isaiah. It comes right after the prophecy against Babylon, and here the focus shifts to Assyria, the power that threatened Judah. God affirms that his plan is sworn and no one will stop it. Scholars often connect it with the Assyrian defeat in the time of Hezekiah, though some also see it as an example of God's judgment on all nations.

For today: when you feel a burden that seems greater than you are, remember that God still governs. Hand it over to him in prayer and trust that he knows when and how to take it away.
exp.28:8:
The passage says the people should stop and be amazed, because they are blind and confused. The word for being clouded in mind is not used in the verse above, so that comment is removed, and the verse's own words "they are drunken, but not with wine" carry the picture: they are staggering like drunkards, yet they have had nothing to drink.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Jerusalem, which is called by a name that appears in the verses that follow. The verses after this one explain that God sent them a deep, sleep-like stupor because they did not want to listen. Many understand this as both a warning and a judgment: their spiritual blindness was real and had consequences.

For today: let us not assume we understand God simply because we know things about the faith. Let us ask him each day for humility to listen to his Word, before the heart hardens and no longer recognizes his voice.
exp.6:8:
Isaiah says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, has only Samaria as its head, and Samaria has only a human king, the son of Remaliah. Then he warns: "If you do not trust, you will not stand firm," meaning that if they do not put their confidence in God, they will not stay steady.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to King Ahaz of Judah. Syria and Ephraim had joined forces against Judah, and Ahaz was terrified. God tells him that these enemies are only men with limited power. In Hebrew, the words for "trust" and "stand firm" sound alike, and that resemblance reinforces the message.

For today: when fear makes you feel that everything is falling apart, remember who is truly greater. Trusting in God, and not only in your own calculations, is what gives you firmness.
exp.56:2:
God firmly calls out a group: "Come closer, you children of the sorceress." A fortune-teller is someone who predicts the future through signs or magic. The words for adulterer and adulteress speak of unfaithfulness, and here they refer mainly to spiritual unfaithfulness: abandoning God for other gods. It is a way of saying that this people followed the bad example of their parents.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he comforted the righteous person who dies without anyone noticing, and now he addresses those who mock and practice idolatry. The contrast is strong: the righteous enter peace, while the rebels are called to account.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we place our trust in instead of God, such as superstitions, horoscopes, or modern idols. God invites us to return to him sincerely, without mocking those who follow him.
exp.44:4:
He says that the Lord is the only God; there is no other beside him. He also promises to gird someone, that is, to clothe him with strength, equip him, and prepare him for a task, even though that person did not know him.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. In this passage he addresses Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he names long before his reign. God would use him so that the people of Israel, in exile in Babylon, could return to their land. The verses before say that all this is for the sake of Israel, his chosen people. In this way everyone would know that only the Lord governs history.

For today: God can work in your life and in your world, even when you do not see him or recognize him. Trust that he is still in control, and seek to know him better.
exp.46:14:
They say that all those who have stood with Babylon for years, her partners and merchants from her youth, will abandon her. Each one will go off on his own way, every one to his own direction, continuing on his course without looking back. No one will come to rescue her when judgment arrives.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Babylon, a symbol of pride and of trust in human power. She depended on astrologers, counselors and trade alliances, and believed herself safe. God shows her that none of that will be able to save her. Many understand that he also speaks of a pride that goes beyond a single city.

For today: examine where you have placed your security, whether money, connections, reputation or plans. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who never abandons anyone who draws near to him with humility.
exp.16:8:
It says that when God's judgment comes, the cities that seemed strong will be left almost empty, like the few fruits left on the branches after the harvest. The word translated as "uppermost branch" refers to the top shoots of the plant. In the end it speaks of ruin and desolation.

Isaiah announces this message against Damascus and the northern kingdom, Israel, which trusted in alliances and fortresses. The verses that follow explain the cause: they forgot God, their rock. This verse is difficult in the original Hebrew, and the translations understand it in different ways, so it is wise to read it with humility.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, work or plans. All of these can fail, but God does not. Seek God first, and he will sustain the rest.
exp.27:0:
It says that a harsh warning is coming, a "woe," against Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel. Its "crown of pride" is its arrogance and its capital, probably Samaria, which sat on a hill beside a fertile valley. The "drunkards" who were "overcome with wine" were its leaders, dazed by wine and luxury. Their glorious beauty is "a fading flower": it wilts quickly.

The prophet Isaiah, sent by God, speaks a few years before Assyria conquered the northern kingdom (around 722 B.C.). The people lived confident in their wealth and power, and forgot God. The verses that follow announce that God will bring a strong invader, like a storm and a flood, who will trample that crown.

For today: whatever fills us with pride or lulls us to sleep, whether success, pleasure, or comfort, fades away. Let us ask God for humility and an awake heart to listen to him.
exp.31:7:
It says that the generous person plans generous things, and that by these noble deeds he stays firm and rises up. "Liberal" here does not speak of politics, but of someone with a noble, giving heart. Acts of generosity are what the word points to. Some translators understand the idea of standing firm as meaning that he will remain steady and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the verses before, he describes the foolish and the greedy, who oppress the poor with deceptive words. Now he sets them in contrast with the noble person. Then he warns the complacent, careless women of Jerusalem that their false sense of security will come to an end.

For today: our thoughts shape our actions. Before the opportunity comes, think about how you could help someone in need, and pray that God will give you a generous heart, determined to do good.
exp.27:22:
It says that God asks for complete attention. He repeats "give ear" twice, as if to say: "Listen truly, not just with your ears." The word "hear" is the same as "hearken," and "my speech" means "what I am saying" or "my word."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he warned the proud leaders of Judah who mocked his warnings, and he spoke of a judgment that would come. Now the tone changes: he calls people to listen to a teaching. Right after, he uses the example of the farmer, who does not plow all the time but does each task in its season. Many understand that in this way God works with wisdom, and his discipline has a purpose.

For today: before you react or doubt God, stop for a moment and listen to his Word with humility. Read a passage slowly and ask: "Lord, what do you want to teach me?"
exp.1:2:
This verse describes many peoples who encourage one another to go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob. They want God to teach them his ways so that they may walk in his paths. "Zion" and "Jerusalem" are the same city, and from there God's teaching will go out. "Law" here means instruction, not only rules.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. He announces what will happen "in the latter days," that is, in a future that God will bring. After the verse comes peace among the nations. Christians often see it fulfilled in Christ and his Church, and others expect it at a future time; it is understood in several ways.

For today: before deciding something important, ask God what he thinks and seek his teaching in the Bible. Coming to him with humility, willing to obey, is the first step toward walking in his paths.
exp.23:3:
This verse says the whole earth falls into ruin. The verse's wording "mourneth and fadeth away" means the earth is worn down and withers, like something that dries up and loses its life. The "haughty people of the earth" are also left weakened: the leaders and the powerful languish too. No one escapes, not even the most important.

The prophet Isaiah, a messenger of God, speaks within a section (chapters 24 to 27) that announces a judgment on the whole earth. The text itself gives the reason: the people broke God's laws and covenant. Scholars debate whether it refers to a near event, to the end of time, or to both, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: sin has consequences that reach everyone, not just a few. We can examine our own lives, return to obeying God with humility, and trust that He remains our refuge.
exp.56:13:
This verse is a command: someone must prepare the way. The source's quoted words for "level the ground" and "clear" must be handled carefully. The verse reads "Cast ye up" and "take up the stumblingblock," so I will explain the sense using words from the verse: preparing the road means building it up and clearing it, and a stumblingblock is an obstacle where someone might fall. The road being prepared is the road of God's people.

God speaks here, having just shown that idols and human alliances do not save, since the wind carries them away. Instead, he promises refuge to whoever waits on him. Now he orders the removal of whatever stands in the way of his people's return. Some read this as a announcement of the return from exile, and others also see it as a picture of the work of Christ. Both readings are possible.

For today: God wants us to come back to him, and sometimes there are obstacles we ourselves can remove, such as a grudge, a habit, or a distraction. Ask him to help you clear that obstacle, and also to help others come near to him without stumbling.
exp.18:15:
It says that when the day of God's judgment comes, the Egyptians will be left without strength and full of fear, "like women." This was a common expression of the time for speaking of people who were frightened and helpless. They will be astonished and tremble before the "raised hand" of God, that is, his power lifted up in action.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks to Judah in the name of God. Egypt was a power in which many trusted instead of trusting in the Lord. Earlier, the text says that God confused their plans. Scholars discuss which historical moment the phrase "in that day" refers to, and it may have a broader scope.

For today: no human strength, not money, power, or plans, gives us ultimate security. Today you can hand your fears over to God and trust in Him rather than in your own resources.
exp.33:0:
God says he calls all the nations to come near and listen. The word for "come near" means the same as the verse's "come near," and "listen" means to pay close attention. The phrase about what fills the earth refers to everything that is in it, that is, the living beings on the earth. The phrase about what the world produces refers to everything the world brings forth. It is a summons to all of creation, as in a court of law.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The verses that follow explain the reason: the Lord is going to judge the nations for their wickedness. This chapter uses very strong and poetic language. Many understand that the mention of Edom, later on, is an example of that universal judgment.

Today we can take seriously what God says, without thinking it does not concern us. Before speaking or defending ourselves, we can pause and listen to his voice in the Bible with humility, and let it correct us and draw us closer to him.
exp.32:7:
The highways lie empty, and no traveler walks them anymore. Someone has broken the agreement, looked down on the cities, and shown no respect for anyone. The word for the great roads is one the verse itself doesn't use, so the verse's note on it can be dropped, and the phrase about the agreement being annulled simply means that an agreement was broken.

The prophet Isaiah describes a time when Assyria threatened Judah, when King Sennacherib invaded the land. The messengers of peace weep because their efforts to make a treaty were ignored. Many understand that the one who broke the covenant was the invader; others see it in a more general way. After this picture of ruin, God himself says that he will rise up.

When everything seems abandoned and broken, do not place your hope in human promises, which can fail. Trust in God, who remains faithful and acts in his own time. Today you can pray about the situation that worries you and rest in him.
exp.64:16:
God says that he is going to create new heavens and a new earth. The word "create" here is the verb that the reader's verse gives as "create," so no further explanation of it is needed. What came before, that is, the pain and anguish of the past, will no longer be remembered or come to mind. God promises a renewal so complete that the old suffering will be forgotten.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a people who have suffered because of their sin and rebellion. He promises to restore his faithful servants. Christians often see here an announcement of the new creation that Revelation 21 takes up again. Some scholars think the text also speaks of a near renewal of Jerusalem, and others of a final fulfillment. Both readings have been held.

For today: if you carry wounds or sorrows, this promise invites you to wait in hope. God not only comforts, he also renews. Bring your pain to him with confidence.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that the righteous king will be like a shelter for his people. He is like a place where a person hides from the strong wind, a refuge from the storm, fresh water in the desert, and the shadow of a great rock when the sun beats down. A hiding place from the wind is a shelter, and a covert from the tempest is a refuge from the storm.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived in fear and injustice because of wicked leaders and threats from other nations. He announces a king who will rule with justice. Many Christians see here a sign of Jesus, the Messiah; others think it first refers to a king like Hezekiah. It can be read in both ways.

For today: when you are tired or afraid, turn to Christ in prayer, and at the same time try to be a refuge for others: listen, help, and treat with justice and tenderness anyone who needs it.
exp.65:15:
It says that God himself will judge all people, using fire and the sword as images of his judgment. "All flesh" means every human being. The ones who fall under that judgment are "the slain of the Lord," and they will be many. The words "rejoice" and "grow green again" are older forms, here rendered as "will rejoice" and "will grow green again."

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, passing on God's words at the end of the book. Earlier, God promises comfort and joy to his faithful servants. Then he points to those who practice a false religion, mixed with things he calls an abomination. Some scholars see here a judgment that is near, and others see a final one; the text allows both readings.

For today: God sees our deeds and thoughts. Examine your heart with honesty and trust in his mercy, seeking a genuine faith and not merely religious appearance.
exp.42:7:
God commands that his people be brought out or brought forward, people who have eyes but do not see, and who have ears but do not hear. The word "bring forth" means "make come out" or "bring to the front." This does not speak of blindness of the body, but of failing to recognize what God has done and said.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, who was in exile. He has just promised to bring his children back from far away. Then he calls them forward as witnesses before the nations, to show that he alone is God and that he does what he announces. His people had seen much, but they did not understand.

For today: it is not enough to have seen and heard of God many times. Ask him to open your eyes and your ears, and think about how he has cared for you. That will help you trust him and speak of him to others.
exp.6:0:
It says that in the days of King Ahaz of Judah, two enemy kings, Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel (the northern kingdom), went up to Jerusalem to attack it. But they could not conquer it. The older forms of the names in the source are rendered here as Ahaz, Uzziah, and Jerusalem, and the word for attacking it means to make war against it.

The book of Isaiah presents this event as a summary of the conflict. The verses that follow tell how the king and the people trembled with fear, and how God sent Isaiah to speak with Ahaz. Some scholars see here a summary of the whole conflict, with the details explained afterward. God wanted Ahaz to trust in Him and not in human alliances.

For today: when a threat seems bigger than you, remember that God can sustain you even when you feel your heart tremble. Before looking for hasty ways out, pray and ask Him to teach you to trust in Him.
exp.31:4:
This verse says that a time is coming when things will be seen as they really are. The stingy person, the one with a small heart, will no longer be given the reputation of being openhearted, a word that here means generous and noble. And the one who clings tightly to what he has will not be called bountiful either.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a promise about a righteous king (Isaiah 32:1). Under that reign, people regain their sight, their hearing, and their understanding. The verses that follow explain that the selfish person shows himself by his actions: he leaves the needy hungry and harms the poor.

For today: do not be impressed by appearances or by reputation. Look at how someone treats the weak. And examine your own heart: ask God to make you truly generous, not just generous in words.
exp.1:19:
In that day, people will throw their idols of silver and gold, the ones they had made to worship, to the moles and to the bats. In other words, they will cast them into dark and abandoned places, as something useless.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had filled their land with silver, gold, and idols. He announces a day when the LORD will appear in his majesty and judge human pride. On that day, what once seemed valuable will be shown to be worthless. Many understand "that day" as a judgment of God; some also connect it to the end of time.

For today: ask yourself where you are placing your trust, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Give that place to God, because he alone is worthy to be worshiped.
exp.49:1:
God asks why, when he came to his people, no one was waiting for him or answered him. Then he asks whether his hand has become "short," that is, weak and unable to rescue. He answers by showing his power: with a single command he dries up the sea and turns rivers into a wilderness.

The Lord is speaking to the people of Israel in exile. They felt that God had abandoned them, like a wife who had been sent away. God answers that the problem was not a lack of power or love on his part, but the people's wickedness and rebellion. He did come and call, but there was no answer.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, honestly examine whether you have been attentive to his call. He still has the power to rescue, and he invites you to respond to him today with confidence.
exp.11:0:
It says that a day will come when God's people will sing to him with gratitude. It acknowledges that God was angry, but that his anger has passed and that now he comforts them. A few older words: "fierce anger" is strong wrath; "turned away" means withdrew; "LORD" is the name of Israel's God.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had been disciplined for their rebellion. This verse is a short song that closes the previous section, where a future king and a restoration are announced. "That day" refers to that time of salvation God promised. Some see it fulfilled in part in the return from exile, and others also in Christ or at the end of time.

For today: if you have felt God's discipline or have failed, do not stay in guilt. God forgives and comforts whoever returns to him. Answer him today with a sincere prayer of gratitude.
exp.35:21:
Three officials of King Hezekiah returned to him with their clothes torn. Eliakim was the one in charge of the palace, Shebna the scribe or secretary, and Joah the recorder, that is, the one who kept the records of the kingdom. They told him what Rabshakeh had said, a senior spokesman of the king of Assyria. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief, distress, or horror.

The Assyrians had surrounded Judah, and Rabshakeh was mocking the LORD, saying that no god had saved his people. The officials obeyed the king's order not to answer him. Now they return to report, troubled by the threats and by the insult against God.

For today: when news or pressure overwhelms you, there is no need to pretend to be strong. You can bring your pain honestly before God, as Hezekiah did, who quickly sought the LORD in prayer.
exp.2:14:
It says that God asks the leaders of his people a sharp question: "What do you think you are doing, crushing my people and grinding the faces of the poor?" "Beat to pieces" means to strike or pound hard, and "grind the faces" is a picture of mistreatment and humiliation. It is an accusation, not a doubt on God's part.

The Lord, the God of hosts, speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is like a trial against the elders and princes of Judah. They had the duty to care for the people, but they took advantage of the poor and kept for themselves what belonged to them. God takes the case of the weak as something personal: he calls them "my people."

For today: if I have any power, whether at work, at home, or in the church, I must use it to protect and not to abuse. God watches how we treat the most vulnerable.
exp.43:26:
This verse says that God has power over the deep waters. He commands them, "Be dry," and they obey. The "rivers" that dry up speak of great currents that seemed impossible to cross. "Deep" means the abyss or the deep waters.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, to a people who would be carried off captive to Babylon. God promises that Jerusalem will be inhabited again and that Cyrus, king of Persia, would help make that happen. Many believe the dried-up waters recall the Red Sea, and others think they allude to how Cyrus took Babylon, though this last point is debated.

For today: when you face an obstacle that seems too big, remember that God can open a way where you see no exit. Trust Him and take the next step in faith.
exp.44:5:
This verse says that God wants all people, from where the sun rises to where it sets, that is, from east to west, to recognize that there is no other God. "Yahweh" is the name of God, and "there is none beside me" means that no one else shares his place.

God speaks to Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he called by name to help free Israel from exile, although Cyrus did not know the true God. Out of love for his chosen people, God uses a foreign king. In this way he shows that he rules over all nations and that his plans are carried out.

For today: when you feel that everything is out of control, remember that God still reigns. Rest in him and pray with confidence, knowing that he can work even through people who do not know him.
exp.44:6:
It says that God is the creator of all things: he forms the light and creates the darkness, he makes peace and creates calamity. The Hebrew word translated here as "calamity" can mean disaster, misfortune or judgment, not necessarily sin. The word "create" in the verse is the same one that means to bring something into being, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

God himself speaks, addressing Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he would use to free Israel from exile in Babylon, although Cyrus did not know him. In that time many peoples believed in several gods, one of light and another of darkness. God declares that there is no other power beside him; everything, including calamities, is under his control and purpose.

For today: when you live through dark or confusing times, remember that nothing escapes the hand of God. You can pray with confidence, even if you do not understand everything, because he still governs and is just.
exp.48:21:
He says that God himself, the Lord GOD, will give a mighty sign to the nations. The phrases "lifting up the hand" and "raising the banner" are gestures of calling, like a signal for people to gather together. As a result, the peoples will bring back the sons and daughters of Israel, carrying them in their arms and upon their shoulders, with care. "Gentiles" here means the nations.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Zion, or Jerusalem, who felt abandoned, alone and without children during the exile. The people doubted that God remembered them. God answers by promising restoration. Some see here the return from Babylon; others also see a broader fulfillment in the future.

For today: when you feel forgotten or without hope, remember that God has not left you. He can work in unexpected ways, and his care is tender. Wait on him with confidence.
exp.40:26:
God says that he was the first to announce these things to Zion, before they happened. And he promises to send Jerusalem a messenger who brings good news. The phrase "good tidings" means good news, and the one who brings it is the messenger. The word "Zion" here refers to God's people and to their city.

The Lord speaks in an imaginary trial against the idols of the nations. He asks who announced beforehand what was going to happen, and no one answers. Only God announces the future and fulfills it. Many understand that the one who comes from the north and the east is Cyrus, king of Persia, although some interpret it differently. The messenger of good news points to the deliverance of Jerusalem, and Christians also see it fulfilled in Christ.

Today we can trust that God keeps what he says. When everything seems uncertain, we can return to his Word and rest in his faithfulness.
exp.52:3:
This verse says that the servant of the Lord took upon himself our sicknesses and our pains, that is, our suffering and our burdens. Yet the people thought God was punishing him: they saw him as struck down, smitten of God, and humbled.

Here a group speaks, looking back with surprise and regret. They had despised him before, but now they understand that his suffering was not punishment for his own fault. The verses that follow make this clear: he was wounded for our rebellions. Christians see Jesus in this passage, though some scholars debate how the passage was originally understood.

For today: when you see someone suffering, do not rush to judge them. And when you suffer, remember that Christ knows pain and walks with you in compassion.
exp.63:3:
It says that from the beginning no one has heard, understood, or seen another god, apart from the LORD, who acts on behalf of those who wait for him. The words "heard" and "understood" here mean that people have not grasped or known anything like this.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, praying on behalf of the people of Israel. He asks that God intervene with power, as he did in the past, and he recalls his wonderful works. The people acknowledge their sin in the verses that follow, but still hold on to the hope that God will save them.

For today: when your situation feels hopeless, do not stop waiting on God. He acts on behalf of those who trust in him. Spend a few minutes in prayer, remembering something God has already done for you, and bring your waiting to him with confidence.
exp.15:9:
This verse says that joy and singing have ended in the fields and vineyards of Moab. No one will shout with gladness or tread grapes in the winepresses (the vats where grapes were trampled to get the wine). The treader was the one who crushed the grapes with his feet. God says, "I have made their vintage shouting to cease," meaning the celebration of the harvest.

Isaiah announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring country of Israel, famous for its vineyards. God is the one speaking, but the prophet also shows sorrow: he weeps for Jazer, Heshbon, and Sibmah. The texts do not explain all the historical details of that destruction. We see that God judges pride, but He takes no pleasure in human suffering.

For today: let us not rejoice in the fall of others, nor trust in our harvests or achievements. May our hearts feel compassion, and may we seek God before the crisis arrives.
exp.55:9:
It says that the watchmen of the people, that is, their leaders, are blind and know nothing. They are like guard dogs that do not bark: they give no warning of danger. "Watchmen" are sentinels who keep watch from a tower. Those who are drowsy and lying down describe people who spend their time stretched out, and loving to slumber shows that they prefer comfort to their duty.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah after the return from exile. He has just promised to gather the scattered, and he also invites the nations.
