But now he denounces the leaders of Israel who neglect the people and seek their own gain, as the following verses show. Interpreters differ on exactly who these leaders are and when this took place.

Today: if you have any responsibility, whether in your family, your church, or your work, do not grow drowsy. Ask the Lord for open eyes, and speak with love and truth when you see a danger.
exp.9:28:
This verse says that the enemy army crossed the passage (the ford of the river or ravine) and camped at Geba, a small town. Seeing it approach, the people of Ramah trembled with fear, and the inhabitants of Gibeah, the city where King Saul was born, fled in flight. The word that means they spent the night there is simply the verb used in the verse for taking up lodging.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He describes, with vivid images, the advance of the Assyrian army toward Jerusalem, naming towns north of the city. Many understand it as an announced march, not necessarily one that had already happened, and scholars discuss the exact route. What matters is that the previous verse promises that God will remove the yoke from his people, and the following text shows that the danger will not have the last word.

For today: when fear advances like an army, remember that God sees the danger and also the deliverance. Tell him honestly what you fear, and trust that he cares for you.
exp.2:24:
This verse announces that the men of Jerusalem will die by the sword, and that its mighty men, that is, its military strength, will fall in battle. "Men" are the men, and "by the sword" means by the sword. "Your strength" refers to the warriors who defended the city.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. Before this, he described the pride of the women, who trusted in their jewels and their beauty, and announced that all of that would be lost. Now judgment reaches the men. Many understand this as a warning of invasion, although the text does not give exact details of when it happened.

For today: do not put your security in what is passing away, such as appearance, money, or strength. Trust in God, and let Him correct your pride before life does it with blows.
exp.34:5:
It says that when God comes to save, those who today cannot walk will leap for joy like a deer, and those who cannot speak will sing. It also promises that waters will break out in the wilderness and streams in the barren land. The verse's "streams" and "wilderness" are the sense here: a torrent is a strong rushing current of water, and a wilderness is an uninhabited, dry place.

Isaiah writes to the people of Judah, who are weary and afraid. Earlier, the prophet tells them to take heart, because God is coming to save them. The verses that follow speak of a "Way of Holiness." Many see it as a promise of restoration for the people; Christians often see in it also a announcement of the work of Christ and of the final restoration. There are several ways of understanding it.

For today: when you feel dry or without strength, do not just stare at the desert. Speak to God honestly, remember his promises, and encourage another person who is discouraged.
exp.64:7:
God uses the image of a cluster of grapes where new wine is still found. Someone sees it and says, "Do not throw it away, for a blessing is in it." In the same way God promises that, for the sake of his servants, he will not destroy the whole people. Here "destroy" means to ruin or throw away.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just announced judgment on a people who burned incense on the mountains and offended him with their idolatry. But even in the midst of punishment, God makes clear that he will preserve a faithful group. He then promises to bring descendants from Jacob and Judah, and that his chosen ones will live again in the land.

For today: God sees value in those who are faithful to him, even if they are few, and he does not lose them in the midst of crises. If you feel small or alone in your faith, remember that he cares for you. He also invites us to live with sincerity, so that we do not keep following what offends him.
exp.42:20:
This verse says that God formed his people with a purpose: that they would speak of his praises and make known how good he is. The phrase "formed" means that he shaped them and brought them into existence as a people. "Shew forth" means that they will declare it openly, so that others will know.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, who was living in the midst of hardship and exile. He promises to do something new: to make a way in the wilderness and give water to his chosen people. Then, in the verses that follow, he rebukes them because they have neglected him. Even so, his purpose for them does not change, and his grace goes forward.

For today: God made us to know him and to speak of his goodness. Today you can tell someone, simply, how God has sustained you in a difficult moment, and thank him out loud.
exp.7:2:
Isaiah says that he came together with his wife, "the prophetess," and she became pregnant and had a son. Then God commanded him to give the boy a very long name: Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The name is usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the plunder."

Isaiah speaks in the first person. Judah was afraid of Damascus and Samaria, which were threatening it. God used the child's name as a sign: before he learned to speak, Assyria would defeat those kingdoms. The witnesses mentioned in the previous chapter testified that the announcement was made before it came to pass.

For today: when fear seems bigger than God, remember that He knows the future and keeps His word. Trust His promises instead of seeking security only in human strength.
exp.28:7:
It says that the nations that attack Jerusalem (Mount Zion) will be left disappointed. They are like a hungry man who dreams he is eating, but wakes up with an empty stomach, or a thirsty man who dreams he is drinking and wakes up weary and still thirsty. The word "or" is used to present the two images as alternatives, and "is found" describes where the enemy is left.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Jerusalem, called Ariel, in a time of threat. God promises that He Himself will intervene and that the enemy multitude will vanish like a dream. The verses that follow show that the people were also spiritually asleep. Some understand this as a historical promise of deliverance, and others also see a broader announcement about God's judgment.

For today: the things that do not come from God promise much but do not satisfy. Seek your rest and your security in Him, who truly feeds the soul.
exp.25:7:
It says that while God acts with his judgments (his just decisions and his works to correct and govern), his people have waited for him with patience. The phrase "to thy name and to the remembrance of thee" means: to who you are and to what you have done, so that the greatest longing of the soul is God himself. The word "remembrance" here refers to the recollection of his renown and his character.

The people of Judah speak in a song of confidence within Isaiah 24–27. They live between oppression and waiting, and they affirm that God is upright and that his ways are just. Interpreters differ about the exact historical moment, but the tone is one of faith in the midst of difficulty.

For today: when justice seems slow in coming, do not let the waiting harden you. Turn it into a time to desire God more and to remember who he is. Pray calmly, read his Word, and trust that he is upright.
exp.23:17:
It says that no one will be able to escape God's judgment. Whoever flees from the terror will fall into a pit (the "pit" is a deep hole in the ground), and whoever climbs out of the pit will be caught in a trap. The "windows from on high" that are opened call to mind the flood of Noah (Genesis 7:11), and the "foundations of the earth" that shake show that everything is shaken.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, in a section describing God's judgment on the whole earth. The cause is that the inhabitants have been unfaithful and have broken the covenant with God. Scholars debate which historical events it refers to, and many also see it as a picture of the final judgment.

For today: we cannot hide our sin or flee from God by our own means. The wisest course is to turn back to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy, for the righteous receive glory (v. 16).
exp.21:15:
God asks Shebna a sharp question: "What are you doing here? Who are you, to have carved yourself a tomb here?" He speaks of a tomb cut out in a high place, hewn into the rock.

Isaiah brings this message from God to Shebna, a high official, the palace steward. It seems he used his position to seek his own honor, with a luxurious tomb, as if he were of royal blood. We know no more details of his life; the text shows only a man more concerned with his fame than with serving. God announces that he will be removed from his post and will die far away.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I work to serve, or to be admired? God gives us responsibilities to bless others, not to raise a monument to our own name.
exp.22:7:
This verse asks a question: who decided the fall of Tyre? Tyre was a city famous for its trade, and it was described as a city whose power and fame made it admired. Its merchants were so wealthy that they had the standing of princes and nobles.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks a message of judgment against Tyre. The question is rhetorical: the answer comes in the next verse, where God himself has decreed it. Tyre trusted in its riches and its reputation, and God shows that no human glory is beyond his authority.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or reputation. All of that can change suddenly. Be thankful for what God gives you, use it with humility, and trust in him more than in what you have.
exp.57:7:
Then the verse says that when the people live the kind of fasting God desires, their lives will be filled with light, like the coming of morning. "Health" here means healing or restoration, and "speedily" means "quickly." The righteousness that goes before them is an upright life that opens the way, and the glory of the Lord will be their rear guard, that is, the one who watches over their back and protects them.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who fasted and carried out religious acts, but who mistreated their workers and neglected the poor. God tells them that true fasting includes freeing the oppressed, sharing bread, and clothing the naked. The promise of the verse is God's response to that obedience.

For today: join your prayer with a concrete act of kindness. This week, share a meal, help someone in need, or deal justly with the people you work alongside.
exp.16:9:
It says the people forgot God, who is here called "the God of your salvation" (salvation here is the same as "health," meaning safety) and "the rock of your strength," that is, the secure place where one takes shelter. Therefore, although they plant beautiful plants and foreign shoots (cuttings brought from other lands, perhaps tied to pagan worship), they will not see fruit.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom, Israel (Ephraim), allied with Damascus. Many understand that they trusted in alliances and in idols, not in God. The text does not make entirely clear what the plants were, and they are interpreted in several ways. The central point is that, without God, the effort comes to nothing.

For today: before you plan and work, pause to remember who sustains you. Set aside a moment each day to give thanks and to place your projects in his hands.
exp.46:3:
This verse is a brief statement of who God is. The people of Israel call him "Redeemer," that is, the one who rescues and sets free his own. His name is "the Lord of hosts," the Lord who holds all power, and he is "the Holy One of Israel," the one who is pure and wholly set apart from everything else.

Isaiah announces the fall of Babylon, called "the daughter of the Chaldeans." She had dominated Israel and was cruel to it. God himself allowed that punishment to fall on his people because of their disobedience, but now he judges Babylon for her lack of mercy. In the midst of that judgment, the prophet reminds us who defends his own.

For today: when you feel trapped by situations stronger than you, remember that God has not forgotten you. Pray to him as your Redeemer and trust in his care, even when deliverance is slow in coming.
exp.43:0:
It says that God speaks to his people and asks them to listen carefully. The opening words mark a shift: after rebukes, a word of comfort comes. God calls Jacob and Israel his servant and reminds them that he chose them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were living under judgment and discouragement, and perhaps felt forgotten. So God reminds them of their identity: they are not an abandoned people, but a chosen one. The verses that follow confirm this with promises of help, of not fearing, and of pouring out his Spirit and his blessing.

For today: when you feel far from God or afraid, stop and listen to what he says about you. Your worth does not depend on your failures, but on his love and his calling. Read his Word and rest in his faithfulness.
exp.42:9:
God says to Israel: "You are my witnesses and my chosen servant." He chose them so that they would know him, believe in him, and understand that he alone is God. The phrase about being "formed" refers to the fact that no other god was made before him, and none will be made after him. God has no beginning and no rival. The name of God is the one the verse calls "the Lord," and the older spelling of certain words has been updated to modern usage.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is like a courtroom: he calls the nations to bring forward witnesses who can show that their gods have announced or done anything. Israel, though spiritually blind and deaf, did see God announce things and save them. In this way, their history proves that the Lord is the only true God.

For today: God also invites us to be witnesses through our lives. Think of a time when God helped you or held you up, and tell someone about it today with simplicity and gratitude.
exp.55:6:
God himself says he will bring a group of people to his holy mountain, that is, to Jerusalem, where the temple stands. There he will fill them with joy. Their whole burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be welcomed, that is, well received. And his house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The words before this one are addressed to foreigners who join themselves to the Lord, love him, and keep his covenant. In that time many thought they were left outside. God promises them a place, a name, and a full welcome in his house.

For today: if God opens the door to all who come to him with sincerity, we too should do the same. This week, invite or warmly welcome someone who feels like an outsider in your church or community, and pray with that person.
exp.59:12:
It says that the finest trees of Lebanon, famous for its fine timber, will be brought to Zion to beautify the temple. The trees named in the verse are the fir, the pine, and the box, all trees with fine wood. The phrase "the place of my feet" refers to the sanctuary, where God makes his presence felt among his people. God promises to honor that place.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, encouraging Jerusalem after its humiliation. He promises restoration and says that the nations will bring their riches. Some see its fulfillment in the return from exile, others in Christ and the Church, and others in a future time. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: God delights in beautifying and honoring the place where he dwells. Offer him the best of your life, your time, and your talents, trusting that he restores what seemed abandoned.
exp.62:1:
Here the prophet asks the warrior who is approaching why his clothing is stained red, like the clothing of someone who has trodden grapes in the winepress, the vat where the juice of the grapes was squeezed out. The reddish color is so intense that it is compared to deep red.

The prophet Isaiah sees God coming from Edom, a people hostile to Israel, as both judge and savior. He himself answers afterward that he has trampled the nations in his anger, and that his clothing was stained. Some understand this as historical judgment on God's enemies; others see it as a announcement of the final judgment. Christians also connect it with Revelation 19, although how it connects is debated.

For today: God is not indifferent to injustice. We can hand over our pain to him, trust that he will do justice, and reject personal revenge. He also saves and redeems his people.
exp.44:14:
This verse says that God, though at times he cannot be seen or understood, is the God who saves. The word "hidest" means that he hides himself, that his purposes and the way he acts are not always clear to us.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. God has just announced that he will use Cyrus to free his people held in captivity, and that the nations will acknowledge that he alone is God. Isaiah responds with wonder: God works in unexpected ways. Some understand this to mean that God works behind the events of history; others see it as an expression of reverence before a mystery.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, do not conclude that he is absent. Trust that he works and saves, even in silence. Tell him honestly what you feel, and wait on him.
exp.0:15:
This verse is a call from God to his people: "Wash you, make you clean" is an invitation to wash away the dirt of sin. "Put away the evil of your doings" means setting aside the wickedness in their actions, and "from before mine eyes" shows that God sees everything. "Cease to do evil" asks for a real change in conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. They kept festivals, brought offerings, and prayed, but their hands were full of blood, meaning there was violence and injustice. For this reason God rejects their empty religion. Even so, he immediately offers them forgiveness: their sins, red as crimson, can become white as snow.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or pray if we mistreat others. Ask God to forgive you and to show you an attitude or habit you need to leave behind, and change it this week with concrete actions.
exp.40:23:
It says that idols and false gods are worth nothing, and that what they do is empty. Here "vanity" means something hollow, without power. "Abomination" is something repugnant. So whoever chooses to trust in those gods becomes like them: they cling to something empty.

God speaks, through Isaiah, in a kind of trial before the nations. He challenges the idols to tell what has happened and what will happen, or to do something, good or bad. They cannot. With this God shows that only He knows and directs history. Then He announces that He will raise up someone from the east, whom many understand to be Cyrus, although the text here does not name him.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we place our trust in that cannot answer: money, success, the opinion of others. Let us hand that trust today to the God who does speak and does fulfill what He says.
exp.57:11:
It says that the people who practice justice and compassion will be used by God to rebuild what lay in ruins. The "ancient wastelands" are the ruins of abandoned cities. The "breaches" are the gaps in a wall, and the "highways" are roads. They are promised that they will be called repairers of the broken places and restorers of paths where people can dwell.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who fasted and kept the rituals, yet who continued to be unjust toward others. He tells them that true fasting means sharing bread, freeing the oppressed, and caring for the afflicted. Many understand the restoration to refer to the rebuilding of the land after the exile, though the message reaches beyond that period.

Today, sincere faith shows itself in helping to repair what is damaged around us: a divided family, a neighbor in need, or a forgotten community. Today, choose one concrete act of service.
exp.42:2:
God presents himself as the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, and your Savior. He says that he gave Egypt, Ethiopia, and Seba as your ransom, that is, as the price of your deliverance. The word "ransom" speaks of a payment to set someone free.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who were suffering exile and were afraid. The Lord reminds them that he created them, redeemed them, and calls them his own. Scholars understand the mention of those nations in several ways; what is certain is that it expresses how much God values his people.

For today: when fear overwhelms you, remember that you belong to God and that he values you deeply. Say to him in prayer: "Lord, you are my Savior; in you I trust."
exp.32:13:
The sinners in Jerusalem (Zion) were filled with fear when they saw God's judgment. Those who look religious but are not truly so are the ones described as "hypocrites." The phrase "were struck with terror" means they were left trembling. The "devouring fire" and "everlasting burnings" describe the holiness of God, who does not tolerate evil. The question is: who can stand close to such a God?

The prophet Isaiah speaks here after announcing punishment against the nations that were enemies of Judah. God calls both those far away and those near to recognize his power. Some understand the fire as God's judgment; others understand it as his holy presence. The answer comes in the verses that follow: the one who lives with justice and righteousness.

For today: it is not enough to only appear good. Ask God for a sincere heart, and practice honesty in small things, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.57:13:
He says that if someone honors the Sabbath and stops pursuing their own profit on that day, God promises them three things: that they will delight themselves in the Lord, that he will make them ride upon the high places of the earth, and that he will feed them with the inheritance of Jacob. The promise that he will feed them with the inheritance of Jacob refers to the land and the blessings promised to Jacob's descendants.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and practiced their religion, but neglected justice and mercy. Before this verse, God asks them to honor the Sabbath as a day of delight and not of their own interests. The final phrase emphasizes that the promise is certain.

For today: set aside time each week to rest and be with God, leaving work and distractions behind, and ask him to teach you to delight in him.
exp.48:4:
Here the servant of the LORD says that God formed him from his mother's womb to be his servant and to bring Jacob back to Him. Even though Israel does not gather or respond, he knows that God values him, and that his God is his strength.

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, who in this passage is called "Israel." He feels tired from work that seems to be in vain. Many Christians see here a prophecy about Jesus, while others first emphasize Israel as a people or a faithful servant within it. God answers by expanding his mission: he will also be a light to the nations.

For today: if you serve God and see little fruit, do not measure your worth by people's response. Rest in the fact that God knows you, values you, and gives you strength to remain faithful.
exp.31:19:
They are blessed who sow beside all waters and let the ox and the donkey roam freely there. "Blessed" means happy or fortunate. The phrase about letting the animals walk through the ground refers to allowing livestock to tread on wet land, something done on moist soil, perhaps to sow or to trample the earth. Scholars do not have one single exact explanation for that image.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. The chapter announces a time of justice, of the Spirit poured out, and of peace for God's people, after judgment. This verse closes the promise with a scene of calm and fruitful work, where the land yields its harvest without threat.

For today: work with hope and generosity, even when you do not see the fruit right away. Sow kindness, prayer, and honest labor, trusting that God cares for what you do in his name.
exp.64:6:
God says he will hold the people accountable for their sins, both their own and those of their ancestors. The phrase "burned incense" means they offered smoke to idols on the mountains and hills, and in this way they provoked him. To "blaspheme" means to speak of him with contempt and dishonor him.

"Therefore will I measure their former work into their bosom" is an expression meaning that he will repay them fully for what they deserve. "Their former work" refers to the sin they had practiced for many years.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He rebukes a rebellious people who practiced idolatry and, at the same time, considered themselves holier than others. God does not overlook that sin, but he promptly promises to save a faithful remnant.

For today: let us not keep repeating inherited mistakes without examining them. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our sins, to leave behind every false refuge, and not to look down on others. His justice is serious, but his mercy is too.
exp.25:19:
God invites his people to go into their rooms, shut their doors, and hide themselves for a brief moment, while his anger passes. The phrase about going into their rooms refers to the private rooms or chambers of the house. The word "indignation" is God's judgment against evil.

The prophet Isaiah speaks these words for God. Before this, the people confessed their helplessness and held to the hope of the resurrection of the dead. After this, God comes out to call to account the wickedness and violence on the earth. Interpreters differ: some see a picture of physical shelter, others a picture of trusting God during judgment. The text does not make this clear.

When everything feels uncertain or unjust, there is no need to respond with fear or haste. You can step aside for a moment, pray, and rest in God, trusting that he cares for his own and will bring about justice in his time.
exp.2:17:
It says that, when the day of judgment comes, God will take away from the women of Jerusalem their adornments. The phrase about the ankle ornaments seems to refer to striking anklets or foot jewelry. The hair nets were ornaments or nets for the hair. The crescent ornaments were pieces shaped like half moons. The exact meaning of some of the Hebrew words is uncertain, and translations vary.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just accused the daughters of Zion of pride: they walked with airs of superiority and made noise to draw attention. This list of jewelry shows a wealth and vanity that hid injustice among the people. By taking them away, God shows them that what they boasted in could not save them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we find our worth. God does not condemn beauty, but he does condemn the pride that seeks admiration. Let us ask him for a humble heart.
exp.4:9:
It says that a large vineyard of ten yoke-measures (a yoke-measure was what a yoke of oxen could plow in one day) would produce only a small skin of wine, that is, a small jar of wine (the Hebrew Bible speaks of a "bath," about 20 to 40 liters, though the exact measure is debated). And thirty measures of seed sown would produce barely three measures of harvest. In other words, a miserable harvest, far less than what was sown.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD to Judah. He has just condemned the wealthy who piled up houses and land without thinking of others. God announces that this greed will bring punishment: fields that yield nothing and empty houses.

For today: accumulating more and more does not bring security or peace. Ask yourself whether you use what you have with generosity and justice, and trust that God is the one who gives true fruit.
exp.55:3:
Here God speaks to the eunuchs, men who in that time were often shut out from the congregation of Israel. He tells them that if they keep his Sabbaths (the days of rest), choose what pleases him, and hold fast to his covenant (his agreement with him), they will have a place among his people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The eunuchs and the foreigners felt rejected, afraid of being left out, like a dry tree with no future and no descendants. God answers that their acceptance does not depend on their background or their condition, but on their faithfulness to him.

Today, if someone feels excluded or without worth, they can remember that God looks at a willing heart. We can draw near to him with confidence and also welcome others who feel left out.
exp.38:3:
Here the prophet Isaiah asks King Hezekiah a second question: what things the messengers saw in his palace. Hezekiah answers frankly that he showed them absolutely everything, keeping nothing back. "Treasures" are his riches and stored goods.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The envoys from Babylon had come from far away, and Hezekiah, pleased with their visit, showed them all his wealth and his weapons. The Bible does not detail everything he was thinking, but God's response in the following verse shows that this was a serious mistake: Babylon would later carry off all of that.

For today: it is worth asking ourselves where we place our trust and what we boast about. Everything we have is a gift from God and can pass away. Before others, it is better to give glory to God than to proudly display what we possess.
exp.39:5:
A voice says, "Cry." He asks, "What shall I cry?" The answer is that all people are like grass, and all their beauty or greatness is like a flower of the field, which lasts only a short time. "Flesh" here means weak and mortal humanity. "Aloud" means "loudly."

We are in the comforting part of Isaiah, where God announces that he is coming to rescue his people. A voice, not clearly identified, gives the command to proclaim. The prophet answers with humility, and the message contrasts human frailty with the faithfulness of God, whose word stands forever, as the following verses say.

For today: do not place your security in success, fame, or strength, which pass away. Rely on the word of God, which does not change. That trust gives you peace when everything around you seems unstable.
exp.24:10:
He says that God will put his hand into the middle of Moab, the way a swimmer moves his arms to move forward in the water. In this way he will bring down, that is, humble, their pride, which is their arrogance. The phrase about the "members of his hands" is hard, and some understand it as skillful movements of the hands. Others think it is Moab who thrashes about without being able to save itself.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a song of praise for God's salvation. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears here as an example of a pride that rises up against God and his people. The message is that God defeats the proud and cares for those who wait on him.

Today we can examine our hearts and ask God to free us from pride. If we trust in him, we do not need to win by our own strength; we can wait with humility and patience for his justice.
exp.29:19:
It says that God will allow hard times, described as "the bread of adversity" and "the water of affliction," that is, suffering and scarcity. But even so, the teachers who speak on God's behalf will no longer hide or disappear. The Hebrew-era word for "teachers" is one the verse above renders as "teachers," and the phrase about being removed means they will not be pushed aside. The people will see them with their own eyes. Some understand this to refer to prophets, and others to God himself as the Teacher.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who trusted in alliances with Egypt instead of trusting in God. He warns them of the consequences, but he also promises that God will show mercy. Suffering is not the final word: after it comes God's guidance and the abandonment of idols.

For today: in your difficult moments, do not turn away from the Word of God. Seek out a church, a faithful teacher, or a daily time of Bible reading. God often uses difficulty so that you will listen to his voice with greater attention.
exp.40:11:
This verse says that Israel's enemies, those who fought and argued against them, will disappear so completely that even if they are sought, they will not be found. The phrase "they shall be as nothing" and the words "as a thing of nought" mean that they will lose all their power and be left without any importance. The word "contend" means to dispute or to be in conflict.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, a small and frightened people surrounded by stronger nations. God wants to calm their fear by reminding them that he is with them, helps them, and sustains them. It is a promise to that people in their specific situation.

For today: when you feel pressure from conflicts or from people who make your life difficult, do not let fear take charge. Pray, trust that God sustains you, and avoid repaying evil with evil. He knows how to care for you.
exp.44:22:
God says he made an oath by himself, because there is no one greater by whom to swear. What has gone out of his mouth is righteous and will not be canceled: every knee will bow before him and every tongue will swear, that is, will declare its loyalty to him.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people in exile who feel forgotten. God presents himself as the only God, Savior, and righteous one, and calls all the nations to look to him and be saved. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, applying it to Christ. Some debate how that final acknowledgment will take place, but the text emphasizes that God has the last word.

Today we can rest: even though the world may seem chaotic, God fulfills what he promises. Decide today to honor him with your life, and trust him when you feel insecure.
exp.20:2:
It says that the prophet feels a very strong pain in his lower back and in his waist, and an anguish comparable to the pains of a woman who is giving birth. The sentence "I was bowed down at the hearing of it" means that he was overcome with sorrow by what he heard, and "I was dismayed at the seeing of it" means that he was filled with fear because of what he saw.

Isaiah speaks, and the passage is a "burden," that is, a message of judgment against Babylon, called "the wilderness of the sea." God shows him a harsh vision: the Persians and the Medes will come to destroy. Many understand that Isaiah suffers because of what he sees, though some think it also expresses the terror of the people before that fall.

For today: God does not ask us to be indifferent to the suffering of the world. We can bring to prayer the tragedies we see, feel compassion, and trust that God is just and in control.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that God's judgment will fall on his people like fire that burns up dry stubble. The dry heads of grain and the dry stalks are consumed in an instant. The rotting of the root and the turning of the blossom into dust describe a people left without life or a future. The reason is plain: they rejected the law of God and despised his word.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the Lord to the kingdom of Judah, in the song of the vineyard and the woes of Isaiah 5. Before this verse, he denounces drunkenness and injustice: judges who acquit the guilty for a bribe and take away the rights of the innocent. The root problem was turning their backs on God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are treating God's word lightly, or bending it to our own convenience. A practical way is to read it each day with humility and to obey what we already understand, including in how we treat others with justice.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that the promised king will find his delight in fearing the Lord, that is, in revering and honoring him. The phrase "quick understanding" means that he will be very sharp, quick to perceive. Moreover, he will not decide based on appearances or on mere rumors: "reprove" here means to rebuke or pass judgment.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, threatened by powerful kingdoms and poorly governed by their leaders. He announces a descendant of Jesse, father of King David, on whom the Spirit of God will rest. Christians see in this branch Jesus; the text describes him as a perfect judge, just toward the poor.

For today: before forming an opinion about someone, do not settle for what you see or for what is being said. Ask, listen calmly, and ask God for wisdom to judge with justice and mercy.
exp.56:0:
It says that righteous and faithful people die, and almost nobody takes it to heart. The phrase translated here as "takes it to heart" means "stops to think." The "devout" are the godly, those who love God. "Gathered" means that they are taken away from this world. No one understands that God takes them away before the trouble arrives, or to spare them from it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's word to a people who had turned away from Him. The leaders and the people lived in idolatry and indifference, and did not value the faithful. The following verse clarifies that the righteous "shall enter into peace" and rest. Afterward God rebukes harshly those who practiced idolatry.

For today: when faithful people are taken away, or when life seems unjust, we can trust that God cares for His own and gives them rest. And let us value today the sincere believers around us, giving them thanks and support.
exp.14:7:
The cry of grief spread through all the land of Moab, from one end to the other. "The borders" are the boundaries or edges of the territory. Eglaim and Beer-elim were places at the edges of the land of Moab; their exact location is not certain. The "howling" is a loud cry of anguish.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a prophecy against Moab, a people who were neighbors of Israel. Before this, the destruction of its cities and fields is described, and afterward God announces further judgment on Dibon. Scholars do not agree on which exact historical event is meant. Even so, the text shows that the judgment reached everyone, and that the prophet also felt compassion for that people.

For today: God cares about the nations and sees the pain of people, even of those who are not his own people. We can learn to weep with those who suffer and to pray for them, instead of rejoicing in their fall. It also reminds us to live in humility before God.
exp.65:0:
God says the heavens are his throne, and the earth is the footstool where he rests his feet. Then he asks: what house could be built for him, and what place could be his resting place? God cannot be contained in any building.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This is the end of the book, and he addresses a people who valued the temple and the sacrifices very highly. The verses that follow show that God is not concerned with rituals offered without a sincere heart. He looks to the humble person, the one who respects his word. Scholars debate which temple is in view, but the central message is clear.

For today: it is not enough to attend a place or keep religious customs. Today you can draw near to God with humility, listening to his word with respect and obeying it from the heart.
exp.1:16:
It says that human pride, both that of each person and that of people in general, will be brought down and humbled. In the end, only God will be lifted up, that is, recognized as the only one who is truly great. The words translated as "loftiness" and "haughtiness" mean thinking oneself superior to others and to God. "Bowed down" means brought down or lowered. "In that day" refers to the day of the Lord, when God will act in judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who trusted in their wealth, their fortresses, their trading ships and their idols. The verses before this one mention towers, walls and the ships of Tarshish, symbols of power and prosperity. Isaiah warns them that none of these will save them before God. Scholars debate exactly which moment "that day" refers to, whether to a near judgment, to the end of time, or to both.

Today we can examine where we place our security: money, achievements or prestige. It is better to humble ourselves now before God than to be humbled later.
exp.1:13:
This verse follows a list of lofty and proud things over which the "day of the LORD" will come. Here the high mountains and the lifted-up hills are mentioned. It is a poetic image: what looks great and firm on the earth will be brought low by God.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in God's name. The cedars, the mountains, the towers and the ships represent people's pride and their trust in their power and wealth. Many understand these images as speaking of proud people, though some also see a judgment on nature and on human works. The central point is that only God is exalted (v. 17).

For today: examine what you trust in, whether your success, your money, or your position. Ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on him and not on what seems high and secure.
exp.39:7:
It says that everything human is temporary, like the grass that dries up and the flower that falls. By contrast, what God says never ends. The old forms of "dries up" and "falls" are not used here; the verse itself says "withereth" and "fadeth." "Shall stand for ever" means it stays firm and does not change.

The passage comes from Isaiah 40, a message of comfort for the people of Judah, who faced exile or its consequences. A voice commands that someone cry out, and the prophet asks what to proclaim. The answer is that human strength is fragile, but God's promise is certain. Then comes the announcement: God comes to his people with power and care.

For today: when you feel weak or see that everything is changing, rely on the Word of God. Read a passage each day and trust his promises more than what passes quickly, such as success, fame, or worries.
exp.47:6:
God says that these new things "are created now", meaning that He is bringing them into being right now. You had not heard of them before, so that you could not say, "I already knew that." "Created" means made or brought into existence.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, a stubborn people who credited events to their idols. God had already announced past events so that they would not attribute them to the idols. Now He reveals new and hidden things, so that they will recognize that only He governs history. Scholars disagree about exactly which new things are meant, but the context points to the deliverance from Babylon.

Today we can give God credit for the good we experience, without saying "I already knew that" or "it was my luck." Thank Him today for one specific blessing.
exp.59:19:
It says that the sun of Jerusalem will never set and its moon will not wane, because God himself will be its light forever. The verse's word "wane" means to lessen or fade out. The days of mourning, the sorrow over a loss, will come to an end.

It is a promise from God through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who had suffered violence and destruction. It speaks of a restored Zion, where there will be salvation and praise. Some believers see it partly fulfilled in the return from exile, others in the work of Christ, and others in the final restoration, as in Revelation 21:23.

For today: when you go through dark moments, remember that God is not merely a temporary help but a light that endures. Place your hope in him, and let his presence sustain you while you wait for the end of your tears.
exp.25:11:
This verse says that the people trust God to give them peace. The word "ordain" means that God will grant it or place it in their hands. Also, they acknowledge that everything they have accomplished and done, God worked in them and through them. Peace is not presented as a human achievement, but as a gift from God.

Here the people of Judah speak in a song of trust within Isaiah's prophecy. Before this, there is talk of a wicked man who does not learn even when shown kindness, and of enemies who do not see the hand of God. Afterward, the believers confess that other lords had dominated them, but that only to God do they call. Some understand "all our works" as the people's victories and achievements; the central idea is the same: God is the one who sustains.

Today, before struggling to achieve tranquility, ask God for his peace. And when something good comes from your effort, thank him, because he gave you the strength to do it.
exp.33:11:
It says that in that land there will no longer be anyone with real authority. The nobles will be called "princes," but they will have no kingdom to rule. All their great ones will be reduced to nothing. "Palaces" are the royal houses; "without a kingdom" means without power or territory.

Isaiah announces here God's judgment on the nations, and in this chapter Edom is mentioned in a special way. He speaks as a prophet, in the name of the Lord. His message is that no human power can stand when God judges. The images of smoke, wild animals and ruins paint a total desolation. Some see poetic and symbolic language; others take it more literally.

For today: do not place your security in titles, money or position, since all of that can disappear. Trust in God, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the land of Judah was full of idols. The people bowed down before objects made by their own hands and fingers. "Also" adds this to the earlier list: riches, horses, and chariots. The phrase "have bowed down" means they worshiped and gave their lives over to them.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, the people of God, and voices his complaint before Him. God had let them go their own way because they trusted foreign diviners, riches, and military strength, not Him. The verses that follow announce judgment, and when God appears, the idols will be of no use at all.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can place our trust in money, success, or what we produce. Ask yourself honestly: where does my heart rest? Give that place to God, because only He can truly hold you up.
exp.36:1:
Verse 2 tells that King Hezekiah sent three groups of men to the prophet Isaiah: Eliakim, who was over the household (the one in charge of the house and the affairs of the palace), Shebna the scribe (who wrote and kept the records), and the elders of the priests. All of them went "covered with sackcloth," a rough clothing used as a sign of grief and humility.

King Hezekiah had just heard the threats and mockery of the Assyrian messenger against Jerusalem and against God. For that reason he tore his clothes, went to the temple, and sent his trusted men to ask Isaiah to pray for the people who were still left.

For today: when a crisis comes that overwhelms you, do not face it alone. Pray to God and seek the support of people of faith who can intercede with you.
exp.40:0:
God calls the islands, that is, the distant lands, and all the peoples to keep silence and listen to him. He asks them to renew their strength, draw near, and present their arguments. The phrase "let them come near together to judgment" means they will come together to a debate or a court, where it will be seen who is right.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah. The verses that follow ask who raised up a righteous man from the east and gave him victory over kings. Many believe this refers to Cyrus of Persia, though some understand it differently. The central idea is that the Lord directs history, and not the idols of the nations.

For today: before you let fear or the voices of the world carry you away, be still and remember who governs history. Bring your concerns before God with confidence, because he can withstand any examination.
exp.46:13:
They say that the astrologers and fortune-tellers of Babylon will be like stubble, that is, light chaff that the wind carries away. The fire will consume them, and they will not even be able to save themselves. No good ember will remain to warm yourself by, nor a fire to sit beside; the fire will be destructive, not a comfort.

God speaks through Isaiah against Babylon, portrayed as a proud queen who trusted in magic, omens, and the study of the stars. He mocks those securities: if they are of any use, let them defend her now. The text stresses that her counselors will not be able to deliver her from judgment.

For today: examine what you trust in to feel secure. It may be horoscopes, superstitions, money, or your own plans. All of these can fail. Hand your fears over to God, who can truly save.
exp.2:12:
God stands up, like a judge in a courtroom, to present his case and pass sentence. To plead a cause means to argue on behalf of a matter in court, and the people mentioned here refers to his own people and, more broadly, to the nations. God is not a passive observer: he acts against injustice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in Judah, at a time when its leaders were abusing the people. Just before this verse, the text speaks of guides who lead people astray, and afterward God accuses the elders and princes of devouring the vineyard and crushing the poor. God himself calls the judgment because his people are being mistreated.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it to serve and not to take advantage of others. And if you have suffered injustice, rest in the knowledge that God sees and will judge with truth.
exp.23:14:
It says that the people should praise the Lord and give him honor. It calls them to do this "in the fires" and "in the isles of the sea," that is, in distant places. The word "glorify" means to honor and to acknowledge his greatness. Some translators understand "in the fires" as "in the east" or "in the regions of light," since the Hebrew can be read in more than one way.

Isaiah speaks in the middle of a judgment that reaches the whole earth. There will be destruction, and only a small remnant will be left, like the few olives that remain after the tree is shaken. That remnant, scattered in faraway lands, sings to God. Scholars do not always agree on exactly who that remnant is, but the text shows that God is praised even in times of judgment.

For today: praise God also in difficult moments, wherever you are. Your situation does not change the fact that he is worthy of honor.
exp.56:5:
God tells his people that their "portion" and their "lot," that is, what they regard as their inheritance and their security, they have placed among the smooth stones of the valley. To those stones they poured out a drink offering and brought gifts. At the end God asks: "Should I receive comfort in these?" In other words, will I not answer with judgment?

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Judah of idolatry: worshiping under the trees, in the valleys, and on high places. Some believe the smooth stones were objects of Canaanite worship, but scholars are not completely certain. God speaks like a husband wounded by unfaithfulness.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your security. Anything we treat as a source of life, whether money, success, or approval, can take the place of God. Return to Him with sincerity, for He forgives those who repent.
exp.9:7:
He says in this verse that the king of Assyria is boasting: "Are not my princes altogether kings?" That is, his leaders and officials have as much authority as a king, and that is why his power seems so vast to him.

Here God speaks through Isaiah and quotes the proud words of the Assyrian king. God uses him as an instrument to discipline his people, but the king does not know this and thinks everything is due to his own strength. That is why God exposes his arrogance, and later in the chapter announces that he will judge him.

For today: when we have success, power or good results, let us not claim all the credit for ourselves. Let us give thanks to God, for he gives and sustains what we have. Humility keeps us grounded.
exp.29:32:
It says that God has long had a place of judgment prepared, called Topheth, for the king. The phrase "set in order and made ready" means arranged and ready. It is a deep and wide place, with a great fire and plenty of wood. The breath of the Lord, his breath, sets it alight like a stream of burning sulfur.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was looking for help in Egypt out of fear of Assyria. He assures them that God himself will break Assyria. Topheth was a place near Jerusalem, later associated with terrible sacrifices. Many believe the "king" is the king of Assyria; others see a more general picture of God's judgment on the proud. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: you do not need to fear the powerful or rely on your own resources. God is just and has the last word. Give your fears to him in prayer and trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.63:1:
This verse says that God's presence would be like a very intense fire, like the one that melts metals or makes water boil. "Melted metals" refers to metals made liquid by heat. "Well known" means known by everyone. "Your enemies" and "the nations" are the peoples who do not acknowledge God. The speaker wishes that God would act with such power that the nations tremble before him.

It is part of a prayer by the prophet Isaiah on behalf of the people of Israel. The people feel far from God and in trouble, and they remember how God saved them before through astonishing deeds. For that reason they beg him to intervene again. Scholars debate at what historical moment this prayer is set, so it is wise not to state that with certainty.

Today we can pray sincerely and without fear, asking God to act in our lives and in our world. Remembering what he has already done gives us confidence to wait on him.
exp.65:4:
God speaks to those who hold his word in reverence, those who tremble at it. He tells them that their own brothers hate them and reject them for the sake of his name. Those brothers mock them, saying, "Let the Lord be glorified," as though they were devout. But God promises to appear for the joy of the faithful, and those who mocked will be put to shame.

The phrase "ashamed" points to people who are put to shame or left disappointed.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. At the end of the book, the people are divided: some worship in an empty way and mix their religion with practices that God rejects, while others are faithful to him from the heart. God comforts the faithful who are pushed aside by their own people, and he assures them that he will do justice.

If you are rejected or mocked for obeying God, do not lose heart. Keep going with humility, trusting that God sees everything and that he himself will make the truth clear in his time.
exp.43:1:
God presents himself as the one who made Israel and shaped it from the womb, that is, from its beginnings as a people. He promises to help it and says: "Fear not." He calls Jacob "my servant" and also "Jesurun," a poetic name for Israel. "Chosen" means that God picked him out.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were living with fear and discouragement, and God reminds them that he has not forgotten them. In the verses that follow, he promises to pour out water on the dry land and his Spirit on their children, as an image of new life and blessing.

For today: when fear or weariness weighs on you, remember that God has known you from the beginning and does not let you go. You can speak to him with confidence, ask him for help, and rest in the knowledge that his care does not depend on your strength, but on his faithfulness.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that the watchman sees a chariot coming with a pair of riders. Then one of them announces, "Babylon is fallen, is fallen!" and that all the images of her gods have been broken and lie shattered on the ground. Here "riders" means horsemen, and "broken" means destroyed or smashed to pieces.

The prophet Isaiah speaks like a sentinel who keeps watch at night from a tower. God shows him, in a vision, the fall of Babylon, the great power that oppressed the nations. Some think it refers to the conquest in 539 B.C. by the Medes and Persians, but the text gives no further details. The message encouraged God's people: no empire lasts forever.

For today: when evil and injustice seem very strong, remember that God still rules. Watch with patience, pray, and trust that no power or idol can stand before Him.
exp.22:16:
After the seventy years of being forgotten have passed, the Lord will "visit" Tyre, meaning he will attend to it and take care of it. The city will return to its trade and its profits.

The word "fornicate" here does not refer to literal sexual immorality. It is used as a picture of a city that trades with all the nations without loyalty to any of them.

The word "face" in the verse means the surface of the earth.

Isaiah prophesies against Tyre, a great trading city of Phoenicia. It is part of a message of judgment against several nations. The seventy years are understood in different ways: some see them as a literal period of time, and others as a symbolic period. What follows is surprising: its profits would be dedicated to the Lord and would serve to feed and clothe those who serve him.

For today: money and work can be either a trap or a blessing. We can ask ourselves whether what we earn serves only us, or whether we also put it at the service of God and of those in need.
exp.44:9:
It is a serious thing to bring a complaint against parents for having brought a child into the world. The words "fathered" and "gave birth" refer to the father who gives life and the mother who brings forth. The "Woe" is a serious warning: someone complains about their origin as if they had no right to question how they were formed.

God speaks through Isaiah, and the passage is addressed to a people in exile who doubted his plans. God had just announced that he would use Cyrus, a foreign king, to help his people. Some may have been troubled by that method. That is why God uses the image of clay and the potter, and now that of parents, to show that it is not fitting to call the one who gives life to account.

Today we can learn to trust God even when we do not understand the way he works. Instead of complaining bitterly, we can bring our questions to him honestly and rest in the knowledge that he knows what he is doing.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that the gates of the city, which were the place of gathering and justice, will be filled with sadness and mourning. Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, will be left alone and without comfort, sitting on the ground. "Sit" in the verse means to take a seat or settle down, and "desolate" means abandoned, without help. Sitting on the ground was a sign of deep mourning.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. Earlier in this chapter, he describes the women of Zion, proud of their luxury and their beauty, while in the city there was injustice toward the poor. The message announces a judgment: what they admired will be lost. This verse uses the image of a widow to show the fall of the city after the war.

For today: let us not place our security in what looks good or in what we possess. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that seeks justice and cares for the needy.
exp.62:13:
It says that the Spirit of the Lord guided Israel with care, the way livestock is led down into a valley: calmly and safely, so that they could rest. The word "beast" here means livestock, and "to lead" means to care for and guide. God did this "to make thyself a glorious name": to show who He is.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, in a prayer that recalls the exodus. He looks back to the crossing of the sea and the desert, with Moses as the guide. He does this because the people feel far from God and ask Him to show His love and His power again, as the verses that follow say.

For today: when you feel lost or tired, remember how God has guided you before. That remembrance can become prayer and hope, because the Shepherd does not change.
exp.14:8:
It says the waters of Dimon will be full of blood. God promises to bring still more disasters on Dimon: lions against those who escape from Moab and against those who remain in that land. "Fill up completely" is what the wording of the verse conveys here, meaning to be filled to the brim. "Additions" are things added, more punishments, and "remnant" refers to those who survive, the remains.

This is part of a prophecy of Isaiah against Moab, Israel's neighbor. God himself speaks ("I will bring"). The Moabites flee weeping and carry their riches to the brook of the willows. Dimon was probably a Moabite town, and its name sounds like the Hebrew word for "blood"; some believe Isaiah is playing on that similarity. Not even fleeing saves them. The "lions" may be real animals or a symbol of new invaders; it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: let us not trust in riches or in human escapes, but in God, who is just and governs the nations. Let us seek refuge in him in time.
exp.56:8:
God tells his people that they went to a "king" carrying fragrant oil and many perfumes, and that they sent messengers far away. "Ointment" means scented oil. At the end it says they lowered themselves to the deepest place, perhaps even to the grave. Some think "the king" is the god Molech, and others think it was a foreign king with whom Judah sought alliances. It is not certain which.

God speaks through Isaiah and accuses Judah of unfaithfulness, like a wife who abandons her husband. They sought security in idols and in foreign powers, instead of trusting God. They wore themselves out in that effort, but they did not repent.

Today we can ask ourselves where we seek security apart from God: money, influence or success. It is better to stop exhausting ourselves on what does not save, and to return to him with trust.
exp.42:8:
All the nations and peoples are said to be gathered together as if for a trial.

The reader is challenged to bring forth someone who announced ahead of time what was going to happen, or who can explain the former things, that is, earlier events that have already been fulfilled. Let them bring their witnesses to prove they are right, and let those who hear them agree that it is true.

God speaks to Israel, his people, who are weary and surrounded by nations with idols. Earlier, the people are described as blind and deaf, even though they have eyes and ears. God calls them to be his witnesses. The challenge shows that only the LORD announces the future and then fulfills it; the idols are silent. Scholars debate which exact events are meant, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when many voices compete for your trust, remember how God has been faithful in your life and in his Word. Write down those signs of his faithfulness and tell someone about them this week.
exp.53:13:
God promises to clothe his people in righteousness, like an adornment that makes them beautiful. He also promises to keep them far from oppression, that is, from the mistreatment of the powerful. Because of this, they will no longer be afraid, since terror will not come near them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Jerusalem, described as a woman who was abandoned and afflicted, but who will now be restored. Many understand that the promise looks toward the return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment in the people of God. Righteousness and peace come from Him, not from human effort.

For today: when fear or injustice surrounds you, remember that your security rests in the character of God and not in your circumstances. Pray asking Him for peace, and seek to live justly in your daily dealings with others.
exp.41:3:
This verse says that the Servant of God will not wear out or give up. Words like "fail" and "discouraged" describe losing strength or courage. He will remain steadfast until he has set justice on the earth. The distant lands, the islands, represent faraway peoples who wait in hope for his teaching and guidance.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, presenting the Servant chosen by God. He is a gentle servant, who does not shout or crush the weak, like a bruised reed. Christians see Jesus here, and the New Testament quotes this passage in Matthew 12. God promises him strength to carry out his mission.

For today: when you feel weary of doing good, remember that Christ does not give up on you. Rest in his strength and keep serving with tenderness.
exp.12:17:
It says that the soldiers who will attack Babylon will be merciless. With bows they will strike down even the young men, and they will show no pity to the babies (the sentence about "fruit of the womb" refers to small children, and the words that follow, "their eye shall not spare," mean that they will feel no pity).

Isaiah prophesies a message from God against Babylon, the proud power of his time. God says he will raise up the Medes to judge her. These are very harsh images of the violence of ancient war, and the text does not present them as something good, but as judgment on a proud and cruel nation. Some scholars see here a historical fulfillment, and others also see a foreshadowing of the final judgment.

Today it reminds us that God does not ignore the pride or the injustice of the powerful. We can trust that he judges with justice, and for that reason we should reject cruelty and treat the vulnerable with compassion.
exp.29:11:
God, here called "the Holy One of Israel," says that his people rejected his message. The word for "despise" means that they set it aside. Instead of trusting in God, they put their security in oppression and perverseness, that is, in deception and wickedness, and leaned on these as on a walking staff.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who did not want to hear warnings. They asked the prophets to say only pleasant things. Moreover, they sought protection in political alliances, especially with Egypt, rather than trusting in God. That is why God announces the consequences to them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we want to hear only what pleases us. God loves us, and for that reason he sometimes corrects us. Listening to his Word with humility, even when it is uncomfortable, is a firmer foundation than any false support.
exp.0:20:
It says that Jerusalem, the city that once was faithful to God, has now become like an unfaithful woman. The image of a prostitute is a strong way to describe unfaithfulness to God. The word for "judgment" here means justice, and fairness is equal and honest treatment for everyone. The word "murderers" shows that where there was once justice, there is now violence and abuse.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah and Jerusalem. God has just offered them a way out: obey and live well, or rebel and suffer the consequences. Here He grieves painfully over what they have become. The verses that follow explain the problem: corrupt leaders who love bribes and neglect the fatherless and the widow.

For today: examine whether your faith shows in how you treat the weak. God does not seek only religious words, but justice and compassion. Today you can help or defend someone who has no one else to do so.
exp.65:8:
It says that God, who gives the ability to bring forth, will not leave unfinished what He has begun. "Shall I bring to the birth" and "cause to bring forth" mean that He opens the womb and gives life. "Shut the womb" is the picture of stopping the birth. The expected answer is no: God completes what He starts.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah, at the end of the book. Zion, that is Jerusalem, appears as a mother who suddenly gives birth to a new people. It is an image of restoration that seems impossible. Scholars see it as a promise for the return from exile, and many also as a foreshadowing of something greater, still to be fulfilled.

For today: if God has started something in your life or in your family, even if it takes a long time or seems stuck, trust that He is faithful to complete it. Wait with prayer and patience.
exp.51:14:
Here the servant of the Lord is said to sprinkle many nations. Sprinkling was a gesture of purification in Israel's worship. The kings shall shut their mouths, that is, they will fall silent out of amazement and respect. "But" introduces what follows, and "were told" means they were given the message. They will see and consider something they had never heard before.

God speaks here, presenting his servant, and the passage continues into Isaiah 53. Before this, the servant is disfigured and suffers, but later he is exalted. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes this verse in Romans 15:21. Some Jews have understood the servant to be Israel; there are various interpretations.

For today: do not be discouraged if the gospel seems small or despised. God can open the eyes of powerful and humble people alike. Share the good news with humility, trusting that God makes understood what no one had understood before.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that God will punish the women of Jerusalem for their pride. The phrase "will leave their heads bare" means stripping the hair from the head or leaving the scalp exposed, something that was a cause of humiliation. The phrase about exposing their private parts speaks of exposing them to public shame. Some think it refers to the nakedness of captives, and others to humiliation in a more general sense.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was living in luxury while the powerful oppressed the poor. The daughters of Zion represent the women of the upper class, who showed themselves proud and vain. God announces that they will lose what made them proud.

For today: examine what you boast about, whether money, appearance, or position. Ask God for a humble heart, and use it to care for those in need instead of showing off.
exp.43:9:
Here God asks a question that sounds like a serious mockery: who would be foolish enough to make a god or cast an idol that is useless for anything? The words "formed" and "molten" speak of shaping and casting metal. "Profitable" means that it neither helps nor benefits anyone.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who were surrounded by nations with idols. God reminds them that he is the only God and that they are his witnesses. He shows them how absurd it is to worship something made by human hands, in order to give them confidence and so that they will not be afraid.

For today: anything we make and then ask to give us security, such as money, success, or the approval of others, can become an idol. Today you can ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and bring that fear to God in prayer.
exp.32:4:
It says that the Lord will be exalted, that is, acknowledged and raised up, because he dwells on high, meaning in a place far above everything. Furthermore, he filled Zion, which is Jerusalem, with righteous decisions and fairness, and with doing what is right. The words quoted here are simply the verse's own terms: "exalted" and "dwelleth," with "on high" describing where he is.

This chapter is a prophecy by Isaiah addressed to Judah. First it speaks of a destroyer and asks God for help (vv. 1-4). Then, in this verse, the prophet declares that God will act and will be honored. The preceding verses show enemy nations fleeing and being stripped of their goods. The following verses promise stability: wisdom, salvation, and the fear of the Lord. Scholars debate which exact historical moment is in view.

For today: when the world seems unjust or disordered, remember that God remains above all. Ask him to fill your home and your work with uprightness, and begin yourself by acting justly in small things.
exp.26:0:
In that day, it says, God himself will intervene with his sword, which is hard, great and strong, against Leviathan. This is a sea monster described as a swift, gliding serpent and as a twisting, coiled serpent full of bends. He will also slay the dragon of the sea.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do at the end of a long section about his judgment on the nations. Leviathan and the dragon are poetic images of evil and chaos that threaten his people. Some believe they represent enemy powers; others, a spiritual force. The text does not make this clear, and it is interpreted in several ways. Next comes the song of the vineyard protected by God.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that evil, however great or twisted it may seem, does not have the last word. God will defeat it, and in the meantime he cares for his own.
exp.48:3:
This verse says that the servant of the Lord feels that his effort was useless. The words "I have laboured in vain" and "I have spent my strength for nought" express that he worked hard and gave all his strength. Even so, he trusts: "yet surely my judgment is with the Lord" means that God is the one who evaluates his work, and "my work with my God" indicates that his reward is in God's hands.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, who is called Israel. Some see him as the people of Israel, others as a faithful servant within the people, and many Christians see Jesus here. He expresses his weariness because it seems there is no fruit, but God answers him that his mission is even greater: to be a light to the nations.

For today: when you serve while weary and do not see results, do not measure your work only by what you can see. Entrust it to God, who sees everything and rewards with justice.
exp.32:5:
It says that, in the days of Zion, there will be stability through wisdom, knowledge, and a powerful salvation. The most valuable thing for the people will be the fear of the LORD, that is, honoring God and living in reverence toward Him. The word "knowledge" in the verse's wording means understanding of what is true. Where the verse says "thy times," it refers to the era in which God sustains His people.

It is a prophecy from Isaiah to Judah, in the midst of threats from invaders and distress. Before this, God is exalted and fills Zion with justice; afterward, messengers are described as weeping and roads as ruined. Many understand that this verse offers hope in the middle of that suffering, although scholars debate which exact moment it refers to.

For today: in times of fear or uncertainty, do not seek security only in money or human plans. Ask God for wisdom and cultivate a sincere respect for Him in everyday life. That reverence is a treasure that is not lost.
exp.5:7:
Here is what the passage says: Isaiah heard the voice of God asking, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Isaiah answered at once, "Here am I; send me."

The words "here am I" are the same as "here I am," and "send me" is the same as "send me." The "us" in "who will go for us" is a form that some understand as the majesty of God, and others as a sign of the Trinity; the Bible does not fully settle it here.

Isaiah is speaking, a man who has just seen the holiness of God in the temple and felt lost because of his sin. A seraph touched his lips with a coal from the altar and declared him forgiven. After that forgiveness, God asks who will go, and Isaiah answers. His mission would be difficult, since the people were not going to respond well.

For today: when we experience God's forgiveness, we can respond with gratitude and availability. We can say, "Here I am," even though we do not know everything that will be asked of us.
exp.43:27:
God says that Cyrus, king of Persia, will be "my shepherd," that is, someone who will carry out His will. Cyrus will cause Jerusalem to be rebuilt and the foundation of the temple to be laid again.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah at a time when Jerusalem was not yet destroyed and the people were not yet in exile. He wants to comfort Israel and show that He governs history. He names Cyrus long before Cyrus reigned. Some believe Isaiah announced this in advance; others think this part was written during the exile. Whatever the case, the message is that God can use a foreign king to fulfill His promises.

For today: when your situation seems to be in ruins, trust that God can work even through unexpected means. Pray, wait patiently, and watch for how He sustains you.
exp.50:22:
The promise here is that the cup of punishment will pass from his people to those who humbled them. The "oppressors" are those who afflicted them. They said to her: "Bow down, that we may pass over," that is, "lie down so that we may walk on you." "You laid your body as the ground, and as the street" describes extreme humiliation, like being trampled just as the floor of a path is trodden underfoot. "Soul" here means the whole person.

The Lord speaks as the one who "pleads," that is, who defends the cause of his people in a court case. Jerusalem had suffered judgment for her sin and was left as one reeling in pain. Now God says that this time is ending and that he himself will deal with those who abused her. Most readers understand this to refer to the nations that oppressed Judah, such as Babylon.

For today: if you have been humbled or mistreated, God sees your pain and does not forget you. You can hand your wound over to him and leave justice in his hands, rather than carrying the burden of revenge.
exp.53:6:
God tells his people that he forsook them for a brief moment, but that he will gather them back with great mercies. "I will gather thee" is like bringing together someone who had been scattered and bringing them back home. "Mercies" are acts of compassion and kindness that they did not deserve.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people, Israel, had suffered the punishment of exile because of their unfaithfulness, and they felt like an abandoned wife. God presents himself as their husband and redeemer. He compares his promise to the one he made to Noah: just as he swore never again to flood the earth, he swears never again to be so angry with them.

For today: if you go through a season when you feel that God is far away, do not conclude that he has abandoned you forever. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that his compassion lasts longer than any trial.
exp.32:21:
This verse says that God fills three roles for his people: he is our judge, the one who decides with justice; our lawgiver, the one who gives the laws for living well; and our king, the one who rules with authority. For that reason it concludes that he himself will save us. The word "lawgiver" refers to the one who establishes the laws.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived threatened by foreign powers. Before this verse, he describes Jerusalem as a secure city, like a firm tent whose stakes are never pulled up. Afterward, he compares the enemies to a poorly built ship that sinks. God is the one who gives the victory and forgives sin.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember that God is not merely a distant helper. He guides, corrects, and rules with justice. You can entrust your decisions to him and trust that he sustains you.
exp.44:11:
God says that he made the earth and created human beings on it. With his own hands he stretched out the heavens, and he gave commands to all their host, that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars.

The Lord, the Holy One of Israel, speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were in trouble and doubted how God was acting. So God reminds them that he is the Creator and that he is in control.
