Right away he announces that he will raise up Cyrus to free the captives. Many understand that this is the meaning of the passage that follows.

When something in your life does not make sense, remember who God is. The one who holds up the universe also cares for you. You can pray with confidence, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.33:9:
It says that the fire and smoke of judgment against that land will not stop. The image is of a place destroyed forever, where no one will ever pass through again or live.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter announces judgment on the nations, and especially on Edom, which here stands as an example of those who oppose God and his people. The case of Zion shows that God defends his own and does justice. The images of pitch and sulfur recall Sodom. Many understand them as poetic and prophetic language, not as a literal description.

For today: God takes justice seriously, and evil will not have the last word. This invites us not to take revenge ourselves, but to trust him, and to live with humility and reverence, seeking his mercy while there is still time.
exp.21:18:
God tells Shebna that he will remove him from the position of power he holds. The phrase "I will drive you out" carries the sense of "I will thrust you out," and the word "thrust" speaks of removing him from his office with force. It is a clear sentence: he will lose his position.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. According to verse 15, the one accused is Shebna, a steward of the palace. The text shows him as someone proud, who cared about his own glory and not about serving the people. God removes him and puts Eliakim in his place, who would care for Jerusalem and for Judah like a father.

For today: any office or influence we have is on loan, not our own. It is wise to use it with humility and to serve others, remembering that God is the one who raises up and the one who takes away.
exp.5:5:
It says that one of the seraphim, heavenly beings who surround God's throne, flew toward Isaiah. He was holding a burning coal in his hand, that is, a glowing ember, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, that is, pincers, so as not to be burned.

Isaiah is speaking, recounting his vision of the temple. He has just seen the holy Lord and feels lost because of his sin and that of his people. The coal comes from the altar, a place tied to sacrifice and forgiveness. Many understand that it shows God himself cleansing and preparing the one he calls. The text does not explain every detail of the gesture.

For today: when you feel unworthy before God, do not hide. Bring your sin to him with sincerity, trust in his forgiveness, and let yourself be cleansed. Then you will be ready to say, "Here I am."
exp.65:20:
God promises that he will take "of them" to be priests and Levites. Priests and Levites were those who served God in the worship of the temple. The word "them" seems to refer to people brought from the nations, although some scholars think it refers to scattered Israelites who return. Both readings exist.

The Lord speaks near the end of Isaiah. He has just announced that his survivors will carry his glory to distant nations that never heard of him. Then he promises new heavens and a new earth, where all flesh will worship him. What is surprising is that priestly service, once limited to one family, is now opened up in a broader way.

For today: God does not look at our origin, but calls us to serve him. Ask him how you can serve others with what you have, without thinking that you are not fit for it.
exp.47:8:
God says that, for the sake of his own name, he will hold back his anger and postpone his punishment. He will do this so that he is praised, and so that he will not completely destroy his people. The verse of the word "defer" is what the reader needs here: it means to hold off or put off, and God's patience is that he gives time and waits, as one who is patient, and that he does not cut them down, as one would cut down a tree.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel (Judah), a people whom he had known as stubborn and rebellious from the beginning. Even so, he does not abandon them because of what the people deserve, but because of his own faithfulness and glory. The verses that follow show that he refines them in the furnace of affliction.

For today: if God has been patient with you despite your failures, do not take that lightly. His patience is mercy that invites repentance. Respond with gratitude and return to him today.
exp.50:21:
God tells his people that he has already taken the cup of punishment out of their hand. The "cup that makes you stagger" is a cup that makes a person reel, and "the dregs" is the bitter sediment at the bottom. "Defends" means he takes up their cause, like a lawyer. God promises: "you will never drink it again."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem had suffered greatly for its sin and was like someone drunk with sorrow, without strength. Now God presents himself as their defender and passes that cup to the oppressors who mistreated them. Scholars debate how this relates to the exile and to the future, but the comfort is clear.

If you feel you carry guilt or suffering with no way out, remember that God can be your defender. Trust in his forgiveness, rest in his care, and rise again with hope.
exp.43:12:
The carpenter measures the wood with a ruler or a cord, marks the outline with red ochre (a reddish dye), carves it with planes, and shapes it with the compass. In this way he makes a figure with the look of a beautiful man, so that it may stand in a house, as an ornament or a shrine.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people tempted by idolatry. With irony, he describes step by step how craftsmen make idols. The point is to show that a god made by human hands cannot be God. The verses that follow show that the same wood serves for warming oneself, cooking, and also for worship.

For today: let us ask ourselves which things made by us, such as money, fame, or success, we treat as if they could save us. Only the Creator deserves our complete trust.
exp.36:11:
Here the king of Assyria asks whether the gods of other nations were able to rescue the peoples that his forefathers conquered. He mentions cities such as Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who lived in Telassar. "Delivered" means "rescued." "Nations" refers to the peoples of other lands. "Which were in" means "who lived in."

Sennacherib speaks through his messengers as he threatens Jerusalem. He wants King Hezekiah to surrender, and to that end he compares the God of Israel with the idols of other peoples. He overlooks the fact that the Lord is not just one god among many.

For today: when threats or voices of fear tell you that God cannot help you, do as Hezekiah did. Bring your worry to God in prayer, lay it before Him, and trust in His power rather than in what you can see.
exp.31:3:
It says that under the just reign that Isaiah announces, people who previously did not understand will begin to comprehend. The "rash" here are hasty people or those lacking discernment, not necessarily foolish. The "stammerers" are those who speak with difficulty, and their tongue will be loosened, that is, freed, to speak with clarity.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks of a righteous king (Isaiah 32:1), whom many Christians relate to Christ, though some think first of Hezekiah. Before that, the people were spiritually blind and deaf. With that king, the truth would be seen and heard, and then the text contrasts this with the wickedness of the miser.

For today: if you find it hard to understand God's Word or to express your faith, ask Him for light and courage. He can give you understanding and simple, clear words to speak of Him.
exp.39:1:
God commands that Jerusalem be spoken to tenderly. He announces three things to her: her time of hard struggle or forced service is over, her sin has been pardoned, and she has received double for her sins.

God speaks to his messengers, probably the prophets, to comfort his people. Isaiah looks ahead to the exile in Babylon, when Jerusalem would lie in ruins. The word "double" is understood in several ways: a punishment that is fully sufficient, or a measure equal to her guilt. The verses that follow announce that God himself is coming to his people.

If you carry guilt that has already been forgiven, remember that God does not speak to you with contempt, but with tenderness. Today you can comfort someone with words of hope, and receive God's forgiveness yourself with confidence.
exp.29:8:
It says that the people of Israel are rebellious. It calls them "lying children," that is, people who say one thing and live another. They would not listen to the law of the Lord, that is, God's teaching and guidance. Here "listen" means to hear and obey.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. At that time, Judah was seeking the protection of Egypt against its enemies, instead of trusting in God. He had told them that their strength would be found in waiting quietly. That is why he commands this message to be written down, so that it would serve as a witness in the future. The verses that follow show that they did not want to hear truths, but pleasant words.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we listen to God only when it suits us. A good practice is to read the Bible with humility, willing to accept what corrects us, not only what comforts us.
exp.58:18:
People from every part of the world, from where the sun sets to where it rises, will come to revere the name of the Lord and to acknowledge his glory. Here "fear" means to honor with awe. The verse also says that the enemy will come like a flood, that is, with overwhelming force, but the Spirit of the Lord will raise a standard against him. Some translators render this as the Spirit will put him to flight; the Hebrew text allows both ideas.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name. The people were living in injustice and sin, and no one was interceding. So God himself acts as a warrior who puts on righteousness as a breastplate. Then he promises a Redeemer for those who turn away from evil.

For today: when you feel that your problems are sweeping you along like a river, remember that God does not leave you alone. Come to him sincerely and trust that his Spirit sustains you.
exp.47:3:
God tells his people that he knows how stubborn they are. He uses strong images: the "neck" is the throat and back of the neck, and calling it a "sinew of iron" means it is rigid and will not bend. The "brow of brass" speaks of a brazen face, one that is not ashamed and will not let itself be corrected.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel. He reminds them that he announced things before they happened, so that they could not credit them to their idols. Their hardness made such clear warnings necessary.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for a spirit willing to listen, to acknowledge our mistakes, and to change course, trusting that his correction comes from his love and faithfulness.
exp.54:3:
This verse says that God has placed someone as a "witness" for the peoples, that is, someone who makes known who God is and what He does. He also set him as a "chief" and "teacher" for the nations, that is, as a guide who leads and instructs. The phrase about "I have given him" is the same as the one in the verse above, and the wording about "firm mercies to David" is as in the verse above.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just invited His people to come and listen, and to promise the sure mercies shown to David. For this reason, many understand this "him" to be a descendant of David, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. Some also apply it to the people of Israel, and this is debated. In any case, God's blessing reaches the nations.

For today: before looking for other guides who do not satisfy, listen to Jesus, and let His teaching direct your decisions this week.
exp.59:1:
This verse says that a very great darkness will cover the earth and all the peoples. But upon the people of God, here called "you," the Lord will shine, and his glory will be seen. The image of the rising sun is used here: God appears like a light that comes up over the horizon. "Shall arise" is the name of the one who gives light.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, especially to Jerusalem (Zion). He announces hope after difficult times: God will restore them, and his light will draw other nations. Many Christians also see in this verse a sign of Christ, the light of the world, although this is interpreted in several ways.

Even when there is dark news around you or moments of pain, God can be your light. Today, ask him to guide you, and try to reflect his goodness in the way you treat others.
exp.41:12:
What it says: This verse describes God as a powerful warrior who goes out to fight.

Context: The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Before this, the peoples of the desert, such as Kedar, sing praise to God. Afterward, the Lord himself says that he has kept silent for a long time, but now he will act. It is a poetic image. Many see it as a promise that God will deliver his people and overcome injustice, in connection with the Servant in chapter 42.

For today: When it seems that God is silent in the face of evil or your pain, remember that his silence is not weakness or forgetfulness. Trust that he will act in his time, and in the meantime, praise him with hope.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that the Lord will strengthen the enemies of Rezin, the king of Syria, and gather them together against him. The word "set up" means to raise or empower. Rezin was an ally of Israel, so God allows his enemies to turn against that alliance.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Ephraim, whose capital was Samaria. They had suffered blows, yet they answered with pride, saying, "The bricks are fallen, but we will rebuild with hewn stones." God warns that his judgment is still in progress. Some understand that Syria and Ephraim would be weakened by Assyria; the text does not detail this here.

For today: when life shakes us, it is not enough to rebuild with pride and carry on as before. God invites us to stop, listen to his correction, and return to him with humility, before making new plans.
exp.23:13:
This verse says that a small group of survivors will raise their voices and sing with joy to honor the greatness of God. Their song will reach the shores, since the sea is what is meant here, and "they shall cry aloud" means they will shout with joy.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the middle of a announcement of judgment on the earth. The cities are left empty and only a few remain, like the olives left over after the tree has been shaken. Even so, these few praise God. Scholars debate exactly who they are: some think of a faithful remnant of Israel, others of believers from all nations. Later on, the prophet himself laments the wickedness of the people.

For today: even when everything seems lost or in ruins, we can choose to praise God. Our joy does not depend on circumstances, but on who He is.
exp.15:13:
God announces that within three years Moab will lose its glory. In that sense, the deadline will be precise. Moab's large population will be reduced to a small, weak remnant.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the preceding chapters mourn its downfall. Moab trusted in its high places and its gods, but they would not save it. Now God sets a date. We do not know for certain which historical event fulfilled this; scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: do not place your security in what seems great, such as money, prestige, or empty religion. All of that can fall quickly. Seek God sincerely now, not only when you are tired and in trouble.
exp.9:9:
It says that the king of Assyria boasts of having conquered kingdoms that worshiped idols. Those kingdoms had more images than Jerusalem and Samaria, that is, they seemed stronger in religious matters. The phrase "my hand hath found" means "my power reached," so the first sentence can be rephrased in the verse's own words as "as my hand hath found the kingdoms." "Graven images" are the statues of their gods.

The one speaking is the king of Assyria, in a proud tone, within a prophecy of Isaiah. God had used Assyria to discipline his people, but this king thought all the credit was his. Therefore, afterward, God says he will judge him for his arrogance. Some understand that the king compares Jerusalem with the peoples he defeated, believing it will fall the same way.

For today: when we succeed, let us remember that everything we achieve depends on God. Humility protects us from believing we are owners of what He has allowed us to have.
exp.59:15:
It says that Zion will be nourished with the riches of the nations and their kings, like a baby who nurses at the breast. "Suck" is an image of care and abundant provision. The result is that she will recognize that the Lord is her Saviour, her Redeemer, and the mighty One of Jacob, that is, the powerful God of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem, a people who had suffered contempt and destruction. He promises them restoration, honor, and peace. Scholars understand this in different ways: as the return from exile, as something fulfilled in Christ and the church, or as a hope still to come.

For today: when you feel abandoned or lacking, remember that your provision comes from God, not only from your own strength. Ask Him to care for you, and trust that He is your Saviour and your strength.
exp.0:29:
It says the people will be like a large tree whose leaves fall off and dry up, and like a garden or orchard that lacks water. The word for the tree is not fully certain, so some translations name a different kind of tree instead. It is an image of weakness and of life that is coming to an end.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which had abandoned the LORD and practiced the worship of idols, probably under trees and in gardens, as the previous verse suggests. Those who trusted in those places will find that they cannot hold them up. So the judgment shows that what seemed strong had no life of its own.

For today: what gives us strength is not what we admire or what appears firm, but staying connected to God. We can ask ourselves what we depend on most, and turn back to Him again each day.
exp.61:1:
It says that when God makes the righteousness of Jerusalem shine, the nations and their kings will see it. The word "nations" here means peoples or groups of people, and "righteousness" includes both the uprightness and the salvation that God gives to her. Also, God will give her a new name, spoken by his own mouth. A new name speaks of a new identity.

The one speaking seems to be the prophet, though some understand it as a voice of the Messiah. He says he will not keep silent until Zion is restored. The people had lived through exile and ruin, and felt abandoned. The verses that follow explain the new name: no longer "Forsaken," but "Hephzibah," which means "my delight is in her."

For today: if you belong to God, your identity is not defined by your failures or by what others have said about you. God names you with love. Today you can live according to what He says about you, and not according to your wounds.
exp.40:17:
He says God will make water break out where it seems impossible: rivers on the bare heights, springs in the middle of the valleys, pools where there had been desert, and fountains in dry ground. The sentence that explains the old wording is dropped, since it refers to words not in the verse above.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to his people Israel, who felt weak, poor, and without resources. Just before this, the verse mentions the afflicted who look for water and cannot find it, and he promises to hear them and not forsake them. Water is an image of provision and care. Scholars understand it both as a concrete promise of help and as a picture of renewal.

For today: when you feel dry or without a way out, bring your need to God honestly. He does not ignore the one who is thirsty, and he can supply what you need in ways you did not expect.
exp.50:5:
God invites his people to look at the sky and the earth, which seem solid and firm. But he says the heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth will wear out like an old garment. Its inhabitants will also pass away. His salvation, however, will last forever, and his righteousness will never come to an end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a discouraged people, probably in a time of exile or pressure. He wants them to trust in him and not in human powers. The verses that follow encourage them not to fear the mockery of people. Some understand the statement that they will vanish literally and others as poetic language; the central message is the same.

For today: when fear, criticism, or insecurity weighs on you, remember that the most solid things in this world are temporary. Place your hope in God's salvation, which endures. Today, bring him one specific worry in prayer.
exp.62:6:
This verse says that the one speaking will remember and recount the goodness of the Lord. Its words for "lovingkindnesses" refer to his love and compassion; "praises" refers to deeds worthy of being celebrated; "goodness" refers to his generosity; and the "mercies" are his tenderness and compassion. All of this he did for the house of Israel, and it was a great deal.

The one speaking seems to be the prophet, who, on behalf of the people, begins a prayer that recalls the past. It comes after a passage about God's judgment against the enemies. Here the tone shifts: from justice to recalling his faithfulness. What follows shows that God had compassion on his people and rescued them.

For today: take stock of what God has done for you. Write down three concrete things and give thanks for them. Remembering strengthens faith when difficult times come.
exp.8:2:
The verse says that God made the people grow, but before, that growth did not bring true joy. Now, before God, the people will rejoice like those who gather the harvest after much labor, or like soldiers who divide the plunder after winning a battle. The goods taken from a defeated enemy are the spoils of war.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat of Assyria. The northern regions, Zebulun and Naphtali, were the first to suffer invasion. The prophet announces that God will bring light and freedom where there was darkness and oppression. Some translations read the text a little differently, since the Hebrew original presents a difficulty, but the central idea is the same: joy that comes from God.

Today you can remember that having more, whether people, achievements, or things, does not fill the heart. True joy is born when God sets free and restores. Ask him to give you that deep joy.
exp.47:16:
This verse says that the Lord, who redeems his people and is completely holy, presents himself as their God. He is the one who teaches what truly benefits, what is good and useful for them. He also guides and directs them along the way they should walk.

Here God himself speaks to Israel, who was in exile in Babylon. Earlier he reminded them that he does not speak in secret and that he directs history. Then he laments that his people did not pay attention to his commandments, for otherwise they would have had peace like a river and numerous descendants. It is an invitation given with tenderness and also with sorrow.

For today: if God leads us for our good, it is worth listening to him before we decide. You can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and pray, asking him for direction, and be willing to obey what you see, even when it costs you.
exp.35:6:
Here the verse says that if the people answer that they trust in the Lord their God, that God would be the same one whose high places and altars Hezekiah had removed. Furthermore, Hezekiah ordered that Judah and Jerusalem worship before only one altar. "High places" are places of worship on the hills.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and make them surrender. He twists what Hezekiah did: that reform aimed to purify worship, but he presents it as if it had offended God. His argument is that of an enemy, not a voice from God.

For today: when someone uses half-truths to sow doubt about your faith, do not let yourself be intimidated. Compare what you hear with the Word of God and keep obeying him, even when others misread your decisions.
exp.20:0:
Isaiah announces a "burden," that is, a heavy message of judgment. He compares the arrival of an enemy to whirlwinds, strong winds that sweep across the southern desert. A "terrible land" is a fearsome land, from which something frightening comes. "The desert of the sea" is a hard expression; many understand it as Babylon, but not everyone is certain.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks and recounts a vision that God shows him. In the verses that follow, which mention the Medes and the Persians, many believe it foretells the fall of Babylon. Isaiah does not rejoice: the vision fills him with anguish and dread.

Today we can remember that no empire or human power escapes the sight of God. When the world seems like a storm, trust that God governs history. And, like Isaiah, learn to feel pain for the suffering of others, without mocking it.
exp.24:9:
He says that the hand of God, that is, his power and his care, will rest securely upon this mountain, which is Zion, where God reveals himself. But Moab will be trodden down like straw that is crushed in the dunghill, the place where manure is piled up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He comes from a great promise: God will defeat death, wipe away every tear, and save his people. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears as an example of pride against God (the following verse). Some believe it represents all who oppose God; others think it speaks of the historical Moab.

For today: trust that God has the last word. If you feel small before injustice, rest in his hand and give up pride, which God resists.
exp.64:3:
He says this rebellious people stays among the graves and spends the nights in desolate places. Furthermore, they eat pork, which the law of Moses forbade, and in their pots there is broth made from unclean things, that is, things forbidden by the law.

God speaks through Isaiah. He complains about a people he patiently called ("I stretched out my hands all day long"), yet who followed their own paths. Many understand these practices to be pagan rituals, perhaps tied to consulting the dead, although scholars are not entirely certain of the details. What is serious is that they combined this with a religion of outward appearance, considering themselves "holier" than others.

For today: examine whether your faith is only appearance. God seeks a sincere heart that obeys him, not a religiosity that considers itself superior to others.
exp.2:21:
It says God lists more of the luxury items of the women of Jerusalem. The fine clothes worn for special occasions are changeable suits of apparel, the short capes or cloaks are mantles, the things that covered or adorned are wimples, and the small items that were probably purses or pins are crisping pins; scholars translate that last word in different ways.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's message to Judah. The women of Zion were proud and vain (v. 16), and the list of adornments points to a society that trusted in its appearance and wealth. God warns that all that brilliance will be taken away: mourning, loss, and humiliation will come through judgment.

For today: it is not wrong to dress simply, but it is worth asking where we place our security. If our worth depends on what we have or how we appear, it is fragile. Let us instead seek a humble and thankful heart before God.
exp.0:8:
It says that, if God had not left a small group of survivors, the people would have ended up completely destroyed, like Sodom and Gomorrah. A "remnant" is a small number left behind, a few who remain. The "Lord of hosts" speaks of God's power over all things.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. Their land was devastated by invaders, and Jerusalem stood like a lonely hut. But the underlying problem was injustice and a religion that was only outward appearance. That is why, in the verse that follows, God calls their leaders "rulers of Sodom." Even so, the remnant that survives shows that God did not abandon them completely.

Today we can recognize that we stand firm by the mercy of God, not by our own merits. That gratitude invites us to return to Him with a sincere heart and to live with justice, not just with religious practices.
exp.0:16:
This verse is an invitation to change one's conduct. "Learn to do well" means that doing good is something you learn and practice. "Seek judgment" means to seek justice. "Relieve the oppressed" is helping to correct the harm suffered by the person who was mistreated. "Judge the fatherless" is defending the cause of the child without a father, and "plead for the widow" is protecting her.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah and Jerusalem. They practiced religion with prayers and offerings, but they lived with injustice and violence. That is why God says he does not hear their prayers. He does not reject prayer itself, but religion without obedience. And right away he offers them forgiveness if they repent.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we might help or defend: someone alone, in need, or ignored. A concrete step is to visit, accompany, or support that person this week, so that our faith shows in actions.
exp.64:0:
God says he let himself be found by people who never asked for him or sought him. To a nation that did not call on his name, he said, "Here I am, here I am."

Isaiah is the prophet through whom God speaks. The verses that follow show a rebellious people, to whom God stretched out his hands all day long. Some understand the "people who did not call on his name" to be the non-Jewish nations, and Paul uses it that way in Romans 10:20. Others see it as referring to Israel itself, since God kept offering himself even to those who did not seek him. Both readings show his initiative.

For today: God seeks us first, even when we are distracted. If you sense his call today, respond simply. And pray for someone far away, trusting that God can also go out to meet them.
exp.26:12:
In that day God has appointed, a great trumpet will sound, a sign of calling. The Israelites who were scattered in Assyria and those driven out or exiled in Egypt will return. They will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to a people who would be punished for their lack of understanding and their idolatry. After the judgment, God promises to gather his people one by one. Assyria and Egypt represent places of exile and oppression. Some see here the return after the exile; others also see a future or spiritual fulfillment. Believers have understood this in several ways.

For today: even if you feel far away, lost, or scattered because of your mistakes or your circumstances, God keeps calling. His discipline is not his final word; his aim is to restore you so that you worship him again. Respond to his call today.
exp.4:2:
In this passage God, speaking as the owner of a vineyard, calls on the people of Jerusalem and the men of Judah to act as judges. He asks them to decide fairly who is in the right: himself or his vineyard.

Isaiah is telling a song or parable. The one who is loved is God, and the vineyard, as verse 7 of the same chapter makes clear, stands for Israel and Judah. God did everything to care for it: he cleared away the stones, built a wall around it, and planted good vines. But it produced wild grapes, that is, bitter ones. God puts the people in the role of jury so that they can see their own failure.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly what fruit we are bearing after so much care from God. This week, think of one area of your life where you have received a great deal, such as teaching, family, or forgiveness, and ask God for help to bear good fruit there, with justice and love.
exp.54:9:
It says that the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there without doing their work. They water the earth, make it sprout and bear fruit, and so there is seed for the one who sows and bread for the one who eats. "Filled" means that it fills the earth and leaves it thoroughly soaked. "Seed" is what is sown.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a discouraged people, probably in exile. After inviting them to return to him and reminding them that his thoughts are higher than ours, he uses this image. The following verse explains it: so is his word, which does not return empty, but accomplishes what he wills.

For today: do not become discouraged if you do not see immediate results when you read, pray, or share the Bible. Like the rain, God's word works quietly. Keep sowing with patience and trust that he will make the fruit grow in its time.
exp.47:2:
He says that God had announced long before what was going to happen. He spoke it with his own mouth, made it known, and then carried it out suddenly, and everything happened just as he had said.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, the people of Jacob. They boasted of being God's people and swore by his name, but without truth or righteousness, that is, with their lips and not with their hearts. God reminds them that he gave warning beforehand, so that they would not credit what happened to their idols, as the following verses say.

For today: God is faithful to his word. We can trust what the Bible says and give him the credit, not luck or other things. And our faith must be sincere, not just words.
exp.32:0:
Here God announces a "woe", that is, a warning of judgment, against a destroyer. This man or nation plundered and betrayed others without having suffered the same. "Treachery" means betrayal or deceit. The final word is clear: when his cycle of abuses comes to an end, he will receive the same treatment he gave.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name at a time of threat against Judah. The text does not name the plunderer, and many think it refers to Assyria, though others see it as a broader description of any oppressor. The following verse shows the people crying out to God and waiting on Him.

For today: do not envy those who prosper by doing harm, nor take revenge on your own. Trust that God sees injustice, and ask Him for mercy and strength, as the people do in the following verse.
exp.44:0:
This verse says that God speaks to Cyrus, whom he calls "his anointed," that is, someone chosen for a mission. God takes him "by the right hand," as one who gives strength and support. He promises that Cyrus will subdue nations, that he will take power away from kings, loosing the loins of kings, as one strips them of their battle belt, and that the gates of the cities will stand open.

It is Jehovah who speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Cyrus was king of Persia, and the Bible presents him as God's instrument for letting the people of Israel, who were exiled in Babylon, return to their land. Cyrus did not know God, yet God uses him all the same. When exactly this prophecy was written is something scholars debate.

For today: God governs history, even through people who do not know him. You can trust that doors which seem closed are no obstacle for him, and that he accomplishes his purposes.
exp.13:1:
Other peoples, the verse says, will help Israel return to its own land, and the Israelites will have those same people as male and female servants. Those who once held Israel captive and oppressed them will now fall under Israel's rule. The old wording in the source means to rule over or dominate, and the word for "possess" is used in an older sense: to hold as property.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a promise from God to the people who would suffer captivity, especially under Babylon. The verse before speaks of the LORD's compassion, and the verse after prepares a mocking song against the king of Babylon. Interpreters differ: some see this promise fulfilled in the return from exile, while others also read it as a promise with a still wider scope.

For today: when you feel crushed by injustice, remember that God sees the pain and can change the course of history. Trust in Him, and let His justice, not your resentment, have the last word.
exp.50:2:
God promises that he will comfort Zion, that is, Jerusalem and his people. Her ruins and abandoned places will be made like the garden of Eden. Where there was desert, there will be a garden like the garden of the Lord. In place of sorrow there will be joy, gladness, thanksgiving and the voice of singing.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to those who seek righteousness and trust in him. He asks them to remember Abraham and Sarah: God called one man alone, blessed him and multiplied him. If he did that with a childless couple, he can raise up his people from their ruins again.

When your life feels like a desert, remember how God has acted before. His comfort is not just an emotion; it is a promise of restoration. Wait on him and give him thanks now.
exp.9:30:
This verse says that the people of Madmenah fell into panic and that the inhabitants of Gebim will gather, probably to flee or to save their belongings. "Was thrown into confusion" means that it was filled with confusion and alarm; those who live there are the ones who dwell in that place.

Isaiah speaks to Judah about the advance of an Assyrian army, which in his description comes down from the north toward Jerusalem. The towns named lie along that route, and the fear runs from place to place. It is not known with certainty where all these places were, but the meaning is clear. The prophet wants the people to feel the threat, so that he can then show that God will bring down the proud invader.

For today: when fear advances like a wave in your life, remember that no threat has the last word. God reigns and can humble what seems invincible. Trust in Him.
exp.56:3:
God asks some of the people pointed questions: Who are you mocking? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? To "mock" is to make fun of someone, and opening the mouth wide and stretching out the tongue is a gesture of contempt. Then he calls them "children of transgression" and "a seed of falsehood," that is, people who turn away from him and live in deception.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Shortly before, the righteous man dies and enters peace. Now God addresses those who practiced idolatry and mocked the faithful. His questions are meant to make them see their sin and realize that, at heart, they are mocking God himself.

For today: before we mock someone for their faith or for the way they live, let us remember that God sees the heart. Let us ask him for humility to correct ourselves and for respect to treat everyone with dignity.
exp.48:15:
God says he has his people "engraved" on the palms of his hands, meaning marked or carved in, like something that will not wear away. "Walls" are the walls of Jerusalem (Zion), which lay in ruins. God keeps them always in view and does not lose sight of them.

The LORD speaks to Zion, the people of Israel in exile. They complained, "The LORD has forsaken me, and my Lord has forgotten me." God answers with the image of a mother who does not abandon her nursing child, and adds that even if she were to forget, he will not forget. Then he promises rebuilding and the return of their children.

For today: when you feel forgotten or overlooked, remember that God does not hold you in memory only, but has you engraved in his hand. Speak to him openly about what hurts, and rest in the knowledge that he continues to think of you and of what you need to rebuild.
exp.25:12:
This verse says that the people acknowledge the Lord as their God. Other lords ruled over them, that is, governed them, but those masters stood apart from you, that is, without reckoning with God. Even so, the people declare that only through God will they remember and honor his name. Having been ruled by others means they exercised power and control.

The speaker is the people of Judah in a song of trust found within Isaiah 24 to 27. They have lived under foreign powers and oppressors. The verses before it speak of peace that comes from God, and the verses after it say that those rulers died and were wiped out. Interpreters debate exactly whom it refers to, but the general sense is clear: God is stronger than any human power.

Today we can ask what things hold authority over our hearts: money, fear, the opinion of others. Today you can choose deliberately to put God first, giving thanks for his name and seeking him in prayer.
exp.45:0:
This verse says that the gods of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, are falling down. Their images are carried on beasts and draft animals. The words for "bowed down" and "fell down" mean that they bend over or collapse. The idols, instead of carrying their people, become a heavy burden for the animals that transport them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Bel (another name for Marduk) and Nebo were important gods of Babylon. The text announces that Babylon will fall and that its idols will be carried away. Then God contrasts this with how he treats Israel: he has sustained them from the womb.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up weighing on us and cannot save us. God, on the other hand, sustains us. Today you can hand him a specific worry and rest in his care.
exp.37:1:
He says that King Hezekiah, when he received the news that he would die, turned toward the wall and prayed to God. "Turned his face toward the wall" means that he turned over in bed so that he was facing the wall. "Lord" is the name of God, and "Hezekiah" is Hezekiah.

The prophet Isaiah had just told him on God's behalf that his sickness was fatal and that he should put his house in order. Hezekiah was king of Judah. Many think he turned away to have privacy with God, although the text does not explain his reason. Afterward, he prays and weeps, and God answers.

When we receive news that breaks us, we can step away for a moment from the noise and the stares to speak with God in complete honesty. He listens to the one who speaks to him with an open heart.
exp.16:0:
It says that God announces judgment on Damascus, the capital of Syria. "Burden" means a heavy message, a prophetic pronouncement. The city will cease to be a city and will be left as a heap of ruins. It is a strong image of total destruction.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, delivering the word of the LORD. Damascus had allied itself with Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, and the next verse says that Ephraim's help would also come to an end. Many understand this as referring to the fall of Damascus before Assyria, around 732 B.C. Some also see a broader fulfillment, but that is debated.

For today: no human power is as firm as it appears. Trusting in alliances, riches, or our own strength is fragile. We can rest in God, who governs the nations and fulfills what he says.
exp.53:2:
It says that God's people, who seemed small and without a future, will spread out in every direction, "on the right hand and on the left." Their descendants will take possession of other nations and will fill again the cities that lie in ruins, that is, cities that were destroyed and abandoned.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem or Israel, which is compared to a barren and abandoned woman. The people were living through the pain of exile and desolation. God promises them restoration and asks them to enlarge their tent in faith. Scholars debate whether the fulfillment refers only to the return from exile or also to the church, which includes people from all nations.

For today: when your situation looks barren or without a way out, do not shut yourself in with fear. Trust God's promises and take steps of faith, praying and serving, preparing room for what He can do.
exp.10:3:
He says that the King who is coming will not judge by favoritism. He will defend the poor with justice and speak with fairness on behalf of the meek, that is, the humble. To "argue" a case means that he will defend the poor or settle their cause. The rod of his mouth and the breath of his lips show that his word has the authority to bring down wickedness. The wicked are the ones who do evil.

Isaiah prophesies in the name of God. He speaks of a descendant of Jesse, the father of David, on whom the Spirit of the Lord rests. Judah was living under unjust leaders, and the prophet promises a different ruler. Christians see Jesus in this announcement. What follows, with the wolf and the lamb, describes the peace that his reign will bring.

For today: trust that God sees those whom no one defends. And strive to treat everyone with justice, without judging only by appearances or by rumors.
exp.4:4:
God announces what he will do with his vineyard. He will take away the hedge, that is, the protection that surrounded it, and for that reason it will be devoured by animals. He will also break down its fence, the wall of stones, and so people will trample it underfoot. "Breach" means to open gaps in a wall. "Trodden down" means trampled underfoot.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God, in a song that uses the image of a disappointed vinedresser. God cared for his vineyard and expected good grapes, but it produced wild, bitter grapes. Verse 7 explains that the vineyard is Israel and Judah, and that God expected justice but found violence. Here the people themselves are called to judge the case.

God cares for us and looks for fruits of justice and mercy, not merely a religion of appearances. Today we can ask ourselves, with humility, what fruit we are bearing in how we treat others, and not take his protection for granted.
exp.59:7:
This verse asks a question full of wonder: who are these that fly like a cloud, and like doves returning to their dovecotes? The word "windows" here refers to the openings of the dovecote. The image shows people arriving in large groups, quickly and eager to return home.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, and God promises to restore her after the punishment. The verses that follow explain that these are her children returning from far away by ships, together with people from other nations who join to worship the LORD. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a broader fulfillment, with peoples from everywhere coming to God.

For today: God rejoices when someone returns to Him, and we too can rejoice and welcome with affection the one who comes back, without reproach.
exp.36:10:
Here the king of Assyria says to Hezekiah: "You know what the Assyrian kings have done to all the countries: they destroyed them completely. Do you think you will be spared?" It is a question meant to frighten and to strip away all hope.

The one speaking is Sennacherib, king of Assyria, through messengers. Jerusalem was under threat. He learns that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, is coming to fight against him, and even so he sends this message to pressure Hezekiah into surrendering. He mocks Judah's trust in God, and he compares the Lord to the gods of other nations.

For today: when threats seem bigger than your faith, do not measure your situation only by what has happened to others. Bring your fear to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and trust that He is greater than any voice that intimidates you.
exp.25:14:
Here the people of God tell the LORD that He made the nation grow, and they repeat it to stress the point. In doing so, God himself was glorified. The phrase "thou art glorified" means "you showed yourself glorious." Also, "you extended it to all the ends of the earth" means that he enlarged the borders. Some understand this to refer to the territory, and others to the fame of God.

The faithful remnant of Judah speaks within a song of trust. They say that other lords ruled over them, but that they acknowledge only God. The oppressors have already fallen, and God restored his people. It is not clear whether Isaiah speaks of a past event or of a hope seen as already fulfilled.

For today: when God blesses you or lifts you up, do not claim the credit. Give him thanks, and let your life show who He is.
exp.13:2:
It says that a day will come when God will give his people rest. They will be relieved from heavy labor, from constant fear, and from the hard bondage they suffered. The word "rest" in this verse means relief and peace, and the bondage it describes is living under the control of others as a servant.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing the word of God. Israel lived under the threat of foreign powers, and Babylon would become its oppressor. For this reason, God promises restoration and justice. The verses that follow show that this relief would come with the fall of the king of Babylon. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see a wider hope.

For today: if you are exhausted or afraid because of a situation that weighs you down, remember that God sees your burden and promises rest. Pray with confidence, keep doing good, and wait on Him, without letting fear have the last word.
exp.31:12:
It says that the land of God's people, which once gave harvests, will be filled with thorns and thistles, that is, weeds that grow where no one tends the field. Even the houses of pleasure and the joyful city will be left deserted. The houses of pleasure were the homes where people enjoyed life in comfort.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the women who are at ease and feel secure, that is, those who live quietly and confident in themselves. He warns them that their false sense of security will come to an end through a coming judgment. Scholars disagree about the exact historical moment, but the message is clear. Still, the passage ends with hope: the Spirit will come from on high, and everything will be restored.

For today: let us not place our security in comfort or in what we have. Let us ask God that his Spirit renew our hearts.
exp.23:16:
It says that God's judgment will come upon all the inhabitants of the earth in a way that cannot be avoided. "Fear" is a sudden dread; "the pit" is a deep hole; "the snare" is a trap for catching animals. These are three images of danger that close in on people without leaving them any way out.

Isaiah 24 speaks of God's judgment upon the whole earth, not only upon one people. The prophet speaks in God's name and explains that humanity has broken His laws and His covenant. In the verses before, some praise God, but Isaiah grieves over so much betrayal. Interpreters debate whether it describes a historical judgment, a future one, or both.

Today it invites us to take God seriously and not to trust in our own security. We can ask ourselves: what am I trusting in? God calls us to return to Him, who is the only true refuge.
exp.62:0:
This verse presents a question and an answer. Someone asks who this figure is who comes from Edom, from the city of Bozrah, with garments stained a deep red. He looks glorious and walks with great strength. He himself answers: he speaks in righteousness and is mighty to save.

Edom was a neighboring people and a frequent enemy of Israel, and Bozrah was one of its important cities. In the verses that follow, the figure appears as a warrior who judges the nations. Many Christians see here the Lord himself, and some connect him with Christ, although there are different interpretations of the details. Edom may represent God's enemies in general.

For today: we can trust that God is just and also mighty to save. When we see so much injustice, we do not have to take revenge; we can hand everything over to him and keep doing good.
exp.21:1:
God speaks to Jerusalem, here called a "valley of vision." He says the city is full of noise, restless, and given to celebration. But its dead did not fall by the sword nor in battle.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. While danger draws near, the people celebrate on their rooftops without taking it seriously. The leaders flee and are captured, and the prophet weeps. It is not known with certainty which moment he has in mind; some scholars think of an Assyrian siege and others of a Babylonian one. It is also unclear how those dead died, perhaps of hunger or disease.

Today, let us not ignore God's warnings with distractions and false cheer. And when others suffer, let us imitate Isaiah: let us weep with them and truly help.
exp.2:1:
God continues the list of what he is going to take away from Jerusalem and Judah: the warrior, the man of war, the judge, the prophet, the one who claims to foretell the future, and the elder. These are the leaders who gave the people security, order, and direction. The word "diviner" here refers to someone who claimed to know the future; the Bible condemns this practice in other passages, so its mention alongside the prophet shows that there was a mixture of true and false guides.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Judah had turned away from God through injustice and idolatry, and the punishment would be the loss of firm leadership, which would bring disorder and weakness.

For today: let us not place our security only in leaders, institutions, or strong people. Let us pray for those who guide us, ask for wisdom for them, and trust first in God, who sustains all things.
exp.37:4:
God tells Isaiah to go to King Hezekiah and give him this message: "I am the God of your ancestor David. I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. I will add fifteen years to your life." The word "add" means that God gives him more time than he had.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and shortly before this Isaiah had told him he would die. The king turned to God, remembered that he had tried to live with sincerity, and wept bitterly. Then God speaks through Isaiah. God also promises to deliver Jerusalem from the king of Assyria, who was threatening it.

For today: God hears sincere prayers and sees our pain. We can speak to him honestly, even in tears, and trust that he listens. He will not always answer as he answered Hezekiah, but he is always attentive to us.
exp.27:15:
God says that he lays in Zion a firm and precious stone, set as a cornerstone and as a secure foundation. A cornerstone is the stone that holds up and aligns the whole building. The phrase "he that believeth shall not make haste" means that the one who trusts will not flee in panic or grasp at false escapes.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. The rulers of Jerusalem mocked and believed they were safe from any punishment because of deceptive agreements, which they called a covenant with death. God contrasts their refuge of lies with a true foundation. The New Testament applies this stone to Christ (1 Peter 2:6).

When pressures come, do not run after quick or deceptive solutions. Build your life on trust in God and in Christ, and wait calmly, because He sustains what is well founded.
exp.39:15:
It says that not even all the wood of Lebanon would be enough to light the fire for a sacrifice worthy of God, nor would all its animals be enough to offer. Lebanon was famous for its cedar forests and its abundance. Even so, all of that falls short before the greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, discouraged and far from their land. He wants to comfort them by showing them who their God is. Before and after this verse, the nations appear as a drop or as dust, and he asks how anyone could make an image of God. Some understand that it is also stressed that God does not need our offerings.

Today we can remember that we do not draw near to God because of how much we give or do. We can worship him with humility and trust, and rest in the fact that he is greater than our fears.
exp.8:9:
It says that the people of Israel, after suffering a blow, respond with pride. The bricks were simple materials, and the hewn stone is carved stone, stronger and more costly. The sycomores were wild fig trees, of little value; the cedars were noble and expensive wood. They say: "The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones; the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars."

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom (Ephraim, Samaria). They had already suffered calamities, but instead of repenting, they spoke with arrogance. God warns that more enemies will come, because their hearts had not changed.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when a difficulty strikes us, we only want to rebuild with our own strength and plans. God may be calling us to stop, to acknowledge our mistakes, and to return to Him in humility before we raise anything up again.
exp.46:2:
It says that Babylon will be exposed and humiliated. "Shame" and "dishonor" speak of her public fall, with no place left to hide. God declares that he will take vengeance, that is, he will do justice. The phrase "I will not meet thee as a man" is difficult: some understand that no one will be able to stop God or plead for her; others, that God will accept no go-between.

God speaks through Isaiah, addressing Babylon as a proud woman who goes from queen to slave. She had been harsh with God's people (v. 6), and she considered herself secure forever. God judges her and, at the same time, presents himself as the Redeemer of Israel.

For today: pride and cruelty do not last, because God sees and does justice. Instead of trusting in your power or your reputation, live with humility and treat others with compassion.
exp.28:6:
This verse says that all the nations that gather to attack Ariel (another name for Jerusalem) will vanish like a dream of the night, which fades away when one wakes up. The siege engines and weapons of attack, and the encirclement that leaves her distressed and with no way out, are what the verse refers to when it speaks of her munition and her distress.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Jerusalem, a city that felt secure but lived with a shallow faith. God announces that he will first correct her, and then rescue her from her enemies suddenly. Scholars debate the exact moment he has in mind, perhaps the time of King Hezekiah and the threat from Assyria, though some also see a broader scope.

For today: when a problem seems enormous and threatening, remember that God is greater. Give him your fear in prayer and trust that he can undo what weighs on you today.
exp.19:3:
This verse explains the meaning of Isaiah's sign. The king of Assyria would lead away captive Egyptians and Ethiopians, young and old, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. A "transmigration" means a group of exiles taken to another land, and the bare buttocks describe a very severe public humiliation.

God speaks through Isaiah. Judah was tempted to trust in Egypt and Ethiopia to defend them against Assyria. Isaiah, walking without a cloak and without sandals as a sign, showed that those nations would fall and would be unable to save anyone. The texts speak of "three years"; some understand this as the whole length of that time and others as a period of the sign, and it is not known for certain.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, or plans. All of these can fail. Simply put, we place our trust first in God, and then use other resources with gratitude.
exp.10:11:
He says that God will raise up a sign or banner for the nations to see. With that sign he will gather the exiled Israelites and the scattered Jews, who are spread out to every corner of the earth. "Corners" means the edges or far ends, and "exiles" are those who were forcibly taken from their land.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks of a future king who comes from the root of Jesse, that is, from David's family. Many Christians see Jesus here; others connect it to the return of Israel, or to both. The peoples of the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah) were divided, and God promises to unite and restore them.

For today: God knows how to gather what is broken and scattered. If there is division in your family or church, seek peace by drawing near to Christ, who is the banner that unites us.
exp.18:8:
It says that those who work in fine flax, that is, those who comb and prepare it to make cloth, and those who weave nets, will be put to shame and dismayed. "Confounded" here means disappointed, with their plans frustrated. Egypt was famous for its flax and its fishing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah in a message against Egypt. If the Nile River dries up, everything that depends on it fails: the plants, the fishing, and the flax industry. The verses that follow show that not even the wise counselors of the pharaoh will be able to solve it. Scholars debate the exact timing of this judgment, but the message is clear: no one stands without God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we depend on most: our work, our money, or our skill. All of that can fail. Let us work with diligence, but place our trust in God, who sustains all things.
exp.44:3:
God says that he called someone by name and gave him a title of honor, even though that person did not know him. The reason is his affection for Jacob and Israel, his chosen people. A servant is someone who serves God. A title of honor is a name given in recognition of someone's standing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the previous verse (45:1) he names Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he calls his anointed. God would use him to open the way for the release of Israel from exile in Babylon. Cyrus was a pagan king, but God would use him to care for his people and to show that he alone is God.

Today we can trust that God works even where he is not recognized. If you are going through a difficult situation, remember that he can move people and circumstances in favor of his children. Rest in his care and give him thanks.
exp.44:21:
It says God invites all people, even those farthest away, to turn their gaze toward him to be saved. "Look unto me" means "look to me"; "be ye saved" means "let yourselves be saved"; and "all the ends of the earth" refers to the most distant corners of the world. The reason is clear: he alone is God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses those who have survived from the nations, people from other peoples who continue to worship wooden idols that cannot save. God shows them that he alone announced what would happen, and that he is a righteous God and Savior. His invitation is universal.

For today: when you feel lost, burdened, or guilty, do not look first to other ways out. Pause, pray, and turn your gaze toward God with confidence. He invites and receives everyone.
exp.36:21:
God answers Hezekiah's prayer with a message for the king of Assyria. He says that Jerusalem, called "the virgin, the daughter of Zion," has despised him and laughed him to scorn. The gesture of shaking the head as the enemy turns away was a sign of mockery.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah had prayed in distress because Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was threatening Jerusalem and mocking God. God answers and declares that the city Sennacherib thought weak will not fall. The verses that follow show that his real sin was insulting the Holy One of Israel.

Today we can learn that when we feel small before a huge problem, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. God hears, and he does not ignore the pride of those who think themselves invincible.
exp.27:7:
The verse describes a disastrous feast. The tables are covered with vomit and filth, and not a single clean corner is left. The word "vomit" refers to what is thrown up from drinking too much, and "filthiness" is the uncleanness that goes with it. It is a deliberately raw image.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the leaders of Judah, including priests and prophets. These men were supposed to guide the people with clarity, but they were drunk on wine and strong drink (fermented drink). Because of this they made mistakes when seeing visions and when pronouncing judgments. Then they mock God's teaching, as if it were meant for children.

Today we can ask ourselves what things cloud our minds and keep us from hearing God. It is not only alcohol; it can be any vice or excess. If we want to guide others with wisdom, we need a sober heart that is attentive to his Word.
exp.27:4:
On that day, the verse says, God himself will be like a crown of glory and a beautiful headpiece for the rest of his people. "The remnant" means those who are left, the faithful few. A "diadem" is a crown or ornament worn on the head.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he had announced the fall of Ephraim (the northern kingdom), whose leaders took pride in their adornments and drank themselves into a stupor. In contrast to that passing crown, which will be trampled underfoot, God promises to be the true crown for those who remain faithful to him. Some believe that "that day" points to the judgment of Assyria, while others see a broader hope.

For today: do not look for your worth in success, fame, or pleasure, which wither quickly. Fix your eyes on God, who gives lasting beauty and dignity to those who trust in him.
exp.12:2:
God himself has given the command to a group of people whom he has set apart for this task. "Sanctified" here means set apart or appointed by God for a purpose, not necessarily people who are perfect. He also called his warriors, his fighters, to carry out his anger. They rejoice in the greatness of God, or they take pride in serving him in this.

God speaks, through Isaiah, in a message against Babylon. The armies that would come are instruments that God uses to judge the pride and violence of that city. Scholars explain in different ways who these "sanctified ones" are: it is generally thought to be the Medes or another army, used by God, although they did not know it.

For today: God rules over the nations and over justice, even when we do not see it. We can rest in the knowledge that no evil goes unanswered, and we should live with humility, without trusting in our own power.
exp.36:12:
This verse is a question that does not seek an answer but aims to mock. It asks where the kings of Hamath, Arphad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah are, that is, of cities that had already been conquered. It means: "They no longer exist, and neither will you be saved." In the older wording, "Hamath" is Hamat and "Arphad" is Arpad, but the verse you read uses the forms given above.

The speaker is the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, speaking through messengers and letters addressed to King Hezekiah of Judah. He wanted to frighten him into surrendering, telling him that the gods of other nations had not rescued them and that the God of Judah would not rescue him either. Hezekiah did not answer with fear, but took the letter to the temple and spread it out before God.

For today: when threats or bad news overwhelm you, do not keep turning them over in your mind. Bring them to God in prayer, honestly, and trust that He is different from everything that seems powerful in this world.
exp.39:18:
This verse describes how an idol is made. The "workman" is a craftsman who prepares a carved or cast image, a figure shaped by hand or melted into form. Then the "goldsmith" covers it with a layer of gold and casts silver chains onto it, which were probably ornaments or silver pieces to decorate the figure. Some scholars think that last phrase is difficult to translate exactly.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to comfort a people who live among nations full of idols. He has just said that the nations are like nothing before the Lord. With an ironic question, he shows how absurd it is to compare God with something that human hands make.

Today we have other "idols": money, success, image. Everything we build and then expect to save us is far too small. Today, place your trust in the God who created everything, not in what you can make for yourself.
exp.64:9:
He says that God will turn two places into lands of rest and abundance for his people. Sharon was a fertile plain beside the Mediterranean Sea, good for grazing. The valley of Achor lay on the other side of the territory, near Jericho, and its name is associated with distress. A fold is a pen or place where livestock rest. A safe pasture is what is meant by the phrase. The promise is for those who sought God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces that, although the people have been rebellious and will be judged, he will not destroy everything. He will preserve a faithful remnant. The contrast is clear: those who seek him receive restoration, and those who worship Fortune and Fate face judgment.

For today: God can transform our valleys of distress into places of rest. If we seek him sincerely, we can trust that he cares for and restores his own, even after difficult times.
exp.38:4:
Isaiah tells King Hezekiah to listen carefully to a message that does not come from him, but from God. The title "Lord of hosts" speaks of the Lord as the one who rules over all power, even over kings and nations.

The prophet Isaiah speaks after Hezekiah showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon. Hezekiah saw no problem in doing so. Many understand that there was pride or overconfidence in his riches, although the text does not say it in so many words. That is why the prophet confronts him and announces what God will say next.

Today we can learn to listen to the word of God even when it is not pleasant. Everything we have is a gift from Him, and trusting in our possessions instead of trusting in Him puts us at risk. Let us ask Him for humility to receive His correction.
exp.8:1:
It says that a people who lived in darkness suddenly saw a great light. The words "darkness" and "the shadow of death" speak of distress, oppression, and danger. "Dwelt" means lived. "Saw" is the plain word for seeing. The light that "shined upon them" is an image of hope and deliverance that comes without them producing it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, in a time of threat from Assyria. The regions of Zebulun and Naphtali, in Galilee, were among the first to suffer invasion. Isaiah announces that God will end that oppression by breaking the yoke of the oppressor. Matthew 4:12-16 quotes this passage and applies it to Jesus, who began his ministry in Galilee.

For today: if you are going through a dark season, you do not have to create the light yourself. Ask God to show you his presence, draw near to Jesus in the Gospels, and share that hope with someone who is walking in darkness today.
exp.48:16:
It says that those who will rebuild Zion will arrive soon, and that those who ruined her will leave her. The "builders" are those who raise up again; the "destroyers" are those who leave a place in ruins. Some versions translate the phrase as "your children come hurrying" instead of "builders," because in Hebrew the two words look alike.

God speaks through Isaiah to Zion, the people of Israel, who felt forgotten in exile. He has just told her that he has not forgotten her: she is engraved on his palms, and he always keeps her ruined walls in mind. This verse promises restoration, return, and repopulation.

For today: if you feel that your life is in ruins, remember that God has not forgotten you. Trust that he can rebuild what is damaged and drive away what was destroying you, even though it may take time.
exp.24:7:
He says that God will destroy death forever. The word "wipe away" means to dry, as the Lord himself will dry the tears from every face. He will also take away the "disgrace," that is, the shame and contempt his people have suffered throughout the earth. And all of this is certain, because the Lord has spoken it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who live surrounded by threats and powerful nations. Earlier, God prepares a feast on "this mountain," which many understand to be Zion or Jerusalem, for all peoples, and he removes the veil that covers the nations. Then the people respond with joy: "This is our God; we have waited for him." Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 15:54, and Revelation 21:4 recalls it.

When pain or loss weighs on you, do not keep it in silence. Bring it before God, who promises to comfort you and one day wipe away your tears.
exp.9:24:
It says that the time of God's anger against his people is very nearly over. "Fury" and "anger" speak of his discipline. "Destruction" means an end or ruin, and here it refers to the enemies, that is, Assyria, not Judah. Some understand that the anger turns against Assyria; the context that follows suggests this.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had been used as a rod to correct Judah for its sin, but Assyria was proud and cruel. God comforts "my people who dwell in Zion" and tells them not to fear. He recalls past deliverances, such as the one from Egypt and the one from Midian, to show that he will rescue them again.

For today: when you go through a trial or a correction, remember that God sets limits on the time of suffering. Trust that he cares for you, and do not let fear control you.
exp.48:14:
It is very rare for a mother to forget the baby she nursed and to stop feeling tenderness for the child she bore. "Feeling compassion" means feeling affection and mercy. The question "Can a woman forget?" is the verse's own wording. Even if some mother were to forget, God affirms that He will never forget His people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people of Israel, discouraged in exile, had said: "The LORD has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me." God answers that complaint with a tender image. He adds that he carries Zion engraved on the palms of his hands, and he promises restoration.

For today: when you feel alone, forgotten, or abandoned, do not trust only what you feel. Tell God honestly what hurts you, and remember this promise. His love for you is firmer than the strongest human love.
exp.64:15:
This verse says that in the future God promises, people will seek blessing and make oaths only in the name of the God of truth, that is, the faithful God who keeps his word. To swear is to affirm something by calling God as witness. It also says that the troubles of the past will be forgotten and hidden from his eyes.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is separating those who despise him, who will suffer, from his servants, who will have joy. Right after this he announces new heavens and a new earth. Some see here a restoration after the exile, others the final renewal of all things; some see both.

For today: if your past or your pain weighs on you, trust that God is faithful and able to heal. And strive to make your words and promises true, as he is.
exp.4:1:
He says that the owner of the vineyard cared for it with great diligence: he cleared the stones from the ground, planted the best vines, built a tower to watch over it, and prepared a winepress, which is the place where grapes are trodden to get the wine. He expected good grapes, but the vineyard yielded wild grapes, that is, sour and worthless ones.

Isaiah sings a song in the name of his beloved, who represents God. Shortly after, the text explains that the vineyard is the people of Israel and Judah. God had given them care, law and protection, but he looked for justice and found injustice (Isaiah 5:7). The final question asks the listeners to recognize the problem.

For today: God has given us much, and he hopes that this will show in our lives through love, honesty and justice. Today we can ask ourselves what fruit we are bearing and ask him for help to change whatever needs changing.
exp.49:8:
He says that the Lord God is the one who helps the speaker, and so no one can truly condemn him. He asks, "Who shall condemn me?" and claims that his accusers are like old clothing that wears out and that the moth eats. The verse of "condemn" and "wax old" is dropped here, since those words do not appear in the verse above; the sentence about declaring someone guilty is removed as well.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, in the third Servant Song of Isaiah. He endures mockery and blows, but he trusts God. Many Christians see here an anticipation of Jesus; others also connect it to Israel or to the prophet himself. His confidence does not come from himself but from God's backing.

When you are accused unjustly, or feel guilty without reason, rest in the fact that God is your helper. Human criticism passes away like worn-out clothing; the faithfulness of God remains.
exp.43:24:
God says that he makes the signs of the diviners fail and makes fools of those who foretell the future. He also turns the wise backward and makes their knowledge foolish. The word "frustrateth" means that he makes their signs come to nothing.

The LORD speaks, the Redeemer of Israel and the Creator of all things. The people are about to be rescued from exile, and God announces it as something certain. While the nations trusted in diviners and counselors, God shows that only he knows and directs the future. The verses that follow confirm this: he will fulfill his word and rebuild Jerusalem.

Today we can let go of the need to control the future through horoscopes, superstitions, or mere human calculation. We can plan wisely, but trusting in God, who keeps what he promises and sustains our lives.
exp.51:11:
It says that God's people will not leave in a hurry or escape like fugitives. God himself will go ahead of them as their guide, and he will also watch over their rear.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God will do. The people were captive in Babylon, and they are called to leave and to live in holiness. The departure from Egypt was in haste (Exodus 12:11); this one will be different, under God's care. Right after this comes the suffering Servant, and many Christians see Jesus there.

For today: when God calls you to leave something harmful or to start over, do not act in panic. Pray, walk one step at a time, and trust that he goes before you and stays with you.
exp.61:6:
It says that those who pray for Jerusalem should not give God any rest. Rest here means a break or pause. They are to keep pressing until he makes it secure and firm, and makes it a source of praise throughout the earth. To make it firm means to establish it, leaving it safe and steady.

Isaiah speaks to a people who were waiting for Jerusalem to be restored. God has set watchmen on its walls, and they keep reminding the Lord of his promises. This is not because God forgets them; rather, persistent prayer joins us to his purpose. Some understand the watchmen to be prophets, while others understand them to be the whole faithful people.

For today: persevere in prayer for what God has promised, whether for your family, your church, or your community. Pray with constancy and hope, trusting that God finishes what he begins.
exp.2:13:
God says he himself will bring the elders and the princes of his people to judgment, that is, their leaders. He accuses them of having consumed the vineyard, an image of God's people, which in Isaiah 5 is compared to a vineyard.
