He also says that in their houses is what was taken from the poor, that is, what they took from the needy. The word "judgment" here means a court hearing, where the case is presented and decided.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, on behalf of God, to Judah and Jerusalem. God appears as a judge who brings his case against the leaders. They were supposed to care for the people, but instead they deceived them and took advantage of the weakest.

For today: if you have any authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it to protect and serve, not to gain advantage for yourself. God sees how we treat the most vulnerable.
exp.52:4:
This verse says that the servant of God was wounded and crushed, but not because of his own wrongs, but because of ours. "Transgressions" are the times we turn away from God; "bruised" means crushed; "wounded" means hurt. "The chastisement of our peace" means the punishment that brings our peace with God. By his wounds, we receive healing.

This passage is part of the prophecy of Isaiah, written to a people who were suffering the consequences of their turning away from God. It speaks of a servant who suffers for others. At first, people thought God was punishing him for his own faults; then they recognize that he was suffering for them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament applies it to Him (1 Peter 2:24). Jews often interpret the servant differently, for example as Israel.

For today: if you carry guilt or shame, come to God with confidence. Christ has already carried that weight, so you can receive forgiveness and begin again with gratitude.
exp.32:10:
It says that God's enemies, and also those who trust in their own plans, "conceive" things of no value: chaff, which is dry straw, and stubble, which are the dry tips of the wheat. What they give birth to will be just as useless. Moreover, their own fire, that is, their fury and evil intentions, will destroy them. "Shall devour you" means that it will bring them to an end.

Here the LORD speaks, through Isaiah, to Judah and to the nations that threatened it, probably Assyria. The land is in mourning, and the fertile places, such as Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel, are laid waste. Then God says that he will rise up. The plans of the proud fail when he acts.

For today: do not place your hope in plans made with pride, resentment or deceit, because they do not bear true fruit. Before you decide, ask God and seek what pleases him.
exp.65:2:
God says that the offerings of certain people are as repugnant to him as murder or a pagan sacrifice. The grain offering, the incense, and the pig, an animal unclean for Israel, are also mentioned in this passage. Those people chose their own way and loved their abominations.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that heaven is his throne and that he does not need a temple made by human hands. He looks to the humble person who trembles at his word. Some believe the people mixed the worship of God with idolatrous practices; the text does not spell this out.

Today: it is not enough to keep rituals, go to church, or give offerings. God seeks a humble heart that obeys his word. Ask him to examine your heart.
exp.65:9:
This verse says that all who love Jerusalem and have mourned for her are invited to rejoice and celebrate with her. "Rejoice" means to take delight with joy, and "mourn" means to be in grief, sad and hurting.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do. The verses before it say that God brings a nation to birth suddenly, and that Zion will have children. Then comes the promise of comfort and peace like a river. Many understand this to refer to the restoration of God's people; others also see a future fulfillment. Interpreters differ on this point.

For today: if you are sad over situations that hurt, such as a family, a church, or a community, God promises comfort. Trust that your sadness is not the end, and let Him lead you little by little into joy.
exp.58:13:
It says that among the people there was no longer any uprightness or justice. "Right" and "justice" had moved away, as if they had been pushed aside. "The public square" was the open place where trials and the affairs of the city were handled, and there truth "stumbled," that is, it fell. "Fairness" means just and upright dealing, and it could not even enter.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and confesses their sins: lies, slander, and rebellion against God. He explains that injustice in society is born from a heart that has drifted away from God. Then the text shows that God sees this situation, is displeased, and promises to act himself to bring salvation.

Today we can begin by being people of our word and of fair dealing in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in the community. Let us speak the truth with love, not repeat gossip, and stand up for those who are treated unjustly, trusting that God upholds justice.
exp.41:11:
This verse is an invitation to give God the honor he deserves. To "give glory" to the Lord means to acknowledge who he is and to praise him. To "declare his praise" means to announce and proclaim what he is like and what he has done. The "islands" were understood as distant lands, beyond the sea.

Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking. He has just presented the Servant of the Lord, who will bring justice and hope. For this reason he calls for a new song from the desert to the sea and the mountains. The praise is not only for Israel but for distant peoples. Afterward, God appears as a warrior who acts after a long silence.

Today we can praise God without keeping it to ourselves. This week, tell someone close to you or far away something specific that God has done in your life, and thank him out loud.
exp.62:15:
Here the people say that God is their true Father. "Ignores" and "does not know us" mean that Abraham and Israel (Jacob), the ancestors, cannot help them and do not know their situation. "Redeemer" is the one who rescues and frees someone; "everlasting" means he has been so from the beginning and forever.

The passage is spoken by the people of Israel, or by a prophet on their behalf, in a prayer of lament. It seems they are in a time of suffering, with the sanctuary trampled by enemies. They remember how God cared for them before and ask where his compassion is now. Many believe it is a prayer from the exile, though the text does not give all the details.

For today: when you feel alone or without support, do not depend only on your family, your history, or your merits. You can come to God honestly, even with your doubts, because he is Father and Redeemer.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that every soldier's clothing in the battle is filled with noise and stained with blood. But that clothing and those weapons will not be kept: they will be burned, and the fire will consume them. "Confused noise" means a great roar of clamor, "garments rolled in blood" means clothing dragged through and soaked, and "fuel of fire" means the food or fuel that the fire feeds on.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under threat and oppression. He announces that God will deliver them, as He did in the days of Midian. The verses that follow say that this deliverance comes with the promised child. Many Christians see in him Jesus. The end of war and of its weapons shows that God will bring true peace.

For today: when you feel that your life is a battle, remember that God promises an ending of peace. Trust in Him and seek to be someone who brings peace, not more conflict.
exp.43:6:
Here God issues a challenge to all the false gods: "Who can do what I do?" He asks who can call, declare, and set in order the events from the time the ancient people existed. To "declare" means to make known or announce; "set it in order for me" means to lay out the evidence before him. Then he invites them to announce what is coming.

Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, who has just said: "I am the first and I am the last." His people were living under pressure and surrounded by religions with idols. God reminds them that he alone knows and directs the future, and that they are his witnesses.

For today: when the future frightens you, remember that God has already spoken and fulfilled his word throughout history. You can rest in him, instead of seeking security in things that you cannot see and that know nothing.
exp.0:17:
God invites the people to come and "reason together," that is, to talk the matter through and settle it, as in a fair trial. He says that even if their sins are like the deepest scarlet or crimson dyes, which are hard to wash out, He will make them as white as snow or as clean wool.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah, a people who kept up their religion but oppressed the fatherless and the widow. First He asks them to change their conduct and do justice; then He warns that obedience brings good and rebellion brings ruin. Forgiveness is offered together with a call to return. Some read this as a question or as irony, but the central idea is the same.

If you carry guilt, come to God honestly, ask for forgiveness, and take one concrete step of justice or kindness toward someone who needs it.
exp.29:18:
This verse says that God's people will once again live in peace in Zion, in Jerusalem. There will be no more weeping, because God, who is compassionate, will show pity to them. When they cry out to Him, He will answer them right away. The word "dwell" in the verse above is the key idea here: it means to live and remain in a place.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to a people who, instead of trusting Him, were looking for protection in Egypt against their enemies. He warns them that consequences will come, but he also promises that God waits patiently to show them mercy. Some think the promise points to relief in the near future, and others think it also points to a fuller restoration to come.

For today: when you feel afflicted or have strayed from the right path, you do not have to hide or solve everything on your own. Cry out to God sincerely. He listens, He has compassion, and He still guides those who return to Him.
exp.36:27:
God tells the king of Assyria that he knows him completely. "Dwelling" refers to where he sits or rests, "going out and coming in" is everything he does, his comings and goings, and "rage" is his anger. Nothing of his life or his pride is hidden from him. God even knows that this rage is aimed against Him.

Speaking through the prophet Isaiah, God addresses Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Hezekiah. God answers that He governs history and that Assyria has been only an instrument in His hands. Then He announces that He will stop the king and make him return the way he came.

For today: God sees everything that happens, including the injustices and abuses that make us suffer. You can rest in the knowledge that no human power is beyond His control. Bring your fears to Him with confidence, and do not take justice into your own hands.
exp.27:27:
This verse says that the farmer threshes the bread grain (wheat), but does not do it without stopping. He does not keep crushing it over and over with the wheel of his cart, nor break it apart with the teeth of the threshing sledge, which was an instrument with sharp edges or stones used to separate the grain from the straw.

Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Judah, who felt secure and mocked his warning. He uses the example of the farmer, whom God himself instructs, to show that God corrects with measure and purpose. Many understand that this refers to God's judgment on his people: it is serious, but it does not seek to destroy. The text gives no further detail.

For today: when you go through a trial or correction, remember that God knows how much pressure is necessary. Trust his wisdom and allow yourself to be shaped, without despairing.
exp.13:17:
This verse says that all the kings of the nations, when they die, rest with honor, each in his own tomb. "Lie" here means they are laid down in death, and "house" in this verse refers to their family tomb or a fitting resting place.

Isaiah is delivering a prophetic taunt against the king of Babylon, whom the text names as the king of Babylon at the beginning of the chapter. The other kings receive an honorable burial, but this one does not. He will be cast out of his tomb and despised, because he was cruel: he destroyed cities, killed his people, and never released the prisoners. Some think he also speaks of a spiritual power behind that pride, but the text is clearly addressed to a human king.

For today: what we leave behind at the end of life depends on how we used the power we had. Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat with justice and compassion those who depend on us.
exp.32:1:
The people ask God to show them mercy. They confess that they have waited for him with patience. They ask that God be their strength, like an arm for them every morning, and also their rescue (the word here means salvation) when hard times come.

The people of Judah speak here, praying in the midst of danger. Earlier, Isaiah announced judgment against a cruel invader who plundered and betrayed; scholars often connect him with Assyria, though the text does not give the name. Faced with that power, the people do not trust in their own strength but cry out to God. Some understand "their arm" as the arm of those who wait; the general sense is the same: dependence on God.

For today: begin each morning by asking God for strength for that day, and trust that he will also sustain you when a difficulty comes that you did not expect. Waiting on him is not standing still, but resting in his help while you do what is yours to do.
exp.42:4:
It says that God speaks to his people and asks them not to be afraid, because he is with them. The word "seed" here means descendants, that is, the children and descendants of Israel. God promises to gather them from the east and the west, that is, from faraway places. "I will bring" means to bring together those who had been scattered.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. His people lived under the threat of exile and scattering. God reminds them that they are precious to him: "you were precious in my eyes, and I have loved you." The promise rests on that love. Many understand it to point to the return from Babylon, and others also see a broader fulfillment in God's people gathered from everywhere.

Today, when you feel afraid or find yourself far from everything, remember that God loves you and is with you. Pray today and say to him: "Lord, I trust in your company."
exp.53:15:
He says that God is the creator of everyone: of the smith who fans the glowing coals and brings out the tool for his work, and also of the destroyer who ruins. The words "created" and "have created" in the verse mean "made." Coals are live embers. Weapons and the people who use them exist under God's power.

God speaks to Jerusalem, the people of Israel, who felt abandoned and vulnerable after the exile. He promises them protection and a secure future. The verses that follow say that no weapon formed against them will prosper. Some understand that God allows the enemy but limits him; the text does not explain how this happens.

When you feel fear for people or situations that threaten you, remember that nothing is outside God's control. You can pray with confidence, do what is right, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for his own, even when you do not always understand how.
exp.21:7:
He says that God removed Judah's protection, that is, he exposed its weakness. A "covering" is what shelters and defends. Then the people looked toward the "armory of the forest house," a storehouse of weapons that Solomon had built (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17). In other words, they sought defense in military means.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the message about the "valley of vision," which is Jerusalem. The city is surrounded by enemies, and its inhabitants rush to build walls, secure water, and prepare weapons. But the prophet rebukes them for not looking to God, who allowed that crisis (v. 11). Scholars debate which exact moment he has in mind, perhaps the Assyrian threat in the time of Hezekiah.

For today: preparing and planning is wise, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before rushing to find solutions, stop and ask God what he wants to tell you in the difficulty.
exp.41:14:
Here God says that he will turn mountains and hills into desolate places, that he will dry up all the grass, that the rivers will become islands (that is, banks of dry land), and that he will dry up the pools.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he will come out like a warrior, after a long silence. The images of drought show his power over nature and his judgment against those who trust in idols. Interpreters debate whether this is figurative language or whether it also refers to concrete events. What follows shows that his aim is to guide his people, like the blind, toward the light.

For today: God is not indifferent or powerless, even when he seems silent. You can trust that he guides your steps, even along paths you do not know, and stop leaning on things that cannot save you.
exp.16:13:
It says that at evening terror comes, but before morning the enemy is no longer there. "Trouble" means dread or disorder; "tread down" means trample or trample upon; "lot" means what falls to them or their fate. In other words, those who oppress and plunder God's people meet this sudden end.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God. Just before, he describes many nations roaring like the sea against Judah. Many scholars think this refers to the Assyrian threat of his time, though not all agree. The verse comforts the people: God rebukes, and the enemy's power scatters like chaff before the wind.

When you feel trampled by problems or injustices that seem enormous, remember that God has the last word. You can rest in Him, pray with confidence, and keep doing good, without letting fear defeat you.
exp.0:12:
God tells the people of Judah to stop bringing empty offerings. The "vain offering" is a worthless gift, the "incense" is the sweet-smelling smoke of burnt offerings, and "endure" here means to put up with or tolerate. The new moons, the sabbaths, and the assemblies were festivals God himself had commanded, yet now he says he cannot stand them, because they are mixed with "iniquity," that is, with wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people kept the rituals, but they lived in injustice, and so their hands were "full of blood," as verse 15 says. God is not rejecting worship itself, but a religion that is only outward show and does not change the heart or conduct.

For today: before you sing, pray, or give an offering, ask yourself whether your daily life matches it. God looks for a sincere heart that also deals justly and compassionately with others.
exp.32:6:
The verse says that the ambassadors of the people cry out outside, in the street, and that the envoys of peace weep bitterly. The word "ambassadors" refers to the representatives sent to negotiate, and the "envoys of peace" were those who carried proposals to avoid war. Their weeping shows that their efforts failed.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah when Assyria was threatening Jerusalem. Many scholars think it refers to the envoys of King Hezekiah, who paid tribute but whom Assyria betrayed when it broke the agreement (see the following verses). Others see it in a more general way. What is clear is that the passage contrasts the failure of human diplomacy with the promise that God will be exalted and will give security to Zion.

When human plans fail and hope runs out, we can weep sincerely before God. But we can also trust that He is our true refuge and treasure.
exp.22:9:
This verse says that the "daughter of Tarshish" must leave her land freely, like a river that overflows and follows its channel, because there is no longer anyone to hold her back or defend her. "Strength" here refers to power or protection. The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain, and some translations understand it differently, for example, as if there were no longer any harbor or wall to hold her. Tarshish was a distant place of sea trade, whose exact location is debated.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God in a prophecy against Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. God himself decreed her fall to humble her pride. When Tyre fell, her trading partners, such as Tarshish, would be left without support.

For today: do not place your security in money, success, or your connections, because all of that can change suddenly. Trust God first, and use what you have with humility.
exp.2:15:
Here Jehovah speaks about the women of Jerusalem. He says they are proud: they walk with their necks held high, look around with flirtatious or brazen eyes, and step along with exaggerated steps, making the ornaments on their ankles jingle.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he accused the leaders of oppressing the poor. Now he points to the pride and luxury of the women of the city, probably a reflection of a society that lived comfortably and vainly while others suffered. The verses that follow announce that God will strip away those ornaments and their false sense of security.

For today: let us examine where we draw our sense of worth. God does not condemn beauty, but pride and indifference toward those in need. Let us ask him for a humble and generous heart.
exp.13:29:
It says that the poorest and most needy will find food and rest in safety, while God will bring Philistia to an end by famine. The phrase "the firstborn of the poor" is an expression meaning the very poorest among the poor. The needy are those in want. The "root" and the "remnant" refer to what is left of that people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah in the year King Ahaz died. The Philistines were rejoicing that a king who had struck them had fallen, but God warns them that something worse is coming. Scholars debate which king is meant by the "broken rod"; it is not entirely clear.

For today: God cares for the weak and judges pride. If you feel small or in need today, trust that he sees your situation. And if things are going well for you, do not become proud or mock the fall of others.
exp.46:4:
God tells Babylon, called "daughter of the Chaldeans," to leave her throne and sit in silence, like someone humbled. The phrase about going into darkness suggests shame, loss of power, and gloom in place of glory. She will no longer be the lady of kingdoms, that is, the great power that ruled over other nations.

God himself speaks here through Isaiah, as the Redeemer of Israel. Babylon had dominated Judah, but it treated the people cruelly, and God judges it for its pride and lack of compassion. Some understand this as a prophecy about the historical fall of Babylon; others also see in it an example of human pride in general.

For today: power, success, and fame are not eternal. If God gives us authority, let us use it with humility and mercy, and not think that our position will be secure forever.
exp.4:6:
It says that the vineyard God had been speaking about is his people: Israel and Judah. God cared for them with affection, like a plant that gave him delight, meaning pleasing and precious to him. He looked for right judgment and justice, but found violence and wrongdoing. He looked for righteousness, but found a cry, the cry of those being oppressed.

Isaiah uses a song-parable about a vineyard. God, the owner, explains why he will take away his protection: his people produced bad fruit. What follows shows concrete examples, such as piling up houses and land without thinking of others.

For today: God is not looking only for religion, but for visible fruits of justice and fair treatment. Today you can ask yourself: how do I treat those who depend on me or have less than I do? Ask God to let your faith show in honest and compassionate decisions.
exp.33:5:
This verse uses the image of a sacrifice to speak of God's judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood and with fat, like the animals offered on the altar: lambs, goats and rams. The word "fat" here simply means the fat of the animals. The city of Bozrah was an important city of Edom, and "slaughter" refers to a great destruction.

Isaiah announces God's judgment against the nations, and here he focuses on Edom, a neighbor of Israel and a frequent enemy of his people. The animals are a poetic picture of Edom's fall. The passage speaks of vengeance and of the cause of Zion, that is, God defends his people and sets right the injustice done to them.

For today: God does not ignore the evil and suffering of his people. We can rest in the fact that he will do justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. And his holiness invites us to live with humility and to repent in time.
exp.13:12:
He says that someone was thinking in his heart: "I will ascend to heaven, I will set my throne higher than the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of the assembly, in the far north." "Throne" is the word for the seat of a king. "The mount of the assembly" is the mountain of gathering, where the gods were thought to meet. "North" is the direction of the verse's final phrase.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. It is a mocking song aimed at the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), who oppressed many nations. His fall from power to the grave is described. Some early Christians have also applied this passage to Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of the human king. This is debated. In both cases, the center is the pride that wants to take the place of God.

Today, when we want to control everything or to be admired without limit, let us remember that God resists the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and serve others without seeking applause.
exp.6:17:
It says that in that day God will call, as with a whistle, the fly from the far reaches of the rivers of Egypt and the bee from the land of Assyria. Here "whistle" means giving a signal to make them come. These are images of armies that will arrive in swarms.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who feared his enemies and did not trust God. Isaiah warns him that although those kings would fall, God would bring something worse: the invasion of Assyria. Egypt and Assyria were neighboring powers, and many understand the text to refer to their armies.

For today: God rules even what seems out of control. So instead of seeking security in alliances or human resources, we can trust Him and obey Him with humility.
exp.33:1:
Here Isaiah says that God is angry with all the nations and with their armies. The word for "destroy" in the original means that God will bring them to ruin, and the image of a place where animals are put to death is a strong picture of judgment. The word "armies" can refer to their forces and to all their power.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and calls all peoples and the whole earth to listen. It is a solemn announcement of worldwide judgment, and the chapter then focuses on Edom. Scholars debate whether it refers only to events close at hand, to the end of time, or to both. What is clear is that God is sovereign over all the nations.

Today we can remember that no human power stands above God. That invites us to trust in Him, to live with humility, and to seek His forgiveness, which is offered in Christ, rather than depending on our own strength or on governments.
exp.4:15:
He says that when God judges, everyone will see how great he is. The Lord of hosts is the Lord who commands all power. To be exalted means to be lifted up and recognized as supreme. To be sanctified means to be shown as holy, set apart, and perfect. His righteousness makes his holiness visible.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. In chapter 5, God compares them to a vineyard that produced bad fruit: injustice, pride, and abuse. Just before this verse, the proud are humbled. Here the result is shown: while human pride falls, God's righteousness is lifted high.

For today: when you see injustice and it seems that no one responds, rest in the fact that God is just and will see everything. And examine your own heart: ask him to take away your pride and teach you to live with honesty and fair treatment toward others.
exp.29:16:
It says the people will be so weak and so afraid that a thousand men will flee at the threat of one alone, and all of them will flee at the threat of five. In the end only a few will be left, alone like a pole on the top of a mountain or like a flag on a hill. A hill is a small rise or height of land.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. The people were looking for military protection in Egypt, with horses and chariots, instead of trusting the Lord, who offered them salvation in quietness and confidence. They said "No." So God warns that the flight they chose would turn against them. Even so, the passage that follows shows that God waits so that he may show mercy.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for quick escapes without prayer, we can stop and trust God. He remains patient and is ready to help anyone who turns back to him.
exp.55:0:
God speaks and calls his people to "keep judgment", that is, to live uprightly, and to "do justice", treating others with honesty and fairness. The reason is that his salvation is near, and also his righteousness, which will soon be made clear.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The verses that follow say that those who obey will be blessed, and that neither the foreigner nor the eunuch, who might feel shut out, should think that God rejects them. Many scholars place this message at the time of the return from exile, though not all agree.

For today: if we are waiting for God's work, we should not sit with our arms folded. Today you can choose to be just in a concrete matter, such as paying what is owed, speaking the truth, or standing up for someone who is being treated with contempt.
exp.6:6:
God declares that the plan of Judah's enemies will fail. The words "It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass" mean that it will not hold firm and will never be carried out. This refers to the "evil counsel," that is, the wicked plan to invade Judah, divide it up, and set up a puppet king, the son of Tabeel.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz, who was very afraid because Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) had allied against him. God sends him a message to calm him: those kings appear strong, but their power is limited. Verse 9 ends with a challenge to believe: if they do not believe, they will not remain.

For today: when plans or pressures threaten you and seem bigger than you are, remember that God rules above them. Trusting Him does not remove the problem at once, but it allows you to face it with firmness and peace, instead of acting out of fear.
exp.13:19:
He says this king will not be buried with honor alongside the other kings. The reason is that he ruined his own country and killed his people. "Seed" means descendants, and "wicked ones" means evildoers. His family will not be remembered with honor.

The prophet Isaiah is delivering a mocking song against the king of Babylon, and the text presents it in poetic form. Dead kings receive a dignified tomb, but this tyrant is cast out like a trampled corpse. God himself then announces that he will wipe out the name of Babylon. Some apply this to one particular king, and others also see a broader picture of human pride.

For today: power used to harm others does not leave a good memory behind. Ask God to help you use your influence, even if it is small, to care for people and not to take advantage of them.
exp.34:3:
It says that frightened and discouraged people (those with a fearful heart) should be encouraged: "Be strong, fear not." God himself is coming. "Vengeance" and "recompence" mean that God will do justice and set right the wrong; "save you" means rescuing his people.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to God's people, who lived in fear before enemies and judgments. After describing the desert that blossoms, he asks them to strengthen the weak. Then it is announced that the blind will see and the lame will leap: signs that God restores. Some see here also a promise that points to Christ; others read it mainly as hope for Israel.

Today, when someone close to you is discouraged, do not give them only advice: tell them gently that God is faithful and that they are not alone. And you, remember that promise when you feel fear.
exp.26:7:
He says that God disciplines his people with measure, that is, with moderation and not without limit. "His shoots" are the branches, an image of the people. God holds back his "strong wind," that is, his fierce judgment, on the day of the hot wind, which is the hot, dry wind from the east. Even when he disciplines, he sets a limit.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, passing on God's word about Israel, which is pictured as a vineyard. The verse before it promises restoration, and the next one explains that the punishment aims to cleanse the idolatry. Some understand "it" to refer to the people and others to the city; the Hebrew text is difficult and is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you go through a correction or a trial, remember that God does not act with unrestrained fury. His discipline has a purpose and a limit, and it seeks to restore your life and your fruit.
exp.59:10:
It says that the gates of Jerusalem will always stand open, by day and by night, and will never be shut. In this way the wealth of the nations will be able to come in freely, and their kings as well, who will be brought to the city, that is, led or guided there.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who had suffered punishment and destruction. He promises them restoration and mercy. The gates were normally shut at night out of fear of enemies; here it is announced that the peace will be so secure that there will be no need to shut them. Some see here a fulfillment in history, and others a future or spiritual fulfillment.

For today: our lives and our church can live with confidence in the peace that God gives, keeping our doors open to receive and welcome everyone with generosity, without living dominated by fear.
exp.8:5:
It says that a child is born, a son whom God gives to his people. The "government on his shoulder" means that the rule will be under his authority. The phrase "is called" simply means that he will be called by these names. His names describe who he is: Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat and oppression of foreign powers. First he announces that God will break the yoke that oppresses them, as in the days of Midian (Judges 7). Then he promises a kingdom without end on the throne of David. Christians see Jesus here; some scholars also see a first fulfillment in a king of that time.

For today: when you feel that everything weighs on you or you don't know what to do, bring your burdens and decisions to Jesus. He counsels with wisdom and gives a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that Israel would be attacked from two sides: the Syrians (Arameans) from the east and the Philistines from the west. They would devour Israel "with open mouth," that is, without difficulty. Even so, God's anger had not subsided, and his hand was still stretched out, ready to correct.

Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel. They had suffered blows, yet they proudly said they would rebuild stronger, with dressed stone and cedars. Instead of turning to God, they trusted in themselves. For this reason God allowed their enemies to keep pressing them.

For today: when crises come, it is not enough to rebuild with our own strength. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but every difficulty is a good moment to stop, pray, and ask what God wants to teach us. Let us return to him with humility.
exp.56:4:
God asks the people of Judah whether they are not ashamed of what they do. Being "inflamed" with idols means they were burning with passion for them. The "tree" was a dense-shaded tree, under which pagan rites were performed. They also sacrificed their children in the valleys and among the rocks, or large boulders.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is accusing the people of unfaithfulness, and for this reason he calls them "children of the sorceress," that is, of a witch. These practices were common among the neighboring peoples, and the people copied them. Scholars debate the exact period when this happened, but the accusation is clear.

For today: we no longer worship under trees, but we can give our hearts to things that are not God, such as money or success. Ask yourself what thing you are more passionate about than God, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.57:10:
This verse promises that God himself will guide and care for his people like a shepherd. The word "guide" in the verse shows what this means: leading and protecting. Times of great need are described as dry seasons. The phrase "satisfy thy soul" means that God will give you contentment. The phrase "make fat thy bones" speaks of giving strength and health. The people will be like a well-watered garden and like a spring whose waters never run dry.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people fasted and appeared religious, but they oppressed others and did not practice justice. God tells them that what he truly desires is that they remove the yoke, give bread to the hungry, and help those who are suffering. Then the blessing will come.

When we generously help someone who is suffering, God takes care of our lives. This week, look for a concrete way to serve someone in need, and trust that God will sustain you.
exp.25:2:
It says that God watches over and keeps in "perfect peace" the person whose mind stays fixed on Him. "Keep" here means to protect, like someone guarding a house. "Stayed" means to remain steady, not letting go. In the original language, the phrase "perfect peace" repeats the word for peace, as if to say complete peace. The reason the verse gives is simple: that person has placed their trust in God.

It is part of a song that Judah will sing "in that day," meaning a future time of salvation. Isaiah writes it for a people living under threat, and he contrasts the city of God, strong because of His protection, with the proud city that God brings low (v. 5). Scholars debate which exact city is meant.

For today: when worry comes, go back to prayer and remember God's promises, instead of repeating your fears. Trusting is a daily decision, and God promises to sustain your heart.
exp.29:12:
This verse compares the people's sin to a high wall that has a crack or a bulging, bent part. That wall looks solid, but it is going to collapse suddenly, without warning. The phrase "this iniquity shall be to you" means that their sin will turn back against them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. They rejected his word, would not listen to the prophets, and put their trust in violence, deceit, and human alliances instead of trusting in God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are relying on for our security. What is built on lies or pride may look firm for a while, but it cannot hold. God invites us to return to him and rest in his word.
exp.58:12:
This verse describes the sin of the people with several strong words. "Transgressing" means breaking faith or betraying trust. "Turning away from our God" means turning your back on him and no longer following him. "Oppression and revolt" are words that do harm and defy God. And sin does not come only from the mouth: the lie is conceived in the heart, that is, the falsehood is formed in the mind before it is spoken.

Here Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people. He includes himself in the message and acknowledges the guilt. Before this verse, the people complain that salvation has not come, but the prophet explains that their own sins separate them from God. Afterward, we see how lying damages justice in society.

For today: before you speak, examine what is in your heart. Ask God for sincerity, and practice telling the truth with love, even when it is costly.
exp.9:4:
God speaks and calls Assyria the rod and staff of his anger. That is, he uses it like a stick to correct. The words "fury" and "wrath" speak of his righteous anger against evil. He says he placed that anger in its hand, meaning that Assyria would be the instrument.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Judah and Israel, who had fallen into injustice and disobedience (see the preceding verses). He warns them that a punishment is coming from far away and that no one will be able to save them without him. Assyria does not know that God is using it; its plans are of conquest and pride. That is why later God will also judge it.

For today: God governs even the nations and the difficult situations. If we go through a correction, we can humbly ask what he wants to teach us, and trust that he remains in control and is just.
exp.32:15:
This verse speaks of the righteous person described earlier: the one who walks in uprightness. That person will dwell in high places, protected as in a fortress of rock. A "place of shelter" means a refuge. Also, bread will be given to them, and their water will be sure, that is, secure and never failing.

The prophet Isaiah writes to Judah when Assyria was threatening and the people trembled before the judgment of God. Sinners grow afraid before the consuming fire, which probably points to the holiness of God. Then the question is asked: who will be able to stand in his presence? This verse answers with a promise of care for the one who lives with integrity.

For today: God cares for the one who seeks to live honestly, even when there is fear or scarcity. Today you can choose one concrete step of integrity, such as turning down an unfair advantage, and trust that God sustains your life.
exp.0:13:
God says he no longer tolerates the religious festivals of his people. The new moon celebrations marked the beginning of each month, and the appointed feasts were the sacred festivals and gatherings. "My soul hates" means that his heart rejects them. "A burden" means something heavy to carry. God shows himself weary of putting up with them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. God himself had commanded those feasts, so the problem was not the feasts. The serious issue was that the people kept them while practicing injustice, and the text says their hands were full of blood. God was asking for a change of life, not just rituals.

For today: going to church, singing, or praying is not enough if during the week we treat others badly or ignore the person in need. Ask God to show you something specific that you need to correct, and do it as part of your worship.
exp.50:14:
This verse says that it is the Lord who divides the sea, that is, who stirs up or splits the sea, and its waves roar. The phrase "The Lord of hosts" is a title that speaks of his power over all that he has made. God reminds his people who he is: the mighty God who rules even the fiercest waters.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to a people in exile who were afraid of their oppressors and had forgotten their Creator. Earlier he rebuked them for fearing a mere man who passes away. Now he comforts them with his greatness. Some see here a memory of the Red Sea, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: when your fears seem like giant waves, remember that God rules the sea. Before you think about your problem, take a moment to pray and to recall who he is.
exp.40:12:
It says that the Lord, the God of his people, takes him by the right hand, like a father who guides his child, and tells him, "Fear not." The word "hold" means to grasp or to take firm hold of someone. The phrase "I will help thee" sounds like it refers to the past, but in the original it is understood as a certain promise: "I will help you" or "I am helping you."

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, his servant, probably at a time of threat from powerful nations. The verses before this one promise that those who oppose them will vanish. God wants to encourage a small and frightened people, reminding them that they are not alone.

For today: when you feel afraid or small before a problem, imagine that God is holding your hand. Pray simply: "Lord, hold me up today." You do not depend on your own strength, but on the one who holds you.
exp.54:1:
This verse says that people spend their money and effort on things that do not nourish or satisfy. "Satisfaction" means being full and content. "Richness" refers to rich, abundant food, an image of joy and fullness. God invites us to listen carefully, to eat what is good, and to truly enjoy ourselves.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, probably to a people in exile or near it, tired and spiritually thirsty. He offers freely what money cannot buy: his grace and his covenant. The verses that follow speak of the promises made to David. Christian interpreters often see in this a sign that points to Christ, although the original text speaks first to Israel.

Today, ask yourself where you are investing your time and energy. Set aside a moment each day to hear God in his Word and in prayer, and let him feed you.
exp.1:5:
It says that God left his people, Israel, because they had filled themselves with customs from the East, practiced divination like the Philistines, and felt secure in alliances with foreigners. "Filled" means full. "Diviners" are those who foretell the future. "Foreign children" can be understood as pacts with foreigners or pagan customs; it is interpreted in several ways.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He has just invited them to walk in the light of the Lord, and now he explains why they are far from it. They were trusting in foreign influences, in riches, in horses and in idols, instead of trusting in God.

For today: check where you rest when you are afraid or need direction. Money, horoscopes, fashions or people can take the place of God. Seek Him first in prayer and in His Word.
exp.17:2:
It says that all the inhabitants of the earth will see a sign lifted up on the mountains and hear the sound of a trumpet. A "banner" is a standard raised to draw attention, and the trumpet serves to give a warning. Both things announce that God is about to act, and no one will be able to ignore it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. A powerful nation, which many understand to be Ethiopia (Cush), sends messengers seeking alliances, probably in the face of the threat from Assyria. Scholars disagree about who raises the banner, but the context shows that God is the one who directs events, watching calmly and intervening in his own time.

For today: when the world seems agitated and we look for security in alliances or human plans, let us remember that God is still in control. We can trust and wait with peace, knowing that he acts in his own time.
exp.20:9:
He says the prophet speaks to his people, whom he calls "my threshing" and "the corn of my floor." These are images of wheat beaten on the threshing floor, the place where the grain was separated out. Isaiah affirms that he invents nothing: he faithfully tells them what he heard from God, the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel.

Isaiah speaks after seeing in vision the fall of Babylon. That news was hard for God's people, who were suffering under the empires. Many understand that the people would be "threshed," that is, tested and broken, though the phrase can be interpreted in other ways. What is clear is that the prophet insists the message comes from God.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, even if it is hard to hear, let us receive it with humility. And if we share anything of him, let us do so faithfully, without adding or taking away anything.
exp.38:5:
Here God announces that a time will come when everything in the palace of Hezekiah, including the riches that his ancestors stored up, will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, delivering a message from the LORD. Hezekiah, king of Judah, had shown all his treasures to Babylonian envoys who visited him. His pride or excessive confidence in human alliances receives a warning here. Babylon was not yet the great power, and the prophecy was fulfilled later, though the historical details are understood in different ways.

For today: what we accumulate is not secure forever. It is wise to receive God's correction with humility, to use what we have with gratitude, and to trust Him more than our possessions or the support of others.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that those who rule over or collect taxes from God's people are called "young men," and that "women" dominate them. The word "oppressors" refers to those who demand payments or tribute. Also, the leaders of the people deceive them and lead their paths astray. Scholars understand "young men" in several ways: immature or weak rulers, or even actual young people. The meaning of "women" is also interpreted differently, perhaps as weak or easily influenced leaders.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God, in Judah. God announces that he will take away good leadership as a consequence of injustice. The verses that follow show that God will judge the elders and princes who took advantage of the poor.

For today: do not follow blindly whoever guides you. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and pray for your leaders, that they may act with justice and wisdom.
exp.33:4:
It says that God's sword, which first becomes drunk, or is filled to the full, in the heavens, will now come down to punish Edom. God calls this people "the people under my curse," that is, a condemned people, set apart for destruction because of their wickedness. The word "judgment" speaks of a fair sentence.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Chapter 34 announces judgment on the nations, and Edom appears as an example of those who oppose God and his people. Scholars debate whether all of this describes a historical event close at hand, a final judgment, or both. The language is poetic and very strong.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook it. We can trust that he will judge with justice, and so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. In the meantime, let us live with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.40:28:
It says that the idols and those who make them are worth nothing. "Iniquity" here speaks of something empty and deceptive, and "molten images" are the idols made from cast metal in molds. Calling them "wind and confusion" means they have no substance or power, like air that slips away.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In this passage he presents a case against the nations and their false gods. He challenges them to announce what is to come or to give counsel, but they answer nothing. Only the Lord declares what will happen and brings good news to Zion and Jerusalem.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others, ends up being like air. Today you can identify where you are trusting too much and place your hope again in the God who really speaks and fulfills his word.
exp.50:15:
God says that he has put his words in the mouth of someone and covered him under the shadow of his hand. The phrases "plant the heavens" and "lay the foundations of the earth" mean "so that he might plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth." What God wants is to declare to Zion: "Thou art my people."

The LORD speaks to Israel, who is distressed and in exile. He wants to comfort them and remind them that he is the Creator and has not forgotten them. Scholars do not agree on who the "you" is: it may be Israel as a nation, the prophet, or the Servant of God. What is clear is that God cares for the one who carries his message.

Today, if you share the Word of God, you do not depend only on your own strength. Speak with confidence and remember that his hand covers you and that you are part of his people.
exp.7:4:
It says that the Lord spoke to Isaiah again. The words in the original that correspond to "again" and the connecting word are short phrases, and the verse itself simply reads "The Lord spake also unto me again, saying." It is a short sentence that introduces a new message from God to the prophet.

Isaiah writes here in the first person. He has just described the birth of his son, whose name was a sign that Assyria would soon defeat Damascus and Samaria. Now God gives him another message: the people of Judah had despised trust in God, the gentle waters of Shiloah, and had sought security in human alliances. For this reason the power of Assyria would come upon them.

God does not remain silent when we turn away. He speaks to us again and again, through His Word and through His Spirit. Today we may ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to Him once more, even if it is to correct us, and to trust in Him more than in our own securities.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that the altar and the monument to the Lord in Egypt will be a sign and a witness that God is present there. When the Egyptians suffer under their oppressors, they will cry out to the Lord, and he will send them a saviour, a great one, who will defend them and set them free.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in God's name about the future of Egypt, a nation that had once been an enemy of Israel. It is a surprising promise: Egypt too would come to know the Lord. Interpreters differ about who this saviour is. Some think of a historical deliverer, and many Christians see a promise that points to Christ. It cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: God hears the cry of anyone who is oppressed, whatever their background. When you suffer, cry out to him with confidence, and let his great mercy teach you to pray also for those who seem far from God.
exp.34:2:
It says that we should give strength and encouragement to those who are exhausted and weak. The phrase that means to strengthen or encourage is not needed here, and neither is the word that means to make firm or give vigor. Hands that are tired and knees that tremble describe people without strength, who are afraid or discouraged.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to God's people with a message of hope. Before this, he describes a desert that blossoms, an image of the restoration that God promises. Then he says that God himself will come to save. For this reason, this call is directed to those who already believe and who should encourage one another while they wait. Scholars debate the exact moment the prophecy refers to, but the central encouragement is clear.

Today we can look out for someone in our family, church, or work who is tired or worried. A phone call, a prayer together, or a concrete offer of help will remind them that God has not forgotten them.
exp.33:6:
This verse says that God's judgment on Edom will be complete. The word "unicorns" in the verse is an old rendering of a Hebrew term (re'em) that most likely refers to wild oxen or large buffalo; it is not the legendary animal. The "bullocks with the bulls" and the images of the land soaked with blood and the dust made fat with fatness show a huge slaughter, described as a sacrifice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do. Edom, a neighbor of Israel, is the example of the nations that oppose God and his people. The language is poetic and exaggerated, and it speaks of divine justice and of the "cause of Zion," that is, God defending his own.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook it. We can rest in the fact that he judges with justice, and so leave vengeance in his hands and live with humility and mercy.
exp.49:0:
Here God speaks to his people through questions. The "bill of divorce" was the document of divorce, and the "creditors" are those who lend money and collect debts. God asks: where is the paper with which I divorced Israel, your mother? To which creditor did I sell you as slaves? There is none. God says they were sold because of their iniquities, and the mother was put away because of their transgressions.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah to a people who were in exile and believed that God had abandoned them forever. God answers that the separation did not happen because of any lack of love or power on his part, but because of the people's sin.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, examine your heart honestly and do not assume that he has abandoned you. Return to him, because his hand has not been shortened to save.
exp.62:9:
This verse says that the people of Israel rebelled and grieved the Holy Spirit of God. Because of this, God, who had cared for them before, stopped acting as their protector and, in a sense, went against them. The word "and" is the meaning of the old connecting word in the verse, "vexed" here is understood as grieve or distress, and "he was turned to be their enemy" means that God himself opposed them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, prayerfully recalling what God did for his people. Before this verse he tells of God's love and compassion; after it he recalls the exodus with Moses. Isaiah shows that Israel's suffering came from their rebellion, not because God stopped loving them.

For today: God is not indifferent to our attitudes. When we resist his guidance, we move away from his care. Today you can examine your heart, recognize where you have resisted God, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.39:26:
This verse says that God's people are complaining: "God does not see my path, and He does not care that justice is done for me." "My way is hidden" means they feel their life is hidden from God's eyes. "My judgment is passed over" means their just cause was ignored. God asks them, with a certain tenderness, why they think this way.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Israel, who was suffering and felt forgotten, probably in a time of exile or under the threat of it (scholars place it in different ways). Earlier, God is shown as the Creator who calls each star by name. If not one star escapes Him, neither does His people. Later, He promises strength to the weary.

When you feel forgotten or ignored by God, do not silence your complaint, but remember what you know of Him: He cares for the stars and also for you. Pray, telling Him honestly what you feel, and ask Him for strength for today.
exp.50:19:
This verse says that the sons of Jerusalem fell without strength and lay in the corners of all the streets. They were like a wild antelope or ox caught in a net, unable to escape. "Fainted" means they were completely weakened. "Full of the fury" and "rebuke" speak of God's judgment upon them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as a grieving mother, after the destruction and famine of judgment. No one comforts or guides her. But the text that follows changes its tone: God, who defends his people, takes away the cup of his anger and promises that she will not drink it again.

For today: even when we live with the hard consequences of our mistakes, God does not abandon us. If you feel without strength today, come to him sincerely; he knows how to comfort and lift up.
exp.52:1:
It says the Servant of the LORD would grow up like a tender shoot, like a root coming up out of dry ground, where almost nothing lives. He would have no imposing figure and no special beauty; when people saw him, they would find nothing attractive that would move them to desire him. The word "appearance" here means good looks, and the word "shoot" means a new young growth.

It is a group speaking with "we," probably the people admitting their mistake. This follows the question of who believed the message. Christians see Jesus here, and the New Testament quotes this chapter in that sense. Some Jewish scholars understand the servant to be Israel; there are different interpretations.

Today it invites us not to measure the worth of people, or of God, by outward appearance, success, or what is eye-catching. God often works through what is humble and simple. We can learn to value what He values.
exp.21:22:
He says that God will set his servant like a peg or nail firmly driven into a secure place, and that he will become a seat of honor for his father's household, that is, a source of respect and dignity. The word for "I will drive it" means "I will fasten him," and "seat of honor" is a throne or place of glory.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He removes Shebna, a proud administrator of the palace, and puts in his place Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, to take care of the king's house. The verses that follow show that the people will lean on him, but also that this burden has limits. Some Christians see here a shadow of Christ (Revelation 3:7); others read only the historical moment.

For today: if God gives you a responsibility, serve it with humility and faithfulness, remembering that your steadiness depends on Him, not on your position.
exp.32:14:
This verse describes the person who can live near God. He walks in righteousness and speaks with truth. He turns away from money gained through violence. He shakes his hands so as not to accept bribes, which are payments meant to corrupt judgment. He stops his ears from hearing plans of violence or bloodshed, and he closes his eyes so as not to look on evil with pleasure.

Isaiah writes in a time of threat for Judah. God has shown his power, and the hypocrites in Zion tremble. Then the question arises: who can stand before a holy God, compared to a consuming fire? This verse and the next answer: the one who lives with integrity will receive protection, food, and will see the King.

For today: practice integrity in small things. Refuse an unfair advantage, do not repeat harmful gossip, and turn your gaze away from what pushes you toward wrong. In this way your life shows that you want to be close to God.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim, who were brothers, fought against each other, and then joined together to attack Judah. "Anger" is God's wrath. "His hand is stretched out" means that his hand was still raised to punish. Although the people were already suffering, the judgment had not ended.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel, which is sometimes called Ephraim. He describes God's punishment for their pride and rebellion. The war, the hunger and the violence between brothers show a people destroying themselves. Scholars understand this as a description of the internal struggles of that time, although not all of them agree on the specific events.

Today this verse invites us to examine our quarrels with family, church or neighbors. When pride and resentment take control, everyone is hurt. Let us ask God for humility, and seek peace before division consumes us.
exp.40:3:
God asks: who did all this, that is, raised up a conqueror and guided history? He himself answers: "I the Lord." He calls the generations from the beginning. He is "the first" and remains the same with "the last," that is, the final ones.

God speaks through Isaiah and challenges the nations that trusted in idols. "The righteous one from the east" is often understood as Cyrus of Persia, though some think of Abraham. The central point is that God directs history, and idols do not.

For today: when the world seems out of control, remember that God was there at the beginning and will be there at the end. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your time are in his hands, and pray with confidence.
exp.64:17:
This verse says that God's people should be glad and rejoice forever in what God is creating.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who have suffered greatly and need hope. He promises new heavens and a new earth, where the pain of the past will be forgotten. Some scholars see here a near restoration, and others see the final promise of a new world. It can also be read as both.

When you are going through a trial, remember that God has not given up on his creation. Take a moment today to thank him for something good you already see, and to trust that he can turn your sorrow into joy.
exp.1:18:
He says that when God rises with power to judge the earth, people will flee to hide in caves and crevices of the rocks. They will be afraid because of the overwhelming presence of the Lord and the brightness of his greatness. Here "terrifying" means something that causes fear and awe. The phrase about shaking the earth speaks of a judgment that shakes all of humanity.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He warns them that human pride and idolatry will not withstand the day of the Lord, a time when God will show that he alone is great. Scholars debate whether the text refers to a near historical judgment, a final one, or both.

For today: examine what you depend on in place of God, such as money, reputation, or your own strength. Today you can surrender these to him with humility, without waiting for everything to be shaken.
exp.2:0:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, is going to take away from Jerusalem and from Judah everything that holds them up. Those who give support are taken away, and so are those who provide protection. He will also take away all the bread that sustains them and all the water they need, that is, the basic food and water needed to live.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. The next chapter lists leaders and capable people who will be gone: judges, prophets, elders, and counselors. The message is a judgment for the people's injustice and pride, since they trusted in their own resources and not in God. Scholars understand the exact timing in different ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not place your security only in your work, your money, or your leaders. Be thankful each day for what God gives you, and trust Him first.
exp.3:5:
It says there will be a shelter, that is, a kind of booth or tent that gives shade, to protect people from the heat of the day. It will also be a refuge and a hiding place from the storm with strong wind, and from the downpour of heavy rain.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks to Judah and Jerusalem, who had fallen into sin and faced judgment. The verses before this one speak of a cleansing that God would bring and of his presence as a cloud and fire over Zion, as in the desert with Israel. This verse closes the promise: God himself will be the protection. Some see here a hope for Israel's future; many Christians also connect it with Christ, although the text does not say so in those words.

When you go through heat, pressure, or storms, do not rush to hide only in your own strength. Draw near to God in prayer, ask him to cleanse you, and trust that his presence is a real refuge.
exp.47:12:
God says that his hand laid the foundations of the earth and that with his right hand he measured the heavens, marking them out with a span, that is, with the width of an open hand. When he called to them, they came together at once, presenting themselves all at the same time, ready to obey.

God himself speaks to Israel, his people, who were in exile and were always tempted to trust in idols. He reminds them that he is the first and the last, the Creator. That is why he can announce in advance what he will do in Babylon and then carry it out.

For today: if the God who formed the earth and the heavens calls you and cares for you, you can entrust him with your worries. What seems enormous to you is not great to him. Rest in his power and in his faithfulness.
exp.61:0:
He says that the speaker will not stay silent or rest for the sake of Zion and Jerusalem. He will keep going until their righteousness shines like the light of dawn, and their salvation, that is, their deliverance, burns like a lit torch. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "I will not rest" means "I will not stop."

The context is a promise of restoration for God's people after punishment and exile. It is not entirely clear who is speaking: some think it is the prophet Isaiah, and others think it is the Servant of the Lord, whom Christians connect with Christ. The verses that follow show the purpose: that the nations would see God's glory in his people.

For today: do not give up praying or serving for your church, your family, or your city. Persevere with hope, trusting that God keeps what he promises.
exp.45:9:
He says that God announces the future from the beginning, that is, he speaks of things that have not yet happened. Where it says "my counsel shall stand," it refers to his plan or purpose, which is not cancelled. "I will do all my pleasure" means he will do everything he desires, and nothing stops him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who were tempted to trust in idols. For that reason he asks them to remember the past and to recognize that he alone is God. The "man of my counsel" that appears later is usually understood to be Cyrus, king of Persia, although the text here does not name him.

For today: when your life feels uncertain, remember how God has sustained you before. Pray with confidence, knowing that his plan is firm even when you cannot see the whole way ahead.
exp.13:23:
Here God makes a solemn oath. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" means the Lord who commands over all powers. It says that what he has thought and determined will come to pass just as he planned it, and nothing will change it.

God speaks through Isaiah. He had just announced the fall of Babylon, and right away he announces that he will break the Assyrian in the land of Judah. With an oath, God gives assurance to his people, who lived threatened by powerful empires. The verses that follow show that his plan reaches all the nations.

For today: when the world seems dominated by unjust powers or by fear, you can rest in the fact that God keeps what he promises. Trust in him, pray calmly, and keep doing good.
exp.0:14:
God says that when his people lift up their hands to pray, he will hide his eyes from them, meaning he will not look on them with favor. Even if they offer many prayers, he will not hear them. The verse for this comes at the end: their hands are full of blood, that is, of violence and injustice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah. The people kept up their rituals, sacrifices, and festivals, but they oppressed the weak. God does not reject prayer itself, but the religion practiced without justice or repentance. The verses that follow show this: he calls them to wash themselves clean and to do good.

Today, it is not enough to pray or go to church if we live harshly toward others. We can ask forgiveness, correct an injustice, and help someone in need. In this way our prayer comes from a sincere heart.
exp.40:27:
He says that God looks among the idols and the nations, searching for someone who can explain what is happening or give good counsel, and He finds no one. He asks them, and no one answers even a word. A counsellor is someone who guides with wisdom. None means that there is no one able to answer.

The Lord speaks here in the middle of an imagined trial against the idols and the nations that follow them (Isaiah 41). He challenges them to show that their gods know the past and the future. Since they cannot announce anything, it becomes clear that they are not gods. By contrast, God announced long ago His plans for Zion and Jerusalem, and He promises to send good news.

Today we can ask ourselves what we place our trust in: money, success, opinions, or our own plans. If these cannot give us firm answers or peace, let us return to God, who speaks the truth and does what He promises.
exp.32:12:
God calls everyone to listen: both those who are far away and those who are near. He wants them to know what he has done and to acknowledge his might.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he has announced judgment on empty plans and the wickedness of the nations, compared to straw and burned thorns. Then the people of Zion become frightened and ask who will be able to stand before a God so holy. The answer describes the one who lives with righteousness and honesty. Some understand "those who are far off" as the nations, and "those who are near" as Israel.

For today: do not take lightly the might and holiness of God. Listen to him with humility, examine your heart, and ask him for help to live with honesty in everyday life.
exp.41:21:
It says that the people of Israel were robbed, trampled, and humiliated. Many were trapped in caves and locked up in prisons. The phrase "robbed and spoiled" means plundered and stripped of everything. No one came to rescue them, and no one said "Give it back." They were like helpless prey.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, describing the condition of Israel, the blind and deaf servant he had spoken of before. The verses that follow explain that this ruin was not an accident: God himself allowed it because the people sinned and refused to walk in his ways or listen to his law. Many understand this to refer to the exile in Babylon, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when we suffer the consequences of ignoring God, we are not without hope. We can listen to his voice, return to him with humility, and trust that he does rescue those who seek him.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that the women of Moab will go about frightened and without direction, like a bird that flees its nest when it is startled. They will be at the shallow crossing places of the river Arnon, on the border of Moab.

God speaks through Isaiah about a judgment that falls on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab is in crisis and its people are fleeing. The verses before and after show them asking Judah for help. Scholars do not agree on every historical detail of this passage, so it is wise to read it with humility.

When life shakes us and we feel like that bird without a nest, we need not run aimlessly. We can seek refuge in God and offer shelter to anyone who is wounded or left without help.
exp.58:15:
What it says: God looks at his people and sees that no one stands up to set right so much injustice. He is astonished that there is no intercessor, that is, someone who steps in between and defends what is right. So he himself acts: his arm, which represents his power, brings salvation, and his own righteousness sustains him.

Context: The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people full of lies, violence and oppression, where even the one who avoided evil was persecuted. God does not ignore this: he sees it, and it grieves him. The verses that follow describe him as a warrior who puts on righteousness as his armor. Many Christians see here a sign of Christ, although the original text speaks first of the liberation of Israel.

For today: God is the one who saves, but he also seeks people willing to intercede and to defend the weak. Today you can pray for someone who suffers injustice and, if it is within your reach, help them with courage and humility.
exp.51:2:
This verse says that God speaks to his people. "For nothing" means freely, without receiving anything in return. Israel was sold without anyone paying a fair price for them. That is why they will also be redeemed "without money": their freedom will not be bought with silver.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem, which lives in captivity and humiliation. God calls her to awake and rise up. Her oppressors did not pay a real price for them, so God owes no ransom to them. He will act on his own account and out of love for his name, which is blasphemed.

For today: if you feel bound by guilt or failure, remember that the freedom God gives is not earned through effort, nor is it paid for. Christians of many traditions see in this a foreshadowing of redemption in Christ. Today you can receive it with gratitude and rise up.
exp.37:9:
He says that Hezekiah, facing his illness, thought he would die young, in the middle of his life. "The gates of the grave" is a poetic way of speaking of Sheol, the place of the dead. "I am deprived of the residue of my years" means that he felt they were taking away the years he still had left to live.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks in a writing he composed after he was healed. He had been gravely ill and God had announced to him that he would die. This verse recalls what he felt in that moment of anguish, before the Lord heard his prayer and added years to his life.

For today: when you feel that your plans are being cut short by an illness or a crisis, do not hide your pain. Hezekiah expressed it honestly and put it in writing. Bringing our fear to God just as it is can open the way to receive his comfort.
exp.25:9:
It says that a wicked person can be shown kindness and mercy, yet still does not learn to live righteously. Even in a land where uprightness and good example prevail, he keeps doing wrong. The words "favour" here mean kindness or compassion; "wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God; and "unjustly" means doing evil. The phrase "will not behold the majesty of the Lord" means that he does not recognize the greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a song of trust by God's people. Earlier he said that when God judges, people learn righteousness. Here he contrasts this: there are those who do not change even when shown kindness. Interpreters understand this as a hardened heart, not merely a lack of information.

For today: do not assume that blessings will change the heart. Ask God for a humble heart, one that recognizes his goodness and responds with gratitude and obedience.
exp.43:16:
This verse describes a man who uses half of a log to cook and warm himself, and with what is left over he makes an image. Then he bows down before it, worships it, and asks it to save him. The leftover piece is the part of the wood that remains, and the carved figure is the image he shapes from it. To bow down or prostrate oneself is what the word translated as "falleth down" means here.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who lived surrounded by nations that worshipped idols. With irony, he shows how absurd idolatry is: the same wood serves for the daily fire and for a "god." The verses that follow say that this person does not reflect, because his mind is closed.

For today: let us review which things, even useful ones, we are putting in God's place, such as money, work, or success. They cannot save us. Let us ask God to help us trust in him alone.
exp.6:19:
God says he will use the king of Assyria like a hired razor. The wording about being shaved is a plain image: with it he will take off the hair of the head, the hair of the feet, and even the beard. In those days, this was a sign of complete humiliation. The phrase about the far side of the river refers to the Euphrates River.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and looked for help from Assyria instead of trusting God. The prophet warns that this power, the one Ahaz asked for help, would end up as an instrument of judgment and harm for Judah. Some scholars see here a reference to later Assyrian invasions.
