For today: when we are afraid, let us not look for security in human solutions that draw us away from God. What seems like help can cost us dearly. Let us pray first and trust in Him.
exp.11:4:
This verse invites us to sing praises to God, because he has done magnificent things, that is, great and admirable works. It also asks that this be known throughout the earth. Here the "psalms" are songs of praise, and "Jehovah" is the name of God.

Isaiah 12 is a brief hymn of gratitude. The prophet speaks, or the people he leads speak, in "that day," a future time of salvation and comfort after the judgment announced in the earlier chapters. God had been angry with his people, but now he comforts and saves them. That is why the song bursts forth. The mention of "all the earth" shows that this joy was not only for Israel, but was to be shared with the nations.

For today: when you remember something good that God has done for you, do not keep it to yourself. Tell someone about it this week, or sing a song of praise out loud as a way of making his works known.
exp.23:2:
This verse says that the land will be completely emptied and stripped bare, like a house that thieves have entered and cleared of everything. The words "utterly" and "utterly" stress that nothing will be left. The reason given is simple: God himself has spoken it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Chapters 24 to 27 describe a judgment that reaches the whole earth, without distinction of rank: priest and people, master and servant. The verses that follow give the reason: the people broke God's laws and violated his covenant. Some see here a judgment on the world of that time, others a foretaste of the end of days; the text allows both readings.

For today: let us not trust in what can be lost, such as money, position, or success. God calls everyone alike to live justly and to return to him with humility, because only his word endures.
exp.43:18:
This verse says that the man who makes an idol does not stop to think. He uses part of the wood to warm himself, bake bread and roast meat, and with what is left he makes a god. Words like "consider" mean to think something through; "turn" means to change something into another thing; "abomination" means something detestable in God's sight; and "bow down" here means to bend low in order to worship.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, which was surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. With irony, he shows how absurd it is to worship a piece of wood that serves for the daily fire. Then he calls Israel to remember that he formed them and does not forget them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by us, such as money, success or image, we are treating as if they could save us. Stop, think calmly, and return to the God who made you.
exp.51:4:
God says that his people were taken away "for nought", that is, without anyone paying anything for them and without any just reason. Those who "rule over them" make them "howl", that is, groan in pain. Furthermore, because of this, God's name is blasphemed all day long.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel in captivity. He mentions Egypt and Assyria as examples of oppressors. The words "what have I here" can be understood in several ways: as a question from God expressing that he does not remain indifferent, or as a lament. In any case, God prepares the announcement of the deliverance that follows.

For today: when you suffer injustice or see people mocking the name of God, remember that he is not indifferent. Pray with confidence and wait for his rescue, without becoming bitter or responding with evil.
exp.17:4:
It says that, just before the harvest, when the grape or fruit is nearly ready and the flower has passed, God cuts off the tender shoots with pruning tools and removes the branches. It is a farming image: the farmer steps in at the right moment, before the fruit is gathered.

Isaiah speaks in God's name to a distant nation, Ethiopia (Cush), in chapter 18. God says he watches in silence, with calm, while the moment comes. Scholars disagree about whom the pruning refers to: it may be the judgment on the nations that threatened Judah, or on the people themselves. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: even when God seems silent, he is not absent. He acts in his own time, and his pruning, though painful, is not carelessness. We can wait with confidence and ask him for patience.
exp.8:18:
It says that because of God's anger the land has been left in darkness, and that the people will be like wood for the fire. In addition, people will lose all tenderness: no one will have compassion for their own brother.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, Israel (also called Ephraim and Manasseh). The people lived in lies, wickedness, and injustice, and they did not repent. That wickedness is described as a fire that gets out of control and ends up consuming them, through divisions and internal struggles. Many understand this as God's judgment through war and chaos.

Today we can remember that sin, if it is not confessed, destroys relationships as well. Let us ask God for a humble and compassionate heart, and let us seek to be reconciled with someone close to us before hardness grows.
exp.29:30:
This verse says that Assyria, which struck others with a rod, that is, with force and violence, will be destroyed by the voice of God. The name for Assyria here is the old form of the word, which is rendered in English as Assyrian, the great enemy empire of that time. The word for being broken means broken into pieces, defeated completely.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was afraid of Assyria and looked for help from Egypt instead of trusting in God. For this reason he reminds them that God is the one who has real power. Earlier, Isaiah speaks of songs of joy for God's people; afterward, he speaks of judgment on Assyria. Scholars debate which exact historical event is in view, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel that someone or something stronger than you is oppressing you, do not place your hope only in human solutions. Pray and trust that God has the last word over all injustice.
exp.8:16:
God says that he will take no pleasure in the young men of the people, nor will he have compassion on their fatherless and widows, because all of them have fallen into wickedness. The young men are those who are in their youth; the impious are those who do not honor God; and those who do evil are the wicked. Even so, God's anger has not subsided: his hand remains stretched out, ready for judgment.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, Israel, also called Ephraim. The leaders and the false prophets had deceived the people, and the corruption reached everyone, even the weakest. Some understand the outstretched hand as judgment, and others also see a door left open to repentance.

For today: let us guard our words and whom we follow. Let us ask God that our mouths speak truth and that our hearts turn to him with humility.
exp.22:1:
The inhabitants of the coast are told to be silent. Here "isle" means the coastal, seafaring region of Phoenicia. The merchants of Sidon, who crossed the sea and filled Tyre with wealth, now have nothing to say. The verse's words "replenished" and "enriched" are rendered here as "filled" and "made rich." The command to be still is an order to stay silent in the face of disaster.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking, announcing a judgment from God against Tyre, the great trading city. Its harbors and businesses depended on seaborne commerce, and its fall would affect all its partners, such as Sidon. Scholars debate exactly how and when this prophecy was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: no human riches are secure.

For today: it is easy to trust in money, work, or economic stability. This verse invites us to give thanks for what we have, but to place our security in God, who does not change or pass away.
exp.22:2:
The verse says that Tyre grew rich from the grain and harvests of Egypt, watered by the many waters of the Nile. The word "seed" in the verse refers to the sown fields, and "harvest" refers to the mature grain. "Mart of nations" means that Tyre was a marketplace where many peoples gathered to trade.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Tyre, a great trading city by the sea. The ships and the merchants mourn because their harbor will be destroyed. The verse recalls where her wealth came from: trade with other peoples. Scholars debate at what historical moment this prophecy was fulfilled.

Today we can be thankful for the work and the goods we have, but without trusting in them as if they were our security. What seems firm today can change soon. It is wise to place our trust in God and to use what we have with generosity.
exp.59:16:
It says that God will change what is poor and worn out into something better: instead of copper, gold; instead of iron, silver; instead of wood, brass; and instead of stones, iron. Furthermore, he will make peace the ruler of his people and righteousness the one who collects what is owed. A tribute is what is paid to an authority, and those who collect it do so with harsh demands.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who felt abandoned and despised. He promises restoration and glory. Many understand this as hope for the return from exile, and others also see a future fulfillment in the kingdom of God. Interpreters explain it in various ways.

For today: when you feel that your life is worn down, surrender that area to God and ask him to place his peace and his righteousness in it, trusting that he knows how to restore.
exp.45:10:
It says God calls from the east a "bird," meaning someone swift and determined like a bird of prey, and brings him from a far country. He calls him "the man that executeth my counsel": the one who will carry out his plan. "I have purposed it" means he has planned it. What God says, he does.

God himself speaks, in a time when Israel was in difficulty. He asks them to remember that he alone is God and that he announces the future before it happens, unlike the idols. Many understand this "bird" to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who would come from the east (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1), though some also see it as a broader picture of God's plans.

For today: when your situation seems out of control, remember that God has a plan and can use even unexpected people and places. Rest in his faithfulness and obey him with confidence.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that Israel will take up a mocking song, or song of victory, against the king of Babylon. The verse of the word "proverb" is removed because that word does not appear in the verse. The "golden city" is Babylon, famous for its wealth. The word "oppressor" in the verse is the one who forces tribute from others, a tyrant.

Isaiah speaks of a future day when God will give rest to his people after the captivity. The verses before this one promise that God will have compassion on Israel. He addresses a people who would suffer oppression, to give them hope that no empire lasts forever.

For today: if you feel oppressed or see injustice, trust that God has the last word. Rest in Him and avoid bitterness, waiting for his justice.
exp.35:19:
Here the spokesman of the king of Assyria asks mockingly whether any god of other nations managed to save his people from the power of Assyria. By this he means that the Lord will not be able to rescue Jerusalem either. The words "delivered" and "out of my hand" mean rescued or saved from someone's power. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high-ranking officer sent by King Sennacherib. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem, in the days of King Hezekiah. He wants to frighten the people into surrendering and not trusting in God. He compares the Lord with the gods of conquered nations, as if he were just one more of them. Hezekiah's officials keep silent, as the king had ordered, and afterward they report everything to him with their clothes torn, a sign of distress.

Today too there are voices that tell us God will not be able to help us, comparing our situation with cases that seem hopeless. Instead of arguing with fear, we can do as Hezekiah did: bring the problem to God in prayer and trust that He is different from everything else.
exp.19:5:
He says that when Egypt falls, the people of this coast will say, "Look what has become of our hope." They had run to Egypt asking for help to be delivered from Assyria, and now they ask themselves, "And how shall we escape?" The word for "isle" can refer to the coast or region of the Mediterranean, and the phrase about fleeing for help means that they had gone looking for refuge.

God speaks through Isaiah. Shortly before, Isaiah had walked naked and barefoot as a sign that Egypt and Ethiopia would be led away captive by Assyria. The peoples of the coast, perhaps including Judah, were trusting in that alliance. Scholars debate exactly who the inhabitant of this isle is, but the message is clear: that hope was false.

For today: check where and in whom you place your security. Money, connections, or plans can fail. Pray and trust God first, and use the rest wisely, without making it your refuge.
exp.39:3:
This verse describes a road being prepared for the Lord. The valleys are raised up, the mountains and hills are brought low, the crooked is made straight, and the rough places become level. It is the language of preparing a real road for a king to pass.

God comforts Jerusalem: her punishment has been completed and her sin has been forgiven. A voice in the wilderness calls for a way to be opened for Jehovah. Many understand this as speaking of the return from exile in Babylon. The Gospels apply this voice to John the Baptist, who was preparing people for Jesus.

For today: preparing the way for God means removing what gets in the way in the heart, such as pride, bitterness, or hidden sins. Today you can speak to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and set straight one specific thing, such as making peace with someone.
exp.31:6:
This verse says that the greedy man (the stingy or wicked person who thinks only of himself) misuses his power. He plans how to deceive the simple, that is, plain and naive people, with clever words. He also uses the courts, or tribunals, to attack the poor and take away what they have.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, in Judah. He is describing the righteous kingdom that will come, and by contrast he shows how fools and wicked people behave. Just before this, he says that the stingy man will no longer be called generous: his actions reveal his heart. Afterward, the text presents the noble person, who plans to do good.

For today: review how you use your words and your influence. May they never be used to take advantage of someone who has less than you. Use what you know and what you have to help with honesty.
exp.56:19:
This verse compares the wicked to the sea during a storm. Its waves never settle, and all they bring up onto the shore is mud and filth, that is, muck and dirt. "Stormy sea" would be rendered here as a sea stirred up by a storm, and the idea of "resting" is simply being at peace and still.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised to heal, guide, and comfort his people, offering peace to both those who are far off and those who are near. Then he warns that whoever lives in rebellion and rejects God does not have that peace. Some understand "the wicked" as those who persist in turning away from God, rather than those who repent.

For today: if your heart is troubled by guilt, pride, or worry, do not keep struggling alone. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge what you have done wrong, and receive his forgiveness and his peace.
exp.39:28:
This verse says that God gives strength to the one who is worn out, and that to the one who has no strength left at all, he increases what little remains. "Strength" here means power or courage, and "increases" means he makes it grow greatly. It speaks not only of bodily tiredness, but of the person who feels they can go on no longer.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, comforting the people of Israel, who were discouraged and believed that God no longer saw their situation. That is why, just before, he reminds them that the LORD is eternal, the creator of all things, who never grows weary and whose wisdom is immense. Many scholars think he is addressing the Israelites in exile, although the exact time is debated.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not pretend that you are fine. Tell God honestly that you are tired, and wait on Him with confidence, asking him for help to take the next step.
exp.61:2:
Verse 3 says that Zion, that is, God's people in Jerusalem, will be like a beautiful crown and a royal ornament. What matters is where it is: not on its own head, but in the hand of the LORD. A royal diadem is a crown or royal band. Glory speaks of beauty and honor.

The speaker seems to be the prophet Isaiah, although some think it is the Messiah. He says he will not keep silent for Jerusalem. The people were discouraged, with the city in ruins. God promises to restore it, give it a new name, and show his righteousness to the nations.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements or on what others think of you. God holds you in his hand and rejoices over you. Today, when you feel discouraged, remember that you belong to him and that he cares for you.
exp.7:1:
Isaiah says that he gathered two men as trustworthy witnesses: Uriah, who was a priest, and Zechariah, son of Jeberechiah. The word that is sometimes rendered as "gathered" means to call together or assemble. A faithful witness was someone whose word could be believed whenever it was challenged.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, following God's command to write a message on a large scroll. That message announced that Syria and Israel would soon be defeated by Assyria. By calling witnesses, Isaiah made it on record that he had said this before it happened. That way, when it came to pass, no one could claim he had made it up afterward. Scholars are not certain about the exact identity of these two men.

God is not afraid of being checked. If something in your life today depends on your word, make sure it is true and reliable, and do not fear that someone will examine it.
exp.50:0:
God calls on those who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord to listen. He asks them to look back to the rock from which they were cut, like a quarry, and to the pit from which they were dug, that is, to their humble origin.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a weary people, probably in a time of exile or discouragement. The verses that follow make clear that this rock is Abraham and Sarah: God called one man, blessed him, and multiplied him. If God made a people out of so little, he can keep his promise to comfort Zion.

For today: when you feel small or without strength, remember where God took you from and how faithful he has been before. That remembrance strengthens your confidence that he can do something new with you.
exp.8:7:
It says that the Lord sent a message to Jacob, that is, to his people Israel, and that this message fell upon them. "Jacob" and "Israel" name the same people here. The message "fell" can be understood as arriving with weight and without being possible to ignore; some read it as a message of judgment that would be fulfilled.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Just before, he announced the promise of a child who would bring peace and everlasting justice. Now the tone changes: the northern kingdom, Israel, with Ephraim and Samaria, responded with pride, saying they would rebuild better what had been destroyed, without turning back to God. The word arrived, but they did not take it seriously.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, let us not let it pass by with pride or with confidence in our own strength. Let us listen with humility and allow it to correct us in time.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the nets of the Egyptian fishermen will be broken, and that those who keep ponds for raising fish will be filled with sorrow. The phrase "fish ponds" refers to pools or tanks where live fish were kept. In some versions, the second part is understood differently: it speaks of the workers or laborers, who are left dejected. There are differences of translation in the Hebrew text.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God, in a prophecy against Egypt. He announces that the Nile, from which the whole country lived, would dry up. Without the river there is no fishing, no flax, and no woven cloth. This shows that God can take away what Egypt believed was secure. The wise men of Pharaoh would not be able to prevent it.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in work, money, or plans. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else breaks.
exp.27:16:
God says he will measure judgment and righteousness with a cord and a level, as a builder does to see whether a wall is straight. Then the hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters will flood the hiding place. "Refuge" is the meaning of the word rendered as "refuge of lies," and a "hiding place" is a place to hide.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. The leaders of Judah felt secure and said they had made a covenant with death, meaning that nothing would happen to them. They trusted in deceptions and false alliances. God answers them that he has placed in Zion a firm stone, and that his own rod of justice will reveal what is crooked.

For today: examine what you are leaning on. If your security rests on excuses, appearances, or lies, it will not withstand the storm. Seek the truth and trust in God, who is a firm foundation.
exp.44:17:
He says that the Lord is the Creator of the heavens and of the earth. He formed the earth, made it, and "established" it, that is, He set it in order and firmly in place. He did not create it "in vain," meaning without purpose or empty, but so that it would be inhabited. And he concludes by affirming that there is no other God besides Him.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier He mocked those who make idols, who will be put to shame, and He promised salvation to Israel. Here He presents himself as the only true God, who does not speak in secret or deceive those who seek Him, unlike the idols that cannot save.

For today: your life is not an accident. The same God who made the world with purpose also has a purpose for you. Seek Him, and not things that cannot save.
exp.29:28:
It says that God's people will have a song of joy, like the song of the night when the Passover was celebrated. They will also have gladness of heart, like that of someone who goes up to the mountain of the Lord with the sound of the pipe. The phrase "the mighty One of Israel" is a title for God, who is their rock and their refuge.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was trusting in an alliance with Egypt against Assyria. Earlier, the prophet describes God's judgment against the nations. Here there is a contrast: while Assyria would be broken, those who are faithful to God would sing. Some think the Passover night recalls the liberation from Egypt.

For today: when you face fear or pressure, remember that God has already rescued you before. Be encouraged to sing or to pray with gratitude, trusting that He is your strength.
exp.18:16:
This verse says that Judah, the land of God's people, will cause fear in Egypt. Every Egyptian who remembers it will be left frightened, that is, they will be astonished. The reason is the counsel of God, which here means his plan or decision, and which he himself determined against Egypt.

Isaiah prophesies about Egypt, which was a great power. Earlier, the text says that no leader or ordinary person will be able to save it, because God will act with his mighty hand. Some understand that Judah becomes a cause for dread because Egypt recognizes that the God of Judah is the one who rules. Interpreters do not agree on how or when this was fulfilled. What follows shows that God's judgment also opens the door for Egypt to come to know him.

For today: let us not trust in power, money, or human leaders. God's plans come to pass, and his judgment often seeks to restore. Trust in him.
exp.29:26:
It says that God draws near from far away, like a judge coming to act. The reference to his anger against evil comes through in the phrase about his face burning with it. His weight is hard to bear, and his lips and tongue, like a consuming fire, speak words of judgment that cannot be stopped.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was looking for help in Egypt instead of trusting God. The passage announces judgment on the nations, probably Assyria according to many interpreters, and at the same time comfort for God's people. The same God who punishes pride also heals his people's brokenness.

For today: do not take God's holiness lightly, but do not forget his care. When you face an unjust situation or feel wounded, trust that God sees, judges with justice, and knows how to heal. Go to him instead of looking for easy ways out.
exp.54:2:
God invites his people to come near and listen closely. "Incline your ear" means paying attention with humility. He promises that whoever listens "shall live," meaning they will have true life. He also promises an everlasting covenant, a bond that does not end, based on "the sure mercies of David," that is, the faithful love he promised to David.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, probably to a people in exile or weary and thirsty. He offers freely what money and effort cannot provide. The verses that follow speak of one who will be a witness and a leader for the nations. Many Christians see here a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David; others first emphasize the promise to Israel.

For today: set aside a moment each day to listen to God, reading his Word calmly. Trust that his love sustains you, even though you have not earned it.
exp.63:7:
Here the people acknowledge that God is their Father and their Creator. They use the image of the potter: they are the clay, and God is the one who formed them with his hands. The verse's word "clay" refers to the soft material the potter shapes. Being "the work of his hand" means that they belong to him and that he made them.

The one speaking is the prophet, on behalf of the people of Israel. After confessing their sin and acknowledging that they deserve nothing, they ask for mercy. It is a prayer of repentance, probably reflecting on the ruin of Jerusalem and its cities, as the following verses show. Scholars debate the exact date, but the tone is one of humility.

For today: when you feel weak or have failed, do not run away from God. Come to him as a child comes to a father, and surrender yourself again into his hands. He can keep shaping your life with patience and love.
exp.41:0:
God presents his servant and says that he will uphold him. He calls him "my chosen one," in whom he delights, that is, in whom he finds great pleasure. He says that he has put his Spirit upon him, and that he will bring forth judgment to the nations, or in other words, bring justice to the nations.

God himself is speaking here, within the Servant Songs in Isaiah. In the original setting, the people were discouraged and needed hope. Jews have seen Israel in this passage, and others have seen a special individual. Christians, following Matthew 12:18-21, see Jesus here, whose justice is gentle: he does not break the bruised reed or snuff out the smoldering wick.

For today: if God works with tenderness and firmness, we can draw near to him even when we are weak or weary. And in how we treat others, let us seek justice without crushing those who are already broken.
exp.18:20:
It says that Egypt, which before did not know the God of Israel, will truly come to know him "in that day." The Egyptians will offer him sacrifice (an animal) and offering (a gift of grain or food). They will also make vows, that is, solemn promises to God, and keep them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Earlier he announced judgment on Egypt, but here he promises something surprising: Egypt, a powerful nation and at times an enemy of Israel, will also cry out to God and be healed. Some see here a future fulfillment, others see a foretaste of the gospel reaching all nations. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: no one is too far away for God to reach. Pray for people or peoples who seem distant from God, and if you made God a promise, keep it with sincerity.
exp.20:7:
The watchman cries out loudly, like a lion, and tells the Lord that he has stood at his post of watch all day and all night, without moving. The watchtower is a high tower from which people kept watch. The word "ward" refers to the post or shift of watching.

God had asked the prophet to set a watchman to report what he saw. Here the watchman answers that he has been faithful and steady, waiting. Shortly afterward he announces the fall of Babylon. Some scholars think the watchman is Isaiah himself; others think he is a symbolic figure. The original text is difficult and is translated in several ways.

For today: faith is sometimes waiting with steadiness. Stay alert and faithful in prayer and in your duty, even when God's answer is slow, trusting that He speaks in his own time.
exp.8:17:
It says that the wickedness of the people is like a fire. It starts by burning what is small, the briers and thorns, but then it catches in the thickest part of the forest, and everything ends up rising like a column of smoke. The thickets of the forest are a dense tangle of bushes, and the phrase "shall kindle" means that the fire will be set alight. The image shows how evil grows and destroys.

Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel (Ephraim). The leaders deceived, the people followed them, and no one was spared from the corruption. Isaiah explains that this wickedness was already consuming the nation from within, and the verses that follow describe violence between brothers. Some scholars also see here a reference to the internal conflicts of that time.

For today: do not minimize the "small" sins, such as lying or resentment, because they can grow out of control. Today, confess to God something you tend to tolerate, and ask him for help to put it out in time.
exp.55:4:
God promises faithful eunuchs a place in his house and within his walls, that is, a sense of belonging among his people. He gives them a name better than that of sons and daughters, an everlasting name that will never be erased.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Eunuchs and foreigners felt excluded, and the law placed restrictions on them (for example, Deuteronomy 23:1). Moreover, a eunuch had no children to carry on his name. God answers that whoever keeps his Sabbaths, chooses what pleases him, and holds fast to his covenant is welcome and remembered forever.

If you ever feel set aside, or believe you lack something needed to be valued before God, remember that he looks at the faith and obedience of the heart. Draw near without fear, and welcome with the same warmth those who feel left outside.
exp.30:8:
It says that Assyria, the mighty empire, will lose its strength through fear. Its stronghold (its rock or place of refuge) will pass away in terror, and its leaders will be struck with dread at the banner (the sign of war). The Lord declares all this, the one whose fire and furnace are in Zion and Jerusalem, that is, his presence that judges and purifies.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking military help in Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. The prophet promises them that God himself will defend Jerusalem and defeat Assyria, without any need for human armies. Some understand the fire and the furnace as protection, and others as judgment; perhaps it includes both.

Today we can remember that no power or problem is greater than God. When you feel fear, or the temptation to rely only on human resources, pray and trust first in the One who cares for his people.
exp.48:10:
It says that God will turn his mountains into a road, meaning that the greatest obstacles will become open paths. "Turn" here means "I will make" or "I will change them into." The "highways" are roads prepared for travel, and "exalted" means they will be raised up and made firm, ready for the passage of his people.

God speaks, addressing his Servant and, through him, Israel, who was held captive in Babylon. He promises to free the prisoners, care for them like a shepherd on the way, and bring them back from distant places. Interpreters see here the return from exile and, for many Christians, also a shadow of the work of Christ.

For today: when you face a problem that looks like a mountain, remember that God can open a way where you see only obstacles. Trust his guidance, take the next step in faith, and ask him to lead you with the tenderness of a shepherd.
exp.37:5:
It says that God promises to save King Hezekiah and Jerusalem from the power of the king of Assyria. "Deliver" means to rescue or bring out of danger, and "defend" means to protect and watch over.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah was very sick, had prayed in tears, and God granted him fifteen more years of life. In addition to that, God renews the promise to defend the city, which was threatened by Assyria. God answers his prayer with personal help and also for his people.

For today: when you face an illness or a threat that overwhelms you, pray sincerely, even with tears. God hears and cares for you. You can trust in his protection, even though he does not always respond in the same way.
exp.48:25:
God promises that those who oppressed his people will suffer the consequences of their own violence. The images are very strong: they will eat their own flesh and be drunk with their own blood as though it were sweet wine. Many understand this as figurative language of judgment, in which the oppressors destroy one another. The goal is that all flesh, that is, all of humanity, will know that the Lord is the Savior, the Redeemer, and the mighty One of Jacob.

The Lord speaks to Israel in exile, a people who felt abandoned and trapped by a greater power. God answers that he himself will defend their cause and rescue his children, even though the captor may seem invincible.

For today: when you feel crushed by an injustice or by a situation stronger than you, do not take revenge. Entrust your cause to God, who sees, defends, and redeems. Rest in the fact that he is faithful to his own.
exp.22:3:
It says that Sidon, the great city by the sea, should be ashamed. The sea itself, called "the strength of the sea," speaks like a woman who never had children: she has not been in labor, has not raised young men, and has not brought up young women. It is a picture of total loss: the city is left empty, without people or a future.

It is part of Isaiah's prophecy against Tyre, the Phoenician city known for sea trade. Sidon, its neighbor, appears here alongside it. Interpreters explain in various ways who is speaking and what the image means, but all agree on the message: the commercial power of these cities would fall, and even the sea would seem to mourn the ruin of its children.

For today: the riches, success and security we build can disappear. It is wise to place our trust in God, who does not change, and not in what seems strong today.
exp.9:3:
He says that, without God's help, the unjust will have no salvation: some will bow down or give up among the prisoners, and others will fall dead. "Without me" can be understood as "without God" or "outside of me"; some read it as "there is nothing left for them but". Even so, God's anger has not calmed down: his hand remains stretched out, that is, ready to keep judging. "Fury" is righteous anger.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just accused the leaders of Judah and Israel of making unjust laws, taking away the rights of the poor, and robbing widows and orphans. He warns that a disaster will come from far away, and the following text mentions Assyria as the instrument of judgment.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the weak. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are just and generous toward those who have less power, and act on their behalf with honesty and mercy.
exp.43:14:
He says that a man uses the same tree for two very different things. He burns one part to warm himself and to bake his bread. With another part he makes a god and kneels before it. The words "red dye" and "bake" describe the wood's color and the act of baking, so the quoted terms are removed from the verse above; the verse simply tells the reader that the wood is used both for heat and for the bread.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people tempted by the idolatry of the neighboring nations. With irony, the prophet shows how absurd it is to worship something a person makes with his own hands. The same piece of wood serves for the fire and for the "god." This contrasts with the living God, who created the trees and human beings.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can give God's place to things we ourselves make or obtain: money, success, image. Ask yourself: what do I expect will save me or give me security? Hand that over to God and trust in him.
exp.53:10:
God speaks to a city that is suffering and calls it "poor thing": she is worn out, battered as if by a storm, and without anyone to comfort her. But he promises to rebuild her with very precious stones. A "carbuncle" was a bright red gemstone, and the "sapphires" were blue stones; scholars debate exactly which minerals are meant. The image speaks of a beauty and a firmness that she did not have.

The Lord is speaking to Jerusalem, the people of Israel, after the pain of exile. He has just promised that his anger has ended, just as he swore there would be no other flood, and that his mercy will not move even if the mountains tremble. The precious stones are poetic language for restoration, not necessarily a literal description.

For today: if you are exhausted from some storm, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell God how you feel and trust that he can lift up again what has fallen, on a firm foundation that is his faithfulness.
exp.9:0:
It says God issues a strong warning, a "woe," against those who make unjust laws. It is not only personal wickedness: it is injustice turned into law.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's message to the people of Judah in the eighth century BC. The verses that follow explain the reason: justice was being denied to the poor, the widows, and the orphans. God asks them what they will do on the day He calls them to account, when destruction comes from afar.

For today: if you have any authority, whether at home, at work, in the church, or in the community, check whether your rules and decisions protect the most vulnerable. And if you do not have such authority, you can still stand up for those who have no voice.
exp.36:16:
What it says: King Hezekiah asks God to listen and to look carefully. He uses human images: bending down to hear and opening the eyes, like someone who draws near to pay full attention. He asks God to hear the words of Sennacherib, who sent messengers to insult the living God. To blaspheme means to speak with contempt against God.

Context: Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks while the Assyrian army surrounds Jerusalem. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had sent a letter mocking Judah's trust in God. Hezekiah took the letter to the temple, laid it before God, and prayed. He did not ask for help out of pride, but because the honor of God's name was at stake.

For today: When a threat or a mockery overwhelms you, do not carry it alone. Present it to God honestly, as Hezekiah did with his letter. Tell him in detail what you are facing, and trust that he sees and hears.
exp.51:5:
God says that his people will come to know his name, that is, to truly know him. This will happen "in that day," when God himself, the one who now speaks through the prophet, makes his presence known. "Here I am, present" means "I am here, I have arrived." Some old words: "Assyria" is the name the verse gives for the nation that held the people captive, and the phrase about oppressing them without cause means that it held them down unjustly.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people who are humbled and held captive, whose name was blasphemed by the nations. God shows that he is not indifferent to that situation. The verses that follow announce to the messenger who proclaims: "Your God reigns." Christians often see here a promise that is fully fulfilled in Christ, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

When you feel forgotten or are in the middle of a trial, remember that God is not far away. His promise is to be present, and knowing him better is the greatest comfort.
exp.63:11:
Here the people ask God whether he will remain still and silent in the face of so much suffering. The words "will you hold back" and "stay silent" carry the same sense as the verse: to refrain from acting, to keep quiet. The phrase "afflict us very sore" means to bring great hardship upon us, to a greatly excessive degree. It is an honest cry: "How long, Lord? Will you do nothing?"

The prophet speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of lament. The cities are deserted and the temple was burned, something many understand as the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. Some think Isaiah looks ahead to that future in advance; others think he speaks from the perspective of the exile. Scholars explain this in different ways. The people acknowledge their sin, yet still ask for mercy.

For today: when you feel that God is silent in the midst of your pain, do not hide your complaint. Bring it to him honestly, as this people did, and trust that God hears and is compassionate, even when his answer is slow in coming.
exp.6:12:
Isaiah speaks to the royal family of Judah. He tells them that they already wear out the people, and now they also wear out God.

King Ahaz was afraid of his enemies. God offered him a sign to strengthen his faith, but Ahaz answered with words that sounded pious, saying he would not put the Lord to the test. In reality, he had already decided to trust in political alliances and not in God. That is why Isaiah rebukes him. Then comes the sign of Immanuel, which means God with us. Scholars understand it in several ways, and Christians see it fulfilled in Christ.

Today: be careful with excuses that sound spiritual but hide distrust. When God invites us to trust Him, let us respond with sincere faith and obedience.
exp.39:22:
He says that God brings the mighty to nothing, that is, the princes and people of great authority. He also makes the judges or rulers of the earth like something empty, meaning without lasting worth.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who felt small and discouraged before the empires of their time. To comfort them, he reminds them who God is: the Creator who is above the whole earth, before whom the inhabitants are like grasshoppers. Before Him, no king has the final word.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated or dazzled by human power, whether political, economic, or social. Governments and great figures pass away, but God endures. Trust in Him, pray for those who govern, and have peace, because your life is in the hands of the Lord.
exp.57:2:
Here the people complain to God: they say they fasted and humbled themselves, but God did not pay attention to them. God answers that, on the very day of their fast, they do whatever suits them and demand more work from their workers. "Labors" here means work or toil, and the word for it is the same one used in the verse ("labours"). The phrase that is no longer in the verse is simply rendered as "you pretended not to notice" or "you turned a blind eye."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He orders him to denounce the sin of his people, who appear to seek God every day but live in injustice. Their religion was a matter of appearances: they fasted, but did not change the way they treated others. The verses that follow show quarreling and mistreatment in the midst of the fast.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious acts if the heart remains selfish. Before you pray, fast, or serve, ask yourself whether you are treating with justice and kindness those who depend on you or live with you.
exp.4:26:
The army that God is going to bring will be strong and tireless. None of its soldiers will grow weary or stumble. They will not doze off or fall into drowsiness. Their belts will be fastened tight at the waist, and the straps of their sandals will not break.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, carrying God's message. He has just described Israel as a vineyard that yielded bitter grapes, despite God's care, because of its injustice and violence. God announces that he will use a distant nation as an instrument of judgment. The text does not say here which nation it is; many think of Assyria, and that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God takes justice seriously, but his correction seeks to bring us back to himself. Today you can ask him to show you something you need to set right, and to obey him without delay.
exp.64:21:
It says that God's people will no longer live under the injustice of working so that others end up with everything. No one will build a house for a stranger to live in, or plant so that someone else eats. The word "dwell" means to live in a place, and the idea of "long enjoy" is that they will keep for a long time what their hands have made. Their lives will be long, like the days of a tree.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises to his faithful people "new heavens and a new earth" (65:17). Many see here a future fulfillment; others think it also describes a restoration after the exile. Christians often see it as a hope that Christ will bring to completion.

For today: God sees honest work and does not forget it. You can work faithfully even when you do not yet see fruit, and you can also help others receive a fair reward for their effort.
exp.61:11:
It says God will give his people new names: "Holy People" and "Redeemed of the Lord." Holy means set apart for God. The redeemed are those who have been bought back by paying a price. Jerusalem will be called "Sought Out," meaning desired and cared for, and "A City Not Forsaken," meaning never abandoned again.

The prophet Isaiah announces a promise of restoration for Israel, probably addressed to a people who were suffering after the exile. They are invited to prepare the way, because the Savior is coming with his reward. Many Christians also see here an anticipation of Christ and his Church, although the text speaks first of Israel.

Today, you can remember that your identity does not depend on your failures or on what others say about you. If you trust God, he sees you as someone redeemed, set apart, and loved. Today you can live with that security.
exp.9:2:
God asks three questions of those who oppressed the poor. The "day of visitation" means the moment when God comes to call people to account. "Destruction" is total ruin, and it would come "from afar." "Flee for help" means seeking refuge. They are asked: what will you do, where will you run for help, and where will you leave your riches or your honor when that day arrives?

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just condemned the rulers who made unjust laws to strip the poor, the widows, and the orphans of their rights. What follows shows that the punishment would come through Assyria, a nation God would use as an instrument of judgment.

For today: God takes notice of how we treat the weak. Today you can ask yourself whether, at work, in your family, or in your community, you defend the vulnerable or take advantage of them, and correct whatever needs correcting before it is too late.
exp.37:13:
This verse says that the king suffered so much that his cries sounded like the cries of birds: the shriek of the crane, the sad song of the swallow, and the coo of the dove. He lifted his eyes to heaven and cried out, "I am oppressed; undertake for me," that is, "I am oppressed and feel crushed." He ends by asking, "Undertake for me," meaning, "Be my support and my strength."

Ezekiah, king of Judah, speaks in a writing of his own after he fell gravely ill. Isaiah had told him he would die, and he felt his life being cut off like cloth that the weaver pulls from the loom. Here he has no clear words, only groaning, and yet he still looks toward God.

For today: when pain leaves you without words, you do not have to speak beautifully to pray. You can bring God your sighs, your weariness, and your fear, and simply ask him, "Hold me up." He hears even the groans.
exp.40:19:
This verse says that God will do all these wonders so that the people may see, know, pay attention, and understand that it was the hand of the Lord who did it. The word translated "consider" here means to take notice or pay attention. The phrase "created it" means that God made it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were tired and afraid, as if in a desert. God promises to turn dry places into rivers, springs, and forests. Then, in the verses that follow, He challenges the idols to show whether they can do anything similar. Many understand this as a promise of comfort and restoration.

For today: when God helps you in a dry or difficult time, do not credit it only to luck or to your own effort. Stop, recognize His hand, and give thanks to Him out loud. In this way your gratitude will also become a witness to others.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that the government of the promised child will grow and that his peace will never end. He will reign on the throne of David, and he will make it firm with judgment, that is, with righteous decisions, and with justice. This holds from now on and forever. The passage ends by affirming that God himself will accomplish it through his zeal, his burning and determined love for his people.

Isaiah speaks to a people threatened by war and darkness, in the time of the divided kingdom. Earlier he had announced the birth of a child with divine titles. Then the text returns to the judgment on Israel for its pride. Christians see Jesus here, the son of David, although Israel first heard it as a promise of a just king.

For today: when the world seems unstable, trust that God will do what he has promised. Ask him for his peace and seek to live with justice in your home and your work.
exp.29:25:
He says that when God heals his people, there will be an extraordinary light: the moon will shine like the sun, and the sun will be seven times stronger. The word for "binds up" means to join back what is broken, and the idea of a "breach" is a fracture, like a broken bone. A "wound" is an open sore. God promises to repair his people's damage.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah, which was trusting in alliances with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Before this verse, the prophet announces judgment, "the great slaughter," and also blessing: water, food, and rest. Many understand the light as poetic language for complete restoration; others see it as a promise for the final future. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: if you are wounded by your mistakes or by pain, do not hide the wound. Bring it to God with humility, because he knows how to heal what seems impossible to repair.
exp.55:5:
This verse says that foreigners who draw near to God to serve him, who love his name and want to be his servants, are also welcome. They are asked to keep the Sabbath without defiling it, that is, without treating it as an ordinary day, and to hold firmly to God's covenant.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. At that time, Israel's law limited the participation of eunuchs and foreigners in certain aspects of worship. Here God declares that his house will be open to them, and that what matters most is loving and obeying him, not the person's origin or condition.

For today: if God receives with joy those who come to him with sincere love, we too should welcome into the church those who arrive from other countries, cultures or backgrounds. You might greet someone new today and offer them a place beside you.
exp.36:4:
The servants of King Hezekiah came to the prophet Isaiah. They went to bring him a message from the king and to ask him to pray.

The king of Assyria had surrounded Judah, and his spokesman mocked the God of Israel. Hezekiah, distressed, did not rely on his own army. He sent his servants to the prophet to seek the word of God and to ask for prayer for the people who remained. Isaiah answered with comfort: "Do not be afraid."

When fear grips us, we do not have to carry it alone. We can pray, and we can also seek out someone of mature faith who will pray with us and remind us of God's promises.
exp.20:6:
He says the watchman sees chariots coming: one with a pair of horsemen, another drawn by donkeys, and another by camels. The word "horsemen" in the verse above refers to men on horseback. On seeing this, he does not stay calm but begins to look much more closely, like someone who knows something important is approaching.

Isaiah recounts a vision about the fall of Babylon. God commands that a watchman be posted to report what he sees, while the leaders of Babylon eat and drink, confident. The chariots with donkeys and camels probably point to an allied army arriving, although interpreters debate the detail. The message: "Babylon is fallen, is fallen."

Today we can learn to be alert and to pray with patience, without letting ourselves be lulled to sleep by comfort. God works even when we do not see it right away. Set aside a moment each day to listen to God attentively, trusting that He is greater than any power in the world.
exp.23:10:
It speaks of cries and laments in the public squares because there is no more wine, which was a sign of celebration. All joy grew dark, that is, it went out like the coming of night, and gladness was driven away, that is, cast out of the land.

Isaiah, a prophet of God, speaks within a section (chapters 24 to 27) that describes a judgment upon the whole earth. Scholars debate which city is meant by the "city of confusion": some think of a particular city, and others of a symbol of humanity living without God. The message is that when the covenant with God is broken, the joys that do not rest on him come to an end.

Today we can ask ourselves what our joy is based on. Pleasures pass away, but God does not. Let us seek in him a gladness that does not depend on circumstances.
exp.30:6:
This verse says that when God acts to save his people, people will throw away the silver and gold idols they made. "Cast away" means to fling far off, with rejection. "Sinful hands" shows that making idols was itself a sin.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Judah was looking for help in Egypt against the threat of Assyria, instead of trusting the Lord. Before this verse, God promises to protect Jerusalem like a bird that shelters its young, and he calls the people to return to him. Afterward, he announces the fall of Assyria. When God's deliverance is seen, the idols will be exposed as worthless.

For today: ask yourself where you place your security, such as money, success, or your own plans, and hand it over to God with confidence.
exp.22:11:
He says that God announces to Sidon, the Phoenician city that was proud and joyful, that its feasting is over. He calls it "virgin" because it thought itself untouched and secure, but now it is "oppressed." Even if it tries to flee to Chittim (probably Cyprus, though some think of other lands of the Mediterranean), it will find no rest there either. "Rest" means peace and repose.

Isaiah prophesies in the name of the LORD against Tyre and Sidon, cities made rich by sea trade. The Lord is the one who "stretched out his hand over the sea" and weakens its power. Scholars debate which exact historical event the prophet has in mind, but the message is clear: no power stands above God.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or our own plans, because they can fall. Let us rest in God, for only in him is there a rest that is not lost.
exp.46:5:
God says he was angry with his people, Israel, and allowed them to be treated as if they had no value. ("I have polluted mine inheritance" means he let his own people be humiliated.) He handed them over into the hands of Babylon. But Babylon showed no mercy: even the elderly were laden with a very heavy burden.

God himself speaks, the Redeemer of Israel, addressing Babylon, called the daughter of the Chaldeans. God used her to discipline his people, but she went too far in cruelty and believed herself unconquerable. For this reason God now announces her fall.

For today: God can correct his own, but he does not approve of abuse by those who hold power. If you have authority over others today, treat them with mercy, especially the weakest, and remember that one day you will give an account to God.
exp.64:20:
It says that God's people will build houses and live in them, and will plant vineyards and enjoy their grapes. Here "dwell" in the verse means "live" or "inhabit." It is a simple picture of peace, stability, and rest from labor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises a new heavens and a new earth, where Jerusalem will be a source of joy and there will be no more weeping. The verses that follow show the contrast: in the past others took what the people built, but now no one will take away the fruit of their labor. Some see here a future fulfillment; others see a promise that already began with the return from exile. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God cares about everyday life, such as home and work. You can trust that He watches over your effort, and in the meantime work with honesty and gratitude, waiting for His promise.
exp.35:7:
The Rabshakeh, a messenger sent by the king of Assyria, mocks Jerusalem with sarcasm. Offering to hand over pledges here means making a bet or a deal, and his polite-sounding request is really a taunt. He offers two thousand horses, but he doubts that Judah has enough riders to mount them. The riders are the horsemen.

The Rabshakeh speaks for King Sennacherib around the year 701 BC. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem and wants to discourage Hezekiah and the people so that they will surrender. He stresses that Judah is militarily weak. Although he claims to speak on behalf of the LORD, his words are propaganda, and the biblical account portrays him as a proud man who mocks God.

Today, voices that belittle us often point out our weaknesses so that we will stop trusting God. We can listen calmly, acknowledge our limitations, and still place our trust in God, not in the taunts or in our own strength.
exp.22:10:
He stretched out his hand over the sea and shook the kingdoms. He also says that the Lord has given a command against Canaan, which here refers to Phoenicia, the region of trading cities such as Tyre and Sidon, that its strongholds be destroyed. The sea is the Mediterranean, from which its wealth came.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter is a message against Tyre, a powerful city made rich by sea trade. The verse before explains the reason: God wants to humble the pride of all human glory. Neither the sea nor riches protect someone who thinks they are untouchable.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, success or reputation. All of that can totter, but God does not. Trust Him first and use what you have with humility.
exp.21:8:
It says that the people of Jerusalem saw that the walls of the city of David had many cracks or breaches, and that there were more and more of them. So they gathered the water of the lower pool (the pool, or reservoir, is the one named in the verse) to have water during an attack.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, sent by God. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy, and the people made practical preparations: repairing walls, storing water, and checking their weapons. The problem, according to the next verse, is that they did not look to God, who had made and formed that city. Scholars debate the exact moment this refers to, but the central message is clear.

It is good to plan and work wisely, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before solving a problem, let us seek God in prayer and place our trust in Him.
exp.49:6:
He says that the Lord God is the one who helps the servant, and so he does not feel humiliated. "I have set my face like flint" means that he stayed firm and determined, like a very hard stone. "Ashamed" means defeated or left in disgrace. He trusts that God will not leave him that way.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, in the third Servant Song in Isaiah. He is obedient, though he suffers blows, mockery, and spitting. Many Christians see here a prophecy of Jesus, who also set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Others read it first as the voice of the prophet himself, and there are also those who see the faithful people. It can be understood in several ways.

For today: when obeying God brings you criticism or mockery, do not depend on the approval of people. Pray asking God for help, and keep going with firmness and gentleness, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.32:9:
Here the text says that God himself steps in. After describing a ruined land, the LORD announces that he will now act. He repeats "now" three times to mark that the moment has come. The words "exalted" and "lifted up" mean that God will be raised high and his greatness will be recognized by all.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the text shows a devastated land: empty roads, broken treaties, and fertile places like Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel withered away. This is often connected to the Assyrian threat during the time of Judah, although scholars debate the details. Then God warns that the plans of the proud will be consumed like straw in the fire.

When everything seems lost and no one else can help, God is not absent. You can hand him your difficult situation and trust that he will act in his own time and in his own way.
exp.58:5:
What it says: The verse compares the actions of wicked people to spider webs. A spider's web is fragile and cannot be made into clothing; it does not warm or cover anyone. In the same way, what these people do gives them no benefit and does not protect them. Their hands are full of injustice.

Context: Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel and explains why they feel that God is far away. The problem is not that God cannot save, but that the people have filled themselves with lies, violence and injustice (vv. 1-2). The prophet describes real sins and shows them with strong images, such as viper's eggs and spider webs.

For today: What is built on deceit or on abuse does not give true security. Today we can ask ourselves whether our work, our words and our businesses are honest. Doing what is right may cost more, but it is the only thing God blesses and the only thing that truly covers us.
exp.55:8:
This verse is a call addressed to the wild animals, the beasts of the field and of the forest, to come and devour. The phrase that would be "come to" today is simply "come and devour." It is a strong image: a prey is left defenseless, and the predators are invited to eat it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before, God promises to gather Israel and to receive people from all nations into his house of prayer. Here the tone shifts: the people are exposed to danger because their guardians, the leaders, fail them. The verses that follow call them blind watchmen and silent dogs. Interpreters debate who the beasts are: they may be enemy nations, but this cannot be known with certainty.

For today: those who care for others, in the church or in the family, must be attentive, speak the truth, and not seek only their own advantage. Caring for others is a serious responsibility.
exp.19:1:
Here God gives the prophet Isaiah a strange command: to take off the sackcloth from his waist and the sandals from his feet. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance. Isaiah obeyed and went about naked and barefoot. It is likely that "naked" means without his outer cloak, wearing only his undergarment, though some think he went further than that.

The Lord speaks at the time when Assyria conquered the Philistine city of Ashdod. Judah was tempted to trust in Egypt and Ethiopia for protection. God used Isaiah as a living sign: in this way the Egyptians and Ethiopians would be led captive, and they would not be able to save anyone. According to the text that follows, Isaiah did this for three years.

Today, the lesson is to trust in God and not in human powers that seem secure. It also invites us to obey God even when it costs us shame or the opinion of others.
exp.65:7:
God asks questions to show something astonishing. No one has seen or heard of such a thing: that an entire land would be born in a single day, or that a nation would appear all at once. "Zion" is Jerusalem, the people of God. The phrase "was in labor" means she suffered pains to give birth. Yet as soon as the labor began, she already had her children.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is comforting his people after times of judgment and sorrow, and he promises to restore Jerusalem. Interpreters differ: some see a return from exile, others the arrival of God's renewed people, and others a fulfillment that is still future.

For today: when your situation seems slow or impossible, remember that God can work in ways you do not expect. Trust that he finishes what he promises, and in the meantime, pray and wait with hope.
exp.6:24:
It says that the hills which used to be worked with a hoe, that is, a tool for digging and cultivating, will no longer be planted. People will not go there because of the thorns and thistles that will cover them. Those lands will serve as pasture for oxen, and the lesser cattle will tread upon them, trampling them down.

Isaiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, in the days of King Ahaz, when the armies of Syria and Israel were threatening. God announces that the land will be left abandoned because of the judgment that is coming, and many understand this to refer to the invasion of Assyria. It is a warning because of the lack of trust in God.

For today: when everything seems lost, do not place your security only in your own resources. Trust in God and seek his direction before you decide.
exp.0:22:
It says that the leaders of Jerusalem have become corrupt. Those who are "rebellious" are the ones who betray justice, and "companions of thieves" are those who join with unjust people. They love gifts and bribes, and for that reason they do not defend the fatherless or attend to the widow's case, that is, to the most defenseless.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, who denounces Judah and Jerusalem. The city that was once faithful and just is now full of injustice. God does not only condemn: the verses that follow announce that he will remove the impurity, like someone who melts metal to draw off its dross.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot pay or defend themselves. We can ask ourselves whether, at work, in church, or in our community, we give fair attention to everyone, without favoring only the person who benefits us.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that God's people, united and restored, will advance swiftly and forcefully against their former enemy neighbors. "They shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines" suggests a swift attack toward the west. "They shall spoil them of the east together" means they will plunder them. Edom, Moab, and Ammon, nations to the east, will be brought under their control.

Isaiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, around the eighth century B.C., announcing what God will do through the future King from David's line (Isaiah 11:1-10). The verses before this one speak of gathering the scattered people and ending the rivalry between Ephraim and Judah. Many see here a promise of restoration; others understand it symbolically, as God's final victory. Interpretations vary.

For today: God can heal divisions among his people and turn rivalry into unity. Ask him to remove envy from you and to help you work in peace with other believers.
exp.26:2:
He says that God himself takes care of his vineyard, which represents his people. He waters it at every moment and watches over it night and day. The word "visit" here means that no one comes to harm it (in other passages, to "visit" can mean to punish).

The Lord speaks, and the song about the vineyard comes after he announces his judgment against Leviathan, an image of evil powers or oppressors (interpreters apply it to different kingdoms or forces). When Isaiah speaks of the vineyard, he means Israel, to whom God promises protection and constant care, without anger toward her.

For today: if your life is in God's hands, you do not depend only on your own strength. Today, when you face what worries you, pray and give it to him, remembering that he cares for you at every moment.
exp.60:2:
This verse promises that God will change the grief of his people into blessing. Ashes and mourning were signs of deep sorrow; in exchange, God gives beauty, the oil of joy (the oil used at festivals), and a garment of praise in place of a heavy spirit. Those who mourn are the ones who weep. In the end, the people are called trees of righteousness, planted by God to display his glory.

The speaker is a servant anointed by God's Spirit, sent to comfort. Isaiah addresses a people struck by exile and ruin. Jesus read the preceding verses in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied them to himself (Luke 4:16-21).

For today: if you are going through grief, bring your sorrow to God with sincerity. He can comfort you and, in time, cause something new to grow in you. Let others walk with you through that process.
exp.6:2:
God tells Isaiah to go out to meet King Ahaz. He is to take his son Shear-jashub, whose name means "a remnant will return." The meeting will take place at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the Fuller's Field, that is, the place where clothes were washed and worked.

The Lord speaks, and Ahaz is the one addressed. Syria and Israel were threatening Jerusalem, and the heart of the king and of the people trembled like trees in the wind. God sends his prophet with a message of calm. Perhaps Ahaz was checking the city's water supply, though the text does not say so with certainty. The name of Isaiah's son was itself a message of hope.

When fear shakes us, God goes out to seek us with words of calm. Before acting in anxiety, stop and listen to what He says in His Word.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that the people of Jerusalem will no longer see that foreign people who inspired fear, whose language sounded strange and hard to understand. The word "fierce" describes a people that causes terror. The phrases "deeper speech" and "stammering tongue" describe a speech that cannot be understood. The promise is that this threat will disappear.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah when Assyria, a foreign power, was oppressing them and collecting tribute. The officials who counted and weighed the spoil were a symbol of that domination. The prophet announces that God will deliver his people, and that they will see the King in his beauty. Scholars debate whether that King is God himself, or King Hezekiah, or a future hope.

Today, God can give us peace in the face of what intimidates us and what we do not understand. When fear speaks loudly, let us remember the King who cares for his own, and trust that He has the last word.
exp.15:5:
We have heard that the people of Judah have heard talk of the pride of Moab. It is an enormous pride: arrogance, haughtiness, and self-importance, that is, thinking oneself superior to others. "Arrogance" here means excessive pride. But God says that "his lies shall not stand firm," that is, his boasting and false confidence will not hold up.

Isaiah announces a message of judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Shortly before, the prophet speaks of refuge for displaced Moabites and of a future just king on David's throne. After this, the text shows Moab's lament because its cities and its vineyards will be destroyed. Scholars discuss which exact historical moment is meant, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: pride seems strong, but it is fragile. Today we can ask God for humility and rest our security in his truth, not in boasting about what we have or who we are.
exp.44:15:
They will be ashamed and humiliated, all of them, and they will go off together in disgrace, those who make idols. "Desconcertados" means bewildered, and "deshonra pública" means public dishonor. Those who make idols are the people who craft images to worship them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel. In the verses before this one, the nations acknowledge that the God of Israel is the only God, though at times he seems hidden, that is, he is not always seen acting. After verse 16, God promises eternal salvation to his people. The contrast is clear: idols fail, but God saves.

Today we can ask ourselves what takes the place of God in our hearts: money, fame, success, or approval. All of these end up disappointing us. Trusting in God gives us a firm hope that does not put us to shame.
exp.58:4:
They hatch vipers' eggs and weave spiders' webs. The wicked are like someone hatching eggs of venomous snakes and spinning webs. Those who are venomous serpents are deadly, and the one who eats of their eggs dies, and if they are crushed, a viper comes out. In other words, what they produce brings only harm and death.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He explains that God is neither deaf nor powerless; what separates them from Him is their sins: violence, lying, and injustice. Their webs are no use for clothing; in other words, their works cannot cover their guilt.

For today: examine what you produce with your words and decisions. What seems small, like a lie or an injustice, can bring harm. Ask God to cleanse you and guide you to act with truth and justice.
exp.28:5:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, will come to visit the city with very powerful signs: thunder, earthquakes, a great noise, violent winds, storm, and a fire that consumes. "You shall be visited" here is not a gentle visit, but God's arrival to act. The "whirlwind" is a wind that spins with great force.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, which is called Ariel. First God humbles her for her pride and her religion of lip service. Then, however, he intervenes against the enemies who attack her. Interpreters debate whether this "visiting" refers to Jerusalem under judgment or to the defense of the city against its enemies. The following context favors the second.

For today: when you feel surrounded or without strength, remember that God rules over every threat. Trust in him, but also let him correct your pride.
exp.18:2:
It says that Egypt will lose the courage and the wisdom that made it feel strong. God himself will bring its plans to nothing. Then, in their despair, the Egyptians will look for answers to idols, to sorcerers, to mediums (the spirit-speakers, people who claimed to speak with spirits) and to diviners. "Counsel" means their plans and their wisdom for governing.

It is a "burden," that is, a message of judgment that God gives to the prophet Isaiah. The LORD speaks, and announces that he will come against Egypt, a powerful nation full of idols. Before this verse it already speaks of divisions and internal fighting. Scholars debate exactly which historical moment it refers to, and there is no single certain answer.

When our plans fail, it is easy to run to anything that promises quick answers. Better that we bring our confusion to God in prayer and to his Word, where true wisdom is found.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that the prophet invites the people of Israel, called "house of Jacob," to walk in the light of the Lord. "Come ye" means "come," and "let us walk" includes the prophet himself. The light represents guidance, truth, and God's presence. To walk is to live day by day according to his direction.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Just before, he describes a future in which many nations will go up to Jerusalem to learn from God, and there will be peace. Then Isaiah shows that his own people were living far from God: they trusted in fortune-tellers, in riches, and in war horses. That is why the verse is an urgent call: do not wait for that future, but start living this way now.

For today: do not trust only in your own resources or plans. Before deciding something important, ask God for direction and search his Word for the step to take today.
exp.16:12:
They say that many nations will make a great noise, like the roar of mighty waters. But God will rebuke them with his word, and they will flee far away. They will be swept off like the chaff, the light husk that is left over when the grain is threshed, which the wind carries away from the mountains, or like the dust that a whirlwind lifts up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C., when Judah faced threats from neighboring powers. This passage follows a message against Damascus and Ephraim. Many understand it to refer to armies, probably Assyria, that attack God's people. The next verse shows that their noise comes to an end in a single night. Scholars do not agree on identifying every historical detail.

Today, when problems seem loud and enormous, remember that God is greater. Bring your fear to him in prayer and trust that he has the final word.
exp.37:2:
Hezekiah asks God to remember how he has lived. To "walk before you in truth" means to live sincerely before God, and "a perfect heart" means a whole heart, without duplicity. He says he has done what is "pleasing" in God's sight, that is, what pleases Him. Then he "wept sore," meaning he wept very hard.

King Hezekiah is speaking while he is very ill. The prophet Isaiah has just told him that he is going to die. He turns his face toward the wall, perhaps to pray in private, and cries out to God. Scholars do not agree on every detail of his request, but God heard his prayer and his tears, and added fifteen years to his life.

For today: you can be completely honest with God in your moments of pain, fear, or distress. Bring Him your tears and your requests with sincerity, trusting that He hears you and cares about you.
exp.2:7:
It says that Jerusalem is ruined and Judah has fallen, and it gives the reason: what they say and what they do goes against the Lord. The phrase "provoke the eyes of his glory" means to provoke or offend God, who sees everything and is glorious.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah. The verses before it describe a society without leaders, so weakened that no one wants to rule. Isaiah explains that this ruin is not bad luck, but the result of turning away from God in words and conduct. The exact historical details are interpreted in several ways.

For today: let us examine whether our words and actions agree with what we say we believe. We can ask God to help us speak the truth and live with integrity, because He hears us and sees us with love.
exp.35:15:
