The messenger of the king of Assyria speaks to the people of Jerusalem and tells them not to listen to Hezekiah. He offers them terms to "make an agreement" with him, that is, to surrender, and to "come out" to him, meaning to give themselves up. In return he promises that each person will be allowed to keep eating from his own vine and fig tree and drinking water from his own cistern. The "cistern" here is the well or water source of each household.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a senior Assyrian officer, when Sennacherib threatens Jerusalem. He wants to sow fear and distrust toward King Hezekiah and toward God. His offer sounds calm, but later he speaks of being carried away to another land, that is, exile.

For today: be wary of easy offers that ask you to abandon your faith in exchange for comfort. Before accepting anything, ask yourself what it will really cost you and what God says about it.
exp.41:22:
God asks his people a question: who among you will listen to this? Who will pay attention and hear, thinking about what is coming? To "listen" here means to give close attention. Being alert to what is ahead means thinking about the future and learning for what comes next.

Here God speaks through Isaiah. Israel has been plundered and humbled, and the people do not understand why. God reminds them that he himself allowed that defeat because of their disobedience. The question is a call, and also a rebuke, because they were not listening or learning.

For today: when we go through hard times, let us not only ask that they end. Let us stop and listen to God, think about what he wants to teach us, and obey him again. Listening today changes what comes tomorrow.
exp.4:5:
It says God will leave his vineyard turned into abandoned ground. No one will prune it (cut back the branches so they bear more fruit) or dig it (loosen the soil). Instead of grapes, thistles and thorns will grow. Furthermore, God will command the clouds not to give rain. "Even to the clouds" means "even to the clouds."

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a song about his vineyard. God cared for that vineyard with great care, but he expected good grapes and received wild (bitter) grapes. The following verses explain that the vineyard is Israel and Judah. God expected justice, and found violence and abuse. For that reason he announces judgment.

For today: God cares for us and expects fruits of justice and compassion. Today you can ask yourself humbly: what fruit is my life bearing, and how do I treat others?
exp.36:26:
They say the people of the conquered cities had lost their strength, were defeated and put to shame. They were as fragile as the grass of the field, as tender green plants, or as the grass that sprouts on rooftops, which dries up quickly because it has no deep root. The phrase about being "before it is grown" means before it has grown up and ripened.

Here God speaks through Isaiah to King Sennacherib of Assyria, who boasted of his conquests and mocked the God of Israel. God answers him that those victories were not his own merit, since God had allowed them from long before. Assyria was only an instrument, and its pride would be judged.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated by powers that seem invincible. God governs history and is greater than any threat. Trust in Him and avoid pride, because everything we have comes from His hand.
exp.6:16:
God says he will bring a time of suffering upon King Ahaz, his people, and his family, a kind of hardship not seen since the northern kingdom (Ephraim) broke away from Judah. That punishment would come through the king of Assyria.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Ahaz, king of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and did not trust God; he preferred to seek help from Assyria. God had offered him a sign, but Ahaz refused it. So what Ahaz was relying on would turn against him. Scholars agree that this refers to the later Assyrian pressure, although they debate some details.

For today: when you are afraid, do not run first to human solutions that ignore God. Pray, ask for his guidance, and trust in him, because what looks like a safe way out can bring more trouble than the one you were trying to avoid.
exp.40:18:
God promises to fill the wilderness with trees: cedars, olive trees, and myrtles, which are trees valued for good timber, fruit, or fragrance, along with thorn trees, beeches, elms, and poplars. The olive trees mentioned here are the ones in the verse, and the phrase "all together" means that they grow side by side. Some of these trees are identified in several ways, so the exact names may vary from one translation to another.

The Lord speaks to his people Israel, who are tired and distressed, probably during the time of exile. He promises that he will hear them and will not abandon them. The flourishing desert is an image of God's care, and the text that follows says that everyone will see that his hand has done it.

For today: when you find yourself in a dry season or a situation with no way out, pray with confidence. God can bring life and hope where you see only emptiness, and his timing and his way of doing it may surprise you.
exp.17:0:
It speaks of a "woe," a warning from God, against a distant land. The land is described as one "shadowing with wings," and this may be understood as a place full of winged insects, of armies, or of ships with sails. It also lies beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which at that time was the kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt. Scholars are not sure exactly what that image means.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. Judah probably faced the threat of Assyria, and some were thinking of seeking help through alliances with Cush. Many believe the message reminds them that God rules over all nations, though this is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. Before rushing to seek human support, it is good to pray and to trust first in God, who has control of history.
exp.36:35:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord went out during the night and struck down 185,000 soldiers in the Assyrian camp. When the others got up, they saw only dead bodies.

King Sennacherib of Assyria had surrounded Judah with threats and mocked God. King Hezekiah prayed, and God answered through the prophet Isaiah, promising to defend Jerusalem for his own honor and because of his promise to David. This account also appears in 2 Kings 19. The Bible does not explain how it happened; it only says it was the work of God's angel.

When you find yourself surrounded by a problem that is bigger than you are, do as Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer with sincerity. He can act in ways you cannot imagine, and his faithfulness does not depend on your strength.
exp.42:21:
God tells his people that they did not call on him in prayer. "Calling upon" means calling on God and asking him for help. Their wearying of him, the verse's word for having grown tired of him, means that they had become bored with him and no longer cared.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he had promised them water in the desert and his care. Here he rebukes them because, despite all his love, they offered sacrifices without a sincere heart. The verses that follow show that their religion had become empty ritual, while their sins weighed heavily on God. Even so, verse 25 announces forgiveness purely by grace.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly pray or only keep religious customs. God desires a close relationship. Take a few minutes today to speak to him honestly, without formulas, and to thank him that he always forgives.
exp.20:14:
It says the people flee from four things: the swords, the drawn sword (the sword that is out of its sheath), the bent bow (the bow that is strung and ready to shoot), and the weight, or harshness, of the battle. These are people who escape from a war and seek to save themselves.

Isaiah announces a burden, that is, a message of judgment, concerning Arabia. He speaks in the name of God. The fugitives arrive in lands such as Dedanim and Tema, and those peoples are asked to give them water and bread. Afterward God announces that within a year the glory of Kedar, another Arab tribe, will be broken. Scholars are not sure which specific invasion is meant.

For today: God sees the exhausted person who flees and calls us to help them. This week, share bread, time, or a kind word with someone who is going through a hard struggle.
exp.49:9:
What it says: Isaiah asks who among the people fears the Lord and obeys the voice of his servant. Then he encourages anyone who walks in darkness (dark moments with no way out) and has no light (hope or guidance) to trust in the name of the Lord and lean on Him, that is, rest on Him like a firm walking staff. "Fear" here means to respect God with reverence.

Context: This is the third Servant Song. Before it, the servant speaks, trusting that God helps him. Here the prophet seems to address the people. Scholars debate who the servant is: some think of Isaiah, others of Israel, and Christians see in him Jesus. Afterward, God warns those who trust in their own light, a light made of human fire.

For today: When you don't understand what is happening in your life, do not invent your own light with hasty solutions. Pray, listen to the Word, and keep trusting God, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.27:9:
It says that the teaching comes repeated and in small portions: one command after another, one line after another, a little here and a little there.

Isaiah speaks to priests and prophets who were drunk and who mocked his message. Many think this verse mimics their mockery, as if they treated Isaiah like a teacher speaking to infants. Others read it as a description of God's own teaching. It is not certain which reading is correct. In any case, since they would not listen, God would speak to them in a foreign tongue, probably through invaders.

Today: do not despise what is simple or repeated. Read a short passage each day, practice it, and return to it. In this way faith grows, little by little.
exp.65:6:
It says that Zion gave birth suddenly, without going through the usual process. Normally childbirth brings long pain and a period of waiting; here everything happens in reverse.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just comforted the faithful who are rejected by their own brothers, and he promises that those who rejected them will be put to shame. Then he announces a restoration so swift that it seems unbelievable: a nation born in a day. Scholars debate whether this refers to the return from exile, to the church, or to a future fulfillment, and it may include several of these meanings.

For today: when your situation seems to move very slowly or has no way out, remember that God does not depend on our timing or on what seems possible. Remain faithful and wait on him with confidence, because he finishes what he begins.
exp.9:33:
He says that God will cut down the densest part of the forest with iron, that is, with an axe, and that Lebanon, famous for its great cedars, will fall by a mighty power. The thickest part of the forest is the densest, most tangled growth of trees.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. Assyria, the empire advancing against Jerusalem, is described as an army that reaches Nob, near the city. The images of the forest and the tall trees stand for the pride of the powerful. Some think Lebanon speaks of Assyria itself; others, that it refers to the fall of its leaders. The text does not make this entirely clear.

God is not impressed by those who seem untouchable. If today you feel small in the face of something that seems enormous, remember that God cares for his people and humbles pride. And if you have power or success, learn to live with humility.
exp.46:0:
It says that Babylon, imagined as a noble and pampered young woman, must come down from her high place and sit in the dust. "Virgin daughter" is a poetic way of speaking about the city and its people. "No throne" means she no longer rules. "Tender and delicate" describes a life of luxury and comfort, which will come to an end.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon was a powerful and proud empire. God announces its fall and the humiliation of those who believed they could not be touched. Isaiah wrote this long before Babylon reached its greatest power, so many read it as a prophecy.

For today: power, money, or success can make us feel secure and proud. This text invites us to live with humility, remembering that everything comes from God and that nothing we have is eternal.
exp.41:18:
Here God asks who is more blind and deaf than his own servant. He calls the one he sent a "messenger" and "perfect," and yet he says that this servant does not see or hear well. "Perfect" can be understood as someone who is at peace with God, or who has been placed in a complete relationship with Him.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked those who trust in idols, and now he turns his gaze to his people, Israel, the servant who sees many things but does not take them seriously. Some believe it refers only to Israel; others also see a contrast with the faithful Servant announced earlier in the chapter.

For today: it is not enough to know the Word or to have heard it many times. Ask God for an attentive heart, and take time today to read a passage slowly, asking what it is asking you to do.
exp.26:3:
He says that God is not angry with his vineyard, which is his people. If someone were to set thorns and briers, that is, enemies or wickedness, as if they were going to fight against him, God would advance against them, trample them underfoot, and burn them all together.

The Lord speaks, and in the passage he tends his vineyard with tenderness, watering it and guarding it day and night. Here God's anger is not against his people, but against whatever threatens them. Scholars debate some details of the image, but the general meaning is God's protection and his invitation to make peace with him.

Today you can trust that God cares for you, even when you feel surrounded by problems. If you have felt that he is angry with you, remember that he invites you to make peace with him. Come near to him sincerely and rest in his care.
exp.42:12:
It says that God existed before there was any time: "before the day was, I am he." No one can snatch anything out of his hand or escape from it. And when God decides to act, no one can stop him. The verse's "who shall let it?" means who can hinder or block it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people who would be carried off to Babylon. God reminds them that only he saves and that they are witnesses to what he has done for them. He gives them assurance before announcing that he will redeem them. Some understand "out of my hand" as God's power to deliver and also to judge.

For today: when you feel that your situation is out of control, remember that God is not caught off guard and is not weakened. You can rest in the knowledge that your life is in hands no one can overcome. Pray with confidence and obey, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.49:7:
He is near who declares me righteous; who will bring a case against me? Let us stand together; who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. The speaker says that God is very close to him and is the one who declares him righteous. For this reason he dares to challenge anyone who accuses him. "Let us stand together" means let us appear together before the judge. "Bring a case against me" means argue or contend the matter in court. "My adversary" is the one who opposes him in the trial.

The speaker is the Servant of the LORD, who endures blows, mockery, and spitting without giving up. Christians see in this an image of Jesus, although the original text also speaks of a faithful servant who trusts in God. His confidence does not come from being perfect in himself, but from God's support.

For today: when you are falsely accused or feel guilty without reason, do not live in fear. Pray, do what is right, and rest in the knowledge that God knows the truth and sustains you.
exp.29:31:
God promises that every blow of punishment against Assyria will come with the sound of tambourines and harps. The "tambourines" are hand drums, and the "lyres" are stringed instruments, similar to harps. The phrase "grounded staff" is difficult: many understand it as the rod of punishment that God has prepared, though others translate it differently.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. Assyria had oppressed the nations with violence, and Judah was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. God announces that Assyria, which struck others with the rod, will be broken by his voice.

For today: you can trust that God brings about justice in his own time. You do not need to take revenge or rely on human powers. Entrust your injustices to God and rest in the knowledge that he cares for you.
exp.54:6:
This verse invites the person who lives in wrongdoing to change direction. The one who lives without regard for God is called "wicked," and the one who acts with evil is called "unrighteous." They are asked to leave behind both their actions and their thoughts, and to return to God. The promise is that He will have mercy and will pardon generously, that is, with great generosity.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a weary people, probably during the time of exile in Babylon. Just before this, God invites people to seek Him while He can still be found. Afterward, He makes clear that His thoughts and ways are higher than ours, which helps explain why His forgiveness is so great.

For today: if something weighs on your conscience, do not wait until you have made yourself right first. Speak to God honestly today, leave that path, and trust that His forgiveness is generous.
exp.2:5:
In times of crisis, the text says, people will be so desperate that a man will take hold of his own brother, of his father's house, and say to him: "You have clothing, be our ruler, and let this ruin be under your hand."

The quoted word "take hold" means to grab or take someone by the hand. "Have clothing" refers to having some clothing, that is, a little means.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He announces that God will remove the provision and the capable leaders, and disorder will come. The poverty will be so great that no one will want to govern, and whoever has a cloak will be seen as a candidate. The verses that follow explain why: the people had turned against God with words and deeds.

For today: let us not seek leadership for comfort or by pretending to be sufficient, and let us pray for honest and wise leaders. When a society turns away from God, it needs to return to Him before seeking only human saviors.
exp.14:4:
Here the pain of Moab after its destruction is described. Those who escape flee as far as Zoar, and they climb up weeping by the slopes of Luhith and Horonaim, which were places along the road. The figure of a young cow in the verse is one of strong, loud crying; some explain it in another way. The word "destruction" in the verse means total ruin.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces a judgment of God upon Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. What is striking is that the prophet says "my heart shall cry out for Moab": he speaks not with mockery but with sorrow. The verses before show whole cities weeping in the streets and on the rooftops.

For today: even when someone suffers the consequences of their own actions, let us not celebrate their fall. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, one that prays and helps with mercy.
exp.12:9:
This verse says that the sky will grow dark: the stars and their constellations will not give their light, the sun will be darkened as soon as it rises, and the moon will not shine. The bright stars are called the stars that shine brightly, and light is what fills the sky with brightness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This chapter announces the day of the Lord against Babylon, a day of judgment against pride and wickedness. The darkness in the sky is poetic language that often describes a very great judgment. Some see it fulfilled in the fall of Babylon, and others also see a reference to the end of the age.

Today this text reminds us that God rules over the nations and that no human power is eternal. We can examine our hearts, lay down pride, and trust God with humility, knowing that his justice is true and that he offers forgiveness to those who come to him.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that God himself will be the judge among the nations and will correct many peoples. As a result, people will turn their weapons into tools for work: the swords into plowshares (the iron tip that opens the ground) and the spears into pruninghooks (for cutting wheat). There will be no more wars, and no one will be trained to fight anymore.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, describes a vision of "the latter days." The nations go up to God's mountain, to Jerusalem, to learn his ways. Then the prophet calls his own people, the house of Jacob, to walk now in the light of the LORD, because at that time they were relying on fortune-tellers and foreign customs.

For today: the peace God promises begins where I live. I can ask myself what "sword" I have at home, at work, or in church, such as a harsh word or a grudge, and turn it into something that serves and builds up.
exp.43:15:
He takes a single piece of wood and uses it for two very different things. With one part he makes a fire: he roasts meat, eats until he is full, and warms himself. He is glad and says, "I am warm, I have seen the fire!" With the rest, as the following verses say, he makes a god.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people tempted by idolatry. With irony, he shows how absurd it is to worship something a person makes himself out of ordinary wood, the same wood he uses to cook.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things, even good ones such as money, work, or success, we have placed in the place of God. What we do or control cannot save us. Today we can thank God for his gifts and trust in him, not in them.
exp.14:1:
He has gone up to Bayit and to Dibon, to the high places, to weep. Over Nebo and over Medeba, the people of Moab will howl, that is, they will lament aloud. Shaving the head and tearing out the beard were signs of deep mourning. "Shaved" means cut bare, and "tear out" means to pull the hair out.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking. This message, called a "burden," is a warning of judgment against Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab wept at its high places, seeking help from its gods. Scholars debate when this destruction happened and who caused it; the text only shows that God sees the nations and that their fall would come suddenly.

For today: do not place your security in things that can fall in a single night, such as money, reputation, or plans. Seek God first; he remains, and he comforts those who weep.
exp.29:1:
Some of the people of Judah set out on the road to Egypt to seek help, but without asking God. "Have not asked at my mouth" means they did not ask for his direction. They wanted to lean on the strength of Pharaoh, the Egyptian king, and take refuge under Egypt's protection.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah faced the threat of Assyria, and its leaders sought an alliance with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. God calls this sin, because it was a way of setting him aside. The passage that follows warns that such help would end in shame.

For today: before making an important decision, whether about money, work, or family, pray first and seek God's guidance in his Word. You may ask for advice and use resources, but do not let them take the place of God.
exp.1:12:
It says the day of the LORD will also come against the cedars of Lebanon, tall and majestic, and against the oaks of Bashan. In other versions, Bashan is associated with oaks or terebinths; the Hebrew word is translated in different ways. These trees are famous for their height and strength.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He warns them that God will judge all human pride. The cedars and the oaks work as images of people, powers, and things that seem imposing. Many understand that this is not an attack on trees, but poetic language about arrogance.

For today: examine what you trust in to feel secure or important, such as your money, your position, or your achievements. Hand that over to God and ask for a humble heart, because only He remains firm.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that in Israel the respected elders and honorable leaders are "the head," that is, those who give orders. But the prophet who teaches lies is "the tail," in other words, the lowest part. "Honourable of face" means someone of a dignified appearance who inspires respect. The verse shows that bad teaching dishonors the one who gives it, no matter what position he holds.

The passage is spoken by the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's judgment on the northern kingdom, Israel. The people did not return to God even after being punished. Their leaders and false prophets were leading them down the wrong path, and so the judgment would reach everyone, from top to bottom.

Today it invites us not to be impressed only by the prestige or appearance of someone who teaches. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to ask God for wisdom to distinguish the truth.
exp.51:1:
God tells Jerusalem to rise up from the ground and shake off the dust, like someone coming out of humiliation. The word "sit down" can be understood as taking a place of dignity, though some translate it "stand up." She is also to loosen the chains from her neck. "Captive daughter of Zion" is a tender way of addressing the city and its people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, announcing to a humbled and captive people that their situation is going to change. The verses that follow explain that they were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without payment. The text looks toward the release from exile, and Christians also read it in light of redemption in Christ.

Today, God invites us not to remain in shame or in old guilt. If He already offers freedom, we can respond with faith: praying, asking forgiveness, accepting His grace, and taking a concrete step to leave behind whatever still holds us bound.
exp.39:2:
This verse says that a voice calls for the way of the Lord to be prepared. The first key word, rendered here as "clear away," means to clean out or clear a path, and the second, "highway," refers to a straight, firm road. The desert and the wilderness are empty and difficult places, yet it is there that God wants to pass. It is like making the route ready so that a king can arrive.

God comforts Jerusalem: her punishment has ended and her sin has been forgiven. The one speaking is an unnamed voice in this passage, and the prophecy announces that God himself will come to his people. The Gospels (Matthew 3:3) apply this voice to John the Baptist, who prepared people for Jesus.

Today we can ask ourselves what obstacles are in our hearts: pride, resentment, or carelessness. Acknowledging them honestly and asking for forgiveness is a way of "making straight the highway" so that God can work in us.
exp.37:6:
It says that God will give Hezekiah a sign, that is, a visible proof, that he will fulfill what he promised. "The LORD" is the name of God. The phrase ends with a colon because the sign is explained in the following verse: the shadow on the dial will go back.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, carrying a message from God to King Hezekiah. The king was seriously ill, had prayed weeping, and God promised him fifteen more years of life and protection against Assyria. The sign confirmed that promise. Some think it was a miracle in the sun or in the shadow; the text only says that the shadow went back, and does not explain how it happened.

For today: God hears our prayers and does not despise our tears. When you doubt his promises, remember how he has kept his word before, and trust him simply.
exp.54:12:
It says that where there used to be thorns and prickly plants, good trees will now grow. The tree mentioned here, the fir, is a cypress or pine tree according to some other translations; the myrtle is a shrub with green leaves and fragrant flowers. To be "cut off" means to be erased or removed. Thus, this transformation will be a lasting sign for the name of the LORD.

God speaks through Isaiah at the end of his message of comfort to the people of Israel. He promises their return and joy after the exile. His word will accomplish what He wants. The thorns represent a land damaged by sin and punishment; the good trees show the change that God brings about.

For today: if there are areas of your life that feel like thorns, such as habits, wounds, or fears, trust that God can change them. Ask Him for His help and let His word keep working in you with patience.
exp.65:12:
God says that he will comfort his people the way a mother comforts her child. The image is of close, tender care, of an embrace and relief. The promise is personal: "I myself will comfort you." And the words that follow announce that this comfort will be experienced in the restored city, Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. The people have gone through pain and ruin, and God promises restoration, peace flowing like a river, and joy. The text then adds that God will also act with justice against his enemies. Some understand this promise for the restored Israel, and others also see a foretaste of the final comfort in Christ.

For today: when you are weary or wounded, do not stay alone with your pain. Come to God in prayer, as a child runs to his mother, and let him comfort you.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that the darkness to come will not be like the distress before. At first, God dealt lightly, or with little weight, with the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, in the north of Israel. Later, the burden grew heavier in the area along the way of the sea, on the other side of the Jordan, in Galilee of the nations, that is, of the foreign peoples. This phrase is difficult, and translators understand it in different ways: some see a contrast between the past affliction and a future relief.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, threatened by the invasion of Assyria. The lands of the north were the first to suffer the blow, and the prophet announces that this darkness will not have the last word, as the following verse shows.

Today, when we go through dark times, we can remember that God knows where we suffer and that our pain is not the end of the story. Let us wait on Him with confidence.
exp.0:3:
God speaks with both grief and firmness. He calls Israel a "sinful nation" and a "people laden with iniquity," because their guilt weighs on them like a heavy load. "Evildoers" and "corrupters" describe a life that has gone crooked and rotten. Then he says three things: they have forsaken the Lord, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger (this is how he is named here), and they have gone away backward, that is, they turned around and walked away from him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just called the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He complains that he raised his children and they rebelled. Even the ox and the donkey recognize their owner, but his people do not. Then he describes the consequences as a body wounded from head to foot.

For today: do not ignore God's calls to return to him. Today, acknowledge in prayer where you have drifted away, and come back to him with humility. He remains a Father ready to heal.
exp.7:20:
They will go through the land hard-pressed and hungry. Because of the hunger they will be filled with anger, and they will speak evil of their king and of their God. The phrase "they will curse" means speaking with anger and contempt. The phrase "lifting up their faces" shows that they will look up toward the sky in anger and defiance. "It" probably refers to the land described earlier, though some understand it differently.

Isaiah speaks in a time of crisis in Judah, when many sought answers from diviners and spirits instead of from God. Isaiah tells them to return to the law and to the testimony, the word of God. Whoever rejects it is left without light and ends in distress and darkness, as the following verse says.

For today: when need comes, let us not blame God or seek answers in dark things. Let us first seek his Word, where there is light and hope.
exp.56:18:
He says that God himself creates "the fruit of the lips": words of peace, praise, and comfort. He announces peace both to the one who is far off and to the one who is near, that is, to those who are at a distance and to those who are close. And he promises: "and I will heal him."

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that he was angry because of his people's greed and rebellion, but that even so he wants to heal them and guide them. The ones who are far off and near are understood in several ways: Jews far from or near Jerusalem, or those who were estranged from God and those who already followed him. Then the text warns that the wicked who reject God have no peace.

For today: if you are far from God, it is not too late to return; his peace and his healing are waiting for you. If you are near, use your words to bring peace and encouragement to others.
exp.12:8:
It says that the day of the Lord is coming near and will be harsh, full of anger and burning fury. Its purpose is to leave the land desolate and to remove the sinners from it. The harsh, cruel quality of that day is what the passage stresses, and the anger it describes is intense.

Isaiah prophesies about Babylon, the great power that would later be judged. God speaks through the prophet to warn that he will punish wickedness and pride. Many understand that the passage was fulfilled in part with the fall of Babylon, and that it also points to a final judgment of God on the world. Christians have read it in both ways.

For today: God is just and does not overlook evil or arrogance. This invites us to live with humility, to repent sincerely, and to trust that he will do justice, without taking revenge ourselves.
exp.28:19:
It says that the end will come for those who harm others. The "terrible one" is the abuser; the "scorner" is the one who mocks what is good and mocks God. The phrase about rising early to pursue wickedness means they got up early to plan evil, eager to carry it out. "Cut off" means cut down, as a tree is cut down.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Their leaders oppressed the weak, bent justice, and silenced anyone who corrected them. Earlier, God promises that the humble and the poor will rejoice in Him. This verse shows the other side: injustice will not last forever.

For today: if you suffer injustice, trust that God sees and will act. And examine your own heart: do you rise up thinking about blessing others or about taking advantage of them? Ask God to make you humble and just.
exp.47:5:
This verse says that the people had already heard and seen God's promises fulfilled, and so they ought now to tell them to others. The words "you have heard it" and "you have seen it" are the verse's own wording, so no further explanation is needed. "New and hidden things" are new announcements, previously unknown to them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, who was stubborn and doubted Him. He had announced events before they happened, so that they would not credit them to their idols. Now He promises new things, probably the deliverance from Babylon, though some also see a broader scope.

For today: God has been faithful to you in the past. Recall one specific occasion when He was, and share it with someone this week. In this way your faith grows, and you do not attribute to chance what God has done.
exp.54:0:
God says he invites everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters. Even those who have no money may come, and they can buy and eat. Wine and milk are offered for free, without money and without cost. The old form of the word "to" is written differently, and "come" carries the sense of "come along." Fullness means abundance, being well satisfied.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. This message is addressed to a weary people, probably in exile or near it, who are seeking comfort. The verses that follow show that God calls them to stop spending their strength on what does not satisfy, and he promises them an everlasting covenant, tied to the promises made to David.

Today, this invitation reminds us that we cannot earn God's favor through effort. If you feel emptiness or weariness, you can draw near to him just as you are, and receive his grace with open hands.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that the righteous person should be encouraged: it will go well with them, because they will enjoy what their own deeds have produced. The phrase "they shall eat the fruit of their doings" is a way of saying that they will receive the result of their work and of how they live. The righteous person is one who lives uprightly before God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, on behalf of the LORD, to Jerusalem and Judah, who were in decline because of their open sin and their wicked leaders. In the midst of that judgment, God leaves a word of comfort for the faithful. The following verse shows the contrast: the wicked will reap their evil.

For today: do not lose heart if doing what is right seems to bring no reward. Remain honest and faithful even in small things, trusting that God sees and cares for those who obey him, even when we do not always understand the manner and timing.
exp.42:25:
It says that God invites his people to an open trial. "Put me in remembrance" means: remind me, present your case. "Let us plead together" means: let us discuss this face to face. "Declare thou, that thou mayest be justified" means: state your reasons to justify yourself, and see whether you have any.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel. He has just told them that he blots out their rebellions for his own sake, not because of their merits. His people had grown weary of God with their sins and their empty sacrifices. Then he reminds them that from their ancestors on they have failed, so they have no defense. It is a challenge that shows salvation is a gift and not something earned.

For today: instead of justifying ourselves before God, we can honestly confess our faults and trust in his forgiveness, which does not depend on what we do, but on his grace.
exp.48:20:
It says that Zion, the city of God, will be amazed to see so many children around her. She felt bereaved of her children, alone, with no settled home, and cast out of her land. So she asks who raised all these, since she had been left abandoned.

God is speaking to Jerusalem, which represents his people in exile in Babylon. They felt forgotten, but God promises to restore her and fill her with people. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a broader fulfillment in God's family, which includes the nations.

For today: when you feel alone, fruitless, or forgotten, remember that God can work in silence and surprise you. Keep trusting in him, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the Lord will wash away the moral filth of the women of Zion and remove the stains of blood shed in Jerusalem. "Filth" refers to impurities; to wash and to cleanse mean to make clean. The "spirit of judgment" and the "spirit of burning" (fire that purifies) speak of a cleansing that corrects and burns away what is bad, the way metal is refined.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. In chapter 3 he denounced the pride and injustice of Jerusalem. Here he promises that, after the punishment, a clean people will remain, called "holy." Some see in this a promise for the future of Israel, and others see a broader picture of God's work.

For today: God not only forgives, he also transforms. We can ask him to cleanse us without fear, even when correcting something in our lives hurts, because his goal is to heal and care for us.
exp.51:9:
This verse says that God "bared his arm," meaning he rolled up his sleeve to act with power, like someone preparing for work or battle. It is a "holy" arm, pure and faithful to his character. He did it in the sight of all the nations. The words translated here as "the ends of the earth" refer to the far limits of the world, and the reference to "salvation" means the rescue or deliverance that comes from God.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were in exile. The watchmen, or sentinels, announce that God is returning to Zion and comforting Jerusalem. A deliverance so clear is promised that even the nations will see it. Many Christians also see in this a announcement of salvation in Christ, and the New Testament connects it with the gospel.

For today: when you feel weak, remember that God acts with power and faithfulness. Trust in his work and share it with others, because his salvation is for everyone.
exp.18:17:
The passage says that, in a future time, five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan, that is, the language of Israel, and will swear allegiance to the Lord, the Lord of hosts. One will be called "The city of destruction." This name is hard: it may mean "destruction" or "sun," and scholars interpret it in different ways.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf within a prophecy about Egypt. First he announces judgment and fear for that nation, but then he shows that God does not abandon it. Egypt, the traditional enemy of Israel, will come to know the true God.

For today: God can change hearts that are far away or distant. So do not give up on any person or any people; pray for them and treat them with hope.
exp.25:5:
It says that the proud city, already brought down to the dust, will be trampled underfoot. The word translated here as "trample" means "will trample it." The ones who trample it are the afflicted and the poor (the needy are the ones in want). In other words, those who were once oppressed now walk over what used to oppress them.

Isaiah 26 is a song of confidence that the people of Judah will sing in the future. Before that, the text invites trust in the LORD, the everlasting strength, because he has humbled the haughty city. Many think that city stands for the pride and violence of the nations; the text does not name it here. Afterward, the song speaks of the upright path of the righteous.

For today: if you feel small or mistreated, do not grow bitter or seek revenge. Trust in God and keep walking uprightly, because he cares for the humble and knows how to put everything in its place.
exp.13:21:
God himself says he will rise up against Babylon and wipe it out completely. The phrase "cut off" means to pull up or erase entirely. "Remnant" refers to the survivors, what is left over. "Son and nephew" speaks of descendants: neither its name, nor its remnant, nor its heirs will remain.

God speaks here, called "the Lord of hosts," that is, the Lord of all power. The verse sits within a taunting song against the king of Babylon, a proud and cruel ruler who oppressed many nations. Isaiah announces that this power will not last. Scholars debate whether the king is one particular person or a symbol of imperial arrogance, and the text leaves that open.

For today: do not lose heart when injustice seems to be winning. God sees and has the last word. Trust that he will do justice in his own time, and examine your own heart so that you do not live with the pride that God so strongly opposes.
exp.13:18:
He says that the king of Babylon, whom Isaiah addresses as "you," will not receive a dignified burial. He will be thrown out of his tomb, like a rotten and disgusting branch. The phrase "abominable branch" refers to a despised branch that is cast away. The phrase "slain with the sword" means those who died in battle. His body will be like that of fallen soldiers, covered with wounds and trampled underfoot.

Isaiah pronounces this poetic mockery against a proud and cruel king. Earlier the text says that the other kings rest with honor in their tombs, but he does not. Many identify him with the king of Babylon; others also see a broader background about pride. God denounces that he destroyed his land and killed his people.

For today: power and fame do not guarantee a good ending. God sees how we use the authority we have, whether in the home, at work, or in the church. Let us ask him for humility to serve and not to crush others.
exp.40:8:
God tells Israel that he took them from the farthest parts of the earth and called them from its most distant corners. He reminds them: "You are my servant." He chose them and never rejected them. The word "rejected" means throwing something away as though it no longer has any use. "The chief men" here is understood as the most remote or most important places; some interpret it differently.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The neighboring nations make idols and encourage one another out of fear. In contrast, God comforts Israel, the people descended from Abraham, reminding them that they were chosen by grace, not because of their merits. The promise continues: "Fear not, for I am with you."

For today: when you feel small, rejected, or out of place, remember that God calls you and does not cast you aside. Tell him in prayer today: "Lord, I trust that you chose me and that you do not let go of me."
exp.36:8:
The verse tells us that the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, received a piece of news: Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, had come out to fight against him. Upon hearing it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah with another message. The phrase "when he heard it" marks the moment the news reached him, and the word "heard" in the verse is the key to the sentence.

Here the account from Isaiah describes the Assyrian invasion of Judah. God had already announced that Sennacherib would hear a rumor and return to his own land. That rumor seems to be this news. Under pressure, Sennacherib tries to make Hezekiah surrender with threats and mockery aimed at his trust in God. The exact military details are debated by scholars, but the text shows how God directs events.

For today: when someone threatens you or makes you doubt God, remember that He governs circumstances, even those you cannot see. Trust and pray, as Hezekiah did.
exp.39:16:
It says that all the nations, compared with God, are like nothing. The phrases "counted as nothing" and "less than nothing" are a strong way of saying that, next to God, the peoples have no weight or worth that can be compared with his. The word "nations" in the verse means nations or peoples. A "bucket" is a small pail, and "dust on the scale" is usually understood as the fine powder left on a balance.

The prophet Isaiah comforts a tired people who are afraid before powerful empires. He reminds them that God is greater than any power, and that not even all of Lebanon, with its forests and animals, would be enough to offer him a worthy offering. Then he goes on to ask who can be compared with God, and he mocks the idols made by craftsmen.

For today: when the fear of governments, crises, or powerful people weighs on you, remember who God is. Pray with confidence, and do not put your hope in anything made by human hands.
exp.50:17:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to a mother, was left alone and without support. Among all the sons she bore and raised, none guides her or takes her by the hand to help her.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem after God's harsh punishment. She has drunk the cup of God's wrath, an image of divine judgment. Her leaders and her people lay fallen and without strength. The abandonment shows how deep the pain was. But this passage prepares the comfort that God offers right after.

For today: when you feel without support, with no one to take you by the hand, do not stay silent or alone. God sees your pain and remains your comfort. And if you know someone who is alone or weary, be the one who reaches out a hand to them.
exp.42:27:
He says that God himself dishonored the leaders of the temple and handed over his people to destruction and mockery. "Profaned" means taking away holiness or honor. "Given to the curse" refers to something handed over to judgment or doom. "Reproaches" is public shame and contempt. "Princes of the sanctuary" are those in charge of worship, priests and officials.

God speaks through Isaiah, in a kind of legal case where he invites Israel to defend itself. He reminds them that their history was marked by sin, including the sin of their teachers. Many understand this verse as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, though the text gives no further details. Just before this, God says he blots out their rebellions for his own sake (v. 25).

For today: do not minimize sin or your need for forgiveness. If God corrects, it is to call you back to him. Confess to him sincerely and receive his grace, without excuses or pride.
exp.7:11:
It says not to call "conspiracy" everything that people call by that name, nor to live in the same fear as they do. Explaining the wording: "conspiracy" and "plot" are how the verse's term is rendered, and the phrase "do not fear" means "do not let yourselves be terrified."

God speaks through Isaiah, who tells that the Lord warned him "with a strong hand" not to follow the path of the people. Judah was threatened by neighboring kings, and the people saw danger and plots everywhere. God calls them to trust him, for "God is with us." Some scholars debate exactly what that "conspiracy" referred to.

Today, faced with alarming news and rumors, we can pause before repeating the fear of others. Before reacting, let us pray, ask for wisdom, and remember that God remains our refuge and the one who deserves our deepest respect.
exp.4:10:
Isaiah says "Woe" to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink and keep drinking until night, until the wine sets them on fire, that is, inflames them and takes control of them. This is not a single slip, but a life given over to drinking from the start of the day.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, within the song of the vineyard (chapter 5). God denounces Judah for its injustice and greed. Feasts with music and wine filled their days, yet they ignored the work of God. For this reason he announces judgment to them: empty houses, poor harvests, and captivity.

For today: examine what occupies the first place in your day and the best of your time. It may be alcohol or some other pleasure. Ask God to be your first thought and your greatest joy.
exp.39:0:
God himself commands that his people be comforted. The repetition of the word "comfort" twice gives it emphasis, like a tender and urgent invitation. Furthermore, God calls them "my people" and presents himself as "your God," that is, he affirms that he remains bound to them.

Here God is speaking, and his message seems directed to those who will carry the news, perhaps the prophets. The verses that follow say that Jerusalem has completed her time of punishment and that her sin has been pardoned. The phrase about receiving "double" is understood in several ways, and it is not certain which is the correct one. What is clear is that God announces relief and a road of return toward him.

Today, if you are tired or burdened with guilt, remember that God speaks with tenderness. You can also be an instrument of comfort: this week, look for someone who is suffering and speak words of hope to them.
exp.56:20:
Those who live with their backs turned to God, the "wicked," do not know true peace. The word "wicked" refers to people who reject God and live without taking him into account. The peace mentioned here is more than calm: it means well-being, wholeness, and a good relationship with God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he offers peace and healing to both those who are far away and those who are near, that is, to those who are distant from him and to those who are close. Then he compares the wicked to a restless sea that cannot be calm and that throws up mire and dirt. The peace is offered, but whoever insists on evil does not receive it.

Today, if you feel restless, ask yourself honestly whether there is something you should let go of and give to God. Returning to him with humility opens the door to his peace and his healing.
exp.58:7:
They never learned the way of peace, the verse says. There is no justice in how they act, and their paths are "crooked," that is, twisted, dishonest. Paths are small roads. Whoever walks those roads will not find peace either.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He shows them that their sins, such as violence and injustice, are the barrier between them and God (v. 2). Then, in the verses that follow, the prophet includes himself with the people, as one who confesses a shared sin.

For today: peace is not found through shortcuts or at the expense of others. Examine today one area where you act with deceit, harshness, or injustice. Confess it to God and ask Him to straighten that path. He forgives and guides anyone who returns to Him sincerely.
exp.28:1:
He says that God himself will bring Ariel into distress, that is, into anguish, trouble, and siege. The city will be left grieving and sorrowful, full of mourning. And at the end he says it will be like Ariel. The name Ariel can sound like "lion of God," but it has also been understood as "hearth of the altar," and so there are several interpretations.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Ariel is a name for Jerusalem, the city of David. The people kept up their feasts and sacrifices, but their hearts were far from God. So the Lord announces a siege that would bring them low.

For today: routine religion does not replace a sincere heart. Ask yourself whether your prayers and your service come from love for God, and ask him to correct whatever is empty in you.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that we should honor God as holy and give him first place in our hearts. "Sanctify" means treating him as unique and sacred. "Fear" and "dread" here do not mean terror, but a deep, reverent respect toward God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The kingdom of Judah was threatened by neighboring powers, and the people lived frightened, seeing conspiracies everywhere. God warns Isaiah not to be carried away by that panic. The verses that follow show that God would be a sanctuary for whoever trusts in him, but a stone of stumbling for whoever rejects him.

When fear of people, of news, or of the future overwhelms us, we can stop and pray: "Lord, you are greater than this." Putting God first brings back our calm and our perspective.
exp.65:5:
This verse describes a great noise coming out of the city and the temple. It is the voice of God himself, who repays his enemies, that is, gives them what they deserve for their actions. The word "noise" here means a loud, roaring sound, like a commotion.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he rebuked those who did evil and did not answer his call. He also encouraged the faithful who were despised for their faith. Here he announces that he himself will intervene. Scholars debate which city and temple are meant: it may be Jerusalem, or it may be a picture of God's judgment.

For today: if you feel rejected for following God, do not seek revenge or despair. Trust that God sees everything and will bring justice in his time. In the meantime, remain faithful and respond when he speaks to you.
exp.39:29:
This verse says that even the young people, who are the strongest and fullest of energy, become exhausted and weakened. The words "youths" and "young men" in the verse both refer to the young. "Flaquean," meaning they lose their strength, and "caen," showing that they stumble or collapse, are rendered here as "shall faint and be weary" and "shall utterly fall."

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were discouraged and felt that God did not see their situation. Many believe he addresses people in exile, though scholars explain this in different ways. Isaiah compares human strength, which runs out, with God, who never grows tired and gives strength to the weak.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. When you feel tired, whether from work, family, or life, acknowledge your limits and pray sincerely. Take a few minutes to wait on God, asking him to sustain you today.
exp.14:2:
They say that the people of Moab will clothe themselves in rough cloth of mourning in their streets. On the rooftops and in the streets, everyone will cry out and weep with grief. The word "howl" means to cry out in anguish, and the phrase "weeping abundantly" suggests they weep without restraint.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces a message of judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Their cities fall in the night, suddenly, and mourning fills the whole land. Even so, the prophet shows his own sorrow: "My heart shall cry out for Moab" (v. 5). Scholars debate which exact invasion is meant; the text does not name it clearly.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, yet the prophet does not rejoice in another's fall. We can learn to weep with those who suffer, even with those far from us, and to pray for them with compassion rather than mockery.
exp.28:22:
Isaiah says that Jacob will see his children, whom God calls "the work of my hands," living among his people. They will honor God's name, that is, they will treat him as holy and set apart. Here "sanctify" means recognizing God as sacred. The reverence the verse describes is not fear in the sense of being frightened, but deep respect shown toward him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he spoke of unjust people who accused others with lies and persecuted those who corrected them at the gate, which was the place where judgments were made. Now God promises to restore his people so that they will no longer be ashamed. Scholars debate when this is fulfilled; many see it in the return from exile and also in a future time.

For today: God continues to work in his people with patience. We can trust that he corrects and renews, and respond by honoring him with sincere respect in what we say and do.
exp.51:3:
It says that God's people went down to Egypt long ago, not to stay there, but to live there as foreigners, as sojourners. Afterward, Assyria oppressed them and carried them off without any just reason. The word "carried off" here means that it took them captive.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, and comforts a people who are suffering. He recalls two oppressions: Egypt and Assyria. There are several ways to interpret which exact moment the verse points to, but the idea is clear: Israel was mistreated unjustly. That is why God promises to rescue them and to show himself present.

For today: when you feel you are suffering without reason, or feel bound and held back, remember that God sees injustice and does not forget you. Bring your pain to him in prayer, trust that he is at work, and shake off discouragement, because his rescue does not depend on what you are able to pay.
exp.28:23:
They who went astray in their thinking and in their way of living will come to understanding with wisdom. Those who complained and criticized will also learn to receive correct teaching. Those whose hearts or minds have wandered away from the truth are the ones who went astray in spirit. People who grumble under their breath, especially against God or against their leaders, are the ones who murmur.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In this chapter he rebukes a people whose hearts are far from him, but now he promises restoration. God will give Israel children who honor his name and fear him. Some understand this promise as hope for Israel in its own time, while others also see a greater fulfillment in the future. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: if you have been complaining or confused, do not stay there. God keeps teaching those who allow themselves to be corrected. Ask him for humility to listen to his Word and to change your attitude.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that God has been a firm refuge for the poor and the needy when they suffer. He is like a coat in the storm and a shade in the strong heat. The needy are those who lack what they need, and the violent blow of the wicked is like a heavy rain beating against a wall, the very face of a wall or building.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks in the form of praise to God. It is in a section where God announces that he will bring down proud and oppressive cities. It is not stated with certainty which city is meant; scholars understand it in several ways, perhaps as a symbol of human pride in general. Afterward, God prepares a banquet for all peoples.

For today: when you feel weak or pressured, turn to God in prayer before looking for other ways out. He cares for the fragile and can be your refuge.
exp.0:23:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord of hosts and the Mighty One of Israel, is going to act. The words "Ah" and "I will ease me" introduce his resolve to act at last. "I will ease me of mine adversaries" and "avenge me of mine enemies" mean that God will do justice and will not leave evil without a response. "Enemies" and "adversaries" refer to those who oppose him.

God speaks through Isaiah. The leaders of Jerusalem had become corrupt: they accepted bribes and did not defend the fatherless or the widow. God's enemies here are his own unjust people. But what follows shows that his judgment seeks to cleanse and restore, not only to punish.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, especially against the weak. We can ask where we fail to be just and how we might help those who have no voice, trusting that God corrects in order to heal.
exp.59:14:
Jerusalem (Zion) went through a period of abandonment and contempt. She was rejected and hated, so lonely that no one even passed through her. But God promises to change that situation: he will make her an everlasting excellence, that is, an honor that does not fade, and a joy that will pass from parents to children.

The passage is God speaking through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Zion. The people had suffered punishment and humiliation, and the text announces their restoration. The nearby verses speak of enemies bowing down and of God as Savior and Redeemer. Many see here a partial fulfillment after the exile and another still to come; interpreters understand it in different ways.

If today you feel forgotten or looked down upon, remember that God can turn abandonment into hope. Trust in his faithfulness, even though the process may take time.
exp.28:20:
This verse describes those who will be removed when God brings justice: people who used their words to make others guilty, who set traps for the one who corrected them in court, and who twisted what was right with empty arguments. The gate was the public place where the elders judged. The phrase about turning aside the just with worthless reasons means that they denied justice to the innocent with arguments that had no value.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. He announces that God will put an end to the oppression of the corrupt leaders in Judah, and that the humble and the poor will rejoice. Then God promises that his people will not be put to shame.

For today: let us guard our words and not attack the one who corrects us with sincerity. If something troubles us, let us seek truth and justice, and honestly defend those who have no voice.
exp.54:5:
It says we should seek God now, while he lets himself be found, and call on him while he is near. "Seek" means to approach him with a sincere desire. "Call on" means to invoke him, to speak to him in prayer. The words "found" and "near" show that God wants to be found.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a passage where he invites everyone, even nations that did not know him, to come to him. The verses that follow explain the call: that the wicked person should leave his evil way and return to God, who pardons generously. Some think that "while he may be found" is a call not to let the opportunity pass; the text does not give an exact date.

For today: do not put off your prayer or your drawing near to God. Today itself, set aside a few minutes to speak to him sincerely and ask him for forgiveness and guidance.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the people turned down the waters of Shiloah, which flow gently and quietly, and chose instead to rejoice in Rezin and in the son of Remaliah. "Rejoice" here means that they took delight in them and placed their trust in them. Rezin was king of Syria, and the son of Remaliah was Pekah, king of Israel.

God speaks through Isaiah in a time of threat for Judah. Shiloah was a spring of water in Jerusalem, and here it probably stands for God's quiet protection, though some also interpret it as the house of David. The people trusted in human alliances more than in God. Therefore, the following text says, the mighty king of Assyria would come upon them like a flooding river.

Today, we sometimes trust in visible resources that seem strong more than in the quiet help of God. Before seeking security in other things, we can stop to pray and trust in Him.
exp.13:31:
This verse says that when the messengers of other nations (the "nations") come to ask what is happening, the answer will be simple: God himself founded Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and there the afflicted of his people will find refuge. "Shall trust in it" means they will run to seek protection.

Isaiah speaks in a message against Philistia, a neighboring nation that had oppressed Israel. He announces that judgment will come upon it, while God's poor will be cared for. Some think the messengers come to ask about the fall of Philistia or to seek alliances; the text does not detail this, and there are different interpretations.

For today: when you feel weak or afflicted, do not place your security in human alliances or in your own strength. Run to God, who remains a firm refuge for his people. And if someone asks you where your hope is, you can answer with the same simplicity: God founded it.
exp.29:14:
God tells his people how they could be saved: by turning back to him and resting, in quietness and trust. "Rest" and "quiet" speak of calm and of not acting out of desperation. "Strength" is the true power that holds us up. But the verse ends in sorrow: "and ye would not." God offered the way, and they rejected it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was threatened by Assyria and sought protection in an alliance with Egypt, which God had not asked for. So the people say, "we will flee upon horses," trusting in military force. God warns them that this plan would collapse like a cracked wall or a broken vessel.

Today, when fear arrives, we often rush to solve everything with our own strength. Before acting, stop to pray, hand your worry over to God, and trust him. Resting in God is not passivity, but choosing his guidance over panic.
exp.15:8:
This verse says that the prophet will weep with a grief as deep as the weeping of the people of Jazer over the vines of Sibmah. He says he will drench with tears Heshbon and Elealeh, two cities of Moab. The phrase "I will water thee" means "I will drench you." The "shouting" is the joyful noise of the harvest, and now that cry of celebration has fallen, that is, it has been silenced by ruin.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Moab, a neighboring country of Israel famous for its vineyards. Its harvests will be destroyed by invaders. It is surprising that Isaiah does not rejoice but mourns for them. Some understand that this reflects the pain of God himself.

For today: even when someone faces the consequences of their actions, we can respond with compassion and not with mockery. Let us ask God for a heart that suffers with those who suffer.
exp.4:28:
This verse describes an enemy army as a lion. Its roar, or loud growl, is like that of young lions. It growls, seizes its prey, and carries it off with no one able to rescue it. It is a picture of strength, speed, and a people that cannot be stopped.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. After the song of the vineyard and several woes against injustice, God announces that he will bring a distant nation as judgment. Many believe this refers to Assyria, although the text does not give the name, and some think of Babylon as well.

For today: God takes justice and faithfulness seriously. If we have neglected something, we can return to him now with humility, knowing that his discipline seeks to restore us and that his mercy remains open.
exp.12:15:
It says that when Babylon falls, its children will be violently thrown down and dashed to pieces before their parents' eyes. The houses will be plundered, and the women will be violated. It is a very harsh description of what happens in a conquest.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, announcing God's judgment on a proud and violent nation. God says he will raise up the Medes as his instrument. The text does not celebrate cruelty, but warns how terrible war is and how terrible the sin of empires is. Interpreters see here both a historical warning and a sign of God's final judgment.

For today: let us not trust in power or wealth, because every human empire falls. And if we suffer violence or injustice, we can trust that God sees and will judge with justice.
exp.28:12:
It says the people come close to God with words and praise, but their heart is far from Him. Their respect toward God no longer comes from loving Him, but is a rule learned from people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at a time when Jerusalem lived with a religion that was only for show, while it trusted in its own plans and alliances. The verses before show that the people did not understand what God was saying, like someone holding a sealed book. Then God announces that He will act and will put human wisdom to shame.

For today: before you sing, pray, or go to church, ask God to examine your heart. Let your worship be sincere, and let your obedience come from loving Him, not just from habit.
exp.28:2:
Here God says he will surround Jerusalem with an enemy army. The phrase for pitching camp is what it means to set up camp around a city; the siege engines are war machines used to attack it; and the siege ramps are towers or earthen mounds raised to assault the walls.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The city is named here as Ariel, a name for Jerusalem, and the text links it to David and to the sacrifices of the temple. Its exact meaning is debated. The people kept up their ceremonies, but without a sincere heart, and God warns that he will bring them low. Many believe this refers to the Assyrian siege, though it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: it is not enough to perform rituals or religious customs if the heart is far from God. We can honestly ask ourselves whether our faith is real or only routine. God corrects us to wake us up, and we can always return to him with humility.
exp.55:2:
This verse says that the foreigner who has joined himself to the Lord must not think, "The Lord will surely separate me from his people." Nor should the eunuch say, "I am a dry tree," that is, someone without fruit or future. The verse's word "joined" means united or drawn near.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. There were people who could feel shut out: foreigners and eunuchs, whom the law restricted in certain aspects of life among the people (Deuteronomy 23:1-8). God assures them that, if they keep his covenant, they will have a place in his house and an enduring name, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel lesser, without value, or out of place, do not define your future by that label. If you have drawn near to God in faith, he receives you. Learn to trust his word more than your fears, and welcome also those who feel excluded.
exp.48:24:
God answers a hard question: who can take the prey away from a strong warrior? He says that he will. The captives of the mighty will be set free. "Contend" means to argue a case or take up a dispute in court, so God promises to defend the cause of his people. "I will contend" means that he himself will take up their case. He also promises to save their children.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Zion, that is, to Israel in exile, who felt abandoned. Their oppressors seemed impossible to overcome. God declares that his power is greater, and so everyone will know that he is Savior and Redeemer.

When you feel that a problem is too big for you, do not face it alone. Bring it to God in prayer, trust that he defends his own, and keep waiting on him, even when the solution takes time.
exp.26:5:
It says that a time will come when the people of God, called Jacob and Israel, will be like a tree that puts down roots, blossoms, and sends out new shoots. They will bear so much fruit that the face of the world (the surface of the earth, the whole world) will be filled. The word "fill" here means to be full.

He speaks within a song about his vineyard (Isaiah 27:2-5). He says that he has no anger against it and invites his enemies, like thorns and thistles, to make peace with him. After the discipline, he promises restoration. Some see here a future fulfillment for Israel, others a blessing that reaches the nations through the people of God.

For today: even when you go through trials or correction, God does not leave you there. His goal is for you to take root again in him and bear fruit. Trust in his process and seek peace with him.
exp.7:15:
It says that God's message should be kept carefully. "Bind up" and "seal" are like closing an important document to protect it. The "testimony" and the "law" are the word that God spoke through Isaiah. The "disciples" are those who listen to him and learn from him.

Here Isaiah speaks, or according to some, the Lord speaks through him. Judah was rejecting God and sought security in political alliances instead of in Him. Many would stumble because they did not believe. That is why the message is entrusted to a faithful group, so that it would remain as proof when it came to pass. Scholars disagree about whether "seal" means keeping it hidden or simply making sure it is authentic.

For today: when many ignore God, do not be discouraged. Keep His Word in your heart, study it with other believers, and trust that God does what He says.
exp.48:1:
He says that God made the Servant's words powerful and piercing, like a sharp sword. He also kept him protected under the shadow of his hand. He made him like a polished arrow, ready to be shot, and kept him hidden in his quiver, the case where arrows are kept.

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, who calls out to the islands and distant peoples to listen to him. God called him from before he was born. In the text, this Servant is called "Israel," and many Christians see in him Jesus, who carries out the mission that Israel was not able to accomplish. Others understand him also as Israel or a faithful remnant. God prepares him and takes care of him before sending him out.

God cares for and prepares his servants, even in times that seem hidden or silent. If you feel kept in the quiver, not doing much, trust: God knows when and where to send you.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that the waters of Nimrim will run dry. So the grass will wither, the tender shoots will fade, and nothing green will be left. The words that the verse calls old forms of "dry up" and "wither" are the same idea as the verse's "is withered away" and "faileth," so the verse's comment on them is replaced here with the verse's own wording. It is the picture of a fertile land left without life.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God about Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. He announces a destruction that leaves the people weeping and fleeing. Nimrim was in the region of Moab, although scholars are not sure of its exact location. It stands out that Isaiah says his heart cries out for Moab: the message of judgment is not delivered coldly, but with pain.

For today: what seems secure, like water, work, or riches, can disappear quickly. Place your trust in God and learn to feel compassion, even for those who suffer the consequences of their own ways.
exp.62:3:
God says that he has kept a day in his heart to bring justice against evil. "Vengeance" here means justice that sets crooked things straight, not an uncontrolled anger. The verse also says that the year of his "redeemed" has come, that is, the time when he rescues his people. "Has come" simply means that the time has arrived.

The Lord speaks, presented as a warrior coming from Edom with his clothes stained, like someone who has trodden grapes in the winepress. He does this alone, because no one else could save. Isaiah shows God judging the oppressors and freeing his people. Some Christians also see in this a look toward Christ; others read it mainly as historical judgment.

For today: if you have suffered injustice, do not take revenge with your own hands. Hand the matter over to God, trust that he will do justice in his time, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.10:7:
This verse says that a nursing infant will play beside the hole of a venomous snake, and a child just weaned will put his hand into the den of a dangerous serpent, without suffering harm.

Isaiah, God's prophet, describes the reign of the Messiah, the descendant of Jesse, father of David. He speaks to a people struck by injustice and fear. Many understand these images as a picture of complete peace, and others see them as poetic language. The verses that follow say that this peace comes because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the LORD.

For today: God promises a peace that heals what we fear most. While it arrives in full, we can seek to know him better and be people who bring peace to our home and work.
exp.4:27:
This verse describes a very well-prepared army. The arrows are sharp, and their bows are drawn tight and ready to shoot. The horses' hooves are as hard as flint, and the chariot wheels spin with the force of a whirlwind.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who had fallen into injustice and disobedience. In chapter 5, the prophet announces that God will bring a distant nation as judgment. Many believe it refers to Assyria, although the text does not give the name here. God is the one who calls that army.

For today: God does not overlook injustice, but his warnings aim to bring us back to him. Today you can ask God in prayer what area of your life needs correction, and respond with humility before the consequences grow.
exp.58:2:
This verse describes the people's sin using the image of a whole body: hands stained with blood, fingers full of wickedness, lips that speak lies, and a tongue that utters twisted things. "Stained" means dirty or soiled. "Wickedness" is injustice, doing what is not right.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. The verse before makes clear that God is able to save and able to hear. The problem is not His power, but that the people's sin had separated them from Him. That is why the prophet shows them plainly what they were doing: violence, deceit, and injustice. Scholars debate the exact date of this passage, but the message is clear.
