For today: before we think that God is far away, it is wise to examine honestly our actions and our words. We can ask for forgiveness and begin to speak the truth and to treat others well.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that when that time comes, the "glory of Jacob," that is, the splendor and strength of the people of Israel, will be made small. The phrase "shall be made thin" means it will diminish. The "fatness of his flesh" speaks of a full, healthy body, and "shall wax lean" means it will become thin and weak.

Isaiah speaks as God's messenger in the midst of a judgment against Damascus and Ephraim (the northern kingdom), which had joined forces against Judah. By trusting in human alliances instead of in God, Ephraim would lose its power. The harvest images that follow show that almost nothing would be left, although a remnant would survive.

For today: let us not place our security in riches, alliances, or our own strength, because all of these can fade. Let us trust in God, who cares for his own even in times of scarcity.
exp.22:0:
The message concerning Tyre: Tyre, the great trading city by the sea, is said to have been destroyed completely, with no houses and no harbor to enter. A "burden" means a heavy message of judgment. The "ships of Tarshish" were large trading vessels, and they are told to howl, that is, to cry out loudly in grief. The name "Chittim" is usually connected with Cyprus; there the sailors learn the news when they return.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, announcing a message from God against Tyre, a wealthy and proud city. Interpreters disagree about which conquest is meant: some think of Babylon, others of Alexander the Great, and others see several stages. The text does not make this clear.

For today: wealth and success are not a safe refuge. Place your trust in God, and use all you have with humility and generosity.
exp.40:15:
God says he will make the enemies like chaff that is blown away. To "fan" grain is to throw threshed grain into the air so the wind carries off the chaff. The phrase "he will scatter them" means that he will scatter them. A "whirlwind" is a strong wind that spins around. By contrast, God's people will not be scattered: they will rejoice in the Lord and take pride, in the good sense, in knowing the Holy One of Israel.

God speaks to Israel, calling them worms and few, that is, weak and small. He encourages them not to fear, because he is their Redeemer. He compares them to a new threshing sledge, a tool that crushes grain, to say that God will use them with power against what looks like a mountain. Interpreters debate exactly who these enemies are; the text does not name them here.

For today: when you feel small before an enormous problem, do not put your trust in your own strength. Bring your fear to God and seek your joy in him, rather than in everything turning out well.
exp.57:12:
If you turn your foot away from the sabbath, that is, if you stop using it to do what you please, and you call it a delight, the holy day of the Lord, honourable, and you honour it without following your own ways, without seeking your own pleasure, and without speaking your own words, a promise will come.

"Turn away thy foot" means to hold back your steps. "Honour" means to show respect.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked a false fast, one that looked religious but ignored justice and compassion toward the needy. Now he shows that the sabbath was meant to be joy and communion with God, not a burden. The blessings that follow speak of restoration and of delight in the Lord.

For today: set aside time each week to rest and seek God without rush or distraction. Quiet the noise, pray, give thanks, and enjoy his presence as a gift, not as an obligation.
exp.30:5:
This verse says that the people should return to God, from whom the Israelites had turned away and had opposed with great stubbornness. The word "turn" means "return." "Deeply revolted" means that their rebellion was great and deeply rooted.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah sought protection in Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. A few verses earlier, God promises to defend Jerusalem like a lion guarding its prey and like birds covering their nest. So this call comes with tenderness: God cares for those who had turned away, and He invites them to come back. Then He announces that they will abandon their idols and that Assyria will fall.

For today: if at any time we trust our own plans, money, or human help more than God, we can stop and return to Him sincerely. He still welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.46:1:
It says that Babylon, once proud and pampered, will be brought low like a slave. She will have to grind grain at the mill, hard work fit for servant women. The words that refer to the hair are the lock of hair; removing the veil and baring the legs to cross the rivers speaks of being left exposed, like a captive led away into exile.

God speaks through Isaiah. Babylon had dominated other peoples, even the people of God, and had believed herself eternal and without rival. God announces that her fall will come, and that He Himself will do justice. Scholars agree that it is an image of humiliation, though not all of them agree on every detail.

For today: pride and power seem firm, but they do not last. God sees injustice and is the Redeemer of his own people. Today you can live with humility and trust that He cares for you and brings about justice in his time.
exp.25:6:
It says that the life of the one who does what is right goes along a straight road, without bending. God, who is perfectly upright, "weighs" that road, meaning he examines it with justice and keeps it level, like someone smoothing a path. The word "just" refers to a person who lives according to the will of God.

These words belong to a song of trust in Judah, in the book of Isaiah. Before this, the text speaks of God humbling the proud city, and the poor trampling it. Afterward, the people say they wait for God and seek him from the early morning. Interpreters disagree about which city is meant, but the message is clear: God corrects the arrogant and cares for the humble.

For today: when your path feels hard, keep doing what is right and trust that God sees your life with justice. Ask him to guide you each morning.
exp.18:21:
God says he will strike Egypt, but not to destroy it; he will strike it in order to heal it. The blow is a correction. Afterward, the Egyptians will turn back to the Lord, and he will receive them with kindness.

Isaiah the prophet speaks, announcing a message from God about Egypt, a nation seen in Israel's thinking as an enemy and oppressor. The immediate context shows that Egypt would cry out to God in its suffering, and God would send them a deliverer. Interpreters differ about when and how this is fulfilled, but all of them see an announcement of hope for the nations.

For today: when God corrects you, do not see it as rejection. His aim is to heal you and draw you closer to himself. Also remember that his mercy reaches even those who seem most distant.
exp.37:10:
He says that Hezekiah, believing himself close to death, thought he would no longer see the LORD (God's name, the short form of "Jehovah") in "the land of the living." He also thought he would no longer see people, the inhabitants of the world, that is, the people who live on the earth.

King Hezekiah of Judah is the one speaking. He wrote this lament when he was seriously ill, before he was healed. He felt as if his life were being cut short in the middle. His grief was not only about losing his life, but about losing fellowship with God in the temple and with the people. Some think it reflects a limited view of the afterlife in his time; the text does not fully explain this.

When pain makes everything seem dark, we can be honest with God, as Hezekiah was. He did not hide his distress. Let us bring our fears to God and value each day of life so that we may stay close to Him and to others.
exp.8:19:
He says that the desperate people will seize violently whatever they find on the right and still be hungry; then they will eat whatever they find on the left and still not be satisfied. The word "snatch" here means to grab or tear away greedily. In the end, each one will devour the flesh of his own arm, a very strong image: they end up harming themselves and their own families.

Some understand "arm" as a relative or neighbor; others see it as a picture of self-destruction.

Speaking on behalf of God, Isaiah announces judgment on the northern kingdom, Israel, for its wickedness and injustice. The nation turns against itself: Manasseh against Ephraim, and both against Judah. It is the internal violence that follows when a people turns away from God.

Today it reminds us that selfishness and rivalry never satisfy and end up destroying families, churches, and communities. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that seeks peace and cares for a brother instead of competing with him.
exp.59:4:
Then Zion will see and be radiant, and her heart will swell with joy and wonder. The phrase "her heart will swell" means that her heart will be filled with joy and amazement. "The multitude of the sea" refers to the wealth and the people of distant lands, and "the strength of the nations" means the goods and power of the nations. All of this will turn toward her.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, after announcing that the glory of God rises upon her. It is a promise of restoration: God will bring the children of the people back from afar and draw the nations to her. Some see this fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also in Christ and the Church. Interpreters understand it in various ways.

For today: when you feel small or without hope, remember that God can restore what seems lost. Trust in Him and keep your heart open to joy and gratitude.
exp.23:22:
It says that the sun and the moon, which seem so bright and powerful, will be overshadowed before the glory of God. "Lord of hosts" means the Lord who commands over all power. The word "reign" means that he will rule, and "ancients" refers to the leaders of his people.

Isaiah speaks in a passage where he announces God's judgment on the earth and on the powers that rise up against him. The verse before speaks of "that day," a time in which God acts. Some understand this as the end of time, while others also see a broader meaning in history. What is clear is that it ends with hope: God reigns.

Today we can remember that nothing we admire or fear stands above God. When something seems too great to us, let us offer it to him in prayer and trust in his rule.
exp.4:21:
It says that God cries out a warning of "woe" against those who pride themselves on being champions at drinking wine and experts at preparing strong drinks. What should bring them shame, they take as a source of pride.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. He is denouncing leaders and powerful people who have turned good into evil and evil into good. The verse that follows shows that this life of excess went hand in hand with injustice: they acquitted the guilty for bribes and took away the rights of the innocent.

For today: examine what you feel proud of. If something controls you, such as alcohol or any other pleasure, ask God for help and seek support from people you trust. A clouded or enslaved mind rarely acts with justice and clarity.
exp.45:4:
God asks a question to make us think: to whom can God be compared? The words "liken" and "equal" mean placing someone on the same level. "Compare" means measuring one thing against another. The implied answer is that no person and no thing is like him.

The Lord speaks to his people Israel, who were surrounded by nations with idols. Earlier he reminded them that he carried them from birth and will carry them into old age. Then he describes how people make idols out of gold and silver, and then the idols must be carried because they cannot move or respond. The contrast is clear: the living God carries his people; idols have to be carried.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we carry as if they could save us: money, success, or approval. When you feel weary, rest in the God who sustains you and listens to you.
exp.58:19:
God says he will send a Redeemer, that is, someone who rescues and sets free, to Zion, meaning Jerusalem and its people. This salvation is for those who turn from wickedness in Jacob, which is another name for Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the people are accused of injustice and sin, and God sees that no one can save them. So he himself acts. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:26-27, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. How it applies to Israel in the future is understood in different ways.

For today: salvation is a gift from God, but it is received by turning back to him. If there is something you need to leave behind, today you can confess it honestly and trust in the forgiveness that the Redeemer offers.
exp.56:17:
God says that he has seen how his people have lived, with their mistakes and their stubbornness, and yet he promises to heal them, to lead them as a shepherd does, and to give them comfort. For the phrase about leading them, the verse speaks of guiding and caring for them, and the wording about giving comfort is clear on its own. The ones who mourn are those who weep and grieve.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he said that he had been angered by the greed of the people, and that they kept on rebelling. But God does not want to stay angry forever, since the human spirit would break under it. His discipline has a limit, and his aim is to restore. Some scholars think this refers to the people in exile, though the message reaches anyone who turns back in repentance.

For today: if you feel wounded by your own mistakes or by a loss, do not hide from God. He already knows your path and offers you healing. Bring him your pain and your guilt today in prayer, and let him lead you.
exp.0:10:
God asks, sadly, what use he has for so many sacrifices. He says he is already full of the burnt offerings of rams and of the fat of well-fed animals. He takes no pleasure in the blood of bulls, lambs, or male goats. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah kept up its temple rituals, yet it lived with injustice, as the following verses show. God is not rejecting here the sacrifices that he himself commanded, but he rejects them when the heart is far from him and there is no obedience.

For today: attending church, singing, or giving offerings is not enough if I mistreat others. Today I can ask myself whether my daily life, my words, and my fair treatment of others match my worship of God.
exp.48:11:
God's people will return from very distant places. Some will come from far away, others from the north and the west, and others from the land of Sinim. The verse of "Sinim" is not fully agreed upon: some think it is a distant region to the east or the south, perhaps Egypt or even China, but this is uncertain.

God speaks to Israel, who lives in exile and feels abandoned. He has already promised to guide them, give them water, and open paths for them. This verse shows that the promise is broad: God will gather his people from every direction. Shortly afterward, Zion says that God has forgotten her, and the Lord answers with tenderness.

For today: if you feel far away or forgotten, remember that God knows where you are and can bring you back. No distance, mistake, or loneliness is too great for his care. Trust his guidance and take the next step toward him.
exp.58:17:
This verse says that God will give each person what they deserve. The words "repay" and "pay" mean responding with justice to what has been done. "Return fury" means paying back anger to those who oppose Him. "The islands" probably refers to distant lands, and they too will receive God's judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of a people full of injustice and wickedness. God sees that no one intercedes or sets things right, so He Himself acts, clothed in righteousness like a soldier in armor. His judgment is not caprice but a response to evil. And right after comes hope: the Redeemer will come to Zion, to those who turn away from their wickedness.

For today: do not take revenge with your own hands; trust that God sees all injustice and will judge it rightly. In the meantime, take up His invitation to turn back to Him, for His redemption is open to whoever repents.
exp.48:19:
This verse says that the children born in times of loss and sorrow are now so many that the place has become too small for them. They say to Zion: "Move aside, so that I may live here." The words "too strait" mean narrow or cramped. The "children of your bereavement" are the children born when she felt alone and without children. "Give place" here means step aside to make room.

God speaks through Isaiah to Jerusalem, called Zion, who felt forsaken during the exile. He promises to restore her and fill her with people. The picture is of a mother who believed she had no children and suddenly sees a huge family. Some also see here a broader promise for the people of God.

For today: when you go through a season of loss or loneliness, do not think that God has finished with you. He can bring fruit and companionship where you did not expect them. And when God gives you more, be ready to make room and receive with generosity.
exp.1:15:
This verse continues a list of great things that people admired. It says that the day of the LORD will also come upon all the ships of Tarshish, meaning the large trading vessels, and upon all the pleasant pictures, meaning beautiful and valuable works of art. Tarshish was a distant place; scholars are not sure where it was.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He warns that God will judge everything they trusted in: mountains, towers, wealth, and luxury. The following verses explain the reason: human pride will be brought low, and only the LORD will be exalted.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, achievements, and beautiful things are not evil in themselves, but they become dangerous when they take the place of God. Today, give thanks for what you have and offer it to Him with humility.
exp.6:9:
This is a brief introduction. It says that God spoke again to King Ahaz, that is, that he continued his message. "Spake again" means "kept speaking" or "spoke once more." "Ahaz" is the older spelling of the name.

The one speaking is the Lord, the LORD of hosts, through the prophet Isaiah. Ahaz, king of Judah, was afraid because Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom) were threatening him. God had just told him to trust, and that if he did not believe, he would not remain firm. Now he gives him another opportunity: he offers him a sign to help him believe. Even so, Ahaz will reject it with an excuse that sounds pious.

For today: God keeps speaking to us with patience, even when we doubt. When you feel fear, do not shut yourself in or look only for human solutions; listen to his Word and respond with sincere faith, not with religious excuses.
exp.31:2:
When the righteous reign comes, it says, people will be able to see and hear clearly. "Shall not be dim" means their eyes will not be clouded or shut. "Shall hearken" means their ears will listen closely and truly understand.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah, who lived among injustice and spiritual blindness. He first announces a just king who will be a refuge and relief, like shade in the heat. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus; others connect it first to King Hezekiah. Both readings are possible. He then says that the foolish will understand.

For today: ask God for eyes and ears that are attentive. Before you give an opinion or pass judgment, take a moment to read God's Word and to listen with humility, both to God and to those who speak to you.
exp.37:7:
God promises that he will turn back the shadow ten steps on the "dial of Ahaz," and so it happens. The word "degrees" can also be understood as "steps" or "stairs," and the "dial" seems to have been a stairway or structure that marked the time by the shadow of the sun. "Went down" means "was turned back."

Isaiah speaks to King Hezekiah, who was gravely ill and had prayed with tears. God promises to heal him and to deliver Jerusalem from the king of Assyria. This sign confirms that God will keep his word. How the phenomenon happened exactly is not explained in the text, and it has been interpreted in several ways.

For today: when your situation seems to have no way out, remember that God is faithful to what he promises. Bring your fears to him in prayer and trust his word, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.11:1:
What it says: The verse affirms that God is the one who saves. "Health" here means salvation, not physical well-being. "I will be confident" means "I will feel secure and trusting." The name of God appears in a short form and a full form. The speaker says they will not be afraid, because God is their strength and the reason for their song.

Context: Isaiah 12 is a short hymn of thanksgiving. The people of God, Israel, speak "in that day," that is, when they are restored after the judgment announced in the earlier chapters. They acknowledge that God was angry, but that his anger passed and he comforted them. Many Christians also see here a look toward the complete salvation in Christ, though the original text speaks first of Israel's deliverance.

For today: When fear overtakes you, do not just stare at the problem. Remember how God has sustained you before, and give thanks out loud, perhaps with a prayer or a simple song.
exp.32:22:
It says a ship was badly prepared: the ropes are slack, the mast is not firm, and the sail cannot be spread. Even so, there will be a great spoil that is divided, and even the lame will take their share. The word "tacklings" in the verse names the ropes that hold the mast and sail, and "loosed" means they have gone slack and are not drawn tight.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and distress. The verses before it present the LORD as judge, lawgiver, and King who saves. Many understand the weak ship to represent the enemies, who cannot control the situation. Others think it describes Jerusalem. The text does not make clear who the subject is, so it is wise to read it with caution.

For today: when you feel weak or poorly prepared, remember that your security does not depend on your own strength but on God, who can give you what you need.
exp.12:14:
It says that, on the day of judgment against Babylon, no one who is captured will escape. "Thrust through" means pierced with a spear. The phrase "joined unto them" means whoever joins with them or enlists alongside them, and "fall by the sword" means they will die by the sword.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, and God himself speaks of its judgment. The verses before this one speak of the day of the Lord, with the heavens and the earth trembling. The verses that follow announce that God will stir up the Medes. It is harsh language, typical of ancient warfare. Interpreters see here the historical fall of Babylon, and some also see an image of God's final judgment against human pride.

For today: God takes injustice and arrogance seriously, and no human power lasts forever. Trust that He judges with justice. And examine your heart: do not join yourself to what God condemns, but seek his mercy.
exp.27:20:
He says that God will rise up to act, as he did at mount Perazim and in the valley of Gibeon. In both places God fought on behalf of his people against their enemies (2 Samuel 5:20; Joshua 10:10-12). Here, however, his judgment will come against his own people. That is why he calls his work "strange": it is not what he most delights in, but it is necessary.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the proud leaders of Judah, who mocked his warnings and trusted in political alliances to protect themselves. God warns them that the judgment is real and that their false refuges will not cover them, like a bed that is too short.

Today, mockery in the face of God's correction hardens the heart. If God points something out to you, listen to it soon and return to him with humility, because his correction seeks to restore you.
exp.27:14:
They said the rulers of Jerusalem felt secure. They claimed to have made a covenant with death and an agreement with the grave, meaning they believed the punishment would not reach them. The overflowing scourge is a destructive storm or flood. Their refuge, they said, was a lie and falsehood.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God, addressing the mocking leaders of Jerusalem. With irony, he quotes what they themselves were saying. Many believe this refers to political alliances, perhaps with Egypt, to protect themselves from Assyria, although the text does not name it here. God then responds with a firm stone in Zion and with just judgment.

For today: examine what refuge you trust. Money, appearances, or a comfortable lie do not withstand the storm. Seek your security in God and in his truth, which does remain firm.
exp.56:15:
God says that he will not keep up his quarrel or stay angry forever. If he did, the human spirit would faint before him, that is, it would be worn out and unable to endure. The word "faint" in the verse above means to grow weak or be drained of strength. The "souls which I have made" are the people God himself created.

God speaks, the High and Lofty One, who dwells with the humble and the broken. His people had fallen into greed and rebellion, and God corrected them. But here he explains that his discipline has a limit. His aim is not to destroy but to heal, guide, and comfort, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel the weight of your mistakes or of a correction, remember that God corrects in order to restore, not to crush you. Draw near to him with humility and let him lift you up.
exp.39:24:
God asks a question: "To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal?" The one speaking is "the Holy One," that is, God himself. The words "or" means "or," and "equal" means "matched," and "shall I be equal" is the same as "to whom will you compare me."

God has just said that powerful rulers are like plants that wither when He blows on them. Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who feel that God does not see their suffering. So God reminds them that no one can be compared to Him, and He invites them to look at the stars, which He calls by name.

Today we may be tempted to trust in money, in leaders, or in our own strength. When something worries you, look up at the sky and remember who God is: nothing is greater than He is, and you can rest in His care.
exp.23:7:
It says that the music and the feasting are over. The tambourines (percussion instruments) no longer sound, the noise of those who were celebrating has ended, and the harp has fallen silent. It is a picture of sorrow: where there was once celebration, there is now stillness and grief.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks in a section that describes a judgment upon the whole earth. According to the text, the cause is that its inhabitants broke God's laws and the everlasting covenant (v. 5). Scholars debate whether it refers to a specific historical event or to a final judgment; the passage may carry both meanings.

For today: the joys of this world can end suddenly, so let us not place our security in them. Let us enjoy with gratitude what God gives, but trust in Him, who remains forever.
exp.58:6:
They run toward evil without a second thought, and they are in a hurry to kill innocent people. Their thoughts are full of "iniquity," which means wickedness and injustice. Wherever they pass, they leave "wasting and destruction," that is, ruin and pain.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He shows them that their sins, such as violence, deceit, and injustice, are the reason God seems far away and why there is no justice among them. Isaiah speaks on behalf of everyone and includes himself in the people's confession.

For today: evil almost always begins in the thoughts. Ask God to examine your mind, and reject today resentment, envy, or the desire to harm others. Take care what you think, because from there your steps are born.
exp.35:3:
Here Rabshakeh, an official of the king of Assyria, speaks to Hezekiah's envoys. He asks them to carry a message: the great king of Assyria wants to know what Judah is relying on to feel secure. Rabshakeh seems to be a title rather than a personal name, and it is usually understood as the chief cupbearer or a high-ranking officer. "Confidence" means security or hope placed in something.

Assyria had invaded Judah and was now threatening Jerusalem. Rabshakeh speaks with pride and wants to discourage the people. His question aims to show that Judah has nothing to trust in, neither its army nor Egypt.

For today: the question serves to examine us. When pressures come, where does my heart rest? Rabshakeh used it to intimidate, but we can answer it honestly before God, who is worthy of trust.
exp.57:4:
God asks whether the fast he wants is only something outward: spending the day afflicted, with the head bowed down like a reed, lying on sackcloth and ashes. "Afflict the soul" means humbling oneself or going without food. The sackcloth was a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning. God answers with two questions: do they call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord? The implied answer is no.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people complain that they fast and God does not respond. But God shows them that they were fasting while seeking their own gain, exploiting others, and quarreling. Their religion looked good, but their hearts were not with God or with their neighbor.

For today: before practicing something spiritual, such as prayer, fasting, or serving, ask yourself whether your treatment of others is in line with it. Today, concretely help someone in need or correct a small injustice you have been ignoring.
exp.65:22:
It says that, in the time God promises, all of humanity will come to worship him, every new moon and every sabbath. "From one new moon to another" refers to the new moon, the start of each month. "All flesh" means all people. [The sentence about the old form "á" is removed, since that word does not appear in the verse.]

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the close of the book. God promises new heavens and a new earth, and that his people will remain. It includes people from other nations, since he will also take priests from among them. The passage contrasts those who worship with those who rebelled. Christians interpret it in different ways: some see it as a picture of the future kingdom, others as symbolic language of universal worship.

For today: make worship a constant habit, not only an occasional one. Set aside a regular time, whether weekly or daily, to give thanks to God, pray, and listen to his Word.
exp.61:7:
God has made a solemn oath. The phrases about his strength and power speak of his might. He promises that he will never again hand over his people's grain for their enemies to eat, nor let foreigners drink the wine that his people worked to produce. Outsiders, meaning oppressors, are the people in view here.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem. Before this, enemies would carry off the people's harvests. Many readers understand this message as encouragement for those who had been exiled or had only recently returned, who were suffering poverty. God assures them of restoration: the fruit of their labor will be for them, and for praising him.

Today, we can trust that God cares for those who work and wait on him. When you feel that your effort is being lost, pray with perseverance, like the watchmen of the previous verse, and rest in God's faithfulness, while continuing to work honestly.
exp.4:11:
It says that at this people's feasts the music and the wine never fail. The harps, the lyres (stringed instruments), the tambourines (hand drums) and the flutes fill the air. But they do not look at or consider what the Lord is doing; that is, they do not take time to recognize his hand or his work.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah. This verse is part of a series of woes, or laments, against the injustice and the careless living of the people. The people were given over to pleasure and forgot God. For this reason the text goes on to announce exile, because of their lack of knowledge of God.

For today: enjoyment is not bad in itself, but it can dull our attention to God. Look for a moment each day to stop, give thanks, and notice what God is doing in your life.
exp.2:20:
The verse says that the Lord will take away the adornments of the women of Jerusalem: the rings, and the nose jewels, that is, the hoops or rings hung from the nose. It is part of a long list of fine jewelry and clothing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The daughters of Zion walked proudly and vainly (v. 16), while the people lived unjustly toward the poor. God warns them that he will remove what gave them pride and security. Some scholars see here a criticism of luxury; others, an announcement of the fall of the city.

Today we can ask ourselves what we depend on to feel valuable: clothing, money, or image. God does not condemn beauty in itself, but pride and indifference toward others. Let us ask him for a humble and generous heart.
exp.29:15:
Here God says that his people rejected the salvation he was offering them. They answered: "No; for we will flee upon horses," that is, they meant to seek escape through military strength and speed. The word "swift" is the one to note in the verse above: it means fast. God answers them with irony: if they flee, they will indeed flee, and those who pursue them will be even swifter than they are.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. The verses just before offered them rest, quietness, and trust in God. Many understand that the people were seeking protection in military alliances, perhaps with Egypt, instead of trusting in God. For that reason the result would be defeat and fear.

When you face a problem, before rushing to your own solutions, stop and pray. Trusting God is not doing nothing, but seeking his direction first and resting in his care.
exp.5:10:
Isaiah, after receiving his call, asks: "Lord, how long?" God answers that the judgment will last until the cities are wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land is utterly desolate.

The prophet Isaiah speaks with God, in the vision where he is sent. God entrusts him with a message for a people who do not want to listen, and Isaiah asks how long that hardness will last. The verses that follow say that, even so, a remnant will remain, like the stump of a felled tree, called the holy seed. Many see judgment here, but also hope.

For today: when you see someone rejecting the truth, or when you face difficult consequences, remember that God does not abandon completely. Trust that He can bring forth new life even where it seems that only a stump is left.
exp.27:2:
It says that the "crown of pride" of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot. "Trodden" means walked on, crushed beneath the feet. The crown represents the pride and glory of Ephraim's leaders, who gave themselves over to wine and vanity. What they considered so beautiful will end up on the ground.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf, probably before the fall of the northern kingdom (Israel, called Ephraim here), which fell to Assyria. Its leaders trusted in their wealth and their strength, and lived in excess. God announces that he will send a powerful force, like a storm and a flood, that will bring them down. But the passage ends with hope: God will be a crown for those who remain faithful to him.

Today we can ask ourselves what we take pride in, or where we place our security. Anything that does not rest on God is fragile. He wants to be our true crown.
exp.64:4:
Here the text describes people who separate themselves from others and say, "Stay where you are, do not come near me, because I am more holy than you." God responds that these people are a "smoke" in his anger, an irritation that does not go away, like a fire that burns all day.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He complains about a people who provoked him with practices of false worship: sacrifices in gardens, rites among the graves, and foods forbidden by the law. The serious thing is that, while they did this, they considered themselves superior to others. God overlooks neither their idolatry nor their pride.

For today: check whether you ever look down on others because you think you are more spiritual. True holiness is not presumed upon and does not push people away; it makes us humble and compassionate, and it brings us closer to God and to others.
exp.19:0:
This verse marks the time when what follows takes place. It says that Sargon, king of Assyria, sent a high military commander (called Tartan in some other versions) to Ashdod, a Philistine city. There he fought against the city and captured it.

The passage is a historical fact that serves as an introduction. Assyria was the dominant power, and Ashdod had looked toward Egypt for help. That is why God speaks right away through Isaiah: Egypt and Ethiopia would not be a safe refuge either. Historians usually place this event around 711 B.C., although the exact dates are debated.

Today we can learn not to place our security in human strengths that seem firm, such as money, connections, or power. When crises come, only God is a refuge that does not fall. Trust in Him first.
exp.39:12:
It says that no one has given lessons or advice to the Spirit of the Lord. It is a rhetorical question: the answer is "no one." The word "or" is simply the ordinary word for "or," and "taught him by counsel" means that no one gave him advice to instruct him.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who feel that God does not see their situation. Just before this, God appears as a tender shepherd and as a powerful Creator who measures the seas and the heavens. With these questions, Isaiah shows that God has perfect wisdom and needs no one's help. For this reason his care can be trusted.

When you do not understand what God allows in your life, do not give him orders or judge him from your limited view. Pray with sincerity, tell him your doubts, and rest in the knowledge that his wisdom is greater than yours. He cares for you as a shepherd cares for his lambs.
exp.39:19:
This verse says that a person of little means, who cannot afford gold or silver for an idol, looks for a wood that will not rot. Then he hires a skilled craftsman to make a carved image that will stay firm and not fall over. Presenting it as an offering to his god is what the source's first quoted phrase refers to, and the second quoted phrase means that it is fixed securely in place.

God speaks through Isaiah to comfort his people, who were or would be in exile, surrounded by idols. With a certain irony, he shows how absurd it is to compare the Creator with something a man makes and must secure so that it does not fall. Right after this, he reminds them who God truly is: the one who stretches out the heavens.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can trust in things that we must hold up ourselves, such as money, success, or our image. Rest better in the God who holds you up.
exp.9:6:
God says that Assyria will be used as his instrument, but the Assyrian king does not see it that way. He does not think of carrying out a purpose of God; in his heart he only wants to destroy and wipe out many nations. To "uproot" means to pull up from the root, and "cut off" means to put an end to them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was full of injustice, and God announces that he will send Assyria as discipline against his people. But Assyria acts with pride and ambition, and for that reason God later says that he will also judge Assyria. God uses this king, but he does not approve of his wickedness.

For today: God can work even through situations and people who do not acknowledge him, and that does not excuse evil. Trust that God governs history, and examine your own motives so that you act with humility and justice.
exp.53:16:
No weapon formed to harm God's people will succeed. Every tongue that accuses them in judgment will be proved wrong. The "inheritance" the servants of the Lord receive is what God gives them as their share, and their righteousness, or their vindication, comes from God.

Speaking through Isaiah, the Lord comforts Jerusalem after promising restoration and peace. The people felt weak and threatened. God reminds them that he is the one who has authority over the blacksmith and over the destroyer, meaning that no enemy is outside his control. Some understand the promise in a general way, as applying to God's people as a whole; others see it fulfilled especially in Christ and his church.

For today: when you are attacked with criticism or lies, do not become bitter or seek revenge. Pray, keep doing good, and rest in the fact that God is your defender. The promise does not say there will be no attacks, but that they will not prevail.
exp.27:3:
He says that the beauty of Ephraim, the thing it was so proud of, will fade like a flower that dries up. Its city sat on a fertile valley, but it will be like the early fig of summer: as soon as someone sees it, they pick it up and eat it right away. The word "fading" describes a flower that withers; the phrase about it being swallowed up speaks of a quick destruction; and "in his hand" means within easy reach.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf against the northern kingdom, called Ephraim, and its capital, Samaria. Its leaders lived in luxury and drunkenness, trusting in their wealth. Isaiah announces that a strong invader will come like a storm. Many understand that he is referring to Assyria, although the text says it through images.

Today, beauty, success, or security can end quickly. Put your trust in God, not in what you boast about. He is the lasting crown.
exp.16:5:
It says that, after the judgment, only a small remnant will be left. It is like when the olive tree is shaken to gather its fruit: on the highest branch only two or three olives remain, and on the fruitful branches, four or five. The "gleaning grapes" are the few fruits left behind after the harvest. The "olive tree" is the tree itself.

Isaiah announces that God will leave Damascus and the northern kingdom, Israel (Jacob), without strength, since they had trusted in human alliances and in their idols. The Lord speaks through the prophet. The judgment is severe, but it is not total: a remnant remains. The verses that follow show that this remnant will turn its eyes back to its Maker.

For today: when life leaves you with little, do not lose hope. God can use those few "olives" to draw you closer to Him and teach you to trust in Him, not in your own securities.
exp.1:6:
It says that the land of Judah was full of silver and gold, with riches without limit. It also had a great many horses and war chariots, so many that they could not be counted. In other words, the country had plenty of money and military strength.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Before this verse, he calls them to walk in the light of the LORD, but he acknowledges that they had turned away from God, mixing themselves with foreign practices and fortune-tellers. Afterward, the text says that their land was also full of idols. Wealth and power were not evil in themselves, but they trusted in these things more than in God.

Today we can ask ourselves where our heart rests: in money, in security, or in God. Be thankful for what you have, but place your trust first in the Lord.
exp.4:16:
After the judgment, the lambs will graze in peace, as if they were in their own pasture. And strangers, that is, outsiders, will eat in the fertile lands that were left empty. The phrase "the waste places of the fat ones" here refers to rich or productive fields that have been abandoned. Some scholars understand the lambs to be the people who survive, and others take them to be simply flocks grazing among ruins. The text allows both readings.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He has just told the parable of the vineyard, which yielded sour grapes, and announced six woes against injustice, greed, and pride. This verse describes how the lands of the powerful would look after the judgment: empty and occupied by others.

Today it reminds us that accumulating wealth and power without justice does not last. What seems secure can be left abandoned. It is worth asking ourselves what we are building and whether it honors God and blesses others.
exp.36:17:
It says that the kings of Assyria did indeed lay waste many nations and their lands. "Countries" refers to the territories around a city or nation. Hezekiah does not deny Assyria's power; he acknowledges it honestly before God.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks here, in prayer within the temple. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was threatening him with a letter, mocking God. Hezekiah presents the actual facts and then recalls that the gods of those nations were made of wood and stone, while the LORD is the living God.

For today: when you face a great problem, there is no need to pretend it does not exist. You can tell God sincerely how serious it is and, at the same time, remind both him and yourself who he is.
exp.10:1:
He says that the Spirit of the Lord will remain permanently upon a future descendant of Jesse. That Spirit is described with six qualities, in three pairs: wisdom and understanding (seeing clearly and grasping things), counsel and might (planning well and having the power to carry it out), knowledge and fear of the Lord (knowing God and respecting Him with reverence). "Rest" means that the Spirit stays, not that it merely passes by.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and of weak kings. Jesse was the father of King David, so the stump and the shoot suggest that the dynasty seemed cut off, but God would cause something new to sprout. Christians see Jesus, the Messiah, here; Jews have read it as a promise of an ideal king.

For today: before deciding something important, ask God for wisdom and reverence toward Him, and do not rely only on your own cleverness or on what you see at first glance.
exp.42:3:
God tells his people that he values them greatly. "Of great worth" means of great value, and "honourable" means worthy of respect. Because of this love, he is willing to give other men and nations in exchange for them. "Life" here refers to the whole life of the person.

The LORD, the Holy One of Israel, speaks to Israel, a people facing exile and fear. The verses before it promise his presence in waters and fire, and the verses after it promise to gather his children from afar. The references to Egypt, Ethiopia and Seba are the language of rescue, and scholars interpret them in different ways, so it is best not to force an exact historical explanation.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements or on what others think of you. When you feel insignificant, remember that God loves you and is with you. Rest in that, and treat others as someone whom he also loves.
exp.54:4:
It says that someone will call nations that he did not know, and those nations, who did not know him either, will come running to him. They will not do so on their own merit, but because of the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who has honored him. The archaic spelling "Á" is the old form of "a", and "Jehová" is the name of God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the verse before, he mentions the covenant with David and someone set up as a witness and teacher to the nations. Many understand the "thou" to be the people of Israel, others see the ideal king who comes from David, and Christians usually see Christ. God invites everyone to come and live.

For today: God can draw people we would never have imagined. Live in such a way that others see God in you, and do not hesitate to kindly invite those who seem far away.
exp.65:11:
God himself promises to bring peace to Jerusalem, and that peace will be abundant, like a river that never runs dry. It also speaks of the riches of the nations that will come like a stream that has overflowed its banks. The people are described as a child: they will nurse, be carried in arms, and be bounced on the knees, being shown tender affection.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. His people had gone through pain, punishment and disappointment. God promises them restoration and joy. The verses that follow compare his comfort to that of a mother. Some understand this as a promise to the restored Israel, and others also see an announcement of God's future kingdom.

For today: if you are weary or wounded, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Come to God honestly and let him comfort you, as a child rests in its mother's arms.
exp.18:7:
The fishermen of Egypt will be filled with sorrow. Those who cast hooks into the river and those who spread nets over the water will grieve over their fate and lose their strength. The word "languish" means to be left without spirit or energy. "Mourn" means to weep and lament.

Isaiah prophesies against Egypt, within a message about God's judgment on that nation. The Nile was the source of life, food, and work for the Egyptians. If the river dried up, fishing, crops, and the trades that depended on it would also come to an end. Scholars do not agree on how or when this was fulfilled; some read it as a general warning that Egypt could not rely on its resources.

For today: examine what your security depends on. Work, money, or plans can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else runs dry.
exp.6:7:
It says that Syria has Damascus as its capital, and that its leader is King Rezin. In other words, Syria is nothing more than that: a human kingdom with limits. Then it announces that within sixty-five years Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) will be broken, meaning destroyed, until it no longer exists as a people.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid because Syria and Israel were planning to attack him. God tells him that those plans will not succeed. The sixty-five years are explained in different ways, and scholars do not agree on how to count them. What is clear is that the northern kingdom would fall.

For today: when problems seem enormous, remember that God rules above every human power. Trust in Him instead of letting fear control you.
exp.63:9:
What it says: The people describe with sorrow how the land has been left. The holy cities are empty, Zion (the mountain where the temple stood) looks like a wilderness, and Jerusalem is a lonely place, without people. "Desolation" here means a place that has been abandoned and laid waste.

Context: The prophet speaks on behalf of the whole people of Israel, in a prayer of repentance. They have just acknowledged that God is their Father and their potter, and they ask him not to remember their sin forever. Many believe it reflects the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile, though some also see it as a prophetic look toward that grief.

For today: When your life feels empty or in ruins, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, acknowledge what has gone wrong, and trust that he, as the potter, can still rebuild what has been broken.
exp.28:11:
This verse speaks of a book that is handed to a person who cannot read. When they are asked to read it, they answer that they cannot. The phrase that the quoted wording renders as "was given" simply means the book is handed over to them. It is the second image in the passage: before, the book was sealed; now, the one who receives it simply cannot read.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing the people of Jerusalem. He tells them that, because of their hardness, they could not understand his message, as if they were in a deep sleep. The verses that follow show the problem: they honored God with their lips, but their hearts were far away. Some interpret the image as a spiritual inability; others, as a judgment of God upon them.

For today: having a Bible or knowing religious words is not enough. Ask God for a humble and willing heart, and read his Word eager to obey it, not merely to keep a custom.
exp.50:10:
This verse promises that the redeemed of the Lord will return to Zion with singing. They will have a joy that never ends, like a crown on their heads. The words "return" and "flee away" in the verse express that the sorrow and mourning will go far away, like someone escaping.

God's people are suffering, probably in exile, and they ask God to act as he did before. They remember the exodus from Egypt and the crossing of the sea. Rahab and the dragon are poetic images of the power of chaos and evil. Then God himself answers with comfort, so that they will not fear human beings.

Today, if you are going through a painful time, remember what God has already done for his people. His past faithfulness encourages you to wait with hope. Pray with confidence and do not let fear rule your heart.
exp.62:14:
Here the people ask God to look down from his holy and glorious heaven. They ask where his zeal (his passion for defending his own) is, along with his strength and his tenderness. The words "bowels" and "mercies" speak of his deep compassion. The phrase "are they restrained?" means: have those expressions of his love toward us been held back or stopped?

The people speaking are Israel, probably in a time of exile or hardship, though scholars place it in different settings. Before this verse they recall how God led them through the wilderness and the sea. Now they feel far from him and confess that he alone is their Father and Redeemer.

For today: when you feel God is distant, you can pray honestly, as they do. Remember what he has already done for you, and ask him with confidence to look on you and help you.
exp.47:20:
It says that when God led his people through dry places, they lacked no water. He made water flow from a rock: he split the great rock and the waters gushed out. "They thirsted not" means they did not go thirsty; "the rock" is a large stone; "led them" refers to his guiding them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just invited the people to leave Babylon with joy and to announce that God has redeemed them. To give them confidence, he reminds them how he cared for their ancestors in the desert after they left Egypt (Exodus 17; Numbers 20). If he cared for them then, he can care for them now. The following verse warns that there is no peace for the wicked.

For today: if God calls you to leave something behind and move forward with him, you can trust that he will also provide what you need along the way. Remember how he has sustained you before, and take the next step in faith.
exp.42:24:
God says that He Himself, and no one else, is the one who wipes out the rebellions of His people. He does this for His own sake, that is, for the sake of His own name and His merciful character, not because the people deserve it. And He promises that He will not remember their sins, meaning that He will not hold them against them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel. The people had neglected their sincere offerings and, worse still, had burdened God with their wrongdoing. Even so, He offers forgiveness. Then He invites them to a court-like exchange, a dialogue in which they can present their defense, and He reminds them that sin goes back a long way.

Today, if you repent, you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry old guilt. Come to God with sincerity, receive His forgiveness as a gift, and live with gratitude.
exp.2:3:
He says that God will take away the capable leaders of the people and put in their place young people without experience. "Young men" are youths, and "children" can be understood as little ones or very immature people. "Princes" and "lords" are rulers. Some think it also speaks of rulers who act immaturely, even if they are not children.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The verses before it list the leaders God would remove: warriors, judges, counselors, and elders. When wise guidance is missing, disorder, violence, and despair would come, as what follows shows. It is the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: let us pray for our leaders and seek wisdom from God. Let us also patiently train the young, so that they grow with character and the fear of the Lord.
exp.0:18:
It says that if the people are willing and obedient, they will enjoy the best of the land. The phrase "if ye be willing" means "if you are willing," and "obedient" means "if you listen and obey." "Ye shall eat the good of the land" speaks of enjoying its fruits and its abundance.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah. He had just invited them to leave injustice, care for the orphan and the widow, and return to Him to be forgiven. Then he warns of the opposite: rebellion brings destruction. God does not force anyone; He sets out two paths and asks them to choose. The people had fallen into violence and injustice, though they still kept their religious rituals.

God offers forgiveness and blessing, but He expects a response from the heart. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God is asking of me that I have been putting off? Obeying Him, even when it costs us, is the path to His good.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that the king of Babylon struck the peoples in anger, and that the wounds he caused never healed. "Ruled as a master" means he dominated like an owner over his subjects. "Rage" refers to violent anger. He also pursued the nations without mercy and without restraint.

God commands Isaiah to raise up a mocking song, that is, a taunting poem, against the king of Babylon. The prophet speaks on God's behalf to a people who were suffering oppression. Scholars debate whether it refers to one particular king or to all of Babylonian power. The text celebrates that God broke the scepter of the oppressors and that the earth rested.

No cruel power lasts forever, however invincible it may seem. If you suffer today from an injustice, trust that God sees and knows how to act in his time. And if you have authority over others, use it to care for them, not to wound them.
exp.20:4:
This verse describes a scene of banquet preparations taking place while, at the same time, a watchman is posted to look out and the leaders are called to get ready for battle. "Anointing the shield" meant coating it with oil so that it was strong and blows would slide off.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. In the passage before, he tells how a vision about the fall of Babylon filled him with anguish and dread. Many understand that the verse shows how the city was feasting with confidence, not noticing that the attack was already coming. Some scholars read it differently, and the text does not make this fully clear.

For today: do not live distracted by comfort. Stay alert and spiritually prepared, praying and trusting God, because troubles often arrive when we least expect them.
exp.26:6:
This verse asks two questions about Israel. It asks whether God punished him with the same severity with which God struck those who struck him, or whether Israel was killed the way his enemies were killed. The implied answer is no: Israel's punishment was much milder.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, presenting God's words about his people, whom God compares to a vineyard. The context shows a God who corrects with measure, not with fury. His aim is to purge the sin of Jacob and restore him, so that he will bear fruit again. Some scholars understand "the one who struck him" as the enemy nations, and others read it differently; the general meaning remains the same.

For today: when God corrects us, he does not do it to destroy us, but to cleanse us and make us bear fruit. Receive his correction with confidence, knowing that his discipline is measured and comes from his love.
exp.24:2:
This verse says that a strong people will honor God, and that a city of violent or harsh people will hold him in respect. Here "shall fear thee" does not speak of terror, but of acknowledging God with awe and reverence. "Strong" means powerful and mighty.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, praising God after announcing his judgment. God brought down a strong and proud city, and the text does not give its name, so scholars interpret it in several ways. Seeing how God cares for the poor and humbles the proud, even the powerful end up acknowledging him. It is a song of gratitude for God's faithfulness.

For today: even if you have power, success, or security, your true strength is in God. Today you can thank him for his works and treat with compassion those who are weak, as he does.
exp.4:20:
This verse is a warning against intellectual pride. Those who are "wise in their own eyes" and "prudent in their own sight" are people who believe they are clever simply because they think so themselves. The word "woe" expresses grief and a warning of judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. This is a series of six "woes" against injustice: greed, drunkenness, mocking God, and twisted justice. Those who asked God to hurry, as if mocking him, and who called evil good, considered themselves wiser than God. Isaiah shows that this pride lies behind their bad decisions.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I accept advice or correction? One practical way to live out humility is to read the Bible with a willingness to be corrected, and to ask the opinion of wise and sincere people before making important decisions.
exp.39:21:
It says that God reigns from on high, over the "circle of the earth." The word "circle" can refer to a round circle or a rounded horizon; it is not certain that the prophet had a sphere in mind. The inhabitants of the earth look as small to him as grasshoppers. God stretches out the heavens like a thin curtain and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in.

Isaiah comforts a discouraged people who live in exile, surrounded by powerful nations and idols. The prophet contrasts the true God with the wooden images that people make. Before and after this verse, he shows that nothing and no one, not kings or rulers, can be compared with the Creator.

For today: when problems or authorities seem enormous, remember who is truly great. Bring your worry to God in prayer, trusting that he is still in control.
exp.6:22:
It says that in that time, a piece of land that had a thousand vines, each worth a thousand pieces of silver, would be abandoned and covered with thorns and thistles. A very valuable vineyard would turn into brush.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid of his enemies and sought help from Assyria instead of trusting God. Isaiah announces that judgment will come because of that lack of faith: the land would be left empty of people. Scholars agree that he speaks of an invasion, though they debate the exact details.

For today: what seems very valuable can be lost if we stop trusting God. We can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, in plans, or in the Lord. He cares for those who lean on Him.
exp.4:24:
God was deeply angry with his people because of their wickedness, and he struck them with his hand. The anger is described as intense wrath; the hills shook with a terrible tremor, and the bodies lying dead in the streets show how severe the judgment was. Even so, his anger has not faded: his hand is still stretched out, ready to correct.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the kingdom of Judah. This comes from the song of the vineyard (chapter 5), where the people produced injustice instead of good fruit. The verses before it condemn those who accepted bribes and despised God's law. Scholars debate which past blow the shaking refers to: some think of an earthquake, others see it as a general picture of judgment.

For today: God takes justice seriously. Today you can examine whether you are honest in your work and your dealings, and return to his word with humility before the correction becomes harsher.
exp.26:11:
The passage says that on that day God will act from the river Euphrates, from the riverbed itself, all the way to the stream of Egypt, a brook on the southern edge of the promised land. Here the word for God's action is understood as shaking or striking, the way an olive tree is shaken to gather its fruit. And the children of Israel will be gathered one by one, that is, personally, leaving no one behind.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Earlier he announced judgment on a city that lacked understanding. Now the tone changes: after the punishment comes the hope of restoration. Interpreters disagree about whether this refers to a historical return or to something still in the future.

For today: God does not treat his people as an anonymous mass; he seeks you one by one. If you feel far away or scattered, you can trust that he knows your name and invites you to come back.
exp.65:16:
This verse speaks of people who perform rituals to "sanctify" and "purify" themselves in gardens, probably in pagan worship, and at the same time eat things that the law called unclean: pork, something repugnant (an abomination), and the mouse. "Consumed" means destroyed. God says that all of them will share the same end.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. In context, He comes to judge with fire those who mixed their worship with idolatrous practices. He says that He knows their works and their thoughts. But judgment is not the final word: afterward He will gather all the nations so that they may see His glory.

For today: it is not enough to have outward religiosity if the heart is divided. Examine honestly what place God has in your thoughts and decisions, and ask Him to cleanse you truly, not merely in appearance.
exp.53:0:
God invites the barren woman, the one who never had children, to sing and shout for joy. The reason is that the children of the forsaken woman will be more than those of the married wife.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, right after the chapter about the suffering Servant (chapter 53). The woman represents Jerusalem or the people of God, who felt abandoned and without a future during the exile. God promises them restoration and growth. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4:27 and applies it to the children of promise.

When you feel empty or unproductive, do not decide by what you see today. Praise God with confidence, because He can bring life where it seems impossible.
exp.42:11:
God says that he announced what was going to happen, then saved his people and made them hear it. No foreign god was among them to do that. For this reason, Israel is a witness that only the LORD is God. The word "hear" here means to listen; a "strange" god is a false or other god; and "witnesses" are those who can tell what they saw.

Here God speaks himself through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, surrounded by peoples who worshiped idols. God reminds them that he had promised, had rescued, and had spoken clearly, something the idols never did. The verses that follow call him the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel.

For today: think about the times God helped you, held you up, or kept his word in your life. This week, tell someone one of those experiences in simple words. Your story can be a testimony that God is faithful.
exp.1:21:
Isaiah says: stop trusting in human beings. The phrase "stop relying on man" means "keep away from him," that is, do not put your trust in him. "Breath" is the air we breathe, the breath that is "in his nostrils": human life depends on a fragile puff of air. The question "what is he worth?" means: what value does he have that you should trust him instead of God?

Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. He has just described the day when God will rise up in majesty, the idols will fall, and the people will flee to hide. Earlier in the chapter he showed a nation full of pride, riches, and false securities. The prophet calls them not to lean on what cannot save them.

For today: when you feel pressure, check where you truly rest. Value and respect people, but do not make them your ultimate security. Place your trust first in God, who does not vanish like a breath.
exp.22:5:
This verse says that the people of Tyre must flee toward Tarshish, a distant place across the sea. The first phrase in the verse is a call to cross over, to go away. "Howl" means to cry out loud in pain. The "inhabitants of the isle" are the people of Tyre and its coastal area.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Tyre, a city very rich from maritime trade. The fall of Tyre would be so great that its inhabitants would seek refuge far away. Scholars do not agree on where Tarshish was; many think of the western Mediterranean, but this is not certain.

For today: wealth and success do not give us true security. Everything can change suddenly. It is wise to place our trust in God, not in what we have, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.43:7:
God tells his people not to be frightened or shaken. He reminds them that he had already announced long ago what he would do. That is why they are his witnesses, that is, people who can vouch that he is faithful. He declares that there is no other God besides him. The word "Rock" here means a secure refuge, and he says he knows of no other.

The Lord himself is speaking, presenting himself as the King and Redeemer of Israel. His people were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols, and God reminds them that only he announces what is coming and then fulfills it. He then contrasts this with idols, which neither see nor understand.

Today, when the future unsettles you, remember the times God sustained you. Tell those stories to others; your testimony strengthens your own trust and that of those who listen to you.
exp.23:8:
It says that there will no longer be feasts with songs and wine. The phrase about not drinking wine with singing means that no one will toast amid songs of joy. And the drink, which once gave pleasure, will taste bitter to those who take it. The little word "á" is an old way of writing "a".

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks on behalf of God. In this chapter he describes a judgment on the whole earth because of the wickedness and rebellion of the people. The harvests are lost, and the music and celebration fall silent. Commentators debate whether it refers to a near event, a final one, or both, and it is fair to say that not everything is entirely clear.

For today: do not place your joy only in passing things such as food, parties, or money. Ask God to be the source of your gladness, because what he gives does not turn bitter.
exp.22:14:
In Isaiah 23:15, Tyre, the great trading city on the coast, would be forgotten for seventy years, "according to the days of one king." That may mean the length of one reign or of one lifetime. Afterward, the city would sing again, returning to its trade and its fame, the way a prostitute goes back to her old ways. Being forgotten means no one would remember the city or go looking for it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf within a message about Tyre (chapter 23). Tyre grew rich through sea trade. The Bible uses the image of a prostitute for its ambitious commerce, which was sold to every kingdom. Commentators do not agree on exactly how the seventy years were fulfilled.

For today: success and wealth do not give lasting security. Ask yourself whether your trust is in God or in your achievements, and use what you have with honesty and generosity.
exp.27:25:
This verse says that the farmer knows what to do at each moment because God himself instructs him. Its comment on the wording of "discretion" is that it means with judgment, with good sense, and in an orderly way.

Isaiah speaks to leaders of Judah who mocked his warnings and trusted in their own alliances. He uses the example of the farmer to show that God does not act without measure: just as the plowman does not plow or thresh forever, God corrects with purpose and with limits. Some believe this speaks of discipline upon his people.

For today: when you go through a trial, trust that God works with wisdom and not without meaning. Ask him for the wisdom you need for each task and each season.
exp.36:0:
When King Hezekiah heard the news, he tore his clothes in a sign of grief, put on sackcloth (a rough cloth that was worn in times of mourning and humiliation), and went into the house of the Lord. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "after hearing this" means "after he had heard this."

The passage is about Hezekiah, king of Judah. Assyria, under its king Sennacherib, had invaded the land, and its spokesman, Rabshakeh, mocked God and threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah felt the weight of the crisis and of the blasphemy. He immediately sent his officials to ask the prophet Isaiah to pray.

When a piece of news crushes us, the first thing does not have to be panic or looking only for human solutions. We can come before God honestly, acknowledge our weakness, and also ask for the prayers of people of faith.
exp.20:5:
God tells the prophet to set a watchman, that is, a lookout who watches closely and reports right away whatever he sees. The lookout's job is simple: keep watch and pass on what is seen.

Isaiah speaks within a prophecy about a message of judgment, which many connect with the fall of Babylon, though not everyone agrees. The prophet is troubled by the vision, while the city seems to carry on with feasting. God tells him to keep watching, and the lookout then sees chariots and horsemen approaching.

For today: do not live distracted or indifferent. Set aside time to pray and to listen carefully to God, and humbly share what you learn from his Word to help others stay prepared.
exp.64:23:
This verse says that God will answer his people even before they ask him for help. And while they are still speaking, he has already heard them. To "call" means to cry out for help with urgency, and to "hear" here means that God has already listened and taken notice.

The Lord is speaking through the prophet Isaiah. He is describing a future restoration, with a new heaven and a new earth (v. 17), where his people will live in peace, without laboring in vain or suffering injustice. Scholars debate whether this is fulfilled in the return from exile, in the age of the church, or at the end of time. Many see a combination of these ideas.

For today: you can pray with confidence, knowing that God is not distant or slow to listen to you. He knows what you need. Do not stop praying, but do so with a sense of rest, without thinking that you have to convince him to attend to you.
exp.59:18:
This verse says that the sun by day and the moon's light by night will no longer be needed. God himself will be the lasting light of his people and their glory. The phrase "everlasting light" means a light that lasts forever, and "glory" here refers to what brings honor and splendor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a city that had gone through suffering and exile. Before this verse he promises peace, justice, and an end to violence. Afterward he says the days of mourning will come to an end. Some understand this as a restoration after the exile, and others as a promise that will be fully fulfilled in the future. Revelation 21:23 uses a similar image, and this helps us read it with Christian hope.

Today, when you find yourself in darkness because of sadness or uncertainty, pray and remember that God is your steady light. Seek him every day, because his presence does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.25:16:
The verse says the people felt like a woman with child who is near the time of her delivery: in sharp pain, groaning and crying out. "With child" means pregnant, and "delivery" means the birth of the baby. "In thy sight" means that this suffering was plainly seen by God.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking on behalf of the people of Israel (Judah). This is part of a song of trust that comes after times of punishment and distress. The people admit that they sought God in their trouble. But the verses that follow say that this pain did not bring the deliverance they had hoped for. Then comes the hope that the dead will live. Interpreters disagree about whether this speaks of the restoration of the nation, of the final resurrection, or of both.

For today: when you suffer and see no results, bring your pain to God honestly. He hears your cries and can give hope beyond what you see right now.

sum.33: God calls all the nations to listen, because he is angry with them and will hand them over to judgment. Edom in particular will suffer its punishment, and its land will be left in ruins, burning and inhabited only by wild animals. The chapter teaches that God acts with justice and that his word is fulfilled.
sum.57: God tells his people that their fasting is fake, because they fast while they fight, exploit others, and look out only for themselves. The kind of fasting that pleases him is ending oppression, sharing bread with the hungry, and helping people in need. If they do this, God promises light, guidance, restoration, and joy, and he also invites them to honor the Sabbath.
sum.63: Isaiah 64 is a prayer from the people asking God to come down and act with power, as he did in the past. They acknowledge that their sins and their "righteousness" are worth nothing, but they rest on the fact that God is their Father and they are the clay in his hands. They ask for forgiveness and help in the face of the destroyed city and temple.
sum.17: Isaiah 18 speaks of a distant land, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, that sends messengers by sea. God says he will watch calmly and, when the time comes, will cut off what seemed ripe, as with pruning knives. In the end, a strong and mistreated people will bring an offering to God on Mount Zion.
sum.62: A glorious warrior comes from Edom with stained clothes, for he has punished the nations and saved his own people. Then the people remember the mercies of God toward Israel, even though they rebelled, and they pray that God would look upon them, because he is their Father and Redeemer.
sum.8: Isaiah announces that the people who walked in darkness will see a great light: a child will be born, called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace, who will reign with justice forever. But Israel, proud and not seeking God, suffers judgment, division, and violence.
sum.32: Isaiah announces that the plunderer will be plundered, and the people cry out to the LORD, asking for mercy. God rises up as judge and king, and he burns up the wicked like thorns. Only those who live with justice and righteousness will dwell securely, and they will see Zion in peace, with their sins forgiven.
sum.1: In the last days, Isaiah announces, all the nations will climb the mountain of the LORD to learn his ways, and there will be peace, with no more wars.
