But the people of Judah have filled themselves with wealth, fortune-tellers, and idols. Because of this, the day of the LORD is coming, a day that will humble all pride, and only God will be exalted.
sum.49: God says that his people were sold and abandoned because of their own wrongdoing, not because he lacked the power to save them. His servant speaks with the teaching God has given him, endures blows and mockery with firmness, and trusts that God is helping him. Whoever walks in darkness must trust in God, and whoever lights their own way with their own fire will suffer pain.
sum.47: God speaks to Israel, a stubborn people who claim to believe in him but do not live in truth. He reminds them that he announced everything beforehand so that they could not credit their idols. For the sake of his own name, he refines them and does not destroy them, and he calls them to leave Babylon. He laments that by disobeying, they lost their peace.
sum.52: Isaiah speaks of a servant of God who is despised and full of sorrow. He suffers in silence like a lamb, even though he never did any wrong. He carried the sins and rebellions of everyone, and through his wounds there is healing and forgiveness. God will lift him up and honor him. Christians see Jesus in this passage.
sum.55: God calls his people to practice justice and keep the Sabbath, and he promises that foreigners and eunuchs who join themselves to him will be accepted, with a place and an everlasting name in his house of prayer for all peoples. But he denounces the blind, self-serving leaders who neglect the people.
sum.54: God invites all who are thirsty to come and receive freely what truly nourishes the soul, and He promises an everlasting covenant. He calls people to seek Him and to turn away from wrongdoing, because He forgives generously. His ways are higher than ours, and His word accomplishes its purpose, bringing joy and renewal.
sum.53: God calls Jerusalem, pictured as a barren and abandoned woman, to rejoice and enlarge her tent, because she will have many children and will no longer live in shame. Although he left her for a brief moment, he promises everlasting compassion, a covenant of peace that will not be shaken, and protection against every attack.
sum.29: God rebukes his rebellious people for seeking help from Egypt instead of from him, and for refusing to listen to his prophets. He warns them of ruin, but offers them salvation through rest and trust. He promises compassion, guidance and blessing, and judgment on Assyria.
sum.48: In Isaiah 49, the servant of the LORD says that God called him from the womb and made him a light to the nations, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Although Zion feels that God has forgotten her, he promises that he will not forget her, will restore her, and will rescue her children.
sum.10: God promises a righteous king who will come from the family of Jesse, filled with the Spirit of the LORD, who will defend the poor and bring a peace so great that even fierce animals will live together in harmony. He also promises to gather his scattered people, end their divisions, and make a way for them, just as he did when they left Egypt.
sum.51: God calls Jerusalem to wake up, rise, and free herself from her chains, because he will redeem her without payment and will make his presence known. Messengers joyfully announce that "your God reigns," and the people must leave clean, for God goes before them. In the end, his servant will be highly exalted, though first he will suffer, and kings will be left speechless.
sum.12: Isaiah announces God's judgment against Babylon. The "day of the LORD" is coming, bringing terror, darkness in the sky, and punishment for arrogance and wickedness. God will stir up the Medes against her, and the proud city will be left desolate, like Sodom and Gomorrah. The lesson is that God humbles pride and judges injustice.
sum.36: Hezekiah, facing the threats and mockery of the king of Assyria, takes the letter to the temple and prays, asking God to show that he alone is God. Through Isaiah, God promises to defend Jerusalem, and an angel defeats the Assyrian army. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.
sum.30: Isaiah warns that it is a mistake to trust in Egypt, its horses, and its chariots, instead of seeking the Holy One of Israel, because the Egyptians are only men. God promises to defend Jerusalem like a lion protecting its prey and like birds guarding their nest. He calls the people to turn back to him and leave their idols, and Assyria will fall.
sum.38: Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, and Hezekiah proudly showed them all his treasures. Isaiah announced to him that one day everything would be carried off to Babylon, including some of his own descendants. Hezekiah accepted the word of God, but his only concern was that there would be peace during his lifetime.
sum.44: God calls Cyrus, who did not know Him, to open doors and free His people, so that it may be shown that He alone is God, the one who holds both light and darkness. No one should argue with their Creator. God invites all nations to look to Him and be saved, and He promises that every knee will bow before Him.
sum.13: God will have compassion on Israel and give them rest. His people will sing a mocking song against the proud king of Babylon, who wanted to make himself equal to God and ended up brought low in the grave. God also announces that he will destroy Assyria, and he warns Philistia not to rejoice, because his plans do not fail and Zion is a refuge for the afflicted.
sum.18: God announces judgment on Egypt: there will be divisions, a harsh ruler, the river will dry up, and the wisdom of its advisers will turn into foolishness. But then Egypt will cry out to God, he will strike it and heal it, and they will know him and worship him. In the end, Egypt, Assyria, and Israel will be blessed together as God's people.
sum.59: God tells Jerusalem to rise and shine, because her glory is coming while darkness covers the other peoples. Nations, kings, and her scattered children will come to her with riches and praise. God promises to restore her, give her peace and justice, and be her everlasting light.
sum.46: God announces that Babylon, proud and secure in itself, will lose its throne and fall into humiliation. It was harsh toward God's people and trusted in its wickedness, its fortune-tellers, and its wisdom. But ruin will come suddenly, and no one will save it, because the Redeemer of Israel is the Holy One.
sum.41: God presents his chosen servant, gentle yet steadfast, who will bring justice and be a light to the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners. God calls the whole earth to sing to him, because he announces new things and will guide the blind. But Israel, deaf and blind, suffered punishment for not following his law.
sum.56: God rebukes his people for following idols and false alliances, while the righteous person dies with no one noticing, yet enters into peace. Although God was angry at their rebellion, he lives with the humble and broken-hearted, and he promises to heal them, guide them, and give them comfort and peace. For the wicked, however, there is no peace.
sum.16: God announces that Damascus will be reduced to ruins, and that Israel (Ephraim) will also grow weak, becoming like a field with almost no harvest, because it forgot God, its rock and its salvation. Even so, some will turn their eyes back to their Creator and leave behind their altars. In the end, the nations that attack his people will be scattered suddenly.
sum.21: God pronounces judgment on Jerusalem, called "the Valley of Vision." Faced with danger, the people trusted in their walls, weapons, and water supply, but they did not look to God. Instead of mourning, they gave themselves over to feasting. God also removes the proud steward Shebna from his office and puts Eliakim in his place, though at the end it is said that this "peg" will also fall.
sum.5: Isaiah sees the Lord seated on his throne, surrounded by seraphim who proclaim his holiness, and he feels unworthy because of his sin. One of the seraphim touches his lips with a coal from the altar, and Isaiah responds, "Here I am, send me." God gives him the task of speaking to a people who will not want to understand, but he promises that a holy remnant will remain.
sum.31: Isaiah announces a righteous king who will be like a shelter and cool water for his people, and who will give clear sight to the eyes and understanding to the foolish. He warns the complacent women that the land will be left desolate, until God pours out his Spirit and brings lasting justice, peace, and security.
sum.20: Isaiah receives a harsh vision about the Desert of the Sea: an army of Persians and Medes is coming to destroy, and the prophet trembles in anguish. The watchman announces that Babylon has fallen with its idols. Then the passage speaks of Dumah and Arabia, where there is night, flight, and a need to help the thirsty. God, who has spoken it, keeps control over the nations.
sum.25: Isaiah 26 is a song of trust in God. He gives perfect peace to those who trust in Him, humbles the proud, and guides the righteous. In their distress, the people wait for God, and it is announced that the dead will live. They are invited to hide for a little while until the wrath passes, for God will come to judge wickedness.
sum.19: God commands Isaiah to walk around without his outer clothing and barefoot for three years, as a sign that Assyria will lead captives away to Egypt and Ethiopia. In this way those who put their trust in them will be put to shame, and they will ask how they can escape. The lesson is that trusting in human powers leads to disappointment.
sum.9: God condemns those who make unjust laws and oppress the poor, widows, and orphans, and He uses Assyria as the rod of His punishment. But Assyria becomes proud, and God promises to judge it as well. A small remnant of Israel will return to trust in the Holy God, and His people should not be afraid.
sum.26: In that day, the LORD will punish Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent of the sea, and he will look after his vineyard day and night. Although Israel will be disciplined for its sin and its city will be left deserted, God promises that it will bloom again. Those scattered from Assyria and Egypt will be gathered together to worship him in Jerusalem.
sum.37: King Hezekiah became gravely ill, and the prophet Isaiah told him to get his affairs in order. Hezekiah wept and prayed to God, and God heard his prayer. He added fifteen years to Hezekiah's life and promised to deliver the city from Assyria, giving him a sign through the shadow on the sundial. Hezekiah thanked God because he had forgiven his sins and healed him.
sum.64: God lets himself be found even by those who were not looking for him, yet he judges his rebellious people who practice idolatry and consider themselves holier than others. Even so, he preserves a faithful remnant who will be blessed. He promises new heavens and a new earth, where there will be joy, long life, work that bears fruit, and peace, and he will answer before they even cry out.
sum.34: Isaiah announces that the desert will burst into bloom with flowers, water, and joy, because God himself is coming to save his people. The weak will be strengthened, the blind will see, the deaf will hear, and the lame will leap. There will be a "Highway of Holiness" on which the redeemed will return to Zion singing, with everlasting joy and without sorrow.
sum.15: Isaiah 16 is a message about Moab. Moab is asked to give shelter to the exiles, but its pride and its lies will not save it. Its vineyards and its joy will be destroyed, and within three years its glory will fall, leaving only a few who are weak. In the middle of this judgment, a throne of mercy and justice is announced in the tent of David.
sum.2: God is taking away from Jerusalem and Judah their leaders and their means of support, and the people fall into disorder, violence, and the oppression of the poor. He will judge the unjust rulers and the proud women of Zion, trading their luxury for mourning and ruin. The righteous will fare well, and the wicked will be repaid according to what they have done.
sum.22: Isaiah announces God's judgment on Tyre, the wealthy trading city, which will fall and be forgotten for seventy years. God decrees this to humble human pride and fame. Afterward Tyre will return to trade, but its profits will be dedicated to the Lord and will serve those who stand before Him.
sum.50: God invites his people to remember Abraham and to trust in his righteousness and salvation, which will last forever, rather than in fear of other people. He promises to comfort Zion, and that the redeemed will return singing. To Jerusalem, crushed and stunned by its punishment, he announces that he has taken the cup of his wrath out of her hand and will place it in the hands of her oppressors.
sum.60: A messenger anointed by God's Spirit brings good news: freedom for captives, comfort for those who mourn, and joy in place of sorrow. God promises to rebuild what was destroyed, to make an everlasting covenant with his people, and to bless them before the nations. The people rejoice, because God clothes them in righteousness and will make praise spring up.
sum.61: God promises that he will not stay silent until Jerusalem shines with his righteousness and salvation. He will give her a new name, she will no longer be called "Forsaken," and she will be loved like a bride. He appoints watchmen who will pray without rest, promises to protect her harvests, and announces that the Savior is coming to call his people "Redeemed."
sum.28: God warns that Jerusalem, called Ariel, will be brought low and besieged, but her enemies will vanish like a dream. The people honor God with their lips, yet their hearts are far from him, and so they become spiritually blind. In the end, God promises to rescue the humble, put an end to the violent, and restore his people.
sum.27: Isaiah warns that Ephraim, proud and drunk, will be brought down, and that its own leaders, priest and prophet, stumble from wine. The mockers of Jerusalem trust in lies, but God lays a firm stone in Zion: whoever believes does not rush. God judges with justice, and like the farmer, acts with wisdom and measure.
sum.58: Isaiah says that God is able to save, but the sins of the people, such as lying, violence, and injustice, have separated them from Him and left them in darkness. Seeing that no one stands up for the truth, God Himself acts to save. He promises that a Redeemer will come to those who repent, and that His Spirit and His words will remain forever.
sum.40: In this chapter God shows that he rules history: he raises up a conqueror and challenges the idols, which can announce nothing and do nothing. To Israel, his chosen servant, he says not to be afraid, because he helps them, sustains them, and redeems them. He also promises to turn the desert into a place of water and trees.
sum.14: Isaiah 15 announces that Moab will be destroyed in the night, and its cities will fall silent. The whole nation will mourn, wearing sackcloth, with shaved heads and cries of anguish, as they flee and their wealth is lost. God speaks with sorrow over Moab, but warns that further calamities will come upon the survivors.
sum.35: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, conquered the fortified cities of Judah and sent Rabshakeh with a large army to Jerusalem. With mockery and threats, Rabshakeh tried to take away the people's confidence in Egypt, in King Hezekiah, and in the Lord, promising peace and a good land if they surrendered. The people remained silent, and the messengers returned distressed to report everything to Hezekiah.
sum.6: When Syria and Israel threatened Jerusalem, King Ahaz was filled with fear, and God sent word through Isaiah telling him not to be afraid and to trust. Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, so God himself gave the sign of the child Immanuel. He also warned that Assyria would bring hard days and desolation to the land.
sum.24: Isaiah praises God for his faithful deeds: he brought down the proud city and was a refuge for the poor and the needy. He promises a banquet for all peoples on his mountain, where he will remove the veil, destroy death, and wipe away every tear. His people will rejoice in his salvation, while Moab, in its pride, will be brought low.
sum.39: God commands that Jerusalem be comforted: her sin has been pardoned, and God himself comes as a tender and powerful shepherd. Before God, the nations, the powerful, and the idols are nothing, and people are like grass that withers. But those who wait on the LORD will receive renewed strength.
sum.23: Isaiah 24 announces that the LORD will judge the whole earth, making no distinction between rich and poor, because its inhabitants broke the laws and the everlasting covenant. Joy disappears, and fear and trembling arrive. In the end, the LORD reigns in glory on Mount Zion, and a few people praise him.
sum.7: God tells Isaiah to give his son the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, as a sign that Assyria would soon come against Damascus and Samaria, and also against Judah, because the people had rejected God and feared other men. Isaiah teaches that people should fear only the LORD, trust his word, and not consult the dead, since whoever turns away from him is left in darkness.
sum.3: Isaiah 4 describes a difficult time, when seven women will seek out one man so that they can take away their shame. It then announces that God will cleanse Jerusalem through judgment and fire, and that those who remain will be called holy. Over Zion God will place a cloud by day and fire by night, as a shelter and protection.
sum.4: God takes care of his people the way a vineyard keeper takes care of his vineyard. But he expected justice and found wickedness and injustice instead. So he pronounces woes on greed, drunkenness, contempt for his word, and corruption, and warns that judgment is coming, with a foreign army.
sum.0: God accuses Judah of rebellion, saying even the oxen and donkeys are not as foolish as his people. He rejects their sacrifices and festivals because they live in injustice. He calls them to wash themselves clean, to seek what is good, and to defend the orphan and the widow. He offers them complete forgiveness if they obey, and he promises to purify and restore Zion with justice.
sum.43: God comforts Israel, his chosen servant, promising him his Spirit and blessing, and declares that he alone is God. He mocks idols, made from the same wood that is used for fire, and calls his people to return to him because he has redeemed them. He announces that Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and he names Cyrus as his shepherd.
sum.11: Isaiah 12 is a song of praise for "that day." The people acknowledge that God has set aside his anger, comforted them, and is their salvation and their strength. Therefore they draw water with joy from the wells of salvation, and everyone is invited to sing and to proclaim his deeds throughout the earth.
sum.45: The idols of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, fall down and have to be carried like a heavy load, while God says that he himself carries his people from birth until old age. The idols cannot speak or save, but God announces the future and carries out his plan. He calls to those who are stubborn of heart and promises to bring his salvation near to Zion.
sum.42: God tells Israel not to be afraid, because he has redeemed them, loves them, and will be with them through the water and through the fire. He promises to gather his people, to be the only Savior, and to do something new, like roads in the desert. Although Israel has worn him out with their sins, God says he will blot out their rebellions for his own sake.
sum.65: God, who made the whole heaven and earth, looks with favor on the humble person who trembles at his word, but he rejects false and rebellious religion. He promises to comfort and bring peace to Jerusalem, to judge its enemies, and to gather people from all nations to see his glory and worship him, while the rebels face a terrible punishment.
